Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Visuddhimaggo

The Path of Purification

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Nidānādikathā

Introductory Account

1.

1.

Sīle [M 1.0001][V 1.0001] patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti. (saṃ. ni. 1.23);

A wise man, established in virtue, developing mind and wisdom, an ardent and discerning bhikkhu—he can disentangle this tangle.

Iti hidaṃ vuttaṃ, kasmā panetaṃ vuttaṃ, bhagavantaṃ kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharantaṃ rattibhāge aññataro devaputto upasaṅkamitvā attano saṃsayasamugghāṭatthaṃ –

Thus was this said. Why was this said? It is said that while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain devaputta approached him during the night to dispel his own doubt, asking:

Antojaṭā bahijaṭā, jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā;

Taṃ taṃ gotama pucchāmi, ko imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti. (saṃ. ni. 1.23) –

The inner tangle, the outer tangle, people are entangled in a tangle. I ask you, Gotama, who can disentangle this tangle?

Imaṃ [V 1.0002] pañhaṃ pucchi. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – jaṭāti taṇhāya jāliniyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sā hi rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu heṭṭhupariyavasena punappunaṃ uppajjanato saṃsibbanaṭṭhena veḷugumbādīnaṃ sākhājālasaṅkhātā jaṭā viyāti jaṭā, sā panesā sakaparikkhāraparaparikkhāresu sakaattabhāvaparaattabhāvesu ajjhattikāyatanabāhirāyatanesu ca uppajjanato antojaṭā bahijaṭāti vuccati. Tāya evaṃ uppajjamānāya jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā. Yathā nāma veḷugumbajaṭādīhi veḷuādayo, evaṃ tāya taṇhājaṭāya sabbāpi ayaṃ sattanikāyasaṅkhātā pajā jaṭitā vinaddhā, saṃsibbitāti attho. Yasmā ca evaṃ jaṭitā. Taṃ taṃ gotama pucchāmīti tasmā taṃ pucchāmi. Gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Ko imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti imaṃ evaṃ tedhātukaṃ jaṭetvā ṭhitaṃ jaṭaṃ ko vijaṭeyya, vijaṭetuṃ ko samatthoti pucchati.

He asked this question. The concise meaning is: 'Tangle' is a term for craving, the entangling net. For it arises repeatedly in relation to objects such as forms, by way of lower and higher manifestations, on account of its interweaving nature, like the tangle formed by the net of branches of bamboo thickets and so forth; thus it is called a 'tangle'. Furthermore, because it arises in relation to one’s own possessions and the possessions belonging to others, one’s own being and the being of others, and the internal and external sense-bases, it is called 'an inner tangle and an outer tangle'. People are entangled by this tangle that thus arises. Just as bamboos are entangled by the tangles of bamboo thickets and so forth, so too is this entire multitude of beings entangled, bound, and interwoven—such is the meaning. And since they are thus entangled, therefore he asks him, 'I ask you, Gotama!' 'Gotama' is addressing the Blessed One by his clan name. He asks, 'Who can disentangle this tangle?'—meaning, 'Who could disentangle this tangle which has thus entangled the triple world, who is capable of disentangling it?'

Evaṃ [M 1.0002] puṭṭho panassa sabbadhammesu appaṭihatañāṇacāro devadevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā catuvesārajjavisārado dasabaladharo anāvaraṇañāṇo samantacakkhu bhagavā tamatthaṃ vissajjento –

When thus questioned, the Blessed One—whose range of knowledge was unimpeded in all phenomena, the deva of devas, Sakka above Sakka, Brahmā above Brahmā, the master of the four confidences, the possessor of the ten powers, possessing unobstructed knowledge, the All-Seeing One—explaining the matter, said:

Sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti. –

Established in virtue, a wise man, developing mind and wisdom, an ardent, discerning bhikkhu—he can disentangle this tangle.

Imaṃ gāthamāha.

He spoke this verse.

2.

2.

Imissā dāni gāthāya, kathitāya mahesinā;

Vaṇṇayanto yathābhūtaṃ, atthaṃ sīlādibhedanaṃ.

Now, of this verse spoken by the Great Seer, explaining the meaning according to reality, with its divisions of virtue and so on.

Sudullabhaṃ labhitvāna, pabbajjaṃ jinasāsane;

Sīlādisaṅgahaṃ khemaṃ, ujuṃ maggaṃ visuddhiyā.

The secure, straight path to purity, comprised of virtue and so on, for those who have obtained the very hard-to-get going-forth in the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

Yathābhūtaṃ ajānantā, suddhikāmāpi ye idha;

Visuddhiṃ nādhigacchanti, vāyamantāpi yogino.

Yogis here who, though desiring purity and striving, do not know things as they really are, fail to attain purity.

Tesaṃ [V 1.0003] pāmojjakaraṇaṃ, suvisuddhavinicchayaṃ;

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, desanānayanissitaṃ.

For their delight, a very clear ascertainment, based on the method of exposition of the residents of the Mahāvihāra.

Visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissaṃ, taṃ me sakkacca bhāsato;

Visuddhikāmā sabbepi, nisāmayatha sādhavoti.

I will expound the Path of Purification. As I diligently expound it, all you who desire purity, O worthy ones, listen carefully.

3. Tattha visuddhīti sabbamalavirahitaṃ accantaparisuddhaṃ nibbānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tassā visuddhiyā maggoti visuddhimaggo. Maggoti adhigamūpāyo vuccati. Taṃ visuddhimaggaṃ bhāsissāmīti attho.

3. Herein, 'purification' should be understood as Nibbāna, which is completely free from all stains and utterly pure. The path to that purification is the 'Path of Purification' (Visuddhimagga). 'Path' is said to be the means of attainment. The meaning is: "I shall expound that Path of Purification."

So panāyaṃ visuddhimaggo katthaci vipassanāmattavaseneva desito. Yathāha –

Now, this Path of Purification is sometimes taught by way of insight alone. As it is said:

“Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti, yadā paññāya passati;

Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā”ti. (dha. pa. 277);

“When one perceives with wisdom that all conditioned things are impermanent, then one becomes disenchanted with suffering—this is the path to purification.”

Katthaci jhānapaññāvasena. Yathāha –

Sometimes, by way of jhāna and wisdom. As it is said:

“Yamhi jhānañca paññā ca, sa ve nibbānasantike”ti. (dha. pa. 372);

“He in whom are jhāna and wisdom, he, indeed, is near to Nibbāna.”

Katthaci kammādivasena. Yathāha –

Sometimes, by way of kamma and so on. As it is said:

“Kammaṃ [M 1.0003] vijjā ca dhammo ca, sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamaṃ;

Etena maccā sujjhanti, na gottena dhanena vā”ti. (ma. ni. 3.387; saṃ. ni. 1.48);

“By kamma, knowledge, and Dhamma, by virtue and the highest life—by these are mortals purified, not by lineage or by wealth.”

Katthaci sīlādivasena. Yathāha –

Sometimes, by way of virtue and so on. As it is said:

“Sabbadā [V 1.0004] sīlasampanno, paññavā susamāhito;

Āraddhavīriyo pahitatto, oghaṃ tarati duttara”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.96);

“One who is ever endowed with virtue, wise, and well concentrated, energetic and resolute, crosses the flood so difficult to cross.”

Katthaci satipaṭṭhānādivasena. Yathāha –

Sometimes, by way of the foundations of mindfulness and so on. As it is said:

“Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā…pe… nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya, yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti (dī. ni. 2.373).

“This, monks, is the direct path for the purification of beings… for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.”

Sammappadhānādīsupi eseva nayo. Imasmiṃ pana pañhābyākaraṇe sīlādivasena desito.

The same principle applies even to the right efforts and so forth. But in this exposition of the question, it is taught by way of virtue and so forth.

4. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – sīle patiṭṭhāyāti sīle ṭhatvā, sīlaṃ paripūrayamānoyeva cettha sīle ṭhitoti vuccati. Tasmā sīlaparipūraṇena sīle patiṭṭhahitvāti ayamettha attho. Naroti satto. Sapaññoti kammajatihetukapaṭisandhipaññāya paññavā. Cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayanti samādhiñceva vipassanañca bhāvayamāno, cittasīsena hettha samādhi niddiṭṭho. Paññānāmena ca vipassanāti. Ātāpīti vīriyavā. Vīriyañhi kilesānaṃ ātāpanaparitāpanaṭṭhena ātāpoti vuccati. Tadassa atthīti ātāpī. Nipakoti nepakkaṃ vuccati paññā, tāya samannāgatoti attho. Iminā padena pārihārikapaññaṃ dasseti. Imasmiñhi pañhābyākaraṇe tikkhattuṃ paññā āgatā. Tattha paṭhamā jātipaññā, dutiyā vipassanāpaññā, tatiyā sabbakiccapariṇāyikā pārihārikapaññā. Saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhatīti bhikkhu. So imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti so iminā ca sīlena iminā ca cittasīsena niddiṭṭhasamādhinā imāya ca tividhāya paññāya iminā ca ātāpenāti chahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu. Seyyathāpi nāma puriso pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya [M 1.0004] sunisitaṃ satthaṃ ukkhipitvā mahantaṃ veḷugumbaṃ vijaṭeyya, evameva sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya samādhisilāyaṃ sunisitaṃ vipassanāpaññāsatthaṃ vīriyabalapaggahitena pārihārikapaññāhatthena ukkhipitvā sabbampi taṃ attano santāne patitaṃ taṇhājaṭaṃ vijaṭeyya sañchindeyya sampadāleyya. Maggakkhaṇe panesa taṃ jaṭaṃ vijaṭeti nāma. Phalakkhaṇe vijaṭitajaṭo sadevakassa lokassa aggadakkhiṇeyyo hoti. Tenāha bhagavā –

4. Here is the brief explanation: "Established in virtue" means standing firm in virtue; one is said to be established in virtue only by fulfilling virtue. Therefore, the meaning here is having established oneself in virtue by fulfilling it. "A person" means a being. "Wise" means endowed with the rebirth-linking wisdom that is conditioned by kamma and birth. "Develops mind and wisdom" means developing both concentration and insight. Here, concentration is indicated by the term "mind," and insight by the term "wisdom." "Ardent" means possessing energy, for energy is called "ardor" because it burns up and scorches the defilements; one who has this is "ardent." "Discerning" means discernment, which is wisdom; the meaning is endowed with that wisdom. By this term, protective wisdom is shown. In this exposition of the question, wisdom is mentioned three times: the first is wisdom by birth, the second is insight wisdom, and the third is protective wisdom that accomplishes all tasks. "A bhikkhu" is one who sees danger in saṃsāra. "He may untangle this tangle" means a bhikkhu endowed with these six qualities: this virtue, this concentration indicated by the term "mind," these three kinds of wisdom, and this ardor. Just as a man, standing on the ground, might lift a well-sharpened knife and untangle a great bamboo thicket, so too, standing on the ground of virtue, lifting the well-sharpened knife of insight wisdom on the whetstone of concentration with the hand of protective wisdom propelled by the power of energy, he may untangle, cut through, and tear asunder all the tangle of craving that has arisen in his own continuity. At the moment of the path, he is said to untangle that tangle. At the moment of fruition, having untangled the tangle, he becomes the foremost worthy of offerings in the world with its devas. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Sīle [V 1.0005] patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ;

Ātāpī nipako bhikkhu, so imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭa”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.23);

A wise person established in virtue, developing mind and wisdom—an ardent, discerning bhikkhu—he may unravel this tangle.

5. Tatrāyaṃ yāya paññāya sapaññoti vutto, tatrāssa karaṇīyaṃ natthi. Purimakammānubhāveneva hissa sā siddhā. Ātāpī nipakoti ettha vuttavīriyavasena pana tena sātaccakārinā paññāvasena ca sampajānakārinā hutvā sīle patiṭṭhāya cittapaññāvasena vuttā samathavipassanā bhāvetabbāti imamatra bhagavā sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena visuddhimaggaṃ dasseti.

5. Herein, with regard to the wisdom by which one is called 'wise,' there is nothing for him to do, for that is indeed accomplished for him by the power of past kamma alone. But as for 'ardent' and 'discerning,' through the energy mentioned here, one should be a constant practitioner, and through wisdom, one who acts with full awareness. Having established oneself in virtue, one should develop the serenity and insight mentioned by way of mind and wisdom; thus the Blessed One herein shows the path of purification through the gateway of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

Ettāvatā hi tisso sikkhā, tividhakalyāṇaṃ sāsanaṃ, tevijjatādīnaṃ upanissayo, antadvayavajjanamajjhimapaṭipattisevanāni, apāyādisamatikkamanupāyo, tīhākārehi kilesappahānaṃ, vītikkamādīnaṃ paṭipakkho, saṃkilesattayavisodhanaṃ, sotāpannādibhāvassa ca kāraṇaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti.

Thus, the threefold training, the threefold excellence of the Dispensation, the supporting condition for the threefold knowledge and the like, the avoidance of the two extremes and the cultivation of the middle way, the means to transcend states of deprivation and the like, the abandonment of defilements in three modes, the antidote to transgressions and the like, the purification of the threefold defilement, and the cause for the state of a stream-enterer and so forth—all these have been revealed.

Kathaṃ? Ettha hi sīlena adhisīlasikkhā pakāsitā hoti, samādhinā adhicittasikkhā, paññāya adhipaññāsikkhā.

How so? Herein, the training in higher virtue is revealed by virtue, the training in higher mind by concentration, and the training in higher wisdom by wisdom.

Sīlena ca sāsanassa ādikalyāṇatā pakāsitā hoti. “Ko cādi kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ, sīlañca suvisuddha”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.369) hi vacanato, “sabbapāpassa akaraṇa”nti (dī. ni. 2.90) ādivacanato ca sīlaṃ sāsanassa ādi, tañca kalyāṇaṃ, avippaṭisārādiguṇāvahattā. Samādhinā majjhekalyāṇatā pakāsitā hoti. “Kusalassa upasampadā”ti (dī. ni. 2.90) ādivacanato hi samādhi sāsanassa majjhe, so ca kalyāṇo, iddhividhādiguṇāvahattā. Paññāya sāsanassa pariyosānakalyāṇatā pakāsitā hoti. “Sacittapariyodāpanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti (dī. ni. 2.90) hi vacanato, paññuttarato [M 1.0005] ca paññā sāsanassa pariyosānaṃ, sā ca kalyāṇaṃ, iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu tādibhāvāvahanato.

And by virtue, the initial excellence of the Dispensation is revealed. For since it is said, "What is the beginning of wholesome qualities? It is virtue, well-purified," and from the statement beginning "the non-doing of all evil," virtue is the beginning of the Dispensation; and it is excellent because it brings qualities beginning with freedom from remorse. By concentration, the middle excellence of the Dispensation is revealed. For from the statement beginning "the attainment of the wholesome," concentration is the middle of the Dispensation; and it is excellent because it brings qualities beginning with psychic powers. By wisdom, the culminating excellence of the Dispensation is revealed. For since it is said, "The purification of one's own mind—this is the Dispensation of the Buddhas," and because wisdom is supreme, wisdom is the culmination of the Dispensation; and it is excellent because it brings about a state of imperturbability with regard to the desirable and undesirable.

“Selo yathā ekaghano, vātena na samīrati;

Evaṃ nindāpasaṃsāsu, na samiñjanti paṇḍitā”ti. (dha. pa. 81); –

As a solid rock is unshaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by praise or blame.

Hi vuttaṃ.

For it was said.

Tathā [V 1.0006] sīlena tevijjatāya upanissayo pakāsito hoti. Sīlasampattiñhi nissāya tisso vijjā pāpuṇāti, na tato paraṃ. Samādhinā chaḷabhiññatāya upanissayo pakāsito hoti. Samādhisampadañhi nissāya cha abhiññā pāpuṇāti, na tato paraṃ. Paññāya paṭisambhidāpabhedassa upanissayo pakāsito hoti. Paññāsampattiñhi nissāya catasso paṭisambhidā pāpuṇāti, na aññena kāraṇena.

Similarly, by virtue, the supporting condition for the threefold knowledge is revealed. For it is by relying on the accomplishment of virtue that one attains the three knowledges, and not beyond that. By concentration, the supporting condition for the sixfold higher knowledge is revealed. For it is by relying on the accomplishment of concentration that one attains the six higher knowledges, and not beyond that. By wisdom, the supporting condition for the varieties of analytical knowledge is revealed. For it is by relying on the accomplishment of wisdom that one attains the four analytical knowledges, and not by any other reason.

Sīlena ca kāmasukhallikānuyogasaṅkhātassa antassa vajjanaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti, samādhinā attakilamathānuyogasaṅkhātassa. Paññāya majjhimāya paṭipattiyā sevanaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti.

And by virtue, the avoidance of the extreme known as indulgence in sensual pleasures is revealed; by concentration, the avoidance of the extreme known as self-mortification. By wisdom, the cultivation of the Middle Way is revealed.

Tathā sīlena apāyasamatikkamanupāyo pakāsito hoti, samādhinā kāmadhātusamatikkamanupāyo, paññāya sabbabhavasamatikkamanupāyo.

Similarly, by virtue, the means to overcome the woeful states is revealed; by concentration, the means to overcome the sensual realm; by wisdom, the means to overcome all states of existence.

Sīlena ca tadaṅgappahānavasena kilesappahānaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti, samādhinā vikkhambhanappahānavasena, paññāya samucchedappahānavasena.

And by virtue, the abandonment of defilements by way of substitution is revealed; by concentration, by way of suppression; and by wisdom, by way of cutting off.

Tathā sīlena kilesānaṃ vītikkamapaṭipakkho pakāsito hoti, samādhinā pariyuṭṭhānapaṭipakkho, paññāya anusayapaṭipakkho.

Similarly, by virtue, the counteragent to the transgression of defilements is revealed; by concentration, the counteragent to their obsession; by wisdom, the counteragent to their underlying tendencies.

Sīlena ca duccaritasaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti, samādhinā taṇhāsaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ, paññāya diṭṭhisaṃkilesavisodhanaṃ.

And by virtue, the purification from the defilement of misconduct is revealed; by concentration, the purification from the defilement of craving; by wisdom, the purification from the defilement of wrong view.

Tathā sīlena sotāpannasakadāgāmibhāvassa kāraṇaṃ pakāsitaṃ hoti, samādhinā anāgāmibhāvassa, paññāya arahattassa. Sotāpanno hi “sīlesu paripūrakārī”ti (a. ni. 3.87) vutto, tathā sakadāgāmī. Anāgāmī [M 1.0006] pana “samādhismiṃ paripūrakārī”ti (a. ni. 3.87). Arahā pana “paññāya paripūrakārī”ti (a. ni. 3.87).

Thus, virtue is revealed as the cause for the state of a stream-enterer and a once-returner, concentration for the state of a non-returner, and wisdom for arahantship. For the stream-enterer is said to be “one who fulfills virtue” (AN 3.87), and so too the once-returner. The non-returner, however, is said to be “one who fulfills concentration” (AN 3.87). The arahant, however, is said to be “one who fulfills wisdom” (AN 3.87).

Evaṃ ettāvatā tisso sikkhā, tividhakalyāṇaṃ sāsanaṃ, tevijjatādīnaṃ upanissayo, antadvayavajjanamajjhimapaṭipattisevanāni, apāyādisamatikkamanupāyo, tīhākārehi kilesappahānaṃ, vītikkamādīnaṃ paṭipakkho, saṃkilesattayavisodhanaṃ, sotāpannādibhāvassa ca kāraṇanti ime nava, aññe ca evarūpā guṇattikā pakāsitā hontīti.

Thus, by this much, the threefold training, the threefold excellence of the Dispensation, the foundation for the threefold knowledge and so on, the avoidance of the two extremes and the cultivation of the Middle Way, the means to transcend states of deprivation and so on, the abandonment of defilements in three ways, the antidote to transgressions and so on, the purification of the threefold defilements, and the cause for becoming a stream-enterer and so on—these nine, and other such threefold qualities, are made clear.

1. Sīlaniddeso

1. The Exposition of Virtue

Sīlasarūpādikathā

The Discussion on the Nature of Virtue and So On

6. Evaṃ [M 1.0007][V 1.0007] anekaguṇasaṅgāhakena sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena desitopi panesa visuddhimaggo atisaṅkhepadesitoyeva hoti. Tasmā nālaṃ sabbesaṃ upakārāyāti vitthāramassa dassetuṃ sīlaṃ tāva ārabbha idaṃ pañhākammaṃ hoti.

6. Though this Path of Purification has thus been taught by way of the gate of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, which encompasses many qualities, it has nevertheless been taught only in a very condensed way; thus it is not adequate for the benefit of all. Therefore, to set forth its elaboration, this inquiry begins first with virtue.

Kiṃ sīlaṃ, kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ, kānassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni, kimānisaṃsaṃ sīlaṃ, katividhaṃ cetaṃ sīlaṃ, ko cassa saṃkileso, kiṃ vodānanti.

What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What is the benefit of virtue? How many kinds of virtue are there? What is its defilement, and what is its cleansing?

Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ. Kiṃ sīlanti pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanādayo dhammā. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “kiṃ sīlanti cetanā sīlaṃ, cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.39). Tattha cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi vā viramantassa vattapaṭipattiṃ vā pūrentassa cetanā. Cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīhi viramantassa virati. Apica cetanā sīlaṃ nāma pāṇātipātādīni pajahantassa satta kammapathacetanā. Cetasikaṃ sīlaṃ nāma “abhijjhaṃ pahāya vigatābhijjhena cetasā viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.217) ādinā nayena vuttā anabhijjhābyāpādasammādiṭṭhidhammā. Saṃvaro sīlanti ettha pañcavidhena saṃvaro veditabbo pātimokkhasaṃvaro, satisaṃvaro, ñāṇasaṃvaro, khantisaṃvaro, vīriyasaṃvaroti. Tattha iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupetoti (vibha. 511) ayaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvaro. Rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatīti (dī. ni. 1.213) ayaṃ satisaṃvaro.

Herein is the explanation. What is virtue? It is the states, such as volition, of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the practice of duties. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “What is virtue? Volition is virtue, a mental factor is virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue” (Paṭi. Ma. 1.39). Therein, ‘volition as virtue’ is the volition of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or of one who fulfills the practice of duties. ‘A mental factor as virtue’ is the abstinence of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth. Furthermore, ‘volition as virtue’ refers to the seven volitions of the courses of action of one who abandons killing living beings and so forth. ‘A mental factor as virtue’ refers to the states of non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view, spoken of in the manner beginning: “Having abandoned covetousness, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness” (Dī. Ni. 1.217). As for ‘restraint as virtue,’ herein restraint is to be understood as fivefold: restraint by the Pātimokkha, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. Therein, “He is endowed, possessed of this restraint of the Pātimokkha” (Vibh. 511)—this is restraint by the Pātimokkha. “He guards the eye faculty, he undertakes restraint in the eye faculty” (Dī. Ni. 1.213)—this is restraint by mindfulness.

Yāni [V 1.0008] sotāni lokasmiṃ, (ajitāti bhagavā;)

Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhiyyareti. (su. ni. 1041);

“Whatever streams there are in the world, Ajita,” said the Blessed One, “mindfulness is their prevention. I declare the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut off.” (Sn. 1041)

Ayaṃ [M 1.0008] ñāṇasaṃvaro. Paccayapaṭisevanampi ettheva samodhānaṃ gacchati. Yo panāyaṃ khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassātiādinā (ma. ni. 1.24; a. ni. 6.58) nayena āgato, ayaṃ khantisaṃvaro nāma. Yo cāyaṃ uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetītiādinā (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 6.58) nayena āgato, ayaṃ vīriyasaṃvaro nāma. Ājīvapārisuddhipi ettheva samodhānaṃ gacchati. Iti ayaṃ pañcavidhopi saṃvaro, yā ca pāpabhīrukānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ sampattavatthuto virati, sabbampetaṃ saṃvarasīlanti veditabbaṃ. Avītikkamo sīlanti samādinnasīlassa kāyikavācasiko anatikkamo. Idaṃ tāva kiṃ sīlanti pañhassa vissajjanaṃ.

This is restraint by wisdom. Reflection on the use of requisites is also included right here. And that which comes by way of enduring cold and heat, and so forth (MN 1.24; AN 6.58), this is called restraint by patience. And that which comes by way of not tolerating an arisen sensual thought, and so forth (MN 1.26; AN 6.58), this is called restraint by energy. Purification of livelihood is also included right here. Thus, this fivefold restraint, and the abstinence concerning things encountered on the part of clansmen who are fearful of evil—all this should be understood as the virtue of restraint. Non-transgression as virtue is the bodily and verbal non-transgression of one who has undertaken virtue. This, then, is the answer to the question, 'What is virtue?'

7. Avasesesu kenaṭṭhena sīlanti sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Kimidaṃ sīlanaṃ nāma. Samādhānaṃ vā, kāyakammādīnaṃ susīlyavasena avippakiṇṇatāti attho. Upadhāraṇaṃ vā, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhānavasena ādhārabhāvoti attho. Etadeva hettha atthadvayaṃ saddalakkhaṇavidū anujānanti. Aññe pana siraṭṭho sīlattho, sītalaṭṭho sīlatthoti evamādināpi nayenettha atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti.

7. As for the remaining questions, in what sense is it virtue? It is virtue in the sense of composing (sīlana). What is this composing? It is either composure (samādhāna), meaning the non-dispersion of bodily actions and so forth by way of good conduct; or it is upholding (upadhāraṇa), meaning the state of being a support by way of being a foundation for wholesome qualities. This indeed is the twofold meaning here that those skilled in the characteristics of words acknowledge. Others, however, explain the meaning here in such ways as: 'virtue has the meaning of head (chief),' 'virtue has the meaning of coolness,' and so on.

8. Idāni kānassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānīti ettha –

8. Now, as to the question, “What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?”:

Sīlanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ tassa, bhinnassāpi anekadhā;

Sanidassanattaṃ rūpassa, yathā bhinnassanekadhā.

Its characteristic is composing (sīlana), even when it is differentiated in many ways; just as being visible is for form, even when it is differentiated in many ways.

Yathā hi nīlapītādibhedena anekadhā bhinnassāpi rūpāyatanassa sanidassanattaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ, nīlādibhedena bhinnassāpi sanidassana bhāvānatikkamanato. Tathā sīlassa cetanādibhedena anekadhā bhinnassāpi yadetaṃ kāyakammādīnaṃ samādhānavasena kusalānañca dhammānaṃ patiṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ sīlanaṃ, tadeva lakkhaṇaṃ, cetanādibhedena bhinnassāpi samādhānapatiṭṭhānabhāvānatikkamanato. Evaṃ lakkhaṇassa panassa –

Just as the characteristic of the form-sphere, even when differentiated in many ways by the distinction of blue, yellow, and so forth, is its being visible, because it does not transgress the state of being visible even when differentiated by blue and so forth; likewise, the characteristic of virtue, even when differentiated in many ways by the distinction of volition and so forth, is that which is called composing (sīlana)—namely, the composure of bodily actions and so forth, and its being a foundation for wholesome qualities—because it does not transgress the state of being composure and a foundation, even when differentiated by the distinction of volition and so forth. Of this virtue thus characterized:

Dussīlyaviddhaṃsanatā[V 1.0009], anavajjaguṇo tathā;

Kiccasampattiatthena, raso nāma pavuccati.

The destruction of moral depravity, and likewise the quality of being blameless, are called its function, in the sense of task and accomplishment.

Tasmā [M 1.0009] idaṃ sīlaṃ nāma kiccaṭṭhena rasena dussīlyaviddhaṃsanarasaṃ, sampattiatthena rasena anavajjarasanti veditabbaṃ. Lakkhaṇādīsu hi kiccameva sampatti vā rasoti vuccati.

Therefore, this virtue should be understood as having the function of destroying moral depravity in the sense of a task, and as having the function of being blameless in the sense of an accomplishment. For among characteristics and so forth, it is the task itself or the accomplishment that is called the function.

Soceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, tayidaṃ tassa viññuhi;

Ottappañca hirī ceva, padaṭṭhānanti vaṇṇitaṃ.

Its manifestation is purity; by the wise, moral shame and moral dread are described as its proximate cause.

Tayidaṃ sīlaṃ kāyasoceyyaṃ vacīsoceyyaṃ manosoceyyanti (a. ni. 3.121) evaṃ vuttasoceyyapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ, soceyyabhāvena paccupaṭṭhāti gahaṇabhāvaṃ gacchati. Hirottappañca panassa viññūhi padaṭṭhānanti vaṇṇitaṃ, āsannakāraṇanti attho. Hirottappe hi sati sīlaṃ uppajjati ceva tiṭṭhati ca. Asati neva uppajjati, na tiṭṭhatīti. Evaṃ sīlassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni veditabbāni.

This virtue, as declared in terms of 'purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind' (AN 3.121), has purity as its manifestation; it manifests as a state of purity and thus becomes comprehensible. Furthermore, moral shame and moral dread are described by the wise as its proximate cause, meaning its immediate cause. For when moral shame and moral dread are present, virtue arises and endures. When they are absent, it neither arises nor endures. Thus, the characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause of virtue should be understood.

Sīlānisaṃsakathā

A Discourse on the Benefits of Virtue

9. Kimānisaṃsaṃ sīlanti avippaṭisārādianekaguṇapaṭilābhānisaṃsaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “avippaṭisāratthāni kho, ānanda, kusalāni sīlāni avippaṭisārānisaṃsānī”ti (a. ni. 11.1).

9. What is the benefit of virtue? Its benefit is the acquisition of many qualities, beginning with freedom from remorse. For it was said: “Ānanda, wholesome virtues have freedom from remorse as their aim and as their benefit” (AN 11.1).

Aparampi vuttaṃ “pañcime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Katame pañca? Idha gahapatayo sīlavā sīlasampanno appamādādhikaraṇaṃ mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigacchati, ayaṃ paṭhamo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ gahapatayo sīlavato sīlasampannassa kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, ayaṃ dutiyo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ gahapatayo sīlavā sīlasampanno yaññadeva parisaṃ upasaṅkamati yadi khattiyaparisaṃ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṃ yadi gahapatiparisaṃ yadi samaṇaparisaṃ, visārado upasaṅkamati amaṅkubhūto, ayaṃ tatiyo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ [V 1.0010] gahapatayo sīlavā sīlasampanno asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti, ayaṃ catuttho ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ gahapatayo sīlavā sīlasampanno kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā [M 1.0010] sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati, ayaṃ pañcamo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.150; a. ni. 5.213; mahāva. 285).

Furthermore, it has been said: "Householders, there are these five benefits for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue. What are the five? Here, householders, a virtuous one, accomplished in virtue, through diligence acquires a great mass of wealth; this is the first benefit for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue. Again, householders, for a virtuous one, accomplished in virtue, a good reputation spreads; this is the second benefit for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue. Again, householders, a virtuous one, accomplished in virtue, enters any assembly—whether of nobles, brahmins, householders, or ascetics—with confidence and without being troubled; this is the third benefit for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue. Again, householders, a virtuous one, accomplished in virtue, dies unconfused; this is the fourth benefit for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue. Again, householders, a virtuous one, accomplished in virtue, upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world; this is the fifth benefit for one who is virtuous and accomplished in virtue" (DN 16; AN 5.213).

Aparepi “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo ca assaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cāti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.65) nayena piyamanāpatādayo āsavakkhayapariyosānā anekā sīlānisaṃsā vuttā. Evaṃ avippaṭisārādianekaguṇānisaṃsaṃ sīlaṃ. Apica –

Moreover, by way of the statement: "If, monks, a monk should wish, 'May I be dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by my fellow monks,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues," and so forth (MN 6), many benefits of virtue, beginning with being dear and agreeable and culminating in the destruction of the taints, have been stated. Thus, virtue has many beneficial qualities, beginning with freedom from remorse. Moreover:

Sāsane kulaputtānaṃ, patiṭṭhā natthi yaṃ vinā;

Ānisaṃsaparicchedaṃ, tassa sīlassa ko vade.

Without which there is no foundation for the sons of the clan in the Dispensation; who can declare the full extent of the benefits of that virtue?

Na gaṅgā yamunā cāpi, sarabhū vā sarasvatī;

Ninnagā vāciravatī, mahī vāpi mahānadī.

Neither the Ganges, nor the Yamunā, nor the Sarabhū, nor the Sarasvatī, nor the Aciravatī, nor the Mahī, nor even a great river,

Sakkuṇanti visodhetuṃ, taṃ malaṃ idha pāṇinaṃ;

Visodhayati sattānaṃ, yaṃ ve sīlajalaṃ malaṃ.

can cleanse that stain of living beings here; whereas the water of virtue indeed cleanses the stain of beings.

Na taṃ sajaladā vātā, na cāpi haricandanaṃ;

Neva hārā na maṇayo, na candakiraṇaṅkurā.

Neither rain-bearing winds, nor yellow sandalwood, nor necklaces, nor jewels, nor the tender rays of the moon,

Samayantīdha sattānaṃ, pariḷāhaṃ surakkhitaṃ;

Yaṃ sameti idaṃ ariyaṃ, sīlaṃ accantasītalaṃ.

can quell the burning in beings here; whereas this noble virtue, well-guarded and utterly cool, does quell it.

Sīlagandhasamo gandho, kuto nāma bhavissati;

Yo samaṃ anuvāte ca, paṭivāte ca vāyati.

What fragrance, indeed, could there be equal to the fragrance of virtue, which wafts equally with the wind and against the wind?

Saggārohaṇasopānaṃ[V 1.0011], aññaṃ sīlasamaṃ kuto;

Dvāraṃ vā pana nibbāna, nagarassa pavesane.

What other stairway for ascending to heaven is equal to virtue? Or what other gate for entering the city of Nibbāna?

Sobhantevaṃ na rājāno, muttāmaṇivibhūsitā;

Yathā sobhanti yatino, sīlabhūsanabhūsitā.

Kings adorned with pearls and gems do not shine so brightly as do ascetics adorned with the ornament of virtue.

Attānuvādādibhayaṃ, viddhaṃsayati sabbaso;

Janeti kittihāsañca, sīlaṃ sīlavataṃ sadā.

Virtue utterly destroys the fear of self-reproach and the like; it always generates renown and joy for the virtuous.

Guṇānaṃ [M 1.0011] mūlabhūtassa, dosānaṃ balaghātino;

Iti sīlassa viññeyyaṃ, ānisaṃsakathāmukhanti.

Thus should this introduction to the discourse on the benefits of virtue be understood—of virtue that is the root of wholesome qualities and the destroyer of the power of defilements.

Sīlappabhedakathā

Discourse on the Divisions of Virtue

10. Idāni yaṃ vuttaṃ katividhaṃ cetaṃ sīlanti, tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ. Sabbameva tāva idaṃ sīlaṃ attano sīlanalakkhaṇena ekavidhaṃ.

Now, as to the question that was asked, 'Of how many kinds is this virtue?', this is the answer. In the first place, all this virtue is of one kind in that it has the characteristic of composing.

Cārittavārittavasena duvidhaṃ. Tathā ābhisamācārikaādibrahmacariyakavasena, viratiavirativasena, nissitānissitavasena, kālapariyantaāpāṇakoṭikavasena, sapariyantāpariyantavasena, lokiyalokuttaravasena ca.

It is twofold by way of observance and avoidance. Likewise, it is twofold by way of good conduct and the fundamentals of the holy life; by way of abstinence and non-abstinence; by way of being dependent and independent; by way of being limited by time and for life; by way of having a limit and being limitless; and by way of being mundane and supramundane.

Tividhaṃ hīnamajjhimapaṇītavasena. Tathā attādhipateyyalokādhipateyyadhammādhipateyyavasena, parāmaṭṭhāparāmaṭṭhapaṭippassaddhivasena, visuddhāvisuddhavematikavasena, sekkhāsekkhanevasekkhanāsekkhavasena ca.

It is threefold by way of being inferior, middling, and excellent. Likewise, it is threefold by way of self-sovereignty, world-sovereignty, and Dhamma-sovereignty; by way of being clung to, not clung to, and tranquillized; by way of being pure, impure, and doubtful; and by way of being that of a trainee, an adept, and one who is neither a trainee nor an adept.

Catubbidhaṃ hānabhāgiyaṭhitibhāgiyavisesabhāgiyanibbedhabhāgiyavasena. Tathā bhikkhubhikkhunīanupasampannagahaṭṭhasīlavasena, pakatiācāradhammatāpubbahetukasīlavasena, pātimokkhasaṃvaraindriyasaṃvaraājīvapārisuddhipaccayasannissitasīlavasena ca.

It is fourfold by way of partaking in decline, in stagnation, in distinction, and in penetration. Likewise, it is fourfold by way of the virtue of monks, of nuns, of those not yet fully ordained, and of householders; by way of natural virtue, customary virtue, virtue as a natural law, and virtue rooted in a past cause; and by way of the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of the sense faculties, the purification of livelihood, and the virtue concerning the requisites.

Pañcavidhaṃ [V 1.0012] pariyantapārisuddhisīlādivasena. Vuttampi cetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “pañca sīlāni – pariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ, apariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ, paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīlaṃ, aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīlaṃ, paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.37). Tathā pahānaveramaṇīcetanāsaṃvarāvītikkamavasena.

10. It is fivefold by way of virtue of limited purity, and so on. This was also stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'There are five kinds of virtue: virtue of limited purity, virtue of unlimited purity, virtue of complete purity, virtue of ungrasped purity, and virtue of pacified purity' (Ps 1.44). Likewise, by way of abandoning, abstinence, intention, restraint, and non-transgression.

11. Tattha ekavidhakoṭṭhāse attho vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Duvidhakoṭṭhāse yaṃ bhagavatā “idaṃ kattabba”nti paññattasikkhāpadapūraṇaṃ, taṃ cārittaṃ. Yaṃ “idaṃ na kattabba”nti paṭikkhittassa akaraṇaṃ, taṃ vārittaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho. Caranti tasmiṃ sīlesu paripūrakāritāya pavattantīti cārittaṃ. Vāritaṃ tāyanti rakkhanti tenāti vārittaṃ. Tattha saddhāvīriyasādhanaṃ cārittaṃ, saddhāsādhanaṃ vārittaṃ. Evaṃ cārittavārittavasena duvidhaṃ.

11. Herein, in the single division, the meaning should be understood in the manner already stated. In the twofold division, the fulfillment of a training rule prescribed by the Blessed One as, ‘This should be done,’ is conduct. The non-performance of what is prohibited as, ‘This should not be done,’ is avoidance. Herein, this is the etymological meaning: They conduct themselves in it, they proceed by way of fulfilling the virtues, thus it is conduct. By it they guard and protect from what is prohibited, thus it is avoidance. Herein, conduct is accomplished by faith and energy, while avoidance is accomplished by faith. Thus, it is twofold by way of conduct and avoidance.

Dutiyaduke [M 1.0012] abhisamācāroti uttamasamācāro. Abhisamācāro eva ābhisamācārikaṃ. Abhisamācāraṃ vā ārabbha paññattaṃ ābhisamācārikaṃ, ājīvaṭṭhamakato avasesasīlassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhāvabhūtanti ādibrahmacariyakaṃ, ājīvaṭṭhamakasīlassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tañhi maggassa ādibhāvabhūtaṃ, pubbabhāgeyeva parisodhetabbato. Tenāha – “pubbeva kho panassa kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ ājīvo suparisuddho hotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.431). Yāni vā sikkhāpadāni khuddānukhuddakānīti vuttāni, idaṃ ābhisamācārikasīlaṃ. Sesaṃ ādibrahmacariyakaṃ. Ubhatovibhaṅgapariyāpannaṃ vā ādibrahmacariyakaṃ. Khandhakavattapariyāpannaṃ ābhisamācārikaṃ. Tassa sampattiyā ādibrahmacariyakaṃ sampajjati. Tenevāha – “so vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ābhisamācārikaṃ dhammaṃ aparipūretvā ādibrahmacariyakaṃ dhammaṃ paripūressatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (a. ni. 5.21). Evaṃ ābhisamācārikaādibrahmacariyakavasena duvidhaṃ.

In the second pair, ‘abhisamācāra’ means noble conduct. ‘Ābhisamācārika’ is abhisamācāra itself. Or, what is prescribed with reference to abhisamācāra is called ābhisamācārika; this is a designation for the virtue remaining apart from that which has livelihood as the eighth factor. ‘Ādibrahmacariyaka’ is that which is the beginning of the holy life of the path; this is a designation for the virtue that has livelihood as the eighth factor. For it is the beginning of the path, since it must be purified in the preliminary stage. Hence it is said: ‘Indeed, his bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are already thoroughly purified beforehand’ (MN 39). Alternatively, the training rules called ‘minor and lesser’ are ābhisamācārika virtue. The rest is ādibrahmacariyaka virtue. Or, what is included in both Vibhaṅgas is ādibrahmacariyaka virtue. What is included in the Khandhakas and the duties is ābhisamācārika virtue. Through the accomplishment of the latter, the ādibrahmacariyaka virtue is accomplished. Therefore it is said: ‘Monks, that a monk could fulfill the virtue of the beginning of the holy life without first fulfilling the virtue of noble conduct—this is not possible’ (AN 5.21). Thus, it is twofold by way of ābhisamācārika and ādibrahmacariyaka.

Tatiyaduke pāṇātipātādīhi veramaṇimattaṃ viratisīlaṃ. Sesaṃ cetanādi aviratisīlanti evaṃ viratiavirativasena duvidhaṃ.

In the third pair, the virtue of abstinence is the mere abstinence from killing living beings, and so on. The remaining factors, such as volition, constitute the virtue of non-abstinence. Thus, it is twofold by way of abstinence and non-abstinence.

Catutthaduke nissayoti dve nissayā taṇhānissayo ca diṭṭhinissayo ca. Tattha yaṃ “imināhaṃ sīlena devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā”ti (dī. ni. 3.320; ma. ni. 1.186; a. ni. 5.206; 7.50) evaṃ [V 1.0013] bhavasampattiṃ ākaṅkhamānena pavattitaṃ, idaṃ taṇhānissitaṃ. Yaṃ “sīlena suddhī”ti evaṃ suddhidiṭṭhiyā pavattitaṃ, idaṃ diṭṭhinissitaṃ. Yaṃ pana lokuttaraṃ lokiyañca tasseva sambhārabhūtaṃ, idaṃ anissitanti evaṃ nissitānissitavasena duvidhaṃ.

In the fourth pair, ‘nissaya’ means two kinds of dependence: dependence on craving and dependence on views. Herein, that virtue which is undertaken while longing for worldly success, thinking, ‘By this virtue I shall become a god or some other divine being,’ is dependent on craving. That virtue which is undertaken with the view of purification, thinking, ‘Purity comes through virtue,’ is dependent on views. But that which is supramundane, and the mundane virtue that serves as its foundation, is non-dependent. Thus, it is twofold by way of being dependent and non-dependent.

Pañcamaduke kālaparicchedaṃ katvā samādinnaṃ sīlaṃ kālapariyantaṃ. Yāvajīvaṃ samādiyitvā tatheva pavattitaṃ āpāṇakoṭikanti evaṃ kālapariyantaāpāṇakoṭikavasena duvidhaṃ.

In the fifth pair, virtue undertaken with a time limit is time-limited virtue. Virtue undertaken for life and maintained accordingly is lifelong virtue. Thus, it is twofold by way of being time-limited and lifelong.

Chaṭṭhaduke lābhayasañātiaṅgajīvitavasena diṭṭhapariyantaṃ sapariyantaṃ nāma. Viparītaṃ apariyantaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “katamaṃ taṃ sīlaṃ sapariyantaṃ? Atthi sīlaṃ lābhapariyantaṃ, atthi sīlaṃ yasapariyantaṃ, atthi [M 1.0013] sīlaṃ ñātipariyantaṃ, atthi sīlaṃ aṅgapariyantaṃ, atthi sīlaṃ jīvitapariyantaṃ. Katamaṃ taṃ sīlaṃ lābhapariyantaṃ? Idhekacco lābhahetu lābhapaccayā lābhakāraṇā yathāsamādinnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamati, idaṃ taṃ sīlaṃ lābhapariyanta”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.38). Eteneva upāyena itarānipi vitthāretabbāni. Apariyantavissajjanepi vuttaṃ “katamaṃ taṃ sīlaṃ na lābhapariyantaṃ? Idhekacco lābhahetu lābhapaccayā lābhakāraṇā yathāsamādinnaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ vītikkamāya cittampi na uppādeti, kiṃ so vītikkamissati, idaṃ taṃ sīlaṃ na lābhapariyanta”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.38). Etenevupāyena itarānipi vitthāretabbāni. Evaṃ sapariyantāpariyantavasena duvidhaṃ.

In the sixth pair, virtue that has a limit with respect to gain, renown, relatives, limbs, or life is called limited virtue. The opposite is unlimited virtue. This is also stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘What is that virtue which is limited? There is virtue limited by gain, there is virtue limited by renown, there is virtue limited by relatives, there is virtue limited by limbs, and there is virtue limited by life. What is that virtue which is limited by gain? Here, someone, for the sake of gain, on account of gain, by reason of gain, transgresses a training rule as undertaken by them; this is that virtue limited by gain’ (Ps i, 44). The others should be elaborated in the same way. In the explanation of the unlimited, it is stated: ‘What is that virtue which is not limited by gain? Here, someone, for the sake of gain, on account of gain, by reason of gain, does not even give rise to the thought of transgressing a training rule as undertaken by them, how then could they transgress it? This is that virtue not limited by gain’ (Ps i, 44). The others should be elaborated in the same way. Thus, it is twofold by way of being limited and unlimited.

Sattamaduke sabbampi sāsavaṃ sīlaṃ lokiyaṃ. Anāsavaṃ lokuttaraṃ. Tattha lokiyaṃ bhavavisesāvahaṃ hoti bhavanissaraṇassa ca sambhāro. Yathāha – “vinayo saṃvaratthāya, saṃvaro avippaṭisāratthāya, avippaṭisāro pāmojjatthāya, pāmojjaṃ pītatthāya, pīti passaddhatthāya, passaddhi sukhatthāya, sukhaṃ samādhatthāya, samādhi yathābhūtañāṇadassanatthāya, yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ nibbidatthāya, nibbidā virāgatthāya, virāgo vimuttatthāya, vimutti vimuttiñāṇadassanatthāya, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ anupādāparinibbānatthāya, etadatthā kathā, etadatthā mantanā, etadatthā upanisā, etadatthaṃ sotāvadhānaṃ, yadidaṃ anupādācittassa vimokkho”ti (pari. 366). Lokuttaraṃ bhavanissaraṇāvahaṃ hoti paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa ca bhūmīti evaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidhaṃ.

In the seventh pair, all virtue connected with the taints is mundane. Virtue unconnected with the taints is supramundane. Herein, the mundane brings about superior states of existence and serves as a foundation for the escape from existence. As it is said: ‘Discipline is for the purpose of restraint, restraint for the purpose of non-remorse, non-remorse for the purpose of joy, joy for the purpose of rapture, rapture for the purpose of tranquility, tranquility for the purpose of happiness, happiness for the purpose of concentration, concentration for the purpose of the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are for the purpose of disenchantment, disenchantment for the purpose of dispassion, dispassion for the purpose of liberation, liberation for the purpose of the knowledge and vision of liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation for the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging. For this purpose is discourse, for this purpose is counsel, for this purpose is the supporting condition, for this purpose is the lending of ear: that is, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging’ (Pvr 13.1.1). The supramundane brings about the escape from existence and is the ground for reviewing knowledge. Thus, it is twofold by way of the mundane and the supramundane.

12. Tikesu [V 1.0014] paṭhamattike hīnena chandena cittena vīriyena vīmaṃsāya vā pavattitaṃ hīnaṃ. Majjhimehi chandādīhi pavattitaṃ majjhimaṃ. Paṇītehi paṇītaṃ. Yasakāmatāya vā samādinnaṃ hīnaṃ. Puññaphalakāmatāya majjhimaṃ. Kattabbamevidanti ariyabhāvaṃ nissāya samādinnaṃ paṇītaṃ. “Ahamasmi sīlasampanno, ime panaññe bhikkhū dussīlā pāpadhammā”ti evaṃ attukkaṃsanaparavambhanādīhi upakkiliṭṭhaṃ vā hīnaṃ. Anupakkiliṭṭhaṃ lokiyaṃ sīlaṃ majjhimaṃ. Lokuttaraṃ paṇītaṃ. Taṇhāvasena vā bhavabhogatthāya pavattitaṃ hīnaṃ. Attano vimokkhatthāya pavattitaṃ majjhimaṃ. Sabbasattānaṃ vimokkhatthāya pavattitaṃ pāramitāsīlaṃ paṇītanti evaṃ hīnamajjhimapaṇītavasena tividhaṃ.

12. In the first triad, virtue that is practiced with inferior desire, mind, energy, or investigation is inferior virtue. That which is practiced with middling desire and so on is middling virtue; that which is practiced with excellent ones is excellent virtue. Or, virtue undertaken out of desire for fame is inferior. That which is undertaken out of desire for the fruit of merit is middling. That which is undertaken relying on the noble state with the thought, 'This is simply what should be done,' is excellent. Or, virtue that is defiled by self-exaltation, disparagement of others, and so on—such as thinking, 'I am accomplished in virtue, but these other monks are immoral, of evil character'—is inferior. Undefiled mundane virtue is middling. Supramundane virtue is excellent. Or, virtue that is practiced through the power of craving for the sake of existence and enjoyments is inferior. That which is practiced for one's own liberation is middling. The virtue of the perfections, practiced for the liberation of all beings, is excellent. Thus, it is threefold by way of inferior, middling, and excellent.

Dutiyattike [M 1.0014] attano ananurūpaṃ pajahitukāmena attagarunā attanigāravena pavattitaṃ attādhipateyyaṃ. Lokāpavādaṃ pariharitukāmena lokagarunā loke gāravena pavattitaṃ lokādhipateyyaṃ. Dhammamahattaṃ pūjetukāmena dhammagarunā dhammagāravena pavattitaṃ dhammādhipateyyanti evaṃ attādhipateyyādivasena tividhaṃ.

In the second triad, that which is undertaken by one wishing to abandon what is unsuitable for oneself, with reverence for oneself and respect for oneself, is virtue predominated by the self. That which is undertaken by one wishing to avoid worldly blame, with reverence for the world and respect for the world, is virtue predominated by the world. That which is undertaken by one wishing to honor the greatness of the Dhamma, with reverence for the Dhamma and respect for the Dhamma, is virtue predominated by the Dhamma. Thus, it is threefold by way of being predominated by the self, and so on.

Tatiyattike yaṃ dukesu nissitanti vuttaṃ, taṃ taṇhādiṭṭhīhi parāmaṭṭhattā parāmaṭṭhaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakassa maggasambhārabhūtaṃ sekkhānañca maggasampayuttaṃ aparāmaṭṭhaṃ. Sekkhāsekkhānaṃ phalasampayuttaṃ paṭippassaddhanti evaṃ parāmaṭṭhādivasena tividhaṃ.

In the third triad, that which was spoken of in the dyads as 'dependent' is 'grasped' because it is affected by craving and views. For the virtuous worldling, that which serves as the requisites for the path, and for the trainees, that which is associated with the path, is 'ungrasped.' For trainees and non-trainees, that which is associated with the fruit is 'pacified.' Thus, it is threefold by way of grasped, ungrasped, and pacified.

Catutthattike yaṃ āpattiṃ anāpajjantena pūritaṃ, āpajjitvā vā puna katapaṭikammaṃ, taṃ visuddhaṃ. Āpattiṃ āpannassa akatapaṭikammaṃ avisuddhaṃ. Vatthumhi vā āpattiyā vā ajjhācāre vā vematikassa sīlaṃ vematikasīlaṃ nāma. Tattha yoginā avisuddhasīlaṃ visodhetabbaṃ, vematike vatthujjhācāraṃ akatvā vimati paṭivinetabbā “iccassa phāsu bhavissatī”ti evaṃ visuddhādivasena tividhaṃ.

In the fourth triad, that which is fulfilled by not falling into an offense, or for which amends have been made after having fallen into one, is pure. For one who has fallen into an offense and has not made amends, it is impure. When there is doubt concerning the object, the offense, or the transgression, the virtue of one who is in doubt is called doubtful virtue. Therein, the yogin should purify impure virtue. In a case of doubt, the doubt should be dispelled without committing the transgression concerning the object, with the thought, 'Thus there will be ease for him.' Thus, it is threefold by way of pure, and so on.

Pañcamattike catūhi ariyamaggehi tīhi ca sāmaññaphalehi sampayuttaṃ sīlaṃ sekkhaṃ. Arahattaphalasampayuttaṃ asekkhaṃ. Sesaṃ nevasekkhanāsekkhanti evaṃ sekkhādivasena tividhaṃ.

In the fifth triad, virtue associated with the four noble paths and the three lower fruits of the contemplative life is the trainee's virtue. Virtue associated with the fruit of arahantship is the non-trainee's virtue. The remainder is neither the trainee's nor the non-trainee's virtue. Thus, it is threefold by way of the trainee's virtue, and so on.

Paṭisambhidāyaṃ pana yasmā loke tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ pakatipi sīlanti vuccati, yaṃ sandhāya [V 1.0015] “ayaṃ sukhasīlo, ayaṃ dukkhasīlo, ayaṃ kalahasīlo, ayaṃ maṇḍanasīlo”ti bhaṇanti, tasmā tena pariyāyena “tīṇi sīlāni, kusalasīlaṃ akusalasīlaṃ abyākatasīlanti (paṭi. ma. 1.39). Evaṃ kusalādivasenapi tividhanti vuttaṃ. Tattha akusalaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetassa sīlassa lakkhaṇādīsu ekenapi na sametīti idha na upanītaṃ, tasmā vuttanayenevassa tividhatā veditabbā.

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, because in the world the natural disposition of various beings is also called 'sīla,' with reference to which they say, 'This one is of pleasant disposition, this one is of painful disposition, this one is of quarrelsome disposition, this one has a disposition for adornment,' therefore, by this alternative meaning, it is said, 'There are three kinds of virtue: wholesome virtue, unwholesome virtue, and indeterminate virtue' (Paṭis. I 43). Thus, it is stated to be threefold also by way of the wholesome and so on. Therein, unwholesome virtue does not accord with even one of the characteristics of the virtue intended in this context, and therefore it is not included here. Therefore, its threefold nature should be understood only in the manner stated above.

13. Catukkesu paṭhamacatukke –

13. In the tetrads, in the first tetrad:

Yodha sevati dussīle, sīlavante na sevati;

Vatthuvītikkame dosaṃ, na passati aviddasu.

Whoever here associates with the immoral, and does not associate with the virtuous; the ignorant one sees no fault in transgressing the object of the rule.

Micchāsaṅkappabahulo[M 1.0015], indriyāni na rakkhati;

Evarūpassa ve sīlaṃ, jāyate hānabhāgiyaṃ.

One who is full of wrong thoughts and does not guard the sense faculties—for such a person, virtue becomes conducive to decline.

Yo panattamano hoti, sīlasampattiyā idha;

Kammaṭṭhānānuyogamhi, na uppādeti mānasaṃ.

But whoever here is content with the accomplishment of virtue, and does not arouse the mind to the practice of meditation subjects,

Tuṭṭhassa sīlamattena, aghaṭantassa uttari;

Tassa taṃ ṭhitibhāgiyaṃ, sīlaṃ bhavati bhikkhuno.

For the monk who is content with mere virtue, not striving for what is higher, that virtue becomes conducive to stagnation.

Sampannasīlo ghaṭati, samādhatthāya yo pana;

Visesabhāgiyaṃ sīlaṃ, hoti etassa bhikkhuno.

But whoever, being accomplished in virtue, strives for the sake of concentration—for this monk, that virtue becomes conducive to distinction.

Atuṭṭho sīlamattena, nibbidaṃ yonuyuñjati;

Hoti nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ, sīlametassa bhikkhunoti.

Not content with mere virtue, one who diligently applies oneself to revulsion—for this monk, that virtue becomes conducive to penetration.

Evaṃ hānabhāgiyādivasena catubbidhaṃ.

Thus, it is fourfold, by way of being conducive to decline and so forth.

Dutiyacatukke [V 1.0016] bhikkhū ārabbha paññattasikkhāpadāni, yāni ca nesaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ paññattito rakkhitabbāni, idaṃ bhikkhusīlaṃ. Bhikkhuniyo ārabbha paññattasikkhāpadāni, yāni ca tāsaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paññattito rakkhitabbāni, idaṃ bhikkhunisīlaṃ. Sāmaṇerasāmaṇerīnaṃ dasasīlāni anupasampannasīlaṃ. Upāsakaupāsikānaṃ niccasīlavasena pañcasikkhāpadāni, sati vā ussāhe dasa, uposathaṅgavasena aṭṭhāti idaṃ gahaṭṭhasīlanti evaṃ bhikkhusīlādivasena catubbidhaṃ.

In the second tetrad, the training rules laid down concerning monks, and those from the rules laid down for nuns which are to be observed by the monks—this is the virtue of monks. The training rules laid down concerning nuns, and those from the rules laid down for monks which are to be observed by the nuns—this is the virtue of nuns. The ten precepts for male and female novices are the virtue of the unordained. For laymen and laywomen, there are the five precepts as constant virtue, or ten if one is able, or the eight precepts as the Uposatha factors—this is the householder’s virtue. Thus, it is fourfold, by way of the virtue of monks and so forth.

Tatiyacatukke uttarakurukānaṃ manussānaṃ avītikkamo pakatisīlaṃ. Kuladesapāsaṇḍānaṃ attano attano mariyādācārittaṃ ācārasīlaṃ. “Dhammatā esā, ānanda, yadā bodhisatto mātukucchiṃ okkanto hoti na bodhisattamātu purisesu mānasaṃ uppajji kāmaguṇūpasaṃhita”nti evaṃ vuttaṃ bodhisattamātusīlaṃ dhammatāsīlaṃ. Mahākassapādīnaṃ pana suddhasattānaṃ, bodhisattassa ca tāsu tāsu jātīsu sīlaṃ pubbahetukasīlanti evaṃ pakatisīlādivasena catubbidhaṃ.

In the third tetrad, the non-transgression of the humans of Uttarakuru is natural virtue. The conduct according to the respective conventions of clans, countries, and sects is customary virtue. “It is the nature of things, Ānanda, that when the Bodhisatta has entered his mother’s womb, no thought connected with sensual pleasures toward any man arises in the Bodhisatta’s mother”—the virtue of the Bodhisatta’s mother, thus spoken of, is virtue based on the nature of things. Moreover, the virtue of pure beings such as Mahākassapa, and of the Bodhisatta in his various births, is virtue rooted in past causes. Thus, virtue is fourfold by way of natural virtue and so forth.

Catutthacatukke yaṃ bhagavatā “idha bhikkhu pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya [M 1.0016] sikkhati sikkhāpadesū”ti (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 1.193) vaṃ vuttaṃ sīlaṃ, idaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana “so cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī, yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati, rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya na nimittaggāhī…pe… manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.22, 411; dī. ni. 1.213; a. ni. 4.198) vuttaṃ, idaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Yā pana ājīvahetupaññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vītikkamassa, “kuhanā lapanā nemittikatā nippesikatā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā”ti evamādīnañca pāpadhammānaṃ vasena pavattā micchājīvā virati, idaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ. “Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevati, yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) ādinā nayena vutto paṭisaṅkhānaparisuddho catupaccayaparibhogo paccayasannissitasīlaṃ nāma.

In the fourth tetrad, the virtue spoken of by the Blessed One thus: "Here, a bhikkhu dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and undertaking to train in the training rules"—this is called the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint. That which is spoken of thus: "Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or features. Since, if he were to dwell with the eye faculty unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and grief might assail him, he practices for its restraint, guards the eye faculty, and undertakes restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear… Having smelled an odor with the nose… Having tasted a flavor with the tongue… Having felt a tactile sensation with the body… Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features… he undertakes restraint of the mind faculty"—this is called the virtue of sense-faculty restraint. Furthermore, the abstinence from wrong livelihood, which proceeds by way of the transgression of the six training rules laid down concerning livelihood, and by way of evil states such as hypocrisy, babbling, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain—this is called the virtue of purity of livelihood. The use of the four requisites, purified by reflection, as stated in the manner: "Reflecting wisely, he uses robes only for the purpose of warding off cold"—this is called the virtue dependent on the requisites.

Pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ

The Virtue of Pātimokkha Restraint

14. Tatrāyaṃ [V 1.0017] ādito paṭṭhāya anupubbapadavaṇṇanāya saddhiṃ vinicchayakathā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Bhikkhūti saṃsāre bhayaṃ ikkhaṇatāya vā bhinnapaṭadharāditāya vā evaṃ laddhavohāro saddhāpabbajito kulaputto. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti ettha pātimokkhanti sikkhāpadasīlaṃ. Tañhi yo naṃ pāti rakkhati, taṃ mokkheti mocayati āpāyikādīhi dukkhehi, tasmā pātimokkhanti vuccati. Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro, kāyikavācasikassa avītikkamassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Pātimokkhameva saṃvaro pātimokkhasaṃvaro. Tena pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvuto pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto, upagato samannāgatoti attho. Viharatīti iriyati. Ācāragocarasampannotiādīnamattho pāḷiyaṃ āgatanayeneva veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

14. Herein, starting from the beginning, is the discourse of analysis together with the word-by-word explanation. Idha: In this Dispensation. Bhikkhu: A son of a good family who has gone forth out of faith, thus designated because he perceives fear in the round of existence or because he wears torn cloths and so on. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto: Here, Pātimokkha refers to the virtue of the training rules. For it protects (pāti) one who observes it, and it liberates (mokkheti) and frees them from sufferings such as those of the lower realms; therefore, it is called Pātimokkha. Saṃvaraṇaṃ saṃvaro: Restraint is the name for non-transgression in bodily and verbal actions. The Pātimokkha itself is restraint; this is Pātimokkha restraint. Tena pātimokkhasaṃvarena saṃvuto pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto: One who is restrained by this Pātimokkha restraint, meaning he has approached and is endowed with it. Viharatīti: He dwells, he conducts himself. Ācāragocarasampannotiādīnamattho: The meaning of terms beginning with 'accomplished in conduct and resort' should be understood according to the method given in the Pāli text itself. Vuttañhetaṃ: For this has been said:

“Ācāragocarasampanno”ti atthi ācāro, atthi anācāro;

“Accomplished in conduct and resort”—there is proper conduct, and there is improper conduct.

Tattha [M 1.0017] katamo anācāro? Kāyiko vītikkamo vācasiko vītikkamo kāyikavācasiko vītikkamo, ayaṃ vuccati anācāro. Sabbampi dussīlyaṃ anācāro. Idhekacco veḷudānena vā pattadānena vā pupphaphalasinānadantakaṭṭhadānena vā cāṭukamyatāya vā muggasūpyatāya vā pāribhaṭyatāya vā jaṅghapesanikena vā aññataraññatarena vā buddhapaṭikuṭṭhena micchāājīvena jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ vuccati anācāro.

Herein, what is improper conduct? Bodily transgression, verbal transgression, or bodily and verbal transgression—this is called improper conduct. All immorality is improper conduct. Here, a certain person makes a living by wrong livelihood, such as by giving bamboo, leaves, flowers, fruits, bathing powder, or tooth-wood; or by flattery, by bean-soup talk, by acting as a nursemaid, or by acting as a messenger, or by any other wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddha. This is called improper conduct.

Tattha katamo ācāro? Kāyiko avītikkamo vācasiko avītikkamo kāyikavācasiko avītikkamo, ayaṃ vuccati ācāro. Sabbopi sīlasaṃvaro ācāro. Idhekacco na veḷudānena vā na pattana pupphana phalana sinānana dantakaṭṭhadānena vā na cāṭukamyatāya vā na muggasūpyatāya vā na pāribhaṭyatāya vā na jaṅghapesanikena vā na aññataraññatarena vā buddhapaṭikuṭṭhena micchāājīvena jīvikaṃ kappeti, ayaṃ vuccati ācāro.

Herein, what is proper conduct? Non-transgression of body, non-transgression of speech, or non-transgression of body and speech—this is called proper conduct. All restraint by virtue is proper conduct. Here, a certain person does not make a living by giving bamboo, leaves, flowers, fruits, bathing powder, or tooth-wood; nor by flattery, nor by bean-soup talk, nor by acting as a nursemaid, nor by acting as a messenger, nor by any other wrong livelihood condemned by the Buddha—this is called proper conduct.

Gocaroti atthi gocaro atthi agocaro.

Regarding resort, there is a proper resort and an improper resort.

Tattha [V 1.0018] katamo agocaro? Idhekacco vesiyāgocaro vā hoti vidhavā, thullakumārikā, paṇḍaka, bhikkhunī, pānāgāragocaro vā hoti, saṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi ananulomikena saṃsaggena, yāni vā pana tāni kulāni assaddhāni appasannāni anopānabhūtāni akkosakaparibhāsakāni anatthakāmāni ahitakāmāni aphāsukakāmāni ayogakkhemakāmāni bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ, tathārūpāni kulāni sevati bhajati payirupāsati, ayaṃ vuccati agocaro.

Therein, what is an improper resort? Here, a certain person resorts to prostitutes, widows, mature maidens, pandakas, or nuns; or he resorts to taverns. He dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, or disciples of sectarians in an unsuitable manner. Or he attends, frequents, and serves such families as are faithless, lacking in confidence, not a source of support, abusive and insulting, who wish for what is not beneficial, who wish for what is not for one's welfare, who wish for discomfort, who do not wish for security from the yokes for monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers. This is called an improper resort.

Tattha katamo gocaro? Idhekacco na vesiyāgocaro vā hoti…pe… na pānāgāragocaro vā hoti, asaṃsaṭṭho viharati rājūhi…pe… titthiyasāvakehi ananulomikena saṃsaggena, yāni vā pana tāni kulāni saddhāni pasannāni opānabhūtāni kāsāvapajjotāni isivātapaṭivātāni atthakāmāni…pe… yogakkhemakāmāni bhikkhūnaṃ…pe… upāsikānaṃ, tathārūpāni kulāni sevati bhajati payirupāsati, ayaṃ vuccati gocaro. Iti iminā ca ācārena iminā ca gocarena upeto [M 1.0018] hoti samupeto upagato samupagato upapanno sampanno samannāgato, tena vuccati “ācāragocarasampanno”ti (vibha. 511).

Therein, what is a proper resort? Here, a certain person does not resort to prostitutes… nor does he resort to taverns. He dwells unassociated with kings… or disciples of sectarians in an unsuitable manner. But he attends, frequents, and serves such families as are faithful, confident, a source of support, illumined by the saffron robe, a shelter for seers, who wish for what is beneficial… who wish for security from the yokes for monks… and female lay followers. This is called a proper resort. Thus, he is endowed with this proper conduct and this proper resort, he is well-endowed, has attained, has well-attained, is possessed of, is accomplished in, and is fully possessed of it; therefore, he is called ‘one accomplished in conduct and resort’.

Api cettha imināpi nayena ācāragocarā veditabbā. Duvidho hi anācāro kāyiko vācasiko ca. Tattha katamo kāyiko anācāro? Idhekacco saṅghagatopi acittīkārakato there bhikkhū ghaṭṭayantopi tiṭṭhati, ghaṭṭayantopi nisīdati, puratopi tiṭṭhati, puratopi nisīdati, uccepi āsane nisīdati, sasīsampi pārupitvā nisīdati, ṭhitakopi bhaṇati, bāhāvikkhepakopi bhaṇati, therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anupāhanānaṃ caṅkamantānaṃ saupāhano caṅkamati, nīce caṅkame caṅkamantānaṃ ucce caṅkame caṅkamati, chamāya caṅkamantānaṃ caṅkame caṅkamati, there bhikkhū anupakhajjāpi tiṭṭhati, anupakhajjāpi nisīdati, navepi bhikkhū āsanena paṭibāhati, jantāgharepi there bhikkhū anāpucchā kaṭṭhaṃ pakkhipati, dvāraṃ pidahati, udakatitthepi there bhikkhū ghaṭṭayantopi otarati, puratopi otarati, ghaṭṭayantopi nhāyati, puratopi nhāyati, ghaṭṭayantopi uttarati, puratopi uttarati, antaragharaṃ pavisantopi there bhikkhū ghaṭṭayantopi gacchati, puratopi gacchati, vokkamma ca therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ purato purato gacchati, yānipi tāni honti kulānaṃ ovarakāni gūḷhāni ca paṭicchannāni ca yattha kulitthiyo [V 1.0019] kulakumāriyo nisīdanti, tatthapi sahasā pavisati, kumārakassapi sīsaṃ parāmasati, ayaṃ vuccati kāyiko anācāro.

Furthermore, in this context, conduct and resort should be understood in this way. For improper conduct is twofold: bodily and verbal. Therein, what is bodily improper conduct? Here, a certain one, even when in the Sangha, being disrespectful, stands jostling the elder monks, sits jostling them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing, speaks while gesticulating with his arms, walks wearing sandals while elder monks walk without sandals, walks on a high walkway while they walk on a low one, walks on a walkway while they walk on the ground, stands encroaching upon the elder monks, sits encroaching upon them, obstructs new monks with a seat, in the steam-bath house adds wood to the fire without asking the elder monks, closes the door, at the bathing place descends jostling the elder monks, descends in front of them, bathes jostling them, bathes in front of them, ascends jostling them, ascends in front of them, when entering the village goes along jostling the elder monks, goes in front of them, and having stepped out of line, walks right in front of the elder monks. He also enters suddenly into the private, concealed inner chambers of families where the women and young ladies of the family are sitting, and he touches a young boy's head. This is called bodily improper conduct.

Tattha katamo vācasiko anācāro? Idhekacco saṅghagatopi acittīkārakato there bhikkhū anāpucchā dhammaṃ bhaṇati. Pañhaṃ vissajjeti, pātimokkhaṃ uddisati, ṭhitakopi bhaṇati, bāhāvikkhepakopi bhaṇati, antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhopi itthiṃ vā kumāriṃ vā evamāha – “itthannāme itthaṃgotte kiṃ atthi, yāgu atthi, bhattaṃ atthi, khādanīyaṃ atthi, kiṃ pivissāma, kiṃ khādissāma, kiṃ bhuñjissāma. Kiṃ vā me dassathā”ti vippalapati, ayaṃ vuccati vācasiko anācāro (mahāni. 87). Paṭipakkhavasena panassa ācāro veditabbo.

Therein, what is verbal improper conduct? Here, a certain one, even when in the Sangha, being disrespectful, teaches the Dhamma without asking leave of the elder monks, answers questions, and recites the Pātimokkha. He speaks while standing and speaks while gesticulating with his arms. Having entered a house, he says to a woman or a girl: “O lady of such-and-such a name, of such-and-such a clan, what is there? Is there gruel? Is there rice? Is there something to eat? What shall we drink? What shall we eat? What shall we consume? Or what will you give me?” Thus he babbles. This is called verbal improper conduct. Proper conduct, however, should be understood by way of its opposite.

Apica [M 1.0019] bhikkhu sagāravo sappatisso hirottappasampanno sunivattho supāruto pāsādikena abhikkantena paṭikkantena ālokitena vilokitena samiñjitena pasāritena okkhittacakkhu iriyāpathasampanno indriyesu guttadvāro bhojane mattaññū jāgariyamanuyutto satisampajaññena samannāgato appiccho santuṭṭho āraddhavīriyo ābhisamācārikesu sakkaccakārī garucittīkārabahulo viharati, ayaṃ vuccati ācāro. Evaṃ tāva ācāro veditabbo.

Furthermore, a monk dwells respectful, deferential, endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, well-robed, well-covered, graceful in his moving forwards and backwards, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching, with downcast eyes, endowed with graceful deportment, with guarded sense-faculties, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, of few wishes, content, with aroused energy, diligent in the observances of proper conduct, and abounding in respect and reverence. This is called conduct. Thus, first, conduct should be understood.

Gocaro pana tividho upanissayagocaro ārakkhagocaro upanibandhagocaroti. Tattha katamo upanissayagocaro? Dasakathāvatthuguṇasamannāgato kalyāṇamitto, yaṃ nissāya assutaṃ suṇāti, sutaṃ pariyodapeti, kaṅkhaṃ vitarati, diṭṭhiṃ ujuṃ karoti, cittaṃ pasādeti. Yassa vā pana anusikkhamāno saddhāya vaḍḍhati, sīlena, sutena, cāgena, paññāya vaḍḍhati, ayaṃ vuccati upanissayagocaro.

Resort, however, is threefold: the supportive resort, the protective resort, and the binding resort. Therein, what is the supportive resort? A good friend endowed with the qualities of the ten topics of discourse, relying on whom one hears what has not been heard, clarifies what has been heard, dispels doubt, straightens one's view, and gladdens the mind. Or one who, by training in emulation of him, grows in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom—this is called the supportive resort.

Katamo ārakkhagocaro? Idha bhikkhu antaragharaṃ paviṭṭho vīthiṃ paṭipanno okkhittacakkhu yugamattadassāvī susaṃvuto gacchati, na hatthiṃ olokento, na assaṃ, na rathaṃ, na pattiṃ, na itthiṃ, na purisaṃ olokento, na uddhaṃ ullokento, na adho olokento, na disāvidisaṃ pekkhamāno gacchati, ayaṃ vuccati ārakkhagocaro.

What is the protective resort? Here, a monk who has entered a village or is walking along a street keeps his eyes downcast, looking only a yoke's length ahead, well-restrained as he goes. He does not look at an elephant, a horse, a chariot, an infantryman, a woman, or a man. He does not look upward or downward or gaze around in different directions as he goes—this is called the protective resort.

Katamo upanibandhagocaro? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā yattha cittaṃ upanibandhati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā [V 1.0020] – “ko ca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno gocaro sako pettiko visayo? Yadidaṃ cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.372), ayaṃ vuccati upanibandhagocaro. Iti iminā ca ācārena iminā ca gocarena upeto…pe… samannāgato. Tenapi vuccati ācāragocarasampannoti.

What is the binding resort? The four foundations of mindfulness, to which the mind is bound. For this was stated by the Blessed One: 'And what, monks, is a monk's own resort, his own ancestral domain? It is these four foundations of mindfulness.' This is called the binding resort. Thus, being endowed with this conduct and this resort… possessed of them, he is therefore said to be 'accomplished in conduct and resort'.

Aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvīti aṇuppamāṇesu asañcicca āpannasekhiyaakusalacittuppādādibhedesu vajjesu bhayadassanasīlo. Samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhāpadesu sikkhitabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ sammā ādāya sikkhati. Ettha ca “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti ettāvatā [M 1.0020] ca puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ dassitaṃ. “Ācāragocarasampanno”tiādi pana sabbaṃ yathāpaṭipannassa taṃ sīlaṃ sampajjati, taṃ paṭipattiṃ dassetuṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Seeing danger in the slightest faults: this means one who is accustomed to seeing danger in faults of even a minute measure, such as breaches of the training rules unintentionally incurred, the arising of unwholesome states of mind, and the like. He undertakes and trains in the training rules: he properly undertakes and trains in whatever is to be trained in among the training rules. And herein, by the words 'restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint,' the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is shown through a teaching based on the individual. But all that follows, beginning with 'accomplished in conduct and resort,' should be understood as having been said to show the practice by which that virtue is perfected for one who practices accordingly.

Indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ

The Virtue of Restraint of the Sense Faculties

15. Yaṃ panetaṃ tadanantaraṃ “so cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā”tiādinā nayena dassitaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ, tattha soti pātimokkhasaṃvarasīle ṭhito bhikkhu. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvāti kāraṇavasena cakkhūti laddhavohārena rūpadassanasamatthena cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvā. Porāṇā panāhu “cakkhu rūpaṃ na passati, acittakattā, cittaṃ na passati, acakkhukattā, dvārārammaṇasaṅghaṭṭe pana cakkhupasādavatthukena cittena passati. Īdisī panesā ‘dhanunā vijjhatī’tiādīsu viya sasambhārakathā nāma hoti, tasmā cakkhuviññāṇena rūpaṃ disvāti ayamevettha attho”ti. Na nimittaggāhīti itthipurisanimittaṃ vā subhanimittādikaṃ vā kilesavatthubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ na gaṇhāti, diṭṭhamatteyeva saṇṭhāti. Nānubyañjanaggāhīti kilesānaṃ anuanubyañjanato pākaṭabhāvakaraṇato anubyañjananti laddhavohāraṃ hatthapādasitahasitakathitavilokitādibhedaṃ ākāraṃ na gaṇhāti, yaṃ tattha bhūtaṃ, tadeva gaṇhāti, cetiyapabbatavāsī mahātissatthero viya.

15. Now, as for the virtue of sense-restraint shown immediately thereafter by the method beginning with ‘he, having seen a form with the eye,’ therein, ‘he’ is the monk established in the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint. ‘Having seen a form with the eye’ means having seen a form with eye-consciousness, which is capable of seeing a form and is conventionally called ‘the eye’ because it is the instrument. The ancients, however, said: ‘The eye does not see a form, for it is without a mind; the mind does not see, for it is without an eye. Rather, upon the collision of the sense-door and the object, the mind, based on the eye-sensitivity, sees. This is what is called a statement including the apparatus, like the expression ‘he shoots with a bow.’ Therefore, the meaning here is precisely ‘one sees a form with eye-consciousness.’ ‘He is not a grasper of the sign’ means he does not grasp a sign that is a basis for defilements—such as the sign of a woman or a man, or a beautiful sign—but stands fast at the mere sight. ‘He is not a grasper of the features’ means he does not grasp the particular features—such as the hand, foot, smiling, laughing, speaking, or glancing—which are conventionally called ‘features’ because they make defilements manifest again and again. He grasps only what is actually there, like the Elder Mahātissa, the dweller of Cetiyapabbata.

Theraṃ kira cetiyapabbatā anurādhapuraṃ piṇḍacāratthāya āgacchantaṃ aññatarā kulasuṇhā sāmikena saddhiṃ bhaṇḍitvā sumaṇḍitapasādhitā devakaññā viya kālasseva anurādhapurato nikkhamitvā [V 1.0021] ñātigharaṃ gacchantī antarāmagge disvā vipallatthacittā mahāhasitaṃ hasi. Thero kimetanti olokento tassā dantaṭṭhike asubhasaññaṃ paṭilabhitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ –

It is said that a certain daughter-in-law of a good family, having quarreled with her husband, was leaving Anuradhapura early in the morning for her relatives’ house, well-adorned and beautified like a celestial maiden. On the way, seeing the Elder coming from Cetiyapabbata to Anuradhapura for his alms-round, her mind became perverted with lust, and she burst into loud laughter. The Elder, wondering, “What is this?” looked at her and, gaining the perception of foulness in her tooth-bones, attained Arahantship. Therefore it is said:

“Tassā dantaṭṭhikaṃ disvā, pubbasaññaṃ anussari;

Tattheva so ṭhito thero, arahattaṃ apāpuṇī”ti.

“Seeing her tooth-bones, he recollected his former perception; standing right there, that Elder attained Arahantship.”

Sāmikopi [M 1.0021] kho panassā anumaggaṃ gacchanto theraṃ disvā “kiñci, bhante, itthiṃ passathā”ti pucchi. Taṃ thero āha –

Her husband, following along the path, saw the Elder and asked, “Venerable sir, did you see a woman?” The Elder said to him:

“Nābhijānāmi itthī vā, puriso vā ito gato;

Apica aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo, gacchatesa mahāpathe”ti.

“I do not know whether it was a woman or a man that went from here; but a collection of bones is going along this great highway.”

Yatvādhikaraṇamenantiādimhi yaṃkāraṇā yassa cakkhundriyāsaṃvarassa hetu etaṃ puggalaṃ satikavāṭena cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ apihitacakkhudvāraṃ hutvā viharantaṃ ete abhijjhādayo dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ anubandheyyuṃ. Tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjatīti tassa cakkhundriyassa satikavāṭena pidahanatthāya paṭipajjati. Evaṃ paṭipajjantoyeva ca rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatītipi vuccati. Tattha kiñcāpi cakkhundriye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā natthi. Na hi cakkhupasādaṃ nissāya sati vā muṭṭhasaccaṃ vā uppajjati. Apica yadā rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, tadā bhavaṅge dvikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhe kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ. Tato vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ. Tato vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ. Tato kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tadanantaraṃ javanaṃ javati.

In the phrase beginning ‘For which reason,’ it is because of non-restraint of the eye faculty that these states such as covetousness would flow into and follow this person who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, with the eye-door unclosed by the door of mindfulness. ‘He practices for its restraint’ means he practices for the purpose of closing that eye faculty with the door of mindfulness. By practicing thus, he guards the eye faculty, and it is also said that he attains restraint in the eye faculty. Herein, although in the eye faculty there is neither restraint nor non-restraint, for neither mindfulness nor forgetfulness arises dependent on the eye sensitivity. Moreover, when a visible object comes into the range of the eye, after the life-continuum has arisen twice and ceased, the functional mind-element, performing the function of adverting, arises and ceases. Thereafter, eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing. Thereafter, the resultant mind-element performs the function of receiving. Thereafter, the resultant, rootless mind-consciousness-element performs the function of investigating. Thereafter, the functional, rootless mind-consciousness-element, performing the function of determining, arises and ceases. Immediately after that, the impulsion runs.
