Tatrāpi neva bhavaṅgasamaye, na āvajjanādīnaṃ aññatarasamaye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā atthi. Javanakkhaṇe pana sace dussīlyaṃ vā muṭṭhasaccaṃ vā aññāṇaṃ vā akkhanti vā kosajjaṃ vā uppajjati, asaṃvaro hoti. Evaṃ honto pana so cakkhundriye asaṃvaroti vuccati. Kasmā? Yasmā tasmiṃ sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni[V 1.0022]. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagare catūsu dvāresu asaṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharadvārakoṭṭhakagabbhādayo susaṃvutā honti, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ arakkhitaṃ agopitameva hoti. Nagaradvārena hi pavisitvā corā yadicchanti, taṃ kareyyuṃ, evameva javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni.

Even there, neither during the life-continuum moment, nor during any of the moments of adverting and so forth, is there restraint or non-restraint. However, if during the impulsion moment immorality, forgetfulness, ignorance, intolerance, or sloth arises, then there is non-restraint. When this occurs, it is called ‘non-restraint in the eye faculty.’ Why? Because when that is present, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. To what is this comparable? Just as in a city where the four gates are unclosed, even if the inner house-doors, storerooms, and chambers are well-closed, still all the goods within the city remain unprotected and unguarded. For thieves, entering through the city gate, may do whatever they wish. Similarly, when immorality and so forth arise during the impulsion, and that non-restraint is present, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting.

Tasmiṃ [M 1.0022] pana sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagaradvāresu saṃvutesu kiñcāpi antogharādayo asaṃvutā honti, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ surakkhitaṃ sugopitameva hoti. Nagaradvāresu hi pihitesu corānaṃ paveso natthi, evameva javane sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīnipi vīthicittāni. Tasmā javanakkhaṇe uppajjamānopi cakkhundriye saṃvaroti vutto.

But when virtue and so forth have arisen in that impulsion, the door is guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. To what is this comparable? Just as when the city gates are closed, even though the inner houses and so on are unclosed, all the goods within the city are well-protected and well-guarded. For when the city gates are shut, there is no entry for thieves. Similarly, when virtue and so forth have arisen during the impulsion, the door is guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses such as adverting. Therefore, restraint, although arising at the impulsion moment, is said to be ‘in the eye faculty’.

Sotena saddaṃ sutvātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Evamidaṃ saṅkhepato rūpādīsu kilesānubandhanimittādiggāhaparivajjanalakkhaṇaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlanti veditabbaṃ.

The same method applies in such cases as ‘having heard a sound with the ear,’ and so on. Thus, in brief, this virtue of restraint of the faculties should be understood as having the characteristic of avoiding the grasping of signs and features that are connected with defilements, in regard to forms and so forth.

Ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ

The Virtue of Purity of Livelihood

16. Idāni indriyasaṃvarasīlānantaraṃ vutte ājīvapārisuddhisīle ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānanti yāni tāni “ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā pāpiccho icchāpakato asantaṃ abhūtaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ ullapati, āpatti pārājikassa. Ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā sañcarittaṃ samāpajjati, āpatti saṅghādisesassa. Ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā ‘yo te vihāre vasati so bhikkhu arahā’ti bhaṇati, paṭivijānantassa āpatti thullaccayassa. Ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhu paṇītabhojanāni agilāno attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pācittiyassa. Ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā bhikkhunī paṇītabhojanāni agilānā attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati, āpatti pāṭidesanīyassa. Ājīvahetu ājīvakāraṇā sūpaṃ vā odanaṃ vā agilāno attano atthāya viññāpetvā bhuñjati[V 1.0023], āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti (pari. 287) evaṃ paññattāni cha sikkhāpadāni, imesaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ.

16. Now, in the virtue of purity of livelihood, which was stated after the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, [this is the explanation] of the six training rules laid down for the sake of livelihood. The six training rules laid down are as follows: (1) 'For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, being of evil desires and overcome by desire, if one boasts of a non-existent, unreal superhuman quality, it is an offense of defeat. (2) For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, if one engages in matchmaking, it is an offense entailing an initial and subsequent meeting of the Sangha. (3) For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, if one says, “The monk living in your monastery is an arahant,” and the other person understands, it is a grave offense. (4) For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, if a monk who is not ill, having requested choice foods for his own sake, consumes them, it is an offense requiring expiation. (5) For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, if a nun who is not ill, having requested choice foods for her own sake, consumes them, it is an offense requiring confession. (6) For the sake of livelihood, for the reason of livelihood, if one who is not ill, having requested curry or boiled rice for one's own sake, consumes it, it is an offense of wrong-doing.' These are the six training rules thus laid down.

Kuhanātiādīsu ayaṃ pāḷi, “tattha katamā kuhanā? Lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa pāpicchassa icchāpakatassa yā paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātena vā sāmantajappitena vā iriyāpathassa vā aṭṭhapanā ṭhapanā saṇṭhapanā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati kuhanā.

In the section on 'deceit' and so forth, this is the Pāli text: 'Herein, what is deceit? For one who, dependent on gain, honor, and fame, is of evil desires and overcome by desire, whatever—whether by means of what is called the partaking of requisites, or by roundabout talk, or by the arranging, establishing, and composing of one's posture—frowning, the habit of frowning, deceit, deceiving, or the state of being deceitful there is, this is called deceit.'

“Tattha [M 1.0023] katamā lapanā? Lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa pāpicchassa icchāpakatassa yā paresaṃ ālapanā lapanā sallapanā ullapanā samullapanā unnahanā samunnahanā ukkācanā samukkācanā anuppiyabhāṇitā cāṭukamyatā muggasūpyatā pāribhaṭyatā, ayaṃ vuccati lapanā.

Herein, what is chattering? For one who, dependent on gain, honor, and fame, is of evil desires and overcome by desire, whatever addressing of others, talking, conversing, praising up, greatly praising up, entrapping talk, greatly entrapping talk, extolling, greatly extolling, agreeable speech, sycophancy, bean-soup talk, and servile behavior there is—this is called chattering.

“Tattha katamā nemittikatā? Lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa pāpicchassa icchāpakatassa yaṃ paresaṃ nimittaṃ nimittakammaṃ obhāso obhāsakammaṃ sāmantajappā parikathā, ayaṃ vuccati nemittikatā.

Herein, what is hinting? For one dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who is of evil desires and overcome by desire, whatever hint to others, act of making a hint, hinting speech, hinting action, roundabout talk, or talking around the subject there is—this is called hinting.

“Tattha katamā nippesikatā? Lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassa pāpicchassa icchāpakatassa yā paresaṃ akkosanā vambhanā garahanā ukkhepanā samukkhepanā khipanā saṃkhipanā pāpanā sampāpanā avaṇṇahārikā parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā, ayaṃ vuccati nippesikatā.

Herein, what is harassment? For one dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who is of evil desires and overcome by desire, whatever abuse of others, scorn, reproach, disparagement, denigration, condemnation, belittling, bringing down, causing ruin, defamation, or backbiting there is—this is called harassment.

“Tattha katamā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā? Lābhasakkārasilokasannissito pāpiccho icchāpakato ito laddhaṃ āmisaṃ amutra harati, amutra vā laddhaṃ āmisaṃ idha āharati. Yā evarūpā āmisena āmisassa eṭṭhi gaveṭṭhi pariyeṭṭhi esanā gavesanā pariyesanā, ayaṃ vuccati lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā”ti (vibha. 862-865).

Herein, what is the striving to win gain with gain? One dependent on gain, honor, and fame, who is of evil desires and overcome by desire, carries material gain obtained here to another place, or brings material gain obtained elsewhere here. Whatever such hankering, seeking, searching, longing, questing, and pursuit of material gain with material gain there is—this is called the striving to win gain with gain.

17. Imissā pana pāḷiyā evamattho veditabbo. Kuhananiddese tāva lābhasakkārasilokasannissitassāti lābhañca sakkārañca kittisaddañca sannissitassa, patthayantassāti [V 1.0024] attho. Pāpicchassāti asantaguṇadīpanakāmassa. Icchāpakatassāti icchāya apakatassa, upaddutassāti attho.

17. The meaning of this Pāli text should be understood as follows. In the exposition of deceit, first, 'dependent on gain, honor, and fame' means one who is dependent on gain, honor, and the sound of fame, that is, one who desires them. 'Of evil desires' means one who desires to display qualities one does not possess. 'Overcome by desire' means one who is harmed by desire, that is, one who is afflicted.

Ito paraṃ yasmā paccayapaṭisevanasāmantajappanairiyāpathasannissitavasena mahāniddese tividhaṃ kuhanavatthu āgataṃ. Tasmā tividhampetaṃ dassetuṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātena vāti evamādi āraddhaṃ. Tattha cīvarādīhi nimantitassa tadatthikasseva sato pāpicchataṃ nissāya paṭikkhipanena, te ca gahapatike attani suppatiṭṭhitasaddhe ñatvā puna tesaṃ “aho ayyo appiccho na kiñci paṭiggaṇhituṃ icchati, suladdhaṃ vata no assa sace appamattakampi kiñci paṭiggaṇheyyā”ti nānāvidhehi upāyehi paṇītāni cīvarādīni [M 1.0024] upanentānaṃ tadanuggahakāmataṃyeva āvikatvā paṭiggahaṇena ca tato pabhuti api sakaṭabhārehi upanāmanahetubhūtaṃ vimhāpanaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ mahāniddese –

Furthermore, because in the Mahāniddesa the threefold basis of deceit is presented by way of the partaking of requisites, roundabout talk, and what is dependent on posture, therefore, to explain this threefold basis, the text begins with “or by means of what is called the partaking of requisites,” and so on. Herein, when invited with robes and so forth, one who is desirous of them, relying on his evil desires, refuses. Then, knowing that those householders have well-established faith in him, when they bring excellent robes and other items through various means, thinking, “Ah, the venerable one has few wishes and does not desire to accept anything. How fortunate we would be if he would accept even a little something,” he accepts, revealing only a desire to favor them. From then on, this act of causing astonishment, which becomes the cause for bringing offerings even by the cartload, is to be understood as the basis of deceit known as the partaking of requisites. For this is said in the Mahāniddesa:

“Katamaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthu? Idha gahapatikā bhikkhuṃ nimantenti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi. So pāpiccho icchāpakato atthiko cīvara…pe… parikkhārānaṃ bhiyyokamyataṃ upādāya cīvaraṃ paccakkhāti. Piṇḍapātaṃ…pe… senāsanaṃ. Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paccakkhāti. So evamāha – ‘kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena cīvarena, etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo susānā vā saṅkārakūṭā vā pāpaṇikā vā nantakāni uccinitvā saṅghāṭiṃ katvā dhāreyya. Kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena piṇḍapātena etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo uñchācariyāya piṇḍiyālopena jīvikaṃ kappeyya. Kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena senāsanena, etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo rukkhamūliko vā assa abbhokāsiko vā. Kiṃ samaṇassa mahagghena gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārena, etaṃ sāruppaṃ yaṃ samaṇo pūtimuttena vā hariṭakīkhaṇḍena vā osadhaṃ kareyyā’ti. Tadupādāya lūkhaṃ cīvaraṃ dhāreti, lūkhaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjati, lūkhaṃ senāsanaṃ paṭisevati, lūkhaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paṭisevati, tamenaṃ gahapatikā evaṃ jānanti ‘ayaṃ samaṇo appiccho santuṭṭho pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho āraddhavīriyo dhutavādo’ti. Bhiyyo bhiyyo nimantenti cīvara…pe… parikkhārehi. So evamāha – ‘tiṇṇaṃ sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavati. Saddhāya sammukhībhāvā saddho kulaputto bahuṃ puññaṃ [V 1.0025] pasavati. Deyyadhammassa…pe… dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ sammukhībhāvāsaddhokulaputto bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavati. Tumhākañcevāyaṃ saddhā atthi, deyyadhammo ca saṃvijjati, ahañca paṭiggāhako, sacehaṃ na paṭiggahessāmi, evaṃ tumhe puññena paribāhirā bhavissanti, na mayhaṃ iminā attho. Apica tumhākaṃyeva anukampāya paṭiggaṇhāmī’ti. Tadupādāya bahumpi cīvaraṃ paṭiggaṇhāti. Bahumpi piṇḍapātaṃ…pe… bhesajjaparikkhāraṃ paṭiggaṇhāti[M 1.0025]. Yā evarūpā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ, idaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthū”ti (mahāni. 87).

“What is the ground of deceit known as partaking of requisites? Here, householders invite a monk with robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites. Being of evil desires, overcome by desire, and wanting requisites, out of a desire for more, he rejects the robe. He rejects the almsfood… the lodging… the medicinal requisites. He says: ‘What need has a recluse for an expensive robe? It is fitting for a recluse to gather rags from a charnel ground, a rubbish heap, or a shop, make them into a patchwork robe, and wear it. What need has a recluse for fine almsfood? It is fitting for a recluse to maintain his life on a lump of food gathered by gleaning. What need has a recluse for a fine dwelling? It is fitting for a recluse to be one who dwells at the foot of a tree or in the open air. What need has a recluse for fine medicinal requisites? It is fitting for a recluse to make medicine from fermented urine or a piece of myrobalan fruit.’ On that account, he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse almsfood, uses a coarse dwelling, and uses coarse medicinal requisites. The householders know him thus: ‘This recluse has few wishes, is content, secluded, unassociated, of aroused energy, and an exponent of ascetic practices.’ They invite him again and again with robes… and other requisites. He then says: ‘Through the presence of three things, a faithful clansman begets much merit. By the presence of faith, a faithful clansman begets much merit. By the presence of the gift… by the presence of those worthy of offerings, a faithful clansman begets much merit. You have faith, the gift is available, and I am the recipient. If I do not accept, you will be excluded from merit. I have no need of this. Yet, out of compassion for you, I accept.’ On that account, he accepts many robes. He accepts much almsfood… many medicinal requisites. Such frowning, the state of frowning, deceit, deceiving, the state of being deceitful—this is the ground of deceit known as partaking of requisites.”

Pāpicchasseva pana sato uttarimanussadhammādhigamaparidīpanavācāya tathā tathā vimhāpanaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha –

Furthermore, for one who is of evil desires, causing astonishment in various ways by speech that reveals the attainment of superhuman states is to be understood as the ground of deceit called allusive speech. As it is said:

“Katamaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthu? Idhekacco pāpiccho icchāpakato sambhāvanādhippāyo ‘evaṃ maṃ jano sambhāvessatī’ti ariyadhammasannissitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati ‘yo evarūpaṃ cīvaraṃ dhāreti, so samaṇo mahesakkho’ti bhaṇati. ‘Yo evarūpaṃ pattaṃ lohathālakaṃ. Dhammakaraṇaṃ parissāvanaṃ kuñcikaṃ, kāyabandhanaṃ upāhanaṃ dhāreti, so samaṇo mahesakkho’ti bhaṇati. Yassa evarūpo upajjhāyo ācariyo samānupajjhāyako, samānācariyako mitto sandiṭṭho sambhatto sahāyo. Yo evarūpe vihāre vasati aḍḍhayoge pāsāde hammiye guhāyaṃ leṇe kuṭiyā kūṭāgāre aṭṭe māḷe uddaṇḍe upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ maṇḍape rukkhamūle vasati, so samaṇo mahesakkho’ti bhaṇati. Atha vā ‘korajikakorajiko bhākuṭikabhākuṭiko kuhakakuhako lapakalapako mukhasambhāviko, ayaṃ samaṇo imāsaṃ evarūpānaṃ santānaṃ vihārasamāpattīnaṃ lābhī’ti tādisaṃ gambhīraṃ gūḷhaṃ nipuṇaṃ paṭicchannaṃ lokuttaraṃ suññatāpaṭisaṃyuttaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Yā evarūpā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ, idaṃ sāmantajappanasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthū”ti (mahāni. 87).

“What is the ground of deceit known as allusive speech? Here, someone who is of evil desires, overcome by desire, aiming for esteem, thinking, ‘Thus people will esteem me,’ speaks words connected with the noble Dhamma, saying, ‘A recluse who wears such a robe is of great influence.’ He says, ‘A recluse who uses such a bowl, a bronze dish, a water pot with a strainer, a water strainer, a key, a belt, or sandals is of great influence.’ He says, ‘A recluse whose preceptor, teacher, fellow resident with the same preceptor, fellow resident with the same teacher, friend, acquaintance, or intimate companion is of such a kind, is of great influence.’ He says, ‘A recluse who dwells in such a dwelling—a gabled building, a mansion, a storied building, a cave, a rock-shelter, a hut, a peaked-roof house, a watchtower, a hall, a storehouse, a service hall, a pavilion, or at the foot of a tree—is of great influence.’ Or else, being extremely hypocritical, a great frowner, a great deceiver, a great chatterer, and a flatterer, he gives a talk that is deep, hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane, and connected with emptiness, saying: ‘This recluse is an obtainer of these kinds of tranquil abidings and attainments.’ Such frowning, the state of frowning, deceit, deceiving, the state of being deceitful—this is the ground of deceit known as allusive speech.”

Pāpicchasseva pana sato sambhāvanādhippāyakatena iriyāpathena vimhāpanaṃ iriyāpathasannissitaṃ kuhanavatthūti veditabbaṃ. Yathāha – “katamaṃ iriyāpathasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthu. Idhekacco pāpiccho icchāpakato sambhāvanādhippāyo ‘evaṃ maṃ jano sambhāvessatī’ti gamanaṃ saṇṭhapeti[V 1.0026], ṭhānaṃ [M 1.0026] saṇṭhapeti, nisajjaṃ saṇṭhapeti, sayanaṃ saṇṭhapeti, paṇidhāya gacchati, paṇidhāya tiṭṭhati, paṇidhāya nisīdati, paṇidhāya seyyaṃ kappeti, samāhito viya gacchati, samāhito viya tiṭṭhati, nisīdati, seyyaṃ kappeti, āpāthakajjhāyī ca hoti, yā evarūpā iriyāpathassa aṭṭhapanā ṭhapanā saṇṭhapanā bhākuṭikā bhākuṭiyaṃ kuhanā kuhāyanā kuhitattaṃ, idaṃ vuccati iriyāpathasaṅkhātaṃ kuhanavatthū”ti (mahāni. 87).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the ground of deceit connected with posture is the act of impressing by means of posture, on the part of one who is of evil desires with the intention of gaining esteem. As it is said: ‘What is the ground of deceit designated as posture? Here, a certain one, being of evil desires, overcome by desire, with the intention of gaining esteem, thinking, “Thus people will esteem me,” composes his walking, composes his standing, composes his sitting, composes his lying down; he walks with deliberation, stands with deliberation, sits with deliberation, lies down with deliberation; he walks as if concentrated, stands as if concentrated, sits as if concentrated, lies down as if concentrated; and he is one who meditates in public view. Whatever such composing, placing, and arranging of posture; such frowning, the state of frowning, deceit, deceiving, the state of being deceitful—this is called the ground of deceit designated as posture.’”

Tattha paccayapaṭisevanasaṅkhātenāti paccayapaṭisevananti evaṃ saṅkhātena paccayapaṭisevanena vā saṅkhātena. Sāmantajappitenāti samīpabhaṇitena. Iriyāpathassa vāti catuiriyāpathassa. Aṭṭhapanātiādi ṭhapanā, ādarena vā ṭhapanā. Ṭhapanāti ṭhapanākāro. Saṇṭhapanāti abhisaṅkharaṇā, pāsādikabhāvakaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhākuṭikāti padhānapurimaṭṭhitabhāvadassanena bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ, mukhasaṅkocoti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhākuṭikaraṇaṃ sīlamassāti bhākuṭiko. Bhākuṭikassa bhāvo bhākuṭiyaṃ. Kuhanāti vimhāpanā. Kuhassa āyanā kuhāyanā. Kuhitassa bhāvo kuhitattanti.

Herein, 'by that designated as the use of requisites' means by that which is designated as 'the use of requisites,' or by the use of requisites so designated. 'By indirect speech' means by speaking nearby. 'Or of posture' means of the four postures. 'Arranging' and so forth means placing, or placing with care. 'Placing' means the manner of placing. 'Setting up' means constructing; that is to say, making an inspiring appearance. 'Frowning' means making a frown by showing a state of being established in foremost striving; that is to say, it means contracting the face. One whose habit is making a frown is a 'frowner' (bhākuṭika). The state of a frowner is 'the state of frowning' (bhākuṭiyaṃ). 'Deception' (kuhanā) is causing astonishment. The way of a deceiver is 'deceiving' (kuhāyanā). The state of having deceived is 'deceitfulness' (kuhitatta).

Lapanāniddese ālapanāti vihāraṃ āgate manusse disvā “kimatthāya bhonto āgatā, kiṃ bhikkhū nimantituṃ, yadi evaṃ gacchatha re, ahaṃ pacchato pattaṃ gahetvā āgacchāmī”ti evaṃ āditova lapanā. Atha vā attānaṃ upanetvā “ahaṃ tisso, mayi rājā pasanno, mayi asuko ca asuko ca rājamahāmatto pasanno”ti evaṃ attupanāyikā lapanā ālapanā. Lapanāti puṭṭhassa sato vuttappakārameva lapanaṃ. Sallapanāti gahapatikānaṃ ukkaṇṭhane bhītassa okāsaṃ datvā datvā suṭṭhu lapanā. Ullapanāti mahākuṭumbiko mahānāviko mahādānapatīti evaṃ uddhaṃ katvā lapanā. Samullapanāti sabbatobhāgena uddhaṃ katvā lapanā.

In the exposition of talking, ālapana is when, upon seeing people who have come to the monastery, one says from the very start: 'For what purpose have you sirs come? Is it to invite the bhikkhus? If so, go on ahead; I will follow behind carrying my bowl.' This is talking from the outset. Or else, presenting oneself, one says: 'I am Tissa; the king is pleased with me, and such and such royal ministers are pleased with me.' This self-promoting talk is ālapana. Lapana is talking in the manner described only when one is asked. Sallapanā is, being afraid of the householders' dissatisfaction, talking very smoothly, repeatedly giving them an opening. Ullapanā is talking by elevating someone, saying he is 'a man of a great family,' 'a great ship-owner,' or 'a great almsgiver.' Samullapanā is talking by elevating someone in every way.

Unnahanāti “upāsakā pubbe īdise kāle navadānaṃ detha, idāni kiṃ na dethā”ti evaṃ yāva “dassāma, bhante, okāsaṃ na labhāmā”tiādīni vadanti, tāva uddhaṃ uddhaṃ nahanā, veṭhanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā ucchuhatthaṃ [M 1.0027] disvā “kuto ābhataṃ upāsakā”ti pucchati. Ucchukhettato, bhanteti. Kiṃ tattha ucchu madhuranti. Khāditvā, bhante, jānitabbanti. “Na, upāsaka, bhikkhussa ucchuṃ dethā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Yā evarūpā nibbeṭhentassāpi veṭhanakathā, sā unnahanā. Sabbatobhāgena punappunaṃ unnahanā samunnahanā.

Unnahanā (coaxing) is when one says to lay devotees: 'Previously at a time like this you would give a new gift; why do you not give now?' and continues in this way until they say: 'We will give, venerable sir, but we have not found an opportunity.' This is called 'tying up higher and higher,' that is, wrapping (veṭhanā). Or else, upon seeing someone with sugarcane in hand, one asks: 'Where did you bring this from, lay devotee?' 'From the sugarcane field, venerable sir.' 'Is the sugarcane there sweet?' 'You will know after chewing it, venerable sir.' Then one says: 'Lay devotee, it is not proper to say, "Give sugarcane to a bhikkhu."' Such talk that wraps around even while one is trying to extricate oneself is unnahanā. Repeated coaxing in every way is samunnahanā.

Ukkācanāti [V 1.0027] “etaṃ kulaṃ maṃyeva jānāti. Sace ettha deyyadhammo uppajjati, mayhameva detī”ti evaṃ ukkhipitvā kācanā ukkācanā, uddīpanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Telakandarikavatthu cettha vattabbaṃ. Sabbatobhāgena pana punappunaṃ ukkācanā samukkācanā.

Ukkācanā (extolling) is proclaiming by exalting, thus: 'This family knows only me. If any gift arises here, they give it only to me.' This is ukkācanā; it is said to be highlighting (uddīpanā). The story of Telakandarika should be told here. Furthermore, repeated extolling in every way is samukkācanā.

Anuppiyabhāṇitāti saccānurūpaṃ dhammānurūpaṃ vā anapaloketvā punappunaṃ piyabhaṇanameva. Cāṭukamyatāti nīcavuttitā attānaṃ heṭṭhato heṭṭhato ṭhapetvā vattanaṃ. Muggasūpyatāti muggasūpasadisatā. Yathā hi muggesu paccamānesu kocideva na paccati, avasesā paccanti, evaṃ yassa puggalassa vacane kiñcideva saccaṃ hoti, sesaṃ alīkaṃ, ayaṃ puggalo muggasūpyoti vuccati. Tassa bhāvo muggasūpyatā. Pāribhaṭyatāti pāribhaṭyabhāvo. Yo hi kuladārake dhāti viya aṅkena vā khandhena vā paribhaṭati, dhāretīti attho. Tassa paribhaṭassa kammaṃ pāribhaṭyuṃ. Pāribhaṭyassa bhāvo pāribhaṭyatāti.

Anuppiyabhāṇitā (ingratiating speech) is simply speaking pleasingly again and again without considering whether it conforms to the truth or to the Dhamma. Cāṭukamyatā (sycophancy) is lowliness of conduct, speaking while placing oneself lower and lower. Muggasūpyatā (lentil-soup-likeness) is being like lentil soup. For just as when lentils are being cooked, only a few do not get cooked while the rest do, so too a person whose speech contains only a little truth while the rest is false is called 'one of lentil-soup-likeness.' His state is muggasūpyatā. Pāribhaṭyatā (acting as a nursemaid) is the state of being an attendant. For one who tends to the children of families on his lap or on his shoulder like a nursemaid (dhāti) is called an attendant (paribhaṭa); the meaning is 'he carries' (dhāreti). The action of that attendant is attendance (pāribhaṭya). The state of attendance is pāribhaṭyatā.

Nemittikatāniddese nimittanti yaṃkiñci paresaṃ paccayadānasaññājanakaṃ kāyavacīkammaṃ. Nimittakammanti khādanīyaṃ gahetvā gacchante disvā “kiṃ khādanīyaṃ labhitthā”tiādinā nayena nimittakaraṇaṃ. Obhāsoti paccayapaṭisaṃyuttakathā. Obhāsakammanti vacchapālake disvā “kiṃ ime vacchā khīragovacchā udāhu takkagovacchā”ti pucchitvā “khīragovacchā, bhante”ti vutte “na khīragovacchā, yadi khīragovacchā siyuṃ, bhikkhūpi khīraṃ labheyyu”nti evamādinā nayena tesaṃ dārakānaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ nivedetvā khīradāpanādikaṃ obhāsakaraṇaṃ. Sāmantajappāti samīpaṃ katvā jappanaṃ. Kulūpakabhikkhu vatthu cettha vattabbaṃ.

In the exposition of hinting, a 'hint' (nimitta) is any bodily or verbal action that generates in others the perception of giving requisites. 'Making a hint' (nimittakamma) is making a hint in such a way as, for example, seeing people going along with food and asking: 'What food did you get?' An 'allusion' (obhāso) is talk connected with requisites. 'The act of making an allusion' (obhāsakamma) is, for example, upon seeing calf-herders, asking: 'Are these calves milk-fed calves or buttermilk-fed calves?' When told, 'They are milk-fed calves, venerable sir,' one replies: 'They cannot be milk-fed calves; if they were, the bhikkhus too would get milk.' The act of making an allusion is to get them to give milk and so on by having the parents of those children informed in this way. Sāmantajappā is talking around the subject. The story of the family-attendant bhikkhu should be told here.

Kulūpako [M 1.0028] kira bhikkhu bhuñjitukāmo gehaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Taṃ disvā adātukāmā gharaṇī “taṇḍulā natthī”ti bhaṇantī taṇḍule āharitukāmā viya paṭivissakagharaṃ gatā. Bhikkhupi antogabbhaṃ pavisitvā olokento kavāṭakoṇe ucchuṃ, bhājane guḷaṃ, piṭake loṇamacchaphāle, kumbhiyaṃ taṇḍule, ghaṭe ghataṃ disvā nikkhamitvā nisīdi. Gharaṇī “taṇḍule nālattha”nti āgatā. Bhikkhu “upāsike ‘ajja bhikkhā na sampajjissatī’ti paṭikacceva nimittaṃ addasa”nti āha. Kiṃ, bhanteti. Kavāṭakoṇe nikkhittaṃ ucchuṃ viya sappaṃ addasaṃ, ‘taṃ paharissāmī’ti olokento bhājane ṭhapitaṃ guḷapiṇḍaṃ viya pāsāṇaṃ, leḍḍukena pahaṭena sappena kataṃ piṭake nikkhittaloṇamacchaphālasadisaṃ phaṇaṃ, tassa taṃ leḍḍuṃ ḍaṃsitukāmassa [V 1.0028] kumbhiyā taṇḍulasadise dante, athassa kupitassa ghaṭe pakkhittaghatasadisaṃ mukhato nikkhamantaṃ visamissakaṃ kheḷanti. Sā “na sakkā muṇḍakaṃ vañcetu”nti ucchuṃ datvā odanaṃ pacitvā ghataguḷamacchehi saddhiṃ sabbaṃ adāsīti. Evaṃ samīpaṃ katvā jappanaṃ sāmantajappāti veditabbaṃ. Parikathāti yathā taṃ labhati tassa parivattetvā kathananti.

It is said that a certain family-attendant bhikkhu, wanting to eat, entered a house and sat down. Seeing him, the lady of the house, not wanting to give, said, 'There is no rice,' and went to a neighbor's house as if to fetch some. The bhikkhu entered the inner chamber and, looking around, saw sugarcane in a corner by the door, jaggery in a vessel, slices of salt-fish in a basket, rice in a pot, and ghee in a jar. Having seen this, he came out and sat down. The lady of the house returned, saying, 'I could not get any rice.' The bhikkhu said, 'Lay-follower, right from the start I saw a sign that I would not get any alms today.' 'What was it, venerable sir?' 'I saw what seemed to be a snake—the sugarcane placed in the corner of the door. As I looked to strike it, I saw what seemed to be a stone—the lump of jaggery placed in a vessel. I saw its hood, made when it was struck by a clod of earth, which was like the slices of salt-fish placed in the basket; and its teeth, like the rice in the pot, as it wished to bite that clod. Then, as it grew angry, venomous saliva, like the ghee put in the jar, came from its mouth.' She thought, 'It is not possible to deceive this shaveling,' and she gave him the sugarcane, cooked rice, and offered him everything along with ghee, jaggery, and fish. Thus, speaking suggestively should be understood as sāmantajappa. Parikathā is speaking in a roundabout way in order to obtain something.

Nippesikatāniddese akkosanāti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanaṃ. Vambhanāti paribhavitvā kathanaṃ. Garahaṇāti assaddho appasannotiādinā nayena dosāropanā. Ukkhepanāti mā etaṃ ettha kathethāti vācāya ukkhipanaṃ. Sabbatobhāgena savatthukaṃ sahetukaṃ katvā ukkhepanā samukkhepanā. Atha vā adentaṃ disvā “aho dānapatī”ti evaṃ ukkhipanaṃ ukkhepanā. Mahādānapatīti evaṃ suṭṭhu ukkhepanā samukkhepanā. Khipanāti kiṃ imassa jīvitaṃ bījabhojinoti evaṃ uppaṇḍanā. Saṃkhipanāti kiṃ imaṃ adāyakoti bhaṇatha, yo niccakālaṃ sabbesampi natthīti vacanaṃ detīti suṭṭhutaraṃ uppaṇḍanā. Pāpanāti adāyakattassa avaṇṇassa vā pāpanaṃ. Sabbatobhāgena pāpanā sampāpanā. Avaṇṇahārikāti evaṃ me avaṇṇabhayāpi dassatīti gehato gehaṃ gāmato gāmaṃ janapadato janapadaṃ avaṇṇaharaṇaṃ. Parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatāti purato madhuraṃ bhaṇitvā parammukhe avaṇṇabhāsitā. Esā hi abhimukhaṃ oloketuṃ [M 1.0029] asakkontassa parammukhānaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ khādanamiva hoti, tasmā parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatāti vuttā. Ayaṃ vuccati nippesikatāti ayaṃ yasmā veḷupesikāya viya abbhaṅgaṃ parassa guṇaṃ nippeseti nipuñchati, yasmā vā gandhajātaṃ nipisitvā gandhamagganā viya paraguṇe nipisitvā vicuṇṇetvā esā lābhamagganā hoti, tasmā nippesikatāti vuccatīti.

In the exposition of nippesikatā (crushing): Akkosanā (reviling) is reviling with the ten grounds for reviling. Vambhanā (disparagement) is speaking contemptuously. Garahaṇā (blaming) is imputing faults in such ways as, 'He is faithless, not devout.' Ukkhepanā (dismissal) is dismissing with speech, saying, 'Do not speak of that here.' Samukkhepanā (thorough dismissal) is dismissing completely, with grounds and reason. Alternatively, seeing one who does not give and saying sarcastically, 'Oh, what an almsgiver!'—this is ukkhepanā (extolling). Saying, 'A great almsgiver!' is samukkhepanā (thorough extolling). Khipanā (belittling) is deriding thus: 'What is this one's living? He is a seed-eater!' Saṃkhipanā (utter belittling) is deriding even more strongly: 'Why do you call this one a non-giver? He is one who always gives the word "there is not" to everyone!' Pāpanā (imputing evil) is imputing the state of being a non-giver or of having a bad reputation. Sampāpanā is imputing evil completely. Avaṇṇahārikā (carrying dispraise) is carrying dispraise from house to house, from village to village, from country to country, thinking, 'He will give even out of fear of my dispraise.' Parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā (backbiting) is speaking sweetly to one's face but speaking dispraise behind one's back. For one who cannot look another in the face, this is like eating the flesh from their back when their back is turned; thus it is called 'backbiting.' This is called nippesikatā because it scrapes away and wipes out another's virtue as if scraping off ointment with a bamboo strip; or because, like one who seeks perfume by grinding fragrant substances, this is a seeking of gain by grinding and pulverizing another's virtues. Thus it is called nippesikatā.

Lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatāniddese nijigīsanatāti magganā. Ito laddhanti imamhā gehā laddhaṃ. Amutrāti amukamhi gehe. Eṭṭhīti icchanā. Gaveṭṭhīti magganā. Pariyeṭṭhīti punappunaṃ magganā. Ādito paṭṭhāya laddhaṃ laddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ tatra tatra kuladārakānaṃ datvā ante khīrayāguṃ labhitvā gatabhikkhuvatthu cettha kathetabbaṃ. Esanātiādīni eṭṭhiādīnameva vevacanāni, tasmā eṭṭhīti esanā. Gaveṭṭhīti gavesanā, pariyeṭṭhīti pariyesanā. Iccevamettha yojanā veditabbā. Ayaṃ kuhanādīnaṃ attho.

In the exposition of pursuing gain with gain: Nijigīsanatā (pursuit) is seeking. 'Gained from here' means gained from this house. 'There' means in such and such a house. Eṭṭhi is wishing. Gaveṭṭhi is seeking. Pariyeṭṭhi is seeking again and again. Here the story should be told of the bhikkhu who, starting from the beginning, gave the alms he had received here and there to the children of the families, and in the end, having received milk-rice, departed. This is the meaning of deceit and the other terms.

Idāni evamādīnañca pāpadhammānanti ettha ādisaddena “yathā vā paneke bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇā [V 1.0029] saddhādeyyāni bhojanāni bhuñjitvā te evarūpāya tiracchānavijjāya micchājīvena jīvikaṃ kappenti. Seyyathidaṃ, aṅgaṃ, nimittaṃ, uppātaṃ, supinaṃ, lakkhaṇaṃ, mūsikacchinnaṃ, aggihomaṃ, dabbihoma”nti (dī. ni. 1.21) ādinā nayena brahmajāle vuttānaṃ anekesaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Iti yvāyaṃ imesaṃ ājīvahetu paññattānaṃ channaṃ sikkhāpadānaṃ vītikkamavasena, imesañca “kuhanā lapanā nemittikatā nippesikatā lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā”ti evamādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ vasena pavatto micchājīvo, yā tasmā sabbappakārāpi micchājīvā virati, idaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho. Etaṃ āgamma jīvantīti ājīvo. Ko so, paccayapariyesanavāyāmo. Pārisuddhīti parisuddhatā. Ājīvassa pārisuddhi ājīvapārisuddhi.

Now, in the phrase 'and such other evil states,' the word 'etcetera' here should be understood to include the many evil states mentioned in the Brahmajāla Sutta, such as: 'Whereas some recluses and brahmins, having partaken of food given in faith, earn their living by wrong livelihood through such a low art as: prognostication from limbs, interpreting omens, interpreting portents, interpreting dreams, interpreting bodily marks, interpreting things gnawed by mice, fire offerings, spoon offerings,' and so on. Thus, whatever wrong livelihood arises from the transgression of these six training rules prescribed for the sake of livelihood, or from such evil states as 'scheming, talking, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain,' the abstinence from all such forms of wrong livelihood is the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhisīla). Herein, this is the meaning of the words: Livelihood (ājīvo) is that by which one lives—that is, the effort to seek requisites. Purity (pārisuddhi) is pureness. The purity of livelihood is ājīvapārisuddhi.

Paccayasannissitasīlaṃ

Virtue Dependent on Requisites

18. Yaṃ panetaṃ tadanantaraṃ paccayasannissitasīlaṃ vuttaṃ, tattha paṭisaṅkhā yonisoti upāyena pathena paṭisaṅkhāya ñatvā, paccavekkhitvāti attho[M 1.0030]. Ettha ca sītassa paṭighātāyātiādinā nayena vuttapaccavekkhaṇameva “yoniso paṭisaṅkhā”ti veditabbaṃ. Tattha cīvaranti antaravāsakādīsu yaṃkiñci. Paṭisevatīti paribhuñjati, nivāseti vā pārupati vā. Yāvadevāti payojanāvadhiparicchedaniyamavacanaṃ, ettakameva hi yogino cīvarapaṭisevane payojanaṃ yadidaṃ sītassa paṭighātāyātiādi, na ito bhiyyo. Sītassāti ajjhattadhātukkhobhavasena vā bahiddhāutupariṇāmanavasena vā uppannassa yassa kassaci sītassa. Paṭighātāyāti paṭihananatthaṃ. Yathā sarīre ābādhaṃ na uppādeti, evaṃ tassa vinodanatthaṃ. Sītabbhāhate hi sarīre vikkhittacitto yoniso padahituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā sītassa paṭighātāya cīvaraṃ paṭisevitabbanti bhagavā anuññāsi. Esa nayo sabbattha. Kevalañhettha uṇhassāti aggisantāpassa. Tassa vanadāhādīsu sambhavo veditabbo. Ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassānanti ettha pana ḍaṃsāti ḍaṃsanamakkhikā, andhamakkhikātipi vuccanti. Makasā makasā eva. Vātāti sarajaarajādibhedā. Ātapoti sūriyātapo. Sarīsapāti ye keci sarantā gacchanti dīghajātikā sappādayo, tesaṃ daṭṭhasamphasso ca phuṭṭhasamphasso cāti duvidho samphasso, sopi cīvaraṃ pārupitvā nisinnaṃ na bādhati, tasmā tādisesu ṭhānesu tesaṃ paṭighātatthāya paṭisevati. Yāvadevāti puna etassa vacanaṃ niyatapayojanāvadhiparicchedadassanatthaṃ[V 1.0030], hirikopīnapaṭicchādanañhi niyatapayojanaṃ, itarāni kadāci kadāci honti. Tattha hirikopīnanti taṃ taṃ sambādhaṭṭhānaṃ. Yasmiṃ yasmiñhi aṅge vivariyamāne hirī kuppati vinassati, taṃ taṃ hiriṃ kopanato hirikopīnanti vuccati. Tassa ca hirikopīnassa paṭicchādanatthanti hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthaṃ. Hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādanatthantipi pāṭho.

18. Now, as for what was said next about the virtue dependent on requisites, therein 'wisely reflecting' means having known and considered by means of a proper method and path; this is the meaning. Here, the reflection mentioned in the manner of 'for the warding off of cold' and so forth should be understood as 'wisely reflecting.' In this context, 'a robe' refers to any garment such as the inner robe and so on. 'One uses' means one makes use of, wears, or puts on. 'Only for' is a term defining the limit and boundary of the purpose, for this much alone is the purpose for a yogī in using a robe—namely, beginning with 'for the warding off of cold'—and no more. 'Of cold' refers to any cold that arises either due to the disturbance of internal elements or due to changes in external weather. 'For the warding off' means for the purpose of striking it down. It is for the purpose of dispelling it so that it does not cause affliction to the body. For when the body is afflicted by cold, the mind becomes distracted and one cannot strive with proper attention; therefore, the Blessed One allowed the use of a robe for the warding off of cold. This same method applies everywhere. Here, however, 'of heat' refers to the heat of a fire. Its occurrence should be understood in contexts like forest fires and so on. Regarding 'contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things'—here, 'gadflies' are biting flies, also called blind flies. 'Mosquitoes' are simply mosquitoes. 'Wind' includes various types such as those with and without dust. 'Sun' means the heat of the sun. 'Creeping things' refers to any long-bodied creatures like snakes and so on that move by slithering. Their contact is of two kinds: the contact of a bite and the contact of a touch. Such contact does not harm one who is seated wearing a robe; therefore, in such places, one uses it for the purpose of warding them off. The repetition of 'only for' is to show the definition of the limit of a fixed purpose, for the covering of the private parts is a fixed purpose, while the others occur only occasionally. Herein, 'that which provokes shame' refers to this or that private place. For when any such limb is exposed, shame is provoked and destroyed; thus, because it provokes shame, it is called 'that which provokes shame.' And 'for the covering of that which provokes shame' is 'hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthaṃ.' There is also the reading 'hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādanatthaṃ.'

Piṇḍapātanti yaṃkiñci āhāraṃ. Yo hi koci āhāro bhikkhuno piṇḍolyena patte patitattā piṇḍapātoti vuccati. Piṇḍānaṃ vā pāto piṇḍapāto, tattha tattha laddhānaṃ bhikkhānaṃ sannipāto samūhoti vuttaṃ hoti. Neva davāyāti na gāmadārakādayo viya davatthaṃ, kīḷānimittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Na madāyāti na muṭṭhikamallādayo viya madatthaṃ, balamadanimittaṃ porisamadanimittañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Na maṇḍanāyāti na antepurikavesiyādayo [M 1.0031] viya maṇḍanatthaṃ, aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ pīṇabhāvanimittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Na vibhūsanāyāti na naṭanaccakādayo viya vibhūsanatthaṃ, pasannacchavivaṇṇatānimittanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettha ca neva davāyāti etaṃ mohūpanissayappahānatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Na madāyāti etaṃ dosūpanissayappahānatthaṃ. Na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāyāti etaṃ rāgūpanissayappahānatthaṃ. Neva davāya na madāyāti cetaṃ attano saṃyojanuppattipaṭisedhanatthaṃ. Na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāyāti etaṃ parassapi saṃyojanuppattipaṭisedhanatthaṃ. Catūhipi cetehi ayoniso paṭipattiyā kāmasukhallikānuyogassa ca pahānaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

‘Almsfood’ means any food whatsoever. For any food, because it has fallen into a bhikkhu's bowl by way of alms-gathering, is called ‘almsfood.’ Or, it is a collection of lumps of food; this means it is said to be the collection, the gathering, of alms received here and there. ‘Not for play’ means not for the purpose of play, as with village boys and others; this is said to mean it is not for the sake of amusement. ‘Not for intoxication’ means not for the purpose of intoxication, as with boxers, wrestlers, and others; this is said to mean it is not for the sake of intoxication with strength and with manliness. ‘Not for adornment’ means not for the purpose of adornment, as with women of the inner palace, courtesans, and others; this is said to mean it is not for the sake of making the major and minor limbs plump. ‘Not for embellishment’ means not for the purpose of embellishment, as with actors, dancers, and others; this is said to mean it is not for the sake of a clear and radiant complexion. Herein, ‘not for play’ is said for the purpose of abandoning that which is a supporting condition for delusion. ‘Not for intoxication’ is said for the purpose of abandoning that which is a supporting condition for aversion. ‘Not for adornment, not for embellishment’ is said for the purpose of abandoning that which is a supporting condition for lust. Furthermore, ‘not for play, not for intoxication’ is said for the purpose of preventing the arising of one's own fetters. ‘Not for adornment, not for embellishment’ is said for the purpose of preventing the arising of others' fetters. It should be understood that by all four of these, the abandonment of improper practice and of indulgence in sensual pleasure is expressed.

Yāvadevāti vuttatthameva. Imassa kāyassāti etassa catumahābhūtikassa rūpakāyassa. Ṭhitiyāti pabandhaṭṭhitatthaṃ. Yāpanāyāti pavattiyā avicchedatthaṃ, cirakālaṭṭhitatthaṃ vā. Gharūpatthambhamiva hi jiṇṇagharasāmiko, akkhabbhañjanamiva ca sākaṭiko kāyassa ṭhitatthaṃ yāpanatthañcesa piṇḍapātaṃ paṭisevati, na davamadamaṇḍanavibhūsanatthaṃ. Apica ṭhitīti jīvitindriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāyāti ettāvatā etassa kāyassa jīvitindriyapavattāpanatthantipi vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Vihiṃsūparatiyāti vihiṃsā nāma jighacchā ābādhaṭṭhena. Tassā uparamatthampesa piṇḍapātaṃ paṭisevati, vaṇālepanamiva uṇhasītādīsu tappaṭikāraṃ viya ca. Brahmacariyānuggahāyāti sakalasāsanabrahmacariyassa ca maggabrahmacariyassa ca anuggahatthaṃ. Ayañhi piṇḍapātapaṭisevanapaccayā kāyabalaṃ nissāya sikkhattayānuyogavasena [V 1.0031] bhavakantāranittharaṇatthaṃ paṭipajjanto brahmacariyānuggahāya paṭisevati, kantāranittharaṇatthikā puttamaṃsaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.63) viya, nadīnittharaṇatthikā kullaṃ (ma. ni. 1.240) viya, samuddanittharaṇatthikā nāvamiva ca.

‘Only for’ has the meaning already stated. ‘Of this body’ means of this material body composed of the four great elements. ‘For its stability’ means for the purpose of its lasting in continuity. ‘For its maintenance’ means for the purpose of its continuing on without interruption, or for the purpose of its lasting for a long time. For just as the owner of a dilapidated house props it up, and as a cart-driver greases the axle, so one uses almsfood for the stability and maintenance of this body, not for play, intoxication, adornment, or embellishment. Moreover, ‘stability’ is a synonym for the life faculty. Therefore, by ‘for the stability and maintenance of this body,’ it should be understood that this is also said for the purpose of causing the life faculty of this body to continue. ‘For the cessation of affliction’: affliction is the name for hunger, in the sense of a disease. One partakes of almsfood for the purpose of subduing it, like applying an ointment to a wound, and like a remedy for heat, cold, and so on. ‘For the support of the holy life’ means for the support of both the holy life of the entire Dispensation and the holy life of the path. For this person, relying on the bodily strength conditioned by the partaking of almsfood, practices for the purpose of crossing the wilderness of existence by means of devotion to the threefold training, and thus partakes of almsfood for the support of the holy life—like those who wish to cross a wilderness eat their son's flesh, like those who wish to cross a river use a raft, and like those who wish to cross the ocean use a ship.

Itipurāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti etaṃ iminā piṇḍapātapaṭisevanena purāṇañca jighacchāvedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṃ aparimitabhojanapaccayaṃ āharahatthakaalaṃsāṭakatatravaṭṭakakākamāsakabhuttavamitakabrāhmaṇānaṃ aññataro viya na uppādessāmītipi paṭisevati, bhesajjamiva gilāno. Atha vā yā adhunā asappāyāparimitabhojanaṃ nissāya purāṇakammapaccayavasena uppajjanato purāṇavedanāti [M 1.0032] vuccati. Sappāyaparimitabhojanena tassā paccayaṃ vināsento taṃ purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi. Yā cāyaṃ adhunā kataṃ ayuttaparibhogakammūpacayaṃ nissāya āyatiṃ uppajjanato navavedanāti vuccati. Yuttaparibhogavasena tassā mūlaṃ anibbattento taṃ navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmīti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ettāvatā yuttaparibhogasaṅgaho attakilamathānuyogappahānaṃ dhammikasukhāpariccāgo ca dīpito hotīti veditabbo.

'Thus I shall dispel an old feeling and not arouse a new feeling.' By this partaking of almsfood, one partakes reflecting: 'I shall dispel the old feeling of hunger and shall not arouse a new feeling due to immoderate eating—like one of those brahmins who eats until his hand must be pulled away, until his lower garment is too tight, until he rolls about on the spot, until a crow could take a morsel from his mouth, or until he vomits'—just as a sick person takes medicine. Alternatively, what is called the 'old feeling' is that which arises now on account of unsuitable and immoderate food, with past kamma as its condition. By suitable and moderate food, destroying its cause, 'I shall dispel that old feeling.' And what is called the 'new feeling' is that which arises in the future on account of the accumulation of kamma from improper use now. By proper use, not bringing its root into being, 'I shall not arouse that new feeling.' In this way the meaning here should be understood. By this much, the inclusion of proper use, the abandoning of devotion to self-mortification, and the non-abandonment of righteous happiness are shown; this should be understood.

Yātrā ca me bhavissatīti parimitaparibhogena jīvitindriyupacchedakassa iriyāpathabhañjakassa vā parissayassa abhāvato cirakālagamanasaṅkhātā yātrā ca me bhavissati imassa paccayāyattavuttino kāyassātipi paṭisevati, yāpyarogī viya tappaccayaṃ. Anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cāti ayuttapariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogaparivajjanena anavajjatā, parimitaparibhogena phāsuvihāro. Asappāyāparimitaparibhogapaccayā aratitandīvijambhitā. Viññūgarahādidosābhāvena vā anavajjatā, sappāyaparimitabhojanapaccayā kāyabalasambhavena phāsuvihāro. Yāvadatthaudarāvadehakabhojanaparivajjanena vā seyyasukhapassasukhamiddhasukhānaṃ pahānato anavajjatā, catupañcālopamattaūnabhojanena catuiriyāpathayogyabhāvapaṭipādanato phāsuvihāro ca me bhavissatītipi paṭisevati. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

‘And my journey will proceed.’ Since, through moderate use, there is no danger of cutting short the life faculty or disrupting the postures, the journey of this body, which depends on requisites for its subsistence, will be able to proceed for a long time; thus he partakes, just as one with a chronic illness partakes of what is suitable for it. ‘And there will be blamelessness and a comfortable abiding.’ Blamelessness comes from avoiding improper seeking, accepting, and using; a comfortable abiding comes from moderate use. Or, since discontent, lethargy, and yawning arise from unsuitable and immoderate use, blamelessness comes from the absence of these and other faults that the wise would censure, while a comfortable abiding comes from the physical strength resulting from suitable and moderate eating. Or, by avoiding eating to fill the belly and thereby abandoning the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining on one's side, and the pleasure of torpor, there is blamelessness. By eating four or five mouthfuls less than one's fill and thereby establishing fitness for the four postures, ‘there will be a comfortable abiding for me.’ Reflecting thus, he partakes. For it has been said:

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

“When four or five mouthfuls are left uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a bhikkhu with a resolute mind.”

Ettāvatā [V 1.0032] ca payojanapariggaho majjhimā ca paṭipadā dīpitā hotīti veditabbā.

By this much, it should be understood that the grasping of the purpose and the Middle Path are shown.

Senāsananti senañca āsanañca. Yattha yattha hi seti vihāre vā aḍḍhayogādimhi vā, taṃ senaṃ. Yattha yattha āsati nisīdati, taṃ āsanaṃ. Taṃ ekato katvā senāsananti vuccati. Utuparissayavinodanapaṭisallānārāmatthanti parisahanaṭṭhena utuyeva utuparissayo. Utuparissayassa [M 1.0033] vinodanatthañca paṭisallānārāmatthañca. Yo sarīrābādhacittavikkhepakaro asappāyo utu senāsanapaṭisevanena vinodetabbo hoti, tassa vinodanatthaṃ ekībhāvasukhatthañcāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāmañca sītapaṭighātādināva utuparissayavinodanaṃ vuttameva. Yathā pana cīvarapaṭisevane hirikopīnapaṭicchādanaṃ niyatapayojanaṃ, itarāni kadāci kadāci bhavantīti vuttaṃ, evamidhāpi niyataṃ utuparissayavinodanaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā ayaṃ vuttappakāro utu utuyeva. Parissayo pana duvidho pākaṭaparissayo ca, paṭicchannaparissayo ca (mahāni. 5). Tattha pākaṭaparissayo sīhabyagghādayo. Paṭicchannaparissayo rāgadosādayo. Ye yattha apariguttiyā ca asappāyarūpadassanādinā ca ābādhaṃ na karonti, taṃ senāsanaṃ evaṃ jānitvā paccavekkhitvā paṭisevanto bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso senāsanaṃ utuparissayavinodanatthaṃ paṭisevatīti veditabbo.

'Dwelling place' means both a resting place and a seat. Wherever one lies down, whether in a monastery or in a half-gabled shelter and so forth, that is the resting place. Wherever one sits, that is the seat. Combining these two, it is called a dwelling place. 'For dispelling the dangers of the climate and for delighting in seclusion': the danger of the climate is the climate itself, in the sense of oppressing. It is for the purpose of dispelling the dangers of the climate and for the purpose of delighting in seclusion. Whatever unfavorable climate causes bodily affliction or mental distraction should be dispelled by using a dwelling place; this is said for the purpose of dispelling it and for the sake of the happiness of solitude. Indeed, the dispelling of the dangers of the climate through protection from cold and so forth has already been mentioned. Just as in the use of robes, the covering of the private parts out of modesty is the primary purpose, while other purposes occur only occasionally, so too here it should be understood that this is said with reference to the primary purpose of dispelling the dangers of the climate. Alternatively, this aforementioned climate is just the climate. Dangers, however, are of two kinds: manifest dangers and concealed dangers. Among them, manifest dangers are lions, tigers, and so forth; concealed dangers are lust, hatred, and so forth. A bhikkhu who partakes of a dwelling place, having known and reviewed it to be one where these dangers do not cause affliction, which would otherwise arise from lack of protection or from seeing unsuitable forms and so on, is to be understood as one who partakes of the dwelling place with wise reflection for the purpose of dispelling the climate and dangers.

Gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāranti ettha rogassa paṭiayanaṭṭhena paccayo, paccanīkagamanaṭṭhenāti attho. Yassa kassaci sappāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Bhisakkassa kammaṃ tena anuññātattāti bhesajjaṃ. Gilānapaccayova bhesajjaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ, yaṃkiñci gilānassa sappāyaṃ bhisakkakammaṃ telamadhuphāṇitādīti vuttaṃ hoti. Parikkhāroti pana “sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi suparikkhataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 7.67) ādīsu parivāro vuccati. “Ratho sīlaparikkhāro, jhānakkho cakkavīriyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.4) ādīsu alaṅkāro. “Ye ca kho ime pabbajitena jīvitaparikkhārā samudānetabbā”ti (ma. ni. 1.191-192) ādīsu sambhāro. Idha pana sambhāropi parivāropi vaṭṭati. Tañhi gilānapaccayabhesajjaṃ jīvitassa parivāropi hoti, jīvitanāsakābādhuppattiyā antaraṃ adatvā rakkhaṇato sambhāropi. Yathā ciraṃ pavattati, evamassa kāraṇabhāvato, tasmā parikkhāroti vuccati. Evaṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjañca taṃ parikkhāro cāti gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāro. Taṃ gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ. Gilānassa yaṃkiñci sappāyaṃ bhisakkānuññātaṃ telamadhuphāṇitādi [V 1.0033] jīvitaparikkhāranti vuttaṃ hoti. Uppannānanti [M 1.0034] jātānaṃ bhūtānaṃ nibbattānaṃ. Veyyābādhikānanti ettha byābādhoti dhātukkhobho, taṃsamuṭṭhānā ca kuṭṭhagaṇḍapīḷakādayo. Byābādhato uppannattā veyyābādhikā. Vedanānanti dukkhavedanā akusalavipākavedanā. Tāsaṃ veyyābādhikānaṃ vedanānaṃ. Abyābajjhaparamatāyāti niddukkhaparamatāya. Yāva taṃ dukkhaṃ sabbaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti tāvāti attho.

In the phrase 'requisite-medicine-and-provision for the sick' (gilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāra): here, 'requisite' (paccaya) is so called in the sense of counteracting illness, that is, in the sense of opposing its course. This is a term for whatever is suitable. 'Medicine' (bhesajja) is a physician's remedy, because it is permitted by him. A requisite for the sick is itself a medicine, hence 'requisite-medicine for the sick'; this means any suitable physician's remedy for the sick, such as oil, honey, and molasses. As for 'provision' (parikkhāra), in passages such as, 'It is well-furnished with the seven city provisions' (AN 7.67), it is called an 'accessory' (parivāra). In passages such as, 'The chariot with virtue as its equipment...' (SN 5.4), it means 'adornment' (alaṅkāra). In passages such as, 'These are the life-provisions that a renunciant should acquire' (MN 1.191–192), it means 'necessaries' (sambhāra). Here, however, both 'necessaries' and 'accessory' are applicable. For that requisite-medicine for the sick is an accessory to life, as it protects it by not allowing an opportunity for a life-destroying illness to arise; and it is also a necessary, as it is a cause for life's long continuance. Therefore, it is called a 'provision.' Thus, it is a requisite-medicine for the sick and it is a provision, hence 'requisite-medicine-and-provision for the sick.' This refers to a provision for life, such as oil, honey, and molasses, that is suitable for the sick and permitted by a physician. 'Having arisen' means having been born, having come to be, having been produced. In 'afflictive' (veyyābādhika): here, 'affliction' (byābādha) refers to a disturbance of the elements, and also to diseases arising from it, such as leprosy, boils, and abscesses. They are called 'afflictive' because they arise from affliction. 'Feelings' refers to painful feelings, feelings that are the result of unwholesome karma. 'Of those afflictive feelings.' 'For the supreme state of non-affliction' means for the supreme state of being without suffering. The meaning is: until all that suffering is abandoned.

Evamidaṃ saṅkhepato paṭisaṅkhā yoniso paccayaparibhogalakkhaṇaṃ paccayasannissitasīlaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vacanattho panettha – cīvarādayo hi yasmā te paṭicca nissāya paribhuñjamānā pāṇino ayanti pavattanti, tasmā paccayāti vuccanti. Te paccaye sannissitanti paccayasannissitaṃ.

Thus, in brief, this virtue dependent on requisites, which is characterized by the use of requisites with wise reflection, should be understood. Herein, the etymology is as follows: because living beings, by depending upon, relying on, and using them, proceed and are sustained, robes and so on are called 'requisites' (paccaya). That which is dependent on those requisites is 'dependent on requisites' (paccayasannissita).

Catupārisuddhisampādanavidhi

The Method of Accomplishing the Fourfold Purity

19. Evametasmiṃ catubbidhe sīle saddhāya pātimokkhasaṃvaro sampādetabbo. Saddhāsādhano hi so, sāvakavisayātītattā sikkhāpadapaññattiyā. Sikkhāpadapaññattiyācanapaṭikkhepo cettha nidassanaṃ. Tasmā yathā paññattaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ anavasesaṃ saddhāya samādiyitvā jīvitepi apekkhaṃ akarontena sādhukaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

19. In this fourfold virtue, the restraint of the Pātimokkha should be accomplished with faith. For it is accomplished through faith, since the establishment of the training precepts transcends the sphere of disciples. The rejection of a request for the establishment of a training precept is an example here. Therefore, having completely undertaken the training precept as prescribed with faith, one should accomplish it well, without any concern even for one's life. For this has been said:

“Kikīva aṇḍaṃ camarīva vāladhiṃ,

Piyaṃva puttaṃ nayanaṃva ekakaṃ;

Tatheva sīlaṃ anurakkhamānakā,

Supesalā hotha sadā sagāravā”ti.

“Like a blue jay her egg,

like a yak her tail,

like a mother her beloved child,

like a one-eyed person their single eye;

so too, while guarding virtue,

be ever devoted and respectful.”

Aparampi vuttaṃ – “evameva kho pahārāda yaṃ mayā sāvakānaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ mama sāvakā jīvitahetupi nātikkamantī”ti (a. ni. 8.19). Imasmiṃ ca panatthe aṭaviyaṃ corehi baddhatherānaṃ vatthūni veditabbāni.

Furthermore, it was said: “Just so, Pahārāda, whatever training precept I have established for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of life” (AN 8.19). And in this connection, the stories of the elders bound by thieves in the forest should be known.

Mahāvattaniaṭaviyaṃ kira theraṃ corā kāḷavallīhi bandhitvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Thero yathānipannova [V 1.0034] sattadivasāni vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anāgāmiphalaṃ pāpuṇitvā tattheva kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbatti.

It is said that in the Mahāvattani forest, thieves bound an elder with black creepers and made him lie down. The elder, just as he was lying, developed insight for seven days and attained the fruit of non-returning; he passed away right there and was reborn in the Brahma world.

Aparampi [M 1.0035] theraṃ tambapaṇṇidīpe pūtilatāya bandhitvā nipajjāpesuṃ. So vanadāhe āgacchante valliṃ acchinditvāva vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi. Dīghabhāṇakaabhayatthero pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ āgacchanto disvā therassa sarīraṃ jhāpetvā cetiyaṃ kārāpesi. Tasmā aññopi saddho kulaputto –

Furthermore, they bound another elder on the island of Tambapaṇṇi with a stinking creeper and made him lie down. When a forest fire approached, he, without cutting the creeper, established insight and, with the simultaneous cessation of defilements and life, attained Parinibbāna. The Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya, arriving with five hundred monks, saw the elder's body, had it cremated, and had a stupa built. Therefore, any other faithful clansman—

Pātimokkhaṃ visodhento, appeva jīvitaṃ jahe;

Paññattaṃ lokanāthena, na bhinde sīlasaṃvaraṃ.

While purifying the Pātimokkha, one should even give up one's life; established by the Lord of the World, one should not break the restraint of virtue.

Yathā ca pātimokkhasaṃvaro saddhāya, evaṃ satiyā indriyasaṃvaro sampādetabbo. Satisādhano hi so, satiyā adhiṭṭhitānaṃ indriyānaṃ abhijjhādīhi ananvāssavanīyato. Tasmā “varaṃ, bhikkhave, tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.235) ādinā nayena ādittapariyāyaṃ samanussaritvā rūpādīsu visayesu cakkhudvārādipavattassa viññāṇassa abhijjhādīhi anvāssavanīyaṃ nimittādiggāhaṃ asammuṭṭhāya satiyā nisedhentena esa sādhukaṃ sampādetabbo. Evaṃ asampādite hi etasmiṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlampi anaddhaniyaṃ hoti aciraṭṭhitikaṃ, asaṃvihitasākhāparivāramiva sassaṃ. Haññate cāyaṃ kilesacorehi, vivaṭadvāro viya gāmo parassa hārīhi. Cittañcassa rāgo samativijjhati, ducchannamagāraṃ vuṭṭhi viya. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

Just as the restraint of the Pātimokkha is accomplished through faith, so too must the restraint of the faculties be accomplished through mindfulness. For it is aided by mindfulness, since the faculties established in mindfulness cannot be assailed by covetousness and other defilements. Therefore, having recollected the Discourse on the All-Ablaze, beginning with the passage: “Better, monks, that the eye-faculty be seared with a red-hot iron spike, burning, blazing, and glowing, than to grasp at the signs and details in forms cognizable by the eye” (SN 35.235), one should accomplish this restraint well by using unlapsed mindfulness to prevent the grasping of signs and details in objects like forms, a grasping which allows covetousness and other defilements to assail the consciousness that arises at the eye-door and other sense doors. For if this is not properly achieved, even the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint is not long-lasting and is of short duration, like a crop whose branches and fences are not well-arranged. And one is assailed by the thieves of defilements, like a village with open gates by external plunderers. And lust pierces his mind, like rain penetrates a poorly roofed house. As it has been said:

“Rūpesu saddesu atho rasesu,

Gandhesu phassesu ca rakkha indriyaṃ;

Ete hi dvārā vivaṭā arakkhitā,

Hananti gāmaṃva parassa hārino”.

“Guard the senses regarding forms, sounds, and also tastes, smells, and touches. For these doors, being open and unguarded, destroy one as external plunderers destroy a village.”

“Yathā [V 1.0035] agāraṃ ducchannaṃ, vuṭṭhī samativijjhati;

Evaṃ abhāvitaṃ cittaṃ, rāgo samativijjhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 13);

“Just as a poorly thatched house is pierced by rain, so an undeveloped mind is pierced by lust.”

Sampādite pana tasmiṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlampi addhaniyaṃ hoti ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, susaṃvihitasākhāparivāramiva sassaṃ. Na haññate cāyaṃ kilesacorehi[M 1.0036], susaṃvutadvāro viya gāmo parassa hārīhi. Na cassa cittaṃ rāgo samativijjhati, succhannamagāraṃ vuṭṭhi viya. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

When this restraint is accomplished, however, the virtue of Pātimokkha-restraint becomes long-lasting and of long duration, like a crop whose fences are well-arranged. And one is not assailed by the thieves of defilements, like a village whose gates are well-closed against external plunderers. Nor does lust pierce his mind, like rain a well-roofed house. And this was said:

“Rūpesu saddesu atho rasesu,

Gandhesu phassesu ca rakkha indriyaṃ;

Ete hi dvārā pihitā susaṃvutā,

Na hanti gāmaṃva parassa hārino”.

“Guard the sense faculties in regard to forms, sounds, and also tastes, smells, and touches. For when these doors are closed and well-restrained, plunderers do not harm one, just as they cannot a village.”

“Yathā agāraṃ succhannaṃ, vuṭṭhī na samativijjhati;

Evaṃ subhāvitaṃ cittaṃ, rāgo na samativijjhatī”ti. (dha. pa. 14);

“As rain does not penetrate a well-roofed house, so lust does not penetrate a well-developed mind.”

Ayaṃ pana atiukkaṭṭhadesanā.

This, however, is a most excellent teaching.

Cittaṃ nāmetaṃ lahuparivattaṃ, tasmā uppannaṃ rāgaṃ asubhamanasikārena vinodetvā indriyasaṃvaro sampādetabbo, adhunāpabbajitena vaṅgīsattherena viya.

The mind, indeed, is quick to change; therefore, arisen passion should be dispelled by attention to the foul, and sense-restraint should be accomplished, just as it was by the newly ordained Elder Vaṅgīsa.

Therassa kira adhunāpabbajitassa piṇḍāya carato ekaṃ itthiṃ disvā rāgo uppajjati. Tato ānandattheraṃ āha –

It is said that for the newly ordained elder, while wandering for alms, lust arose upon seeing a certain woman. Then he said to the Elder Ānanda:

“Kāmarāgena ḍayhāmi, cittaṃ me pariḍayhati;

Sādhu nibbāpanaṃ brūhi, anukampāya gotamā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.212; theragā. 1232);

“I am burned by sensual lust, my mind is utterly burned. Good sir, tell me the way of extinguishing it; out of compassion, O Gotama.”

Thero [V 1.0036] āha –

The Elder said:

“Saññāya vipariyesā, cittaṃ te pariḍayhati;

Nimittaṃ parivajjehi, subhaṃ rāgūpasañhitaṃ;

Asubhāya cittaṃ bhāvehi, ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ. (saṃ. ni. 1.212; theragā. 1233-1234);

“Through a perversion of perception, your mind is burned. Avoid the sign of the beautiful that is connected with lust. Develop the mind on the foul, one-pointed and well-concentrated.”

“Saṅkhāre parato passa, dukkhato no ca attato;

Nibbāpehi mahārāgaṃ, mā ḍayhittho punappuna”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.212);

“See conditioned formations as other, as suffering, and not as self. Extinguish the great lust; do not be burned again and again.”

Thero rāgaṃ vinodetvā piṇḍāya cari. Apica indriyasaṃvarapūrakena bhikkhunā kuraṇḍakamahāleṇavāsinā cittaguttattherena viya corakamahāvihāravāsinā mahāmittattherena viya ca bhavitabbaṃ. Kuraṇḍakamahāleṇe kira sattannaṃ buddhānaṃ abhinikkhamanacittakammaṃ manoramaṃ ahosi, sambahulā bhikkhū senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantā cittakammaṃ disvā “manoramaṃ, bhante[M 1.0037], cittakamma”nti āhaṃsu. Thero āha “atirekasaṭṭhi me, āvuso, vassāni leṇe vasantassa cittakammaṃ atthītipi na jānāmi, ajja dāni cakkhumante nissāya ñāta”nti. Therena kira ettakaṃ addhānaṃ vasantena cakkhuṃ ummīletvā leṇaṃ na ullokitapubbaṃ. Leṇadvāre cassa mahānāgarukkhopi ahosi. Sopi therena uddhaṃ na ullokitapubbo. Anusaṃvaccharaṃ bhūmiyaṃ kesaranipātaṃ disvāvassa pupphitabhāvaṃ jānāti.

The Elder, having dispelled passion, went for alms. Moreover, a monk fulfilling the restraint of the senses should be like the Elder Cittagutta, who dwelt in the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave, and like the Elder Mahāmitta, who dwelt in the Coraka Great Monastery. It is said that in the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave there was a delightful mural painting depicting the great renunciation of the seven Buddhas. Many monks, wandering on a tour of the dwellings, saw the painting and said, 'Venerable sir, the painting is delightful!' The Elder said, 'Friends, for over sixty years that I have lived in this cave, I did not even know that this painting existed. Only today, relying on those with eyes, have I become aware of it.' It is said that for that entire length of time he dwelt there, the Elder had never opened his eyes and looked up at the cave. A great nāga tree also stood at the cave's entrance, and even that the Elder had never looked up at. Each year, he knew of its flowering only by seeing the fallen pollen on the ground.

Rājā therassa guṇasampattiṃ sutvā vanditukāmo tikkhattuṃ pesetvā anāgacchante there tasmiṃ gāme taruṇaputtānaṃ itthīnaṃ thane bandhāpetvā lañjāpesi “tāva dārakā thaññaṃ mā labhiṃsu, yāva thero na āgacchatī”ti. Thero dārakānaṃ anukampāya mahāgāmaṃ agamāsi. Rājā sutvā “gacchatha bhaṇe, theraṃ pavesetha sīlāni gaṇhissāmī”ti antepuraṃ abhiharāpetvā vanditvā bhojetvā “ajja, bhante, okāso natthi, sve sīlāni gaṇhissāmīti therassa pattaṃ gahetvā thokaṃ anugantvā deviyā saddhiṃ vanditvā nivatti. Thero rājā vā vandatu devī vā, “sukhī hotu, mahārājā”ti vadati. Evaṃ sattadivasā gatā. Bhikkhū āhaṃsu “kiṃ, bhante, tumhe raññepi [V 1.0037] vandamāne deviyāpi vandamānāya “sukhī hotu, mahārāja”icceva vadathāti. Thero “nāhaṃ, āvuso, rājāti vā devīti vā vavatthānaṃ karomī”ti vatvā sattāhātikkamena “therassa idha vāso dukkho”ti raññā vissajjito kuraṇḍakamahāleṇaṃ gantvā rattibhāge caṅkamaṃ ārūhi. Nāgarukkhe adhivatthā devatā daṇḍadīpikaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ atiparisuddhaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi. Thero “kiṃ nu me ajja kammaṭṭhānaṃ ativiya pakāsatī”ti attamano majjhimayāmasamanantaraṃ sakalaṃ pabbataṃ unnādayanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tasmā aññopi attatthakāmo kulaputto –

Hearing of the Elder's virtues, the king, wishing to pay homage, sent for him three times. When the Elder did not come, the king had the breasts of the young mothers in that village bound and sealed, saying, 'Let the infants not receive milk until the Elder comes.' Out of compassion for the infants, the Elder went to the great village. Hearing this, the king said, 'Go, sirs, bring the Elder inside; I will undertake the precepts.' He had the Elder brought to the inner palace, paid homage, and offered him a meal, saying, 'Today, venerable sir, there is no opportunity; tomorrow I will undertake the precepts.' Taking the Elder's bowl and following him a short distance, the king, together with the queen, paid homage and turned back. Whether the king or the queen paid homage, the Elder would say, 'May the great king be happy.' Thus seven days passed. The monks asked, 'Venerable sir, why is it that when the king pays homage, and also when the queen pays homage, you only say, "May the great king be happy"?' The Elder replied, 'Friends, I make no distinction of 'king' or 'queen'.' After seven days had passed, the king, thinking, 'The Elder's stay here is difficult,' dismissed him. The Elder went to Kuraṇḍaka Mahāleṇa and, during the night, ascended his meditation walk. A deity dwelling in a nāga tree stood holding a torch. Then his meditation subject became exceedingly pure and clear. The Elder, delighted, thought, 'Why is my meditation subject so exceptionally clear today?' Just after the middle watch, causing the entire mountain to resound, he attained arahantship. Therefore, any other clansman who seeks his own welfare—

Makkaṭova araññamhi, vane bhantamigo viya;

Bālo viya ca utrasto, na bhave lolalocano.

Like a monkey in the wilderness, like a deer roaming in the woods, and like a frightened child, one should not be of restless eyes.

Adho khipeyya cakkhūni, yugamattadaso siyā;

Vanamakkaṭalolassa, na cittassa vasaṃ vaje.

One should cast one's eyes downwards, looking ahead a yoke's length. One should not fall under the sway of a mind that is restless like a forest monkey.

Mahāmittattherassāpi [M 1.0038] mātu visagaṇḍakarogo uppajji, dhītāpissā bhikkhunīsu pabbajitā hoti. Sā taṃ āha – “gaccha ayye, bhātu santikaṃ gantvā mama aphāsukabhāvaṃ ārocetvā bhesajjamāharā”ti. Sā gantvā ārocesi. Thero āha – “nāhaṃ mūlabhesajjādīni saṃharitvā bhesajjaṃ pacituṃ jānāmi, apica te bhesajjaṃ ācikkhissaṃ – “ahaṃ yato pabbajito, tato paṭṭhāya na mayā lobhasahagatena cittena indriyāni bhinditvā visabhāgarūpaṃ olokitapubbaṃ, iminā saccavacanena mātuyā me phāsu hotu, gaccha idaṃ vatvā upāsikāya sarīraṃ parimajjā”ti. Sā gantvā imamatthaṃ ārocetvā tathā akāsi. Upāsikāya taṃkhaṇaṃyeva gaṇḍo pheṇapiṇḍo viya vilīyitvā antaradhāyi, sā uṭṭhahitvā “sace sammāsambuddho dhareyya, kasmā mama puttasadisassa bhikkhuno jālavicitrena hatthena sīsaṃ na parāmaseyyā”ti attamanavācaṃ nicchāresi. Tasmā –

A poisonous boil arose on the mother of the Elder Mahāmitta; her daughter had also gone forth among the bhikkhunīs. The mother said to her, 'Go, venerable one, go to your brother, inform him of my discomfort, and bring back medicine.' She went and informed him. The Elder said, 'I do not know how to gather roots and herbs to prepare medicine, but I will tell you a remedy: "Since I went forth, never have I, with a mind accompanied by greed, broken the restraint of my senses and looked upon a form of the opposite sex. By this statement of truth, may my mother be at ease. Go, say this and stroke the laywoman’s body."' She went, delivered the message, and did as instructed. Instantly, the laywoman’s boil dissolved like a lump of foam and disappeared. Rising up, she joyfully exclaimed, 'If the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One were present, why would he not stroke the head of a monk like my son with his hand, adorned with its net-like markings?' Therefore—

Kulaputtamāni aññopi, pabbajitvāna sāsane;

Mittattherova tiṭṭheyya, vare indriyasaṃvare.

Let another son of good family, having gone forth in the Dispensation, stand like the Elder Mitta in the supreme restraint of the senses.

Yathā [V 1.0038] pana indriyasaṃvaro satiyā, tathā vīriyena ājīvapārisuddhi sampādetabbā. Vīriyasādhanā hi sā, sammāraddhavīriyassa micchājīvappahānasambhavato. Tasmā anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ pahāya vīriyena piṇḍapātacariyādīhi sammā esanāhi esā sampādetabbā parisuddhuppādeyeva paccaye paṭisevamānena aparisuddhuppāde āsīvise viya parivajjayatā. Tattha apariggahitadhutaṅgassa saṅghato, gaṇato, dhammadesanādīhi cassa guṇehi pasannānaṃ gihīnaṃ santikā uppannā paccayā parisuddhuppādā nāma. Piṇḍapātacariyādīhi pana atiparisuddhuppādāyeva. Pariggahitadhutaṅgassa piṇḍapātacariyādīhi dhutaguṇe cassa pasannānaṃ santikā dhutaṅganiyamānulomena uppannā parisuddhuppādā nāma. Ekabyādhivūpasamatthañcassa pūtihariṭakīcatumadhuresu uppannesu “catumadhuraṃ aññepi sabrahmacārino paribhuñjissantī”ti cintetvā hariṭakīkhaṇḍameva paribhuñjamānassa dhutaṅgasamādānaṃ patirūpaṃ hoti. Esa hi “uttamaariyavaṃsiko bhikkhū”ti vuccati. Ye panete cīvarādayo paccayā, tesu yassa kassaci bhikkhuno ājīvaṃ parisodhentassa [M 1.0039] cīvare ca piṇḍapāte ca nimittobhāsaparikathāviññattiyo na vaṭṭanti. Senāsane pana apariggahitadhutaṅgassa nimittobhāsaparikathā vaṭṭanti. Tattha nimittaṃ nāma senāsanatthaṃ bhūmiparikammādīni karontassa “kiṃ, bhante, kariyati, ko kārāpetī”ti gihīhi vutte “na koci”ti paṭivacanaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ nimittakammaṃ. Obhāso nāma “upāsakā tumhe kuhiṃ vasathā”ti. Pāsāde, bhanteti. “Bhikkhūnaṃ pana upāsakā pāsādo na vaṭṭatī”ti vacanaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi evarūpaṃ obhāsakammaṃ. Parikathā nāma “bhikkhusaṅghassa senāsanaṃ sambādha”nti vacanaṃ, yā vā panaññāpi evarūpā pariyāyakathā. Bhesajje sabbampi vaṭṭati. Tathā uppannaṃ pana bhesajjaṃ roge vūpasante paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, na vaṭṭatīti.

Just as restraint of the senses is to be accomplished by mindfulness, so too should purity of livelihood be accomplished by energy. For it is achieved by energy, since abandoning wrong livelihood is possible for one whose energy is rightly initiated. Therefore, having abandoned improper and unsuitable seeking, this purity should be accomplished with energy through proper means of seeking, such as going on the alms-round, partaking only of purely arisen requisites while avoiding impurely arisen ones as if they were venomous snakes. In this regard, for one who has not undertaken the ascetic practices, requisites that have arisen from the Sangha, from a group, or from laypeople who are devoted on account of his virtues—such as his teaching of the Dhamma—are called 'purely arisen.' But requisites obtained by means of the alms-round and so on are 'exceedingly purely arisen.' For one who has undertaken the ascetic practices, requisites arising by means of the alms-round and so on, or from those devoted to his ascetic virtues in accordance with the rules of the ascetic practices, are called 'purely arisen.' And when, for the purpose of curing a certain illness, fermented myrobalan and the four sweets have been received, it is suitable for his undertaking of the ascetic practice to consume only a piece of myrobalan, thinking, 'Other fellow monks will also partake of the four sweets.' Such a one is called 'a monk of the supreme noble lineage.' As for these requisites, such as robes and so on, for any monk purifying his livelihood, signs, allusions, roundabout talk, and direct requests concerning robes and alms-food are not permissible. However, concerning lodging, for one who has not undertaken the ascetic practices, signs, allusions, and roundabout talk are permissible. Here, a 'sign' means that when a monk is preparing the ground for a lodging and is asked by laypeople, 'What is being done, venerable sir? Who is having it done?', he replies, 'No one'; or any other such act of making a sign. An 'allusion' means saying, 'Lay devotees, where do you live?'—'In a mansion, venerable sir.'—'But, lay devotees, a mansion is not allowable for monks'; or any other such act of making an allusion. 'Roundabout talk' means saying, 'The Sangha’s lodging is crowded,' or any other such indirect speech. Regarding medicine, all of these are permissible. However, as for medicine thus obtained, when the illness has subsided, is it permissible to use it, or not?

Tattha vinayadharā “bhagavatā dvāraṃ dinnaṃ, tasmā vaṭṭatī”ti vadanti. Suttantikā pana “kiñcāpi āpatti na hoti, ājīvaṃ pana kopeti, tasmā na vaṭṭati”cceva vadanti.

Therein, the Vinaya masters say, 'The Blessed One has given an opening; therefore it is allowable.' But the Sutta masters say, 'Even though there is no offense, it impairs one's livelihood; therefore it is not allowable.'

Yo pana bhagavatā anuññātāpi nimittobhāsaparikathāviññattiyo akaronto appicchatādiguṇeyeva nissāya jīvitakkhayepi paccupaṭṭhite aññatreva obhāsādīhi uppannapaccaye paṭisevati, esa “paramasallekhavuttī”ti vuccati, seyyathāpi thero sāriputto.

But one who, though they are permitted by the Blessed One, does not engage in signs, allusions, roundabout talk, or direct requests, but lives relying solely on qualities such as having few wishes, and, even when the destruction of life is imminent, partakes only of requisites that have arisen apart from such means—this one is called 'one of the highest austere conduct,' like the Elder Sāriputta.

So kirāyasmā ekasmiṃ samaye pavivekaṃ brūhayamāno mahāmoggallānattherena saddhiṃ aññatarasmiṃ [V 1.0039] araññe viharati, athassa ekasmiṃ divase udaravātābādho uppajjitvā atidukkhaṃ janesi. Mahāmoggallānatthero sāyanhasamaye tassāyasmato upaṭṭhānaṃ gato theraṃ nipannaṃ disvā taṃ pavattiṃ pucchitvā “pubbe te, āvuso, kena phāsu hotī”ti pucchi. Thero āha, “gihikāle me, āvuso, mātā sappimadhusakkarādīhi yojetvā asambhinnakhīrapāyāsaṃ adāsi, tena me phāsu ahosī”ti. Sopi āyasmā “hotu, āvuso, sace mayhaṃ vā tuyhaṃ vā puññaṃ atthi, appeva nāma sve labhissāmā”ti āha.

It is said that the Venerable One, at one time, while cultivating seclusion, was dwelling in a certain forest with the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Then, one day, a stomach ailment arose in him, causing great pain. In the evening, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna went to attend to that Venerable One and, seeing him lying down, inquired about his condition. He asked, 'Friend, what used to bring you comfort before?' The Elder replied, 'In my lay life, friend, my mother gave me thick milk-rice mixed with ghee, honey, sugar, and so on. That brought me comfort.' That Venerable One said, 'So be it, friend. If either I or you has any merit, perhaps we shall obtain it tomorrow.'

Imaṃ pana nesaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā sutvā “sve ayyassa pāyāsaṃ uppādessāmī”ti tāvadeva therassa upaṭṭhākakulaṃ [M 1.0040] gantvā jeṭṭhaputtassa sarīraṃ āvisitvā pīḷaṃ janesi. Athassa tikicchānimittaṃ sannipatite ñātake āha – “sace sve therassa evarūpaṃ nāma pāyāsaṃ paṭiyādetha, taṃ muñcissāmī”ti. Te “tayā avuttepi mayaṃ therānaṃ nibaddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ demā”ti vatvā dutiyadivase tathārūpaṃ pāyāsaṃ paṭiyādiyiṃsu.

Now, a deity dwelling in a tree at the edge of the walking path heard their conversation and thought, 'Tomorrow, I will provide the Elder with milk-rice.' At that very moment, she went to the household that attended upon the Elder, possessed the eldest son, and caused him distress. When his relatives gathered to determine a cure, she said, 'If you prepare such-and-such milk-rice for the Elder tomorrow, I will release him.' They replied, 'Even without your telling us, we regularly give alms-food to the Elders.' The next day, they prepared milk-rice of that kind.

Mahāmoggallānatthero pātova āgantvā “āvuso, yāva ahaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā āgacchāmi, tāva idheva hohī”ti vatvā gāmaṃ pāvisi.
