Te manussā paccuggantvā therassa pattaṃ gahetvā vuttappakārassa pāyāsassa pūretvā adaṃsu. Thero gamanākāraṃ dassesi. Te “bhuñjatha – bhante, tumhe, aparampi dassāmā”ti theraṃ bhojetvā puna pattapūraṃ adaṃsu. Thero gantvā “handāvuso sāriputta, paribhuñjā”ti upanāmesi. Theropi taṃ disvā “atimanāpo pāyāso, kathaṃ nu kho uppanno”ti cintento tassa uppattimūlaṃ disvā āha – “āvuso moggallāna, aparibhogāraho piṇḍapāto”ti. Sopāyasmā “mādisena nāma ābhataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ na paribhuñjatī”ti cittampi anuppādetvā ekavacaneneva pattaṃ mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā ekamante nikujjesi. Pāyāsassa saha bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhānā therassa ābādho antaradhāyi, tato paṭṭhāya pañcacattālīsa vassāni na puna uppajji. Tato mahāmoggallānaṃ āha – “āvuso, vacīviññattiṃ nissāya uppanno pāyāso antesu nikkhamitvā bhūmiyaṃ carantesupi paribhuñjituṃ ayuttarūpo”ti. Imañca udānaṃ udānesi –

The Elder Mahāmoggallāna came in the morning and said, 'Friend, wait here until I return from my alms round,' then entered the village. The people went out to meet him, took his bowl, filled it with the prepared milk-rice, and offered it. The Elder indicated his intention to leave. They said, 'Venerable sir, eat! We will give more.' After feeding the Elder, they filled his bowl again. The Elder returned and offered it, saying, 'Come, friend Sāriputta, partake of this.' Seeing it, the Elder Sāriputta thought, 'This milk-rice is most delightful. How did it come about?' Discerning its origin, he said, 'Friend Moggallāna, this almsfood is unfit for consumption.' The Venerable Moggallāna, without giving rise to the thought, 'He does not partake of almsfood brought by one such as me,' upon that single utterance took the bowl by its rim and overturned it in a secluded spot. As the milk-rice touched the ground, the Elder’s ailment vanished, and it never arose again for forty-five years thereafter. Then, he said to Mahāmoggallāna, 'Friend, this milk-rice, arisen through verbal intimation, is unsuitable to be consumed even by intestinal worms that, having come out, crawl on the ground.' And he uttered this inspired utterance:

“Vacīviññattivipphārā, uppannaṃ madhupāyasaṃ;

Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ, sājīvo garahito mama.

“This sweet milk-rice, arisen from the diffusion of verbal intimation; if I were to eat it, my livelihood would be censured.

“Yadipi [V 1.0040] me antaguṇaṃ, nikkhamitvā bahi care;

Neva bhindeyyaṃ ājīvaṃ, cajamānopi jīvitaṃ.

“Even if my entrails were to emerge and crawl outside, I would not break my livelihood, even while giving up my life.”

“Ārādhemi sakaṃ cittaṃ, vivajjemi anesanaṃ;

Nāhaṃ buddhappaṭikuṭṭhaṃ, kāhāmi ca anesana”nti.

“I satisfy my own mind, I avoid improper seeking; I will not do what is censured by the Buddha, nor engage in improper seeking.”

Ciragumbavāsikaambakhādakamahātissattheravatthupi cettha kathetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi.

Here, the story of the Elder Mahātissa, the mango-eater who dwelt in the long thicket, should also be told. Thus, in every way.

“Anesanāya [M 1.0041] cittampi, ajanetvā vicakkhaṇo;

Ājīvaṃ parisodheyya, saddhāpabbajito yatī”ti.

“Without generating even a thought for improper seeking, the discerning one, a striver who has gone forth in faith, should purify his livelihood.”

Yathā ca vīriyena ājīvapārisuddhi, tathā paccayasannissitasīlaṃ paññāya sampādetabbaṃ. Paññāsādhanaṃ hi taṃ, paññavato paccayesu ādīnavānisaṃsadassanasamatthabhāvato. Tasmā pahāya paccayagedhaṃ dhammena samena uppanne paccaye yathāvuttena vidhinā paññāya paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjantena sampādetabbaṃ.

Just as purity of livelihood is to be accomplished through energy, so too should virtue dependent on the requisites be accomplished by wisdom. For that is achieved by wisdom, since the wise are capable of seeing the dangers and benefits in requisites. Therefore, abandoning greed for requisites, one should accomplish it by wisely reflecting upon and partaking of the requisites that have arisen lawfully and equitably by the stated method.

Tattha duvidhaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ paccayānaṃ paṭilābhakāle, paribhogakāle ca. Paṭilābhakālepi hi dhātuvasena vā paṭikūlavasena vā paccavekkhitvā ṭhapitāni cīvarādīni tato uttari paribhuñjantassa anavajjova paribhogo, paribhogakālepi. Tatrāyaṃ sanniṭṭhānakaro vinicchayo –

Here, reflection on requisites is twofold: at the time of obtaining them and at the time of using them. For if robes and other requisites have been set aside after reflection on them in terms of their elements or repulsiveness at the time of obtaining, their subsequent use is blameless; so too is their use when reflection occurs at the time of consumption. In this regard, the following is the definitive determination:

Cattāro hi paribhogā theyyaparibhogo, iṇaparibhogo, dāyajjaparibhogo, sāmiparibhogoti. Tatra saṅghamajjhepi nisīditvā paribhuñjantassa dussīlassa paribhogo theyyaparibhogo nāma. Sīlavato apaccavekkhitvā paribhogo iṇaparibhogo nāma. Tasmā cīvaraṃ paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ, piṇḍapāto ālope ālope, tathā asakkontena purebhattapacchābhattapurimayāmamajjhimayāmapacchimayāmesu. Sacassa apaccavekkhatova aruṇaṃ uggacchati, iṇaparibhogaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhati. Senāsanampi paribhoge paribhoge paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Bhesajjassa paṭiggahaṇepi paribhogepi satipaccayatāva vaṭṭati. Evaṃ santepi paṭiggahaṇe satiṃ katvā [V 1.0041] paribhoge akarontasseva āpatti, paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpatti.

There are four kinds of use: theft-use, debt-use, inheritance-use, and ownership-use. Among these, the use by an immoral person who consumes requisites even while seated in the midst of the Sangha is called theft-use. The use by a virtuous person without reflection is called debt-use. Therefore, robes should be reflected upon at each use, almsfood at each mouthful. For one unable to do so, reflection should occur before meals, after meals, or during the first, middle, or last watches of the night. If dawn breaks while one is still failing to reflect, one remains in the category of debt-use. Lodgings too should be reflected upon at each use. For medicine, it is proper that mindfulness be the condition for both receiving and using. Even so, if one has been mindful at reception but does not reflect when using, there is an offense. But if one is not mindful at reception yet reflects when using, there is no offense.

Catubbidhā hi suddhi desanāsuddhi, saṃvarasuddhi, pariyeṭṭhisuddhi, paccavekkhaṇasuddhīti. Tattha desanāsuddhi nāma pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Tañhi desanāya sujjhanato desanāsuddhīti vuccati. Saṃvarasuddhi nāma indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ. Tañhi “na puna evaṃ karissāmī”ti cittādhiṭṭhānasaṃvareneva sujjhanato saṃvarasuddhīti vuccati. Pariyeṭṭhisuddhi nāma ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Tañhi anesanaṃ pahāya dhammena samena paccaye uppādentassa pariyesanāya suddhattā pariyeṭṭhisuddhīti [M 1.0042] vuccati. Paccavekkhaṇasuddhi nāma paccayasannissitasīlaṃ. Tañhi vuttappakārena paccavekkhaṇena sujjhanato paccavekkhaṇasuddhīti vuccati. Tena vuttaṃ “paṭiggahaṇe pana satiṃ akatvā paribhoge karontassa anāpattī”ti.

Purity is fourfold: purity of declaration, purity of restraint, purity of seeking, and purity of reflection. Herein, purity of declaration is the virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint. It is called purity of declaration because it is purified by declaration. Purity of restraint is the virtue of sense restraint. It is called purity of restraint because it is purified by restraint with the mental resolution, 'I will not do this again.' Purity of seeking is the virtue of purity of livelihood. It is called purity of seeking because it is purified by the search of one who abandons improper seeking and acquires requisites righteously and equitably. Purity of reflection is the virtue dependent on requisites. It is called purity of reflection because it is purified by reflection in the manner described. Hence it is said: 'But for one who has not been mindful at reception but reflects when using, there is no offense.'

Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ paccayaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo nāma. Te hi bhagavato puttā, tasmā pitusantakānaṃ paccayānaṃ dāyādā hutvā te paccaye paribhuñjanti. Kiṃpanete bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjanti, udāhu gihīnaṃ paccaye paribhuñjantīti. Gihīhi dinnāpi bhagavatā anuññātattā bhagavato santakā honti, tasmā bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjantīti veditabbā. Dhammadāyādasuttañcettha sādhakaṃ.

For the seven trainees, the use of requisites is called inheritance-use. For they are the Blessed One's children; therefore, as heirs to their father's possessions, they use these requisites. But do they use the Blessed One's requisites, or the requisites of laypeople? Even though given by laypeople, since they are permitted by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that they use the Blessed One's requisites. The Dhammadāyāda Sutta is evidence here.

Khīṇāsavānaṃ paribhogo sāmiparibhogo nāma. Te hi taṇhāya dāsabyaṃ atītattā sāmino hutvā paribhuñjanti.

For those whose taints are destroyed, use is called ownership-use. Since they have transcended the bondage of craving, they use things as owners.

Imesu paribhogesu sāmiparibhogo ca dāyajjaparibhogo ca sabbesaṃ vaṭṭati. Iṇaparibhogo na vaṭṭati. Theyyaparibhoge kathāyeva natthi. Yo panāyaṃ sīlavato paccavekkhitaparibhogo, so iṇaparibhogassa paccanīkattā āṇaṇyaparibhogo vā hoti, dāyajjaparibhogeyeva vā saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Sīlavāpi hi imāya sikkhāya samannāgatattā sekkhotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Imesu pana paribhogesu yasmā sāmiparibhogo aggo, tasmā taṃ patthayamānena bhikkhunā vuttappakārāya paccavekkhaṇāya paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjantena paccayasannissitasīlaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Evaṃ karonto hi kiccakārī hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Among these kinds of use, use as an owner and use as an heir are suitable for all. Use as a debtor is not suitable. Use as a thief is not even worth mentioning. As for this use with reflection by a virtuous one, being the opposite of use as a debtor, it is either use free from debt or is included under use as an heir. For even a virtuous one, being endowed with this training, is counted as a learner. Among these kinds of use, since use as an owner is the highest, a bhikkhu aspiring to it should accomplish the virtue dependent on requisites by using them after reflecting in the prescribed manner. By doing so, he becomes one who does what ought to be done. And it has been said:

“Piṇḍaṃ [V 1.0042] vihāraṃ sayanāsanañca,

Āpañca saṅghāṭirajūpavāhanaṃ;

Sutvāna dhammaṃ sugatena desitaṃ,

Saṅkhāya seve varapaññasāvako.

“Almsfood, dwelling, bed and seat, and water and the dust-warding outer robe; having heard the Dhamma taught by the Well-Gone One, the disciple of supreme wisdom uses them with reflection.

“Tasmā [M 1.0043] hi piṇḍe sayanāsane ca,

Āpe ca saṅghāṭirajūpavāhane;

Etesu dhammesu anūpalitto,

Bhikkhu yathā pokkhare vāribindu. (su. ni. 393-394);

“Therefore, in almsfood, bed and seat, in water and the dust-warding outer robe, a bhikkhu is unstained by these things, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.”

“Kālena laddhā parato anuggahā,

Khajjesu bhojjesu ca sāyanesu ca;

Mattaṃ sa jaññā satataṃ upaṭṭhito,

Vaṇassa ālepanarūhane yathā.

“Having received in due season helpful support from others, with hard foods, soft foods, and savories, one should know the measure, with mindfulness ever established, as with anointing a wound for its healing.

“Kantāre puttamaṃsaṃva, akkhassabbhañjanaṃ yathā;

Evaṃ āhāre āhāraṃ, yāpanatthamamucchito”ti.

“As with one’s own child’s flesh in the wilderness, or as with greasing an axle, so should one take food, uninfatuated, for mere sustenance.”

Imassa ca paccayasannissitasīlassa paripūrakāritāya bhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhitasāmaṇerassa vatthu kathetabbaṃ. So hi sammā paccavekkhitvā paribhuñji. Yathāha –

And to illustrate the complete fulfillment of this virtue dependent on requisites, the story of the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew, should be told. For he used things with proper reflection. As he said:

“Upajjhāyo maṃ bhuñjamānaṃ, sālikūraṃ sunibbutaṃ;

Mā heva tvaṃ sāmaṇera, jivhaṃ jhāpesi asaññato.

“While I was eating cooled, fine rice, my preceptor said to me, ‘Novice, do not burn your tongue through being unrestrained.’

“Upajjhāyassa vaco sutvā, saṃvegamalabhiṃ tadā;

Ekāsane nisīditvā, arahattaṃ apāpuṇiṃ.

“Having heard my preceptor’s words, I then gained a sense of spiritual urgency. Sitting in that one seat, I attained Arahantship.

“Sohaṃ [V 1.0043] paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, cando pannaraso yathā;

Sabbāsavaparikkhīṇo, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti.

“I am now of fulfilled resolve, like the moon on the fifteenth day. With all taints extinguished, there is now no further becoming.”

“Tasmā aññopi dukkhassa, patthayanto parikkhayaṃ;

Yoniso paccavekkhitvā, paṭisevetha paccaye”ti.

“Therefore, another, also desiring the destruction of suffering, should make use of the requisites after having wisely reflected.”

Evaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlādivasena catubbidhaṃ.

Thus, it is fourfold, by way of the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint and so on.

Paṭhamasīlapañcakaṃ

The First Pentad of Virtue

20. Pañcavidhakoṭṭhāsassa paṭhamapañcake anupasampannasīlādivasena attho veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

20. In the first pentad of the fivefold division, the meaning should be understood by way of the virtue of the unordained, and so on. For this has been said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Katamaṃ [M 1.0044] pariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ? Anupasampannānaṃ pariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ, idaṃ pariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Katamaṃ apariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ? Upasampannānaṃ apariyantasikkhāpadānaṃ, idaṃ apariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Katamaṃ paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīlaṃ? Puthujjanakalyāṇakānaṃ kusaladhamme yuttānaṃ sekkhapariyante paripūrakārīnaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhānaṃ pariccattajīvitānaṃ, idaṃ paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Katamaṃ aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīlaṃ? Sattannaṃ sekkhānaṃ, idaṃ aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīlaṃ. Katamaṃ paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīlaṃ? Tathāgatasāvakānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ tathāgatānaṃ arahantānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ, idaṃ paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.37).

“What is the virtue of limited purity? That of the unordained with their limited training rules—this is the virtue of limited purity. What is the virtue of unlimited purity? That of the ordained with their unlimited training rules—this is the virtue of unlimited purity. What is the virtue of complete purity? That of virtuous worldlings who are devoted to wholesome states, who fulfill them up to the limit of a learner, who are unconcerned about body and life, having relinquished life—this is the virtue of complete purity. What is the virtue of ungrasped purity? That of the seven learners—this is the virtue of ungrasped purity. What is the virtue of tranquillized purity? That of the Tathāgata’s disciples who are destroyers of the taints, of Paccekabuddhas, of Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones—this is the virtue of tranquillized purity.”

Tattha anupasampannānaṃ sīlaṃ gaṇanavasena sapariyantattā pariyantapārisuddhisīlanti veditabbaṃ. Upasampannānaṃ –

Herein, the virtue of the unordained should be understood as the virtue of limited purity because it is limited by way of enumeration. That of the ordained—

“Nava koṭisahassāni, asītisatakoṭiyo;

Paññāsasatasahassāni, chattiṃsā ca punāpare.

“Nine thousand crores, and eighty hundred crores; fifty hundred thousands, and thirty-six besides.

“Ete [V 1.0044] saṃvaravinayā, sambuddhena pakāsitā;

Peyyālamukhena niddiṭṭhā, sikkhā vinayasaṃvare”ti. –

“These disciplines of restraint were proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One; the training in the restraint of the Vinaya is indicated by way of abbreviation.”

Evaṃ gaṇanavasena sapariyantampi anavasesavasena samādānabhāvañca lābhayasañātiaṅgajīvitavasena adiṭṭhapariyantabhāvañca sandhāya apariyantapārisuddhisīlanti vuttaṃ, ciragumbavāsikaambakhādakamahātissattherassa sīlamiva. Tathā hi so āyasmā –

Thus, although limited by way of enumeration, it is called ‘the virtue of unlimited purity’ with reference to its being undertaken without remainder and to its limit not being seen in terms of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, and life, like the virtue of the Elder Mahātissa, the dweller of Ciragumba, who did not eat the mangoes. For that venerable one—

“Dhanaṃ caje aṅgavarassa hetu, aṅgaṃ caje jīvitaṃ rakkhamāno;

Aṅgaṃ dhanaṃ jīvitañcāpi sabbaṃ, caje naro dhammamanussaranto”ti. –

“One should give up wealth for the sake of a precious limb; one should give up a limb while protecting one's life. A person, recollecting the Dhamma, should give up limb, wealth, and life—everything.”

Imaṃ sappurisānussatiṃ avijahanto jīvitasaṃsayepi sikkhāpadaṃ avītikkamma tadeva apariyantapārisuddhisīlaṃ nissāya upāsakassa piṭṭhigatova arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Yathāha –

Not forsaking this recollection of a true person, even when his life was in danger, he did not transgress the training rule, and relying on that very virtue of unlimited purity, he attained Arahantship while on the lay follower's back. As it is said:

“Na pitā napi te mātā, na ñāti napi bandhavo;

Karotetādisaṃ kiccaṃ, sīlavantassa kāraṇā.

“He is not your father, nor your mother, nor a relative, nor a kinsman; yet for the sake of a virtuous one, he performs such a deed.

Saṃvegaṃ [M 1.0045] janayitvāna, sammasitvāna yoniso;

Tassa piṭṭhigato santo, arahattaṃ apāpuṇī”ti.

“Having aroused a sense of spiritual urgency and having reflected wisely, while on his back, he attained Arahantship.”

Puthujjanakalyāṇakānaṃ sīlaṃ upasampadato paṭṭhāya sudhotajātimaṇi viya suparikammakatasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ca atiparisuddhattā cittuppādamattakenapi malena virahitaṃ arahattasseva padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, tasmā paripuṇṇapārisuddhīti vuccati, mahāsaṅgharakkhitabhāgineyyasaṅgharakkhitattherānaṃ viya.

The virtue of virtuous worldlings, from their higher ordination onwards, is like a well-washed natural gem or well-wrought gold. Being exceedingly pure and free from the stain of even a mere thought-arising, it serves as the proximate cause for Arahantship itself. Therefore, it is called 'complete purity,' like that of the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita and his nephew, the Elder Saṅgharakkhita.

Mahāsaṅgharakkhitattheraṃ kira atikkantasaṭṭhivassaṃ maraṇamañce nipannaṃ bhikkhusaṅgho lokuttarādhigamaṃ pucchi. Thero “natthi me lokuttaradhammo”ti āha. Athassa upaṭṭhāko daharabhikkhu āha – “bhante, tumhe parinibbutāti samantā dvādasayojanā manussā sannipatitā, tumhākaṃ puthujjanakālakiriyāya mahājanassa vippaṭisāro bhavissatī”ti. Āvuso, ahaṃ “metteyyaṃ bhagavantaṃ passissāmī”ti na vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesiṃ. Tena hi maṃ nisīdāpetvā [V 1.0045] okāsaṃ karohīti. So theraṃ nisīdāpetvā bahi nikkhanto. Thero tassa saha nikkhamanāva arahattaṃ patvā accharikāya saññaṃ adāsi. Saṅgho sannipatitvā āha – “bhante, evarūpe maraṇakāle lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattentā dukkaraṃ karitthā”ti. Nāvuso etaṃ dukkaraṃ, apica vo dukkaraṃ ācikkhissāmi – “ahaṃ, āvuso, pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya asatiyā aññāṇapakataṃ kammaṃ nāma na passāmī”ti. Bhāgineyyopissa paññāsavassakāle evameva arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti.

It is said that when the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, having passed sixty years, was lying on his deathbed, the community of monks asked him about his attainment of the supramundane. The Elder replied, “I have no supramundane state.” Then his attendant, a young monk, said, “Venerable sir, people from twelve yojanas all around have gathered, hearing that you are about to attain final Nibbāna. If you pass away as an ordinary person, the great assembly will be disappointed.” “Friend, I did not establish insight meditation with the thought, ‘I will see the Blessed One Metteyya.’ Therefore, help me to sit up and give me the opportunity.” The young monk helped the Elder to sit up and then went outside. As soon as he went out, the Elder attained Arahantship and gave a sign with a snap of his fingers. The assembled Saṅgha said, “Venerable sir, in producing a supramundane state at such a time of death, you have done what is difficult.” “Friends, this is not difficult. However, I will tell you what is difficult: ‘Friends, from the time of my ordination, I do not recall any act whatsoever done out of mindlessness or ignorance.’” His nephew also attained Arahantship at the age of fifty in this very way.

“Appassutopi ce hoti, sīlesu asamāhito;

Ubhayena naṃ garahanti, sīlato ca sutena ca.

“If one has little learning and is not well-composed in virtue, they blame him on both counts: regarding virtue and regarding learning.

“Appassutopi ce hoti, sīlesu susamāhito;

Sīlato naṃ pasaṃsanti, tassa sampajjate sutaṃ.

“If one has little learning but is well-composed in virtue, they praise him on account of his virtue, and his learning is successful.

“Bahussutopi ce hoti, sīlesu asamāhito;

Sīlato naṃ garahanti, nāssa sampajjate sutaṃ.

“If one has much learning but is not well-composed in virtue, they blame him on account of his virtue, and his learning is not successful.

“Bahussutopi ce hoti, sīlesu susamāhito;

Ubhayena naṃ pasaṃsanti, sīlato ca sutena ca.

“If one has much learning and is well-composed in virtue, they praise him on both counts: on account of his virtue and on account of his learning.

“Bahussutaṃ [M 1.0046] dhammadharaṃ, sappaññaṃ buddhasāvakaṃ;

Nekkhaṃ jambonadasseva, ko taṃ ninditumarahati;

Devāpi naṃ pasaṃsanti, brahmunāpi pasaṃsito”ti. (a. ni. 4.6);

“One who has much learning, who bears the Dhamma, is wise, a disciple of the Buddha—like an ornament of Jambu-river gold, who is worthy to blame him? Even the devas praise him; he is praised by Brahmā as well.”

Sekkhānaṃ pana sīlaṃ diṭṭhivasena aparāmaṭṭhattā, puthujjanānaṃ vā pana rāgavasena aparāmaṭṭhasīlaṃ aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhīti veditabbaṃ, kuṭumbiyaputtatissattherassa sīlaṃ viya. So hi āyasmā tathārūpaṃ sīlaṃ nissāya arahatte patiṭṭhātukāmo verike āha –

Furthermore, the virtue of trainees, because it is not clung to by way of views, is to be known as purity of non-clinging. Alternatively, for ordinary people, virtue that is not clung to by way of lust is to be known as purity of non-clinging, like the virtue of the Elder Tissa, son of a householder. Indeed, that venerable one, desiring to be established in Arahantship by relying on such virtue, said to the robbers: –

“Ubho [V 1.0046] pādāni bhinditvā, saññapessāmi vo ahaṃ;

Aṭṭiyāmi harāyāmi, sarāgamaraṇaṃ aha”nti.

“Break both my legs, and I will give you a sign. I am disgusted by and ashamed of a death with lust.”

“Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, sammasitvāna yoniso;

Sampatte aruṇuggamhi, arahattaṃ apāpuṇi”nti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373);

“Having thought thus, having reflected with wise attention, at the rising of the sun, I attained Arahantship.”

Aññataropi mahāthero bāḷhagilāno sahatthā āhārampi paribhuñjituṃ asakkonto sake muttakarīse palipanno samparivattati, taṃ disvā aññataro daharo “aho dukkhā jīvitasaṅkhārā”ti āha. Tamenaṃ mahāthero āha – “ahaṃ, āvuso, idāni miyyamāno saggasampattiṃ labhissāmi, natthi me ettha saṃsayo, imaṃ pana sīlaṃ bhinditvā laddhasampatti nāma sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya paṭiladdhagihibhāvasadisī”ti vatvā “sīleneva saddhiṃ marissāmī”ti tattheva nipanno tameva rogaṃ sammasanto arahattaṃ patvā bhikkhusaṅghassa imāhi gāthāhi byākāsi –

Another great elder, being severely ill and unable to eat food even with his own hand, lay fallen and rolling about in his own urine and feces. Seeing him, a certain junior monk said, “Alas, how painful are the life-formations!” The great elder said to him: “Friend, if I were to die now, I would obtain heavenly fortune; I have no doubt about this. But the fortune gained by breaking this virtue would be like regaining the state of a householder after having renounced the training.” And saying, “I will die together with my virtue,” he lay right there, and contemplating that very illness, he attained Arahantship and declared it to the Saṅgha with these verses: –

“Phuṭṭhassa me aññatarena byādhinā,

Rogena bāḷhaṃ dukhitassa ruppato;

Parisussati khippamidaṃ kaḷevaraṃ,

Pupphaṃ yathā paṃsuni ātape kataṃ.

“For me, afflicted by a certain disease, severely pained and tormented by sickness, this body quickly dries up, like a flower placed in the dust and in the sun.

“Ajaññaṃ jaññasaṅkhātaṃ, asuciṃ sucisammataṃ;

Nānākuṇapaparipūraṃ, jaññarūpaṃ apassato.

“Ignoble, it is reckoned noble; impure, it is considered pure; filled with various kinds of carrion—for one who does not see the deceptive nature of this form.

“Dhiratthu [M 1.0047] maṃ āturaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, duggandhiyaṃ asuci byādhidhammaṃ;

Yatthappamattā adhimucchitā pajā, hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyā”ti.

“Shame on this ailing, putrid body, foul-smelling, impure, and subject to disease, in which beings, heedless and infatuated, abandon the path leading to a good destination.”

Arahantādīnaṃ pana sīlaṃ sabbadarathappaṭippassaddhiyā parisuddhattā paṭippassaddhipārisuddhīti veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ pariyantapārisuddhiādivasena pañcavidhaṃ.

Furthermore, the virtue of Arahants and others, being purified by the complete calming of all distress, is to be known as purity of tranquility. Thus, by way of purity of limitation and so forth, it is fivefold.

Dutiyasīlapañcakaṃ

The Second Pentad of Virtue

Dutiyapañcake [V 1.0047] pāṇātipātādīnaṃ pahānādivasena attho veditabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ –

In the second pentad, the meaning should be understood by way of abandoning the taking of life and so forth. For this was stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Pañca sīlāni pāṇātipātassa pahānaṃ sīlaṃ, veramaṇī sīlaṃ, cetanā sīlaṃ, saṃvaro sīlaṃ, avītikkamo sīlaṃ. Adinnādānassa, kāmesumicchācārassa, musāvādassa, pisuṇāya vācāya, pharusāya vācāya, samphappalāpassa, abhijjhāya, byāpādassa, micchādiṭṭhiyā, nekkhammena kāmacchandassa, abyāpādena byāpādassa, ālokasaññāya thinamiddhassa, avikkhepena uddhaccassa, dhammavavatthānena vicikicchāya, ñāṇena avijjāya, pāmojjena aratiyā, paṭhamena jhānena nīvaraṇānaṃ, dutiyena jhānena vitakkavicārānaṃ, tatiyena jhānena pītiyā, catutthena jhānena sukhadukkhānaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyā rūpasaññāya paṭighasaññāya nānattasaññāya, viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpattiyā ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāya, ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyā viññāṇañcāyatanasaññāya, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā ākiñcaññāyatanasaññāya, aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāya, dukkhānupassanāya sukhasaññāya, anattānupassanāya attasaññāya, nibbidānupassanāya nandiyā, virāgānupassanāya rāgassa, nirodhānupassanāya samudayassa, paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādānassa, khayānupassanāya ghanasaññāya, vayānupassanāya āyūhanassa, vipariṇāmānupassanāya dhuvasaññāya, animittānupassanāya nimittassa, appaṇihitānupassanāya paṇidhiyā, suññatānupassanāya abhinivesassa, adhipaññādhammavipassanāya sārādānābhinivesassa, yathābhūtañāṇadassanena sammohābhinivesassa, ādīnavānupassanāya ālayābhinivesassa, paṭisaṅkhānupassanāya appaṭisaṅkhāya, vivaṭṭanānupassanāya saññogābhinivesassa, sotāpattimaggena diṭṭhekaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0048] kilesānaṃ, sakadāgāmimaggena oḷārikānaṃ kilesānaṃ, anāgāmimaggena aṇusahagatānaṃ kilesānaṃ, arahattamaggena sabbakilesānaṃ pahānaṃ sīlaṃ, veramaṇī, cetanā, saṃvaro, avītikkamo sīlaṃ. Evarūpāni sīlāni cittassa avippaṭisārāya saṃvattanti, pāmojjāya saṃvattanti, pītiyā saṃvattanti, passaddhiyā saṃvattanti, somanassāya saṃvattanti, āsevanāya saṃvattanti, bhāvanāya saṃvattanti, bahulīkammāya saṃvattanti, alaṅkārāya saṃvattanti, parikkhārāya saṃvattanti, parivārāya saṃvattanti, pāripūriyā saṃvattanti, ekantanibbidāya virāgāya [V 1.0048] nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.41).

There are five aspects of virtue: the abandoning of taking life is virtue, abstention is virtue, volition is virtue, restraint is virtue, non-transgression is virtue. Virtue is the abandoning of taking what is not given, of sexual misconduct, of false speech, of divisive speech, of harsh speech, of idle chatter, of covetousness, of ill will, of wrong view; by renunciation, the abandoning of sensual desire; by non-ill will, the abandoning of ill will; by the perception of light, the abandoning of sloth and torpor; by non-distraction, the abandoning of restlessness; by the discrimination of phenomena, the abandoning of doubt; by knowledge, the abandoning of ignorance; by joy, the abandoning of discontent; by the first jhāna, the abandoning of the hindrances; by the second jhāna, the abandoning of applied thought and sustained thought; by the third jhāna, the abandoning of rapture; by the fourth jhāna, the abandoning of pleasure and pain; by the attainment of the base of infinite space, the abandoning of the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity; by the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, the abandoning of the perception of the base of infinite space; by the attainment of the base of nothingness, the abandoning of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness; by the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the abandoning of the perception of the base of nothingness; by contemplation of impermanence, the abandoning of the perception of permanence; by contemplation of suffering, the abandoning of the perception of pleasure; by contemplation of non-self, the abandoning of the perception of self; by contemplation of disenchantment, the abandoning of delight; by contemplation of dispassion, the abandoning of passion; by contemplation of cessation, the abandoning of origination; by contemplation of relinquishment, the abandoning of grasping; by contemplation of destruction, the abandoning of the perception of solidity; by contemplation of dissolution, the abandoning of accumulation; by contemplation of change, the abandoning of the perception of stability; by contemplation of the signless, the abandoning of signs; by contemplation of the desireless, the abandoning of desire; by contemplation of emptiness, the abandoning of insistence; by insight into phenomena with higher wisdom, the abandoning of insistence on taking things as essential; by knowledge and vision of things as they are, the abandoning of insistence on delusion; by contemplation of drawbacks, the abandoning of insistence on attachment; by contemplation of reflection, the abandoning of non-reflection; by contemplation of turning away, the abandoning of insistence on bondage; by the path of stream-entry, the abandoning of defilements rooted in fixed view; by the path of once-returning, the abandoning of gross defilements; by the path of non-returning, the abandoning of subtle defilements; by the path of arahantship, the abandoning of all defilements is virtue; abstention, volition, restraint, and non-transgression are also virtue. Such virtues conduce to non-remorse of mind, to delight, to rapture, to tranquility, to gladness, to cultivation, to development, to making much of, to adornment, to requisites, to accompaniment, to completion, to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to calm, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna.

Ettha ca pahānanti koci dhammo nāma natthi aññatra vuttappakārānaṃ pāṇātipātādīnaṃ anuppādamattato. Yasmā pana taṃ taṃ pahānaṃ tassa tassa kusaladhammassa patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena upadhāraṇaṃ hoti, vikampābhāvakaraṇena ca samādānaṃ. Tasmā pubbe vutteneva upadhāraṇasamādhānasaṅkhātena sīlanaṭṭhena sīlanti vuttaṃ. Itare cattāro dhammā tato tato veramaṇivasena, tassa tassa saṃvaravasena, tadubhayasampayuttacetanāvasena, taṃ taṃ avītikkamantassa avītikkamanavasena ca cetaso pavattisabbhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttā. Sīlaṭṭho pana tesaṃ pubbe pakāsitoyevāti. Evaṃ pahānasīlādivasena pañcavidhaṃ.

Here, 'abandoning' is not some phenomenon apart from the mere non-arising of the aforementioned kinds, such as the taking of life. However, since that abandoning serves as the foundation for each corresponding wholesome state by way of upholding, and as a commitment by way of preventing wavering, it is therefore called 'virtue' in the sense of sīla as previously explained, which is characterized by upholding and commitment. The other four phenomena are stated with reference to the existence of mental activity: by way of abstaining from each, by way of restraining each, by way of the volition associated with both, and by way of the non-transgression of one who does not transgress in each instance. But the meaning of virtue for these has already been explained. Thus, it is fivefold, by way of virtue as abandoning and so on.

Ettāvatā ca kiṃ sīlaṃ? Kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ? Kānassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni? Kimānisaṃsaṃ sīlaṃ? Katividhaṃ cetaṃ sīlanti? Imesaṃ pañhānaṃ vissajjanaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

And with this, the explanation of these questions is concluded: What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What are the benefits of virtue? And how many kinds of virtue are there?

Sīlasaṃkilesavodānaṃ

The Defilement and Purification of Virtue

21. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “ko cassa saṃkileso, kiṃ vodāna”nti. Tatra vadāma – khaṇḍādibhāvo sīlassa saṃkileso, akhaṇḍādibhāvo vodānaṃ. So pana khaṇḍādibhāvo lābhayasādihetukena bhedena ca sattavidhamethunasaṃyogena ca saṅgahito.

21. But as it was said, 'What is its defilement, and what is its purification?' In this regard, we say: The state of being broken and so forth is the defilement of virtue; the state of being unbroken and so forth is its purification. That state of being broken and so forth is comprised of breaking due to gain, honor, and so forth, and by the seven kinds of sexual union.

Tathā hi yassa sattasu āpattikkhandhesu ādimhi vā ante vā sikkhāpadaṃ bhinnaṃ hoti, tassa sīlaṃ pariyante chinnasāṭako viya khaṇḍaṃ nāma [M 1.0049] hoti. Yassa pana vemajjhe bhinnaṃ, tassa majjhe chiddasāṭako viya chiddaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa paṭipāṭiyā dve tīṇi bhinnāni, tassa piṭṭhiyā vā kucchiyā vā uṭṭhitena visabhāgavaṇṇena kāḷarattādīnaṃ aññatarasarīravaṇṇā gāvī viya sabalaṃ nāma hoti. Yassa antarantarā bhinnāni, tassa antarantarā visabhāgavaṇṇabinduvicitrā gāvī viya kammāsaṃ nāma hoti. Evaṃ tāva lābhādihetukena bhedena khaṇḍādibhāvo hoti.

For example, if, among the seven groups of offenses, a training rule of someone is broken at the beginning or at the end, their virtue is called 'fragmented,' like a garment cut at the edge. If, however, it is broken in the middle, their virtue is called 'pierced,' like a garment with a hole in the middle. If two or three are broken in sequence, their virtue is called 'spotted,' like a cow of a certain body color, such as black or red, with a dissimilar color appearing on its back or belly. If they are broken intermittently, their virtue is called 'variegated,' like a cow speckled with spots of dissimilar color here and there. Thus, the state of being fragmented and so forth arises from breaking due to gain and so forth.

Evaṃ [V 1.0049] sattavidhamethunasaṃyogavasena. Vuttañhi bhagavatā –

The state of being broken and so forth also occurs by way of the seven kinds of sexual union. For it was said by the Blessed One—

“Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā sammā brahmacārī paṭijānamāno na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃdvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati, apica kho mātugāmassa ucchādanaṃ parimaddanaṃ nhāpanaṃ sambāhanaṃ sādiyati, so tadassādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjati, idampi kho, brāhmaṇa, brahmacariyassa khaṇḍampi chiddampi sabalampi kammāsampi. Ayaṃ vuccati, brāhmaṇa, aparisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carati saṃyutto methunena saṃyogena, na parimuccati jātiyā. Jarāya maraṇena…pe… na parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Here, brahmin, some ascetic or brahmin, while professing to live the holy life correctly, does not engage in sexual union with women, but still enjoys being anointed, massaged, bathed, and rubbed by women. He relishes that, delights in it, and finds satisfaction in it. This, too, brahmin, is a holy life that is fragmented, pierced, spotted, and variegated. This, brahmin, is called living an impure holy life, bound by sexual union, not freed from birth, aging, death… I say he is not freed from suffering.”

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco samaṇo vā…pe… paṭijānamāno na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃ dvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati. Napi mātugāmassa ucchādanaṃ…pe… sādiyati. Apica kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ sañjagghati saṃkīḷati saṃkelāyati, so tadassādeti…pe… na parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Furthermore, brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin... does not engage in sexual union with women, nor does he enjoy being anointed... by women. Yet he jokes, plays, and frolics with women. He relishes that... I say he is not freed from suffering.”

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco samaṇo vā…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena saddhiṃ dvayaṃ dvayasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati. Napi mātugāmassa ucchādanaṃ…pe… sādiyati. Napi mātugāmena saddhiṃ sañjagghati saṃkīḷati saṃkelāyati. Apica kho mātugāmassa cakkhunā cakkhuṃ upanijjhāyati pekkhati, so tadassādeti…pe… na parimuccati dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Furthermore, brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin... does not engage in sexual union with women. Nor does he enjoy being anointed... by women. Nor does he joke, play, or frolic with women. But he looks intently at a woman with his eyes and gazes at her, and he relishes that... I say he is not freed from suffering.”

“Puna [M 1.0050] caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco samaṇo vā…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena… napi mātugāmassa… napi mātugāmena… napi mātugāmassa…pe… pekkhati. Apica kho mātugāmassa saddaṃ suṇāti tirokuṭṭā vā tiropākārā vā hasantiyā vā bhaṇantiyā vā gāyantiyā vā rodantiyā vā, so tadassādeti…pe… dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Furthermore, brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin... does not engage in sexual union with women... nor does he look intently at a woman with his eyes and gaze at her. Yet he hears the sound of a woman from behind a wall or behind a fence, whether laughing, speaking, singing, or crying, and he relishes that... I say he is not freed from suffering.”

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco samaṇo vā…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena… napi mātugāmassa… napi mātugāmena… napi mātugāmassa…pe… rodantiyā [V 1.0050] vā. Apica kho yānissa tāni pubbe mātugāmena saddhiṃ hasitalapitakīḷitāni, tāni anussarati, so tadassādeti…pe… dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Furthermore, brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin... does not engage in sexual union with women... nor does he hear the sound of a woman... crying. Yet he recalls his former laughter, talk, and play with women, and he relishes that... I say he is not freed from suffering.”

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco samaṇo vā…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena…pe… napi mātugāmassa…pe… napi yānissa tāni pubbe mātugāmena saddhiṃ hasitalapitakīḷitāni, tāni anussarati. Apica kho passati gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgībhūtaṃ paricārayamānaṃ, so tadassādeti…pe… dukkhasmāti vadāmi.

“Furthermore, brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin... does not engage in sexual union with women... nor does he recall his former laughter, talk, and play with women. Yet he sees a householder or a householder’s son endowed with, possessed of, and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, and he relishes that... I say he is not freed from suffering.”

“Puna caparaṃ, brāhmaṇa, idhekacco samaṇo vā…pe… na heva kho mātugāmena…pe… napi passati gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā…pe… paricārayamānaṃ. Apica kho aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati ‘imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā’ti. So tadassādeti, taṃ nikāmeti, tena ca vittiṃ āpajjati. Idampi kho, brāhmaṇa, brahmacariyassa khaṇḍampi chiddampi sabalampi kammāsampī”ti (a. ni. 7.50).

“Furthermore, brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin... does not engage in sexual union with women... nor does he see a householder or a householder’s son enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure. But rather, aspiring to a certain group of gods, he lives the holy life, thinking, ‘By this virtue, or by this observance, or by this austerity, or by this holy life, may I become a god or some other deity!’ He savors that, longs for it, and attains satisfaction in it. This too, brahmin, is a holy life that is broken, holed, spotted, and blemished.”

Evaṃ lābhādihetukena bhedena ca sattavidhamethunasaṃyogena ca khaṇḍādibhāvo saṅgahitoti veditabbo.

Thus, it should be understood that the state of being broken, etc., is comprised of the breaking for the sake of gain and so forth, and by the seven kinds of sexual union.

Akhaṇḍādibhāvo pana sabbaso sikkhāpadānaṃ abhedena, bhinnānañca sappaṭikammānaṃ paṭikammakaraṇena, sattavidhamethunasaṃyogābhāvena ca, aparāya [M 1.0051] ca “kodho upanāho makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sātheyyaṃ thambho sārambho māno atimāno mado pamādo”tiādīnaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ anuppattiyā, appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāsallekhatādīnañca guṇānaṃ uppattiyā saṅgahito.

The unbroken state, however, is comprised of complete adherence to the precepts without violation, of repairing what is broken by means of appropriate remedial action, of the absence of the seven kinds of sexual union, of the non-arising of evil qualities such as ‘anger, hostility, denigration, malice, envy, miserliness, hypocrisy, craftiness, stubbornness, presumption, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, and heedlessness,’ and of the arising of qualities such as having few wants, contentment, and the paring away of defilements.

Yāni hi sīlāni lābhādīnampi atthāya abhinnāni, pamādadosena vā bhinnānipi paṭikammakatāni[V 1.0051], methunasaṃyogehi vā kodhupanāhādīhi vā pāpadhammehi anupahatāni, tāni sabbaso akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsānīti vuccanti. Tāniyeva bhujissabhāvakaraṇato ca bhujissāni, viññūhi pasatthattā viññupasatthāni, taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhattā aparāmaṭṭhāni, upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā saṃvattayantīti samādhisaṃvattanikāni ca honti. Tasmā nesaṃ esa ‘akhaṇḍādibhāvo vodāna’nti veditabbo.

Those virtues which, even for the sake of gain and so on, remain unbroken, or even if broken through the fault of heedlessness, are restored, or are not corrupted by sexual unions, anger, resentment, and other evil qualities—these are called unbroken, unpierced, unblemished, and unspotted. Because they make one free, they are called ‘freeing.’ Because they are praised by the wise, they are called ‘praised by the wise.’ Because they are not clung to through craving and wrong view, they are called ‘unclung to.’ And because they lead to access concentration or absorption concentration, they are called ‘conducive to concentration.’ Therefore, this quality of being unbroken and so on should be understood as ‘purification.’

Taṃ panetaṃ vodānaṃ dvīhākārehi sampajjati sīlavipattiyā ca ādīnavadassanena, sīlasampattiyā ca ānisaṃsadassanena. Tattha “pañcime, bhikkhave, ādīnavā dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.149; a. ni. 5.213) evamādisuttanayena sīlavipattiyā ādīnavo daṭṭhabbo.

This purification, however, is accomplished in two ways: by seeing the danger in moral failure and by seeing the benefit in moral success. Herein, the danger in moral failure should be seen according to the method of the discourse beginning: "Monks, there are these five dangers for an immoral person, one who has failed in morality" (Dī. Ni. 2.149; A. Ni. 5.213).

Apica dussīlo puggalo dussīlyahetu amanāpo hoti devamanussānaṃ, ananusāsanīyo sabrahmacārīnaṃ, dukkhito dussīlyagarahāsu, vippaṭisārī sīlavataṃ pasaṃsāsu, tāya ca pana dussīlyatāya sāṇasāṭako viya dubbaṇṇo hoti. Ye kho panassa diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanti, tesaṃ dīgharattaṃ apāyadukkhāvahanato dukkhasamphasso. Yesaṃ deyyadhammaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti, tesaṃ namahapphalakaraṇato appaggho. Anekavassagaṇikagūthakūpo viya dubbisodhano. Chavālātamiva ubhato paribāhiro. Bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānantopi abhikkhuyeva gogaṇaṃ anubandhagadrabho viya. Satatubbiggo sabbaverikapuriso viya. Asaṃvāsāraho matakaḷevaraṃ viya. Sutādiguṇayuttopi sabrahmacārīnaṃ apūjāraho susānaggi viya brāhmaṇānaṃ. Abhabbo visesādhigame andho viya rūpadassane. Nirāso saddhamme caṇḍālakumārako viya rajje. Sukhitosmīti maññamānopi dukkhitova aggikkhandhapariyāye vuttadukkhabhāgitāya.

Furthermore, an immoral person, on account of his immorality, is displeasing to gods and humans, not amenable to instruction from his fellows in the holy life, afflicted when his immorality is censured, and remorseful when the virtuous are praised. Because of that immorality, he becomes of poor appearance like a hempen cloth. He is of painful contact to those who follow his example, bringing them suffering in the lower realms for a long time. He is of little worth to those whose offerings he accepts, as he does not make them of great fruit. He is as hard to purify as a cesspool of excrement accumulated over many years. Like a firebrand from a funeral pyre, he is excluded from both sides. Even while claiming to be a bhikkhu, he is no true bhikkhu, but is like a donkey following a herd of cattle. He is ever agitated, like a man who is an enemy to all. He is unfit for communion, like a corpse. Though endowed with learning and other qualities, he is unworthy of veneration by his fellows in the holy life, like a charnel ground fire for brahmins. He is incapable of attaining distinction, like a blind man in seeing forms. He is without hope in the true Dhamma, like an outcaste boy regarding kingship. Though he may think, 'I am happy,' he is truly miserable, being a partaker of the suffering spoken of in the Discourse on the Mass of Fire.

Dussīlānañhi [M 1.0052] pañcakāmaguṇaparibhogavandanamānanādisukhassādagadhitacittānaṃ tappaccayaṃ anussaraṇamattenāpi hadayasantāpaṃ janayitvā uṇhalohituggārappavattanasamatthaṃ atikaṭukaṃ dukkhaṃ dassento sabbākārena paccakkhakammavipāko bhagavā āha –

Indeed, to show the extremely bitter suffering of the immoral—whose minds are greedy for the taste of happiness from enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, from homage, veneration, and so forth—a suffering capable of causing the vomiting of hot blood, generated by the heart-burning that arises even from the mere recollection of that cause, the Blessed One, who in every way directly perceived the result of kamma, said:

“Passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, amuṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūta’nti? Evaṃ, bhanteti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ amuṃ [V 1.0052] mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ āliṅgetvā upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, yaṃ khattiyakaññaṃ vā brāhmaṇakaññaṃ vā gahapatikaññaṃ vā mudutalunahatthapādaṃ āliṅgetvā upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vāti. Etadeva, bhante, varaṃ yaṃ khattiyakaññaṃ vā…pe… upanipajjeyya vā. Dukkhaṃ hetaṃ, bhante, yaṃ amuṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ…pe… upanipajjeyya vāti. Ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave, yathā etadeva tassa varaṃ dussīlassa pāpadhammassa asucisaṅkassarasamācārassa paṭicchannakammantassa assamaṇassa samaṇapaṭiññassa abrahmacārissa brahmacāripaṭiññassa antopūtikassa avassutassa kasambujātassa yaṃ amuṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ…pe… upanipajjeyya vā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tatonidānaṃ hi so, bhikkhave, maraṇaṃ vā nigaccheyya maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ, na tveva tappaccayā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjeyyā”ti (a. ni. 7.72).

“Bhikkhus, do you see that great mass of fire, blazing, flaming, and glowing?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “What do you think, bhikkhus? Which would be better—to embrace and sit or lie down beside that great mass of fire, blazing, flaming, and glowing, or to embrace and sit or lie down beside a khattiya maiden, a brahmin maiden, or a householder's maiden with soft, tender hands and feet?” “Venerable sir, it would be better to embrace and sit or lie down beside a khattiya maiden, a brahmin maiden, or a householder's maiden with soft, tender hands and feet. For it is painful, venerable sir, to embrace and sit or lie down beside that great mass of fire, blazing, flaming, and glowing.” “I declare to you, bhikkhus, I make known to you, that for an immoral person—of evil nature, of impure and dubious conduct, with secret deeds, not an ascetic but one who claims to be an ascetic, not a celibate but one who claims to be a celibate, rotten within, oozing with desire, having become like rubbish—it would indeed be better to embrace and sit or lie down beside that great mass of fire, blazing, flaming, and glowing. For what reason? Because of that, bhikkhus, he might meet with death or suffering equal to death, but not on that account would he, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell.”

Evaṃ aggikkhandhupamāya itthipaṭibaddhapañcakāmaguṇaparibhogapaccayaṃ dukkhaṃ dassetvā eteneva upāyena –

Thus, having shown the suffering caused by indulgence in the five strands of sensual pleasure connected with women through the simile of a mass of fire, in this same way—

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ balavā puriso daḷhāya vāḷarajjuyā ubho jaṅghā veṭhetvā ghaṃseyya, sā chaviṃ chindeyya, chaviṃ chetvā cammaṃ chindeyya, cammaṃ chetvā maṃsaṃ chindeyya, maṃsaṃ chetvā nhāruṃ chindeyya, nhāruṃ chetvā aṭṭhiṃ chindeyya, aṭṭhiṃ chetvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca tiṭṭheyya, yaṃ vā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ [M 1.0053] vā brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ vā gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā abhivādanaṃ sādiyeyyā”ti ca.

“What do you think, bhikkhus? Which would be better: that a strong man should bind both shins with a strong horsehair rope and rub them, so that it cuts through the outer skin; and having cut through the outer skin, it cuts through the inner skin; and having cut through the inner skin, it cuts through the flesh; and having cut through the flesh, it cuts through the sinews; and having cut through the sinews, it cuts through the bone; and having cut through the bone, it should strike the bone marrow and stop there; or that one should consent to the homage of wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ balavā puriso tiṇhāya sattiyā teladhotāya paccorasmiṃ pahareyya, yaṃ vā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ vā brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ vā gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā añjalikammaṃ sādiyeyyā”ti ca.

“What do you think, bhikkhus? Which would be better: that a strong man should strike one on the chest with a sharp, oil-polished spear, or that one should consent to the gesture of reverence from wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ balavā puriso tattena ayopaṭṭena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena kāyaṃ sampaliveṭheyya, yaṃ vā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ [V 1.0053] vā brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ vā gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā saddhādeyyaṃ cīvaraṃ paribhuñjeyyā”ti ca.

“What do you think, bhikkhus? Which would be better: that a strong man should wrap one's body with a hot iron plate—blazing, flaming, and glowing—or that one should use robes given in faith by wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ balavā puriso tattena ayosaṅkunā ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena mukhaṃ vivaritvā tattaṃ lohaguḷaṃ ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ mukhe pakkhipeyya, taṃ tassa oṭṭhampi ḍaheyya, mukhampi, jivhampi, kaṇṭhampi, udarampi ḍaheyya, antampi antaguṇampi ādāya adhobhāgaṃ nikkhameyya, yaṃ vā khattiya… brāhmaṇa… gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā saddhādeyyaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjeyyā”ti ca.

“What do you think, bhikkhus? Which would be better: that a strong man, having opened one’s mouth with a red-hot iron pincer—blazing, flaming, and glowing—were to thrust a red-hot iron ball—blazing, flaming, and glowing—into one’s mouth? It would burn one’s lips, mouth, tongue, throat, and stomach, and taking with it the intestines and mesentery, would exit from the lower part. Or that one were to partake of the almsfood given in faith by wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ balavā puriso sīse vā gahetvā khandhe vā gahetvā tattaṃ ayomañcaṃ vā ayopīṭhaṃ vā ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ abhinisīdāpeyya vā abhinipajjāpeyya vā, yaṃ vā khattiya… brāhmaṇa… gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā saddhādeyyaṃ mañcapīṭhaṃ paribhuñjeyyā”ti ca.

“What do you think, bhikkhus? Which would be better: that a strong man, seizing one by the head or shoulders, were to force one to sit or lie upon a red-hot iron couch or seat—blazing, flaming, and glowing; or that one were to use a couch or seat given in faith by wealthy khattiyas, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ balavā puriso uddhaṃpādaṃ adhosiraṃ gahetvā tattāya ayokumbhiyā pakkhipeyya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya[M 1.0054], so tattha pheṇuddehakaṃ paccamāno sakimpi uddhaṃ gaccheyya, sakimpi adho gaccheyya, sakimpi tiriyaṃ gaccheyya, yaṃ vā khattiya… brāhmaṇa… gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā saddhādeyyaṃ vihāraṃ paribhuñjeyyā”ti cāti (a. ni. 7.72).

“What do you think, monks? Which is better—that a strong man, having seized him with feet up and head down, were to plunge him into a red-hot iron cauldron, ablaze, flaming, and glowing, where he would be cooked, emitting foam, sometimes rising up, sometimes going down, sometimes moving sideways; or that one were to enjoy a dwelling given in faith by nobles, brahmins, or wealthy householders?”

Imāhi vāḷarajjutiṇhasattiayopaṭṭaayoguḷaayomañcaayopīṭhaayokumbhīupamāhi abhivādanaañjalikammacīvarapiṇḍapātamañcapīṭhavihāraparibhogapaccayaṃ dukkhaṃ dassesi. Tasmā –

Through these similes—the horse-hair rope, the sharp spear, the iron plate, the iron ball, the iron bed, the iron seat, and the iron cauldron—he showed the suffering that is contingent upon the enjoyment of respectful greetings, reverential salutations, robes, almsfood, beds, seats, and dwellings. Therefore:

Aggikkhandhāliṅganadukkhādhikadukkhakaṭukaphalaṃ;

Avijahato kāmasukhaṃ, sukhaṃ kuto bhinnasīlassa.

For one who does not abandon sensual pleasure, the fruit is bitter suffering, exceeding the pain of embracing a mass of fire; for one of broken virtue, whence is happiness?

Abhivādanasādiyane[V 1.0054], kiṃ nāma sukhaṃ vipannasīlassa;

Daḷhavāḷarajjughaṃsanadukkhādhikadukkhabhāgissa.

In delighting in reverential homage, what happiness is there for one whose virtue has failed, for one who partakes of suffering exceeding the pain of being rubbed by a strong horse-hair rope?

Saddhānamañjalikammasādiyane kiṃ sukhaṃ asīlassa;

Sattippahāradukkhādhimattadukkhassa yaṃhetu.

In delighting in the reverential gestures of the faithful, what happiness is there for the immoral, for whom this is a cause of suffering far exceeding the pain of a spear thrust?

Cīvaraparibhogasukhaṃ, kiṃ nāma asaṃyatassa;

Yena ciraṃ anubhavitabbo, niraye jalitaayopaṭṭasamphasso.

The pleasure of using robes—what is it for the unrestrained, by which one must long endure contact with blazing iron sheets in hell?

Madhuropi piṇḍapāto, halāhalavisūpamo asīlassa;

Ādittā gilitabbā, ayoguḷā yena cirarattaṃ.

Even sweet almsfood is like deadly poison to the immoral, by which one must swallow blazing iron balls for a long time.

Sukhasammatopi dukkho, asīlino mañcapīṭhaparibhogo;

Yaṃ bādhissanti ciraṃ, jalitaayomañcapīṭhāni.

Even what is considered pleasant, the use of beds and seats, is suffering for the immoral, who will long be tormented by beds and seats of blazing iron.

Dussīlassa vihāre, saddhādeyyamhi kā nivāsa rati;

Jalitesu nivasitabbaṃ, yena ayokumbhimajjhesu.

For the immoral one, what delight is there in dwelling in a monastery given in faith, who must dwell amidst blazing iron cauldrons?

Saṅkasarasamācāro, kasambujāto avassuto pāpo;

Antopūtīti ca yaṃ, nindanto āha lokagaru.

“He whose conduct is like a cesspool, born of defilement, corrupt, and wicked, is inwardly rotten”—so the Teacher of the world declared in censure.

Dhī jīvitaṃ asaññatassa, tassa samaṇajanavesadhārissa;

Assamaṇassa upahataṃ, khatamattānaṃ vahantassa.

Fie on the life of the unrestrained, of him who wears the guise of an ascetic but is no ascetic, bearing a ruined and wounded self.

Gūthaṃ [M 1.0055] viya kuṇapaṃ viya, maṇḍanakāmā vivajjayantīdha;

Yaṃ nāma sīlavanto, santo kiṃ jīvitaṃ tassa.

Just as those fond of adornment shun excrement or a corpse, so do the virtuous and peaceful shun him. Indeed, what is the life of such a one?

Sabbabhayehi [V 1.0055] amutto, mutto sabbehi adhigamasukhehi;

Supihitasaggadvāro, apāyamaggaṃ samārūḷho.

Not freed from all fears, deprived of all the happiness of attainment, with the gates of heaven firmly shut, he has ascended the path to the woeful states.

Karuṇāya vatthubhūto, kāruṇikajanassa nāma ko añño;

Dussīlasamo dussī, latāya iti bahuvidhā dosāti.

Indeed, who else is an object of compassion for compassionate people than one like the immoral person? Thus, the faults of immorality are manifold.

Evamādinā paccavekkhaṇena sīlavipattiyaṃ ādīnavadassanaṃ vuttappakāraviparītato sīlasampattiyā ānisaṃsadassanañca veditabbaṃ. Apica –

By such reflection, the danger in the failure of virtue should be seen, and by the opposite of the way described, the benefit in the accomplishment of virtue should be understood. Furthermore:

Tassa pāsādikaṃ hoti, pattacīvaradhāraṇaṃ;

Pabbajjā saphalā tassa, yassa sīlaṃ sunimmalaṃ.

For him whose virtue is perfectly pure, the bearing of the bowl and robes is inspiring, and his going forth is fruitful.

Attānuvādādibhayaṃ, suddhasīlassa bhikkhuno;

Andhakāraṃ viya raviṃ, hadayaṃ nāvagāhati.

The fear of self-reproach and so forth does not enter the heart of a monk of pure virtue, just as darkness does not enter the sun.

Sīlasampattiyā bhikkhu, sobhamāno tapovane;

Pabhāsampattiyā cando, gagane viya sobhati.

A monk, shining with the accomplishment of virtue in the ascetic’s grove, is as beautiful as the moon shining in the sky with the accomplishment of light.

Kāyagandhopi pāmojjaṃ, sīlavantassa bhikkhuno;

Karoti api devānaṃ, sīlagandhe kathāva kā.

Even the bodily fragrance of a virtuous monk brings joy to the devas; what then is there to say of the fragrance of his virtue?

Sabbesaṃ gandhajātānaṃ, sampattiṃ abhibhuyyati;

Avighātī disā sabbā, sīlagandho pavāyati.

The fragrance of virtue surpasses the excellence of all kinds of fragrances; unhindered, the fragrance of virtue wafts in all directions.

Appakāpi katā kārā, sīlavante mahapphalā;

Hontīti sīlavā hoti, pūjāsakkārabhājanaṃ.

Even small deeds done for the virtuous become of great fruit; thus, the virtuous one becomes a worthy recipient of homage and offerings.

Sīlavantaṃ na bādhanti, āsavā diṭṭhadhammikā;

Samparāyikadukkhānaṃ, mūlaṃ khanati sīlavā.

The taints pertaining to this present life do not afflict the virtuous one; the virtuous one digs up the root of suffering in future lives.

Yā manussesu sampatti, yā ca devesu sampadā;

Na sā sampannasīlassa, icchato hoti dullabhā.

Whatever prosperity there is among humans, and whatever success among the devas, is not difficult for one accomplished in virtue to attain, should he desire it.

Accantasantā [V 1.0056] pana yā, ayaṃ nibbānasampadā;

Mano sampannasīlassa, tameva anudhāvati.

The mind of one accomplished in virtue, however, runs towards that very accomplishment of Nibbāna, which is supremely peaceful.

Sabbasampattimūlamhi[M 1.0056], sīlamhi iti paṇḍito;

Anekākāravokāraṃ, ānisaṃsaṃ vibhāvayeti.

Thus, the wise one should discern the benefit in virtue—the root of all attainments—which is of many kinds and forms.

Evañhi vibhāvayato sīlavipattito ubbijjitvā sīlasampattininnaṃ mānasaṃ hoti. Tasmā yathāvuttaṃ imaṃ sīlavipattiyā ādīnavaṃ imañca sīlasampattiyā ānisaṃsaṃ disvā sabbādarena sīlaṃ vodāpetabbanti.

Indeed, for one who discerns in this way, the mind recoils from the failure of virtue and inclines towards the accomplishment of virtue. Therefore, having seen this danger of the failure of virtue and this benefit of the accomplishment of virtue as stated, one should purify virtue with all respect.

Ettāvatā ca “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti imissā gāthāya sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena desite visuddhimagge sīlaṃ tāva paridīpitaṃ hoti.

And thus far, in the Path of Purification, which is expounded by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, virtue has been elucidated through this verse: “A wise person established in virtue.”

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, made for the joy of good people,

Sīlaniddeso nāma paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter, called the Exposition of Virtue.

2. Dhutaṅganiddeso

2. Exposition of the Ascetic Practices

22. Idāni [M 1.0057][V 1.0057] yehi appicchatāsantuṭṭhitādīhi guṇehi vuttappakārassa sīlassa vodānaṃ hoti, te guṇe sampādetuṃ yasmā samādinnasīlena yoginā dhutaṅgasamādānaṃ kātabbaṃ. Evañhissa appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāsallekhapavivekāpacayavīriyārambhasubharatādiguṇasalilavikkhālitamalaṃ sīlañceva suparisuddhaṃ bhavissati, vatāni ca sampajjissanti. Iti anavajjasīlabbataguṇaparisuddhasabbasamācāro porāṇe ariyavaṃsattaye patiṭṭhāya catutthassa bhāvanārāmatāsaṅkhātassa ariyavaṃsassa adhigamāraho bhavissati. Tasmā dhutaṅgakathaṃ ārabhissāma.

22. Now, since the purification of virtue of the kind described comes about by means of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, and so forth, a yogin who has undertaken virtue should undertake the ascetic practices in order to bring about those qualities. For in this way, his virtue—its defilement washed away by the water of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, seclusion, non-accumulation, arousal of energy, and ease of maintenance—will become thoroughly purified, and his observances will be fulfilled. Thus, with all his conduct purified by the quality of blameless virtue and observances, established in the three ancient noble lineages, he will become worthy of attaining the fourth noble lineage, known as delight in meditative cultivation. Therefore, we shall begin the discourse on the ascetic practices.

Bhagavatā hi pariccattalokāmisānaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhānaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃyeva ārādhetukāmānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ terasadhutaṅgāni anuññātāni. Seyyathidaṃ – paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ, tecīvarikaṅgaṃ, piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ, sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ, ekāsanikaṅgaṃ, pattapiṇḍikaṅgaṃ, khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ, āraññikaṅgaṃ, rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ, abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ, sosānikaṅgaṃ, yathāsanthatikaṅgaṃ, nesajjikaṅganti. Tattha –

Indeed, the Blessed One has permitted thirteen ascetic practices for sons of good families who have abandoned worldly allurements, are indifferent to body and life, and wish to accomplish the conforming practice. They are as follows: the rag-robe-wearer's practice, the triple-robe-wearer's practice, the alms-food-eater's practice, the house-to-house-wanderer's practice, the one-sessioner's practice, the bowl-food-eater's practice, the later-food-refuser's practice, the forest-dweller's practice, the tree-root-dweller's practice, the open-air-dweller's practice, the charnel-ground-dweller's practice, the any-lodging-user's practice, and the sitter's practice. Therein—

Atthato lakkhaṇādīhi, samādānavidhānato;

Pabhedato bhedato ca, tassa tassānisaṃsato.

By meaning, by characteristic, and so forth; by the method of undertaking; by classification and by breaking; and by the benefits of each.

Kusalattikato ceva, dhutādīnaṃ vibhāgato;

Samāsabyāsato cāpi, viññātabbo vinicchayo.

And from the wholesome triad, by the classification of the ascetic practices and so forth, and also by concise and extended explanation, the determination is to be understood.

23. Tattha atthatoti tāva rathikasusānasaṅkārakūṭādīnaṃ yattha katthaci paṃsūnaṃ upari ṭhitattā abbhuggataṭṭhena tesu tesu paṃsukūlamivāti paṃsukūlaṃ, atha vā paṃsu viya kucchitabhāvaṃ ulatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, kucchitabhāvaṃ gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ laddhanibbacanassa paṃsukūlassa dhāraṇaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ[V 1.0058], taṃ sīlamassāti paṃsukūliko. Paṃsukūlikassa aṅgaṃ paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ. Aṅganti kāraṇaṃ vuccati. Tasmā yena samādānena so paṃsukūliko hoti, tassetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ.

23. Herein, first, as to meaning: because it stands upon dust anywhere on roads, in cemeteries, on rubbish heaps, and so forth, and is thus prominent like a dust-heap, it is called 'paṃsukūla.' Alternatively, because it goes to a foul state like dust, it is 'paṃsukūla'; that is to say, it becomes foul. The wearing of a 'paṃsukūla' (rag-robe), which has this etymology, is also called 'paṃsukūla.' One for whom that is his practice is a 'paṃsukūlika.' The factor of a 'paṃsukūlika' is the 'paṃsukūlikaṅga.' The word 'aṅga' is used in the sense of 'cause.' Therefore, it should be understood that this is a designation for the undertaking by which one becomes a 'paṃsukūlika.'

Eteneva nayena saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgaantaravāsakasaṅkhātaṃ ticīvaraṃ sīlamassāti tecīvariko. Tecīvarikassa aṅgaṃ tecīvarikaṅgaṃ.

By this same method, one for whom the three robes—namely the double-robe, the upper robe, and the inner robe—are his practice is a 'tecīvariko' (triple-robe wearer). The factor of a 'tecīvariko' is the 'tecīvarikaṅga' (triple-robe-wearer's practice).

Bhikkhāsaṅkhātānaṃ [M 1.0058] pana āmisapiṇḍānaṃ pātoti piṇḍapāto, parehi dinnānaṃ piṇḍānaṃ patte nipatananti vuttaṃ hoti. Taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ uñchati taṃ taṃ kulaṃ upasaṅkamanto gavesatīti piṇḍapātiko. Piṇḍāya vā patituṃ vatametassāti piṇḍapātī, patitunti carituṃ, piṇḍapātī eva piṇḍapātiko. Piṇḍapātikassa aṅgaṃ piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ.

Now, 'piṇḍapāta' is the falling of lumps of material food designated as alms; that is to say, the falling into the bowl of lumps given by others. One who seeks that alms-food, approaching family after family, is a 'piṇḍapātiko.' Or, one whose vow it is to go for alms is a 'piṇḍapātī'; 'to go' means to wander. A 'piṇḍapātī' is just a 'piṇḍapātiko.' The factor of a 'piṇḍapātika' is the 'piṇḍapātikaṅga.'

Dānaṃ vuccati avakhaṇḍanaṃ, apetaṃ dānatoti apadānaṃ, anavakhaṇḍananti attho. Saha apadānena sapadānaṃ, avakhaṇḍanarahitaṃ anugharanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sapadānaṃ carituṃ idamassa sīlanti sapadānacārī, sapadānacārī eva sapadānacāriko. Tassa aṅgaṃ sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ.

'Dāna' is said to be 'breaking off.' 'Apadāna' is 'without breaking off'; the meaning is 'uninterrupted.' 'Sapadāna' is 'with non-breaking'; that is to say, from house to house without interruption. One for whom it is his practice to wander without interruption is a 'sapadānacārī'; a 'sapadānacārī' is just a 'sapadānacāriko.' His factor is the 'sapadānacārikaṅga.'

Ekāsane bhojanaṃ ekāsanaṃ, taṃ sīlamassāti ekāsaniko. Tassa aṅgaṃ ekāsanikaṅgaṃ.

Eating in one sitting is 'ekāsana.' One for whom that is his practice is an 'ekāsaniko.' His factor is the 'ekāsanikaṅga.'

Dutiyabhājanassa paṭikkhittattā kevalaṃ ekasmiṃyeva patte piṇḍo pattapiṇḍo. Idāni pattapiṇḍagahaṇe pattapiṇḍasaññaṃ katvā pattapiṇḍo sīlamassāti pattapiṇḍiko. Tassa aṅgaṃ pattapiṇḍikaṅgaṃ.

Because a second vessel is rejected, the alms-food in only one bowl is 'pattapiṇḍa.' Now, applying the designation 'pattapiṇḍa' to the act of eating from a single bowl, one for whom that is his practice is a 'pattapiṇḍika.' The factor of such a one is the 'pattapiṇḍikaṅga.'

Khalūti paṭisedhanatthe nipāto. Pavāritena satā pacchā laddhaṃ bhattaṃ pacchābhattaṃ nāma, tassa pacchābhattassa bhojanaṃ pacchābhattabhojanaṃ, tasmiṃ pacchābhattabhojane pacchābhattasaññaṃ katvā pacchābhattaṃ sīlamassāti pacchābhattiko. Na pacchābhattiko khalupacchābhattiko. Samādānavasena paṭikkhittātirittabhojanassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vuttaṃ khalūti eko sakuṇo. So mukhena phalaṃ gahetvā tasmiṃ patite puna aññaṃ na khādati. Tādiso ayanti khalupacchābhattiko. Tassa aṅgaṃ khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ.

'Khalu' is a particle in the sense of prohibition. Food obtained afterwards by one who has indicated satisfaction is called 'pacchābhatta.' The eating of that 'pacchābhatta' is 'pacchābhattabhojana.' Applying the designation 'pacchābhatta' to the eating of that later food, one for whom that is his practice is a 'pacchābhattika.' One who is not a 'pacchābhattika' is a 'khalupacchābhattika.' This is the designation for one who has rejected extra food by way of undertaking the practice. In the commentary, however, it is said: 'Khalu' is a certain bird. Having taken a fruit in its beak, if that fruit falls, it does not eat another. One who is like that is a 'khalupacchābhattika.' The factor of such a one is the 'khalupacchābhattikaṅga.'

Araññe [V 1.0059] nivāso sīlamassāti āraññiko. Tassa aṅgaṃ āraññikaṅgaṃ.

One for whom dwelling in the forest is his practice is a forest-dweller ('āraññika'). The factor of such a one is the 'āraññikaṅga.'

Rukkhamūle nivāso rukkhamūlaṃ, taṃ sīlamassāti rukkhamūliko. Rukkhamūlikassa aṅgaṃ rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ. Abbhokāsikasosānikaṅgesupi eseva nayo.

Dwelling at the root of a tree is 'rukkhamūla.' One for whom that is his practice is a 'rukkhamūliko.' The factor of a 'rukkhamūliko' is the 'rukkhamūlikaṅga.' This same method applies also to the open-air dweller's factor ('abbhokāsikaṅga') and the charnel-ground dweller's factor ('sosānikaṅga').

Yadeva [M 1.0059] santhataṃ yathāsanthataṃ, idaṃ tuyhaṃ pāpuṇātīti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ uddiṭṭhasenāsanassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmiṃ yathāsanthate viharituṃ sīlamassāti yathāsanthatiko. Tassa aṅgaṃ yathāsanthatikaṅgaṃ.

'Yathāsanthata' means 'just as it is spread out.' This is the designation for a lodging assigned first with the words, 'This falls to you.' One for whom it is his practice to dwell in that which is 'as spread out' is a 'yathāsanthatiko.' The factor of such a one is the 'yathāsanthatikaṅga.'

Sayanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā nisajjāya viharituṃ sīlamassāti nesajjiko. Tassa aṅgaṃ nesajjikaṅgaṃ.

Having rejected lying down, one for whom it is his practice to dwell in the sitting posture is a 'nesajjiko' (a sitter). The factor of such a one is the 'nesajjikaṅga.'

Sabbāneva panetāni tena tena samādānena dhutakilesattā dhutassa bhikkhuno aṅgāni, kilesadhunanato vā dhutanti laddhavohāraṃ ñāṇaṃ aṅgaṃ etesanti dhutaṅgāni. Atha vā dhutāni ca tāni paṭipakkhaniddhunanato aṅgāni ca paṭipattiyātipi dhutaṅgāni. Evaṃ tāvettha atthato viññātabbo vinicchayo.

Moreover, all these are factors of a monk who is 'one who has shaken off' ('dhuta') because he has shaken off defilements by means of this or that undertaking. Or, they are 'dhutaṅgas' because knowledge—which has received the designation 'dhuta' from its shaking off of defilements—is a factor ('aṅga') of them. Alternatively, they are also 'dhutaṅgas' because they are both 'dhuta' (things that shake off), due to their shaking off of opposing states, and they are 'aṅgas' (factors) of the practice. Thus, the analysis here is to be understood in terms of its meaning.

Sabbāneva panetāni samādānacetanālakkhaṇāni. Vuttampi cetaṃ “yo samādiyati, so puggalo. Yena samādiyati, cittacetasikā ete dhammā. Yā samādānacetanā, taṃ dhutaṅgaṃ. Yaṃ paṭikkhipati, taṃ vatthū”ti. Sabbāneva ca loluppaviddhaṃsanarasāni, nilloluppabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānāni appicchatādiariyadhammapadaṭṭhānāni. Evamettha lakkhaṇādīhi veditabbo vinicchayo.

Moreover, all these have the characteristic of the volition of undertaking. It has also been said: 'The person who undertakes is the individual. The mental states and their concomitants by which one undertakes are these phenomena. The volition of undertaking is the ascetic practice. That which one rejects is the object.' Moreover, all these have the function of dispelling craving, the manifestation of non-craving, and are the proximate cause for noble qualities such as having few wishes. Thus, the determination here should be understood by means of these characteristics and so on.

Samādānavidhānatotiādīsu pana pañcasu sabbāneva dhutaṅgāni dharamāne bhagavati bhagavatova santike samādātabbāni. Parinibbute mahāsāvakassa santike. Tasmiṃ asati khīṇāsavassa, anāgāmissa, sakadāgāmissa, sotāpannassa, tipiṭakassa, dvipiṭakassa, ekapiṭakassa, ekasaṅgītikassa, aṭṭhakathācariyassa. Tasmiṃ asati dhutaṅgadharassa, tasmimpi asati cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ sammajjitvā ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā sammāsambuddhassa santike vadantena viya [V 1.0060] samādātabbāni, apica sayampi samādātuṃ vaṭṭati eva. Ettha ca cetiyapabbate dve bhātikattherānaṃ jeṭṭhakabhātu dhutaṅgappicchatāya vatthu kathetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ tāva sādhāraṇakathā.

Furthermore, concerning the five points beginning with the method of undertaking, all the ascetic practices should be undertaken in the presence of the Blessed One himself while he is living. After his final passing, they should be undertaken in the presence of a great disciple. In his absence, in the presence of one who has destroyed the corruptions, a non-returner, a once-returner, a stream-enterer, a master of the Three Piṭakas, of the Two Piṭakas, of one Piṭaka, of one Collection, or a teacher of the commentaries. In the absence of such a one, in the presence of an observer of the ascetic practices. In the absence of even that one, after sweeping the courtyard of a shrine and sitting on one's heels, they should be undertaken as if speaking in the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One. Moreover, it is also permissible to undertake them by oneself. Here, the story of the elder brother of the two sibling elders on Cetiyapabbata, on account of his having few wishes with regard to the ascetic practices, should be told. This, for now, is the general discussion.

1. Paṃsukūlikaṅgakathā

1. The Explanation of the Refuse-Rag Wearer's Practice

24. Idāni ekekassa samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃse vaṇṇayissāma. Paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ tāva “gahapatidānacīvaraṃ paṭikkhipāmi, paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti [M 1.0060] imesu dvīsu vacanesu aññatarena samādinnaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāvettha samādānaṃ.

24. Now we shall explain for each practice its method of undertaking, procedure, grades, breaking, and benefits. The refuse-rag wearer's practice, to begin with, is undertaken with one of these two phrases: 'I refuse a robe given by a householder,' or 'I undertake the refuse-rag wearer's practice.' This, then, is the undertaking.

Evaṃ samādinnadhutaṅgena pana tena sosānikaṃ, pāpaṇikaṃ, rathiyacoḷaṃ, saṅkāracoḷaṃ, sotthiyaṃ, nhānacoḷaṃ, titthacoḷaṃ, gatapaccāgataṃ, aggiḍaḍḍhaṃ, gokhāyitaṃ, upacikākhāyitaṃ, undūrakhāyitaṃ, antacchinnaṃ, dasācchinnaṃ, dhajāhaṭaṃ, thūpacīvaraṃ, samaṇacīvaraṃ, ābhisekikaṃ, iddhimayaṃ, panthikaṃ, vātāhaṭaṃ, devadattiyaṃ, sāmuddiyantietesu aññataraṃ cīvaraṃ gahetvā phāletvā dubbalaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya thiraṭṭhānāni dhovitvā cīvaraṃ katvā porāṇaṃ gahapaticīvaraṃ apanetvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ.

One who has thus undertaken this ascetic practice should take a cloth from any of these sources: a charnel ground, a shop, a street, a refuse heap, childbirth, a bathing place, a ford, from one who has gone to and returned from a charnel ground, one scorched by fire, chewed by a cow, eaten by termites, gnawed by rats, torn at the center, torn at the fringe, a banner, a stupa-offering, a monk's possession, a royal consecration, one created by psychic power, the wayside, one carried by the wind, one given by a deity, or one cast up by the sea. Having taken such a cloth, he should tear it, discard the weak parts, wash the strong parts, and make it into a robe. Then, having set aside his old householder's robe, he should use it.

Tattha sosānikanti susāne patitakaṃ. Pāpaṇikanti āpaṇadvāre patitakaṃ. Rathiyacoḷanti puññatthikehi vātapānantarena rathikāya chaḍḍitacoḷakaṃ. Saṅkāracoḷanti saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍitacoḷakaṃ. Sotthiyanti gabbhamalaṃ puñchitvā chaḍḍitavatthaṃ. Tissāmaccamātā kira satagghanakena vatthena gabbhamalaṃ puñchāpetvā paṃsukūlikā gaṇhissantīti tālaveḷimagge chaḍḍāpesi. Bhikkhū jiṇṇakaṭṭhānatthameva gaṇhanti. Nhānacoḷanti yaṃ bhūtavejjehi sasīsaṃ nhāpitā kāḷakaṇṇicoḷanti chaḍḍetvā gacchanti.

Therein, 'from a charnel ground' means fallen in a charnel ground. 'From a shop' means fallen at a shop door. 'From a street' refers to a rag discarded in the street through a window by those seeking merit. 'From a refuse heap' is a rag discarded in a rubbish heap. 'From childbirth' is a cloth discarded after wiping away uterine blood. It is said that the mother of the minister Tissa, after having uterine blood wiped with a cloth worth a hundred, had it discarded on the Tālaveḷi road, intending that the refuse-rag wearers would take it. Bhikkhus take it only for the purpose of mending worn-out parts. 'From a bathing place' refers to what is discarded by those who, having been bathed from head to toe by exorcists, depart, considering it an 'inauspicious cloth' (kāḷakaṇṇicoḷa).

Titthacoḷanti nhānatitthe chaḍḍitapilotikā. Gatapaccāgatanti yaṃ manussā susānaṃ gantvā paccāgatā nhatvā chaḍḍenti. Aggiḍaḍḍhanti agginā ḍaḍḍhappadesaṃ. Tañhi manussā chaḍḍenti. Gokhāyitādīni pākaṭāneva. Tādisānipi hi manussā chaḍḍenti. Dhajāhaṭanti nāvaṃ ārohantā dhajaṃ bandhitvā ārūhanti. Taṃ tesaṃ dassanātikkame gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Yampi yuddhabhūmiyaṃ dhajaṃ bandhitvā ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ dvinnampi senānaṃ gatakāle gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

'From a ford' means a worn cloth discarded at a bathing ford. 'From one who has gone to and returned' refers to what people discard after going to a charnel ground, returning, and then bathing. 'Scorched by fire' means a cloth with a part burned by fire. For people discard such a thing. 'Chewed by a cow' and the like are self-evident. For people discard such things too. 'A banner' refers to a flag that is tied when boarding a ship. It is permissible to take it after they are out of sight. Also, a flag that has been set up on a battlefield may be taken after both armies have departed.

Thūpacīvaranti [V 1.0061] vammikaṃ parikkhipitvā balikammaṃ kataṃ. Samaṇacīvaranti bhikkhusantakaṃ. Ābhisekikanti rañño abhisekaṭṭhāne chaḍḍitacīvaraṃ. Iddhimayanti ehibhikkhucīvaraṃ. Panthikanti antarāmagge patitakaṃ. Yaṃ pana sāmikānaṃ satisammosena patitaṃ, taṃ thokaṃ rakkhitvā gahetabbaṃ. Vātāhaṭanti vātena paharitvā dūre pātitaṃ, taṃ pana sāmike apassantena [M 1.0061] gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Devadattiyanti anuruddhattherassa viya devatāhi dinnakaṃ. Sāmuddiyanti samuddavīcīhi thale ussāritaṃ.

A 'stupa-offering' is a cloth with which an anthill has been draped and a ritual offering made. A 'monk's possession' is that which belongs to a bhikkhu. A 'royal consecration' cloth is a robe discarded at a king’s consecration site. One 'created by psychic power' is the robe of an 'ehi bhikkhu.' 'From the wayside' is that which has fallen in the middle of a road. However, that which has fallen due to an owner’s lapse of memory should be watched for a short time before being taken. 'Carried by the wind' is that which has been blown by the wind and cast far away; it is permissible for one who does not see the owner to take it. 'Given by a deity' is that which is given by deities, as in the case of the Elder Anuruddha. 'Cast up by the sea' is that which is cast ashore by ocean waves.

Yaṃ pana saṅghassa demāti dinnaṃ, coḷakabhikkhāya vā caramānehi laddhaṃ, na taṃ paṃsukūlaṃ. Bhikkhudattiyepi yaṃ vassaggena gāhetvā vā dīyati, senāsanacīvaraṃ vā hoti, na taṃ paṃsukūlaṃ. No gāhāpetvā dinnameva paṃsukūlaṃ. Tatrapi yaṃ dāyakehi bhikkhussa pādamūle nikkhittaṃ, tena pana bhikkhunā paṃsukūlikassa hatthe ṭhapetvā dinnaṃ, taṃ ekatosuddhikaṃ nāma. Yaṃ bhikkhuno hatthe ṭhapetvā dinnaṃ, tena pana pādamūle ṭhapitaṃ, tampi ekatosuddhikaṃ. Yaṃ bhikkhunopi pādamūle ṭhapitaṃ, tenāpi tatheva dinnaṃ, taṃ ubhatosuddhikaṃ. Yaṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā laddhaṃ, hattheyeva ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ anukkaṭṭhacīvaraṃ nāma. Iti imaṃ paṃsukūlabhedaṃ ñatvā paṃsukūlikena cīvaraṃ paribhuñjitabbanti idamettha vidhānaṃ.

However, that which is given with the words, 'We give this to the Saṅgha,' or that which is obtained by those going about for cloth-alms, is not a refuse-rag. In the case of a gift from a bhikkhu, that which is given after having been accepted according to seniority, or that which is a robe belonging to the lodging, is not a refuse-rag. Only that which is given without one having been made to accept it is a refuse-rag. Therein, when donors place a robe at a bhikkhu’s feet, and that bhikkhu then gives it to a refuse-rag wearer by placing it in his hands, it is called 'pure on one side' (ekatosuddhika). When it is given by placing it in a bhikkhu’s hands, and he then places it at the refuse-rag wearer's feet, that too is 'pure on one side.'
