When it is placed at a bhikkhu’s feet, and he gives it in that same way, it is 'pure on both sides' (ubhatosuddhika). When it is received by being placed in the hands and given by being placed in the hands, it is called a 'non-superior robe' (anukkaṭṭhacīvara). Having understood this classification of refuse-rags, the refuse-rag wearer should use the robe. This is the procedure in this matter.

Ayaṃ pana pabhedo, tayo paṃsukūlikā ukkaṭṭho majjhimo mudūti. Tattha sosānikaṃyeva gaṇhanto ukkaṭṭho hoti. Pabbajitā gaṇhissantīti ṭhapitakaṃ gaṇhanto majjhimo. Pādamūle ṭhapetvā dinnakaṃ gaṇhanto mudūti.

This, furthermore, is the classification: there are three types of refuse-rag wearers—the superior, the middling, and the inferior. Among them, one who takes only from a charnel ground is the superior. One who takes what has been set aside with the thought, 'Renunciants will take it,' is the middling. One who takes what has been given by being placed at his feet is the inferior.

Tesu yassa kassaci attano ruciyā gihidinnakaṃ sāditakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

For any one of these, should he, following his own preference, consent to a robe given by a householder, the ascetic practice is broken at the moment of consent. This is the breaking in this case.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, “paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ nissāya pabbajjā”ti (mahāva. 128) vacanato nissayānurūpapaṭipattisabbhāvo, paṭhame ariyavaṃse patiṭṭhānaṃ, ārakkhadukkhābhāvo, aparāyattavuttitā, corabhayena abhayatā, paribhogataṇhāya abhāvo, samaṇasāruppaparikkhāratā, “appāni ceva sulabhāni ca tāni ca anavajjānī”ti (a. ni. 4.27; itivu. 101) bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇitapaccayatā, pāsādikatā, appicchatādīnaṃ phalanipphatti, sammāpaṭipattiyā anubrūhanaṃ, pacchimāya janatāya diṭṭhānugatiāpādananti.

These, now, are the benefits: in accordance with the words, 'The going-forth is dependent on rag-robes' (Mahāvagga 128), there is the presence of a practice that is in conformity with the dependence; establishment in the first noble lineage; the absence of the suffering of guarding; a life not dependent on others; freedom from fear of thieves; the absence of craving for their use; suitability as a recluse's requisite; being a requisite praised by the Blessed One as 'few, easily obtained, and blameless' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.27; Itivuttaka 101); inspiring confidence; the accomplishment of the fruit of fewness of wishes and so on; the fostering of right practice; and setting an example for future generations to follow.

Mārasenavighātāya[V 1.0062], paṃsukūladharo yati;

Sannaddhakavaco yuddhe, khattiyo viya sobhati.

For destroying the army of Māra, the ascetic who wears rag-robes shines like a warrior in battle, clad in armor.

Pahāya [M 1.0062] kāsikādīni, varavatthāni dhāritaṃ;

Yaṃ lokagarunā ko taṃ, paṃsukūlaṃ na dhāraye.

Having abandoned fine cloths such as those from Kāsi, who would not wear that rag-robe which was worn by the Teacher of the world?

Tasmā hi attano bhikkhu, paṭiññaṃ samanussaraṃ;

Yogācārānukūlamhi, paṃsukūle rato siyāti.

Therefore, a bhikkhu, remembering his own pledge, should delight in the rag-robe, which is suitable for a yogī's practice.

Ayaṃ tāva paṃsukūlikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This, for now, is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, grades, breaking, and benefits of the rag-robe-wearer's practice.

2. Tecīvarikaṅgakathā

2. The Exposition on the Triple-Robe-Wearer's Practice

25. Tadanantaraṃ pana tecīvarikaṅgaṃ “catutthakacīvaraṃ paṭikkhipāmi, tecīvarikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

25. Next, the triple-robe-wearer's practice is undertaken with one of these statements: 'I refuse a fourth robe; I undertake the triple-robe-wearer's practice.'

Tena pana tecīvarikena cīvaradussaṃ labhitvā yāva aphāsukabhāvena kātuṃ vā na sakkoti, vicārakaṃ vā na labhati, sūciādīsu vāssa kiñci na sampajjati, tāva nikkhipitabbaṃ. Nikkhittapaccayā doso natthi. Rajitakālato pana paṭṭhāya nikkhipituṃ na vaṭṭati, dhutaṅgacoro nāma hoti. Idamassa vidhānaṃ.

When one who observes the triple-robe-wearer's practice has obtained robe-cloth, it may be set aside for as long as he is unable to make it up due to some difficulty, or does not find someone to see to it, or is not supplied with a needle and so on. There is no fault on account of its having been set aside. But from the time it is dyed, it is not allowable to set it aside; he becomes what is called a 'thief of the ascetic practice.' This is the procedure for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭhena rajanakāle paṭhamaṃ antaravāsakaṃ vā uttarāsaṅgaṃ vā rajitvā taṃ nivāsetvā itaraṃ rajitabbaṃ. Taṃ pārupitvā saṅghāṭi rajitabbā. Saṅghāṭiṃ pana nivāsetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Idamassa gāmantasenāsane vattaṃ. Āraññake pana dve ekato dhovitvā rajituṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā pana kañci disvā sakkoti kāsāvaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā uparikātuṃ, evaṃ āsanne ṭhāne nisīditabbaṃ. Majjhimassa rajanasālāyaṃ rajanakāsāvaṃ nāma hoti, taṃ nivāsetvā vā pārupitvā vā rajanakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Mudukassa sabhāgabhikkhūnaṃ cīvarāni nivāsetvā vā pārupitvā vā rajanakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tatraṭṭhakapaccattharaṇampi [V 1.0063] tassa vaṭṭati. Pariharituṃ pana na vaṭṭati. Sabhāgabhikkhūnaṃ cīvarampi antarantarā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Dhutaṅgatecīvarikassa pana catutthaṃ vattamānaṃ aṃsakāsāvameva vaṭṭati. Tañca kho vitthārato vidatthi, dīghato tihatthameva vaṭṭati.

In terms of grades, this practitioner is also threefold. Herein, for the strict practitioner, at the time of dyeing, first either the inner robe or the upper robe should be dyed, and having worn that, the other should be dyed. Having put on that one, the outer robe should be dyed. However, it is not permissible to wear the outer robe as an inner robe. This is his practice in a monastery near a village. But in a forest monastery, it is permissible to wash and dye two together. However, one should sit in a nearby place so that if one sees anyone, one is able to pull the robe over oneself. For the moderate practitioner, there is a so-called 'dyeing robe' in the dyeing hall; it is permissible to wear or wrap it while doing the dyeing work. For the lenient practitioner, it is permissible to wear or wrap the robes of fellow monks while doing the dyeing work. A sitting-cloth spread out there is also permissible for him. However, it is not permissible to carry it around. The robes of fellow monks are also permissible to be used from time to time. However, for one observing the three-robe ascetic practice, only a shoulder-cloth is permissible as a fourth robe that is in use. And that, indeed, is permissible to be only one span in width and three cubits in length.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi catutthakacīvaraṃ sāditakkhaṇeyeva dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, however, the ascetic practice is broken at the very moment of consenting to a fourth robe. This is the breaking in this matter.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0063] panānisaṃso, tecīvariko bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti kāyaparihārikena cīvarena. Tenassa pakkhino viya samādāyeva gamanaṃ, appasamārambhatā, vatthasannidhiparivajjanaṃ, sallahukavuttitā, atirekacīvaraloluppappahānaṃ, kappiye mattakāritāya sallekhavuttitā, appicchatādīnaṃ phalanipphattīti evamādayo guṇā sampajjantīti.

These, now, are the benefits: a bhikkhu who wears the three robes is content with a robe sufficient to protect the body. For him, like a bird, travel is simply a matter of taking his wings with him. There is little activity, avoidance of accumulating cloth, lightness of living, abandonment of greed for additional robes, a life of austerity through moderation in what is permissible, and the accomplishment of fruits such as fewness of wishes and so on—such qualities are thus attained.

Atirekavatthataṇhaṃ, pahāya sannidhivivajjito dhīro;

Santosasukharasaññū, ticīvaradharo bhavati yogī.

Having abandoned craving for extra cloth, the wise one, avoiding accumulation, knows the taste of the happiness of contentment; the yogī becomes a wearer of the three robes.

Tasmā sapattacaraṇo, pakkhīva sacīvarova yogivaro;

Sukhamanuvicaritukāmo, cīvaraniyame ratiṃ kayirāti.

Therefore, just as a bird moves about with its own wings, the supreme yogī, desiring to wander happily with only his robes, should take delight in the limitation of robes.

Ayaṃ tecīvarikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, grades, breaking, and benefits of the triple-robe-wearer's practice.

3. Piṇḍapātikaṅgakathā

3. The Exposition on the Alms-Food-Eater's Practice

26. Piṇḍapātikaṅgampi “atirekalābhaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, piṇḍapātikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

26. The alms-food-eater's practice is also undertaken with one of these statements: “I refuse extra gains; I undertake the alms-food-eater's practice.”

Tena pana piṇḍapātikena “saṅghabhattaṃ, uddesabhattaṃ, nimantanabhattaṃ, salākabhattaṃ, pakkhikaṃ, uposathikaṃ, pāṭipadikaṃ, āgantukabhattaṃ, gamikabhattaṃ, gilānabhattaṃ, gilānupaṭṭhākabhattaṃ, vihārabhattaṃ, dhurabhattaṃ, vārakabhatta”nti etāni cuddasa bhattāni na sāditabbāni. Sace pana “saṅghabhattaṃ gaṇhathā”tiādinā nayena avatvā “amhākaṃ gehe saṅgho bhikkhaṃ gaṇhātu, tumhepi bhikkhaṃ [V 1.0064] gaṇhathā”ti vatvā dinnāni honti, tāni sādituṃ vaṭṭanti. Saṅghato nirāmisasalākāpi vihāre pakkabhattampi vaṭṭatiyevāti idamassa vidhānaṃ.

That alms-food-eater should not consent to these fourteen kinds of meals: a meal for the Sangha, a meal for a specific group, a meal by invitation, a meal by ticket, a fortnightly meal, an observance-day meal, a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal, a meal for newcomers, a meal for those departing, a meal for the sick, a meal for those nursing the sick, a meal offered at a monastery, a meal offered at the entrance to the village, and a meal given by turn. But if, without using phrases such as, “Accept the meal for the Sangha,” it is given by saying, “Let the Sangha receive alms-food in our house; you too may receive alms-food,” then it is allowable to consent to it. A ticket from the Sangha for requisites other than food and a meal cooked in the monastery are also allowable. This is the procedure for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭho puratopi pacchatopi āhaṭabhikkhaṃ gaṇhati, pattadvāre ṭhatvā pattaṃ gaṇhantānampi deti, paṭikkamanaṃ āharitvā dinnabhikkhampi gaṇhati, taṃ divasaṃ pana nisīditvā bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhati. Majjhimo taṃ divasaṃ nisīditvāpi gaṇhati, svātanāya pana nādhivāseti. Mudukosvātanāyapi punadivasāyapi bhikkhaṃ adhivāseti. Te ubhopi serivihārasukhaṃ na labhanti, ukkaṭṭhova labhati. Ekasmiṃ kira [M 1.0064] gāme ariyavaṃso hoti, ukkaṭṭho itare āha – “āyāmāvuso, dhammasavanāyā”ti. Tesu eko ekenamhi, bhante, manussena nisīdāpitoti āha. Aparo mayā, bhante, svātanāya ekassa bhikkhā adhivāsitāti. Evaṃ te ubho parihīnā. Itaro pātova piṇḍāya caritvā gantvā dhammarasaṃ paṭisaṃvedesi.

By way of division, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Herein, the strict one accepts alms brought from a house further on his route or from one already passed; standing at the door of the house he has reached, he also gives his bowl to those who would take it; and he also accepts alms brought to the eating hall. However, on that day, he does not accept alms by sitting and waiting for them. The moderate one accepts alms even while sitting and waiting on that day, but he does not consent to an invitation for the next day. The lenient one consents to an invitation for the next day and also for the day after. Both of these latter two do not obtain the happiness of living at will; only the strict one obtains it. It is said that in a certain village, a discourse on the Noble Traditions was being held. The strict practitioner said to the others, “Come, venerable sirs, let us go to listen to the Dhamma.” One of them said, “Venerable sir, I have been asked by a certain person to sit and wait for a meal.” The other said, “Venerable sir, I have consented to receive alms from someone for tomorrow.” Thus, both of them missed out. The other one, having gone for alms early in the morning, went and experienced the taste of the Dhamma.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi saṅghabhattādiatirekalābhaṃ sāditakkhaṇeva dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

However, for all three of these, the ascetic observance is broken at the very moment of consenting to an extra gain, such as a meal for the Sangha. This is the breaking of the observance in this case.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, “piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjā”ti (a. ni. 4.27; itivu. 101) vacanato nissayānurūpapaṭipattisabbhāvo, dutiye ariyavaṃse patiṭṭhānaṃ, aparāyattavuttitā, “appāni ceva sulabhāni ca tāni ca anavajjānī”ti bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇitapaccayatā, kosajjanimmaddanatā, parisuddhājīvatā, sekhiyapaṭipattipūraṇaṃ, aparapositā, parānuggahakiriyā, mānappahānaṃ, rasataṇhānivāraṇaṃ, gaṇabhojanaparamparabhojanacārittasikkhāpadehi anāpattitā, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitā, sammāpaṭipattibrūhanaṃ, pacchimajanatānukampananti.

These are the benefits: (1) having a practice that conforms to the dependence, according to the saying, “The going forth depends on the morsel of almsfood”; (2) establishment in the second noble tradition; (3) living without dependence on others; (4) possessing requisites praised by the Blessed One as “few, easily obtained, and blameless”; (5) the subduing of idleness; (6) purity of livelihood; (7) fulfillment of the Sekhiya training; (8) not being supported by others; (9) the act of helping others; (10) the abandonment of conceit; (11) the prevention of craving for tastes; (12) not incurring an offense regarding the training rules on group meals, consecutive meals, and meal-round practice; (13) a way of life that conforms to fewness of wishes and other such virtues; (14) the cultivation of right practice; and (15) compassion for future generations.

Piṇḍiyālopasantuṭṭho, aparāyattajīviko;

Pahīnāhāraloluppo, hoti cātuddiso yati.

Content with morsels of almsfood, with a livelihood not dependent on others, and having abandoned greed for food, the ascetic wanders unhindered in the four directions.

Vinodayati [V 1.0065] kosajjaṃ, ājīvassa visujjhati;

Tasmā hi nātimaññeyya, bhikkhācariyāya sumedhaso.

He dispels idleness, his livelihood is purified; therefore, indeed, one of good wisdom should not disdain the practice of going for alms.

Evarūpassa hi –

For of such a one:

“Piṇḍapātikassa bhikkhuno,

Attabharassa anaññaposino;

Devāpi pihayanti tādino,

No ce lābhasilokanissito”ti.

Even the gods hold dear that steadfast monk who lives on alms, who supports himself and not another, so long as he is not dependent on gain and fame.

Ayaṃ piṇḍapātikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the exposition on the ascetic practice of eating only almsfood, concerning its undertaking, procedure, grades, breaking, and benefits.

4. Sapadānacārikaṅgakathā

4. The Discourse on the Ascetic Practice of Going for Alms in Unbroken Sequence

27. Sapadānacārikaṅgampi [M 1.0065] “loluppacāraṃ paṭikkhipāmi, sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

27. The ascetic practice of going for alms in unbroken sequence is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I reject selective wandering for alms. I undertake the ascetic practice of going for alms in unbroken sequence.”

Tena pana sapadānacārikena gāmadvāre ṭhatvā parissayābhāvo sallakkhetabbo. Yassā racchāya vā gāme vā parissayo hoti, taṃ pahāya aññattha carituṃ vaṭṭati. Yasmiṃ gharadvāre vā racchāya vā gāme vā kiñci na labhati, agāmasaññaṃ katvā gantabbaṃ. Yattha kiñci labhati, taṃ pahāya gantuṃ na vaṭṭati. Iminā ca bhikkhunā kālataraṃ pavisitabbaṃ, evañhi aphāsukaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya aññattha gantuṃ sakkhissati. Sace panassa vihāre dānaṃ dentā antarāmagge vā āgacchantā manussā pattaṃ gahetvā piṇḍapātaṃ denti vaṭṭati. Iminā ca maggaṃ gacchantenāpi bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ sampattagāmaṃ anatikkamitvā caritabbameva. Tattha alabhitvā vā thokaṃ labhitvā vā gāmapaṭipāṭiyā caritabbanti idamassa vidhānaṃ.

Now, that practitioner of going for alms in unbroken sequence should, while standing at the village gate, ascertain that there is no danger. If there is danger in a certain street or village, it is permissible to leave it and go elsewhere. If he receives nothing at a certain house door, street, or village, he should consider it a 'non-village' and proceed. Where he does receive something, it is not permissible to leave that area and go on. This monk should enter the village rather early, for in that way he will be able to leave an unsuitable place and go elsewhere. Furthermore, if people giving alms in the monastery, or people approaching him on the path, take his bowl and offer almsfood, it is permissible. And this monk, even while travelling, upon reaching a village at the time for the alms-round, must not bypass it but should go for alms there. Whether he receives nothing there or only a little, he should proceed through the village in sequential order. This is the procedure for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭho purato āhaṭabhikkhampi pacchato āhaṭabhikkhampi paṭikkamanaṃ āharitvā diyyamānampi na gaṇhati, pattadvāre pana pattaṃ vissajjeti[V 1.0066]. Imasmiñhi dhutaṅge mahākassapattherena sadiso nāma natthi. Tassapi pattavissaṭṭhaṭṭhānameva paññāyati. Majjhimo purato vā pacchato vā āhaṭampi paṭikkamanaṃ āhaṭampi gaṇhati, pattadvārepi pattaṃ vissajjeti, na pana bhikkhaṃ āgamayamāno nisīdati. Evaṃ so ukkaṭṭhapiṇḍapātikassa anulometi. Muduko taṃ divasaṃ nisīditvā āgameti.

By way of division, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Herein, the strict one does not accept alms brought from a house in front, nor from a house behind, nor those brought to the eating hall; he only hands over his bowl at the door of the house he has reached. Indeed, in this ascetic practice, there is none like the Elder Mahākassapa. For him, too, only the instance of handing over his bowl is known. The moderate one accepts alms brought from in front or from behind, and those brought to the eating hall; he also hands over his bowl at the door of the house he has reached; however, he does not sit and wait for alms. In this respect, he is similar to the strict practitioner of eating only almsfood. The lenient one sits and waits for an invitation on that day.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi loluppacāre uppannamatte dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

However, for all three of these, the ascetic observance is broken the very moment they engage in selective wandering for alms. This is the breaking of the observance in this case.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, kulesu niccanavakatā, candūpamatā, kulamaccherappahānaṃ, samānukampitā, kulūpakādīnavābhāvo, avhānānabhinandanā, abhihārena anatthikatā, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

These are the benefits: one is always new to the families; one is like the moon; one abandons possessiveness regarding families; one has equal compassion for all; there is an absence of the faults associated with being intimate with families; one does not delight in invitations; one has no need for specially brought food; and one’s conduct conforms with fewness of wishes and other such virtues.

Candūpamo [M 1.0066] niccanavo kulesu,

Amaccharī sabbasamānukampo;

Kulūpakādīnavavippamutto,

Hotīdha bhikkhu sapadānacārī.

Like the moon, ever new among families, free from possessiveness, and with equal compassion for all; liberated from the faults of being intimate with families—such is the monk in this world who goes for alms in unbroken sequence.

Loluppacārañca pahāya tasmā,

Okkhittacakkhu yugamattadassī;

Ākaṅkhamāno bhuvi sericāraṃ,

Careyya dhīro sapadānacāranti.

Therefore, abandoning selective wandering for alms, with downcast eyes, seeing only a yoke’s length ahead, the wise one who desires to roam freely on the earth should practice the observance of going for alms in unbroken sequence.

Ayaṃ sapadānacārikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the exposition on the ascetic practice of going for alms in unbroken sequence, concerning its undertaking, procedure, grades, breaking, and benefits.

5. Ekāsanikaṅgakathā

5. The Discourse on the Ascetic Practice of Eating in One Session

28. Ekāsanikaṅgampi “nānāsanabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, ekāsanikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

28. The ascetic practice of eating in one session is undertaken with one of the following statements: “I reject eating in various sessions. I undertake the ascetic practice of eating in one session.”

Tena [V 1.0067] pana ekāsanikena āsanasālāyaṃ nisīdantena therāsane anisīditvā “idaṃ mayhaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti patirūpaṃ āsanaṃ sallakkhetvā nisīditabbaṃ. Sacassa vippakate bhojane ācariyo vā upajjhāyo vā āgacchati, uṭṭhāya vattaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero panāha “āsanaṃ vā rakkheyya bhojanaṃ vā, ayañca vippakatabhojano, tasmā vattaṃ karotu, bhojanaṃ pana mā bhuñjatū”ti. Idamassa vidhānaṃ.

Now, that practitioner of eating in one sitting, when sitting in the meal hall, should not sit on an elder's seat but, having marked a suitable seat with the thought, 'This will be for me,' should sit down. If his teacher or preceptor arrives while his meal is unfinished, it is proper to rise and perform his duties. The Elder Tipiṭakacūḷābhaya, however, said: 'He should guard either the seat or the meal. And this one's meal is unfinished; therefore, let him perform his duties, but let him not eat the meal.' This is the procedure for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭho appaṃ vā hotu bahu vā, yamhi bhojane hatthaṃ otāreti, tato aññaṃ gaṇhituṃ na labhati. Sacepi manussā “therena na kiñci bhutta”nti sappiādīni āharanti, bhesajjatthameva vaṭṭanti, na āhāratthaṃ. Majjhimo yāva patte bhattaṃ na khīyati, tāva aññaṃ gaṇhituṃ labhati. Ayañhi bhojanapariyantiko nāma hoti. Muduko yāva āsanā na vuṭṭhāti tāva bhuñjituṃ labhati. So hi udakapariyantiko vā hoti yāva pattadhovanaṃ na gaṇhāti tāva bhuñjanato, āsanapariyantiko vā yāva na vuṭṭhāti tāva bhuñjanato.

As to the distinctions, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Therein, the strict practitioner, whether it be little or much, once he has lowered his hand into the food, is not allowed to take anything else. Even if people, thinking, “The elder has not eaten anything,” bring ghee and other items, these are permissible only for the purpose of medicine, not for the purpose of food. The moderate practitioner is allowed to take more as long as the food in his bowl is not exhausted. Indeed, this one is called “one for whom the meal is the limit.” The mild practitioner is allowed to eat as long as he does not rise from his seat. Indeed, he is either one who is “limited by water,” in that he eats as long as he has not taken the bowl-washing water, or one who is “limited by the seat,” in that he eats as long as he has not risen.

Imesaṃ [M 1.0067] pana tiṇṇampi nānāsanabhojanaṃ bhuttakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, however, the ascetic practice is broken at the moment of eating a meal at various sittings. This is the breaking in this case.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, appābādhatā, appātaṅkatā, lahuṭṭhānaṃ, balaṃ, phāsuvihāro, anatirittapaccayā anāpatti, rasataṇhāvinodanaṃ appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

And these are the benefits: fewness of illness, fewness of affliction, lightness of body, strength, dwelling at ease, not incurring an offense regarding leftover food, the dispelling of craving for tastes, and conduct that is in conformity with such qualities as fewness of wishes.

Ekāsanabhojane rataṃ,

Na yatiṃ bhojanapaccayā rujā;

Visahanti rase alolupo,

Parihāpeti na kammamattano.

Illnesses arising from food do not overcome the monk who delights in eating in one sitting. Not being greedy for tastes, he does not neglect his own task.

Iti phāsuvihārakāraṇe,

Sucisallekharatūpasevite;

Janayetha visuddhamānaso,

Ratimekāsanabhojane yatīti.

Therefore, in this practice of eating in one sitting—a cause for dwelling at ease, frequented by those delighting in pure austerity—a monk with a purified mind should generate delight.

Ayaṃ ekāsanikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, distinctions, breaking, and benefits of the one-sessioner's practice.

6. Pattapiṇḍikaṅgakathā

6. The Explanation of the Bowl-Food-Eater's Practice

29. Pattapiṇḍikaṅgampi [V 1.0068] “dutiyakabhājanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, pattapiṇḍikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

29. The bowl-food-eater's practice is also undertaken with one of these statements: 'I reject a second vessel,' or 'I undertake the bowl-food-eater's practice.'

Tena pana pattapiṇḍikena yāgupānakāle bhājane ṭhapetvā byañjane laddhe byañjanaṃ vā paṭhamaṃ khāditabbaṃ, yāgu vā pātabbā. Sace pana yāguyaṃ pakkhipati, pūtimacchakādimhi byañjane pakkhitte yāgu paṭikūlā hoti, appaṭikūlameva ca katvā bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmā tathārūpaṃ byañjanaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana madhusakkarādikaṃ appaṭikūlaṃ hoti, taṃ pakkhipitabbaṃ. Gaṇhantena ca pamāṇayuttameva gaṇhitabbaṃ. Āmakasākaṃ hatthena gahetvā khādituṃ vaṭṭati. Tathā pana akatvā patteyeva pakkhipitabbaṃ. Dutiyakabhājanassa pana paṭikkhittattā aññaṃ rukkhapaṇṇampi na vaṭṭatīti idamassa vidhānaṃ.

Now, by that bowl-food-eater, at the time of drinking gruel, when a condiment is received placed in a vessel, either the condiment should be eaten first or the gruel should be drunk. But if one puts it into the gruel, when a condiment such as rotten fish is put in, the gruel becomes disagreeable, and it is proper to eat only after making it not disagreeable. Therefore, this was said in reference to such a condiment. But whatever is not disagreeable, such as honey and sugar, may be put in. And when receiving, only a suitable amount should be received. It is proper to take raw greens with the hand and eat them. However, not doing so, they should be put into the bowl itself. And since a second vessel is rejected, not even another tree leaf is proper. This is the procedure for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭhassa aññatra ucchukhādanakālā kacavarampi chaḍḍetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Odanapiṇḍamacchamaṃsapūvepi bhinditvā [M 1.0068] khādituṃ na vaṭṭati. Majjhimassa ekena hatthena bhinditvā khādituṃ vaṭṭati, hatthayogī nāmesa. Muduko pana pattayogī nāma hoti, tassa yaṃ sakkā hoti patte pakkhipituṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ hatthena vā dantehi vā bhinditvā khādituṃ vaṭṭati.

As to the distinctions, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Therein, for the strict practitioner, apart from the time of eating sugarcane, it is not proper to discard even refuse. It is not proper to eat even lumps of rice, fish, meat, or cakes after breaking them. For the moderate practitioner, it is proper to break and eat with one hand; he is called a 'hand-user.' But the mild practitioner is called a 'bowl-user'; for him, whatever can be put into the bowl, all that may be broken by hand or teeth and eaten.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi dutiyakabhājanaṃ sāditakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, the ascetic practice is broken at the moment of accepting a second vessel. This is the breaking in this case.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, nānārasataṇhāvinodanaṃ. Atricchatāya pahānaṃ, āhāre payojanamattadassitā, thālakādipariharaṇakhedābhāvo, avikkhittabhojitā, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

And these are the benefits: the dispelling of craving for various tastes, the abandoning of excessive desire, seeing only the purpose in food, the absence of weariness from carrying plates and the like, undistracted eating, and conduct in conformity with qualities like fewness of wishes.

Nānābhājanavikkhepaṃ, hitvā okkhittalocano;

Khaṇanto viya mūlāni, rasataṇhāya subbato.

Having abandoned the distraction of various vessels, with downcast eyes, the well-disciplined one digs up, as it were, the roots of craving for tastes.

Sarūpaṃ [V 1.0069] viya santuṭṭhiṃ, dhārayanto sumānaso;

Paribhuñjeyya āhāraṃ, ko añño pattapiṇḍikoti.

Bearing contentment as if it were his very form, with a joyful mind, he should partake of food. Who else is a practitioner of eating only from the bowl?

Ayaṃ pattapiṇḍikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, distinctions, breaking, and benefits concerning the practice of eating only from the bowl.

7. Khalupacchābhattikaṅgakathā

7. The Explanation of the Practice of Refusing Subsequent Food

30. Khalupacchābhattikaṅgampi “atirittabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, khalupacchābhattikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

30. The practice of refusing subsequent food is also undertaken by one of these statements: 'I reject leftover food; I undertake the practice of refusing subsequent food.'

Tena pana khalupacchābhattikena pavāretvā puna bhojanaṃ kappiyaṃ kāretvā na bhuñjitabbaṃ. Idamassa vidhānaṃ.

By that practitioner of refusing subsequent food, having made a declaration of sufficiency, one should not have food made allowable again and eat it. This is the procedure for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭho yasmā paṭhamapiṇḍe pavāraṇā nāma natthi, tasmiṃ pana ajjhohariyamāne aññaṃ paṭikkhipato hoti, tasmā evaṃ pavārito paṭhamapiṇḍaṃ ajjhoharitvā dutiyapiṇḍaṃ na bhuñjati. Majjhimo yasmiṃ bhojane pavārito, tadeva bhuñjati. Muduko pana yāva āsanā na vuṭṭhāti tāva bhuñjati.

As to the distinctions, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Therein, for the strict practitioner, since there is no declaration of sufficiency regarding the first morsel, but when that is being consumed, he refuses another, therefore, having thus made a declaration of sufficiency, he consumes the first morsel but does not eat a second morsel. The moderate practitioner eats only that food with which he was eating when he made the declaration of sufficiency. But the mild practitioner eats as long as he does not rise from his seat.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi pavāritānaṃ kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā bhuttakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, having made the declaration of sufficiency, the ascetic practice is broken at the moment of eating after having had food made allowable. This is the breaking in this case.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0069] panānisaṃso, anatirittabhojanāpattiyā dūrabhāvo, odarikattābhāvo, nirāmisasannidhitā, puna pariyesanāya abhāvo, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

And these are the benefits: being far from the offense of eating food that is not a leftover, absence of gluttony, not storing up provisions, absence of further searching, and conduct in conformity with qualities such as fewness of wishes.

Pariyesanāya khedaṃ, na yāti na karoti sannidhiṃ dhīro;

Odarikattaṃ pajahati, khalupacchābhattiko yogī.

The wise one does not experience weariness from searching, nor does he make a store. The yogi who refuses subsequent food abandons gluttony.

Tasmā [V 1.0070] sugatapasatthaṃ, santosaguṇādivuḍḍhisañjananaṃ;

Dose vidhunitukāmo, bhajeyya yogī dhutaṅgamidanti.

Therefore, wishing to shake off faults, the yogi should cultivate this ascetic practice, praised by the Sugata, which generates growth in virtues like contentment.

Ayaṃ khalupacchābhattikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, grades, breaking, and benefits of the practice of refusing subsequent food.

8. Āraññikaṅgakathā

8. Discourse on the Forest-Dweller's Practice

31. Āraññikaṅgampi “gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, āraññikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

31. The forest-dweller's practice is also undertaken by one of these statements: "I reject a dwelling near a village; I undertake the forest-dweller's practice."

Tena pana āraññikena gāmantasenāsanaṃ pahāya araññe aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Tattha saddhiṃ upacārena gāmoyeva gāmantasenāsanaṃ.

That forest-dweller, having abandoned a dwelling near a village, should let the dawn rise upon him in the forest. Therein, a dwelling near a village is the village itself together with its vicinity.

Gāmo nāma yo koci ekakuṭiko vā anekakuṭiko vā parikkhitto vā aparikkhitto vā samanusso vā amanusso vā antamaso atirekacātumāsaniviṭṭho yo koci satthopi.

A village is any place with one hut or many huts, enclosed or unenclosed, inhabited by humans or uninhabited, or even any caravan that has been settled for more than four months.

Gāmūpacāro nāma parikkhittassa gāmassa sace anurādhapurasseva dve indakhīlā honti, abbhantarime indakhīle ṭhitassa thāmamajjhimassa purisassa leḍḍupāto. Tassa lakkhaṇaṃ yathā taruṇamanussā attano balaṃ dassentā bāhaṃ pasāretvā leḍḍuṃ khipanti, evaṃ khittassa leḍḍussa patanaṭṭhānabbhantaranti vinayadharā. Suttantikā pana kākanivāraṇaniyamena khittassāti vadanti. Aparikkhittagāme yaṃ sabbapaccantimassa gharassa dvāre ṭhito mātugāmo bhājanena udakaṃ chaḍḍeti, tassa patanaṭṭhānaṃ gharūpacāro. Tato vuttanayena eko leḍḍupāto gāmo, dutiyo gāmūpacāro.

The vicinity of a village is defined as follows: For an enclosed village, if, like Anurādhapura, it has two gate-posts, it is the distance of a clod-throw by a man of medium strength standing at the inner gate-post. Its characteristic is this: The Vinaya experts say it is the area within the landing spot of a clod thrown as young men, displaying their strength, throw a clod by extending their arm. But the Sutta experts say it is the distance of a clod thrown according to the rule for scaring away crows. In an unenclosed village, the landing spot of water that a woman standing at the door of the outermost house throws from a vessel is the vicinity of the house. From that point, by the method stated, one clod-throw is the village, and a second is the village-vicinity.

Araññaṃ pana vinayapariyāye tāva “ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (pārā. 92) vuttaṃ. Abhidhammapariyāye “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā, sabbametaṃ [M 1.0070] arañña”nti (vibha. 529) vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana suttantikapariyāye “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ. Taṃ āropitena ācariyadhanunā parikkhittassa gāmassa [V 1.0071] indakhīlato aparikkhittassa paṭhamaleḍḍupātato paṭṭhāya yāva vihāraparikkhepā minitvā vavatthapetabbaṃ.

In the Vinaya context, it is said, 'Excluding the village and its vicinity, all of that is wilderness' (Pārā. 92). In the Abhidhamma context, it is said, 'Everything outside the gate-post is wilderness' (Vibh. 529). But in this Sutta context, the characteristic is this: 'A wilderness dwelling is at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths.' That should be measured and determined using a teacher's bow, starting from the gate-post of an enclosed village or from the first clod-throw of an unenclosed one, up to the monastery's boundary.

Sace pana vihāro aparikkhitto hoti, yaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ senāsanaṃ vā bhattasālā vā dhuvasannipātaṭṭhānaṃ vā bodhi vā cetiyaṃ vā dūre cepi senāsanato hoti, taṃ paricchedaṃ katvā minitabbanti vinayaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana vihārassapi gāmasseva upacāraṃ nīharitvā ubhinnaṃ leḍḍupātānaṃ antarā minitabbanti vuttaṃ. Idamettha pamāṇaṃ.

If the monastery is unenclosed, it is said in the Vinaya commentaries that the measurement should be made by defining a boundary that includes the very first lodging, or dining hall, or regular assembly place, or Bodhi tree, or shrine, even if it is far from the lodging. But in the Majjhima commentary, it is said that the vicinity of the monastery should be drawn out just like that of a village, and the measurement taken between the two clod-throws. This is the measure here.

Sacepi āsanne gāmo hoti, vihāre ṭhitehi mānusakānaṃ saddo suyyati, pabbatanadīādīhi pana antaritattā na sakkā ujuṃ gantuṃ. Yo tassa pakatimaggo hoti, sacepi nāvāya sañcaritabbo, tena maggena pañcadhanusatikaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Yo pana āsannagāmassa aṅgasampādanatthaṃ tato tato maggaṃ pidahati, ayaṃ dhutaṅgacoro hoti.

Even if a village is nearby, and the voices of people are heard by those staying in the monastery, but it is not possible to go directly because of being obstructed by mountains, rivers, and so on. Whatever its natural path may be, even if it must be traversed by boat, the five hundred bow-lengths should be measured along that path. But whoever blocks paths here and there in order to fulfill the factor of distance from a nearby village is a thief of the ascetic practice.

Sace pana āraññikassa bhikkhuno upajjhāyo vā ācariyo vā gilāno hoti, tena araññe sappāyaṃ alabhantena gāmantasenāsanaṃ netvā upaṭṭhātabbo. Kālasseva pana nikkhamitvā aṅgayuttaṭṭhāne aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Sace aruṇuṭṭhānavelāyaṃ tesaṃ ābādho vaḍḍhati, tesaṃyeva kiccaṃ kātabbaṃ. Na dhutaṅgasuddhikena bhavitabbanti idamassa vidhānaṃ.

If a wilderness-dwelling bhikkhu's preceptor or teacher is ill, and he cannot find what is suitable in the wilderness, he should take them to a village dwelling and attend to them. But he should leave early and cause the dawn to arise in a place that fulfills the conditions for the practice. If their illness worsens at the time of dawn's arising, their needs should be attended to. He should not be one whose purification is merely by the ascetic practice—this is its regulation.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭhena sabbakālaṃ araññe aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Majjhimo cattāro vassike māse gāmante vasituṃ labhati. Muduko hemantikepi.

In terms of its divisions, this practice is also threefold. Among these, for the strict practitioner, dawn must be made to arise in the forest at all times. The moderate practitioner is permitted to dwell near a village for the four months of the rainy season. The lenient practitioner may do so even during the cool season.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi yathā paricchinne kāle araññato āgantvā gāmantasenāsane dhammassavanaṃ suṇantānaṃ aruṇe uṭṭhitepi dhutaṅgaṃ na bhijjati. Sutvā gacchantānaṃ antarāmagge uṭṭhitepi na bhijjati. Sace pana uṭṭhitepi dhammakathike muhuttaṃ nipajjitvā gamissāmāti niddāyantānaṃ aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahati, attano vā ruciyā gāmantasenāsane aruṇaṃ uṭṭhapenti, dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjatīti ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, if they return from the forest at the appointed time and listen to the Dhamma in a village dwelling, their ascetic practice is not broken even if dawn arises while they are listening. Nor is it broken if dawn arises on the way back after listening. However, if, even after the Dhamma-speaker has risen, they lie down for a moment, thinking, "We will leave after a short rest," and dawn arises while they are sleeping, or if they willingly cause dawn to arise in a village dwelling, their ascetic practice is broken—this is the breaking here.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0071] panānisaṃso, āraññiko bhikkhu araññasaññaṃ manasikaronto bhabbo aladdhaṃ vā [V 1.0072] samādhiṃ paṭiladdhuṃ laddhaṃ vā rakkhituṃ, satthāpissa attamano hoti. Yathāha – “tenāhaṃ, nāgita, tassa bhikkhuno attamano homi araññavihārenā”ti (a. ni. 6.42; 8.86). Pantasenāsanavāsino cassa asappāyarūpādayo cittaṃ na vikkhipanti, vigatasantāso hoti, jīvitanikantiṃ jahati, pavivekasukharasaṃ assādeti, paṃsukūlikādibhāvopi cassa patirūpo hotīti.

This is the benefit: A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, attending to the perception of the forest, is capable of attaining unobtained concentration or maintaining what has been obtained. The Teacher is also pleased with him, as it is said: "Therefore, Nāgita, I am pleased with that bhikkhu because of his forest dwelling" (AN 6.42; 8.86). For one who dwells in remote lodgings, unsuitable sights and so forth do not distract the mind; he becomes free from dread, abandons craving for life, savors the taste of the bliss of seclusion, and the state of being a rag-robe wearer and so forth is suitable for him.

Pavivitto asaṃsaṭṭho, pantasenāsane rato;

Ārādhayanto nāthassa, vanavāsena mānasaṃ.

Secluded, unassociated, delighting in remote lodgings, gladdening the Protector's mind with forest dwelling.

Eko araññe nivasaṃ, yaṃ sukhaṃ labhate yati;

Rasaṃ tassa na vindanti, api devā saindakā.

The happiness a striving one obtains dwelling alone in the forest—even the gods with Indra do not find its flavor.

Paṃsukūlañca esova, kavacaṃ viya dhārayaṃ;

Araññasaṅgāmagato, avasesadhutāyudho.

Wearing the rag-robe like armor, having gone to the forest battle, armed with the remaining ascetic practices.

Samattho nacirasseva, jetuṃ māraṃ savāhiniṃ;

Tasmā araññavāsamhi, ratiṃ kayirātha paṇḍitoti.

He is capable of conquering Māra with his army before long; therefore, a wise one should cultivate delight in forest dwelling.

Ayaṃ āraññikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, divisions, grounds for breaking, and benefits of the forest-dweller's practice.

9. Rukkhamūlikaṅgakathā

9. The Discourse on the Tree-Root Dweller's Practice

32. Rukkhamūlikaṅgampi “channaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

32. The tree-root-dweller's practice is also undertaken with one of these statements: 'I reject a roofed dwelling,' or 'I undertake the tree-root-dweller's practice.'

Tena pana rukkhamūlikena sīmantarikarukkhaṃ, cetiyarukkhaṃ, niyyāsarukkhaṃ, phalarukkhaṃ, vaggulirukkhaṃ, susirarukkhaṃ, vihāramajjhe ṭhitarukkhanti ime rukkhe vivajjetvā vihārapaccante ṭhitarukkho gahetabboti idamassa vidhānaṃ.

However, a tree-root dweller should avoid these trees: a tree on a boundary, a shrine tree, a tree that exudes sap, a fruit tree, a tree inhabited by bats, a hollow tree, and a tree standing in the middle of a monastery. A tree standing at the edge of the monastery should be chosen—this is the rule for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭho yathārucitaṃ rukkhaṃ gahetvā paṭijaggāpetuṃ na labhati. Pādena paṇṇasaṭaṃ apanetvā vasitabbaṃ. Majjhimo taṃ ṭhānaṃ sampattehiyeva paṭijaggāpetuṃ labhati. Mudukena ārāmikasamaṇuddese pakkositvā sodhāpetvā samaṃ kārāpetvā [V 1.0073] vālukaṃ okirāpetvā pākāraparikkhepaṃ kārāpetvā dvāraṃ [M 1.0072] yojāpetvā vasitabbaṃ. Mahadivase pana rukkhamūlikena tattha anisīditvā aññattha paṭicchanne ṭhāne nisīditabbaṃ.

In terms of classification, this practice is also of three kinds. Herein, the strict practitioner is not allowed to have his chosen tree tended; he must remove the fallen leaves with his foot and dwell there. The moderate practitioner is allowed to have the place tended only by those who happen to come there. The mild practitioner may call a monastery attendant or a novice to have the place cleaned, leveled, have sand scattered, a surrounding wall built, and a gate installed before dwelling there. On great festival days, however, a tree-root dweller should not sit there, but should sit elsewhere in a sheltered place.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi channe vāsaṃ kappitakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Jānitvā channe aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpitamatteti aṅguttarabhāṇakā. Ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, the ascetic practice is broken the moment they resolve to dwell under a roof. The Aṅguttara reciters say it is broken merely by allowing the dawn to arise while one is knowingly under a roof. This is the breaking point herein.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ nissāya pabbajjāti (mahāva. 128) vacanato nissayānurūpapaṭipattisabbhāvo, appāni ceva sulabhāni ca tāni ca anavajjānīti (a. ni. 4.27; itivu. 101) bhagavatā saṃvaṇṇitapaccayatā, abhiṇhaṃ tarupaṇṇavikāradassanena aniccasaññāsamuṭṭhāpanatā, senāsanamaccherakammārāmatānaṃ abhāvo, devatāhi sahavāsitā, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

This, in turn, is the benefit: the existence of a practice suitable for the 'dependence,' in accordance with the statement, “The going forth is dependent on the lodging at the root of a tree”; the quality of having requisites praised by the Blessed One as being “few, easily obtained, and blameless”; the arising of the perception of impermanence by frequently seeing the changing of the tree's leaves; the absence of stinginess regarding lodging and of delight in construction work; dwelling together with deities; and conduct that conforms with having few desires and so forth.

Vaṇṇito buddhaseṭṭhena, nissayoti ca bhāsito;

Nivāso pavivittassa, rukkhamūlasamo kuto.

Praised by the Best of Buddhas, and spoken of as a 'dependence'; for one who is secluded, what dwelling is there equal to the root of a tree?

Āvāsamaccherahare, devatā paripālite;

Pavivitte vasanto hi, rukkhamūlamhi subbato.

Indeed, the well-disciplined one dwells in seclusion at the root of a tree—a place that removes stinginess regarding dwellings and is guarded by deities.

Abhirattāni nīlāni, paṇḍūni patitāni ca;

Passanto tarupaṇṇāni, niccasaññaṃ panūdati.

Beholding the reddish, dark-hued, yellow, and fallen leaves of trees, one dispels the perception of permanence.

Tasmā hi buddhadāyajjaṃ, bhāvanābhiratālayaṃ;

Vivittaṃ nātimaññeyya, rukkhamūlaṃ vicakkhaṇoti.

Therefore, a wise person should not disdain the secluded root of a tree, the heritage of the Buddha, an abode for delighting in spiritual cultivation.

Ayaṃ rukkhamūlikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breaking, and benefits of the tree-root-dweller's practice.

10. Abbhokāsikaṅgakathā

10. The Discourse on the Open-Air-Dweller's Practice

33. Abbhokāsikaṅgampi [V 1.0074] “channañca rukkhamūlañca paṭikkhipāmi, abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

33. The open-air-dweller's practice is also undertaken with one of these statements: 'I reject a roofed dwelling and the root of a tree,' or 'I undertake the open-air-dweller's practice.'

Tassa pana abbhokāsikassa dhammassavanāya vā uposathatthāya vā uposathāgāraṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace paviṭṭhassa devo vassati, deve vassamāne anikkhamitvā vassūparame nikkhamitabbaṃ. Bhojanasālaṃ vā aggisālaṃ vā pavisitvā vattaṃ kātuṃ, bhojanasālāya there bhikkhū bhattena āpucchituṃ, uddisantena vā uddisāpentena vā channaṃ pavisituṃ, bahi dunnikkhittāni mañcapīṭhādīni anto pavesetuñca vaṭṭati. Sace maggaṃ gacchantena vuḍḍhatarānaṃ [M 1.0073] parikkhāro gahito hoti, deve vassante maggamajjhe ṭhitaṃ sālaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. Sace na kiñci gahitaṃ hoti, sālāya ṭhassāmīti vegena gantuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pakatigatiyā gantvā paviṭṭhena pana yāva vassūparamā ṭhatvā gantabbanti idamassa vidhānaṃ. Rukkhamūlikassāpi eseva nayo.

However, for such an open-air dweller, it is allowable to enter an observance hall for listening to the Dhamma or for the purpose of the observance day. If it rains after he has entered, he should not leave while it is raining but should leave when the rain stops. It is also allowable for him to enter a meal hall or a fire hall to perform his duties; to inform the elder bhikkhus in the meal hall about the meal; to enter a roofed place when reciting or having a recitation done; and to bring inside any beds, benches, and so forth, that have been left outside in a disorderly way. If, while traveling, he is carrying the requisites of elder bhikkhus and it begins to rain, it is allowable for him to enter a hall situated on the road. If he is carrying nothing, it is not allowable for him to hurry to a hall with the thought, 'I will take shelter in the hall.' Rather, having proceeded at his normal pace and entered, he should remain there until the rain stops and then depart. This is the procedure for him. This same principle also applies to the tree-root dweller.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭhassa rukkhaṃ vā pabbataṃ vā gehaṃ vā upanissāya vasituṃ na vaṭṭati. Abbhokāseyeva cīvarakuṭiṃ katvā vasitabbaṃ. Majjhimassa rukkhapabbatagehāni upanissāya anto appavisitvā vasituṃ vaṭṭati. Mudukassa acchannamariyādaṃ pabbhārampi sākhāmaṇḍapopi pīṭhapaṭopi khettarakkhakādīhi chaḍḍitā tatraṭṭhakakuṭikāpi vaṭṭatīti.

In terms of classification, this practice is also of three kinds. For the strict practitioner, it is not allowable to dwell in dependence on a tree, a mountain, or a house. He should make a hut of robes right in the open and dwell there. For the moderate practitioner, it is allowable to dwell in dependence on a tree, a mountain, or a house, without entering inside. For the mild practitioner, an open-fronted cave, a bower of branches, a screen of cloth, or a small temporary hut abandoned by field-watchers and others is also allowable.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi vāsatthāya channaṃ vā rukkhamūlaṃ vā paviṭṭhakkhaṇe dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Jānitvā tattha aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpitamatteti aṅguttarabhāṇakā. Ayamettha bhedo.

For all three of these, however, the ascetic practice is broken at the moment they enter a roofed dwelling or the root of a tree for the purpose of dwelling. The Aṅguttara reciters say that it is broken merely by knowingly allowing dawn to arise there. This is the breaking point herein.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, āvāsapalibodhupacchedo, thinamiddhapanūdanaṃ, “migā viya asaṅgacārino, aniketā viharanti bhikkhavo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.224) pasaṃsāya anurūpatā, nissaṅgatā, cātuddisatā, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

This, however, is the benefit: the cutting off of the impediment of dwellings, the dispelling of sloth and torpor, conformity with the praise, 'Like deer, bhikkhus wander unattached, living without a home,' non-attachment, being able to go in any of the four directions, and a mode of conduct in accordance with such qualities as having few wants.

Anagāriyabhāvassa[V 1.0075], anurūpe adullabhe;

Tārāmaṇivitānamhi, candadīpappabhāsite.

In a dwelling fitting for the homeless state, not difficult to obtain, under a canopy of star-jewels, illuminated by the lamp of the moon,

Abbhokāse vasaṃ bhikkhu, migabhūtena cetasā;

Thinamiddhaṃ vinodetvā, bhāvanārāmataṃ sito.

A bhikkhu dwelling in the open air, with a mind that has become like a deer's, having dispelled sloth and torpor, resorts to delight in meditation.

Pavivekarasassādaṃ, nacirasseva vindati;

Yasmā tasmā hi sappañño, abbhokāsarato siyāti.

Soon he finds the savor of seclusion; therefore, indeed, a wise person should delight in the open air.

Ayaṃ abbhokāsikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breaking, and benefits of the open-air-dweller's practice.

11. Sosānikaṅgakathā

11. The Discourse on the Charnel-Ground-Dweller's Practice

34. Sosānikaṅgampi [M 1.0074] “na susānaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, sosānikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

34. The charnel-ground-dweller's practice is also undertaken with one of these statements: 'I reject a non-charnel ground,' or 'I undertake the charnel-ground-dweller's practice.'

Tena pana sosānikena yaṃ manussā gāmaṃ nivesantā “idaṃ susāna”nti vavatthapenti, na tattha vasitabbaṃ. Na hi matasarīre ajjhāpite taṃ susānaṃ nāma hoti, jhāpitakālato pana paṭṭhāya sacepi dvādasavassāni chaḍḍitaṃ, taṃ susānameva.

However, such a charnel-ground dweller should not dwell in a place that people, when establishing a village, designate as 'this is a charnel ground.' For it is not called a charnel ground before a dead body has been cremated there. But from the time of cremation onwards, even if it has been abandoned for twelve years, it is still a charnel ground.

Tasmiṃ pana vasantena caṅkamamaṇḍapādīni kāretvā mañcapīṭhaṃ paññapetvā pānīyaparibhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā dhammaṃ vācentena na vasitabbaṃ. Garukaṃ hi idaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ, tasmā uppannaparissayavighātatthāya saṅghattheraṃ vā rājayuttakaṃ vā jānāpetvā appamattena vasitabbaṃ. Caṅkamantena addhakkhikena āḷāhanaṃ olokentena caṅkamitabbaṃ.

However, while dwelling there, one should not do so having had walking paths, pavilions, and so on constructed, having had a bed and chair set up, having had water for drinking and use provided, or while teaching the Dhamma. For this is a weighty ascetic practice. Therefore, to ward off any danger that has arisen, one should inform a senior elder of the Saṅgha or a royal official and dwell with heedfulness. While doing walking meditation, one should walk looking at the cremation ground with half-closed eyes.

Susānaṃ gacchantenāpi mahāpathā ukkamma uppathamaggena gantabbaṃ. Divāyeva ārammaṇaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Evañhissa taṃ rattiṃ bhayānakaṃ na bhavissati, amanussā rattiṃ viravitvā viravitvā āhiṇḍantāpi na kenaci paharitabbā. Ekadivasampi susānaṃ agantuṃ na vaṭṭati. Majjhimayāmaṃ [V 1.0076] susāne khepetvā pacchimayāme paṭikkamituṃ vaṭṭatīti aṅguttarabhāṇakā. Amanussānaṃ piyaṃ tilapiṭṭhamāsabhattamacchamaṃsakhīratelaguḷādikhajjabhojjaṃ na sevitabbaṃ. Kulagehaṃ na pavisitabbanti idamassa vidhānaṃ.

Even when going to the charnel ground, one should deviate from the main road and go by a side path. An object should be marked out during the day itself. Thus, it will not be terrifying for him at night. And although non-human beings wander around at night, crying out repeatedly, they should not be struck by anyone. One must not fail to go to the charnel ground even for a single day. The Aṅguttara reciters say that it is proper to spend the middle watch in the charnel ground and return in the last watch. Food dear to non-human beings—such as sesame paste, bean-rice, fish, meat, milk, oil, and molasses—should not be consumed. One should not enter a family's home. This is the rule for him.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭhena yattha dhuvaḍāhadhuvakuṇapadhuvarodanāni atthi, tattheva vasitabbaṃ. Majjhimassa tīsu ekasmimpi sati vaṭṭati. Mudukassa vuttanayena susānalakkhaṇaṃ pattamatte vaṭṭati.

By way of division, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Therein, the strict practitioner should dwell only where there are constant burnings, constant corpses, and constant lamentations. For the middling practitioner, it is allowable if even one of these three is present. For the mild practitioner, it is allowable in a place that has merely attained the characteristics of a charnel ground in the way described.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi na susānamhi vāsaṃ kappanena dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Susānaṃ agatadivaseti aṅguttarabhāṇakā. Ayamettha bhedo.

However, for all three of these, the ascetic practice is broken by making one's dwelling in a place that is not a charnel ground. The Aṅguttara reciters say it is broken on the day one does not go to the charnel ground. This is the breaking here.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso maraṇassatipaṭilābho, appamādavihāritā, asubhanimittādhigamo, kāmarāgavinodanaṃ, abhiṇhaṃ kāyasabhāvadassanaṃ, saṃvegabahulatā [M 1.0075] ārogyamadādippahānaṃ, bhayabheravasahanatā, amanussānaṃ garubhāvanīyatā, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

And these are the benefits: the gaining of mindfulness of death, dwelling heedfully, attainment of the sign of the unattractive, removal of sensual desire, frequent seeing of the nature of the body, abundance of spiritual urgency, abandoning intoxication with health and so on, endurance of fear and dread, being regarded with respect by non-humans, and conduct in conformity with fewness of wishes and so on.

Sosānikañhi maraṇānusatippabhāvā,

Niddāgatampi na phusanti pamādadosā;

Sampassato ca kuṇapāni bahūni tassa,

Kāmānubhāvavasagampi na hoti cittaṃ.

For the charnel-ground dweller, by the power of mindfulness of death, the faults of heedlessness do not touch him even when asleep. And for him, seeing many corpses, his mind does not come under the sway of sensual power.

Saṃvegameti vipulaṃ na madaṃ upeti,

Sammā atho ghaṭati nibbutimesamāno;

Sosānikaṅgamitinekaguṇāvahattā,

Nibbānaninnahadayena nisevitabbanti.

He attains abundant spiritual urgency, he does not fall into intoxication, and then strives rightly, seeking Nibbāna. Because the charnel-ground practice brings forth these many qualities, it should be cultivated by one whose heart is inclined towards Nibbāna.

Ayaṃ sosānikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, divisions, breaking, and benefits of the charnel-ground practice.

12. Yathāsanthatikaṅgakathā

12. The Discourse on the Any-Lodging-As-Allotted Practice

35. Yathāsanthatikaṅgampi [V 1.0077] “senāsanaloluppaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, yathāsanthatikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

35. The any-lodging-as-allotted practice is also undertaken by means of one of these statements: "I reject greed for lodgings," or "I undertake the any-lodging-as-allotted practice."

Tena pana yathāsanthatikena yadassa senāsanaṃ “idaṃ tuyhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti gāhitaṃ hoti, teneva tuṭṭhabbaṃ, na añño uṭṭhāpetabbo. Idamassa vidhānaṃ.

That practitioner of the any-lodging-as-allotted practice should be content with whatever lodging has been assigned to him with the words, "This falls to you," and he should not displace another. This is his rule.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭho attano pattasenāsanaṃ dūreti vā accāsanneti vā amanussadīghajātikādīhi upaddutanti vā uṇhanti vā sītalanti vā pucchituṃ na labhati. Majjhimo pucchituṃ labhati. Gantvā pana oloketuṃ na labhati. Muduko gantvā oloketvā sacassa taṃ na ruccati, aññaṃ gahetuṃ labhati.

By way of division, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Herein, the strict practitioner is not allowed to ask about the lodging he has received, whether it is far or too near, or troubled by non-human beings, serpents, and so on, or whether it is hot or cold. The middling practitioner is allowed to ask, but he is not allowed to go and inspect it. The mild practitioner is allowed to go and inspect it, and if it does not suit him, he is allowed to take another.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi senāsanaloluppe uppannamatte dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjatīti ayamettha bhedo.

However, for all three of these, the ascetic practice is broken the moment greed for lodgings arises. This is the breaking here.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, “yaṃ laddhaṃ tena tuṭṭhabba”nti (jā. 1.1.136; pāci. 793) vuttovādakaraṇaṃ, sabrahmacārīnaṃ hitesitā, hīnapaṇītavikappapariccāgo, anurodhavirodhappahānaṃ, atricchatāya dvārapidahanaṃ, appicchatādīnaṃ anulomavuttitāti.

And these are the benefits: following the advice, "one should be content with what has been obtained"; seeking the welfare of fellow practitioners; abandoning the discrimination between inferior and superior; abandoning partiality and opposition; closing the door to excessive desire; and conduct in conformity with fewness of wishes, and so on.

Yaṃ [M 1.0076] laddhaṃ tena santuṭṭho, yathāsanthatiko yati;

Nibbikappo sukhaṃ seti, tiṇasantharakesupi.

Content with what he has gained, the ascetic who accepts his allotted place, free from discrimination, sleeps happily, even on a pallet of grass.

Na so rajjati seṭṭhamhi, hīnaṃ laddhā na kuppati;

Sabrahmacārinavake, hitena anukampati.

He is not attached to the best; having received the inferior, he is not angered. He has compassion for junior fellow practitioners for their welfare.

Tasmā ariyasatāciṇṇaṃ, munipuṅgavavaṇṇitaṃ;

Anuyuñjetha medhāvī, yathāsanthatarāmatanti.

Therefore, let the wise one diligently apply himself to the delight in whatever lodging is allotted, a practice frequented by the noble ones and praised by the bull among sages.

Ayaṃ yathāsanthatikaṅge samādānavidhānappabhedabhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, divisions, breaking, and benefits concerning the any-lodging-as-allotted practice.

13. Nesajjikaṅgakathā

13. The Discourse on the Sitter's Practice

36. Nesajjikaṅgampi [V 1.0078] “seyyaṃ paṭikkhipāmi, nesajjikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmī”ti imesaṃ aññataravacanena samādinnaṃ hoti.

36. The sitter's practice, too, is undertaken by one of these statements: "I reject lying down; I undertake the sitter's practice."

Tena pana nesajjikena rattiyā tīsu yāmesu ekaṃ yāmaṃ uṭṭhāya caṅkamitabbaṃ. Iriyāpathesu hi nipajjitumeva na vaṭṭati. Idamassa vidhānaṃ.

That practitioner of the sitter's practice should rise and walk during one of the three watches of the night. For among the postures, it is only lying down that is not permissible. This is his rule.

Pabhedato pana ayampi tividho hoti. Tattha ukkaṭṭhassa neva apassenaṃ, na dussapallatthikā, na āyogapaṭṭo vaṭṭati. Majjhimassa imesu tīsu yaṃkiñci vaṭṭati. Mudukassa apassenampi dussapallatthikāpi āyogapaṭṭopi bibbohanampi pañcaṅgopi sattaṅgopi vaṭṭati. Pañcaṅgo pana piṭṭhiapassayena saddhiṃ kato. Sattaṅgo nāma piṭṭhiapassayena ca ubhatopassesu apassayehi ca saddhiṃ kato. Taṃ kira miḷābhayattherassa akaṃsu. Thero anāgāmī hutvā parinibbāyi.

By way of division, this practitioner is also of three kinds. Therein, for the strict practitioner, neither a back-rest, nor a cloth-binding, nor a supporting strap is permissible. For the middling practitioner, any one of these three is permissible. For the mild practitioner, a back-rest, a cloth-binding, a supporting strap, a pillow, a five-limbed chair, and a seven-limbed chair are permissible. The five-limbed chair is made with a back-rest. The seven-limbed chair is made with a back-rest and with supports on both sides. They say that they made it for the Elder Miḷābhaya. The Elder, having become a non-returner, attained final Nibbāna.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇampi seyyaṃ kappitamatte dhutaṅgaṃ bhijjati. Ayamettha bhedo.

However, for all three of these, the ascetic practice is broken the moment one lies down. This is the breaking here.

Ayaṃ panānisaṃso, “seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 3.320; ma. ni. 1.186) vuttassa cetaso vinibandhassa upacchedanaṃ, sabbakammaṭṭhānānuyogasappāyatā, pāsādikairiyāpathatā, vīriyārambhānukūlatā, sammāpaṭipattiyā anubrūhananti.

And this is the benefit: the cutting off of the mind's bondage, spoken of thus: “He dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness” (Dī. Ni. 3.320; Ma. Ni. 1.186); suitability for engaging in all meditation subjects; having an inspiring deportment; being conducive to the arousal of energy; and the furtherance of right practice.

Ābhujitvāna pallaṅkaṃ, paṇidhāya ujuṃ tanuṃ;

Nisīdanto vikampeti, mārassa hadayaṃ yati.

Having folded his legs crosswise and set his body erect, the ascetic, as he sits, makes Māra's heart tremble.

Seyyasukhaṃ [M 1.0077] middhasukhaṃ, hitvā āraddhavīriyo;

Nisajjābhirato bhikkhu, sobhayanto tapovanaṃ.

Having abandoned the pleasure of lying down and the pleasure of drowsiness, with energy aroused, the bhikkhu delighting in sitting beautifies the ascetic grove.

Nirāmisaṃ pītisukhaṃ, yasmā samadhigacchati;

Tasmā samanuyuñjeyya, dhīro nesajjikaṃ vatanti.

Since one attains joy and happiness free from sensual pleasures, therefore, the wise one should devote himself to the sitter's vow.

Ayaṃ nesajjikaṅge samādāna vidhānappabheda bhedānisaṃsavaṇṇanā.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, divisions, breaking, and benefits concerning the sitter's practice.

Dhutaṅgapakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse on the Ascetic Practices

37. Idāni [V 1.0079] –

37. Now:

Kusalattikato ceva, dhutādīnaṃ vibhāgato;

Samāsabyāsato cāpi, viññātabbo vinicchayoti. –

From the wholesome triad, and from the classification of the ascetic practices and so forth, and from the concise and the extended, the determination should be understood.

Imissā gāthāya vasena vaṇṇanā hoti.

The explanation proceeds by way of this verse.

Tattha kusalattikatoti sabbāneva hi dhutaṅgāni sekkhaputhujjanakhīṇāsavānaṃ vasena siyā kusalāni, siyā abyākatāni, natthi dhutaṅgaṃ akusalanti.

Herein, 'from the wholesome triad' means: indeed, all ascetic practices, with respect to trainees, worldlings, and those with cankers destroyed, may be wholesome or they may be indeterminate. There is no ascetic practice that is unwholesome.

Yo pana vadeyya “pāpiccho icchāpakato āraññiko hotīti ādivacanato (a. ni. 5.181; pari. 325) akusalampi dhutaṅga”nti. So vattabbo – na mayaṃ “akusalacittena araññe na vasatī”ti vadāma. Yassa hi araññe nivāso, so āraññiko. So ca pāpiccho vā bhaveyya appiccho vā. Imāni pana tena tena samādānena dhutakilesattā dhutassa bhikkhuno aṅgāni, kilesadhunanato vā dhutanti laddhavohāraṃ ñāṇaṃ aṅgametesanti dhutaṅgāni. Atha vā dhutāni ca tāni paṭipakkhaniddhunanato aṅgāni ca paṭipattiyātipi dhutaṅgānīti vuttaṃ. Na ca akusalena koci dhuto nāma hoti, yassetāni aṅgāni bhaveyyuṃ, na ca akusalaṃ kiñci dhunāti, yesaṃ taṃ aṅgantikatvā dhutaṅgānīti vucceyyuṃ. Nāpi akusalaṃ cīvaraloluppādīni ceva niddhunāti paṭipattiyā ca aṅgaṃ hoti. Tasmā suvuttamidaṃ “natthi akusalaṃ dhutaṅga”nti.

If someone were to say, 'Even an unwholesome thing is an ascetic practice, due to the statement that “a forest dweller is one with evil wishes, overcome by desire” (A. Ni. 5.181; Pari. 325) and so on,' they should be told: We do not say, 'One does not dwell in the forest with an unwholesome mind.' For whoever dwells in the forest is a forest dweller, and he may be one with evil wishes or one with few wishes. However, these are ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) because, through this or that undertaking, they are limbs (aṅga) of a bhikkhu who has shaken off (dhuta) defilements; or because the knowledge which, from shaking off defilements, is termed 'dhuta' is their limb (aṅga). Or alternatively, it is said that they are ascetic practices because they are both 'shaking' (dhuta) since they shake off opposing factors, and they are 'limbs' (aṅga) of the practice. But no one is called 'shaken off' (dhuta) by means of the unwholesome, for whom these might be limbs; nor does the unwholesome shake off anything, that it should become their 'dhuta' component, causing them to be called ascetic practices. Nor does the unwholesome shake off things like greed for robes, nor is it a limb of practice. Therefore, it is well said: 'There is no unwholesome ascetic practice.'

“Yesampi [M 1.0078] kusalattikavinimuttaṃ dhutaṅgaṃ, tesaṃ atthato dhutaṅgameva natthi. Asantaṃ kassa dhunanato dhutaṅgaṃ nāma bhavissati. Dhutaguṇe samādāya vattatīti vacanavirodhopi ca nesaṃ āpajjati, tasmā taṃ na gahetabba”nti ayaṃ tāva kusalattikato vaṇṇanā.

For those for whom an ascetic practice is devoid of the wholesome triad, in reality there is no ascetic practice at all. By shaking off what non-existent thing would there be something called an ascetic practice? Furthermore, for them a contradiction also arises with the statement, 'One lives having undertaken the qualities that shake off defilements.' Therefore, that view should not be accepted. This, in the first place, is the explanation from the wholesome triad.

Dhutādīnaṃ [V 1.0080] vibhāgatoti dhuto veditabbo. Dhutavādo veditabbo. Dhutadhammā veditabbā. Dhutaṅgāni veditabbāni. Kassa dhutaṅgasevanā sappāyāti veditabbaṃ.

'From the classification of the dhuta and so forth' means: the dhuta should be understood. The dhutavāda should be understood. The dhuta qualities should be understood. The ascetic practices should be understood. For whom the cultivation of the ascetic practices is suitable should be understood.

Tattha dhutoti dhutakileso vā puggalo kilesadhunano vā dhammo.

Herein, 'dhuta' means either a person who has shaken off defilements, or a state that shakes off defilements.

Dhutavādoti ettha pana atthi dhuto na dhutavādo, atthi na dhuto dhutavādo, atthi neva dhuto na dhutavādo, atthi dhuto ceva dhutavādo ca.

Now, in this context of 'dhutavāda', there is one who is dhuta but not a dhutavāda; there is one who is not dhuta but is a dhutavāda; there is one who is neither dhuta nor a dhutavāda; and there is one who is both dhuta and a dhutavāda.

Tattha yo dhutaṅgena attano kilese dhuni, paraṃ pana dhutaṅgena na ovadati, nānusāsati bākulatthero viya, ayaṃ dhuto na dhutavādo. Yathāha, “tayidaṃ āyasmā bākulo dhuto na dhutavādo”ti. Yo pana na dhutaṅgena attano kilese dhuni, kevalaṃ aññe dhutaṅgena ovadati anusāsati upanandatthero viya, ayaṃ na dhuto dhutavādo. Yathāha, “tayidaṃ āyasmā upanando sakyaputto na dhuto dhutavādo”ti. Yo ubhayavipanno lāḷudāyī viya, ayaṃ neva dhuto na dhutavādo. Yathāha, “tayidaṃ āyasmā lāḷudāyī neva dhuto na dhutavādo”ti. Yo pana ubhayasampanno dhammasenāpati viya, ayaṃ dhuto ceva dhutavādo ca. Yathāha, “tayidaṃ āyasmā sāriputto dhuto ceva dhutavādo cāti.

Herein, one who has shaken off his own defilements by means of an ascetic practice, but does not advise or instruct others by means of an ascetic practice, like the Elder Bākula, is dhuta but not a dhutavāda. As it is said: 'Indeed, the Venerable Bākula is dhuta but not a dhutavāda.' One who has not shaken off his own defilements by means of an ascetic practice, but only advises and instructs others by means of an ascetic practice, like the Elder Upananda the Sakyan, is not dhuta but is a dhutavāda. As it is said: 'Indeed, the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan is not dhuta but is a dhutavāda.' One who is deficient in both, like the Elder Lāḷudāyī, is neither dhuta nor a dhutavāda. As it is said: 'Indeed, the Venerable Lāḷudāyī is neither dhuta nor a dhutavāda.' One who is accomplished in both, like the General of the Dhamma, is both dhuta and a dhutavāda. As it is said: 'Indeed, the Venerable Sāriputta is both dhuta and a dhutavāda.'

Dhutadhammā veditabbāti appicchatā, santuṭṭhitā, sallekhatā, pavivekatā, idamatthitāti ime dhutaṅgacetanāya parivārakā pañca dhammā “appicchataṃyeva nissāyā”tiādivacanato (a. ni. 5.181; pari. 325) dhutadhammā nāma, tattha appicchatā ca santuṭṭhitā ca alobho. Sallekhatā ca pavivekatā ca dvīsu dhammesu anupatanti alobhe ca amohe ca. Idamatthitā ñāṇameva. Tattha [M 1.0079] ca alobhena paṭikkhepavatthūsu lobhaṃ, amohena tesveva ādīnavapaṭicchādakaṃ mohaṃ dhunāti. Alobhena ca anuññātānaṃ paṭisevanamukhena pavattaṃ kāmasukhānuyogaṃ, amohena dhutaṅgesu atisallekhamukhena pavattaṃ attakilamathānuyogaṃ dhunāti. Tasmā ime dhammā dhutadhammāti veditabbā.

'The dhuta qualities should be understood' means: having few wishes, contentment, the expunging of defilements, seclusion, and principled aspiration—these five qualities, which are accessories to the volition for the ascetic practices, are called 'dhuta qualities' because of such statements as 'relying on having few wishes' (A. Ni. 5.181; Pari. 325). Herein, having few wishes and contentment are non-greed. The expunging of defilements and seclusion fall under two states: non-greed and non-delusion. Principled aspiration is simply wisdom. And herein, by non-greed one shakes off greed for objects to be rejected, and by non-delusion one shakes off the delusion that obscures the dangers in those same objects. By non-greed one shakes off indulgence in sensual pleasure that arises through the partaking of what is allowed, and by non-delusion one shakes off the practice of self-mortification that arises through excessive austerity in the ascetic practices. Therefore, these qualities should be understood as the dhuta qualities.

Dhutaṅgāni veditabbānīti terasa dhutaṅgāni veditabbāni paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ…pe… nesajjikaṅganti. Tāni atthato lakkhaṇādīhi ca vuttāneva.

'The ascetic practices should be understood' means: the thirteen ascetic practices should be understood, namely, the rag-robe wearer's practice... up to... the sitter's practice. These have already been explained in terms of their meaning, characteristics, and so on.

Kassa [V 1.0081] dhutaṅgasevanā sappāyāti rāgacaritassa ceva mohacaritassa ca. Kasmā? Dhutaṅgasevanā hi dukkhāpaṭipadā ceva sallekhavihāro ca. Dukkhāpaṭipadañca nissāya rāgo vūpasammati. Sallekhaṃ nissāya appamattassa moho pahīyati. Āraññikaṅgarukkhamūlikaṅgapaṭisevanā vā ettha dosacaritassāpi sappāyā. Tattha hissa asaṅghaṭṭiyamānassa viharato dosopi vūpasammatīti ayaṃ dhutādīnaṃ vibhāgato vaṇṇanā.

For whom is the cultivation of the ascetic practices suitable? It is suitable for one of a lustful temperament and for one of a deluded temperament. Why? Because the cultivation of the ascetic practices is both a difficult practice and a life of effacement. By relying on the difficult practice, lust is allayed. By relying on effacement, the delusion of a heedful one is abandoned. Here, the cultivation of the forest-dweller's practice and the tree-root-dweller's practice are also suitable for one of a hateful temperament. For there, by dwelling without friction, his hatred is also allayed. This is the explanation by way of the classification of the ascetic practices and so forth.

Samāsabyāsatoti imāni pana dhutaṅgāni samāsato tīṇi sīsaṅgāni, pañca asambhinnaṅgānīti aṭṭheva honti. Tattha sapadānacārikaṅgaṃ, ekāsanikaṅgaṃ, abbhokāsikaṅganti imāni tīṇi sīsaṅgāni. Sapadānacārikaṅgañhi rakkhanto piṇḍapātikaṅgampi rakkhissati. Ekāsanikaṅgañca rakkhato pattapiṇḍikaṅgakhalupacchābhattikaṅgānipi surakkhanīyāni bhavissanti. Abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ rakkhantassa kiṃ atthi rukkhamūlikaṅgayathāsanthatikaṅgesu rakkhitabbaṃ nāma. Iti imāni tīṇi sīsaṅgāni, āraññikaṅgaṃ, paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ, tecīvarikaṅgaṃ, nesajjikaṅgaṃ, sosānikaṅganti imāni pañca asambhinnaṅgāni cāti aṭṭheva honti.

By way of the concise and the extended: Now, these ascetic practices, in brief, are indeed eight: three chief practices and five unmixed practices. Therein, the practice of eating almsfood in sequence, the practice of eating in one session, and the practice of dwelling in the open air—these are the three chief practices. For one who maintains the practice of eating almsfood in sequence will also maintain the practice of eating only almsfood. And for one who maintains the practice of eating in one session, the practice of eating from one bowl and the practice of refusing food offered later will also be easy to maintain. For one who maintains the practice of dwelling in the open air, what is there to maintain regarding the practice of dwelling at the root of a tree and the practice of accepting any lodging? Thus, these are the three chief practices; and the practice of dwelling in the forest, the practice of wearing rag-robes, the practice of wearing only three robes, the sitter's practice, and the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground—these are the five unmixed practices. Thus there are indeed eight.

Puna dve cīvarapaṭisaṃyuttāni, pañca piṇḍapātapaṭisaṃyuttāni, pañca senāsanapaṭisaṃyuttāni, ekaṃ vīriyapaṭisaṃyuttanti evaṃ cattārova honti. Tattha nesajjikaṅgaṃ vīriyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ. Itarāni pākaṭāneva.

Furthermore, there are two connected with robes, five connected with almsfood, five connected with lodgings, and one connected with energy—thus there are just four groups. Therein, the sitter's practice is connected with energy. The others are evident.

Puna sabbāneva nissayavasena dve honti paccayanissitāni dvādasa, vīriyanissitaṃ ekanti. Sevitabbāsevitabbavasenapi dveyeva honti. Yassa hi dhutaṅgaṃ sevantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhati, tena sevitabbāni. Yassa sevato hāyati, tena na sevitabbāni. Yassa pana sevatopi asevatopi vaḍḍhateva, na hāyati, tenāpi pacchimaṃ janataṃ anukampantena sevitabbāni. Yassāpi [M 1.0080] sevatopi asevatopi na vaḍḍhati, tenāpi sevitabbāniyeva āyatiṃ vāsanatthāyāti.

Again, all of them are twofold by way of dependence: twelve are dependent on requisites, and one is dependent on energy. They are also twofold by way of what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated. For one whose meditation subject grows by cultivating an ascetic practice, it should be cultivated by him. For one whose meditation subject declines by cultivating it, it should not be cultivated by him. However, for one for whom it grows and does not decline, whether cultivating it or not, it should also be cultivated by him out of compassion for future generations. And for one for whom it does not grow, whether cultivating it or not, it should still be cultivated by him for the sake of imprinting a habit for the future.

Evaṃ sevitabbāsevitabbavasena duvidhānipi sabbāneva cetanāvasena ekavidhāni honti. Ekameva hi dhutaṅgaṃ samādānacetanāti. Aṭṭhakathāyampi vuttaṃ “yā cetanā, taṃ dhutaṅganti vadantī”ti.

Thus, although they are twofold by way of what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated, all of them become of a single kind by way of volition. For an ascetic practice is simply the volition of undertaking. It is also said in the Commentary: 'That which is volition, they call an ascetic practice.'

Byāsato [V 1.0082] pana bhikkhūnaṃ terasa, bhikkhunīnaṃ aṭṭha, sāmaṇerānaṃ dvādasa, sikkhamānasāmaṇerīnaṃ satta, upāsakaupāsikānaṃ dveti dvācattālīsa honti. Sace pana abbhokāse āraññikaṅgasampannaṃ susānaṃ hoti, ekopi bhikkhu ekappahārena sabbadhutaṅgāni paribhuñjituṃ sakkoti. Bhikkhunīnaṃ pana āraññikaṅgaṃ khalupacchābhattikaṅgañca dvepi sikkhāpadeneva paṭikkhittāni, abbhokāsikaṅgaṃ, rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ, sosānikaṅganti imāni tīṇi dupparihārāni. Bhikkhuniyā hi dutiyikaṃ vinā vasituṃ na vaṭṭati. Evarūpe ca ṭhāne samānacchandā dutiyikā dullabhā. Sacepi labheyya saṃsaṭṭhavihārato na mucceyya. Evaṃ sati yassatthāya dhutaṅgaṃ seveyya, svevassā attho na sampajjeyya. Evaṃ paribhuñjituṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya pañca hāpetvā bhikkhunīnaṃ aṭṭheva hontīti veditabbāni. Yathāvuttesu pana ṭhapetvā tecīvarikaṅgaṃ sesāni dvādasa sāmaṇerānaṃ, satta sikkhamānasāmaṇerīnaṃ veditabbāni. Upāsakaupāsikānaṃ pana ekāsanikaṅgaṃ, pattapiṇḍikaṅganti imāni dve patirūpāni ceva sakkā ca paribhuñjitunti dve dhutaṅgānīti evaṃ byāsato dvecattālīsa hontīti ayaṃ samāsabyāsato vaṇṇanā.

By way of expansion, however, there are thirteen for monks, eight for nuns, twelve for male novices, seven for female probationers and female novices, and two for laymen and laywomen, thus making forty-two. However, if there is an open-air charnel ground endowed with the qualities of a forest dwelling, even a single monk can undertake all the ascetic practices at once. For nuns, however, the forest-dweller's practice and the practice of refusing food offered later are both prohibited by the training rules themselves. The open-air-dweller's practice, the tree-root-dweller's practice, and the charnel-ground-dweller's practice—these three are difficult to maintain. Indeed, it is not proper for a nun to dwell without a companion. And in such a place, a companion of like mind is rare. Even if she should find one, she would not be freed from living in association. In that case, the very purpose for which she might undertake an ascetic practice would not be fulfilled for her. Thus, due to the inability to undertake five of them, it should be understood that for nuns there are only eight. Among those mentioned, however, omitting the three-robe-wearer's practice, the remaining twelve should be understood as being for male novices, and seven for female probationers and female novices. For laymen and laywomen, however, the one-sessioner's practice and the bowl-food-eater's practice—these two are both suitable and possible to undertake; thus, there are two ascetic practices. In this way, by way of expansion, there are forty-two. This is the description by way of summary and expansion.

Ettāvatā ca “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti imissā gāthāya sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena desite visuddhimagge yehi appicchatāsantuṭṭhitādīhi guṇehi vuttappakārassa sīlassa vodānaṃ hoti, tesaṃ sampādanatthaṃ samādātabbadhutaṅgakathā bhāsitā hoti.

And thus far, in the Path of Purification, which is taught by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom in accordance with the verse, 'A wise person, established in virtue...,' the discourse on the ascetic practices to be undertaken has been delivered for the accomplishment of those qualities—such as fewness of wishes and contentment—by which the purification of virtue of the kind described takes place.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Path of Purification, composed for the delight of good people,

Dhutaṅganiddeso nāma dutiyo paricchedo.

The Second Chapter, named the Exposition of the Ascetic Practices.

3. Kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddeso

3. The Exposition of the Taking Up of Meditation Subjects

38. Idāni [M 1.0081][V 1.0083] yasmā evaṃ dhutaṅgapariharaṇasampāditehi appicchatādīhi guṇehi pariyodāte imasmiṃ sīle patiṭṭhitena “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño, cittaṃ paññañca bhāvaya”nti vacanato cittasīsena niddiṭṭho samādhi bhāvetabbo. So ca atisaṅkhepadesitattā viññātumpi tāva na sukaro, pageva bhāvetuṃ, tasmā tassa vitthārañca bhāvanānayañca dassetuṃ idaṃ pañhākammaṃ hoti.

38.
