Now, since one established in this virtue—purified by qualities such as fewness of wishes, accomplished through the observance of the ascetic practices—should develop the concentration indicated by the heading 'mind,' in accordance with the saying, 'A wise person, established in virtue, should develop mind and wisdom'; and since this concentration, because it has been taught too briefly, is not easy even to understand, let alone to develop; therefore, to show its details and the method of development, this questioning is undertaken.

Ko samādhi? Kenaṭṭhena samādhi? Kānassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni? Katividho samādhi? Ko cassa saṃkileso? Kiṃ vodānaṃ? Kathaṃ bhāvetabbo? Samādhibhāvanāya ko ānisaṃsoti?

What is concentration? In what sense is it concentration? What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? How many kinds of concentration are there? What is its defilement? What is its purification? How should it be developed? What is the benefit of developing concentration?

Tatridaṃ vissajjanaṃ. Ko samādhīti samādhi bahuvidho nānappakārako. Taṃ sabbaṃ vibhāvayituṃ ārabbhamānaṃ vissajjanaṃ adhippetañceva atthaṃ na sādheyya, uttari ca vikkhepāya saṃvatteyya, tasmā idhādhippetameva sandhāya vadāma, kusalacittekaggatā samādhi.

Here is the answer. As to 'What is concentration?': Concentration is of many kinds and various types. An explanation that attempts to analyze all of that would not accomplish the intended purpose and would, moreover, lead to distraction. Therefore, we speak here only with reference to what is intended: one-pointedness of wholesome mind is concentration.

Kenaṭṭhena samādhīti samādhānaṭṭhena samādhi. Kimidaṃ samādhānaṃ nāma? Ekārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ samaṃ sammā ca ādhānaṃ, ṭhapananti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā yassa dhammassānubhāvena ekārammaṇe cittacetasikā samaṃ sammā ca avikkhipamānā avippakiṇṇā ca hutvā tiṭṭhanti, idaṃ samādhānanti veditabbaṃ.

As to 'In what sense is it concentration?': It is concentration in the sense of composing (samādhāna). What is this composing? It is said to be the even and right placing, the establishing, of mind and mental factors on a single object. Therefore, that by the power of which the mind and mental factors, having become undistracted and unscattered, stand evenly and rightly on a single object—this should be understood as composing.

Kānassa lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānīti ettha pana avikkhepalakkhaṇo samādhi, vikkhepaviddhaṃsanaraso, avikampanapaccupaṭṭhāno. “Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti vacanato pana sukhamassa padaṭṭhānaṃ.

Here, as to 'What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?': Concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction, the function of destroying distraction, and the manifestation of non-wavering. However, happiness is its proximate cause, in accordance with the saying, 'The mind of the happy one becomes concentrated.'

39. Katividho [V 1.0084] samādhīti avikkhepalakkhaṇena tāva ekavidho. Upacāraappanāvasena duvidho, tathā lokiyalokuttaravasena sappītikanippītikavasena sukhasahagataupekkhāsahagatavasena ca. Tividho hīnamajjhimapaṇītavasena[M 1.0082], tathā savitakkasavicārādivasena pītisahagatādivasena parittamahaggatappamāṇavasena ca. Catubbidho dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiññādivasena, tathā parittaparittārammaṇādivasena catujhānaṅgavasena hānabhāgiyādivasena kāmāvacarādivasena adhipativasena ca. Pañcavidho pañcakanaye pañcajhānaṅgavasenāti.

39. As to the question, 'How many kinds of concentration are there?': Firstly, it is of one kind by the characteristic of non-distraction. It is of two kinds by way of access and absorption; likewise, by way of mundane and supramundane, by way of being with joy and without joy, and by way of being accompanied by pleasure and accompanied by equanimity. It is of three kinds by way of inferior, middling, and superior; likewise, by way of being with initial and sustained thought, etc., by way of being accompanied by joy, etc., and by way of being limited, sublime, and immeasurable. It is of four kinds by way of painful practice with slow direct knowledge, etc.; likewise, by way of limited concentration with a limited object, etc., by way of the four jhāna factors, by way of being conducive to decline, etc., by way of pertaining to the sense sphere, etc., and by way of dominance. It is of five kinds in the fivefold method by way of the five jhāna factors.

Samādhiekakadukavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Ones and Twos Concerning Concentration

Tattha ekavidhakoṭṭhāso uttānatthoyeva. Duvidhakoṭṭhāse channaṃ anussatiṭṭhānānaṃ maraṇassatiyā upasamānussatiyā āhāre paṭikūlasaññāya catudhātuvavatthānassāti imesaṃ vasena laddhacittekaggatā, yā ca appanāsamādhīnaṃ pubbabhāge ekaggatā, ayaṃ upacārasamādhi. “Paṭhamassa jhānassa parikammaṃ paṭhamassa jhānassa anantarapaccayena paccayo”ti ādivacanato pana yā parikammānantarā ekaggatā, ayaṃ appanāsamādhīti evaṃ upacārappanāvasena duvidho.

Therein, the onefold division is of plain meaning. In the twofold division, the one-pointedness of mind obtained by way of these ten subjects—the six recollection subjects, mindfulness of death, mindfulness of peace, perception of repulsiveness in food, and the analysis of the four elements—and the one-pointedness that occurs in the preliminary stage of the absorption concentrations, this is access concentration. However, from the statement beginning, “The preparation for the first jhāna is a condition for the first jhāna by way of an immediately proximate condition,” the one-pointedness that is immediately after the preparation is absorption concentration. Thus, by way of access and absorption, it is twofold.

Dutiyaduke tīsu bhūmīsu kusalacittekaggatā lokiyo samādhi. Ariyamaggasampayuttā ekaggatā lokuttaro samādhīti evaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidho.

In the second dyad, the one-pointedness of wholesome consciousness in the three planes is mundane concentration. The one-pointedness associated with the Noble Path is supramundane concentration. Thus, by way of mundane and supramundane, it is twofold.

Tatiyaduke catukkanaye dvīsu pañcakanaye tīsu jhānesu ekaggatā sappītiko samādhi. Avasesesu dvīsu jhānesu ekaggatā nippītiko samādhi. Upacārasamādhi pana siyā sappītiko, siyā nippītikoti evaṃ sappītikanippītikavasena duvidho.

In the third dyad, the one-pointedness in the two jhānas of the fourfold system and the three jhānas of the fivefold system is concentration with joy. In the remaining two jhānas, the one-pointedness is concentration without joy. Access concentration, however, may be with joy or it may be without joy; thus, by way of being with joy and without joy, it is twofold.

Catutthaduke catukkanaye tīsu pañcakanaye catūsu jhānesu ekaggatā sukhasahagato samādhi. Avasesasmiṃ upekkhāsahagato samādhi. Upacārasamādhi pana siyā sukhasahagato, siyā upekkhāsahagatoti evaṃ sukhasahagataupekkhāsahagatavasena duvidho.

In the fourth dyad, the one-pointedness of mind in the three jhānas of the fourfold system and the four jhānas of the fivefold system is concentration accompanied by pleasure. In the remaining jhāna, it is concentration accompanied by equanimity. Access concentration, however, may be accompanied by pleasure or by equanimity; thus, it is twofold by way of being accompanied by pleasure and accompanied by equanimity.

Samādhitikavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Triad of Concentration

Tikesu [V 1.0085] paṭhamattike paṭiladdhamatto hīno, nātisubhāvito majjhimo, subhāvito vasippatto paṇītoti evaṃ hīnamajjhimapaṇītavasena tividho.

Among the triads, in the first triad, concentration that is merely obtained is inferior; that which is not very well-developed is middling; and that which is well-developed and has reached mastery is superior. Thus, it is threefold by way of being inferior, middling, and superior.

Dutiyattike [M 1.0083] paṭhamajjhānasamādhi saddhiṃ upacārasamādhinā savitakkasavicāro. Pañcakanaye dutiyajjhānasamādhi avitakkavicāramatto. Yo hi vitakkamatteyeva ādīnavaṃ disvā vicāre adisvā kevalaṃ vitakkappahānamattaṃ ākaṅkhamāno paṭhamajjhānaṃ atikkamati, so avitakkavicāramattaṃ samādhiṃ paṭilabhati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Catukkanaye pana dutiyādīsu pañcakanaye tatiyādīsu tīsu jhānesu ekaggatā avitakkāvicāro samādhīti evaṃ savitakkasavicārādivasena tividho.

In the second triad, the concentration of the first jhāna together with access concentration is with initial and sustained thought. In the fivefold system, the concentration of the second jhāna is without initial thought, with sustained thought only. For one who, seeing a drawback only in initial thought but not in sustained thought, wishes for merely the abandoning of initial thought and transcends the first jhāna, attains concentration without initial thought, with sustained thought only. This was said with reference to that. However, in the fourfold system, the one-pointedness in the second and following jhānas, and in the fivefold system, in the three jhānas from the third onwards, is concentration without initial and sustained thought. Thus, it is threefold by way of being with initial and sustained thought, etc.

Tatiyattike catukkanaye ādito dvīsu pañcakanaye ca tīsu jhānesu ekaggatā pītisahagato samādhi. Tesveva tatiye ca catutthe ca jhāne ekaggatā sukhasahagato samādhi. Avasāne upekkhāsahagato. Upacārasamādhi pana pītisukhasahagato vā hoti upekkhāsahagato vāti evaṃ pītisahagatādivasena tividho.

In the third triad, the one-pointedness of mind in the first two jhānas of the fourfold system and in the first three jhānas of the fivefold system is concentration accompanied by joy. In those same systems, in the third jhāna and in the fourth jhāna, the one-pointedness of mind is concentration accompanied by pleasure. In the final jhāna, it is accompanied by equanimity. Access concentration, however, is accompanied by joy and pleasure or by equanimity; thus it is threefold by way of being accompanied by joy, etc.

Catutthattike upacārabhūmiyaṃ ekaggatā paritto samādhi. Rūpāvacarārūpāvacarakusale ekaggatā mahaggato samādhi. Ariyamaggasampayuttā ekaggatā appamāṇo samādhīti evaṃ parittamahaggatappamāṇavasena tividho.

In the fourth triad, one-pointedness in the access realm is limited concentration. One-pointedness in wholesome states of the form and formless realms is sublime concentration. One-pointedness associated with the Noble Path is immeasurable concentration. Thus, it is threefold by way of being limited, sublime, and immeasurable.

Samādhicatukkavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Tetrad of Concentration

Catukkesu paṭhamacatukke atthi samādhi dukkhāpaṭipado dandhābhiñño, atthi dukkhāpaṭipado khippābhiñño, atthi sukhāpaṭipado dandhābhiñño, atthi sukhāpaṭipado khippābhiññoti.

In the first tetrad, there is concentration with painful practice and slow direct knowledge; there is concentration with painful practice and quick direct knowledge; there is concentration with pleasant practice and slow direct knowledge; and there is concentration with pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge.

Tattha paṭhamasamannāhārato paṭṭhāya yāva tassa tassa jhānassa upacāraṃ uppajjati, tāva pavattā samādhibhāvanā paṭipadāti vuccati. Upacārato pana paṭṭhāya yāva appanā, tāva pavattā [V 1.0086] paññā abhiññāti vuccati. Sā panesā paṭipadā ekaccassa dukkhā hoti, nīvaraṇādipaccanīkadhammasamudācāragahaṇatāya kicchā asukhāsevanāti attho. Ekaccassa tadabhāvena sukhā. Abhiññāpi ekaccassa dandhā hoti mandā asīghappavatti. Ekaccassa khippā amandā sīghappavatti.

Herein, starting from the initial application of mind until the access concentration of each respective jhāna arises, the development of concentration that occurs during that time is called 'the path.' And starting from access concentration until absorption, the wisdom that occurs during that time is called 'direct knowledge.' For some, this path is painful—meaning it is difficult and its cultivation is unpleasant—due to the denseness of the constant occurrence of opposing states, such as the hindrances. For some, due to the absence of that, it is pleasant. Direct knowledge, too, for some is slow: it is dull, and its arising is not swift. For another, it is quick: not dull, with a swift arising.

Tattha yāni parato sappāyāsappāyāni ca palibodhupacchedādīni pubbakiccāni ca appanākosallāni ca vaṇṇayissāma, tesu yo asappāyasevī [M 1.0084] hoti, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā dandhā ca abhiññā hoti. Sappāyasevino sukhā paṭipadā khippā ca abhiññā. Yo pana pubbabhāge asappāyaṃ sevitvā aparabhāge sappāyasevī hoti, pubbabhāge vā sappāyaṃ sevitvā aparabhāge asappāyasevī, tassa vomissakatā veditabbā. Tathā palibodhupacchedādikaṃ pubbakiccaṃ asampādetvā bhāvanamanuyuttassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Vipariyāyena sukhā. Appanākosallāni pana asampādentassa dandhā abhiññā hoti. Sampādentassa khippā.

Herein, we will describe later the suitable and unsuitable conditions, the preliminary duties such as cutting off impediments, and the skills in absorption. Among these, for one who resorts to what is unsuitable, the practice is painful and direct knowledge is slow. For one who resorts to what is suitable, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is quick. But for one who, having resorted to the unsuitable in the earlier stage, resorts to the suitable in the later stage—or having resorted to the suitable in the earlier stage, resorts to the unsuitable in the later stage—it should be understood as mixed. Furthermore, for one who engages in the development without having accomplished the preliminary duties, such as cutting off impediments, the practice is painful. In the opposite case, it is pleasant. And for one who does not accomplish the skills in absorption, direct knowledge is slow. For one who accomplishes them, it is quick.

Apica taṇhāavijjāvasena samathavipassanādhikāravasena cāpi etāsaṃ pabhedo veditabbo. Taṇhābhibhūtassa hi dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Anabhibhūtassa sukhā. Avijjābhibhūtassa ca dandhā abhiññā hoti. Anabhibhūtassa khippā. Yo ca samathe akatādhikāro, tassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti. Katādhikārassa sukhā. Yo pana vipassanāya akatādhikāro hoti, tassa dandhā abhiññā hoti, katādhikārassa khippā. Kilesindriyavasena cāpi etāsaṃ pabhedo veditabbo. Tibbakilesassa hi mudindriyassa dukkhā paṭipadā hoti dandhā ca abhiññā, tikkhindriyassa pana khippā abhiññā. Mandakilesassa ca mudindriyassa sukhā paṭipadā hoti dandhā ca abhiññā. Tikkhindriyassa pana khippā abhiññāti.

Furthermore, the distinction among these is to be understood by way of craving and ignorance, and also by way of proficiency in serenity and insight. For one oppressed by craving, the practice is painful; for one not oppressed, it is pleasant. For one oppressed by ignorance, direct knowledge is slow; for one not oppressed, it is quick. For one who has not made proficiency in serenity, the practice is painful; for one who has made proficiency, it is pleasant. But for one who has not made proficiency in insight, direct knowledge is slow; for one who has made proficiency, it is quick. The distinction among these is also to be understood by way of the defilements and faculties. For one with intense defilements and dull faculties, the practice is painful and direct knowledge is slow; but for one with sharp faculties, direct knowledge is quick. For one with mild defilements and dull faculties, the practice is pleasant and direct knowledge is slow; but for one with sharp faculties, direct knowledge is quick.

Iti imāsu paṭipadāabhiññāsu yo puggalo dukkhāya paṭipadāya dandhāya ca abhiññāya samādhiṃ pāpuṇāti, tassa so samādhi dukkhāpaṭipado dandhābhiññoti vuccati. Esa nayo sesattayepīti evaṃ dukkhāpaṭipadādandhābhiññādivasena catubbidho.

Thus, among these practices and direct knowledges, for the person who attains concentration through a painful practice and slow direct knowledge, that concentration of his is called 'that of painful practice and slow direct knowledge.' This method is to be understood for the remaining three as well. Thus, it is fourfold by way of 'painful practice and slow direct knowledge,' and so on.

Dutiyacatukke atthi samādhi paritto parittārammaṇo, atthi paritto appamāṇārammaṇo, atthi appamāṇo parittārammaṇo, atthi appamāṇo appamāṇārammaṇoti. Tattha yo samādhi appaguṇo [V 1.0087] uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ na sakkoti, ayaṃ paritto. Yo pana avaḍḍhite ārammaṇe pavatto, ayaṃ parittārammaṇo. Yo paguṇo subhāvito, uparijhānassa paccayo bhavituṃ sakkoti, ayaṃ appamāṇo. Yo ca vaḍḍhite ārammaṇe pavatto, ayaṃ appamāṇārammaṇo. Vuttalakkhaṇavomissatāya pana vomissakanayo veditabbo. Evaṃ parittaparittārammaṇādivasena catubbidho.

In the second tetrad: there is concentration that is limited with a limited object; there is concentration that is limited with an immeasurable object; there is concentration that is immeasurable with a limited object; there is concentration that is immeasurable with an immeasurable object. Therein, that concentration which is of little quality and cannot serve as a condition for a higher jhāna, this is 'limited.' But that which occurs in an unexpanded object, this is 'with a limited object.' That which is proficient and well-developed, and can serve as a condition for a higher jhāna, this is 'immeasurable.' And that which occurs in an expanded object, this is 'with an immeasurable object.' But by the mixing of the stated characteristics, the mixed method is to be understood. Thus, it is fourfold by way of 'limited with a limited object,' and so on.

Tatiyacatukke [M 1.0085] vikkhambhitanīvaraṇānaṃ vitakkavicārapītisukhasamādhīnaṃ vasena pañcaṅgikaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, tato vūpasantavitakkavicāraṃ tivaṅgikaṃ dutiyaṃ, tato virattapītikaṃ duvaṅgikaṃ tatiyaṃ, tato pahīnasukhaṃ upekkhāvedanāsahitassa samādhino vasena duvaṅgikaṃ catutthaṃ. Iti imesaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ aṅgabhūtā cattāro samādhī honti. Evaṃ catujhānaṅgavasena catubbidho.

In the third tetrad, for one with hindrances suppressed, the first jhāna is five-factored by means of applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, and concentration. Then, with applied and sustained thought subsided, the second jhāna is three-factored. Then, with joy faded away, the third jhāna is two-factored. Then, with bliss abandoned, the fourth jhāna is two-factored by means of concentration together with equanimous feeling. Thus, there are four concentrations that are the constituent parts of these four jhānas. In this way, it is fourfold by way of the factors of the four jhānas.

Catutthacatukke atthi samādhi hānabhāgiyo, atthi ṭhitibhāgiyo, atthi visesabhāgiyo, atthi nibbedhabhāgiyo. Tattha paccanīkasamudācāravasena hānabhāgiyatā, tadanudhammatāya satiyā saṇṭhānavasena ṭhitibhāgiyatā, uparivisesādhigamavasena visesabhāgiyatā, nibbidāsahagatasaññāmanasikārasamudācāravasena nibbedhabhāgiyatā ca veditabbā. Yathāha, “paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhiṃ kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti hānabhāginī paññā. Tadanudhammatā sati santiṭṭhati ṭhitibhāginī paññā. Avitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti visesabhāginī paññā. Nibbidāsahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti virāgūpasañhitā nibbedhabhāginī paññā”ti (vibha. 799). Tāya pana paññāya sampayuttā samādhīpi cattāro hontīti. Evaṃ hānabhāgiyādivasena catubbidho.

In the fourth tetrad, there is concentration that partakes of decline, concentration that partakes of stability, concentration that partakes of distinction, and concentration that partakes of penetration. Herein, the state of partaking of decline is to be understood by means of the arising of what is opposed; the state of partaking of stability, by means of the establishment of mindfulness in conformity with that; the state of partaking of distinction, by means of the attainment of a higher distinction; and the state of partaking of penetration, by means of the arising of perception and attention accompanied by disenchantment. As it is said: 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and attention accompanied by sensual desire arise—this is wisdom partaking of decline. Mindfulness in conformity with that stands firm—this is wisdom partaking of stability. Perceptions and attention accompanied by the non-discursive arise—this is wisdom partaking of distinction. Perceptions and attention accompanied by disenchantment arise—this is wisdom associated with dispassion, partaking of penetration' (Vibh. 799). Now, the concentrations associated with that wisdom are also four. Thus, it is fourfold by way of that which partakes of decline, and so on.

Pañcamacatukke kāmāvacaro samādhi, rūpāvacaro samādhi, arūpāvacaro samādhi, apariyāpanno samādhīti evaṃ cattāro samādhī. Tattha sabbāpi upacārekaggatā kāmāvacaro samādhi. Tathā rūpāvacarādikusalacittekaggatā itare tayoti evaṃ kāmāvacarādivasena catubbidho.

In the fifth tetrad, there is concentration pertaining to the sense-sphere, concentration pertaining to the form-sphere, concentration pertaining to the formless-sphere, and unincluded concentration; thus there are four concentrations. Herein, all one-pointedness of access is concentration pertaining to the sense-sphere. Likewise, the one-pointedness in wholesome consciousness of the form-sphere and so on are the other three. Thus, it is fourfold by way of that pertaining to the sense-sphere, and so on.

Chaṭṭhacatukke “chandaṃ ce bhikkhu adhipatiṃ karitvā labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassekaggataṃ, ayaṃ vuccati chandasamādhi…pe… vīriyaṃ ce bhikkhu…pe… cittaṃ ce bhikkhu…pe… vīmaṃsaṃ ce bhikkhu adhipatiṃ karitvā labhati samādhiṃ, labhati cittassekaggataṃ[V 1.0088], ayaṃ vuccati vīmaṃsāsamādhī”ti (vibha. 432; saṃ. ni. 3.825) evaṃ adhipativasena catubbidho.

In the sixth tetrad: "If a bhikkhu, making desire the dominant factor, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind, this is called concentration with desire as the dominant factor... If a bhikkhu, making investigation the dominant factor, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind, this is called concentration with investigation as the dominant factor" (Vibh. 432; SN 51.20). Thus, it is fourfold by way of dominance.

Pañcake [M 1.0086] yaṃ catukkabhede vuttaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ, taṃ vitakkamattātikkamena dutiyaṃ, vitakkavicārātikkamena tatiyanti evaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā pañca jhānāni veditabbāni. Tesaṃ aṅgabhūtā ca pañca samādhīti evaṃ pañcajhānaṅgavasena pañcavidhatā veditabbā.

In the pentad, the second jhāna mentioned in the tetrad classification is to be understood as divided into two: the second by transcending mere applied thought, and the third by transcending applied and sustained thought. Thus, there are five jhānas to be understood. And the concentrations that are their constituent factors are also five. Thus, the fivefold nature of concentration is to be understood by way of the factors of the five jhānas.

40. Ko cassa saṃkileso kiṃ vodānanti ettha pana vissajjanaṃ vibhaṅge vuttameva. Vuttañhi tattha “saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyo dhammo. Vodānanti visesabhāgiyo dhammo”ti (vibha. 828). Tattha “paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhiṃ kāmasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti hānabhāginī paññā”ti (vibha. 799) iminā nayena hānabhāgiyadhammo veditabbo. “Avitakkasahagatā saññāmanasikārā samudācaranti visesabhāginī paññā”ti (vibha. 799) iminā nayena visesabhāgiyadhammo veditabbo.

40. Furthermore, regarding 'What is its defilement, and what is its purification?', the answer is indeed stated in the Vibhaṅga. For it is said there: 'Defilement is a state belonging to the part of decline. Purification is a state belonging to the part of distinction' (Vibh. 828). Therein, the state belonging to the part of decline is to be understood by this method: 'For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions and instances of attention accompanied by sensual pleasures arise; the wisdom belongs to the part of decline' (Vibh. 799). The state belonging to the part of distinction is to be understood by this method: 'Perceptions and instances of attention accompanied by that which is without initial thought arise; the wisdom belongs to the part of distinction' (Vibh. 799).

Dasapalibodhavaṇṇanā

An Exposition on the Ten Impediments

41. Kathaṃ bhāvetabboti ettha pana yo tāva ayaṃ lokiyalokuttaravasena duvidhotiādīsu ariyamaggasampayutto samādhi vutto, tassa bhāvanānayo paññābhāvanānayeneva saṅgahito. Paññāya hi bhāvitāya so bhāvito hoti. Tasmā taṃ sandhāya evaṃ bhāvetabboti na kiñci visuṃ vadāma.

41. Now, regarding 'How should it be developed?': that concentration associated with the Noble Path, which was previously mentioned in passages such as 'twofold by way of mundane and supramundane,' its method of development is included only within the method for developing wisdom. For when wisdom is developed, that concentration is also developed. Therefore, with reference to it, we do not state anything separately, such as, 'It should be developed in this way.'

Yo panāyaṃ lokiyo, so vuttanayena sīlāni visodhetvā suparisuddhe sīle patiṭṭhitena yvāssa dasasu palibodhesu palibodho atthi, taṃ upacchinditvā kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano cariyānukūlaṃ cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesu aññataraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā samādhibhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ vihāraṃ pahāya anurūpe vihāre viharantena khuddakapalibodhupacchedaṃ katvā sabbaṃ bhāvanāvidhānaṃ aparihāpentena bhāvetabboti ayamettha saṅkhepo.

As for this mundane concentration, it is to be developed by one who, having purified the moral precepts in the manner described and being established in perfectly pure morality, has cut off whatever impediment he has among the ten impediments; has approached a good friend who gives a meditation subject; has taken up a meditation subject from among the forty suitable to his own temperament; has abandoned a dwelling unsuitable for the development of concentration and dwells in a suitable one; has cut off the minor impediments; and does not neglect any part of the procedure of development. This is the summary here.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0089] pana vitthāro, yaṃ tāva vuttaṃ “yvāssa dasasu palibodhesu palibodho atthi, taṃ upacchinditvā”ti, ettha –

This, however, is the detailed explanation. Regarding what was first said, “For whom there is an impediment among the ten impediments, having cut it off,” here—

Āvāso ca kulaṃ lābho, gaṇo kammañca pañcamaṃ;

Addhānaṃ ñāti ābādho, gantho iddhīti te dasāti. –

A dwelling, supporters, gain, a group, and new work as the fifth; travel, relatives, illness, the study of scriptures, and supernormal power—these are the ten.

Ime [M 1.0087] dasa palibodhā nāma. Tattha āvāsoyeva āvāsapalibodho. Esa nayo kulādīsu.

These are called the ten impediments. Therein, a dwelling itself is the impediment of a dwelling. This is the method for supporters and the others.

Tattha āvāsoti ekopi ovarako vuccati ekampi pariveṇaṃ sakalopi saṅghārāmo. Svāyaṃ na sabbasseva palibodho hoti. Yo panettha navakammādīsu ussukkaṃ vā āpajjati, bahubhaṇḍasannicayo vā hoti, yena kenaci vā kāraṇena apekkhavā paṭibaddhacitto, tasseva palibodho hoti, na itarassa.

Therein, 'dwelling' refers to a single cell, a single monastic compound, or an entire monastery. This is not an impediment for everyone. It is an impediment only for one who becomes anxious about new work and so on, or accumulates many possessions, or for whatever reason has longing and a bound mind; it is not an impediment for another.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – dve kira kulaputtā anurādhapurā nikkhamitvā anupubbena thūpārāme pabbajiṃsu. Tesu eko dve mātikā paguṇā katvā pañcavassiko hutvā pavāretvā pācinakhaṇḍarājiṃ nāma gato. Eko tattheva vasati. Pācinakhaṇḍarājigato tattha ciraṃ vasitvā thero hutvā cintesi “paṭisallānasāruppamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ, handa naṃ sahāyakassāpi ārocemī”ti. Tato nikkhamitvā anupubbena thūpārāmaṃ pāvisi. Pavisantaṃyeva ca naṃ disvā samānavassikatthero paccuggantvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahetvā vattaṃ akāsi. Āgantukatthero senāsanaṃ pavisitvā cintesi “idāni me sahāyo sappiṃ vā phāṇitaṃ vā pānakaṃ vā pesessati. Ayañhi imasmiṃ nagare ciranivāsī”ti. So rattiṃ aladdhā pāto cintesi “idāni upaṭṭhākehi gahitaṃ yāgukhajjakaṃ pesessatī”ti. Tampi adisvā “pahiṇantā natthi, paviṭṭhassa maññe dassatī”ti pātova tena saddhiṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Te dve ekaṃ vīthiṃ caritvā uḷuṅkamattaṃ yāguṃ labhitvā āsanasālāyaṃ nisīditvā piviṃsu. Tato āgantuko cintesi “nibaddhayāgu maññe natthi, bhattakāle idāni manussā paṇītaṃ bhattaṃ dassantī”ti, tato bhattakālepi piṇḍāya caritvā laddhameva bhuñjitvā itaro āha – “kiṃ, bhante, sabbakālaṃ evaṃ yāpethā”ti? Āmāvusoti. Bhante, pācinakhaṇḍarāji phāsukā, tattha gacchāmāti. Thero nagarato [V 1.0090] dakkhiṇadvārena nikkhamanto kumbhakāragāmamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Itaro āha – “kiṃ pana, bhante, imaṃ maggaṃ paṭipannatthā”ti? Nanu tvamāvuso, pācinakhaṇḍarājiyā vaṇṇaṃ abhāsīti? Kiṃ pana, bhante, tumhākaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ vasitaṭṭhāne na koci atirekaparikkhāro atthīti? Āmāvuso mañcapīṭhaṃ saṅghikaṃ, taṃ paṭisāmitameva, aññaṃ kiñci natthīti. Mayhaṃ pana, bhante[M 1.0088], kattaradaṇḍo telanāḷi upāhanatthavikā ca tatthevāti. Tayāvuso, ekadivasaṃ vasitvā ettakaṃ ṭhapitanti? Āma, bhante. So pasannacitto theraṃ vanditvā “tumhādisānaṃ, bhante, sabbattha araññavāsoyeva. Thūpārāmo catunnaṃ buddhānaṃ dhātunidhānaṭṭhānaṃ, lohapāsāde sappāyaṃ dhammassavanaṃ mahācetiyadassanaṃ theradassanañca labbhati, buddhakālo viya pavattati. Idheva tumhe vasathā”ti dutiyadivase pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā sayameva agamāsīti. Īdisassa āvāso na palibodho hoti.

Here is the story: Two sons of good family, it is said, departed from Anurādhapura and, in due course, went forth at the Thūpārāma. Among them, one, having made the two Mātikās proficient, having become of five vassas and performed the Pavāraṇā, went to a place named Pācinakhaṇḍarāji. The other dwelt right there. The one who went to Pācinakhaṇḍarāji, having dwelt there for a long time and become a Thera, thought: “This place is suitable for seclusion. Come now, let me inform my companion also.” Having departed from there, he, in due course, entered the Thūpārāma. Seeing him just as he was entering, the Thera of equal seniority went out to meet him, received his bowl and robe, and performed the duties. The visiting Thera, having entered the dwelling, thought: “Now my companion will send me ghee, or molasses, or a drink, for he has been a long-term resident in this city.” Having received nothing during the night, in the morning he thought: “Now he will send the gruel and solid food brought by the supporters.” Not seeing that either, he thought: “There are no supporters sending anything; I suppose they will give to him when he has entered the village for alms.” Early in the morning, he entered the village together with him. The two of them, having walked one street and received gruel of about a ladle’s measure, sat down in a sitting hall and drank it. Then the visitor thought: “I suppose there is no regular gruel. Now at mealtime, people will give fine food.” Then, at mealtime also, having gone for alms and eaten only what was received, the visitor asked: “Venerable sir, do you always sustain yourselves in this way?” “Yes, friend.” “Venerable sir, Pācinakhaṇḍarāji is comfortable; let us go there.” As the Thera was leaving the city by the southern gate, he took the road to the potters’ village. The other asked: “But why, venerable sir, have you taken this road?” “Friend, did you not praise Pācinakhaṇḍarāji?” “But venerable sir, in the place where you have lived for so long, is there not any extra requisite?” “Yes, friend. The bed and chair are communal property and were put away. There is nothing else.” “But as for me, venerable sir, my walking staff, oil tube, and sandal bag are still right there.” “Friend, having stayed for only one day, you have left behind so much?” “Yes, venerable sir.” He, with a confident mind, having paid homage to the Thera, said: “For noble ones like you, venerable sir, every place is a forest dwelling. The Thūpārāma is the place where the relics of the four Buddhas are enshrined. In the Lohapāsāda, one obtains suitable hearing of the Dhamma, seeing the Great Cetiya, and seeing the great elders. It is as if it were the time of a Buddha. You should dwell right here.” On the second day, taking his bowl and robe, he went away by himself. For such a one, an abode is not an impediment.

Kulanti ñātikulaṃ vā upaṭṭhākakulaṃ vā. Ekaccassa hi upaṭṭhākakulampi “sukhitesu sukhito”tiādinā (vibha. 888; saṃ. ni. 4.241) nayena saṃsaṭṭhassa viharato palibodho hoti, so kulamānusakehi vinā dhammassavanāya sāmantavihārampi na gacchati. Ekaccassa mātāpitaropi palibodhā na honti, koraṇḍakavihāravāsittherassa bhāgineyyadaharabhikkhuno viya.

Family means a family of relatives or a family of supporters. Indeed, for a certain monk who dwells intimately associated, even a family of supporters becomes an impediment by the method of 'when they are happy, he is happy,' etc. (Vibh. 888; Saṃ. Ni. 4.241). That monk cannot go even to a nearby monastery to hear the Dhamma without the people of the family. For a certain monk, even his mother and father are not impediments, as in the case of the young monk, the nephew of the elder who lived at the Koraṇḍaka monastery.

So kira uddesatthaṃ rohaṇaṃ agamāsi. Therabhaginīpi upāsikā sadā theraṃ tassa pavattiṃ pucchati. Thero ekadivasaṃ daharaṃ ānessāmīti rohaṇābhimukho pāyāsi. Daharopi “ciraṃ me idha vutthaṃ, upajjhāyaṃ dāni passitvā upāsikāya ca pavattiṃ ñatvā āgamissāmī”ti rohaṇato nikkhami. Te ubhopi gaṅgātīre samāgacchiṃsu. So aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle therassa vattaṃ katvā “kuhiṃ yāsī”ti pucchito tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Thero suṭṭhu te kataṃ, upāsikāpi sadā pucchati, ahampi etadatthameva āgato, gaccha tvaṃ, ahaṃ pana idheva imaṃ vassaṃ vasissāmīti taṃ uyyojesi. So vassūpanāyikadivaseyeva taṃ vihāraṃ patto. Senāsanampissa pitarā kāritameva pattaṃ.

It is said that he went to Rohaṇa for instruction. The elder's sister, a lay devotee, always asked the elder about his news. One day, the elder set out towards Rohaṇa, thinking, "I will bring the young one." The young one also thought, "I have stayed here a long time. Now, having seen my preceptor and learned of the lay devotee's news, I will return," and he left Rohaṇa. The two of them met on the bank of the Ganges. After performing his duties for the elder at the foot of a certain tree, when asked, "Where are you going?", he informed him of the matter. The elder said, "It is well done by you. The lay devotee also always asks, and I too have come for this very purpose. You go. As for me, I will stay right here for this rains-retreat." So he sent him on his way. That young monk reached that monastery on the very day of entering the rains-retreat. The very lodging that had been built by his father fell to his lot.

Athassa pitā dutiyadivase āgantvā “kassa, bhante, amhākaṃ senāsanaṃ patta”nti pucchanto “āgantukassa daharassā”ti sutvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā āha – “bhante, amhākaṃ [V 1.0091] senāsane vassaṃ upagatassa vattaṃ atthī”ti. Kiṃ upāsakāti? Temāsaṃ amhākaṃyeva ghare bhikkhaṃ gahetvā pavāretvā gamanakāle āpucchitabbanti. So tuṇhibhāvena adhivāsesi. Upāsakopi gharaṃ gantvā “amhākaṃ āvāse eko [M 1.0089] āgantuko ayyo upagato sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo”ti āha. Upāsikā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādesi. Daharopi bhattakāle ñātigharaṃ agamāsi. Na naṃ koci sañjāni.

Then, on the second day, his father came and, while asking, 'Venerable sirs, to whom has our dwelling been assigned?' and hearing, 'To a young visiting monk,' he approached him, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, there is a duty for one who has entered the rains-retreat in our dwelling.' 'What is it, lay follower?' 'For the three months, you are to receive alms-food only in our house, and having performed the Pavāraṇā, you are to take leave at the time of departure.' He consented by his silence. The lay follower also went home and said, 'A visiting noble one has entered the rains-retreat in our dwelling; he should be respectfully attended to.' The female lay supporter, saying, 'Very well,' accepted and prepared excellent hard and soft food. The young monk also went to his relatives' house at mealtime. No one recognized him.

So temāsampi tattha piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā vassaṃvuttho “ahaṃ gacchāmī”ti āpucchi. Athassa ñātakā “sve, bhante, gacchathā”ti dutiyadivase ghareyeva bhojetvā telanāḷiṃ pūretvā ekaṃ guḷapiṇḍaṃ navahatthañca sāṭakaṃ datvā “gacchatha, bhante”ti āhaṃsu. So anumodanaṃ katvā rohaṇābhimukho pāyāsi.

Having consumed alms-food there for the three months, and having completed the rains-retreat, he took leave, saying, 'I am going.' Then his relatives said, 'Venerable sir, please go tomorrow.' On the second day, having fed him right there at home, and having filled a nāḷi measure with oil, they gave him a lump of jaggery and a nine-cubit cloth, and said, 'Venerable sir, please go.' Having given a blessing, he departed, facing towards Rohaṇa.

Upajjhāyopissa pavāretvā paṭipathaṃ āgacchanto pubbe diṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva taṃ addasa. So aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle therassa vattaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ thero pucchi “kiṃ, bhaddamukha, diṭṭhā te upāsikā”ti? So “āma, bhante”ti sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā tena telena therassa pāde makkhetvā guḷena pānakaṃ katvā tampi sāṭakaṃ therasseva datvā theraṃ vanditvā “mayhaṃ, bhante, rohaṇaṃyeva sappāya”nti agamāsi. Theropi vihāraṃ āgantvā dutiyadivase koraṇḍakagāmaṃ pāvisi.

His preceptor also, having performed the Pavāraṇā and coming to meet him on the path, saw him right at the place where he had been seen before. The young monk performed his duties for the elder at the root of a certain tree. Then the elder asked him, 'My good man, did you see the lay supporter?' He replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' and having related the whole affair, he anointed the elder’s feet with that oil, made a drink with the jaggery, and gave that cloth also to the elder himself. Having paid homage to the elder, he departed, saying, 'Venerable sir, Rohaṇa alone is suitable for me.' The elder also, having come to the monastery, entered the village of Koraṇḍaka on the second day.

Upāsikāpi “mayhaṃ bhātā mama puttaṃ gahetvā idāni āgacchatī”ti sadā maggaṃ olokayamānāva tiṭṭhati. Sā taṃ ekakameva āgacchantaṃ disvā “mato me maññe putto, ayaṃ thero ekakova āgacchatī”ti therassa pādamūle nipatitvā paridevamānā rodi. Thero “nūna daharo appicchatāya attānaṃ ajānāpetvāva gato”ti taṃ samassāsetvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā pattatthavikato taṃ sāṭakaṃ nīharitvā dasseti.

The laywoman also stood always watching the road, thinking, 'My brother is now coming, having brought my son.' Seeing him coming all alone, she thought, 'I think my son is dead; this elder comes all alone!' and falling at the elder's feet, she lamented and wept. The elder, thinking, 'Surely the young one, due to having few wishes, has gone without making himself known,' consoled her, related the whole matter, and taking that cloth out from his bowl-bag, showed it to her.

Upāsikā pasīditvā puttena gatadisābhimukhā urena nipajjitvā namassamānā āha – “mayhaṃ puttasadisaṃ vata maññe bhikkhuṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā bhagavā rathavinītapaṭipadaṃ (ma. ni. 1.252 ādayo), nālakapaṭipadaṃ (su. ni. 684 ādayo), tuvaṭṭakapaṭipadaṃ (su. ni. 921 ādayo), catupaccayasantosabhāvanārāmatādīpakaṃ mahāariyavaṃsapaṭipadañca (a. ni. 4.28; dī. ni. 3.309) desesi[V 1.0092]. Vijātamātuyā nāma gehe temāsaṃ bhuñjamānopi ‘ahaṃ [M 1.0090] putto tvaṃ mātā’ti na vakkhati, aho acchariyamanusso”ti. Evarūpassa mātāpitaropi palibodhā na honti, pageva aññaṃ upaṭṭhākakula”nti.

The laywoman, filled with faith, lay down on her chest facing the direction her son had gone, and paying homage, said: 'Surely, I think, the Blessed One, having made a monk like my son a personal witness, taught the practice of the Rathavinīta, the practice of the Nālakapaṭipada, the practice of the Tuvaṭṭaka, and the practice of the Great Noble Traditions, which illuminates contentment with the four requisites and delight in cultivation. Even while eating for three months in the house of the very mother who gave him birth, he would not say, “I am your son, you are my mother.” Oh, what a wonderful man! For such a one, even his mother and father are not impediments; how much more so another supporting family!'

Lābhoti cattāro paccayā. Te kathaṃ palibodhā honti? Puññavantassa hi bhikkhuno gatagataṭṭhāne manussā mahāparivāre paccaye denti. So tesaṃ anumodento dhammaṃ desento samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na okāsaṃ labhati. Aruṇuggamanato yāva paṭhamayāmo, tāva manussasaṃsaggo na upacchijjati. Puna balavapaccūseyeva bāhullikapiṇḍapātikā āgantvā “bhante, asuko upāsako upāsikā amacco amaccadhītā tumhākaṃ dassanakāmā”ti vadanti, so gaṇhāvuso, pattacīvaranti gamanasajjova hotīti niccabyāvaṭo, tasseva te paccayā palibodhā honti. Tena gaṇaṃ pahāya yattha naṃ na jānanti, tattha ekakena caritabbaṃ. Evaṃ so palibodho upacchijjatīti.

Gain means the four requisites. How do they become impediments? Indeed, for a monk of great merit, wherever he goes, people give requisites with a large retinue. While giving blessings to them and teaching the Dhamma, he finds no opportunity to practice the duties of a recluse. From the rising of the dawn until the first watch, his association with people does not cease. Again, very early in the morning, alms-gathering monks who desire many things come and say, 'Venerable sir, such-and-such a male lay devotee, female lay devotee, minister, or minister's daughter wishes to see you.' He, ready to go, says, 'Friend, take the bowl and robe.' Thus, he is constantly busy, and for such a one, those very requisites become impediments. Therefore, having abandoned the group, he should wander alone where they do not know him. In this way, that impediment is cut off.

Gaṇoti suttantikagaṇo vā ābhidhammikagaṇo vā, yo tassa uddesaṃ vā paripucchaṃ vā dento samaṇadhammassa okāsaṃ na labhati, tasseva gaṇo palibodho hoti, tena so evaṃ upacchinditabbo. Sace tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahu gahitaṃ hoti, appaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ, taṃ niṭṭhapetvā araññaṃ pavisitabbaṃ. Sace appaṃ gahitaṃ, bahu avasiṭṭhaṃ, yojanato paraṃ agantvā antoyojanaparicchede aññaṃ gaṇavācakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ime āyasmā uddesādīhi saṅgaṇhatū”ti vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ alabhamānena “mayhamāvuso, ekaṃ kiccaṃ atthi, tumhe yathāphāsukaṭṭhānāni gacchathā”ti gaṇaṃ pahāya attano kammaṃ kattabbanti.

A group means a group of Suttanta experts or a group of Abhidhamma experts. If a monk, while giving recitation or instruction to that group, does not get an opportunity to practice the duties of a recluse, for that very monk, the group becomes an impediment. Therefore, it should be cut off by him in this way: If those monks have learned much and little remains, having completed that remainder, he should enter the forest. If little has been learned and much remains, without going beyond a yojana, within the boundary of a yojana, he should approach another teacher of the group and say, 'May the venerable one support these monks with recitation and so on.' If unable to find such a teacher, he should say, 'Friends, I have a certain duty; you may go to places of comfort,' and, having abandoned the group, he should do his own task.

Kammanti navakammaṃ. Taṃ karontena vaḍḍhakīādīhi laddhāladdhaṃ jānitabbaṃ, katākate ussukkaṃ āpajjitabbanti sabbadā palibodho hoti. Sopi evaṃ upacchinditabbo, sace appaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti niṭṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace bahu, saṅghikañce navakammaṃ, saṅghassa vā saṅghabhārahārakabhikkhūnaṃ vā niyyādetabbaṃ. Attano santakañce, attano bhārahārakānaṃ niyyādetabbaṃ. Tādise alabhantena saṅghassa pariccajitvā gantabbanti.

Undertaking means new construction. While engaged in this, one must ascertain what has been received and what has not been received from carpenters and others, and be zealous regarding what has been done and what remains to be done; for this reason, it is always an impediment. It, too, should be severed thus: If little remains, it should be completed. If much remains, and it is the Sangha's new construction, it should be handed over to the Sangha or to monks responsible for the Sangha’s burdens. If it is his own property, it should be handed over to those who bear his burden. If such a person is not found, he should relinquish it to the Sangha and depart.

Addhānanti [M 1.0091] maggagamanaṃ. Yassa hi katthaci pabbajjāpekkho vā hoti, paccayajātaṃ vā [V 1.0093] kiñci laddhabbaṃ hoti. Sace taṃ alabhanto na sakkoti adhivāsetuṃ, araññaṃ pavisitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karontassapi gamikacittaṃ nāma duppaṭivinodanīyaṃ hoti, tasmā gantvā taṃ kiccaṃ tīretvāva samaṇadhamme ussukkaṃ kātabbanti.

Journey means traveling on a path. Indeed, for someone who anticipates ordination somewhere, or who needs to obtain some requisite, if, being unable to obtain it, he cannot bear it, even while dwelling in the forest and performing the duties of a recluse, the thought of traveling is difficult to remove. Therefore, he should go, complete that task, and only then strive diligently in the duties of a recluse.

Ñātīti vihāre ācariyupajjhāyasaddhivihārikaantevāsikasamānupajjhāyakasamānācariyakā, ghare mātā pitā bhātāti evamādikā. Te gilānā imassa palibodhā honti, tasmā so palibodho upaṭṭhahitvā tesaṃ pākatikakaraṇena upacchinditabbo.

Relatives are those in the monastery such as teachers, preceptors, co-residents, pupils, those under the same preceptor, or those under the same teacher; and at home, mother, father, brother, and so forth. If they are sick, they become an impediment for this person; therefore, that impediment should be severed by attending to them and restoring them to their normal condition.

Tattha upajjhāyo tāva gilāno sace lahuṃ na vuṭṭhāti, yāvajīvampi paṭijaggitabbo. Tathā pabbajjācariyo upasampadācariyo saddhivihāriko upasampāditapabbājitaantevāsikasamānupajjhāyakā ca. Nissayācariyauddesācariyanissayantevāsikauddesantevāsikasamānācariyakā pana yāva nissayauddesā anupacchinnā, tāva paṭijaggitabbā. Pahontena tato uddhampi paṭijaggitabbā eva. Mātāpitūsu upajjhāye viya paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Sacepi hi te rajje ṭhitā honti, puttato ca upaṭṭhānaṃ paccāsīsanti, kātabbameva. Atha tesaṃ bhesajjaṃ natthi, attano santakaṃ dātabbaṃ. Asati bhikkhācariyāya pariyesitvāpi dātabbameva. Bhātubhaginīnaṃ pana tesaṃ santakameva yojetvā dātabbaṃ. Sace natthi attano santakaṃ tāvakālikaṃ datvā pacchā labhantena gaṇhitabbaṃ. Alabhantena na codetabbā. Aññātakassa bhaginisāmikassa bhesajjaṃ neva kātuṃ na dātuṃ vaṭṭati. “Tuyhaṃ sāmikassa dehī”ti vatvā pana bhaginiyā dātabbaṃ. Bhātujāyāyapi eseva nayo. Tesaṃ pana puttā imassa ñātakā evāti tesaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

Among these, first, if the preceptor is sick and does not recover quickly, he should be cared for even for his entire life. Similarly, the teacher who gives the going-forth, the teacher who gives the higher ordination, the co-resident, the pupil to whom one has given the higher ordination, the pupil to whom one has given the going-forth, and those who have the same preceptor should also be cared for throughout their lives. However, the dependence teacher, the instruction teacher, the dependence pupil, the instruction pupil, and those who have the same teacher should be cared for as long as the dependence and instruction are not severed. By one who is able, they should be cared for even after that. One should attend to one's mother and father as one would to a preceptor. Indeed, even if they are established in kingship, if they expect attendance from their son, it must be done. Then, if they have no medicine, one's own property should be given. If one does not have any, having sought it by going for alms, it should be given. For brothers and sisters, however, having prepared only their own property, it should be given. If they have none, having given one's own property for a temporary period, it should be taken back later when one receives it. If one does not receive it back, they should not be pressed for it. It is not proper to either prepare or give medicine for a sister's husband who is not a relative. However, having said, 'Give this to your husband,' it should be given to the sister. This same method should be understood for a brother's wife as well. However, their children are indeed this monk's relatives, therefore it is proper to prepare it for them.

Ābādhoti yokoci rogo. So bādhayamāno palibodho hoti, tasmā bhesajjakaraṇena upacchinditabbo. Sace pana katipāhaṃ bhesajjaṃ karontassapi na vūpasammati, nāhaṃ tuyhaṃ dāso, na bhaṭako, taṃyeva [M 1.0092] hi posento anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe dukkhaṃ pattoti attabhāvaṃ garahitvā samaṇadhammo kātabboti.

Illness is any disease whatsoever. When it is afflicting, it is an impediment; therefore, it should be cut off by the preparation of medicine. However, if it does not subside for one who is preparing medicine for a few days, having reproached one's own individuality, thinking: 'I am not your slave, nor your hired servant. Indeed, by nourishing only you, I have attained suffering in this round of saṃsāra which has an inconceivable beginning,' the duty of a recluse should be performed.

Ganthoti [V 1.0094] pariyattiharaṇaṃ. Taṃ sajjhāyādīhi niccabyāvaṭassa palibodho hoti, na itarassa. Tatrimāni vatthūni –

Scriptural study is the mastery of the teachings. It is an impediment for one who is constantly occupied with recitation and so on, but not for another. Herein, these are the stories:

Majjhimabhāṇakadevatthero kira malayavāsidevattherassa santikaṃ gantvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ yāci. Thero kīdisosi, āvuso, pariyattiyanti pucchi. Majjhimo me, bhante, paguṇoti. Āvuso, majjhimo nāmeso dupparihāro, mūlapaṇṇāsaṃ sajjhāyantassa majjhimapaṇṇāsako āgacchati, taṃ sajjhāyantassa uparipaṇṇāsako. Kuto tuyhaṃ kammaṭṭhānanti? Bhante, tumhākaṃ santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ labhitvā puna na olokessāmīti kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ekūnavīsativassāni sajjhāyaṃ akatvā vīsatime vasse arahattaṃ patvā sajjhāyatthāya āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ “vīsati me, āvuso, vassāni pariyattiṃ anolokentassa, apica kho kataparicayo ahamettha ārabhathā”ti vatvā ādito paṭṭhāya yāva pariyosānā ekabyañjanepissa kaṅkhā nāhosi.

It is said that the Elder Deva, a reciter of the Majjhima Nikāya, went to the Elder Deva of Malayavāsa and requested a subject of meditation. The Elder asked, 'Friend, what is your proficiency in the scriptures?' 'Venerable sir, the Majjhima Nikāya is well-practiced by me,' he replied. 'Friend, this Majjhima Nikāya is difficult to maintain; while reciting the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa comes to mind, and while reciting that, the Uparipaṇṇāsa comes to mind. Whence will there be a subject of meditation for you?' 'Venerable sir, having received a subject of meditation from you, I will not look back at the texts again.' Having taken the subject of meditation, for nineteen years he did not recite, and in the twentieth year, he attained Arahantship. To the monks who came for the purpose of recitation, he said, 'Friends, for twenty years I have not looked at the scriptures; yet I am well-practiced in this. You may begin.' Having spoken thus, from the beginning to the very end, not even in a single syllable did any doubt arise for him.

Karuḷiyagirivāsīnāgattheropi aṭṭhārasavassāni pariyattiṃ chaḍḍetvā bhikkhūnaṃ dhātukathaṃ uddisi. Tesaṃ gāmavāsikattherehi saddhiṃ saṃsandentānaṃ ekapañhopi uppaṭipāṭiyā āgato nāhosi.

The Elder Nāga residing at Karuḷiyagiri also, having abandoned the study of the scriptures for eighteen years, taught the Dhātukathā to the monks. When those monks compared their learning with the village-dwelling elders, not even a single point came forth out of its proper sequence.

Mahāvihārepi tipiṭakacūḷābhayatthero nāma aṭṭhakathaṃ anuggahetvāva pañcanikāyamaṇḍale tīṇi piṭakāni parivattessāmīti suvaṇṇabheriṃ paharāpesi. Bhikkhusaṅgho katamācariyānaṃ uggaho, attano ācariyuggahaññeva vadatu, itarathā vattuṃ na demāti āha. Upajjhāyopi naṃ attano upaṭṭhānamāgataṃ pucchi “tvamāvuso, bheriṃ paharāpesī”ti? Āma, bhante. Kiṃ kāraṇāti? Pariyattiṃ, bhante, parivattessāmīti. Āvuso abhaya, ācariyā idaṃ padaṃ kathaṃ vadantīti? Evaṃ vadanti, bhanteti. Thero hunti paṭibāhi. Puna so aññena aññena pariyāyena evaṃ vadanti bhanteti tikkhattuṃ āha. Thero sabbaṃ hunti paṭibāhitvā “āvuso, tayā [M 1.0093] paṭhamaṃ kathito eva ācariyamaggo, ācariyamukhato pana anuggahitattā ‘evaṃ ācariyā vadantī’ti saṇṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi. Gaccha attano ācariyānaṃ santike suṇāhī”ti. Kuhiṃ, bhante, gacchāmīti? Gaṅgāya parato rohaṇajanapade tulādhārapabbatavihāre sabbapariyattiko mahādhammarakkhitatthero nāma vasati, tassa santikaṃ gacchāti. Sādhu, bhanteti theraṃ vanditvā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ therassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīdi. Thero kasmā āgatosīti [V 1.0095] pucchi. Dhammaṃ sotuṃ, bhanteti. Āvuso abhaya, dīghamajjhimesu maṃ kālena kālaṃ pucchanti. Avasesaṃ pana me tiṃsamattāni vassāni na olokitapubbaṃ. Apica tvaṃ rattiṃ mama santike parivattehi. Ahaṃ te divā kathayissāmīti. So sādhu, bhanteti tathā akāsi. Pariveṇadvāre mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā gāmavāsino divase divase dhammassavanatthāya āgacchanti. Thero rattiṃ parivatti. Taṃ divā kathayanto anupubbena desanaṃ niṭṭhapetvā abhayattherassa santike taṭṭikāya nisīditvā “āvuso, mayhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathehī”ti āha. Bhante, kiṃ bhaṇatha, nanu mayā tumhākameva santike sutaṃ? Kimahaṃ tumhehi aññātaṃ kathessāmīti? Tato naṃ thero añño esa, āvuso, gatakassa maggo nāmāti āha. Abhayathero kira tadā sotāpanno hoti. Athassa so kammaṭṭhānaṃ datvā āgantvā lohapāsāde dhammaṃ parivattento thero parinibbutoti assosi. Sutvā “āharathāvuso, cīvara”nti cīvaraṃ pārupitvā “anucchaviko, āvuso, amhākaṃ ācariyassa arahattamaggo. Ācariyo no, āvuso, uju ājānīyo. So attano dhammantevāsikassa santike taṭṭikāya nisīditvā ‘mayhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathehī’ti āha. Anucchaviko, āvuso, therassa arahattamaggo”ti. Evarūpānaṃ gantho palibodho na hotīti.

At the Mahāvihāra, an Elder named Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, without having mastered the commentaries, had a golden drum beaten, announcing, 'I will recite the three Piṭakas in the assembly that has learned the five Nikāyas.' The Saṅgha of bhikkhus said, 'Of which teachers is his learning? Let him state only his own teachers’ method of learning; otherwise, we will not permit him to speak.' His preceptor, when he came to attend upon him, asked, 'Friend, did you have the drum beaten?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'For what reason?' 'Friend Abhaya, how do the teachers explain this passage?' 'Thus they explain it, venerable sir.' The Elder rejected it with a 'Hum!' Again, he answered with another and another explanation, saying three times, 'Thus they explain it, venerable sir.' The Elder, having rejected all of them with a 'Hum!', said, 'Friend, what you first spoke was indeed the path of the teachers, but since you did not receive it from the teachers' own mouths, you were not able to establish firmly that "thus the teachers explain it." Go and listen in the presence of your own teachers.' 'Where, venerable sir, should I go?' 'Beyond the river Gaṅgā, in the Rohaṇa country, at the Tulādhārapabbata monastery, dwells an Elder named Mahādhammarakkhita, who has mastered all the scriptures. Go to him.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' he said, and having paid homage to the Elder, he went with five hundred bhikkhus into the presence of the other Elder. Having paid homage, he sat down. That Elder asked, 'Why have you come?' 'To hear the Dhamma, venerable sir.' 'Friend Abhaya, they question me from time to time on the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas. But as for the rest, it has been about thirty years since I have looked at them. However, you should recite in my presence at night, and I will explain it to you by day.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' he said, and did so. Having had a great pavilion built at the gate of the monastic cell, the villagers came day by day to listen to the Dhamma. Elder Abhaya recited at night. Explaining that by day, the other Elder gradually completed the exposition. Then, sitting on a rush mat near Elder Abhaya, he said, 'Friend, explain the meditation subject to me.' 'Venerable sir, what are you saying? Was it not in your very presence that I learned it? What could I explain that is unknown to you?' Then the Elder said to him, 'Friend, this path of one who has practiced is another path.' It is said that Elder Abhaya at that time became a stream-enterer. Then, having given him the meditation subject, Abhaya returned. While reciting the Dhamma in the Lohapāsāda, he heard that the Elder had attained Parinibbāna. Hearing this, he said, 'Friends, bring the robe!' and having donned the robe, he said, 'Friends, fitting for our teacher was the path to Arahantship. Friends, our teacher was upright, a thoroughbred. He sat on a rush mat near his own pupil of the Dhamma and requested, "Explain the meditation subject to me." Friends, fitting for the Elder was the path to Arahantship.' For such ones, the scriptures are no obstacle.

Iddhīti pothujjanikā iddhi. Sā hi uttānaseyyakadārako viya taruṇasassaṃ viya ca dupparihārā hoti. Appamattakeneva bhijjati. Sā pana vipassanāya palibodho hoti, na samādhissa, samādhiṃ patvā pattabbato. Tasmā vipassanatthikena iddhipalibodho upacchinditabbo, itarena avasesāti ayaṃ tāva palibodhakathāya vitthāro.

By 'supernormal power' is meant the supernormal power of an ordinary person. For it is as difficult to maintain as an infant who can only lie on its back or as a tender crop. It is destroyed by even a slight disturbance. That supernormal power is an obstacle to insight, but not to concentration, because it is to be attained only after having reached concentration. Therefore, one who desires insight should cut off the obstacle of supernormal power; the other, only the remaining obstacles. This, for now, is the detailed account in the discussion of obstacles.

Kammaṭṭhānadāyakavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Giver of a Meditation Subject

42. Kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ [M 1.0094] kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvāti ettha pana duvidhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānañca. Tattha sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma bhikkhusaṅghādīsu mettā maraṇassati ca. Asubhasaññātipi eke.

42. Now, here in the text beginning 'having approached a good friend, a giver of a meditation subject,' the meditation subject is of two kinds: the meditation subject suitable for all situations and the meditation subject to be constantly maintained. Among these, loving-kindness towards the community of monks and others, and mindfulness of death, are called the meditation subject suitable for all situations. Some also say that the perception of unattractiveness is a meditation subject suitable for all situations.

Kammaṭṭhānikena hi bhikkhunā paṭhamaṃ tāva paricchinditvā sīmaṭṭhakabhikkhusaṅghe sukhitā hontu abyāpajjāti mettā bhāvetabbā. Tato sīmaṭṭhakadevatāsu. Tato gocaragāmamhi issarajane. Tato [V 1.0096] tattha manusse upādāya sabbasattesu. So hi bhikkhusaṅghe mettāya sahavāsīnaṃ muducittataṃ janeti. Athassa te sukhasaṃvāsā honti. Sīmaṭṭhakadevatāsu mettāya mudukatacittāhi devatāhi dhammikāya rakkhāya susaṃvihitarakkho hoti. Gocaragāmamhi issarajane mettāya mudukatacittasantānehi issarehi dhammikāya rakkhāya surakkhitaparikkhāro hoti. Tattha manussesu mettāya pasāditacittehi tehi aparibhūto hutvā vicarati. Sabbasattesu mettāya sabbattha appaṭihatacāro hoti. Maraṇassatiyā pana avassaṃ mayā maritabbanti cintento anesanaṃ pahāya uparūpari vaḍḍhamānasaṃvego anolīnavuttiko hoti. Asubhasaññāparicitacittassa panassa dibbānipi ārammaṇāni lobhavasena cittaṃ na pariyādiyanti.

For a monk devoted to meditation should, first of all, having delimited the scope, develop loving-kindness towards the community of monks within the boundary, thinking: 'May they be happy, may they be free from distress.' Then, towards the deities within the boundary. Then, towards the ruling people in the alms-village. Then, towards all beings, beginning with the humans there. Indeed, by means of loving-kindness towards the community of monks, he generates a gentleness of heart in his fellow residents. Then they become pleasant to live with for him. By means of loving-kindness towards the deities of the boundary, he becomes one who is well-protected with righteous protection by those deities whose minds have been made gentle. By means of loving-kindness towards the ruling people in the alms-village, he becomes one whose requisites are well-protected with righteous protection by those rulers whose mental continuums have been made gentle. By means of loving-kindness towards the people there, he moves about without being despised by those people whose minds have been made confident. By means of loving-kindness towards all beings, he becomes one whose movement is unobstructed everywhere. Furthermore, with mindfulness of death, reflecting, 'I must surely die,' having abandoned improper seeking, he has a sense of urgency that grows ever stronger and becomes one whose conduct is unshrinking. And for one whose mind is familiar with the perception of unattractiveness, even divine objects do not overwhelm his mind through the power of greed.

Evaṃ bahūpakārattā sabbattha atthayitabbaṃ icchitabbanti ca adhippetassa yogānuyogakammassa ṭhānañcāti sabbatthakakammaṭṭhānanti vuccati.

Thus, because it is of great benefit, and because it is to be desired in all situations, and because it is the basis for the intended task of meditative practice, it is called the 'meditation subject for all situations'.

Cattālīsāya pana kammaṭṭhānesu yaṃ yassa cariyānukūlaṃ, taṃ tassa niccaṃ pariharitabbattā uparimassa ca uparimassa bhāvanākammassa padaṭṭhānattā pārihāriyakammaṭṭhānanti vuccati. Iti imaṃ duvidhampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ yo deti, ayaṃ kammaṭṭhānadāyako nāma. Taṃ kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ.

Now, among the forty meditation subjects, that which is suitable to one's temperament is called the 'meditation subject to be maintained' (pārihāriya-kammaṭṭhāna), because it should always be maintained by that person and because it is the proximate cause for higher and higher meditative practice. Thus, one who gives this twofold meditation subject is called a 'giver of meditation subjects' (kammaṭṭhānadāyaka). That giver of meditation subjects...

Kalyāṇamittanti –

...the 'good friend' (kalyāṇamitta) is one who is:

Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojakoti. (a. ni. 7.37);

He is dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem, an admonisher and patient of speech, a speaker of profound discourse, and one who does not engage you in a wrong place.

Evamādiguṇasamannāgataṃ ekantena hitesiṃ vuddhipakkhe ṭhitaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ.

...a good friend who is endowed with such virtues, solely intent on one's welfare, and established in the faction of growth.

“Mamaṃ [M 1.0095] hi, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma jātidhammā sattā jātiyā parimuccantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.129; 5.2) ādivacanato pana sammāsambuddhoyeva sabbākārasampanno kalyāṇamitto. Tasmā tasmiṃ sati tasseva bhagavato santike gahitakammaṭṭhānaṃ sugahitaṃ hoti. Parinibbute pana tasmiṃ asītiyā mahāsāvakesu yo dharati, tassa [V 1.0097] santike gahetuṃ vaṭṭati. Tasmiṃ asati yaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetukāmo hoti, tasseva vasena catukkapañcakajjhānāni nibbattetvā jhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā āsavakkhayappattassa khīṇāsavassa santike gahetabbaṃ.

From the saying beginning, 'Indeed, Ānanda, by relying on me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth,' it follows that the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is the good friend complete in all aspects. Therefore, while he is present, a meditation subject taken in the presence of that very Blessed One is well-taken. But when he has attained Parinibbāna, it is proper to take it from whichever of the eighty great disciples is still living. If such a one is not present, one who wishes to take a meditation subject should, by means of that very subject, produce the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, develop insight that has jhāna as its proximate cause, and then take it in the presence of one who has destroyed the taints, who has reached the destruction of the cankers.

Kiṃ pana khīṇāsavo ahaṃ khīṇāsavoti attānaṃ pakāsetīti? Kiṃ vattabbaṃ, kārakabhāvaṃ hi jānitvā pakāseti. Nanu assaguttatthero āraddhakammaṭṭhānassa bhikkhuno “kammaṭṭhānakārako aya”nti jānitvā ākāse cammakhaṇḍaṃ paññāpetvā tattha pallaṅkena nisinno kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesīti.

But does one who has destroyed the taints reveal himself, saying, 'I am one who has destroyed the taints'? What need is there to ask? Indeed, knowing the state of the practitioner, he reveals himself. Did not the Elder Assagutta, knowing of a monk who was practicing the meditation subject, 'This is a practitioner of the meditation subject,' spread out a piece of leather in the sky and, sitting there cross-legged, teach the meditation subject?

Tasmā sace khīṇāsavaṃ labhati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce labhati, anāgāmisakadāgāmisotāpannajhānalābhīputhujjanatipiṭakadharadvipiṭakadharaekapiṭakadharesu purimassa purimassa santike. Ekapiṭakadharepi asati yassa ekasaṅgītipi aṭṭhakathāya saddhiṃ paguṇā, ayañca lajjī hoti, tassa santike gahetabbaṃ. Evarūpo hi tantidharo vaṃsānurakkhako paveṇīpālako ācariyo ācariyamatikova hoti, na attanomatiko hoti. Teneva porāṇakattherā “lajjī rakkhissati lajjī rakkhissatī”ti tikkhattuṃ āhaṃsu.

Therefore, if one finds one who has destroyed the taints, that is excellent. If one does not, then one should learn from a Non-returner, a Once-returner, a Stream-enterer, a worldling who has attained jhāna, one who knows the three Piṭakas, one who knows two Piṭakas, or one who knows one Piṭaka—in the presence of each preceding one in turn. If even one who knows one Piṭaka is not available, one should learn in the presence of a person who is proficient in even a single Nikāya together with its commentary, and who is also conscientious. For such a person—a bearer of the scriptures, a preserver of the lineage, a guardian of the teaching-tradition—is a teacher who adheres to the teachers' view and is not one who follows his own opinion. For that very reason, the ancient elders said three times: 'The conscientious one will protect! The conscientious one will protect!'

Pubbe vuttakhīṇāsavādayo cettha attanā adhigatamaggameva ācikkhanti. Bahussuto pana taṃ taṃ ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā uggahaparipucchānaṃ visodhitattā ito cito ca suttañca kāraṇañca sallakkhetvā sappāyāsappāyaṃ yojetvā gahanaṭṭhāne gacchanto mahāhatthī viya mahāmaggaṃ dassento kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessati. Tasmā evarūpaṃ kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa vattapaṭipattiṃ katvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Among these, the aforementioned destroyers of the taints and so on declare only the path they themselves have attained. A very learned person, however, having approached various teachers and having clarified his learning and questioning, having marked well the Sutta passages and the reasoning from here and there, and having applied what is suitable and unsuitable, will teach the meditation subject like a great elephant that, when going into a dense place, shows a great path. Therefore, having approached such a good friend who is a giver of a meditation subject, and having performed the duties towards him, one should receive the meditation subject.

Sace [M 1.0096] panetaṃ ekavihāreyeva labhati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ, no ce labhati, yattha so vasati, tattha gantabbaṃ. Gacchantena ca na dhotamakkhitehi pādehi upāhanā ārūhitvā chattaṃ gahetvā telanāḷimadhuphāṇitādīni gāhāpetvā antevāsikaparivutena gantabbaṃ. Gamikavattaṃ pana pūretvā attano pattacīvaraṃ sayameva gahetvā antarāmagge yaṃ yaṃ vihāraṃ pavisati sabbattha vattapaṭipattiṃ kurumānena sallahukaparikkhārena paramasallekhavuttinā hutvā gantabbaṃ.

If one finds such a teacher in the very same monastery, that is excellent. If one does not, one should go to where he dwells. And when going, one should not go with feet washed and anointed, wearing sandals, holding a sunshade, having oil-tubes, honey, molasses, and so on carried by others, and surrounded by pupils. Rather, one should go having fulfilled the duties of a traveler, carrying one's own bowl and robes oneself; and on the way, in every monastery one enters, one should be performing the proper duties, having light requisites and a life of utmost austerity.

Taṃ [V 1.0098] vihāraṃ pavisantena antarāmaggeyeva dantakaṭṭhaṃ kappiyaṃ kārāpetvā gahetvā pavisitabbaṃ, na ca “muhuttaṃ vissametvā pādadhovanamakkhanādīni katvā ācariyassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti aññaṃ pariveṇaṃ pavisitabbaṃ. Kasmā? Sace hissa tatra ācariyassa visabhāgā bhikkhū bhaveyyuṃ, te āgamanakāraṇaṃ pucchitvā ācariyassa avaṇṇaṃ pakāsetvā “naṭṭhosi, sace tassa santikaṃ āgato”ti vippaṭisāraṃ uppādeyyuṃ, yena tatova paṭinivatteyya, tasmā ācariyassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā ujukaṃ tattheva gantabbaṃ.

When entering that monastery, one should have a tooth-cleaner made allowable on the way and take it with one when entering. And one should not think, "I will rest a while, wash my feet, anoint them, and then go to the teacher’s presence," and enter another enclosure. Why? For if there should be monks there who are incompatible with the teacher, they might ask the reason for coming, speak ill of the teacher, and cause remorse by saying, "You are ruined if you have come to his presence," by which one might turn back from that very spot. Therefore, one should ask for the teacher’s dwelling place and go straight there.

Sace ācariyo daharataro hoti, pattacīvarapaṭiggahaṇādīni na sāditabbāni. Sace vuḍḍhataro hoti, gantvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā ṭhātabbaṃ. “Nikkhipāvuso, pattacīvara”nti vuttena nikkhipitabbaṃ. “Pānīyaṃ pivā”ti vuttena sace icchati pātabbaṃ. “Pāde dhovāhī”ti vuttena na tāva pādā dhovitabbā. Sace hi ācariyena ābhataṃ udakaṃ bhaveyya, na sāruppaṃ siyā. “Dhovāhāvuso, na mayā ābhataṃ, aññehi ābhata”nti vuttena pana yattha ācariyo na passati, evarūpe paṭicchanne vā okāse, abbhokāse vihārassāpi vā ekamante nisīditvā pādā dhovitabbā.

If the teacher is younger, one should not consent to his taking of one's bowl and robes, and so on. If he is older, one should go, pay respects to the teacher, and stand. When told, “Friend, put down the bowl and robes,” one should put them down. When told, “Drink water,” if one wishes, one should drink. When told, “Wash your feet,” the feet should not be washed right away. For if it were water brought by the teacher, it would not be suitable. But when told, “Wash, friend; it was not brought by me, but by others,” then one should wash the feet, having sat down in a place where the teacher does not see, such as in a secluded place, or in an open space, or at one side of the monastery.

Sace ācariyo telanāḷiṃ āharati uṭṭhahitvā ubhohi hatthehi sakkaccaṃ gahetabbā. Sace hi na gaṇheyya, “ayaṃ bhikkhu ito eva paṭṭhāya sambhogaṃ kopetī”ti ācariyassa aññathattaṃ bhaveyya. Gahetvā pana na āditova pādā makkhetabbā. Sace hi taṃ ācariyassa gattabbhañjanatelaṃ bhaveyya, na sāruppaṃ siyā. Tasmā sīsaṃ makkhetvā [M 1.0097] khandhādīni makkhetabbāni. “Sabbapārihāriyatelamidaṃ, āvuso, pādepi makkhehī”ti vuttena pana thokaṃ sīse katvā pāde makkhetvā “imaṃ telanāḷiṃ ṭhapemi, bhante”ti vatvā ācariye gaṇhante dātabbā.

If the teacher brings an oil-tube, one should rise and receive it respectfully with both hands. For if one does not take it, the teacher might have a change of mind, thinking: “This monk, from this very moment, is violating the communion.” Having received it, one should not immediately anoint the feet. For if it is the teacher’s body-anointing oil, it would not be suitable. Therefore, one should anoint the head and then the shoulders and other parts. But if told, “Friend, this is oil for all purposes, anoint the feet too,” then after placing a little on the head, one should anoint the feet and say, “Venerable sir, I will set this oil-tube down,” and give it to the teacher as he takes it.

Āgatadivasato paṭṭhāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ me, bhante, kathetha iccevaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Dutiyadivasato pana paṭṭhāya sace ācariyassa pakatiupaṭṭhāko atthi, taṃ yācitvā vattaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace yācitopi na deti, okāse laddheyeva kātabbaṃ. Karontena khuddakamajjhimamahantāni tīṇi dantakaṭṭhāni upanāmetabbāni. Sītaṃ uṇhanti duvidhaṃ mukhadhovanaudakañca nhānodakañca paṭiyādetabbaṃ. Tato yaṃ ācariyo tīṇi divasāni paribhuñjati, tādisameva niccaṃ upanāmetabbaṃ. Niyamaṃ akatvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā paribhuñjantassa yathāladdhaṃ upanāmetabbaṃ. Kiṃ bahunā [V 1.0099] vuttena? Yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā “antevāsikena, bhikkhave, ācariyamhi sammā vattitabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ sammā vattanā, kālasseva uṭṭhāya upāhanā omuñcitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā dantakaṭṭhaṃ dātabbaṃ, mukhodakaṃ dātabbaṃ, āsanaṃ paññapetabbaṃ. Sace yāgu hoti, bhājanaṃ dhovitvā yāgu upanāmetabbā”ti (mahāva. 78) ādikaṃ khandhake sammāvattaṃ paññattaṃ, taṃ sabbampi kātabbaṃ.

From the day of arrival, one should not say, “Venerable sir, teach me the meditation subject.” But starting from the second day, if the teacher has a regular attendant, one should request him and perform the duties. If, even after being requested, he does not give permission, it should be done only when an opportunity is found. While doing so, one should present three tooth-sticks—small, medium, and large. Both cold and hot water for washing the face and for bathing should be prepared. Then, whatever kind of water the teacher uses for three days, that same kind should always be presented. For a teacher who uses whatever is at hand without a fixed preference, whatever is obtained should be presented. What need is there to say more? Whatever proper conduct was prescribed by the Blessed One in the Khandhaka—such as: “Monks, a resident pupil should conduct himself properly towards his teacher. Herein, this is the proper conduct: rising early, removing the sandals, arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, a tooth-stick should be given, water for the face should be given, a seat should be prepared. If there is rice gruel, having washed the bowl, the rice gruel should be presented”—all of that should be done.

Evaṃ vattasampattiyā garuṃ ārādhayamānena sāyaṃ vanditvā yāhīti vissajjitena gantabbaṃ, yadā so kissāgatosīti pucchati, tadā āgamanakāraṇaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Sace so neva pucchati, vattaṃ pana sādiyati, dasāhe vā pakkhe vā vītivatte ekadivasaṃ vissajjitenāpi agantvā okāsaṃ kāretvā āgamanakāraṇaṃ ārocetabbaṃ. Akāle vā gantvā kimatthamāgatosīti puṭṭhena ārocetabbaṃ. Sace so pātova āgacchāti vadati, pātova gantabbaṃ.

Thus, while pleasing the teacher by the fulfillment of duties, having paid respects in the evening, one should depart when dismissed with ‘Go!’ When he asks, “Why have you come?”, then the reason for coming should be stated. If he does not ask but approves of the duties, after ten days or a fortnight has passed, on one day, even though dismissed, one should not depart, but having created an opportunity, one should inform him of the reason for coming. Or, having gone at an improper time and being asked, “For what purpose have you come?”, one should inform him. If he says, “Come in the early morning,” one should go in the early morning.

Sace panassa tāya velāya pittābādhena vā kucchi pariḍayhati, aggimandatāya vā bhattaṃ na jīrati, añño vā koci rogo bādhati, taṃ yathābhūtaṃ āvikatvā attano sappāyavelaṃ ārocetvā tāya velāya upasaṅkamitabbaṃ. Asappāyavelāya hi vuccamānampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sakkā hoti manasikātunti. Ayaṃ kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvāti ettha vitthāro.

However, if at that time his stomach burns due to a bile disorder, or his food is not digested due to weak digestion, or some other illness afflicts him, having revealed that illness truthfully and having informed of his own suitable time, he should approach at that time. For, a meditation subject, even when taught at an unsuitable time, cannot be attended to. This is the detailed explanation here regarding “having approached a virtuous friend, a giver of a meditation subject.”

Cariyāvaṇṇanā

Description of Temperaments

43. Idāni [M 1.0098] attano cariyānukūlanti ettha cariyāti cha cariyā rāgacariyā, dosacariyā, mohacariyā, saddhācariyā, buddhicariyā, vitakkacariyāti. Keci pana rāgādīnaṃ saṃsaggasannipātavasena aparāpi catasso, tathā saddhādīnanti imāhi aṭṭhahi saddhiṃ cuddasa icchanti. Evaṃ pana bhede vuccamāne rāgādīnaṃ saddhādīhipi saṃsaggaṃ katvā anekā cariyā honti, tasmā saṅkhepena chaḷeva cariyā veditabbā. Cariyā, pakati, ussannatāti atthato ekaṃ. Tāsaṃ vasena chaḷeva puggalā honti rāgacarito, dosacarito, mohacarito, saddhācarito, buddhicarito, vitakkacaritoti.

43. Now, regarding the phrase 'suitable for one's own temperament': here, 'temperament' refers to six temperaments: lustful temperament, hateful temperament, deluded temperament, faithful temperament, intelligent temperament, and discursive temperament. Some, however, desire fourteen temperaments, positing four others by way of the combination and conjunction of lust, etc., and similarly four more from faith, etc., thus making eight additional temperaments. However, if the division is spoken of in this way, by making a combination of lust, etc., with faith, etc., there would be many temperaments. Therefore, in brief, only six temperaments should be understood. 'Temperament' (cariyā), 'nature' (pakati), and 'predominance' (ussannatā) are one in meaning. According to these, there are six types of individuals: one of lustful temperament, one of hateful temperament, one of deluded temperament, one of faithful temperament, one of intelligent temperament, and one of discursive temperament.

Tattha [V 1.0100] yasmā rāgacaritassa kusalappavattisamaye saddhā balavatī hoti, rāgassa āsannaguṇattā. Yathā hi akusalapakkhe rāgo siniddho nātilūkho, evaṃ kusalapakkhe saddhā. Yathā rāgo vatthukāme pariyesati, evaṃ saddhā sīlādiguṇe. Yathā rāgo ahitaṃ na pariccajati, evaṃ saddhā hitaṃ na pariccajati, tasmā rāgacaritassa saddhācarito sabhāgo.

Among them, because for a person of lustful temperament, faith is strong at the time of the arising of wholesome consciousness, due to its qualities being proximate to lust. For, just as in the unwholesome aspect, lust is smooth and not too harsh, so too in the wholesome aspect is faith. Just as lust seeks sensual objects, so faith seeks virtues such as morality. Just as lust does not abandon what is unbeneficial, so faith does not abandon what is beneficial. Therefore, a person of faithful temperament is akin to one of lustful temperament.

Yasmā pana dosacaritassa kusalappavattisamaye paññā balavatī hoti, dosassa āsannaguṇattā. Yathā hi akusalapakkhe doso nissineho na ārammaṇaṃ allīyati, evaṃ kusalapakkhe paññā. Yathā ca doso abhūtampi dosameva pariyesati, evaṃ paññā bhūtaṃ dosameva. Yathā doso sattaparivajjanākārena pavattati, evaṃ paññā saṅkhāraparivajjanākārena, tasmā dosacaritassa buddhicarito sabhāgo.

Furthermore, because for a person of hateful temperament, wisdom is strong at the time of the arising of wholesome consciousness, due to its qualities being proximate to hatred. For, just as in the unwholesome aspect, hatred is without affection and does not cling to an object, so too in the wholesome aspect is wisdom. And just as hatred seeks out even a non-existent fault, so wisdom seeks out a real fault. Just as hatred proceeds in the manner of avoiding beings, so wisdom proceeds in the manner of avoiding conditioned formations. Therefore, a person of intelligent temperament is akin to one of hateful temperament.

Yasmā pana mohacaritassa anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya vāyamamānassa yebhuyyena antarāyakarā vitakkā uppajjanti, mohassa āsannalakkhaṇattā. Yathā hi moho paribyākulatāya anavaṭṭhito, evaṃ vitakko nānappakāravitakkanatāya. Yathā ca moho apariyogāhaṇatāya cañcalo. Tathā vitakko lahuparikappanatāya, tasmā mohacaritassa vitakkacarito sabhāgoti.

Furthermore, because for a person of deluded temperament, when striving for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, obstructive thoughts mostly arise, due to its characteristic being proximate to delusion. For, just as delusion is unsettled due to perplexity, so discursive thought is unsettled due to thinking in various ways. And just as delusion is unsteady due to not fathoming, so discursive thought is unsteady due to quick conceptualization. Therefore, a person of discursive temperament is akin to one of deluded temperament.
