Apare taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena aparāpi tisso cariyā vadanti. Tattha taṇhā rāgoyeva, māno ca taṃsampayuttoti tadubhayaṃ rāgacariyaṃ nātivattati[M 1.0099]. Mohanidānattā ca diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhicariyā mohacariyameva anupatati.

Other teachers speak of three other temperaments by way of craving, conceit, and views. Therein, craving is just lust, and conceit is associated with it; therefore, the two of them do not go beyond the lustful temperament. And because views have delusion as their cause, the temperament of views follows only the deluded temperament.

44. Tā panetā cariyā kinnidānā? Kathañca jānitabbaṃ “ayaṃ puggalo rāgacarito, ayaṃ puggalo dosādīsu aññataracarito”ti? Kiṃ caritassa puggalassa kiṃ sappāyanti?

44. Now, what is the cause of these temperaments? And how is it to be known: “This person is of a lustful temperament; this person is of one of the other temperaments, such as the hateful one”? For a person of which temperament, what is suitable?

Tatra purimā tāva tisso cariyā pubbāciṇṇanidānā, dhātudosanidānā cāti ekacce vadanti. Pubbe kira iṭṭhappayogasubhakammabahulo rāgacarito hoti, saggā vā cavitvā idhūpapanno. Pubbe chedanavadhabandhanaverakammabahulo dosacarito hoti, nirayanāgayonīhi vā cavitvā idhūpapanno. Pubbe majjapānabahulo sutaparipucchāvihīno ca mohacarito hoti, tiracchānayoniyā [V 1.0101] vā cavitvā idhūpapannoti evaṃ pubbāciṇṇanidānāti vadanti. Dvinnaṃ pana dhātūnaṃ ussannattā puggalo mohacarito hoti pathavīdhātuyā ca āpodhātuyā ca. Itarāsaṃ dvinnaṃ ussannattā dosacarito. Sabbāsaṃ samattā pana rāgacaritoti. Dosesu ca semhādhiko rāgacarito hoti. Vātādhiko mohacarito. Semhādhiko vā mohacarito. Vātādhiko rāgacaritoti evaṃ dhātudosanidānāti vadanti.

Herein, some say that, firstly, the first three temperaments have past habitual practice as their cause and have the elements and humors as their cause. It is said that in a past life, one who abounded in desirable conduct and beautiful deeds is of a lustful temperament, or one who has passed away from a heavenly realm and arisen here. In a past life, one who abounded in deeds of cutting, killing, binding, and hostility is of a hateful temperament, or one who has passed away from the realms of hell or nāgas and arisen here. In a past life, one who abounded in consuming intoxicants and was devoid of learning and inquiry is of a deluded temperament, or one who has passed away from the animal realm and arisen here. Thus, they say, 'they have past habitual practice as their cause.' Furthermore, a person is of a deluded temperament due to the predominance of two elements: the earth element and the water element. Due to the predominance of the other two, one is of a hateful temperament. However, due to the balance of all, one is of a lustful temperament. And among the humors, one with an excess of phlegm is of a lustful temperament. One with an excess of wind is of a deluded temperament. Or, one with an excess of phlegm is of a deluded temperament; one with an excess of wind is of a lustful temperament. Thus, they say, 'they have the elements and humors as their cause.'

Tattha yasmā pubbe iṭṭhappayogasubhakammabahulāpi saggā cavitvā idhūpapannāpi ca na sabbe rāgacaritāyeva honti, na itare vā dosamohacaritā. Evaṃ dhātūnañca yathāvutteneva nayena ussadaniyamo nāma natthi. Dosaniyame ca rāgamohadvayameva vuttaṃ, tampi ca pubbāparaviruddhameva. Saddhācariyādīsu ca ekissāpi nidānaṃ na vuttameva. Tasmā sabbametaṃ aparicchinnavacanaṃ.

In that regard, because not all who in a past life abounded in desirable conduct and beautiful deeds, nor all who have passed away from a heavenly realm and arisen here, are exclusively of a lustful temperament; nor are the others exclusively of hateful or deluded temperaments. Similarly, for the elements, too, in the manner just stated, there is no such thing as a fixed rule of predominance. And in the fixed rule concerning the humors, only the pair of lust and delusion was stated, and that, too, is self-contradictory. Moreover, concerning the faithful temperament and so on, the cause of not even one was stated. Therefore, all this is an indeterminate statement.

Ayaṃ panettha aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ matānusārena vinicchayo, vuttañhetaṃ ussadakittane (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 498) “ime sattā pubbahetuniyāmena lobhussadā dosussadā mohussadā alobhussadā adosussadā amohussadā ca honti.

Now, herein, this is the decision in accordance with the view of the commentary teachers. For this was stated in the 'Enumeration of Predominances': 'These beings, by the fixed rule of a past cause, are predominant in greed, predominant in hatred, predominant in delusion, predominant in non-greed, predominant in non-hatred, and predominant in non-delusion.'

Yassa [M 1.0100] hi kammāyūhanakkhaṇe lobho balavā hoti alobho mando, adosāmohā balavanto dosamohā mandā, tassa mando alobho lobhaṃ pariyādātuṃ na sakkoti. Adosāmohā pana balavanto dosamohe pariyādātuṃ sakkoti. Tasmā so tena kammena dinnapaṭisandhivasena nibbatto luddho hoti sukhasīlo akkodhano paññavā vajirūpamañāṇo.

For one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed is strong and non-greed is weak, while non-hatred and non-delusion are strong and hatred and delusion are weak, that person's weak non-greed is not able to overcome greed. But the strong non-hatred and non-delusion are able to overcome hatred and delusion. Therefore, having been reborn by means of the rebirth-linking given by that kamma, that person becomes greedy, of pleasant disposition, unangered, wise, and possessing diamond-like knowledge.

Yassa pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe lobhadosā balavanto honti alobhādosā mandā, amoho balavā moho mando, so purimanayeneva luddho ceva hoti duṭṭho ca. Paññavā pana hoti vajirūpamañāṇo dattābhayatthero viya.

Furthermore, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed and hatred are strong and non-greed and non-hatred are weak, while non-delusion is strong and delusion is weak, such a person, by the previous method, is both greedy and malicious. But he is wise, possessing diamond-like knowledge, like the Elder Dattābhaya.

Yassa kammāyūhanakkhaṇe lobhādosamohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva luddho ceva hoti dandho ca, sīlako pana hoti akkodhano (bākulatthero viya).

For one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, that person, by the previous method, is both greedy and sluggish, but is virtuous and unangered, like the Elder Bākula.

Tathā [V 1.0102] yassa kammāyūhanakkhaṇe tayopi lobhadosamohā balavanto honti alobhādayo mandā, so purimanayeneva luddho ceva hoti duṭṭho ca mūḷho ca.

Similarly, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, all three—greed, hatred, and delusion—are strong, and non-greed and the others are weak, that person, by the previous method, is greedy, malicious, and deluded.

Yassa pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe alobhadosamohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva aluddho appakileso hoti dibbārammaṇampi disvā niccalo, duṭṭho pana hoti dandhapañño ca.

Furthermore, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, that person, by the previous method, is ungreedy and has few defilements, remaining unperturbed even upon seeing a divine object; but he is malicious and of slow wisdom.

Yassa pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe alobhādosamohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva aluddho ceva hoti aduṭṭho sīlako ca, dandho pana hoti.

Furthermore, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, non-hatred, and delusion are strong while the others are weak, that person, by the previous method, is both ungreedy and non-hating, and virtuous; but he is sluggish.

Tathā yassa kammāyūhanakkhaṇe alobhadosāmohā balavanto honti itare mandā, so purimanayeneva aluddho ceva hoti paññavā ca, duṭṭho ca pana hoti kodhano.

Similarly, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, non-greed, hatred, and non-delusion are strong while the others are weak, that person, by the previous method, is both ungreedy and wise; but he is malicious and angry.

Yassa [M 1.0101] pana kammāyūhanakkhaṇe tayopi alobhādosāmohā balavanto honti lobhādayo mandā, so purimanayeneva mahāsaṅgharakkhitatthero viya aluddho aduṭṭho paññavā ca hotī”ti.

Furthermore, for one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, all three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are strong while greed and the others are weak, that person, by the previous method, like the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita, is ungreedy, non-hating, and wise.

Ettha ca yo luddhoti vutto, ayaṃ rāgacarito. Duṭṭhadandhā dosamohacaritā. Paññavā buddhicarito. Aluddhaaduṭṭhā pasannapakatitāya saddhācaritā. Yathā vā amohaparivārena kammunā nibbatto buddhicarito, evaṃ balavasaddhāparivārena kammunā nibbatto saddhācarito. Kāmavitakkādiparivārena kammunā nibbatto vitakkacarito. Lobhādinā vomissaparivārena kammunā nibbatto vomissacaritoti. Evaṃ lobhādīsu aññataraññataraparivāraṃ paṭisandhijanakaṃ kammaṃ cariyānaṃ nidānanti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, among these, the one who is called 'greedy' is of a lustful temperament. The malicious and the dull are of hateful and deluded temperaments respectively. The one with wisdom is of an intelligent temperament. The non-greedy and non-malicious, due to their naturally serene disposition, are of a faithful temperament. Or, just as one produced by kamma accompanied by non-delusion is of an intelligent temperament, so too one produced by kamma accompanied by strong faith is of a faithful temperament. One produced by kamma accompanied by sensual thought and the like is of a discursive temperament. One produced by kamma with a mixed accompaniment of greed and so on is of a mixed temperament. Thus, it should be known that the kamma which produces rebirth-linking, accompanied by one or another of these factors like greed, is the cause of the temperaments.

45. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ kathañca jānitabbaṃ ayaṃ puggalo rāgacaritotiādi. Tatrāyaṃ nayo.

45. Now, as for what was said, 'And how is it to be known that this person is of a lustful temperament?' and so on, herein is the method.

Iriyāpathato kiccā, bhojanā dassanādito;

Dhammappavattito ceva, cariyāyo vibhāvayeti.

By way of deportment, duties, food, seeing and so on, and by the occurrence of mental states, one should discern the temperaments.

Tattha [V 1.0103] iriyāpathatoti rāgacarito hi pakatigamanena gacchanto cāturiyena gacchati, saṇikaṃ pādaṃ nikkhipati, samaṃ nikkhipati, samaṃ uddharati, ukkuṭikañcassa padaṃ hoti. Dosacarito pādaggehi khaṇanto viya gacchati, sahasā pādaṃ nikkhipati, sahasā uddharati, anukaḍḍhitañcassa padaṃ hoti. Mohacarito paribyākulāya gatiyā gacchati, chambhito viya padaṃ nikkhipati, chambhito viya uddharati, sahasānupīḷitañcassa padaṃ hoti. Vuttampi cetaṃ māgaṇḍiyasuttuppattiyaṃ –

Therein, regarding 'by way of deportment': a person of lustful temperament, when walking with a natural gait, walks with grace; they place their foot gently, place it evenly, and lift it evenly; and their footprint is arched. A person of hateful temperament walks as if digging the ground with the tips of their feet; they place their foot abruptly, lift it abruptly, and their footprint is dragged at the rear. A person of deluded temperament walks with a confused gait; they place their foot as if startled, lift it as if startled, and their footprint is hastily pressed down. And this was also said in the origin story of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta:

“Rattassa hi ukkuṭikaṃ padaṃ bhave,

Duṭṭhassa hoti anukaḍḍhitaṃ padaṃ;

Mūḷhassa hoti sahasānupīḷitaṃ,

Vivaṭṭacchadassa idamīdisaṃ pada”nti.

For one who is passionate, the footprint would be arched; for one who is malicious, the footprint is dragged at the rear; for one who is deluded, the footprint is hastily pressed down; for one whose covering is removed, the footprint is of this kind.

Ṭhānampi [M 1.0102] rāgacaritassa pāsādikaṃ hoti madhurākāraṃ, dosacaritassa thaddhākāraṃ, mohacaritassa ākulākāraṃ. Nisajjāyapi eseva nayo. Rāgacarito ca ataramāno samaṃ seyyaṃ paññapetvā saṇikaṃ nipajjitvā aṅgapaccaṅgāni samodhāya pāsādikena ākārena sayati, vuṭṭhāpiyamāno ca sīghaṃ avuṭṭhāya saṅkito viya saṇikaṃ paṭivacanaṃ deti. Dosacarito taramāno yathā vā tathā vā seyyaṃ paññapetvā pakkhittakāyo bhākuṭiṃ katvā sayati, vuṭṭhāpiyamāno ca sīghaṃ vuṭṭhāya kupito viya paṭivacanaṃ deti. Mohacarito dussaṇṭhānaṃ seyyaṃ paññapetvā vikkhittakāyo bahulaṃ adhomukho sayati, vuṭṭhāpiyamāno ca huṅkāraṃ karonto dandhaṃ vuṭṭhāti. Saddhācaritādayo pana yasmā rāgacaritādīnaṃ sabhāgā, tasmā tesampi tādisova iriyāpatho hotīti. Evaṃ tāva iriyāpathato cariyāyo vibhāvaye.

Even the standing of one with a lustful temperament is inspiring of confidence and has a graceful manner; for one with a hateful temperament, it has a stiff manner; for one with a deluded temperament, it has a confused manner. This same method applies also to sitting. One with a lustful temperament, not hurrying, prepares the bed evenly, lies down gently, composes their limbs and members, and sleeps in a manner that inspires confidence. And when being roused, not rising quickly, as if reluctant, they reply gently. One with a hateful temperament, hurrying, prepares the bed haphazardly, throws their body down, and sleeps with a frown. And when being roused, they rise quickly and reply as if angry. One with a deluded temperament prepares the bed in a disorderly manner, lies down with scattered limbs, and mostly sleeps face down. And when being roused, making a groaning sound, they rise sluggishly. Furthermore, since those of faithful temperament and so on are of a similar nature to those of lustful temperament and so on, their deportment is also of a similar kind. Thus, in the first place, one should discern the temperaments by way of deportment.

Kiccāti sammajjanādīsu ca kiccesu rāgacarito sādhukaṃ sammajjaniṃ gahetvā ataramāno vālikaṃ avippakiranto sinduvārakusumasantharamiva santharanto suddhaṃ samaṃ sammajjati. Dosacarito gāḷhaṃ sammajjaniṃ gahetvā taramānarūpo ubhato vālikaṃ ussārento kharena saddena asuddhaṃ visamaṃ sammajjati. Mohacarito sithilaṃ sammajjaniṃ gahetvā samparivattakaṃ āḷolayamāno asuddhaṃ visamaṃ sammajjati.

Furthermore, regarding duties: In duties such as sweeping, one with a lustful temperament takes the broom well and, not hurrying, not scattering the sand, but spreading it as if strewing sinduvāra flowers, sweeps cleanly and evenly. One with a hateful temperament takes the broom tightly and, being of a hurried nature, pushes the sand to both sides with a harsh sound, sweeping uncleanly and unevenly. One with a deluded temperament takes the broom loosely and, turning it this way and that while stirring up the sand and rubbish, sweeps uncleanly and unevenly.

Yathā sammajjane, evaṃ cīvaradhovanarajanādīsupi sabbakiccesu nipuṇamadhurasamasakkaccakārī [V 1.0104] rāgacarito. Gāḷhathaddhavisamakārī dosacarito. Anipuṇabyākulavisamāparicchinnakārī mohacarito. Cīvaradhāraṇampi ca rāgacaritassa nātigāḷhaṃ nātisithilaṃ hoti pāsādikaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ. Dosacaritassa atigāḷhaṃ aparimaṇḍalaṃ. Mohacaritassa sithilaṃ paribyākulaṃ. Saddhācaritādayo tesaṃyevānusārena veditabbā, taṃ sabhāgattāti. Evaṃ kiccato cariyāyo vibhāvaye.

As in sweeping, so too in all duties such as washing and dyeing robes, the one of lustful temperament acts skillfully, finely, evenly, and respectfully. The one of hateful temperament acts firmly, stiffly, and unevenly. The one of deluded temperament acts unskillfully, confusedly, unevenly, and indistinctly. Furthermore, the wearing of the robe by one of lustful temperament is neither too tight nor too loose; it is pleasing and well-rounded. For one of hateful temperament, it is too tight and not well-rounded. For one of deluded temperament, it is loose and disarranged. The faithful type and others should be understood in accordance with these, because of sharing their nature. Thus, one should distinguish the temperaments by their actions.

Bhojanāti rāgacarito siniddhamadhurabhojanappiyo hoti, bhuñjamāno ca nātimahantaṃ parimaṇḍalaṃ ālopaṃ katvā rasapaṭisaṃvedī ataramāno bhuñjati, kiñcideva ca sāduṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ āpajjati[M 1.0103]. Dosacarito lūkhaambilabhojanappiyo hoti, bhuñjamāno ca mukhapūrakaṃ ālopaṃ katvā arasapaṭisaṃvedī taramāno bhuñjati, kiñcideva ca asāduṃ labhitvā domanassaṃ āpajjati. Mohacarito aniyataruciko hoti, bhuñjamāno ca aparimaṇḍalaṃ parittaṃ ālopaṃ katvā bhājane chaḍḍento mukhaṃ makkhento vikkhittacitto taṃ taṃ vitakkento bhuñjati. Saddhācaritādayopi tesaṃyevānusārena veditabbā, taṃsabhāgattāti. Evaṃ bhojanato cariyāyo vibhāvaye.

Regarding food, the one of lustful temperament is fond of rich and sweet food. While eating, they make a moderately-sized, well-rounded morsel, savor the various tastes, eat unhurriedly, and experience joy upon receiving something delicious. The one of hateful temperament is fond of coarse and sour food. While eating, they make a mouthful, do not savor the taste, eat hurriedly, and experience displeasure upon receiving something unpleasant. The one of deluded temperament has unfixed tastes. While eating, they make an irregular, small morsel, drop food in the bowl, smear their mouth, and eat with a distracted mind, thinking of this and that. The faithful type and others should also be understood in accordance with these, because of sharing their nature. Thus, one should distinguish the temperaments by their eating.

Dassanāditoti rāgacarito īsakampi manoramaṃ rūpaṃ disvā vimhayajāto viya ciraṃ oloketi, parittepi guṇe sajjati, bhūtampi dosaṃ na gaṇhāti, pakkamantopi amuñcitukāmova hutvā sāpekkho pakkamati. Dosacarito īsakampi amanoramaṃ rūpaṃ disvā kilantarūpo viya na ciraṃ oloketi, parittepi dose paṭihaññati, bhūtampi guṇaṃ na gaṇhāti, pakkamantopi muñcitukāmova hutvā anapekkho pakkamati. Mohacarito yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ disvā parapaccayiko hoti, paraṃ nindantaṃ sutvā nindati, pasaṃsantaṃ sutvā pasaṃsati, sayaṃ pana aññāṇupekkhāya upekkhakova hoti. Esa nayo saddasavanādīsupi. Saddhācaritādayo pana tesaṃyevānusārena veditabbā, taṃsabhāgattāti. Evaṃ dassanādito cariyāyo vibhāvaye.

Regarding seeing and so on: one of lustful temperament, upon seeing even a slightly pleasing form, gazes at it for a long time as if amazed, becomes attached to even a minor virtue, and does not take note of even an actual fault. Even when departing, they leave with longing, as if unwilling to let go. One of hateful temperament, upon seeing even a slightly unpleasing form, does not gaze at it for long, as if weary, is offended by even a minor fault, and does not take note of even an actual virtue. Even when departing, they leave without longing, as if eager to be free of it. One of deluded temperament, upon seeing any form whatsoever, relies on others; hearing another criticize it, they criticize it; hearing another praise it, they praise it. They themselves, however, are merely indifferent through an equanimity of ignorance. This same method applies also to hearing sounds and so on. As for those of faithful temperament and so on, they are to be understood in accordance with those very ones, due to having a similar nature. Thus, one should discern the temperaments from seeing and so on.

Dhammappavattito cevāti rāgacaritassa ca māyā, sāṭheyyaṃ, māno, pāpicchatā, mahicchatā, asantuṭṭhitā, siṅgaṃ, cāpalyanti evamādayo dhammā bahulaṃ pavattanti. Dosacaritassa kodho, upanāho, makkho, paḷāso, issā, macchariyanti evamādayo. Mohacaritassa thinaṃ, middhaṃ, uddhaccaṃ, kukkuccaṃ, vicikicchā, ādhānaggāhitā, duppaṭinissaggitāti evamādayo. Saddhācaritassa [V 1.0105] muttacāgatā, ariyānaṃ dassanakāmatā, saddhammaṃ sotukāmatā, pāmojjabahulatā, asaṭhatā, amāyāvitā, pasādanīyesu ṭhānesu pasādoti evamādayo. Buddhicaritassa sovacassatā, kalyāṇamittatā, bhojanemattaññutā, satisampajaññaṃ, jāgariyānuyogo, saṃvejanīyesu ṭhānesu saṃvego, saṃviggassa ca yoniso padhānanti evamādayo. Vitakkacaritassa bhassabahulatā, gaṇārāmatā, kusalānuyoge arati, anavaṭṭhitakiccatā, rattiṃ dhūmāyanā[M 1.0104], divā pajjalanā, hurāhuraṃ dhāvanāti evamādayo dhammā bahulaṃ pavattantīti. Evaṃ dhammappavattito cariyāyo vibhāvaye.

And by the manifestation of qualities: For one of a lustful nature, deceit, fraud, conceit, evil desires, great desires, discontent, craftiness, and fickleness—these and other such evil qualities frequently arise. For one of a hateful nature, anger, resentment, contempt, rivalry, envy, and stinginess—these and other such qualities frequently arise. For one of a deluded nature, sloth, torpor, restlessness, worry, doubt, obstinate adherence, and difficulty in relinquishing—these and other such evil qualities frequently arise. For one of a faithful nature, open-handed generosity, desire to see the noble ones, desire to hear the true Dhamma, abundance of joy, honesty, absence of deceit, and confidence in inspiring situations—these and other such wholesome qualities frequently arise. For one of an intelligent nature, obedience, good friendship, moderation in food, mindfulness and clear comprehension, dedication to wakefulness, a sense of urgency in stirring situations, and for one who is stirred, wise effort—these and other such qualities frequently arise. For one of a speculative nature, excessive talk, delight in company, lack of delight in wholesome pursuits, instability in tasks, smoldering by night, blazing by day, and rushing here and there—these and other such qualities frequently arise. In this way, one should discern the temperaments by the manifestation of qualities.

Yasmā pana idaṃ cariyāvibhāvanavidhānaṃ sabbākārena neva pāḷiyaṃ na aṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgataṃ, kevalaṃ ācariyamatānusārena vuttaṃ, tasmā na sārato paccetabbaṃ. Rāgacaritassa hi vuttāni iriyāpathādīni dosacaritādayopi appamādavihārino kātuṃ sakkonti. Saṃsaṭṭhacaritassa ca puggalassa ekasseva bhinnalakkhaṇā iriyāpathādayo na upapajjanti. Yaṃ panetaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu cariyāvibhāvanavidhānaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva sārato paccetabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “cetopariyañāṇassa lābhī ācariyo cariyaṃ ñatvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessati, itarena antevāsiko pucchitabbo”ti. Tasmā cetopariyañāṇena vā taṃ vā puggalaṃ pucchitvā jānitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ puggalo rāgacarito, ayaṃ dosādīsu aññataracaritoti.

However, since this method of explaining temperaments has not come in the Pāḷi or the commentaries in any way, but is stated merely according to the views of the teachers, it should not be trusted as authoritative. For the postures and deportments stated for one of a lustful temperament can also be performed by those of a hateful temperament and others who dwell heedfully. And for a single person of mixed temperament, postures and so forth with distinct characteristics are not suitable. But that method of explaining temperaments which is stated in the commentaries, that indeed should be trusted as authoritative. For it has been said: 'A teacher who is an obtainer of the knowledge of discerning others' minds, having known the temperament, will declare the meditation subject; by another, the pupil should be questioned.' Therefore, it should be known either by the knowledge of discerning others' minds or by questioning that person thus: 'This person is of a lustful temperament; this one is of one or another temperament among hate and the others.'

46. Kiṃ caritassa puggalassa kiṃ sappāyanti ettha pana senāsanaṃ tāva rāgacaritassa adhotavedikaṃ bhūmaṭṭhakaṃ akatapabbhārakaṃ tiṇakuṭikaṃ paṇṇasālādīnaṃ aññataraṃ rajokiṇṇaṃ jatukābharitaṃ oluggaviluggaṃ atiuccaṃ vā atinīcaṃ vā ujjaṅgalaṃ sāsaṅkaṃ asucivisamamaggaṃ, yattha mañcapīṭhampi maṅkuṇabharitaṃ durūpaṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ, yaṃ olokentasseva jigucchā uppajjati, tādisaṃ sappāyaṃ. Nivāsanapārupanaṃ antacchinnaṃ olambavilambasuttakākiṇṇaṃ jālapūvasadisaṃ sāṇi viya kharasamphassaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ bhārikaṃ kicchapariharaṇaṃ sappāyaṃ. Pattopi dubbaṇṇo mattikāpatto vā āṇigaṇṭhikāhato ayopatto vā garuko dussaṇṭhāno sīsakapālamiva jeguccho vaṭṭati. Bhikkhācāramaggopi amanāpo anāsannagāmo visamo vaṭṭati. Bhikkhācāragāmopi yattha manussā apassantā viya caranti, yattha ekakulepi bhikkhaṃ alabhitvā nikkhamantaṃ “ehi, bhante”ti āsanasālaṃ pavesetvā yāgubhattaṃ datvā gacchantā gāvī viya vaje pavesetvā anapalokentā gacchanti, tādiso vaṭṭati[V 1.0106]. Parivisakamanussāpi dāsā vā kammakarā vā dubbaṇṇā duddasikā kiliṭṭhavasanā duggandhā jegucchā, ye acittīkārena yāgubhattaṃ chaḍḍentā viya parivisanti, tādisā sappāyā. Yāgubhattakhajjakampi lūkhaṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ sāmākakudrūsakakaṇājakādimayaṃ [M 1.0105] pūtitakkaṃ bilaṅgaṃ jiṇṇasākasūpeyyaṃ yaṃkiñcideva kevalaṃ udarapūramattaṃ vaṭṭati. Iriyāpathopissa ṭhānaṃ vā caṅkamo vā vaṭṭati. Ārammaṇaṃ nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu yaṃkiñci aparisuddhavaṇṇanti idaṃ rāgacaritassa sappāyaṃ.

46. Herein, as to what is suitable for a person of what temperament, first, for one of a lustful temperament, a dwelling is suitable that is one among such as a monastery with an unwashed platform, one standing on the ground, an unprepared mountain slope, a grass hut, or a leaf hut; which is strewn with dust, filled with bats, dilapidated and crumbling, either too high or too low, with rough and saline ground, inspiring dread, and with an unclean and uneven path; where even the bed and chair are filled with bedbugs, of deteriorated appearance and poor shape, which arouses disgust in one merely upon looking at it. The lower and upper robes are suitable if they are torn at the edges, strewn with dangling and trailing threads, like a net-cake, rough to the touch like hemp cloth, soiled, heavy, and difficult to maintain. The alms-bowl, too, is suitable if it is of poor color—either a clay bowl or an iron bowl whose beauty is ruined by pegs and patches—heavy, ill-shaped, and disgusting like a human skull. The path for the alms-round, too, is suitable if it is unpleasant, not near a village, and uneven. The village for the alms-round, too, is suitable if it is one where people act as if they do not see him; where, upon his leaving even a single house without receiving alms, they do not call out, “Come, venerable sir,” lead him into a seating hall, and give him gruel and rice; and where, after giving, they depart without looking back, just as they herd cows into a pen and depart. Such a village is suitable. The people who serve, too, are suitable if they are slaves or laborers—of poor appearance, unpleasant to behold, wearing soiled clothes, foul-smelling, and disgusting, who serve gruel and rice disrespectfully, as if throwing it away. Gruel, rice, and hard food, too, are suitable if they are coarse, of poor color, made of millet, kudrūsaka, broken rice, and so forth; or if it is putrid buttermilk, sour gruel, or a curry of old vegetables; or just anything at all that is merely for filling the stomach. For him, the suitable bodily postures are standing or walking. As for the meditation object, among the color kasiṇas—blue and so on—any one with an impure color is suitable. All this is suitable for one of a lustful temperament.

Dosacaritassa senāsanaṃ nātiuccaṃ nātinīcaṃ chāyūdakasampannaṃ suvibhattabhittithambhasopānaṃ supariniṭṭhitamālākammalatākammanānāvidhacittakammasamujjalasamasiniddhamudubhūmitalaṃ brahmavimānamiva kusumadāmavicitravaṇṇacelavitānasamalaṅkataṃ supaññattasucimanoramattharaṇamañcapīṭhaṃ tattha tattha vāsatthāya nikkhittakusumavāsagandhasugandhaṃ yaṃ dassanamatteneva pītipāmojjaṃ janayati, evarūpaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa pana senāsanassa maggopi sabbaparissayavimutto sucisamatalo alaṅkatapaṭiyattova vaṭṭati. Senāsanaparikkhāropettha kīṭamaṅkuṇadīghajātimūsikānaṃ nissayaparicchindanatthaṃ nātibahuko, ekamañcapīṭhamattameva vaṭṭati. Nivāsanapārupanampissa cīnapaṭṭasomārapaṭṭakoseyyakappāsikasukhumakhomādīnaṃ yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ, tena tena ekapaṭṭaṃ vā dupaṭṭaṃ vā sallahukaṃ samaṇasāruppena surattaṃ suddhavaṇṇaṃ vaṭṭati. Patto udakapupphuḷamiva susaṇṭhāno maṇi viya sumaṭṭho nimmalo samaṇasāruppena suparisuddhavaṇṇo ayomayo vaṭṭati. Bhikkhācāramaggo parissayavimutto samo manāpo nātidūranāccāsannagāmo vaṭṭati. Bhikkhācāragāmopi yattha manussā “idāni ayyo āgamissatī”ti sittasammaṭṭhe padese āsanaṃ paññāpetvā paccuggantvā pattaṃ ādāya gharaṃ pavesetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā sakkaccaṃ sahatthā parivisanti, tādiso vaṭṭati. Parivesakā panassa ye honti abhirūpā pāsādikā sunhātā suvilittā dhūpavāsakusumagandhasurabhino nānāvirāgasucimanuññavatthābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitā sakkaccakārino, tādisā sappāyā. Yāgubhattakhajjakampi vaṇṇagandharasasampannaṃ ojavantaṃ manoramaṃ sabbākārapaṇītaṃ yāvadatthaṃ vaṭṭati. Iriyāpathopissa seyyā vā nisajjā vā vaṭṭati, ārammaṇaṃ nīlādīsu vaṇṇakasiṇesu yaṃkiñci suparisuddhavaṇṇanti idaṃ dosacaritassa sappāyaṃ.

For one of a hateful temperament, a dwelling is suitable that is not too high and not too low, endowed with shade and water, having well-divided walls, pillars, and stairs; having a ground surface that is radiant, even, smooth, and soft, with well-finished garland-work, creeper-work, and various kinds of artistic designs; like a Brahma-mansion, well-adorned with canopies of cloth of variegated colors and with garlands of flowers; having well-arranged, clean, and delightful coverings, beds, and chairs; fragrant with the scent of perfumes and flowers placed here and there for perfuming; which by its mere sight generates rapture and joy—such a dwelling is suitable. Furthermore, the path to that dwelling should be free from all dangers, clean, level, and adorned and well-prepared; this is suitable. In this dwelling, the furnishings should not be too many, for the purpose of preventing insects, bedbugs, snakes, and mice from taking up residence; only a single bed and chair are suitable. For him, as for the under-robe and outer-robe, whatever is excellent among cloths from China, cloths from the Somāra country, silk, fine cotton, fine linen, and so on—a single-layered or double-layered one that is light, well-dyed, of pure color, and suitable for a recluse, is suitable. The bowl should be well-formed like a water bubble, well-polished like a gem, spotless, of a perfectly pure color suitable for a recluse, and made of iron; this is suitable. The alms-round path should be free from dangers, even, pleasant, with a village for alms that is not too far and not too near; this is suitable. The alms-round village is also suitable if it is one where people, thinking, 'Now the noble one will come,' having prepared a seat in a place that has been sprinkled with water and swept, having gone out to meet him, taking his bowl, having led him into the house, having seated him on the prepared seat, serve him respectfully with their own hands—such a one is suitable. Furthermore, his servers are suitable if they are beautiful, pleasing, well-bathed, well-anointed, fragrant with the scent of incense, perfumes, and flowers, adorned with clean and delightful clothes and ornaments of various dyes, and acting respectfully—such ones are suitable. Gruel, rice, and hard food are also suitable if they are endowed with color, scent, and taste, nutritious, delightful, excellent in all aspects, and as much as is wanted. For him, the posture of either lying down or sitting is suitable. The object of meditation should be any one among the color kasiṇas, such as blue, etc., that is of a perfectly pure color. This is suitable for one of a hateful temperament.

Mohacaritassa [M 1.0106] senāsanaṃ disāmukhaṃ asambādhaṃ vaṭṭati, yattha nisinnassa vivaṭā disā khāyanti[V 1.0107], iriyāpathesu caṅkamo vaṭṭati. Ārammaṇaṃ panassa parittaṃ suppamattaṃ sarāvamattaṃ vā (khuddakaṃ) na vaṭṭati. Sambādhasmiñhi okāse cittaṃ bhiyyo sammohamāpajjati, tasmā vipulaṃ mahākasiṇaṃ vaṭṭati. Sesaṃ dosacaritassa vuttasadisamevāti idaṃ mohacaritassa sappāyaṃ.

For one of a deluded temperament, a dwelling that is uncrowded and faces an open direction, where the directions appear open when one is seated, is suitable. Among the postures, walking is suitable. However, for him, a small meditation object—the size of a small measuring bowl or the size of a large pot lid—is not suitable. For in a confined space, the mind falls into even greater delusion. Therefore, a vast, great kasiṇa is suitable. The rest is just as was said for one of a hateful temperament. This is what is suitable for one of a deluded temperament.

Saddhācaritassa sabbampi dosacaritamhi vuttavidhānaṃ sappāyaṃ. Ārammaṇesu cassa anussatiṭṭhānampi vaṭṭati.

For one of a faithful temperament, all the provisions stated in the section on the hateful temperament are suitable. And among the meditation objects, the recollection subjects are also suitable for him.

Buddhicaritassa senāsanādīsu idaṃ nāma asappāyanti natthi.

For one of an intelligent temperament, there is nothing among dwellings and so forth that can be called unsuitable.

Vitakkacaritassa senāsanaṃ vivaṭaṃ disāmukhaṃ yattha nisinnassa ārāmavanapokkharaṇīrāmaṇeyyakāni gāmanigamajanapadapaṭipāṭiyo nīlobhāsā ca pabbatā paññāyanti, taṃ na vaṭṭati, tañhi vitakkavidhāvanasseva paccayo hoti, tasmā gambhīre darīmukhe vanappaṭicchanne hatthikucchipabbhāramahindaguhāsadise senāsane vasitabbaṃ. Ārammaṇampissa vipulaṃ na vaṭṭati. Tādisañhi vitakkavasena sandhāvanassa paccayo hoti. Parittaṃ pana vaṭṭati.

For one of a speculative temperament, a dwelling that is open and faces a direction where, when one is seated, delightful parks, groves, and ponds, rows of villages, towns, and districts, and mountains with a blue-green hue are visible, is not suitable. For such a place is a condition for the wandering of speculative thought. Therefore, one should dwell in a dwelling at the entrance of a deep ravine, covered by the forest, like the Mahinda Cave on the Hatthikucchi mountain slope. A vast meditation object is also not suitable for him, for such an object is a condition for the mind's wandering by way of speculative thought. A small one, however, is suitable.

Sesaṃ rāgacaritassa vuttasadisamevāti idaṃ vitakkacaritassa sappāyaṃ. Ayaṃ attano cariyānukūlanti ettha āgatacariyānaṃ pabhedanidānavibhāvanasappāyaparicchedato vitthāro. Na ca tāva cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ sabbākārena āvikataṃ. Tañhi anantarassa mātikāpadassa vitthāre sayameva āvibhavissati.

The rest is just as was said for one of a lustful temperament. This is what is suitable for one of a speculative temperament. This is the detailed explanation—by way of the sections on classification, cause, analysis, and suitability—of the temperaments that have been discussed in the context of the phrase 'in accordance with one's own temperament.' And yet, the meditation subject suitable for one's temperament has not yet been revealed in all its aspects. For it will become clear by itself in the detailed explanation of the immediately following matrix heading.

Cattālīsakammaṭṭhānavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Forty Meditation Subjects

47. Tasmā yaṃ vuttaṃ cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesu aññataraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāti ettha saṅkhātaniddesato, upacārappanāvahato, jhānappabhedato, samatikkamato, vaḍḍhanāvaḍḍhanato, ārammaṇato, bhūmito, gahaṇato, paccayato, cariyānukūlatoti imehi tāva dasahākārehi kammaṭṭhānavinicchayo veditabbo.

47. Therefore, regarding what was said—'having taken one of the forty meditation subjects'—herein the discernment of meditation subjects should be known for now by these ten aspects: by way of enumeration and explanation, by way of leading to access and absorption, by way of the classification of jhānas, by way of transcending, by way of development and non-development, by way of the object, by way of the plane, by way of grasping, by way of conditions, and by way of suitability to one's temperament.

Tattha [M 1.0107] saṅkhātaniddesatoti cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesūti hi vuttaṃ, tatrimāni cattālīsa kammaṭṭhānāni [V 1.0108] dasa kasiṇā, dasa asubhā, dasa anussatiyo, cattāro brahmavihārā, cattāro āruppā, ekā saññā, ekaṃ vavatthānanti.

Therein, as to 'by way of enumeration and explanation': for it was said, 'among forty meditation subjects.' Therein, these are the forty meditation subjects: ten kasiṇas, ten foulnesses, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four formless states, one perception, and one defining.

Tattha pathavīkasiṇaṃ, āpokasiṇaṃ, tejokasiṇaṃ, vāyokasiṇaṃ, nīlakasiṇaṃ, pītakasiṇaṃ, lohitakasiṇaṃ, odātakasiṇaṃ, ālokakasiṇaṃ, paricchinnākāsakasiṇanti ime dasa kasiṇā.

Therein, the earth kasiṇa, water kasiṇa, fire kasiṇa, air kasiṇa, blue kasiṇa, yellow kasiṇa, red kasiṇa, white kasiṇa, light kasiṇa, and the delimited-space kasiṇa—these are the ten kasiṇas.

Uddhumātakaṃ, vinīlakaṃ, vipubbakaṃ, vicchiddakaṃ, vikkhāyitakaṃ, vikkhittakaṃ, hatavikkhittakaṃ, lohitakaṃ, puḷuvakaṃ, aṭṭhikanti ime dasa asubhā.

The bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut-up, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked-and-scattered, the bloody, the worm-infested, and the skeleton—these are the ten foulnesses.

Buddhānussati, dhammānussati, saṅghānussati, sīlānussati, cāgānussati, devatānussati, maraṇānussati, kāyagatāsati, ānāpānassati, upasamānussatīti imā dasa anussatiyo.

Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of death, mindfulness directed to the body, mindfulness of breathing, and recollection of peace—these are the ten recollections.

Mettā, karuṇā, muditā, upekkhāti ime cattāro brahmavihārā.

Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—these are the four divine abidings.

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ, ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ime cattāro āruppā. Āhāre paṭikūlasaññā ekā saññā. Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ ekaṃ vavatthānanti evaṃ saṅkhātaniddesato vinicchayo veditabbo.

The base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are the four formless states. The perception of loathsomeness in food is the one perception. The defining of the four elements is the one defining. Thus the discernment should be known by way of enumeration and explanation.

Upacārappanāvahatoti ṭhapetvā kāyagatāsatiñca ānāpānassatiñca avasesā aṭṭha anussatiyo, āhāre paṭikūlasaññā, catudhātuvavatthānanti imāneva hettha dasakammaṭṭhānāni upacāravahāni. Sesāni appanāvahāni. Evaṃ upacārappanāvahato.

As to 'by way of leading to access and absorption': setting aside mindfulness directed to the body and mindfulness of breathing, the remaining eight recollections, the perception of loathsomeness in food, and the defining of the four elements—herein, these ten meditation subjects alone lead to access. The remaining ones lead to absorption. Thus it is by way of leading to access and absorption.

Jhānappabhedatoti appanāvahesu cettha ānāpānassatiyā saddhiṃ dasa kasiṇā catukkajjhānikā honti. Kāyagatāsatiyā saddhiṃ dasa asubhā paṭhamajjhānikā. Purimā tayo brahmavihārā tikajjhānikā. Catutthabrahmavihāro cattāro ca āruppā catutthajjhānikāti evaṃ jhānappabhedato.

By way of the classification of jhānas: Herein, among those meditation subjects leading to absorption, the ten kasiṇas together with mindfulness of breathing are associated with four jhānas. The ten kinds of foulness together with mindfulness of the body are associated with the first jhāna. The first three divine abidings are associated with three jhānas. The fourth divine abiding and the four formless attainments are associated with the fourth jhāna. Thus, by way of the classification of jhānas.

Samatikkamatoti dve samatikkamā aṅgasamatikkamo ca ārammaṇasamatikkamo ca. Tattha sabbesupi [V 1.0109] tikacatukkajjhānikesu kammaṭṭhānesu aṅgasamatikkamo [M 1.0108] hoti vitakkavicārādīni jhānaṅgāni samatikkamitvā tesvevārammaṇesu dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ pattabbato. Tathā catutthabrahmavihāre. Sopi hi mettādīnaṃyeva ārammaṇe somanassaṃ samatikkamitvā pattabboti. Catūsu pana āruppesu ārammaṇasamatikkamo hoti. Purimesu hi navasu kasiṇesu aññataraṃ samatikkamitvā ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ pattabbaṃ. Ākāsādīni ca samatikkamitvā viññāṇañcāyatanādīni. Sesesu samatikkamo natthīti evaṃ samatikkamato.

By way of transcending: There are two kinds of transcending—the transcending of factors and the transcending of object. Herein, in all meditation subjects associated with the three or four jhānas, there is transcending of factors, since having transcended the jhāna factors such as initial thought and sustained thought, one attains the second jhāna, etc., in the same objects. Similarly, in the fourth divine abiding, one attains it by transcending joy in the same object as loving-kindness, etc. But in the four formless attainments, there is transcending of object. For by transcending any one of the first nine kasiṇas, the base of the infinity of space is to be attained; and by transcending space, etc., the base of the infinity of consciousness, etc., are to be attained. In the remaining ones, there is no transcending. Thus, by way of transcending.

Vaḍḍhanāvaḍḍhanatoti imesu cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesu dasa kasiṇāneva vaḍḍhetabbāni. Yattakañhi okāsaṃ kasiṇena pharati, tadabbhantare dibbāya sotadhātuyā saddaṃ sotuṃ dibbena cakkhunā rūpāni passituṃ parasattānañca cetasā cittamaññātuṃ samattho hoti. Kāyagatāsati pana asubhāni ca na vaḍḍhetabbāni. Kasmā? Okāsena paricchinnattā ānisaṃsābhāvā ca. Sā ca nesaṃ okāsena paricchinnatā bhāvanānaye āvibhavissati. Tesu pana vaḍḍhitesu kuṇaparāsiyeva vaḍḍhati, na koci ānisaṃso atthi. Vuttampi cetaṃ sopākapañhābyākaraṇe, “vibhūtā bhagavā rūpasaññā avibhūtā aṭṭhikasaññā”ti. Tatra hi nimittavaḍḍhanavasena rūpasaññā vibhūtāti vuttā. Aṭṭhikasaññā avaḍḍhanavasena avibhūtāti vuttā.

Regarding development and non-development: Among these forty meditation subjects, only the ten kasiṇas are to be developed. For to whatever extent one pervades a region with a kasiṇa, within that area one becomes capable of hearing sounds with the divine ear-element, of seeing forms with the divine eye, and of knowing the minds of other beings with one's own mind. However, mindfulness directed to the body and the foulness meditations are not to be developed. Why? Because they are limited by their location and because there is no benefit. And their being limited by location will become apparent in the method of development. For when these are developed, only a heap of corpses increases; there is no benefit whatsoever. This was also stated in the explanation of Sopāka's question: 'O Blessed One, the perception of form is expansive; the perception of a skeleton is not expansive.' For there, the perception of form is said to be expansive by way of the development of the sign, whereas the perception of a skeleton is said to be not expansive by way of its non-development.

Yaṃ panetaṃ “kevalaṃ aṭṭhisaññāya, apharī pathaviṃ ima”nti (theragā. 18) vuttaṃ, taṃ lābhissa sato upaṭṭhānākāravasena vuttaṃ. Yatheva hi dhammāsokakāle karavīkasakuṇo samantā ādāsabhittīsu attano chāyaṃ disvā sabbadisāsu karavīkasaññī hutvā madhuraṃ giraṃ nicchāresi, evaṃ theropi aṭṭhikasaññāya lābhittā sabbadisāsu upaṭṭhitaṃ nimittaṃ passanto kevalāpi pathavī aṭṭhikabharitāti cintesīti.

As for that which was stated, 'With the perception of a skeleton, he pervaded this entire earth' (Theragāthā 18), that was said by way of the mode of its appearance to one who is an obtainer of that perception. For just as in the time of King Dhammāsoka, a karavīka bird, seeing its own reflection on the mirror-walls all around and thus perceiving karavīka birds in all directions, uttered a sweet sound; so too the elder, being an obtainer of the perception of a skeleton and seeing the sign appearing in all directions, thought, 'The entire earth is filled with skeletons.'

Yadi evaṃ yā asubhajjhānānaṃ appamāṇārammaṇatā vuttā, sā virujjhatīti. Sā ca na virujjhati. Ekacco hi uddhumātake vā aṭṭhike vā mahante nimittaṃ gaṇhāti. Ekacco appake. Iminā pariyāyena ekaccassa parittārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ hoti. Ekaccassa appamāṇārammaṇanti. Yo vā etaṃ vaḍḍhane ādīnavaṃ apassanto vaḍḍheti. Taṃ sandhāya “appamāṇārammaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Ānisaṃsābhāvā pana na vaḍḍhetabbānīti.

If so, it might be argued that this contradicts the statement that the foulness jhānas have an immeasurable object. But it is not contradicted. For one person takes up the sign in a large bloated corpse or skeleton, while another takes it up in a small one. In this way, for one person the jhāna has a limited object, while for another it has an immeasurable object. Or else, it was said with reference to one who, not seeing the danger in developing it, develops it nonetheless. However, because there is no benefit, they are not to be developed.

Yathā [M 1.0109][V 1.0110] ca etāni, evaṃ sesānipi na vaḍḍhetabbāni. Kasmā? Tesu hi ānāpānanimittaṃ tāva vaḍḍhayato vātarāsiyeva vaḍḍhati, okāsena ca paricchinnaṃ. Iti sādīnavattā okāsena ca paricchinnattā na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Brahmavihārā sattārammaṇā, tesaṃ nimittaṃ vaḍḍhayato sattarāsiyeva vaḍḍheyya, na ca tena attho atthi, tasmā tampi na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā”ti (dī. ni. 1.556) ādi, taṃ pariggahavaseneva vuttaṃ. Ekāvāsadviāvāsādinā hi anukkamena ekissā disāya satte pariggahetvā bhāvento ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvāti vutto. Na nimittaṃ vaḍḍhento. Paṭibhāganimittameva cettha natthi. Yadayaṃ vaḍḍheyya, parittaappamāṇārammaṇatāpettha pariggahavaseneva veditabbā. Āruppārammaṇesupi ākāsaṃ kasiṇugghāṭimattā. Tañhi kasiṇāpagamavaseneva manasi kātabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ vaḍḍhayatopi na kiñci hoti. Viññāṇaṃ sabhāvadhammattā. Na hi sakkā sabhāvadhammaṃ vaḍḍhetuṃ. Viññāṇāpagamo viññāṇassa abhāvamattattā. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanārammaṇaṃ sabhāvadhammattāyeva na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Sesāni animittattā. Paṭibhāganimittañhi vaḍḍhetabbaṃ nāma bhaveyya. Buddhānussatiādīnañca neva paṭibhāganimittaṃ ārammaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā taṃ na vaḍḍhetabbanti evaṃ vaḍḍhanāvaḍḍhanato.

And just as these should not be developed, so too the rest should not be developed. Why? For among those, in the case of one who develops the sign of mindfulness of breathing, only the mass of wind increases, and it is delimited by location. Thus, because of its faultiness and because of being delimited by location, it should not be developed. The divine abidings have beings as their object; for one who develops their sign, only the mass of beings would increase, and there is no benefit in that. Therefore, that too should not be developed. As for what was said, "With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, pervading one direction," etc., that was said only in the sense of encompassing. Indeed, one who develops meditation by successively encompassing beings in one direction—by way of those in one residence, two residences, etc.—is said to be "pervading one direction," not one who is developing the sign. And here there is no counterpart sign at all that this yogi might develop. Here, the state of having a limited or immeasurable object should also be understood only in the sense of encompassing. Also among the objects of the formless attainments, space is merely the removal of the kasiṇa. Indeed, it should be attended to only by way of the removal of the kasiṇa. For one who develops it beyond that, nothing further arises. Consciousness should not be developed because it is a phenomenon with its own intrinsic nature; indeed, it is not possible to develop a phenomenon with its own intrinsic nature. The absence of consciousness should not be developed because it is merely the absence of consciousness. The object of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should not be developed precisely because it is a phenomenon with its own intrinsic nature. The remaining subjects should not be developed because they are without a counterpart sign. Indeed, it is the counterpart sign that would be what is called 'to be developed'. And the object of recollection of the Buddha, etc., is not a counterpart sign; therefore, it should not be developed. Thus, by way of what is to be developed and what is not to be developed.

Ārammaṇatoti imesu ca cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesu dasakasiṇā, dasaasubhā, ānāpānassati, kāyagatāsatīti imāni dvāvīsatipaṭibhāganimittārammaṇāni. Sesāni na paṭibhāganimittārammaṇāni. Tathā dasasu anussatīsu ṭhapetvā ānāpānassatiñca kāyagatāsatiñca avasesā aṭṭha anussatiyo, āhāre paṭikūlasaññā, catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ, nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti imāni dvādasa sabhāvadhammārammaṇāni. Dasa kasiṇā, dasa asubhā, ānāpānassati, kāyagatāsatīti imāni dvāvīsati nimittārammaṇāni. Sesāni cha na vattabbārammaṇāni. Tathā vipubbakaṃ, lohitakaṃ, puḷuvakaṃ, ānāpānassati, āpokasiṇaṃ, tejokasiṇaṃ, vāyokasiṇaṃ, yañca ālokakasiṇe sūriyādīnaṃ obhāsamaṇḍalārammaṇanti imāni aṭṭha calitārammaṇāni, tāni ca kho pubbabhāge, paṭibhāgaṃ pana sannisinnameva hoti. Sesāni na calitārammaṇānīti evaṃ ārammaṇato.

The determination by way of the object is to be understood. Among these forty meditation subjects, the ten kasiṇas, the ten kinds of foulness, mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness of the body—these twenty-two have the counterpart sign as their object. The remaining do not have the counterpart sign as their object. Similarly, among the ten recollections, having set aside mindfulness of breathing and mindfulness of the body, the remaining eight recollections, the perception of repulsiveness in regard to food, the defining of the four elements, the base of infinite consciousness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these twelve have natural phenomena as their object. The ten kasiṇas, the ten kinds of foulness, mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness of the body—these twenty-two have a sign as their object. The remaining six have objects that are not to be specified. Likewise, the festering corpse, the bloody corpse, the worm-infested corpse, mindfulness of breathing, the water kasiṇa, the fire kasiṇa, the air kasiṇa, and that which has as its object the luminous disc of the sun, etc., in the light kasiṇa—these eight have a moving object. And indeed, they are moving only in the preliminary stage; the counterpart sign, however, is indeed still. The remaining do not have a moving object. Thus is the determination by way of the object.

Bhūmitoti [M 1.0110] ettha ca dasa asubhā, kāyagatāsati, āhāre paṭikūlasaññāti imāni dvādasa devesu nappavattanti. Tāni dvādasa, ānāpānassati cāti imāni terasa brahmaloke nappavattanti[V 1.0111]. Arūpabhave pana ṭhapetvā cattāro āruppe aññaṃ nappavattati. Manussesu sabbānipi pavattantīti evaṃ bhūmito.

The determination by way of the plane is to be understood. Herein, the ten kinds of foulness, mindfulness of the body, and the perception of repulsiveness in regard to food—these twelve do not occur among the devas. Those twelve, and also mindfulness of breathing—these thirteen do not occur in the Brahma world. In the formless existence, however, having set aside the four formless attainments, no other meditation subject occurs. Among humans, all of them occur. Thus is the determination by way of the plane.

Gahaṇatoti diṭṭhaphuṭṭhasutaggahaṇatopettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Tatra ṭhapetvā vāyokasiṇaṃ sesā nava kasiṇā, dasa asubhāti imāni ekūnavīsati diṭṭhena gahetabbāni. Pubbabhāge cakkhunā oloketvā nimittaṃ nesaṃ gahetabbanti attho. Kāyagatāsatiyaṃ tacapañcakaṃ diṭṭhena, sesaṃ sutenāti evaṃ tassā ārammaṇaṃ diṭṭhasutena gahetabbaṃ. Ānāpānassati phuṭṭhena, vāyokasiṇaṃ diṭṭhaphuṭṭhena, sesāni aṭṭhārasa sutena gahetabbāni. Upekkhābrahmavihāro, cattāro āruppāti imāni cettha na ādikammikena gahetabbāni. Sesāni pañcatiṃsa gahetabbānīti evaṃ gahaṇato.

The determination by way of grasping is to be understood by way of grasping through what is seen, touched, or heard. Among these, setting aside the air kasiṇa, the remaining nine kasiṇas and the ten kinds of foulness—these nineteen—are to be grasped by what is seen. The meaning is that in the preliminary stage, their sign is to be grasped by looking with the eye. In mindfulness of the body, the pentad of the skin is to be grasped by what is seen, and the rest by what is heard; thus its object is to be grasped by what is seen and heard. Mindfulness of breathing is to be grasped by what is touched, the air kasiṇa by what is seen and touched, and the remaining eighteen by what is heard. Furthermore, the divine abiding of equanimity and the four immaterial attainments—these are not to be grasped here by a beginner. The remaining thirty-five are to be grasped. Thus is the determination by way of grasping.

Paccayatoti imesu pana kammaṭṭhānesu ṭhapetvā ākāsakasiṇaṃ sesā nava kasiṇā āruppānaṃ paccayā honti, dasa kasiṇā abhiññānaṃ, tayo brahmavihārā catutthabrahmavihārassa, heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ āruppaṃ uparimassa uparimassa, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ nirodhasamāpattiyā, sabbānipi sukhavihāravipassanābhavasampattīnanti evaṃ paccayato.

The determination by way of condition is to be understood. Now, among these meditation subjects, setting aside the space kasiṇa, the remaining nine kasiṇas are conditions for the immaterial attainments; the ten kasiṇas are conditions for the direct knowledges; the three divine abidings are conditions for the fourth divine abiding; each lower immaterial attainment is a condition for the one above it; the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of cessation; and all of them are conditions for pleasant abiding in the present life, for insight, and for the accomplishment of existence. Thus is the determination by way of condition.

Cariyānukūlatoti cariyānaṃ anukūlatopettha vinicchayo veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – rāgacaritassa tāva ettha dasa asubhā, kāyagatāsatīti ekādasa kammaṭṭhānāni anukūlāni. Dosacaritassa cattāro brahmavihārā, cattāri vaṇṇakasiṇānīti aṭṭha. Mohacaritassa, vitakkacaritassa ca ekaṃ ānāpānassati kammaṭṭhānameva. Saddhācaritassa purimā cha anussatiyo. Buddhicaritassa maraṇassati, upasamānussati, catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, āhāre paṭikūlasaññāti cattāri. Sesakasiṇāni, cattāro ca āruppā sabbacaritānaṃ anukūlāni. Kasiṇesu ca yaṃkiñci parittaṃ vitakkacaritassa, appamāṇaṃ mohacaritassāti.

The determination by way of suitability to temperament is to be understood. It is as follows: for one of greedy temperament, the ten kinds of foulness and mindfulness of the body—these eleven meditation subjects—are suitable. For one of hateful temperament, the four divine abidings and the four color kasiṇas—these eight—are suitable. For one of deluded temperament and for one of discursive temperament, only the one meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is suitable. For one of faithful temperament, the first six recollections are suitable. For one of intelligent temperament, mindfulness of death, recollection of peace, defining of the four elements, and perception of repulsiveness in food—these four—are suitable. The remaining kasiṇas and the four immaterial attainments are suitable for all temperaments. And among the kasiṇas, any small one is suitable for one of discursive temperament, while an immeasurable one is suitable for one of deluded temperament.

Evamettha [M 1.0111] cariyānukūlato vinicchayo veditabboti sabbañcetaṃ ujuvipaccanīkavasena ca atisappāyavasena ca vuttaṃ. Rāgādīnaṃ pana avikkhambhikā saddhādīnaṃ vā anupakārā kusalabhāvanā nāma natthi. Vuttampi cetaṃ meghiyasutte –

Thus, the determination here by way of suitability to temperament is to be understood. And all this has been stated by way of direct opposition and by way of extreme suitability. However, there is no so-called wholesome development that does not suppress greed and so forth, or that is not helpful to faith and so forth. This was also stated in the Meghiya Sutta:

“Cattāro dhammā uttari bhāvetabbā. Asubhā bhāvetabbā rāgassa pahānāya. Mettā bhāvetabbā byāpādassa [V 1.0112] pahānāya. Ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāya. Aniccasaññā bhāvetabbā asmimānasamugghātāyā”ti.

“Four things are to be further developed. The meditation on foulness is to be developed for the abandoning of greed. Loving-kindness is to be developed for the abandoning of ill will. Mindfulness of breathing is to be developed for the cutting off of discursive thought. The perception of impermanence is to be developed for the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.’”

Rāhulasuttepi “mettaṃ, rāhula, bhāvanaṃ bhāvehī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.120) nayena ekasseva satta kammaṭṭhānāni vuttāni. Tasmā vacanamatte abhinivesaṃ akatvā sabbattha adhippāyo pariyesitabboti ayaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāti ettha kammaṭṭhānakathā vinicchayo.

In the Rāhula Sutta too, seven meditation subjects were taught to a single individual, in the manner beginning with, “Rāhula, develop the meditation on loving-kindness.” Therefore, without clinging to mere words, the underlying intention should be sought in all cases. This is the determination of the discussion on meditation subjects in the context of “having taken up a meditation subject.”

48. Gahetvāti imassa pana padassa ayamatthadīpanā. “Tena yoginā kammaṭṭhānadāyakaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā”ti ettha vuttanayeneva vuttappakāraṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā buddhassa vā bhagavato ācariyassa vā attānaṃ niyyātetvā sampannajjhāsayena sampannādhimuttinā ca hutvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācitabbaṃ.

48. Now, of this term “having taken up,” this is the elucidation of the meaning. Following the very method stated in the context of “That yogī, having approached a good friend who is a giver of a meditation subject,” one should approach a good friend of the kind described, surrender oneself to the Buddha, the Blessed One, or to one's teacher, and with a perfected intention and a perfected resolve, request a meditation subject.

Tatra “imāhaṃ bhagavā attabhāvaṃ tumhākaṃ pariccajāmī”ti evaṃ buddhassa bhagavato attā niyyātetabbo. Evañhi aniyyātetvā pantesu senāsanesu viharanto bheravārammaṇe āpāthamāgate santhambhituṃ asakkonto gāmantaṃ osaritvā gihīhi saṃsaṭṭho hutvā anesanaṃ āpajjitvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpuṇeyya. Niyyātitattabhāvassa panassa bheravārammaṇe āpāthamāgatepi bhayaṃ na uppajjati. “Nanu tayā, paṇḍita, purimameva attā buddhānaṃ niyyātito”ti paccavekkhato panassa somanassameva uppajjati. Yathā hi purisassa uttamaṃ kāsikavatthaṃ bhaveyya, tassa tasmiṃ mūsikāya vā kīṭehi vā khādite uppajjeyya domanassaṃ[M 1.0112]. Sace pana taṃ acīvarakassa bhikkhuno dadeyya, athassa taṃ tena bhikkhunā khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ kariyamānaṃ disvāpi somanassameva uppajjeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, one should surrender oneself to the Buddha, the Blessed One, thinking: 'I relinquish this being of mine to you, O Blessed One.' For if one does not surrender in this way, while dwelling in remote abodes, when terrifying objects appear, one may be unable to compose oneself and might descend to the village, mingle with householders, engage in improper seeking, and meet with ruin and misfortune. But for one who has surrendered their being, even when terrifying objects appear, fear does not arise. On the contrary, for one reflecting thus: 'O wise one, have you not already surrendered yourself to the Buddhas?'—only joy arises. Just as if a man possessed the finest Kāsi cloth, sorrow might arise for him if it were eaten by rats or insects. But if he were to give it to a robe-less monk, even seeing it being torn to shreds by that monk, only joy would arise in him. This accomplishment is to be understood in this way.

Ācariyassa niyyātentenāpi “imāhaṃ, bhante, attabhāvaṃ tumhākaṃ pariccajāmī”ti vattabbaṃ. Evaṃ aniyyātitattabhāvo hi atajjanīyo vā hoti, dubbaco vā anovādakaro, yenakāmaṃgamo vā ācariyaṃ anāpucchāva yatthicchati, tattha gantā, tamenaṃ ācariyo āmisena vā dhammena vā na saṅgaṇhāti, gūḷhaṃ ganthaṃ na sikkhāpeti. So imaṃ duvidhaṃ saṅgahaṃ alabhanto sāsane patiṭṭhaṃ na labhati, nacirasseva dussīlyaṃ vā gihibhāvaṃ vā pāpuṇāti. Niyyātitattabhāvo pana neva atajjanīyo hoti, na yenakāmaṃgamo, suvaco ācariyāyattavuttiyeva [V 1.0113] hoti. So ācariyato duvidhaṃ saṅgahaṃ labhanto sāsane vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ pāpuṇāti cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissattherassa antevāsikā viya.

When surrendering oneself to the teacher, one should say, 'Venerable sir, I relinquish this being of mine to you.' For one who has not so surrendered their being is either not to be reproved, or is difficult to admonish and unamenable to advice; they go wherever they please without asking the teacher. The teacher does not support them with material aid or with the Dhamma, nor teach them profound texts. Not receiving these two forms of support, they find no footing in the Dispensation and before long fall into immorality or revert to lay life. But one who has surrendered their being is not beyond reproof, nor do they go wherever they please; they are easy to admonish and their livelihood is dependent on the teacher. Receiving the two forms of support from the teacher, they attain growth, development, and abundance in the Dispensation, like the pupils of the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissa.

Therassa kira santikaṃ tayo bhikkhū āgamaṃsu. Tesu eko “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākamatthāyā”ti vutte sataporise papāte patituṃ ussaheyyanti āha. Dutiyo “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākamatthāyā”ti vutte imaṃ attabhāvaṃ paṇhito paṭṭhāya pāsāṇapiṭṭhe ghaṃsento niravasesaṃ khepetuṃ ussaheyyanti āha. Tatiyo “ahaṃ, bhante, tumhākamatthāyā”ti vutte assāsapassāse uparundhitvā kālakiriyaṃ kātuṃ ussaheyyanti āha. Thero bhabbāvatime bhikkhūti kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Te tassa ovāde ṭhatvā tayopi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti ayamānisaṃso attaniyyātane. Tena vuttaṃ “buddhassa vā bhagavato ācariyassa vā attānaṃ niyyātetvā”ti.

It is said that three monks came to the Elder. Among them, one said: 'Venerable sir, if it were for your sake, I would dare to leap from a cliff a hundred men high.' The second said: 'Venerable sir, if it were for your sake, I would dare to grind this being on a stone slab, starting from the heel, until it was completely worn away.' The third said: 'Venerable sir, if it were for your sake, I would dare to stop my in-and-out breathing and die.' The Elder, thinking, 'These monks are truly capable,' taught them a meditation subject. Abiding in his instruction, all three attained arahantship. This is the benefit of surrendering oneself. Therefore it was said: 'Having surrendered oneself to the Buddha, the Blessed One, or to one’s teacher.'

49. Sampannajjhāsayena sampannādhimuttinā ca hutvāti ettha pana tena yoginā alobhādīnaṃ vasena chahākārehi sampannajjhāsayena bhavitabbaṃ. Evaṃ sampannajjhāsayo hi tissannaṃ bodhīnaṃ aññataraṃ pāpuṇāti. Yathāha, “cha ajjhāsayā bodhisattānaṃ bodhiparipākāya saṃvattanti, alobhajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā lobhe dosadassāvino, adosajjhāsayā [M 1.0113] ca bodhisattā dose dosadassāvino, amohajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā mohe dosadassāvino, nekkhammajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā gharāvāse dosadassāvino, pavivekajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā saṅgaṇikāya dosadassāvino, nissaraṇajjhāsayā ca bodhisattā sabbabhavagatīsu dosadassāvino”ti. Ye hi keci atītānāgatapaccuppannā sotāpannasakadāgāmianāgāmikhīṇāsavapaccekabuddhasammāsambuddhā, sabbe te imeheva chahākārehi attanā attanā pattabbaṃ visesaṃ pattā. Tasmā imehi chahākārehi sampannajjhāsayena bhavitabbaṃ. Tadadhimuttatāya pana adhimuttisampannena bhavitabbaṃ. Samādhādhimuttena samādhigarukena samādhipabbhārena, nibbānādhimuttena nibbānagarukena nibbānapabbhārena ca bhavitabbanti attho.

49. Herein, regarding the phrase 'having become one with a perfected disposition and perfected resolve,' furthermore, that yogi should be possessed of a perfected disposition in six aspects by way of non-greed and so forth. For one who is thus possessed of a perfected disposition attains one of the three kinds of enlightenment. As it is said: 'Six dispositions of bodhisattas conduce to the maturation of enlightenment. Bodhisattas with a disposition of non-greed see the fault in greed; bodhisattas with a disposition of non-hatred see the fault in hatred; bodhisattas with a disposition of non-delusion see the fault in delusion; bodhisattas with a disposition of renunciation see the fault in the household life; bodhisattas with a disposition of seclusion see the fault in company; and bodhisattas with a disposition of escape see the fault in all states of existence and destinies.' For whosoever, in the past, future, or present, are stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arahants, Paccekabuddhas, or Sammāsambuddhas, all of them have attained the special state that was to be attained by each of them respectively through these very six aspects. Therefore, one should be possessed of a perfected disposition through these six aspects. Furthermore, through being resolved on that goal, one should be possessed of perfected resolve. The meaning is that one should be inclined towards concentration, revere concentration, and gravitate towards concentration; and be inclined towards Nibbāna, revere Nibbāna, and gravitate towards Nibbāna.

50. Evaṃ sampannajjhāsayādhimuttino panassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācato cetopariyañāṇalābhinā ācariyena cittācāraṃ oloketvā cariyā jānitabbā. Itarena kiṃ caritosi? Ke vā te dhammā bahulaṃ samudācaranti? Kiṃ vā te manasikaroto phāsu hoti? Katarasmiṃ vā te kammaṭṭhāne [V 1.0114] cittaṃ namatīti evamādīhi nayehi pucchitvā jānitabbā. Evaṃ ñatvā cariyānukūlaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetabbaṃ.

50. Furthermore, when a meditation subject is requested by this person who is possessed of a perfected disposition and resolve, a teacher who has obtained the knowledge of others' minds should know his temperament by observing the conduct of his mind. Another teacher should know the temperament by asking with such methods as these: 'What is your temperament? Or what states frequently arise in you? Or what, when you attend to it, becomes comfortable for you? Or towards which meditation subject does your mind incline?' Having known thus, a meditation subject suitable to the temperament should be taught.

Kathentena ca tividhena kathetabbaṃ. Pakatiyā uggahitakammaṭṭhānassa ekaṃ dve nisajjāni sajjhāyaṃ kāretvā dātabbaṃ. Santike vasantassa āgatāgatakkhaṇe kathetabbaṃ. Uggahetvā aññatra gantukāmassa nātisaṃkhittaṃ nātivitthārikaṃ katvā kathetabbaṃ.

And it should be explained by the teacher in three ways. For one who has previously taken up a meditation subject, it should be given after having him recite it for one or two sittings. For a disciple living nearby, it should be explained at the moment of each arrival. For a disciple who wishes to go elsewhere after learning it, it should be explained neither too briefly nor too elaborately.

Tattha pathavīkasiṇaṃ tāva kathentena cattāro kasiṇadosā, kasiṇakaraṇaṃ, katassa bhāvanānayo, duvidhaṃ nimittaṃ, duvidho samādhi, sattavidhaṃ sappāyāsappāyaṃ, dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ, vīriyasamatā, appanāvidhānanti ime nava ākārā kathetabbā. Sesakammaṭṭhānesupi tassa tassa anurūpaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ tesaṃ bhāvanāvidhāne āvibhavissati.

Therein, when explaining the earth kasiṇa first, these nine aspects should be explained: the four faults of a kasiṇa, the making of a kasiṇa, the method for developing what has been made, the two kinds of sign, the two kinds of concentration, the seven kinds of suitability and unsuitability, the tenfold skill in absorption, the balancing of energy, and the procedure for absorption. In the remaining meditation subjects as well, what is appropriate to each should be explained. All of that will become clear in the section on the method of their development.

Evaṃ kathiyamāne pana kammaṭṭhāne tena yoginā nimittaṃ gahetvā sotabbaṃ. Nimittaṃ gahetvāti idaṃ heṭṭhimapadaṃ, idaṃ uparimapadaṃ, ayamassa attho[M 1.0114], ayamadhippāyo, idamopammanti evaṃ taṃ taṃ ākāraṃ upanibandhitvāti attho. Evaṃ nimittaṃ gahetvā sakkaccaṃ suṇantena hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti. Athassa taṃ nissāya visesādhigamo sampajjati, na itarassāti ayaṃ gahetvāti imassa padassa atthaparidīpanā.

While the meditation subject is being explained in this way, the yogi should grasp the key points and listen. 'Grasping the key points' means: 'This is the lower phrase, this is the upper phrase, this is its meaning, this is its intention, this is the simile'—thus connecting each such aspect. For by grasping the key points in this way and listening attentively, the meditation subject is well-grasped. Then, relying on that, special attainment is accomplished for him, but not for the other. This is the explanation of the meaning of this word, gahetvā (having grasped).

Ettāvatā kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano cariyānukūlaṃ cattālīsāya kammaṭṭhānesu aññataraṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāti imāni padāni sabbākārena vitthāritāni hontīti.

Thus far, the words 'having approached a good friend and taken up a meditation subject suitable to one's disposition from among the forty meditation subjects' have been explained in detail in every way.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, made for the delight of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the development of concentration,

Kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddeso nāma

the exposition named 'The Taking Up of a Meditation Subject',

Tatiyo paricchedo.

is the Third Chapter.

4. Pathavīkasiṇaniddeso

4. 4. The Exposition of the Earth Kasiṇa

51. Idāni [M 1.0115][V 1.0115] yaṃ vuttaṃ “samādhibhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ vihāraṃ pahāya anurūpe vihāre viharantenā”ti ettha yassa tāvācariyena saddhiṃ ekavihāre vasato phāsu hoti, tena tattheva kammaṭṭhānaṃ parisodhentena vasitabbaṃ. Sace tattha phāsu na hoti, yo añño gāvute vā aḍḍhayojane vā yojanamattepi vā sappāyo vihāro hoti, tattha vasitabbaṃ. Evañhi sati kammaṭṭhānassa kismiñcideva ṭhāne sandehe vā satisammose vā jāte kālasseva vihāre vattaṃ katvā antarāmagge piṇḍāya caritvā bhattakiccapariyosāneyeva ācariyassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā taṃdivasamācariyassa santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā dutiyadivase ācariyaṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā antarāmagge piṇḍāya caritvā akilamantoyeva attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgantuṃ sakkhissati. Yo pana yojanappamāṇepi phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ na labhati, tena kammaṭṭhāne sabbaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā suvisuddhaṃ āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ katvā dūrampi gantvā samādhibhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ vihāraṃ pahāya anurūpe vihāre vihātabbaṃ.

51. Now, regarding what was said, 'Having abandoned a monastery unsuitable for the development of concentration, one should dwell in a suitable monastery': Herein, for whichever meditator it is comfortable to live in the same monastery with his teacher, he should dwell right there, purifying the meditation subject. If it is not comfortable there, he should dwell in whatever other suitable monastery there is, a gāvuta, half a yojana, or even a yojana away. For, this being so, if doubt or forgetfulness should arise in any place regarding the meditation subject, he can perform his duties in the monastery early, wander for alms on the way, and only after the meal is finished, go to the teacher's dwelling place. Having purified the meditation subject in the teacher's presence on that day, and on the second day, having paid respects to the teacher and departed, he can wander for alms on the way and will be able to return to his own dwelling place without fatigue. But whoever does not find a comfortable place even within the measure of a yojana, he, having cut off all knotty points in the meditation subject and having made the meditation subject thoroughly purified and connected with attention, should go even far, and having abandoned a monastery unsuitable for the development of concentration, should dwell in a suitable monastery.

Ananurūpavihāro

The Unsuitable Monastery

52. Tattha ananurūpo nāma aṭṭhārasannaṃ dosānaṃ aññatarena samannāgato. Tatrime aṭṭhārasa dosā – mahattaṃ, navattaṃ, jiṇṇattaṃ, panthanissitattaṃ, soṇḍī, paṇṇaṃ, pupphaṃ, phalaṃ, patthanīyatā, nagarasannissitatā, dārusannissitatā, khettasannissitatā, visabhāgānaṃ puggalānaṃ atthitā, paṭṭanasannissitatā, paccantasannissitatā, rajjasīmasannissitatā, asappāyatā, kalyāṇamittānaṃ alābhoti imesaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ dosānaṃ aññatarena dosena samannāgato ananurūpo nāma. Na tattha vihātabbaṃ.

52. Therein, what is called an unsuitable monastery is one endowed with any one of eighteen faults. Herein, these are the eighteen faults: being too large, being new, being dilapidated, being situated by a road, having a pond, proximity to vegetables, proximity to flowers, proximity to fruit trees, being an object of desire, being situated near a town, being situated near a forest for timber, being situated near a field, the presence of uncongenial persons, being situated near a port, being situated near a border region, being situated near the border of a kingdom, unsuitability, and the lack of good friends. A monastery endowed with any one of these eighteen faults is called unsuitable. One should not dwell there.

Kasmā? Mahāvihāre tāva bahū nānāchandā sannipatanti, te aññamaññaṃ paṭiviruddhatāya vattaṃ [V 1.0116] na karonti. Bodhiyaṅgaṇādīni asammaṭṭhāneva honti. Anupaṭṭhāpitaṃ pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ gocaragāme piṇḍāya [M 1.0116] carissāmīti pattacīvaramādāya nikkhanto sace passati vattaṃ vā akataṃ pānīyaghaṭaṃ vā rittaṃ, athānena vattaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhāpetabbaṃ. Akaronto vattabhede dukkaṭaṃ āpajjati. Karontassa kālo atikkamati, atidivā paviṭṭho niṭṭhitāya bhikkhāya kiñci na labhati. Paṭisallānagatopi sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhūnaṃ uccāsaddena saṅghakammehi ca vikkhipati. Yattha pana sabbaṃ vattaṃ katameva hoti, avasesāpi ca saṅghaṭṭanā natthi. Evarūpe mahāvihārepi vihātabbaṃ.

Why? In a great monastery, for instance, many of various inclinations gather, and due to being in opposition to one another, they do not perform their duties. The Bodhi-tree enclosure and other such places remain unswept. Drinking water and water for use are not set up. Therein, if this yogi, having taken his bowl and robe thinking, 'I will wander for alms in the alms-resort village,' goes out and sees that a duty is undone or that a water pot is empty, then the duty must be done by him, and water must be set up. One who does not do so incurs a dukkaṭa offense for the breach of duty. For the one who does it, time passes by; having entered very late in the day, when the alms-food is finished, he gets nothing. Even when gone to seclusion, he is distracted by the loud noise of the novices and young monks, and by the formal acts of the Sangha. However, where all duties are already done, and there is no remaining conflict, one should dwell even in such a great monastery.

Navavihāre bahu navakammaṃ hoti, akarontaṃ ujjhāyanti. Yattha pana bhikkhū evaṃ vadanti “āyasmā yathāsukhaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ karotu, mayaṃ navakammaṃ karissāmā”ti evarūpe vihātabbaṃ.

In a new monastery, there is much new work; they criticize one who does not do it. However, where the monks speak thus: 'Let the Venerable Sir practice the duty of a recluse at ease; we will do the new work,' in such a place one should dwell.

Jiṇṇavihāre pana bahu paṭijaggitabbaṃ hoti, antamaso attano senāsanamattampi appaṭijaggantaṃ ujjhāyanti, paṭijaggantassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ parihāyati.

Furthermore, in an old monastery, there is much to be repaired. They criticize one who does not repair even so much as his own lodging. For one who does the repairing, the meditation subject declines.

Panthanissite mahāpathavihāre rattindivaṃ āgantukā sannipatanti. Vikāle āgatānaṃ attano senāsanaṃ datvā rukkhamūle vā pāsāṇapiṭṭhe vā vasitabbaṃ hoti. Punadivasepi evamevāti kammaṭṭhānassa okāso na hoti. Yattha pana evarūpo āgantukasambādho na hoti, tattha vihātabbaṃ.

In a monastery situated on a great road, visitors gather day and night. To those who have arrived at an unseemly hour, having given one's own lodging, one must dwell at the foot of a tree or on a stone slab. On the next day also, it is just the same; therefore, there is no opportunity for the meditation subject. However, where such crowding by visitors does not occur, there one should dwell.

Soṇḍī nāma pāsāṇapokkharaṇī hoti, tattha pānīyatthaṃ mahājano samosarati, nagaravāsīnaṃ rājakulūpakattherānaṃ antevāsikā rajanakammatthāya āgacchanti, tesaṃ bhājanadārudoṇikādīni pucchantānaṃ asuke ca asuke ca ṭhāneti dassetabbāni honti, evaṃ sabbakālampi niccabyāvaṭo hoti.

A soṇḍī is a stone reservoir. Many people gather there for water. The disciples of the city-dwelling great elders, who are teachers to the royal family, come for the purpose of dyeing robes. When they ask for vessels, wooden troughs, and the like, it must be pointed out to them, 'It is in such and such a place and in such and such a place.' In this way, he is constantly occupied at all times.

Yattha nānāvidhaṃ sākapaṇṇaṃ hoti, tatthassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā divāvihāraṃ nisinnassāpi santike sākahārikā gāyamānā paṇṇaṃ uccinantiyo visabhāgasaddasaṅghaṭṭanena kammaṭṭhānantarāyaṃ karonti.

In a monastery where there is a grove of various edible greens, even for one who is sitting in daytime seclusion having taken up a meditation subject, women gathering greens nearby, singing as they pluck them, create an obstacle to his meditation subject through the impact of their unsuitable voices.

Yattha [V 1.0117] pana nānāvidhā mālāgacchā supupphitā honti, tatrāpi tādisoyeva upaddavo.

Again, in a monastery where various flowering shrubs are in full bloom, there too the trouble should be understood as being of the very same kind.

Yattha [M 1.0117] nānāvidhaṃ ambajambupanasādiphalaṃ hoti, tattha phalatthikā āgantvā yācanti, adentassa kujjhanti, balakkārena vā gaṇhanti, sāyanhasamaye vihāramajjhe caṅkamantena te disvā “kiṃ upāsakā evaṃ karothā”ti vuttā yathāruci akkosanti. Avāsāyapissa parakkamanti.

In a monastery where there are various kinds of fruits such as mango, rose-apple, and jackfruit, those who desire fruit come and beg. Towards the monk who does not give, they become angry, or they take by force. In the evening, when they are seen by a monk walking in the middle of the monastery and are asked, 'Lay disciples, why do you do this?', they revile him as they please. They also strive to make him unable to live there.

Patthanīye pana leṇasammate dakkhiṇagirihatthikucchicetiyagiricittalapabbatasadise vihāre viharantaṃ ayamarahāti sambhāvetvā vanditukāmā manussā samantā osaranti, tenassa na phāsu hoti, yassa pana taṃ sappāyaṃ hoti, tena divā aññatra gantvā rattiṃ vasitabbaṃ.

Again, in a desirable monastery regarded by the world as a place of Arahants, similar to Dakkhiṇagiri, Hatthikucchi, Cetiyagiri, and Cittalapabbata, people esteem a yogi dwelling there, thinking, 'This one is an Arahant,' and desiring to pay homage, they gather all around. Because of that, it is not comfortable for him. However, for whomever that place is suitable, he should go elsewhere by day and dwell there at night.

Nagarasannissite visabhāgārammaṇāni āpāthamāgacchanti, kumbhadāsiyopi ghaṭehi nighaṃsantiyo gacchanti, okkamitvā maggaṃ na denti, issaramanussāpi vihāramajjhe sāṇiṃ parikkhipitvā nisīdanti.

In a monastery situated near a city, unsuitable sense-objects come into the range of the senses. Water-carrying slave women also go along, jostling with their pots; stepping aside from the path, they do not give way. Powerful men also sit in the middle of the monastery, having set up a curtain enclosure.

Dārusannissaye pana yattha kaṭṭhāni ca dabbupakaraṇarukkhā ca santi, tattha kaṭṭhahārikā pubbe vuttasākapupphahārikā viya aphāsuṃ karonti, vihāre rukkhā santi, te chinditvā gharāni karissāmāti manussā āgantvā chindanti. Sace sāyanhasamayaṃ padhānagharā nikkhamitvā vihāramajjhe caṅkamanto te disvā “kiṃ upāsakā evaṃ karothā”ti vadati, yathāruci akkosanti, avāsāyapissa parakkamanti.

Again, in a monastery that is dependent on a forest, where there is firewood and trees suitable for building materials, female wood-gatherers cause discomfort like the previously mentioned female vegetable-gatherers and flower-gatherers. People come and cut the trees in the monastery, thinking, 'Having cut these, we will make houses.' If a meditator, having come out from the meditation hall in the evening and walking in the middle of the monastery, sees them and says, 'Lay devotees, why do you do this?', they revile him as they please and even strive to make him unable to dwell there.

Yo pana khettasannissito hoti samantā khettehi parivārito, tattha manussā vihāramajjheyeva khalaṃ katvā dhaññaṃ maddanti, pamukhesu sayanti, aññampi bahuṃ aphāsuṃ karonti.
