Yatrāpi mahāsaṅghabhogo hoti, ārāmikā kulānaṃ gāvo rundhanti, udakavāraṃ paṭisedhenti, manussā vīhisīsaṃ gahetvā “passatha tumhākaṃ ārāmikānaṃ kamma”nti saṅghassa dassenti. Tena tena kāraṇena rājarājamahāmattānaṃ gharadvāraṃ gantabbaṃ hoti, ayampi khettasannissiteneva saṅgahito.

Again, a monastery that is dependent on fields is surrounded on all sides by fields. There, people make a threshing floor right in the middle of the monastery and thresh grain, they sleep in the monastery entrances, and they cause much other discomfort. Also, where there is great property of the Sangha, the monastery attendants impound the cattle of the families, and they block the turn for water. People, taking an ear of grain, show it to the Sangha, saying, 'Behold the deed of your monastery attendants!' For these various reasons, it becomes necessary to go to the house-doors of kings and great ministers. This case is also included under being dependent on fields.

Visabhāgānaṃ puggalānaṃ atthitāti yattha aññamaññaṃ visabhāgaverī bhikkhū viharanti, ye kalahaṃ [V 1.0118] karontā mā, bhante, evaṃ karothāti vāriyamānā etassa paṃsukūlikassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya naṭṭhāmhāti vattāro bhavanti.

Regarding 'the presence of persons of dissimilar nature': this is where monks, who are mutually hostile due to their dissimilar natures, dwell. When they are making a quarrel and are restrained, being told, 'Venerable sirs, do not do so,' they are ones who say, 'From the time this rag-robe wearer arrived, we have been ruined.'

Yopi [M 1.0118] udakapaṭṭanaṃ vā thalapaṭṭanaṃ vā nissito hoti, tattha abhiṇhaṃ nāvāhi ca satthehi ca āgatamanussā okāsaṃ detha, pānīyaṃ detha, loṇaṃ dethāti ghaṭṭayantā aphāsuṃ karonti.

Also, a monastery may be dependent on a water-port or a land-port. There, people who have constantly arrived by boats and by caravans cause discomfort, harassing the monks by saying, 'Give us a place to stay! Give us drinking water! Give us salt!'

Paccantasannissite pana manussā buddhādīsu appasannā honti.

Again, in a monastery dependent on a border region, the people are not devout towards the Buddha and so on.

Rajjasīmasannissite rājabhayaṃ hoti. Tañhi padesaṃ eko rājā na mayhaṃ vase vattatīti paharati, itaropi na mayhaṃ vase vattatīti. Tatrāyaṃ bhikkhu kadāci imassa rañño vijite vicarati, kadāci etassa. Atha naṃ “carapuriso aya”nti maññamānā anayabyasanaṃ pāpenti.

In the vicinity of a kingdom's border, there is fear of kings. For in that region, one king attacks, thinking, 'This does not fall under my authority,' and the other also attacks, thinking, 'This does not fall under my authority.' There, this monk sometimes wanders in the territory of this king, and sometimes in that of the other. Then, thinking, 'This is a spy,' they bring him to misfortune and ruin.

Asappāyatāti visabhāgarūpādiārammaṇasamosaraṇena vā amanussapariggahitatāya vā asappāyatā. Tatridaṃ vatthu. Eko kira thero araññe vasati. Athassa ekā yakkhinī paṇṇasāladvāre ṭhatvā gāyi. So nikkhamitvā dvāre aṭṭhāsi, sā gantvā caṅkamanasīse gāyi. Thero caṅkamanasīsaṃ agamāsi. Sā sataporise papāte ṭhatvā gāyi. Thero paṭinivatti. Atha naṃ sā vegenāgantvā gahetvā “mayā, bhante, na eko na dve tumhādisā khāditā”ti āha.

Unsuitability is due to the convergence of dissimilar objects, such as forms, or due to being possessed by non-human beings. In this regard, there is this story. A certain elder, it is said, was living in the forest. Then a certain female yakkha stood at the door of his leaf-hut and sang. He came out and stood at the door. She went and sang at the head of the walking path. The elder went to the head of the walking path. She stood on a precipice a hundred persons deep and sang. The elder turned back. Then she, approaching swiftly, seized him and said, 'Venerable sir, I have eaten not one, not two, like you.'

Kalyāṇamittānaṃ alābhoti yattha na sakkā hoti ācariyaṃ vā ācariyasamaṃ vā upajjhāyaṃ vā upajjhāyasamaṃ vā kalyāṇamittaṃ laddhuṃ. Tattha so kalyāṇamittānaṃ alābho mahādosoyevāti imesaṃ aṭṭhārasannaṃ dosānaṃ aññatarena samannāgato ananurūpoti veditabbo. Vuttampi cetaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu –

The non-obtaining of good friends is where it is not possible to find a good friend who is a teacher, or like a teacher, a preceptor, or like a preceptor. There, this non-obtaining of good friends is indeed a great fault. A dwelling endowed with any one of these eighteen faults should be known as unsuitable. And this has been stated in the commentaries:

Mahāvāsaṃ navāvāsaṃ, jarāvāsañca panthaniṃ;

Soṇḍiṃ paṇṇañca pupphañca, phalaṃ patthitameva ca.

A dwelling that is too large, a new dwelling, a dilapidated dwelling, and one near a road; one with a pond, one near edible greens, one near flowers, one near fruit, and one that is much sought-after.

Nagaraṃ dārunā khettaṃ, visabhāgena paṭṭanaṃ;

Paccantasīmāsappāyaṃ, yattha mitto na labbhati.

One near a city, one near timber, one near a field, one with those of dissimilar views, one near a port; one in a border region, one on a boundary, an unsuitable one, and one where a good friend is not to be found.

Aṭṭhārasetāni [V 1.0119] ṭhānāni, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ yathāti.

Having understood these eighteen places, the wise one should avoid them from afar, just as one would a path fraught with danger.

Anurūpavihāro

The Suitable Dwelling

53. Yo [M 1.0119] pana gocaragāmato nātidūranāccāsannatādīhi pañcahaṅgehi samannāgato, ayaṃ anurūpo nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “kathañca, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ nātidūraṃ hoti nāccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannaṃ, divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ, appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa appakasireneva uppajjanti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā, te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhati ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ imassa ko attho’ti, tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttānīkaronti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhaṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.11).

53. Furthermore, that monastery which is endowed with five factors, such as being neither too far from nor too near to the alms-resort village, is called a suitable one. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'And how, bhikkhus, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, bhikkhus, a lodging is neither too far nor too near, and is convenient for coming and going; by day it is not crowded, and at night it is quiet and free from noise; it is free from contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. Moreover, for one dwelling in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines as a support for the sick arise with little difficulty. Furthermore, in that lodging dwell elder bhikkhus who are learned, who have mastered the traditions, who are bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikās. From time to time, one approaches them to question and inquire: ‘Venerable sirs, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones then reveal what has not been revealed, make plain what has not been made plain, and they dispel doubt concerning various matters that are grounds for doubt. In this way, bhikkhus, a lodging is endowed with five factors.' (A. Ni. 10.11)

Ayaṃ “samādhibhāvanāya ananurūpaṃ vihāraṃ pahāya anurūpe vihāre viharantenā”ti ettha vitthāro.

This is the detailed explanation here of the phrase: 'by one who dwells in a suitable monastery, having abandoned a monastery unsuitable for the development of concentration.'

Khuddakapalibodhā

The Minor Impediments

54. Khuddakapalibodhupacchedaṃ katvāti evaṃ patirūpe vihāre viharantena yepissa te honti khuddakapalibodhā, tepi upacchinditabbā. Seyyathidaṃ, dīghāni kesanakhalomāni chinditabbāni. Jiṇṇacīvaresu daḷhīkammaṃ vā tunnakammaṃ vā kātabbaṃ. Kiliṭṭhāni vā rajitabbāni. Sace patte malaṃ hoti, patto pacitabbo. Mañcapīṭhādīni sodhetabbānīti. “Ayaṃ khuddakapalibodhupacchedaṃ katvā”ti ettha vitthāro.

54. Regarding the phrase 'having cut off the minor impediments': by one dwelling thus in a suitable monastery, whatever minor impediments there may be for him, those too should be cut off. That is to say: long hair of the head, nails, and body hair should be cut. On worn-out robes, the work of reinforcement or darning should be done. Or, soiled robes should be dyed. If there is dirt in the bowl, the bowl should be fired. Beds, chairs, and so forth should be cleaned. This is the detailed explanation here of 'having cut off the minor impediments.'

Bhāvanāvidhānaṃ

The Method of Development

55. Idāni [V 1.0120] sabbaṃ bhāvanāvidhānaṃ aparihāpentena bhāvetabboti ettha ayaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbakammaṭṭhānavasena vitthārakathā hoti.

55. Now, in the context of the statement, 'One should develop, not neglecting any part of the entire method of development,' this will be a detailed exposition by means of all meditation subjects, beginning with the earth kasiṇa.

Evaṃ [M 1.0120] upacchinnakhuddakapalibodhena hi bhikkhunā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantena bhattasammadaṃ paṭivinodetvā pavivitte okāse sukhanisinnena katāya vā akatāya vā pathaviyā nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Indeed, a bhikkhu who has thus cut off the minor impediments, having returned from the alms-round after the meal, having dispelled the drowsiness from the meal, and sitting comfortably in a secluded place, should apprehend the sign on the earth, whether it is prepared or unprepared. For this has been said:

“Pathavīkasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto pathaviyaṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti kate vā akate vā sāntake, no anantake, sakoṭiye, no akoṭiye, savaṭṭume, no avaṭṭume, sapariyante, no apariyante, suppamatte vā sarāvamatte vā. So taṃ nimittaṃ suggahitaṃ karoti, sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāreti, suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapeti. So taṃ nimittaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāretvā suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetvā ānisaṃsadassāvī ratanasaññī hutvā cittīkāraṃ upaṭṭhapetvā sampiyāyamāno tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ upanibandhati ‘addhā imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇamhā muccissāmī’ti. So vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti.

“One who apprehends the earth kasiṇa apprehends the sign on the earth—whether prepared or unprepared; with a limit, not without a limit; with a boundary, not without a boundary; circular, not non-circular; with a perimeter, not without a perimeter; about the size of a small winnowing basket or a dish. He makes that sign well-grasped; he retains it well; he establishes it well. Having made that sign well-grasped, having retained it well, and having established it well, seeing its benefit, perceiving it as a treasure, establishing regard, and delighting in it, he binds his mind to that object, thinking: ‘Surely, by this practice, I shall be freed from aging and death.’ He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna.”

Tattha yena atītabhavepi sāsane vā isipabbajjāya vā pabbajitvā pathavīkasiṇe catukkapañcakajjhānāni nibbattitapubbāni, evarūpassa puññavato upanissayasampannassa akatāya pathaviyā kasitaṭṭhāne vā khalamaṇḍale vā nimittaṃ uppajjati, mallakattherassa viya. Tassa kirāyasmato kasitaṭṭhānaṃ olokentassa taṃṭhānappamāṇameva nimittaṃ udapādi. So taṃ vaḍḍhetvā pañcakajjhānāni nibbattetvā jhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Therein, for one who in a past existence had also gone forth either in the Dispensation or in the ascetic life and had previously produced the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the earth kasiṇa—for such a meritorious person endowed with supporting conditions—the sign arises on unprepared earth, on a plowed place, or on a threshing floor, as it did for the Elder Mallaka. It is said that for that venerable one, while he was looking at the plowed place, a sign of the very size of that place arose. He, having developed it, produced the fivefold jhānas, and having established insight which has jhāna as its proximate cause, attained Arahantship.

Yo panevaṃ akatādhikāro hoti, tena ācariyasantike uggahitakammaṭṭhānavidhānaṃ avirādhetvā cattāro kasiṇadose pariharantena kasiṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Nīlapītalohitaodātasambhedavasena hi cattāro pathavīkasiṇadosā. Tasmā nīlādivaṇṇaṃ mattikaṃ aggahetvā gaṅgāvahe mattikāsadisāya aruṇavaṇṇāya mattikāya kasiṇaṃ kātabbaṃ. Tañca kho vihāramajjhe sāmaṇerādīnaṃ [V 1.0121] sañcaraṇaṭṭhāne na kātabbaṃ. Vihārapaccante pana paṭicchannaṭṭhāne pabbhāre vā paṇṇasālāya vā saṃhārimaṃ vā tatraṭṭhakaṃ vā kātabbaṃ. Tatra saṃhārimaṃ catūsu daṇḍakesu pilotikaṃ [M 1.0121] vā cammaṃ vā kaṭasārakaṃ vā bandhitvā tattha apanītatiṇamūlasakkharakathalikāya sumadditāya mattikāya vuttappamāṇaṃ vaṭṭaṃ limpetvā kātabbaṃ. Taṃ parikammakāle bhūmiyaṃ attharitvā oloketabbaṃ. Tatraṭṭhakaṃ bhūmiyaṃ padumakaṇṇikākārena khāṇuke ākoṭetvā vallīhi vinandhitvā kātabbaṃ. Yadi sā mattikā nappahoti, adho aññaṃ pakkhipitvā uparibhāge suparisodhitāya aruṇavaṇṇāya mattikāya vidatthicaturaṅgulavitthāraṃ vaṭṭaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etadeva hi pamāṇaṃ sandhāya “suppamattaṃ vā sarāvamattaṃ vā”ti vuttaṃ. “Sāntake no anantake”tiādi panassa paricchedatthāya vuttaṃ.

But a person who has not made such a supporting condition should make the kasiṇa without failing in the method for the meditation subject learned in the presence of a teacher, while avoiding the four kasiṇa faults. For there are four faults of the earth kasiṇa due to the admixture of blue, yellow, red, or white. Therefore, not taking clay of blue or other such colors, the kasiṇa should be made with dawn-colored clay similar to that on a riverbank. And it should not be made in the middle of the monastery in a place where novices and others walk about. But it should be made at the edge of the monastery, in a concealed place, on a mountain slope or in a leaf hut, either as a portable one or a fixed one. Among these, the portable one should be made by tying a piece of old cloth, leather, or a mat to four sticks, and on that, plastering a circle of the prescribed size with well-kneaded clay from which grass, roots, gravel, and potsherds have been removed. During the preliminary work, it should be spread on the ground and looked at. The fixed one should be made on the ground in the shape of a lotus pericarp by driving in stakes and binding them with creepers. If that clay is not sufficient, other clay should be put underneath, and on the upper part, a circle with a diameter of one span and four finger-breadths should be made with well-cleaned, dawn-colored clay. Indeed, it was with reference to this very measure that it was said: “about the size of a small winnowing basket or a dish.” But “with a limit, not without a limit,” and so forth, was said for the purpose of defining its boundary.

56. Tasmā evaṃ vuttappamāṇaparicchedaṃ katvā rukkhapāṇikā visabhāgavaṇṇaṃ samuṭṭhapeti. Tasmā taṃ aggahetvā pāsāṇapāṇikāya ghaṃsetvā samaṃ bherītalasadisaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā nhatvā āgantvā kasiṇamaṇḍalato aḍḍhateyyahatthantare padese paññatte vidatthicaturaṅgulapādake suatthate pīṭhe nisīditabbaṃ. Tato dūratare nisinnassa hi kasiṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, āsannatare kasiṇadosā paññāyanti. Uccatare nisinnena gīvaṃ onamitvā oloketabbaṃ hoti, nīcatare jaṇṇukāni rujanti. Tasmā vuttanayeneva nisīditvā “appassādā kāmā”tiādinā nayena kāmesu ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā kāmanissaraṇe sabbadukkhasamatikkamupāyabhūte nekkhamme jātābhilāsena buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇānussaraṇena pītipāmojjaṃ janayitvā “ayaṃ dāni sā sabbabuddha paccekabuddha ariyasāvakehi paṭipannā nekkhammapaṭipadā”ti paṭipattiyā sañjātagāravena “addhā imāya paṭipadāya pavivekasukharasassa bhāgī bhavissāmī”ti ussāhaṃ janayitvā samena ākārena cakkhūni ummīletvā nimittaṃ gaṇhantena bhāvetabbaṃ.

56. Therefore, having made the boundary of the prescribed measure, a wooden trowel produces a dissimilar color. Therefore, not taking that, one should smooth it with a stone trowel, make it even like the surface of a great drum, sweep that place, bathe, and come to sit on a well-spread seat with legs a span and four finger-breadths high, placed in a spot within two and a half cubits from the kasiṇa-circle. Indeed, for one sitting too far away, the kasiṇa does not appear; for one sitting too close, the kasiṇa's faults become apparent. For one sitting on a seat that is too high, one must bend the neck to look; for one sitting on a seat that is too low, the knees ache. Therefore, having sat down in the prescribed manner, one should reflect on the danger in sensual pleasures by the method beginning with, “Sensual pleasures are of little delight.” With desire arisen for renunciation—which is the escape from sensual pleasures and the means for overcoming all suffering—and having generated rapture and gladness by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha; with respect arisen for the practice, thinking, “This is now that path of renunciation practiced by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples,” and having generated enthusiasm by thinking, “Surely, by this practice I shall become a partaker of the taste of the bliss of seclusion,” one should develop it by opening the eyes in a balanced manner while apprehending the sign.

Atiummīlayato hi cakkhu kilamati, maṇḍalañca ativibhūtaṃ hoti, tenassa nimittaṃ nuppajjati. Atimandaṃ ummīlayato maṇḍalamavibhūtaṃ hoti, cittañca līnaṃ hoti, evampi nimittaṃ nuppajjati. Tasmā ādāsatale mukhanimittadassinā viya samenākārena cakkhūni ummīletvā nimittaṃ gaṇhantena bhāvetabbaṃ, na vaṇṇo paccavekkhitabbo, na lakkhaṇaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Apica vaṇṇaṃ [M 1.0122] amuñcitvā nissayasavaṇṇaṃ katvā ussadavasena paṇṇattidhamme cittaṃ [V 1.0122] paṭṭhapetvā manasi kātabbaṃ. Pathavī mahī, medinī, bhūmi, vasudhā, vasundharātiādīsu pathavīnāmesu yamicchati, yadassa saññānukūlaṃ hoti, taṃ vattabbaṃ. Apica pathavīti etadeva nāmaṃ pākaṭaṃ, tasmā pākaṭavaseneva pathavī pathavīti bhāvetabbaṃ. Kālena ummīletvā kālena nimīletvā āvajjitabbaṃ. Yāva uggahanimittaṃ nuppajjati, tāva kālasatampi kālasahassampi tato bhiyyopi eteneva nayena bhāvetabbaṃ.

Indeed, for one opening the eyes too widely, the eye becomes fatigued, and the circle becomes too distinct; thereby the sign does not arise for him. For one opening the eyes too faintly, the circle is indistinct, and the mind is sluggish; even so the sign does not arise. Therefore, like one seeing the reflection of one’s face in a mirror, it should be developed by opening the eyes in a balanced manner and apprehending the sign; the color should not be reviewed, nor should the characteristic be attended to. Moreover, without abandoning the color, taking the support together with its color, one should establish the mind on the conceptual object by way of its prominence and attend to it. Among the names for earth—such as pathavī, mahī, medinī, bhūmi, vasudhā, vasundharā, and so forth—one should utter whichever one wishes, whichever is agreeable to one’s perception. However, this very name ‘pathavī’ is well-known; therefore, by the power of the well-known name, it should be developed as ‘pathavī, pathavī’. One should attend, at times opening the eyes and at times closing them. For as long as the learning sign does not arise, for that long it should be developed by this very method, even for a hundred periods of time, a thousand periods of time, or even more than that.

57. Tassevaṃ bhāvayato yadā nimīletvā āvajjantassa ummīlitakāle viya āpāthamāgacchati, tadā uggahanimittaṃ jātaṃ nāma hoti. Tassa jātakālato paṭṭhāya na tasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīditabbaṃ. Attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā tattha nisinnena bhāvetabbaṃ. Pādadhovanapapañcaparihāratthaṃ panassa ekapaṭalikupāhanā ca kattaradaṇḍo ca icchitabbo. Athānena sace taruṇo samādhi kenacideva asappāyakāraṇena nassati, upāhanā āruyha kattaradaṇḍaṃ gahetvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā nimittaṃ ādāya āgantvā sukhanisinnena bhāvetabbaṃ, punappunaṃ samannāharitabbaṃ, takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ kātabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ karontassa anukkamena nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, kilesā sannisīdanti, upacārasamādhinā cittaṃ samādhiyati, paṭibhāganimittaṃ uppajjati.

57. When, as he thus develops, the sign comes into range for him when he attends with eyes closed, just as it does when his eyes are open, then the learning sign is said to have arisen. From the time of its arising, one should not sit in that place. Having entered one’s dwelling place, one should develop it while seated there. But for the sake of avoiding the trouble of washing the feet, single-soled slippers and a walking stick should be desired by him. Then, if the tender concentration is lost due to some unsuitable cause, he should put on the slippers, take the walking stick, go to that place, apprehend the sign, return, and develop it while comfortably seated. It should be repeatedly attended to; it should be struck by thought and struck by applied thought. As he does so, the hindrances are gradually suppressed, the defilements subside, the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration, and the counterpart sign arises.

Tatrāyaṃ purimassa ca uggahanimittassa imassa ca viseso, uggahanimitte kasiṇadoso paññāyati, paṭibhāganimittaṃ thavikato nihatādāsamaṇḍalaṃ viya sudhotasaṅkhathālaṃ viya valāhakantarā nikkhantacandamaṇḍalaṃ viya meghamukhe balākā viya uggahanimittaṃ padāletvā nikkhantamiva tato sataguṇaṃ sahassaguṇaṃ suparisuddhaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Tañca kho neva vaṇṇavantaṃ, na saṇṭhānavantaṃ. Yadi hi taṃ īdisaṃ bhaveyya, cakkhuviññeyyaṃ siyā oḷārikaṃ sammasanupagaṃ tilakkhaṇabbhāhataṃ, na panetaṃ tādisaṃ. Kevalañhi samādhilābhino upaṭṭhānākāramattaṃ saññajametanti.

Herein, this is the difference between the former learning sign and this one: in the learning sign, the kasiṇa faults are apparent; but the counterpart sign appears—as if having broken through the learning sign and emerged—having become a hundred times, a thousand times, more purified than that, like a mirror-disc taken out of its case, like a well-polished conch-bowl, like the moon-disc emerged from among the clouds, or like a heron in the mouth of a cloud. And indeed, it is neither possessed of color nor possessed of shape. For if it were such, it would be cognizable by eye-consciousness, gross, subject to comprehension, and struck by the three characteristics; but it is not like that. For it is merely a mode of appearance for one who has gained concentration, something born of perception.

58. Uppannakālato ca panassa paṭṭhāya nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāneva honti, kilesā sannisinnāva, upacārasamādhinā cittaṃ samāhitamevāti.

58. Furthermore, from the time of its arising, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, the defilements are indeed settled, and the mind is indeed concentrated with access concentration.

Duvidho [M 1.0123] hi samādhi upacārasamādhi ca appanāsamādhi ca. Dvīhākārehi cittaṃ samādhiyati [V 1.0123] upacārabhūmiyaṃ vā paṭilābhabhūmiyaṃ vā. Tattha upacārabhūmiyaṃ nīvaraṇappahānena cittaṃ samāhitaṃ hoti. Paṭilābhabhūmiyaṃ aṅgapātubhāvena.

Indeed, concentration is of two kinds: access concentration and absorption concentration. The mind is concentrated in two ways: either in the access stage or in the attainment stage. Therein, in the access stage, the mind is concentrated through the abandonment of the hindrances. In the attainment stage, it is through the manifestation of the factors.

Dvinnaṃ pana samādhīnaṃ idaṃ nānākāraṇaṃ, upacāre aṅgāni na thāmajātāni honti, aṅgānaṃ athāmajātattā, yathā nāma daharo kumārako ukkhipitvā ṭhapiyamāno punappunaṃ bhūmiyaṃ patati, evameva upacāre uppanne cittaṃ kālena nimittamārammaṇaṃ karoti, kālena bhavaṅgamotarati. Appanāyaṃ pana aṅgāni thāmajātāni honti, tesaṃ thāmajātattā, yathā nāma balavā puriso āsanā vuṭṭhāya divasampi tiṭṭheyya, evameva appanāsamādhimhi uppanne cittaṃ sakiṃ bhavaṅgavāraṃ chinditvā kevalampi rattiṃ kevalampi divasaṃ tiṭṭhati, kusalajavanapaṭipāṭivaseneva pavattatīti.

Now, this is the distinction between the two concentrations: in access concentration, the factors are not possessed of strength. Because the factors are not possessed of strength, just as a tender young boy, when lifted up and placed, repeatedly falls to the ground, even so, when access concentration has arisen, the mind at times takes the sign as its object and at times sinks into the life-continuum. But in absorption, the factors are possessed of strength; because they are possessed of strength, just as a strong man, having risen from his seat, could stand even for a whole day, even so, when absorption concentration has arisen, the mind, having cut off the turn of the life-continuum just once, remains for an entire night or an entire day, proceeding solely by the power of the sequence of wholesome impulsion.

Tatra yadetaṃ upacārasamādhinā saddhiṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ uppannaṃ, tassa uppādanaṃ nāma atidukkaraṃ. Tasmā sace teneva pallaṅkena taṃ nimittaṃ vaḍḍhetvā appanaṃ adhigantuṃ sakkoti, sundaraṃ. No ce sakkoti, athānena taṃ nimittaṃ appamattena cakkavattigabbho viya rakkhitabbaṃ. Evañhi –

Therein, the causing of this counterpart sign to arise together with access concentration is extremely difficult to accomplish. Therefore, if one is able, with that very same cross-legged posture, to develop that sign and attain absorption, it is excellent. If one is not able, then that sign should be guarded by this yogi with diligence, like the embryo of a wheel-turning monarch. For thus—

Nimittaṃ rakkhato laddha-parihāni na vijjati;

Ārakkhamhi asantamhi, laddhaṃ laddhaṃ vinassati.

For one who guards the sign, there is no decline of what has been gained; when there is no guarding, whatever is gained is lost.

Sattasappāyā

The Seven Suitable Things

59. Tatrāyaṃ rakkhaṇavidhi –

59. Therein, this is the method of guarding:

Āvāso gocaro bhassaṃ, puggalo bhojanaṃ utu;

Iriyāpathoti sattete, asappāye vivajjaye.

Dwelling, alms-resort, speech, person, food, climate, and posture—these seven, being unsuitable, should be avoided.

Sappāye satta sevetha, evañhi paṭipajjato;

Nacireneva kālena, hoti kassaci appanā.

One should resort to the seven suitable things; for one who practices thus, in a short time indeed, absorption occurs for a certain one.

Tatrassa [V 1.0124] yasmiṃ āvāse vasantassa anuppannaṃ vā nimittaṃ nuppajjati, uppannaṃ vā vinassati, anupaṭṭhitā ca sati na upaṭṭhāti, asamāhitañca cittaṃ na samādhiyati, ayaṃ asappāyo. Yattha nimittaṃ uppajjati ceva thāvarañca hoti[M 1.0124], sati upaṭṭhāti, cittaṃ samādhiyati nāgapabbatavāsīpadhāniyatissattherassa viya, ayaṃ sappāyo. Tasmā yasmiṃ vihāre bahū āvāsā honti, tattha ekamekasmiṃ tīṇi tīṇi divasāni vasitvā yatthassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, tattha vasitabbaṃ. Āvāsasappāyatāya hi tambapaṇṇidīpamhi cūḷanāgaleṇe vasantā tattheva kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā pañcasatā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Sotāpannādīnaṃ pana aññattha ariyabhūmiṃ patvā tattha arahattappattānañca gaṇanā natthi. Evamaññesupi cittalapabbatavihārādīsu.

Therein, for one residing in a dwelling where an unarisen sign does not arise, or an arisen sign vanishes, and unestablished mindfulness does not become established, and an unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated—this is unsuitable. Where a sign arises and is also stable, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated—like for the Elder Padhāniyatissa, resident of Nāgapabbata—this is suitable. Therefore, in a monastery where there are many dwellings, one should reside for three days in each, and wherever one's mind becomes one-pointed, one should reside there. Indeed, due to the suitability of the dwelling, five hundred monks residing in the Cūḷanāga cave on the island of Tambapaṇṇī, having taken up their meditation subject right there, attained Arahantship. Furthermore, there is no counting of the stream-enterers and so on, and of those who, having attained the noble stage elsewhere, then attained Arahantship there. The same applies to other places like the Cittalapabbata Monastery and so on.

Gocaragāmo pana yo senāsanato uttarena vā dakkhiṇena vā nātidūre diyaḍḍhakosabbhantare hoti sulabhasampannabhikkho, so sappāyo. Viparīto asappāyo.

Furthermore, an alms-resort village that is not too far from the dwelling—within one and a half kosas to the north or to the south—and where alms-food is easily obtained and abundant, that is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable.

Bhassanti dvattiṃsatiracchānakathāpariyāpannaṃ asappāyaṃ, tañhissa nimittantaradhānāya saṃvattati. Dasakathāvatthunissitaṃ sappāyaṃ, tampi mattāya bhāsitabbaṃ.

Speech that is included in the thirty-two kinds of worldly talk is unsuitable, for it leads to the disappearance of one's sign. Speech that is based on the ten topics of conversation is suitable, but that too should be spoken with measure.

Puggalopi atiracchānakathiko sīlādiguṇasampanno, yaṃ nissāya asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ thirataraṃ hoti, evarūpo sappāyo. Kāyadaḷhībahulo pana tiracchānakathiko asappāyo. So hi taṃ kaddamodakamiva acchaṃ udakaṃ malīnameva karoti, tādisañca āgamma koṭapabbatavāsīdaharasseva samāpattipi nassati, pageva nimittaṃ.

A person who does not engage in worldly talk and is endowed with virtues such as morality, by relying on whom an unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, or a concentrated mind becomes more stable—such a person is suitable. But one who is devoted to strengthening the body and who speaks worldly talk is unsuitable. For he makes that yogi impure, just as muddy water makes clear water muddy. And by associating with such a person, even meditative attainment is lost, as in the case of the young monk, resident of Koṭapabbata—how much more so the sign.

Bhojanaṃ pana kassaci madhuraṃ, kassaci ambilaṃ sappāyaṃ hoti. Utupi kassaci sīto, kassaci uṇho sappāyo hoti. Tasmā yaṃ bhojanaṃ vā utuṃ vā sevantassa phāsu hoti, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā thirataraṃ hoti, taṃ bhojanaṃ so ca utu sappāyo. Itaraṃ bhojanaṃ itaro ca utu asappāyo.

Furthermore, as for food, for some sweet food is suitable, for some sour food is suitable. As for the season, for some a cold season is suitable, for some a hot season is suitable. Therefore, whatever food or season is comfortable for one who partakes of it, and by which an unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, or a concentrated mind becomes more stable—that food and that season are suitable. Other food and other season are unsuitable.

Iriyāpathesupi kassaci caṅkamo sappāyo hoti, kassaci sayanaṭṭhānanisajjānaṃ aññataro. Tasmā taṃ āvāsaṃ viya tīṇi divasāni upaparikkhitvā yasmiṃ iriyāpathe asamāhitaṃ [V 1.0125] vā cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhitaṃ vā thirataraṃ hoti, so sappāyo. Itaro asappāyoti veditabbo.

Among the postures too, for some, walking is suitable; for some, one of the others—lying down, standing, or sitting—is suitable. Therefore, having tested it for three days like a dwelling, in whichever posture an unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, or a concentrated mind becomes more stable, that posture is suitable. The other should be understood as unsuitable.

Iti [M 1.0125] imaṃ sattavidhaṃ asappāyaṃ vajjetvā sappāyaṃ sevitabbaṃ. Evaṃ paṭipannassa hi nimittāsevanabahulassa nacireneva kālena hoti kassaci appanā.

Thus, having avoided these seven kinds of unsuitable things, one should resort to what is suitable. Indeed, for a certain practitioner who practices thus and frequently resorts to the sign, absorption arises in no long time.

Dasavidhaappanākosallaṃ

The Tenfold Skill in Absorption

60. Yassa pana evampi paṭipajjato na hoti, tena dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ sampādetabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ nayo, dasāhākārehi appanākosallaṃ icchitabbaṃ, vatthuvisadakiriyato, indriyasamattapaṭipādanato, nimittakusalato, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsitabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti, yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanato, samāhitapuggalasevanato, tadadhimuttatoti.

60. Furthermore, for one for whom absorption does not arise even when practicing thus, the tenfold skill in absorption should be accomplished. Herein is the method: skill in absorption should be sought in ten ways: by purification of the basis, by balancing the spiritual faculties, by skill in the sign, by uplifting the mind at the time it should be uplifted, by restraining the mind at the time it should be restrained, by gladdening the mind at the time it should be gladdened, by regarding the mind with equanimity at the time it should be so regarded, by avoiding unconcentrated persons, by associating with concentrated persons, and by being inclined towards that.

61. Tattha vatthuvisadakiriyā nāma ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomāni dīghāni honti, sarīraṃ vā sedamalaggahitaṃ, tadā ajjhattikavatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Yadā panassa cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ hoti, tadā bāhiravatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Ajjhattikabāhire ca vatthumhi avisade uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ hoti, aparisuddhāni dīpakapallikavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Aparisuddhena ñāṇena saṅkhāre sammasato saṅkhārāpi avibhūtā honti, kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjato kammaṭṭhānampi vuḍḍhiṃ viruḷhiṃ vepullaṃ na gacchati. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti parisuddhaṃ, parisuddhāni dīpakapallikavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Parisuddhena ca ñāṇena saṅkhāre sammasato saṅkhārāpi vibhūtā honti, kammaṭṭhānamanuyuñjato kammaṭṭhānampi vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ gacchati.

61. Herein, the act of purifying the basis is the making of the internal and external bases to be clear. For when one’s hair of the head, nails, and body hair are long, or the body is smeared with sweat and grime, then the internal basis is unclear and impure. But when one’s robe is worn out, stained, and foul-smelling, or the lodging is untidy, then the external basis is unclear and impure. And when the internal and external bases are unclear, the knowledge that arises in dependence on mind and mental factors is also impure, just as the light of a lamp flame that has arisen in dependence on an impure lamp-dish, wick, and oil is impure. For one contemplating formations with impure knowledge, the formations are also indistinct, and for one practicing a meditation subject, the meditation subject also does not attain growth, increase, or abundance. But when the internal and external bases are clear, the knowledge that arises in dependence on mind and mental factors is also clear and pure, just as the light of a lamp flame that has arisen in dependence on a pure lamp-dish, wick, and oil is pure. And for one contemplating formations with pure knowledge, the formations are also distinct, and for one practicing a meditation subject, the meditation subject also attains growth, increase, and abundance.

62. Indriyasamattapaṭipādanaṃ [V 1.0126] nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti itarāni mandāni, tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ[M 1.0126], satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, atha neva saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ, tasmā taṃ passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatrāpi soṇattheravatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā. Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño muddhappasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati, bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti. Ubhinnaṃ samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ abhibhavati. Balavavīriyaṃ mandasamādhiṃ vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā uddhaccaṃ abhibhavati. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati. Vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati, tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti. Apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati. Evañhi so lakkhaṇapaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ pana samatāyapi appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato kosajjapakkhena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati, tasmā sā loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu, sabbakammikaamacco viya ca sabbarājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbā. Tenāha – “sati ca pana sabbatthikā vuttā bhagavatā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittañhi satipaṭisaraṇaṃ, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā ca sati, na vinā satiyā cittassa paggahaniggaho hotī”ti.

62. Balancing the faculties means making the faculties of faith and so on equal in function. For if a yogi's faith faculty is strong and the others are weak, then the energy faculty cannot perform its function of exertion, the mindfulness faculty its function of establishing, the concentration faculty its function of non-distraction, and the wisdom faculty its function of seeing. Therefore, that faith faculty should be reduced by reviewing the true nature of things or by not attending to it in the way that it became strong. The story of Elder Vakkali is an example here. But if the energy faculty is strong, then the faith faculty cannot perform its function of conviction, nor can the others perform their respective functions. Therefore, it should be reduced by developing tranquility and so on. In that case, the story of Elder Soṇa should be cited. Similarly, when any one faculty is strong, it should be understood that the others are incapable of performing their own functions. Specifically, the equality of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is praised here. For one with strong faith and weak wisdom is foolishly credulous and places faith in an unworthy object. One with strong wisdom and weak faith tends towards craftiness; like a disease caused by a remedy, he becomes difficult to cure. With the equality of the two, one places faith only in a worthy object. One with strong concentration and weak energy is overcome by laziness, since concentration is on the side of laziness. One with strong energy and weak concentration is overcome by restlessness, since energy is on the side of restlessness. Concentration yoked with energy, however, cannot fall into laziness. Energy yoked with concentration cannot fall into restlessness. Therefore, the two pairs should be made equal. For with the equality of the two pairs, absorption is achieved. Moreover, for one devoted to concentration, even strong faith is fitting. Thus, believing and placing full confidence, one will attain absorption. In the case of concentration and wisdom, for one devoted to concentration, strong one-pointedness is fitting, for in this way one attains absorption. For one devoted to insight, strong wisdom is fitting, for in this way one attains the penetration of the characteristics. But with the equality of the two as well, absorption is certainly achieved. Mindfulness, however, should be strong everywhere. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness by means of faith, energy, and wisdom, which are on the side of restlessness, and from falling into laziness by means of concentration, which is on the side of laziness. Therefore, it is to be desired everywhere, like the flavoring of salt in all sauces, and like an all-purpose minister in all the king's affairs. Hence it is said: 'Mindfulness is declared by the Blessed One to be universally applicable. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its recourse, and mindfulness has protection as its manifestation. Without mindfulness, there is no uplifting and restraining of the mind.'

63. Nimittakosallaṃ nāma pathavīkasiṇādikassa cittekaggatānimittassa akatassa karaṇakosallaṃ, katassa ca bhāvanākosallaṃ, bhāvanāya laddhassa rakkhaṇakosallañca, taṃ idha adhippetaṃ.

63. Skill in the sign is skill in producing the sign that is the cause for one-pointedness of mind, such as the earth kasiṇa, when it has not yet been produced; skill in developing it when it has been produced; and skill in protecting it when it has been attained through development. It is this skill in protecting that is intended here.

64. Kathañca [M 1.0127][V 1.0127] yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti? Yadāssa atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadā passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo tayo abhāvetvā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

64. And how does one uplift the mind when it should be uplifted? When one’s mind is sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so on, then, without developing the three enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility, one develops the enlightenment factors beginning with investigation of states. For this has been said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, allāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, allāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, udakavātañca dadeyya, paṃsukena ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletunti? No hetaṃ, bhante. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, akālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, akālo samādhi…pe… akālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi dusamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti. Yasmiṃ ca kho, bhikkhave, līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi susamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, mukhavātañca dadeyya, na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletunti? Evaṃ bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. If he were to throw wet grass on it, wet cow-dung, and wet sticks, apply a wind mixed with water, and scatter dust on it, would that man be able to kindle a small fire?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “So too, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, it is not the time to develop the tranquility enlightenment factor, not the time to develop the concentration enlightenment factor… not the time to develop the equanimity enlightenment factor. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is hard to rouse with those factors. But when the mind is sluggish, it is the time to develop the investigation of phenomena enlightenment factor, the time to develop the energy enlightenment factor, the time to develop the rapture enlightenment factor. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is easy to rouse with those factors. Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. If he were to throw dry grass on it, dry cow-dung, and dry sticks, blow on it with his mouth, and not scatter dust on it, would that man be able to kindle a small fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

Ettha ca yathāsakamāhāravasena dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, the development of the investigation of phenomena enlightenment factor and the others should be understood according to their respective foods. For this has been said:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā sāvajjānavajjā dhammā hīnappaṇītā dhammā kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā. Tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya uppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa [M 1.0128] bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, blameworthy and blameless phenomena, inferior and superior phenomena, dark and bright phenomena with their counterparts. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.”

Tathā [V 1.0128] “atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu. Tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya uppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Similarly: “Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of striving. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy.”

Tathā “atthi, bhikkhave, pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā dhammā. Tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya uppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Similarly: “Bhikkhus, there are phenomena that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of rapture, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of rapture.”

Tattha sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇapaṭivedhavasena pavattamanasikāro kusalādīsu yoniso manasikāro nāma. Ārambhadhātuādīnaṃ uppādanavasena pavattamanasikāro ārambhadhātuādīsu yoniso manasikāro nāma. Tattha ārambhadhātūti paṭhamavīriyaṃ vuccati. Nikkamadhātūti kosajjato nikkhantattā tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātūti paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavataraṃ. Pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā dhammāti pana pītiyā eva etaṃ nāmaṃ. Tassāpi uppādakamanasikārova yoniso manasikāro nāma.

Therein, attention that occurs by means of penetrating the intrinsic and general characteristics is called 'wise attention' in regard to wholesome states, etc. Attention that occurs by means of producing the element of initiative, etc., is called 'wise attention' in regard to the element of initiative, etc. Therein, 'the element of initiative' is called initial effort. 'The element of exertion' is stronger than that because of having departed from laziness. 'The element of striving' is even stronger than that because of advancing to stage after stage. But 'phenomena that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of rapture' is just a name for preceding rapture itself. The attention that produces it is also called 'wise attention'.

Apica satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paripucchakatā, vatthuvisadakiriyā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanā, duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā, paññavantapuggalasevanā, gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, seven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena: being inquisitive; clarifying the basis; bringing the faculties to equipoise; avoiding persons of dull wisdom; associating with persons of wisdom; reflecting on the domain of profound knowledge; and inclination to that.

Ekādasadhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti apāyādibhayapaccavekkhaṇatā, vīriyāyattalokiyalokuttaravisesādhigamānisaṃsadassitā, “buddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakehi gatamaggo mayā gantabbo, so ca na sakkā kusītena gantu”nti evaṃ gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā, dāyakānaṃ mahapphalabhāvakaraṇena piṇḍāpacāyanatā, “vīriyārambhassa vaṇṇavādī me satthā, so ca anatikkamanīyasāsano amhākañca bahūpakāro paṭipattiyā ca pūjiyamāno pūjito hoti na itarathā”ti evaṃ satthu [M 1.0129] mahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, “saddhammasaṅkhātaṃ me mahādāyajjaṃ gahetabbaṃ, tañca na sakkā kusītena gahetu”nti evaṃ dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā, ālokasaññāmanasikārairiyāpathaparivattanaabbhokāsasevanādīhi [V 1.0129] thinamiddhavinodanatā, kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā, āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā, sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Eleven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy: reflecting on the dangers beginning with the lower realms; seeing the benefits of attaining worldly and supramundane distinctions through energy; reflecting on the course of practice thus: “The path trodden by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples must be trodden by me, and it cannot be trodden by a lazy person”; honoring the alms-food by making it of great fruit for the donors; reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher thus: “My Teacher praises the undertaking of energy, his teaching is not to be transgressed, and he is greatly helpful to us; and being honored by practice, he is honored, not otherwise”; reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance thus: “I must receive the great inheritance known as the true Dhamma, and it cannot be received by a lazy person”; dispelling sloth and torpor by means of attending to the perception of light, changing postures, frequenting open spaces, and so on; avoiding lazy persons; associating with energetic persons; reflecting on the right exertions; and inclination to that.

Ekādasadhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti buddhānussati, dhamma… saṅgha… sīla… cāga… devatānussati, upasamānussati, lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā, siniddhapuggalasevanatā, pasādaniyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Iti imehi ākārehi ete dhamme uppādento dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti nāma. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti.

Eleven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoiding coarse persons, associating with gentle persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and inclination to that. Thus, by these means, by giving rise to these states, one is said to develop the enlightenment factors beginning with investigation of phenomena. In this way, at a time when the mind should be roused, one rouses the mind.

65. Kathaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti? Yadāssa accāraddhavīriyatādīhi uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādayo tayo abhāvetvā passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

65. How does one restrain the mind when it should be restrained? When one's mind is agitated due to excessively exerted energy and so on, then, not having developed the three enlightenment factors beginning with investigation-of-dhammas, one develops the three enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya…pe… na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti? No hetaṃ, bhante. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, akālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, akālo vīriya…pe… akālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi duvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Yasmiṃ ca kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi suvūpasamayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya…pe… paṃsukena [M 1.0130] ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti? Evaṃ, bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Suppose, monks, a person wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. If he were to throw dry grass into it… and not sprinkle it with dust, would that person, monks, be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “So too, monks, when the mind is agitated, that is not the time for developing the enlightenment factor of investigation-of-dhammas, not the time for energy… not the time for developing the enlightenment factor of rapture. For what reason? An agitated mind, monks, is difficult to calm with these states. And when, monks, the mind is agitated, that is the time for developing the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the time for developing the enlightenment factor of concentration, the time for developing the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For what reason? An agitated mind, monks, is easily calmed with these states. Suppose, monks, a person wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. If he were to throw wet grass into it… and sprinkle it with dust, would that person, monks, be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

Etthāpi [V 1.0130] yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena passaddhisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Here too, the development of the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility should be understood by way of their respective nutriment. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Atthi, bhikkhave, kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi. Tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya uppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

“There is, monks, bodily tranquility and mental tranquility. Frequent wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.”

Tathā “atthi, bhikkhave, samathanimittaṃ abyagganimittaṃ. Tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya uppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Similarly: “There is, monks, the sign of serenity and the sign of non-agitation. Frequent wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.”

Tathā “atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhāniyā dhammā. Tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya uppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Similarly: “There are, monks, things that are a foundation for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Frequent wise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity.”

Tattha yathāssa passaddhiādayo uppannapubbā, taṃ ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā tesaṃ uppādanavasena pavattamanasikārova tīsupi padesu yoniso manasikāro nāma. Samathanimittanti ca samathassevetamadhivacanaṃ. Avikkhepaṭṭhena ca tasseva abyagganimittanti.

Here, according to how tranquility and the others have previously arisen, observing that manner, the very attention that proceeds for the sake of their arising is called ‘wise attention’ in all three instances. And ‘the sign of serenity’ is a designation for serenity itself. And ‘the sign of non-agitation’ is a designation for that very thing in the sense of non-distraction.

Apica satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paṇītabhojanasevanatā, utusukhasevanatā, iriyāpathasukhasevanatā, majjhattapayogatā, sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā, passaddhakāyapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, seven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: partaking of fine food, partaking of pleasant weather, partaking of a comfortable posture, maintaining a balanced effort, avoiding persons with agitated bodies, associating with persons with tranquil bodies, and being inclined towards that.

Ekādasa [M 1.0131] dhammā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti vatthuvisadatā, nimittakusalatā, indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā, samaye cittassa niggahaṇatā, samaye cittassa paggahaṇatā[V 1.0131], nirassādassa cittassa saddhāsaṃvegavasena sampahaṃsanatā, sammāpavattassa ajjhupekkhanatā, asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā, samāhitapuggalasevanatā, jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā, tadadhimuttatāti.

Eleven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: clarity of the object, skill in the meditative sign, bringing the faculties to equipoise, restraining the mind when appropriate, arousing the mind when appropriate, gladdening a dispirited mind by means of faith and a sense of urgency, looking on with equanimity at a mind that is proceeding well, avoiding a person who is unconcentrated, associating with a person who is concentrated, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and inclination towards that.

Pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti sattamajjhattatā, saṅkhāramajjhattatā, sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā, tadadhimuttatāti. Iti imehākārehi ete dhamme uppādento passaddhisambojjhaṅgādayo bhāveti nāma. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti.

Five things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: impartiality towards beings, impartiality towards formations, avoiding a person who is attached to beings and formations, associating with a person who is impartial towards beings and formations, and inclination towards that. Thus, in these ways, by causing these states to arise, one is said to develop the enlightenment factors beginning with tranquility. Thus, at a time when the mind should be restrained, one restrains the mind.

66. Kathaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti? Yadāssa paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadā naṃ aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇānussaraṇena cassa pasādaṃ janeti. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti.

66. How does one gladden the mind at a time when it should be gladdened? When that yogi's mind is dispirited due to weakness in the application of wisdom or through not attaining the bliss of tranquility, one should arouse a sense of urgency in it by reviewing the eight bases for spiritual urgency. The eight bases for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death (these four); the suffering of the plane of misery as the fifth; suffering in the past rooted in the round of existence; suffering in the future rooted in the round of existence; and suffering in the present rooted in the search for food. And one generates confidence in that mind by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha. Thus, at a time when the mind should be gladdened, one gladdens the mind.

Kathaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati? Yadāssa evaṃ paṭipajjato alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāssa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati, sārathi viya samappavattesu assesu. Evaṃ yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati.

How, at the time when the mind should be regarded with equanimity, does one regard it with equanimity? When, for one practicing thus, the mind is not sluggish, not agitated, not without savor, is proceeding evenly regarding the object, and has entered upon the path of tranquility, then one does not engage in uplifting, suppressing, or gladdening it—like a charioteer with horses that are proceeding evenly. Thus, at the time when the mind should be regarded with equanimity, one regards it with equanimity.

Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā nāma nekkhammapaṭipadaṃ anāruḷhapubbānaṃ anekakiccapasutānaṃ vikkhittahadayānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā pariccāgo.

Avoiding unconcentrated persons means the abandoning from afar of those individuals who have not previously ascended the path of renunciation, are engaged in many activities, and have scattered minds.

Samāhitapuggalasevanatā nāma nekkhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannānaṃ samādhilābhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanaṃ.

Associating with concentrated persons means approaching from time to time those individuals who have entered upon the path of renunciation and have gained concentration.

Tadadhimuttatā [M 1.0132] nāma samādhiadhimuttatā samādhigarusamādhininnasamādhipoṇasamādhipabbhāratāti attho.

Inclination towards that means inclination towards concentration; that is, regarding concentration as important, inclining towards concentration, sloping towards concentration, and being disposed towards concentration—such is the meaning.

Evametaṃ [V 1.0132] dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ sampādetabbaṃ.

Thus, this tenfold skill in absorption should be accomplished.

67.

67.

Evañhi sampādayato, appanākosallaṃ imaṃ;

Paṭiladdhe nimittasmiṃ, appanā sampavattati.

For one who thus accomplishes this skill in absorption, when the counterpart sign is gained, absorption proceeds.

Evañhi paṭipannassa, sace sā nappavattati;

Tathāpi na jahe yogaṃ, vāyametheva paṇḍito.

If, for one who practices thus, that absorption does not proceed, still the wise one should not abandon the effort, but should indeed continue to strive.

Hitvā hi sammāvāyāmaṃ, visesaṃ nāma māṇavo;

Adhigacche parittampi, ṭhānametaṃ na vijjati.

For, having abandoned right effort, that a person might attain even a slight distinction—such a case does not exist.

Cittappavattiākāraṃ, tasmā sallakkhayaṃ budho;

Samataṃ vīriyasseva, yojayetha punappunaṃ.

Therefore, the wise one, discerning the mode of the mind's proceeding, should again and again apply balance to their energy.

Īsakampi layaṃ yantaṃ, paggaṇhetheva mānasaṃ;

Accāraddhaṃ nisedhetvā, samameva pavattaye.

One should indeed uplift the mind when it tends even slightly towards sluggishness; having restrained the over-exerted mind, one should make it proceed evenly.

Reṇumhi uppaladale, sutte nāvāya nāḷiyā;

Yathā madhukarādīnaṃ, pavatti sammavaṇṇitā.

As the proceeding of bees and the like on pollen, on a lotus petal, on a spider's thread, in a boat, or in an oil-tube is well-described;

Līnauddhatabhāvehi, mocayitvāna sabbaso;

Evaṃ nimittābhimukhaṃ, mānasaṃ paṭipādayeti.

Thus, having completely freed the mind from the states of sluggishness and agitation, one should direct it towards the counterpart sign.

Nimittābhimukhapaṭipādanaṃ

Directing Towards the Sign

68. Tatrāyamatthadīpanā – yathā hi acheko madhukaro asukasmiṃ rukkhe pupphaṃ pupphitanti ñatvā tikkhena vegena pakkhando taṃ atikkamitvā paṭinivattento khīṇe reṇumhi sampāpuṇāti. Aparo acheko mandena javena pakkhando khīṇeyeva sampāpuṇāti. Cheko pana samena javena pakkhando sukhena puppharāsiṃ sampatvā yāvadicchakaṃ reṇuṃ ādāya madhuṃ sampādetvā madhurasamanubhavati.

68. Here is the explanation of the meaning: Just as an unskilled bee, knowing that flowers have bloomed on a certain tree, flies forth with sharp speed, overshoots it, and turning back, arrives when the pollen is exhausted. Another unskilled one, flying forth with sluggish speed, arrives only when it is exhausted. But a skilled one, flying forth with even speed, easily reaches the mass of flowers, takes as much pollen as it desires, prepares honey, and experiences the taste of honey.

Yathā [M 1.0133][V 1.0133] ca sallakattaantevāsikesu udakathālagate uppalapatte satthakammaṃ sikkhantesu eko acheko vegena satthaṃ pātento uppalapattaṃ dvidhā vā chindati, udake vā paveseti. Aparo acheko chijjanapavesanabhayā satthakena phusitumpi na visahati. Cheko pana samena payogena tattha satthapahāraṃ dassetvā pariyodātasippo hutvā tathārūpesu ṭhānesu kammaṃ katvā lābhaṃ labhati.

And just as when the apprentices of a surgeon are practicing their knife-work on a lotus leaf placed in a water vessel, one unskilled apprentice, striking swiftly with the knife, either cuts the lotus leaf in two or makes it sink into the water. Another unskilled apprentice, fearing it might be cut or sink, does not even dare to touch it with the knife. But a skilled apprentice, demonstrating the knife-strike there with even application, and having become perfected in skill, performs the work in such places and obtains a profit.

Yathā ca yo catubyāmappamāṇaṃ makkaṭasuttamāharati, so cattāri sahassāni labhatīti raññā vutte eko achekapuriso vegena makkaṭasuttamākaḍḍhanto tahiṃ tahiṃ chindatiyeva. Aparo acheko chedanabhayā hatthena phusitumpi na visahati. Cheko pana koṭito paṭṭhāya samena payogena daṇḍake vedhetvā āharitvā lābhaṃ labhati.

And just as when the king declared, “Whoever brings a spider's thread four fathoms in measure receives four thousand,” one unskilled man, hastily pulling the spider's thread, breaks it here and there. Another unskilled man, fearing it might break, does not even dare to touch it with his hand. But a skilled man, starting from the end, with even application, winds it onto a stick and brings it, thus obtaining the reward.

Yathā ca acheko niyāmako balavavāte laṅkāraṃ pūrento nāvaṃ videsaṃ pakkhandāpeti. Aparo acheko mandavāte laṅkāraṃ oropento nāvaṃ tattheva ṭhapeti. Cheko pana mandavāte laṅkāraṃ pūretvā balavavāte aḍḍhalaṅkāraṃ katvā sotthinā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇāti.

And just as an unskilled pilot, when the wind is strong, fills the sail and makes the ship rush to a foreign land. Another unskilled pilot, when the wind is weak, lowers the sail and keeps the ship right there. But the skilled pilot, when the wind is weak, fills the sail, and when the wind is strong, makes it half-sail, and reaches the desired place safely.

Yathā ca yo telena achaḍḍento nāḷiṃ pūreti, so lābhaṃ labhatīti ācariyena antevāsikānaṃ vutte eko acheko lābhaluddho vegena pūrento telaṃ chaḍḍeti. Aparo acheko telachaḍḍanabhayā āsiñcitumpi na visahati. Cheko pana samena payogena pūretvā lābhaṃ labhati.

Furthermore, just as when a teacher said to his disciples, 'Whoever fills a tube with a fine opening with oil without spilling it obtains a reward,' one unskilled disciple, greedy for the reward, while filling it with speed, spills the oil. Another unskilled one, from fear of spilling the oil, does not even dare to pour it. The skilled one, however, having filled it with even application, obtains the reward.

Evameva eko bhikkhu uppanne nimitte sīghameva appanaṃ pāpuṇissāmīti gāḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ karoti, tassa cittaṃ accāraddhavīriyattā uddhacce patati, so na sakkoti appanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Eko accāraddhavīriyatāya dosaṃ disvā kiṃ dānime appanāyāti vīriyaṃ hāpeti, tassa cittaṃ atilīnavīriyattā kosajje patati, sopi na sakkoti appanaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Yo pana īsakampi līnaṃ līnabhāvato uddhataṃ uddhaccato mocetvā samena payogena [M 1.0134] nimittābhimukhaṃ pavatteti, so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti, tādisena bhavitabbaṃ. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya etaṃ vuttaṃ –

Just so, when the counterpart sign has arisen for a certain bhikkhu, he makes strong effort, thinking, 'I will quickly reach absorption!' His mind, due to excessively exerted effort, falls into agitation, and he is not able to reach absorption. Another, seeing the fault in excessively exerted effort, relaxes his effort, thinking, 'What now is the use of absorption for me?' His mind, due to overly slack effort, falls into laziness, and he too is not able to reach absorption. But whichever bhikkhu, having freed a mind that is even slightly slack from its state of slackness and an agitated mind from its state of agitation, makes it proceed towards the counterpart sign with even application, he reaches absorption. One should be like such a one. With reference to this meaning, this was said:

Reṇumhi uppaladale, sutte nāvāya nāḷiyā;

Yathā madhukarādīnaṃ, pavatti sammavaṇṇitā.

On pollen, on a lotus petal, on a thread, in a boat, in a tube; just as the proceeding of bees and the like is well described,

Līnauddhatabhāvehi[V 1.0134], mocayitvāna sabbaso;

Evaṃ nimittābhimukhaṃ, mānasaṃ paṭipādayeti.

Having freed it completely from the states of slackness and agitation, thus one should direct the mind towards the counterpart sign.

Paṭhamajjhānakathā

The Discourse on the First Jhāna

69. Iti evaṃ nimittābhimukhaṃ mānasaṃ paṭipādayato panassa idāni appanā ijjhissatīti bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā pathavī pathavīti anuyogavasena upaṭṭhitaṃ tadeva pathavīkasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanamuppajjati. Tato tasmiṃyevārammaṇe cattāri pañca vā javanāni javanti. Tesu avasāne ekaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ, sesāni kāmāvacarāni. Pakaticittehi balavataravitakkavicārapītisukhacittekaggatāni yāni appanāya parikammattā parikammānītipi, yathā gāmādīnaṃ āsannapadeso gāmūpacāro nagarūpacāroti vuccati, evaṃ appanāya āsannattā samīpacārattā vā upacārānītipi, ito pubbe parikammānaṃ, upari appanāya ca anulomato anulomānītipi vuccanti. Yañcettha sabbantimaṃ, taṃ parittagottābhibhavanato, mahaggatagottabhāvanato ca gotrabhūtipi vuccati. Agahitaggahaṇena panettha paṭhamaṃ parikammaṃ, dutiyaṃ upacāraṃ, tatiyaṃ anulomaṃ, catutthaṃ gotrabhu. Paṭhamaṃ vā upacāraṃ, dutiyaṃ anulomaṃ, tatiyaṃ gotrabhu, catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vā appanācittaṃ. Catutthameva hi pañcamaṃ vā appeti, tañca kho khippābhiññadandhābhiññavasena. Tato paraṃ javanaṃ patati. Bhavaṅgassa vāro hoti.

69. Furthermore, for this yogi who directs his meditation mind towards the counterpart sign, when the thought arises, 'Now absorption will be accomplished,' the mind-door adverting consciousness arises. It does so after cutting off the life-continuum and taking as its object that very earth-kasiṇa which has appeared through the application, 'earth, earth.' After that, on that very object, four or five impulsions run. Among these, the one at the end is a fine-material sphere consciousness, while the remaining are sense-sphere consciousnesses. These sense-sphere impulsions, possessing stronger initial application, sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness than ordinary consciousnesses, are also called 'preparatory' (parikamma) because they are a preparation for absorption. And just as the area near a village is called the 'village-approach' (gāmūpacāra) or 'town-approach' (nagarūpacāra), so too, because of their nearness to absorption or because they move in its vicinity, they are also called 'access' (upacāra). And because they conform to the preceding preparatory states and the subsequent absorption, they are also called 'conformity' (anuloma). And that which is the very last among these is also called 'change-of-lineage' (gotrabhū) because it overcomes the lineage of the limited and develops the lineage of the exalted. Herein, by grasping what has not been grasped, the first is preparatory, the second is access, the third is conformity, and the fourth is change-of-lineage. Alternatively, the first is access, the second is conformity, the third is change-of-lineage, and the fourth or fifth is the absorption consciousness. For indeed, it is the fourth or the fifth that attains absorption, and that is in accordance with whether one has quick or slow direct knowledge. After that, the impulsion lapses, and it becomes the turn of the life-continuum.

Ābhidhammikagodattatthero pana “purimā purimā kusalā dhammā pacchimānaṃ pacchimānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ āsevanapaccayena paccayo”ti (paṭṭhā. 1.1.12) imaṃ suttaṃ vatvā āsevanapaccayena pacchimo pacchimo dhammo balavā hoti, tasmā chaṭṭhepi sattamepi appanā hotīti āha, taṃ aṭṭhakathāsu “attano matimattaṃ therasseta”nti vatvā paṭikkhittaṃ. Catutthapañcamesuyeva pana appanā hoti. Parato javanaṃ patitaṃ nāma hoti, bhavaṅgassa āsannattāti vuttaṃ[M 1.0135]. Tameva vicāretvā vuttattā na sakkā paṭikkhipituṃ. Yathā hi puriso chinnapapātābhimukho dhāvanto ṭhātukāmopi pariyante pādaṃ katvā ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti papāte eva patati, evaṃ chaṭṭhe vā sattame vā appetuṃ na sakkoti, bhavaṅgassa āsannattā. Tasmā catutthapañcamesuyeva appanā hotīti veditabbā.

The Venerable Godatta, the Abhidhammika, however, having stated the text, "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding wholesome states by way of the repetition condition" (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.12), declared that, due to the repetition condition, the succeeding state becomes strong; therefore, absorption occurs even in the sixth or seventh moment. But the commentaries have rejected this, stating, "This is merely the elder's personal opinion." Absorption, in fact, occurs only in the fourth or fifth moments. The subsequent impulsion is said to be 'fallen' because of its proximity to the life-continuum, as has been stated. Since this very point was stated after due consideration, it cannot be rejected. For just as a man running toward a precipice, though wishing to stop, cannot place his foot at the edge and stand, but instead falls over the precipice, so too is it impossible to attain absorption in the sixth or seventh moment due to proximity to the life-continuum. Therefore, it should be understood that absorption occurs only in the fourth or fifth moments.

Sā [V 1.0135] ca pana ekacittakkhaṇikāyeva. Sattasu hi ṭhānesu addhānaparicchedo nāma natthi paṭhamappanāyaṃ, lokiyābhiññāsu, catūsu maggesu, maggānantaraphale, rūpārūpabhavesu bhavaṅgajjhāne, nirodhassa paccaye nevasaññānāsaññāyatane, nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa phalasamāpattiyanti. Ettha maggānantaraphalaṃ tiṇṇaṃ upari na hoti. Nirodhassa paccayo nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ dvinnamupari na hoti. Rūpārūpesu bhavaṅgassa parimāṇaṃ natthi, sesaṭṭhānesu ekameva cittanti. Iti ekacittakkhaṇikāyeva appanā. Tato bhavaṅgapāto. Atha bhavaṅgaṃ vocchinditvā jhānapaccavekkhaṇatthāya āvajjanaṃ, tato jhānapaccavekkhaṇanti.

And that absorption, however, lasts for only a single mind-moment. For in seven instances, there is no delimitation of duration: in the first absorption; in the mundane direct knowledges; in the four paths; in the fruition immediately following the path; in the life-continuum absorption in the form and formless existences; in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a condition for cessation; and in the fruition attainment of one emerging from cessation. Herein, the fruition immediately following the path does not occur for more than three moments. The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as a condition for cessation does not occur for more than two moments. In the form and formless realms, there is no measure for the life-continuum; in the remaining instances, there is only a single mind-moment. Thus, absorption lasts for only a single mind-moment. After that, there is a falling into the life-continuum. Then, having cut off the life-continuum, adverting arises for the purpose of reviewing the absorption, followed by the reviewing of the absorption.

Ettāvatā ca panesa vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati (dha. sa. 160; dī. ni. 1.226). Evamanena pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇaṃ.

Furthermore, by this much, this meditator, being secluded indeed from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Thus, this meditator has attained the first jhāna with the earth kasiṇa as its object, which has five factors abandoned, is endowed with five factors, possesses threefold goodness, and is complete with ten characteristics.

70. Tattha vivicceva kāmehīti kāmehi viviccitvā vinā hutvā apakkamitvā. Yo panāyamettha evakāro, so niyamatthoti veditabbo. Yasmā ca niyamattho, tasmā tasmiṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇasamaye avijjamānānampi kāmānaṃ tassa paṭhamajjhānassa paṭipakkhabhāvaṃ kāmapariccāgeneva cassa adhigamaṃ dīpeti.

70. Herein, 'being secluded indeed from sensual pleasures' means: having been secluded from sensual pleasures, having become free from them, having moved away from them. Furthermore, as for this particle 'eva' herein, it should be known as having the meaning of definiteness. And because it has the meaning of definiteness, it therefore clarifies that, at the time of entering and abiding in the first jhāna, sensual pleasures are an opponent to that first jhāna—even though they are not present—and that the attainment of this jhāna is only through the abandoning of sensual pleasures.

Kathaṃ? “Vivicceva kāmehī”ti evañhi niyame kariyamāne idaṃ paññāyati, nūna jhānassa kāmā paṭipakkhabhūtā yesu sati idaṃ nappavattati, andhakāre sati padīpobhāso viya. Tesaṃ pariccāgeneva cassa [M 1.0136] adhigamo hoti, orimatīrapariccāgena pārimatīrasseva. Tasmā niyamaṃ karotīti.

How so? For when the definite statement, 'Being secluded indeed from sensual pleasures,' is made, this becomes clear: surely, sensual pleasures are the opponents of this jhāna, in the presence of which this jhāna does not arise, just as the light of a lamp does not arise in the presence of darkness. And the attainment of this jhāna occurs only through their abandoning, just like the attainment of the far shore through the abandoning of the near shore. Therefore, He makes a definite statement.

Tattha siyā, kasmā panesa pubbapadeyeva vutto, na uttarapade, kiṃ akusalehi dhammehi aviviccāpi jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyyāti? Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃnissaraṇato hi pubbapade esa vutto. Kāmadhātusamatikkamanato hi kāmarāgapaṭipakkhato ca idaṃ jhānaṃ kāmānameva nissaraṇaṃ. Yathāha, “kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhamma”nti (dī. ni. 3.353). Uttarapadepi pana yathā “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 1.139; a. ni. 4.241) ettha [V 1.0136] evakāro ānetvā vuccati, evaṃ vattabbo. Na hi sakkā ito aññehipi nīvaraṇasaṅkhātehi akusaladhammehi avivicca jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. Tasmā “vivicceva kāmehi vivicceva akusalehi dhammehī”ti evaṃ padadvayepi esa daṭṭhabbo. Padadvayepi ca kiñcāpi viviccāti iminā sādhāraṇavacanena tadaṅgavivekādayo, kāyavivekādayo ca sabbepi vivekā saṅgahaṃ gacchanti, tathāpi kāyaviveko cittaviveko vikkhambhanavivekoti tayo eva idha daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, a question might arise: 'Why is this particle eva stated only in the first phrase and not in the latter? Could one attain and dwell in jhāna even without being secluded from unwholesome states?' But this should not be seen in such a way. For this particle eva is stated in the first phrase because [jhāna] is the escape from them [i.e., sensual pleasures]. Indeed, because it is the means for transcending the sensual realm and because it is the opponent of sensual lust, this jhāna is specifically the escape from sensual pleasures. As it is said: 'This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation.' However, in the latter phrase also, just as in the text, 'Here only, O monks, is the ascetic; here is the second ascetic,' the particle eva is brought in and stated, so too should it be brought in and stated here. For it is not possible to attain and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states known as the hindrances. Therefore, this [particle] should be understood in both phrases thus: 'secluded indeed from sensual pleasures, secluded indeed from unwholesome states.'
