And although in both phrases, by this general term 'secluded,' all seclusions—such as seclusion by substitution and so on, and bodily seclusion and so on—are included, nevertheless, here, only three are to be understood: bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion by suppression.

Kāmehīti iminā pana padena ye ca niddese “katame vatthukāmā, manāpiyā rūpā”tiādinā (mahāni. 1) nayena vatthukāmā vuttā, ye ca tattheva vibhaṅge ca “chando kāmo, rāgo kāmo, chandarāgo kāmo, saṅkappo kāmo, rāgo kāmo, saṅkapparāgo kāmo, ime vuccanti kāmā”ti (mahāni. 1; vibha. 564) evaṃ kilesakāmā vuttā, te sabbepi saṅgahitāicceva daṭṭhabbā. Evañhi sati vivicceva kāmehīti vatthukāmehipi viviccevāti attho yujjati, tena kāyaviveko vutto hoti. Vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti kilesakāmehi sabbākusalehi vā viviccāti attho yujjati, tena cittaviveko vutto hoti. Purimena cettha vatthukāmehi vivekavacanato eva kāmasukhapariccāgo, dutiyena kilesakāmehi vivekavacanato nekkhammasukhapariggaho vibhāvito hoti. Evaṃ vatthukāmakilesakāmavivekavacanatoyeva ca etesaṃ paṭhamena saṃkilesavatthuppahānaṃ, dutiyena saṃkilesappahānaṃ. Paṭhamena lolabhāvassa hetupariccāgo, dutiyena bālabhāvassa. Paṭhamena ca payogasuddhi[M 1.0137], dutiyena āsayaposanaṃ vibhāvitaṃ hotīti viññātabbaṃ. Esa tāva nayo kāmehīti ettha vuttakāmesu vatthukāmapakkhe.

Now, by this phrase 'from sensual pleasures' (kāmehi), it should be understood that all are indeed included: both the sensual objects (vatthukāma) spoken of in the Niddesa by the method beginning, 'What are the sensual objects? Agreeable, dear forms...' and the sensual defilements (kilesakāma) spoken of in that same text and in the Vibhaṅga thus, 'Desire is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, desirous lust is sensual pleasure, intention is sensual pleasure, lust is sensual pleasure, intentional lust is sensual pleasure—these are called sensual pleasures.' For when this is so, the meaning of 'secluded indeed from sensual pleasures' as 'secluded indeed from sensual objects' is fitting; by that, bodily seclusion is spoken of. The meaning of 'secluded from unwholesome states' as 'secluded from sensual defilements or from all unwholesome states' is fitting; by that, mental seclusion is spoken of. And here, by the former phrase, through the very statement of seclusion from sensual objects, the abandoning of sensual pleasure is clarified; by the second, through the statement of seclusion from sensual defilements, the embracing of the bliss of renunciation is clarified. And thus, precisely by this statement of seclusion from sensual objects and sensual defilements, the abandoning of the basis of defilement is clarified by the first of these phrases, and the abandoning of defilement by the second. By the first, the abandoning of the cause of flightiness is clarified; by the second, that of the state of foolishness. And by the first, purity of application is clarified; by the second, the nurturing of the disposition. Thus it should be understood. This, for now, is the method regarding the aspect of sensual objects among the sensual pleasures spoken of here in the phrase 'from sensual pleasures'.

Kilesakāmapakkhe pana chandoti ca rāgoti ca evamādīhi anekabhedo kāmacchandoyeva kāmoti adhippeto. So ca akusalapariyāpannopi samāno “tattha katamo kāmo chando kāmo”tiādinā (vibha. 564) nayena vibhaṅge jhānapaṭipakkhato visuṃ vutto. Kilesakāmattā vā purimapade vutto, akusalapariyāpannattā dutiyapade. Anekabhedato cassa kāmatoti avatvā kāmehīti vuttaṃ.

Now, in the aspect of sensual defilements (kilesakāma), by such terms as 'desire' (chanda) and 'lust' (rāga), it is sensual desire (kāmacchanda) itself, which has many divisions, that is intended by 'sensual pleasure' (kāma). And although it is included in the unwholesome, it is spoken of separately in the Vibhaṅga by the method beginning, 'Therein, what is sensual pleasure? Desire is sensual pleasure...' because it is an opponent to jhāna. Alternatively, it is spoken of in the first phrase because it is a sensual defilement, and in the second phrase because it is included in the unwholesome. And because of its many divisions, instead of saying kāmato (from sensual pleasure), the plural kāmehi (from sensual pleasures) is used.

Aññesampi ca dhammānaṃ akusalabhāve vijjamāne “tattha katame akusalā dhammā, kāmacchando”tiādinā [V 1.0137] nayena vibhaṅge upari jhānaṅgānaṃ paccanīkapaṭipakkhabhāvadassanato nīvaraṇāneva vuttāni. Nīvaraṇāni hi jhānaṅgapaccanīkāni, tesaṃ jhānaṅgāneva paṭipakkhāni viddhaṃsakāni vighātakānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi samādhi kāmacchandassa paṭipakkho, pīti byāpādassa, vitakko thinamiddhassa, sukhaṃ uddhaccakukkuccassa, vicāro vicikicchāyāti peṭake vuttaṃ.

Although other states also have an unwholesome nature, only the hindrances are mentioned in the Vibhaṅga—by the method beginning, 'Therein, what are the unwholesome states? Sensual desire...'—because it shows that they are the adversaries of the jhāna factors to be discussed later, and that those jhāna factors are their counterparts. For the hindrances are indeed the adversaries of the jhāna factors, and it is said that the jhāna factors themselves are their counterparts, destroyers, and suppressors. For so it is stated in the Peṭakopadesa: concentration is the counterpart to sensual desire, rapture to ill will, applied thought to sloth and torpor, happiness to restlessness and remorse, and sustained thought to doubt.

Evamettha vivicceva kāmehīti iminā kāmacchandassa vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hoti. Vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti iminā pañcannampi nīvaraṇānaṃ, agahitaggahaṇena pana paṭhamena kāmacchandassa, dutiyena sesanīvaraṇānaṃ. Tathā paṭhamena tīsu akusalamūlesu pañcakāmaguṇabhedavisayassa lobhassa, dutiyena āghātavatthubhedādivisayānaṃ dosamohānaṃ. Oghādīsu vā dhammesu paṭhamena kāmoghakāmayogakāmāsavakāmupādānaabhijjhākāyaganthakāmarāgasaṃyojanānaṃ, dutiyena avasesaoghayogāsavaupādānaganthasaṃyojanānaṃ. Paṭhamena ca taṇhāya taṃsampayuttakānañca, dutiyena avijjāya taṃsampayuttakānañca. Apica paṭhamena lobhasampayuttānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ cittuppādānaṃ, dutiyena sesānaṃ catunnaṃ akusalacittuppādānaṃ vikkhambhanaviveko vutto hotīti veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāva vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehīti ettha atthappakāsanā.

Thus, herein, by 'secluded indeed from sensual pleasures' is meant the seclusion by suppression of sensual desire. By 'secluded from unwholesome states' is meant the seclusion by suppression of all five hindrances. Alternatively, by way of taking up what was not yet taken, the first phrase refers to sensual desire, and the second to the remaining hindrances. Similarly, among the three unwholesome roots, the first phrase refers to greed, which has as its object the various five strands of sensual pleasure, while the second refers to aversion and delusion, which have as their objects the various grounds for resentment and so on. Or, among states such as the floods, the first phrase refers to the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, the taint of sensuality, the clinging to sensuality, the bodily knot of covetousness, and the fetter of sensual passion; the second refers to the remaining floods, yokes, taints, clingings, bodily knots, and fetters. And the first refers to craving and its associated states, while the second refers to ignorance and its associated states. Furthermore, it should be understood that the seclusion by suppression is spoken of in reference to, with the first phrase, the eight consciousness-arisings associated with greed, and with the second, the remaining four unwholesome consciousness-arisings. This, for now, is the explanation of the meaning herein of 'secluded indeed from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states.'

71. Ettāvatā [M 1.0138] ca paṭhamassa jhānassa pahānaṅgaṃ dassetvā idāni sampayogaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ savitakkaṃ savicārantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vitakkanaṃ vitakko, ūhananti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanalakkhaṇo, āhananapariyāhananaraso. Tathā hi tena yogāvacaro ārammaṇaṃ vitakkāhataṃ vitakkapariyāhataṃ karotīti vuccati. Ārammaṇe cittassa ānayanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

71. And thus, having shown the factor of abandonment of the first jhāna, now, to show its associated factor, the phrase 'with applied thought, with sustained thought,' etc., is stated. Therein, applying the mind is applied thought (vitakka); it is said to be directing. This has the characteristic of directing the mind onto an object. Its function is striking and striking all around. For so it is said that by means of it, the yogī makes the object struck and struck all around by applied thought. Its manifestation is the leading of the mind to the object.

Vicaraṇaṃ vicāro, anusañcaraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāyaṃ ārammaṇānumajjanalakkhaṇo, tattha sahajātānuyojanaraso, cittassa anuppabandhanapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Moving about is sustained thought (vicāra); it is said to be moving about continuously. This has the characteristic of repeatedly examining the object. Its function is to yoke the co-arisen states to that object. Its manifestation is the continuous binding of the mind.

Santepi ca nesaṃ katthaci avippayoge oḷārikaṭṭhena pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena ca ghaṇḍābhighāto viya cetaso paṭhamābhinipāto vitakko. Sukhumaṭṭhena anumajjanasabhāvena ca ghaṇḍānuravo viya [V 1.0138] anuppabandho vicāro. Vipphāravā cettha vitakko paṭhamuppattikāle paripphandanabhūto cittassa ākāse uppatitukāmassa pakkhino pakkhavikkhepo viya padumābhimukhapāto viya ca gandhānubandhacetaso bhamarassa. Santavutti vicāro nātiparipphandanabhāvo cittassa ākāse uppatitassa pakkhino pakkhappasāraṇaṃ viya, paribbhamanaṃ viya ca padumābhimukhapatitassa bhamarassa padumassa uparibhāge. Dukanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “ākāse gacchato mahāsakuṇassa ubhohi pakkhehi vātaṃ gahetvā pakkhe sannisīdāpetvā gamanaṃ viya ārammaṇe cetaso abhiniropanabhāvena pavatto vitakko. Vātaggahaṇatthaṃ pakkhe phandāpayamānassa gamanaṃ viya anumajjanabhāvena pavatto vicāro”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ anuppabandhena pavattiyaṃ yujjati. So pana nesaṃ viseso paṭhamadutiyajjhānesu pākaṭo hoti.

And although in some cases they are not dissociated, applied thought (vitakka) is the initial impact of the mind, due to its grossness and its being a forerunner, like the initial striking of a bell. Sustained thought (vicāra), which is the continuous binding, is due to its subtlety and its nature of repeatedly examining, like the reverberation of a bell. Herein, applied thought is agitated, being the mind's trembling at the time of its first arising, like the flapping of the wings of a bird that wishes to fly up into the sky, and like the descent towards a lotus of a bee whose mind follows the scent. Sustained thought has a calm activity, being the state of the mind's non-excessive agitation, like the spreading of the wings of a bird that has flown up into the sky, and like the circling above the upper part of the lotus by a bee that has descended towards the lotus. But in the commentary to the Dukanipāta, it is said: 'Applied thought, which occurs by way of directing the mind onto an object, is like the flight of a great bird going in the sky, which, having caught the wind with both wings, flies with its wings settled. Sustained thought, which occurs by way of examining, is like the flight of one who makes the wings tremble in order to catch the wind.' That statement is suitable for its continuous occurrence. But that distinction between them becomes manifest in the first and second jhānas.

Apica malaggahitaṃ kaṃsabhājanaṃ ekena hatthena daḷhaṃ gahetvā itarena hatthena cuṇṇatelavālaṇḍupakena parimajjantassa daḷhagahaṇahattho viya vitakko, parimajjanahattho viya vicāro. Tathā kumbhakārassa daṇḍappahārena cakkaṃ bhamayitvā bhājanaṃ karontassa uppīḷanahattho viya vitakko, ito cito ca sañcaraṇahattho viya vicāro. Tathā maṇḍalaṃ karontassa majjhe [M 1.0139] sannirumbhitvā ṭhitakaṇṭako viya abhiniropano vitakko, bahi paribbhamanakaṇṭako viya anumajjano vicāro. Iti iminā ca vitakkena iminā ca vicārena saha vattati rukkho viya pupphena phalena cāti idaṃ jhānaṃ “savitakkaṃ savicāra”nti vuccati. Vibhaṅge pana “iminā ca vitakkena iminā ca vicārena upeto hoti samupeto”tiādinā (vibha. 565) nayena puggalādhiṭṭhānā desanā katā. Attho pana tatrāpi evameva daṭṭhabbo.

Furthermore, for one polishing a soiled bronze bowl, having firmly grasped it with one hand and polishing it with the other hand using a polishing brush with powder and oil, applied thought should be understood as being like the hand that holds firmly, and sustained thought as being like the hand that polishes. Likewise, for a potter who, having made the wheel spin by striking it with a stick, is making a pot, applied thought should be understood as being like the hand that presses down, and sustained thought as being like the hand that moves here and there. Likewise, for one drawing a circle, the directing applied thought should be understood as being like the pin fixed in the center, while the examining sustained thought should be understood as being like the pin revolving around the outside. Thus, because this jhāna occurs together with this applied thought and this sustained thought—like a tree with its flower and fruit—it is called 'with applied thought and with sustained thought.' In the Vibhaṅga, however, the teaching is given with the person as its basis, by the method beginning with, 'He is endowed and fully endowed with this applied thought and this sustained thought.' However, the meaning even there should be understood in just this same way.

Vivekajanti ettha vivitti viveko, nīvaraṇavigamoti attho. Vivittoti vā viveko, nīvaraṇavivitto jhānasampayuttadhammarāsīti attho. Tasmā vivekā, tasmiṃ vā viveke jātanti vivekajaṃ.

Herein, regarding 'born of seclusion' (vivekajaṃ): seclusion (vivitti) is viveka; the meaning is the removal of the hindrances. Or, viveka is that which is secluded (vivitto); the meaning is the aggregate of states associated with jhāna which is secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, it is 'born of seclusion' (vivekajaṃ) because it is born from that seclusion (vivekā), or born in that seclusion (viveke).

72. Pītisukhanti ettha pīṇayatīti pīti. Sā sampiyāyanalakkhaṇā, kāyacittapīnanarasā, pharaṇarasā vā, odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā. Sā panesā khuddikā pīti, khaṇikāpīti, okkantikāpīti, ubbegāpīti, pharaṇāpītīti pañcavidhā hoti. Tattha khuddikāpīti sarīre lomahaṃsamattameva kātuṃ sakkoti. Khaṇikāpīti khaṇe khaṇe vijjuppādasadisā [V 1.0139] hoti. Okkantikāpīti samuddatīraṃ vīci viya kāyaṃ okkamitvā okkamitvā bhijjati. Ubbegāpīti balavatī hoti kāyaṃ uddhaggaṃ katvā ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇappattā. Tathā hi puṇṇavallikavāsī mahātissatthero puṇṇamadivase sāyaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā candālokaṃ disvā mahācetiyābhimukho hutvā “imāya vata velāya catasso parisā mahācetiyaṃ vandantī”ti pakatiyā diṭṭhārammaṇavasena buddhārammaṇaṃ ubbegāpītiṃ uppādetvā sudhātale pahaṭacitrageṇḍuko viya ākāse uppatitvā mahācetiyaṅgaṇeyeva patiṭṭhāsi. Tathā girikaṇḍakavihārassa upanissaye vattakālakagāme ekā kuladhītāpi balavabuddhārammaṇāya ubbegāpītiyā ākāse laṅghesi.

72. Herein, in the term pītisukha, 'that which gladdens' (pīṇayati) is pīti (joy). Its characteristic is delighting, its function is to cause the body and mind to flourish, or to pervade, and its manifestation is exhilaration. Now, this joy is of five kinds: minor joy, momentary joy, showering joy, uplifting joy, and all-pervading joy. Among these, minor joy is only able to cause the hairs of the body to stand on end. Momentary joy occurs moment by moment, like flashes of lightning. Showering joy, like a wave on the seashore, repeatedly descends upon the body and breaks. Uplifting joy is powerful, able to make the body rise up and leap into the air. For so it is that the Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Puṇṇavallika, went to the shrine courtyard in the evening on a full-moon day. Seeing the moonlight and facing the Great Shrine, he thought, 'Indeed, at this very time, the four assemblies are worshipping the Great Shrine!' By way of an object habitually seen, he aroused uplifting joy with the Buddha as its object and, like a decorated ball struck on a plastered surface, leapt up into the air and landed right in the Great Shrine courtyard. Similarly, in the village of Vattakālaka, a dependency of the Girikaṇḍaka Monastery, a certain daughter of a good family, by means of powerful uplifting joy with the Buddha as its object, also leapt into the air.

Tassā kira mātāpitaro sāyaṃ dhammassavanatthāya vihāraṃ gacchantā “amma tvaṃ garubhārā akāle vicarituṃ na sakkosi, mayaṃ tuyhaṃ pattiṃ katvā dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti agamaṃsu. Sā gantukāmāpi tesaṃ vacanaṃ paṭibāhituṃ [M 1.0140] asakkontī ghare ohīyitvā gharājire ṭhatvā candālokena girikaṇḍake ākāsacetiyaṅgaṇaṃ olokentī cetiyassa dīpapūjaṃ addasa, catasso ca parisā mālāgandhādīhi cetiyapūjaṃ katvā padakkhiṇaṃ karontiyo bhikkhusaṅghassa ca gaṇasajjhāyasaddaṃ assosi. Athassā “dhaññāvatime, ye vihāraṃ gantvā evarūpe cetiyaṅgaṇe anusañcarituṃ, evarūpañca madhuradhammakathaṃ sotuṃ labhantī”ti muttarāsisadisaṃ cetiyaṃ passantiyā eva ubbegāpīti udapādi. Sā ākāse laṅghitvā mātāpitūnaṃ purimataraṃyeva ākāsato cetiyaṅgaṇe oruyha cetiyaṃ vanditvā dhammaṃ suṇamānā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro āgantvā “amma tvaṃ katarena maggena āgatāsī”ti pucchiṃsu. Sā “ākāsena āgatāmhi, na maggenā”ti vatvā “amma ākāsena nāma khīṇāsavā sañcaranti, tvaṃ kathaṃ āgatā”ti vuttā āha – “mayhaṃ candālokena cetiyaṃ ālokentiyā ṭhitāya buddhārammaṇā balavapīti uppajji. Athāhaṃ neva attano ṭhitabhāvaṃ, na nisinnabhāvaṃ aññāsiṃ, gahitanimitteneva pana ākāse laṅghitvā cetiyaṅgaṇe patiṭṭhitāmhī”ti.

Her parents, it is said, going to the monastery in the evening to listen to the Dhamma, told her, 'Dear daughter, you are heavy with child and cannot go about at an unsuitable time. We will listen to the Dhamma after making a share of merit for you,' and they went. Although she wished to go, being unable to refuse their words, she remained at home. Standing in the forecourt of the house, she gazed in the moonlight at the courtyard of the cetiya on the mountain peak and saw the offering of lamps to the cetiya. She also saw the four assemblies making offerings to the cetiya with flowers, scents, and so on while circumambulating it, and she heard the sound of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus chanting in unison. Then, as she was looking at the cetiya, which resembled a heap of pearls, this thought arose: 'Fortunate indeed are these people who, having gone to the monastery, get to circumambulate in such a cetiya courtyard and to hear such a sweet Dhamma discourse!' At that, uplifting joy arose in her. She leaped into the sky and, descending from the sky into the cetiya courtyard even before her parents, she paid homage to the cetiya and stood listening to the Dhamma. Then her parents arrived and asked her, 'Dear daughter, by which path did you come?' She replied, 'I came through the sky, not by the road.' When they said, 'Dear daughter, only those whose taints are destroyed travel through the sky. How did you come?' she answered, 'As I stood gazing at the cetiya in the moonlight, a strong joy with the Buddha as its object arose in me. Then I was not aware of my state of standing, nor of my state of sitting. But, by the very meritorious sign that had been grasped, I leaped into the sky and was established in the cetiya courtyard.'

Evaṃ ubbegāpīti ākāse laṅghāpanappamāṇā hoti. Pharaṇāpītiyā pana uppannāya sakalasarīraṃ dhamitvā pūritavatthi viya mahatā udakoghena pakkhandapabbatakucchi viya ca anuparipphuṭaṃ hoti.

Thus, uplifting joy is capable of making one leap in the sky. But when pervading joy arises, the entire body is completely pervaded, like a bladder filled by blowing, or like a mountain cavern inundated by a great flood of water.

Sā [V 1.0140] panesā pañcavidhā pīti gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī duvidhaṃ passaddhiṃ paripūreti kāyapassaddhiñca cittapassaddhiñca. Passaddhi gabbhaṃ gaṇhantī paripākaṃ gacchantī duvidhampi sukhaṃ paripūreti kāyikañca cetasikañca. Sukhaṃ gabbhaṃ gaṇhantaṃ paripākaṃ gacchantaṃ tividhaṃ samādhiṃ paripūreti khaṇikasamādhiṃ upacārasamādhiṃ appanā samādhinti. Tāsu yā appanāsamādhissa mūlaṃ hutvā vaḍḍhamānā samādhisampayogaṃ gatā pharaṇāpīti, ayaṃ imasmiṃ atthe adhippetā pītīti.

Furthermore, this fivefold rapture, by conceiving and maturing, fulfills the twofold tranquility: tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Tranquility, by conceiving and maturing, fulfills the twofold happiness: bodily and mental. Happiness, by conceiving and maturing, fulfills the threefold concentration: momentary concentration, access concentration, and absorption concentration. Among these, that pervasive rapture which, having become the root of absorption concentration, develops and attains association with concentration—this is intended as 'rapture' in this context.

73. Itaraṃ pana sukhanaṃ sukhaṃ, suṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati ca kāyacittābādhanti sukhaṃ, taṃ sātalakkhaṇaṃ, sampayuttānaṃ upabrūhanarasaṃ, anuggahapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Satipi ca nesaṃ katthaci avippayoge iṭṭhārammaṇapaṭilābhatuṭṭhi pīti. Paṭiladdharasānubhavanaṃ sukhaṃ. Yattha pīti, tattha sukhaṃ. Yattha sukhaṃ, tattha na niyamato pīti. Saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā pīti. Vedanākkhandhasaṅgahitaṃ sukhaṃ. Kantārakhinnassa [M 1.0141] vanantudakadassanasavanesu viya pīti. Vanacchāyāpavesanaudakaparibhogesu viya sukhaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye pākaṭabhāvato cetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Iti ayañca pīti idañca sukhaṃ assa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne atthīti idaṃ jhānaṃ pītisukhanti vuccati.

73. Furthermore, as for the other term, happiness (sukha) is a state of well-being; or, because it thoroughly consumes (suṭṭhu khādati) and destroys (khanati) bodily and mental affliction, it is called 'happiness' (sukha). It has the characteristic of gratification, the function of enhancing associated states, and its manifestation is support. And although they are inseparable in certain cases, rapture is the delight in obtaining a desirable object, while happiness is the experience of the flavor of what has been obtained. Where there is rapture, there is happiness. Where there is happiness, there is not necessarily rapture. Rapture is included in the aggregate of formations. Happiness is included in the aggregate of feeling. Rapture is like the delight of a person exhausted in the wilderness upon seeing or hearing of a forest grove and water. Happiness is like entering the forest shade and making use of the water. And it should be understood that this is said because of their prominence at their respective times. Thus, because this rapture and this happiness belong to this jhāna, or exist in this jhāna, this jhāna is called 'possessing rapture and happiness' (pītisukha).

Atha vā pīti ca sukhañca pītisukhaṃ, dhammavinayādayo viya. Vivekajaṃ pītisukhamassa jhānassa, asmiṃ vā jhāne atthīti evampi vivekajaṃpītisukhaṃ. Yatheva hi jhānaṃ, evaṃ pītisukhampettha vivekajameva hoti, tañcassa atthi, tasmā ekapadeneva “vivekajaṃpītisukha”ntipi vattuṃ yujjati. Vibhaṅge pana “idaṃ sukhaṃ imāya pītiyā sahagata”ntiādinā (vibha. 567) nayena vuttaṃ. Attho pana tatthāpi evameva daṭṭhabbo.

Alternatively, rapture and happiness are rapture-and-happiness, like the Dhamma and Vinaya, etc. The rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion belongs to this jhāna, or exists in this jhāna; thus, this jhāna is also called 'possessing rapture-and-happiness born of seclusion'. For just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too the rapture-and-happiness herein is born of seclusion alone, and it exists for this jhāna; therefore, it is fitting to say 'born-of-seclusion-rapture-and-happiness' even as a single term. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated by the method beginning with, “This happiness is accompanied by this rapture,” etc. Yet, the meaning there too should be understood in just this same way.

Paṭhamaṃ jhānanti idaṃ parato āvibhavissati. Upasampajjāti upagantvā, pāpuṇitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasampādayitvā vā, nipphādetvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vibhaṅge pana “upasampajjāti paṭhamassa jhānassa lābho paṭilābho patti sampatti phusanā sacchikiriyā upasampadā”ti vuttaṃ. Tassāpi evamevattho daṭṭhabbo. Viharatīti tadanurūpena iriyāpathavihārena itivuttappakārajhānasamaṅgī hutvā attabhāvassa iriyaṃ vuttiṃ pālanaṃ yapanaṃ yāpanaṃ cāraṃ vihāraṃ abhinipphādeti[V 1.0141]. Vuttañhetaṃ vibhaṅge “viharatīti iriyati vattati pāleti yapeti yāpeti carati viharati, tena vuccati viharatī”ti (vibha. 540).

The phrase 'the first jhāna' will become clear later. 'Enters upon' means having approached, having attained. Or, it means having produced, having accomplished. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is said: “'Enters upon' means the gaining, re-gaining, attainment, complete attainment, contact, realization, and entering upon of the first jhāna.” Its meaning should also be understood in just this same way. ‘Dwells’ means that, being endowed with the jhāna of the kind thus described, by means of a posture and mode of dwelling suitable to it, one accomplishes the deportment, occurrence, maintenance, sustenance, carrying on, moving about, and abiding of one's individual existence. For this has been said in the Vibhaṅga: “'Dwells' means one moves, continues, maintains, sustains, carries on, behaves, abides; therefore, it is said 'one dwells'”.

Pañcaṅgavippahīnādi

The abandoning of the five factors, and so on.

74. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgata”nti, tattha kāmacchando, byāpādo, thinamiddhaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ, vicikicchāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ nīvaraṇānaṃ pahānavasena pañcaṅgavippahīnatā veditabbā. Na hi etesu appahīnesu jhānaṃ uppajjati. Tenassetāni pahānaṅgānīti vuccanti. Kiñcāpi hi jhānakkhaṇe aññepi akusalā dhammā pahīyanti, tathāpi etāneva visesena jhānantarāyakarāni. Kāmacchandena hi nānāvisayappalobhitaṃ cittaṃ na ekattārammaṇe samādhiyati. Kāmacchandābhibhūtaṃ vā taṃ na kāmadhātuppahānāya paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati. Byāpādena cārammaṇe paṭihaññamānaṃ na nirantaraṃ pavattati[M 1.0142]. Thinamiddhābhibhūtaṃ akammaññaṃ hoti. Uddhaccakukkuccaparetaṃ avūpasantameva hutvā paribbhamati. Vicikicchāya upahataṃ jhānādhigamasādhikaṃ paṭipadaṃ nārohati. Iti visesena jhānantarāyakarattā etāneva pahānaṅgānīti vuttānīti.

74. Now, as for what was said—'having abandoned five factors, possessing five factors'—herein, the state of having abandoned five factors should be understood through the abandonment of the five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. For jhāna does not arise unless these are abandoned. Therefore, they are called its factors of abandonment. Although other unwholesome states are also abandoned at the moment of jhāna, these alone are specifically obstructive to jhāna. For a mind allured by sensual desire toward various objects does not become concentrated on a single object. Or, overcome by sensual desire, it does not undertake the path for abandoning the sensual realm. A mind afflicted by ill will toward an object does not proceed uninterruptedly. Overcome by sloth and torpor, it becomes unwieldy. Afflicted by restlessness and remorse, it remains unquiet and wanders about. Afflicted by doubt, it does not ascend the path leading to the attainment of jhāna. Thus, because they are specifically obstructive to jhāna, these alone are called the factors of abandonment.

Yasmā pana vitakko ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropeti, vicāro anuppabandhati, tehi avikkhepāya sampāditappayogassa cetaso payogasampattisambhavā pīti pīṇanaṃ, sukhañca upabrūhanaṃ karoti. Atha naṃ sasesasampayuttadhammaṃ etehi abhiniropanānuppabandhanapīṇanaupabrūhanehi anuggahitā ekaggatā ekattārammaṇe samaṃ sammā ca ādhiyati, tasmā vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittekaggatāti imesaṃ pañcannaṃ uppattivasena pañcaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. Uppannesu hi etesu pañcasu jhānaṃ uppannaṃ nāma hoti. Tenassa etāni pañca samannāgataṅgānīti vuccanti. Tasmā na etehi samannāgataṃ aññadeva jhānaṃ nāma atthīti gahetabbaṃ. Yathā pana aṅgamattavaseneva caturaṅginī senā, pañcaṅgikaṃ tūriyaṃ, aṭṭhaṅgiko ca maggoti vuccati, evamidampi aṅgamattavaseneva pañcaṅgikanti vā pañcaṅgasamannāgatanti vā vuccatīti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, because applied thought applies the mind to the object and sustained thought keeps it connected, joy—arising from the accomplishment of the effort—brings gratification to the mind whose effort has been accomplished by these two for the sake of non-distraction, and happiness brings about its augmentation. Then, one-pointedness, assisted by these acts of applying, sustaining, gratifying, and augmenting, places that mind, together with its remaining associated states, evenly and rightly upon a single object. Therefore, the state of being endowed with five factors is to be understood by way of the arising of these five: applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. For when these five have arisen, jhāna is said to have arisen. Therefore, these five are called its constituent factors. Thus, it should not be held that there exists any other jhāna apart from that which is endowed with these. Just as an army is called 'four-limbed,' a musical ensemble 'five-factored,' and the path 'eight-factored' merely on the basis of their components, so too, it should be understood that this jhāna is called 'five-factored' or 'endowed with five factors' merely on the basis of its components.

Etāni ca pañcaṅgāni kiñcāpi upacārakkhaṇepi atthi, atha kho upacāre pakaticittato [V 1.0142] balavatarāni. Idha pana upacāratopi balavatarāni rūpāvacaralakkhaṇappattāni. Ettha hi vitakko suvisadena ākārena ārammaṇe cittaṃ abhiniropayamāno uppajjati. Vicāro ativiya ārammaṇaṃ anumajjamāno. Pītisukhaṃ sabbāvantampi kāyaṃ pharamānaṃ. Tenevāha – “nāssa kiñci sabbāvato kāyassa vivekajena pītisukhena apphuṭaṃ hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.228). Cittekaggatāpi heṭṭhimamhi samuggapaṭale uparimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ viya ārammaṇesu phusitā hutvā uppajjati, ayametesaṃ itarehi viseso. Tattha cittekaggatā kiñcāpi savitakkaṃ savicāranti imasmiṃ pāṭhe na niddiṭṭhā, tathāpi vibhaṅge “jhānanti vitakko vicāro pīti sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti (vibha. 569) evaṃ vuttattā aṅgameva. Yena hi adhippāyena bhagavatā uddeso kato, soyeva tena vibhaṅge pakāsitoti.

And although these five factors exist even at the moment of access concentration, in access they are stronger than in an ordinary mind. Here, however, they are even stronger than in access, having attained the characteristic of the fine-material sphere. For here, applied thought arises, directing the mind onto the object with a very clear aspect. Sustained thought arises, exceedingly examining the object. Joy and happiness arise, pervading the entire body. For that reason, He said: 'There is nothing whatsoever of his entire body that is not pervaded by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.' One-pointedness of mind also arises, having made firm contact with the objects like an upper lid on a lower casket; this is their distinction from the others. Therein, although one-pointedness of mind is not specified in this text—'with applied thought, with sustained thought'—nevertheless, because it is stated thus in the Vibhaṅga: 'Jhāna is applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind,' it is indeed a factor. For with whatever intention the summary was made by the Blessed One, that very intention was declared by Him in the Vibhaṅga.

Tividhakalyāṇaṃ

The Threefold Goodness

75. Tividhakalyāṇaṃ [M 1.0143] dasalakkhaṇasampannanti ettha pana ādimajjhapariyosānavasena tividhakalyāṇatā. Tesaṃyeva ca ādimajjhapariyosānānaṃ lakkhaṇavasena dasalakkhaṇasampannatā veditabbā.

75. Furthermore, in the phrase 'of threefold goodness, endowed with ten characteristics,' the state of threefold goodness is to be understood by way of the beginning, middle, and end. And the state of being endowed with ten characteristics is to be understood by way of the characteristics of these very beginning, middle, and end.

Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi –

Therein, this is the Pāli text:

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, ādissa kati lakkhaṇāni? Ādissa tīṇi lakkhaṇāni, yo tassa paribandho, tato cittaṃ visujjhati, visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Yañca paribandhato cittaṃ visujjhati, yañca visuddhattā cittaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati, yañca paṭipannattā tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Paṭhamassa jhānassa paṭipadāvisuddhi ādi, ādissa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ ādikalyāṇañceva hoti tilakkhaṇasampannañca.

“For the first jhāna, the purity of the path is the beginning, the cultivation of equanimity is the middle, and gladdening is the end. The purity of the path is the beginning of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the beginning have? The beginning has three characteristics. Whatever impediment it has, the mind is purified from that. Because it is purified, the mind enters upon the intermediate sign of serenity. Because it has entered upon it, the mind rushes forward there. That the mind is purified from the impediment, that because it is purified the mind enters upon the intermediate sign of serenity, and that because it has entered upon it the mind rushes forward there—these are the three characteristics of the beginning. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is good in the beginning and is endowed with three characteristics.

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Majjhassa [V 1.0143] tīṇi lakkhaṇāni, visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Yañca visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati, yañca ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Paṭhamassa jhānassa upekkhānubrūhanā majjhe, majjhassa imāni tīṇi lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ majjhekalyāṇañceva hoti tilakkhaṇasampannañca.

The cultivation of equanimity is the middle of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the middle have? The middle has three characteristics. One regards the purified mind with equanimity; one regards the mind that has entered upon serenity with equanimity; one regards the mind established in oneness with equanimity. That one regards the purified mind with equanimity, that one regards the mind that has entered upon serenity with equanimity, and that one regards the mind established in oneness with equanimity—these are the three characteristics of the middle. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is good in the middle and is endowed with three characteristics.”

“Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, pariyosānassa kati lakkhaṇāni? Pariyosānassa cattāri lakkhaṇāni, tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ anativattanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, indriyānaṃ ekarasaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, tadupagavīriyavāhanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā, āsevanaṭṭhena sampahaṃsanā. Paṭhamassa jhānassa sampahaṃsanā pariyosānaṃ, pariyosānassa imāni cattāri lakkhaṇāni. Tena vuccati paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇañceva hoti catulakkhaṇasampannañcā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.158).

“Elation is the culmination of the first jhāna. How many characteristics does the culmination have? The culmination has four characteristics: elation by way of the non-transgression of the states that have arisen there; elation by way of the single function of the faculties; elation by way of bearing the appropriate energy; and elation by way of repeated practice. Elation is the culmination of the first jhāna, and the culmination has these four characteristics. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is excellent in its culmination and endowed with four characteristics.”

Tatra [M 1.0144] paṭipadāvisuddhi nāma sasambhāriko upacāro. Upekkhānubrūhanā nāma appanā. Sampahaṃsanā nāma paccavekkhaṇāti evameke vaṇṇayanti. Yasmā pana “ekattagataṃ cittaṃ paṭipadāvisuddhipakkhandañceva hoti upekkhānubrūhitañca ñāṇena ca sampahaṃsita”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.158) pāḷiyaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā antoappanāyameva āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi, tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā, dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā ca veditabbā.

Therein, some explain thus: purification of the path is the access concentration with its requisites; development of equanimity is absorption; elation is reviewing. However, since it is said in the Pāli, “The mind that has attained unification is an approach to the purification of the path, is developed by equanimity, and is made elated by knowledge,” therefore, within absorption itself, purification of the path should be understood by way of the approach; development of equanimity should be understood by way of the function of equanimity as neutrality therein; and elation should be understood by way of the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that purifies by establishing the state of the non-transgression, etc., of phenomena.

Kathaṃ? Yasmiñhi vāre appanā uppajjati, tasmiṃ yo nīvaraṇasaṅkhāto kilesagaṇo tassa jhānassa paribandho, tato cittaṃ visujjhati. Visuddhattā āvaraṇavirahitaṃ hutvā majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati. Majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ nāma samappavatto appanāsamādhiyeva. Tadanantaraṃ pana purimacittaṃ ekasantatipariṇāmanayena tathattamupagacchamānaṃ majjhimaṃ samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati nāma, evaṃ paṭipannattā tathattupagamanena tattha pakkhandati nāma. Evaṃ tāva purimacitte vijjamānākāranipphādikā paṭhamassa jhānassa uppādakkhaṇeyeva āgamanavasena paṭipadāvisuddhi veditabbā.

How so? Indeed, at the time when absorption arises, the mind is purified from that which is the impediment to that jhāna, namely, the group of defilements called the hindrances. Due to being purified, having become free from obstruction, it enters upon the intermediate sign of serenity. The intermediate sign of serenity is simply the absorption-concentration itself, which proceeds evenly. Furthermore, the preceding consciousness, by attaining that very state through the method of transformation into a single continuity, is said to enter upon the intermediate sign of serenity. Because it has thus entered upon it, through the attainment of that state, it is said to leap into it. Thus, for now, the purification of the path—which accomplishes the modes existing in the preceding consciousness—should be understood by way of the approach at the very moment of the arising of the first jhāna.

Evaṃ [V 1.0144] visuddhassa pana tassa puna visodhetabbābhāvato visodhane byāpāraṃ akaronto visuddhaṃ cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Samathabhāvupagamanena samathapaṭipannassa puna samādhāne byāpāraṃ akaronto samathapaṭipannaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Samathapaṭipannabhāvato eva cassa kilesasaṃsaggaṃ pahāya ekattena upaṭṭhitassa puna ekattupaṭṭhāne byāpāraṃ akaronto ekattupaṭṭhānaṃ ajjhupekkhati nāma. Evaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhāya kiccavasena upekkhānubrūhanā veditabbā.

Furthermore, with regard to that mind thus purified, since there is no need for it to be purified again, one, not making an effort in purifying, is said to regard the purified mind with equanimity. With regard to the mind that has entered upon serenity through having attained the state of serenity, one, not making an effort in concentrating it again, is said to regard that which has entered upon serenity with equanimity. And with regard to this mind, which, just because of its state of having entered upon serenity, is established in unification after having abandoned association with defilements, one, not making an effort again in establishing unification, is said to regard that which is established in unification with equanimity. Thus, the development of equanimity should be understood by way of the function of equanimity as neutrality therein.

Ye panete evaṃ upekkhānubrūhite tattha jātā samādhipaññāsaṅkhātā yuganaddhadhammā aññamaññaṃ anativattamānā hutvā pavattā, yāni ca saddhādīni indriyāni nānākilesehi vimuttattā vimuttirasena ekarasāni hutvā pavattāni, yañcesa tadupagaṃ tesaṃ anativattanaekarasabhāvānaṃ anucchavikaṃ vīriyaṃ vāhayati, yā cassa tasmiṃ khaṇe pavattā āsevanā, sabbepi te ākārā yasmā ñāṇena saṃkilesavodānesu taṃ taṃ ādīnavañca ānisaṃsañca [M 1.0145] disvā tathā tathā sampahaṃsitattā visodhitattā pariyodāpitattā nipphannāva, tasmā “dhammānaṃ anativattanādibhāvasādhanena pariyodāpakassa ñāṇassa kiccanipphattivasena sampahaṃsanā veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ.

Furthermore, those paired states called concentration and wisdom, born therein and thus developed by equanimity, proceed without transgressing one another. And the faculties, such as faith, being liberated from various defilements, proceed with a single taste through the taste of liberation. And one produces that energy which is suitable for their state of non-transgression and single taste. And whatever repeated practice occurs at that moment—all these aspects are indeed accomplished because, through knowledge, having seen the respective danger and benefit in defilements and purifications, they are in that way gladdened, purified, and thoroughly cleansed. Therefore, it was said: “Elation should be understood as the accomplishment of the function of the knowledge that purifies by establishing the state of non-transgression and other qualities of phenomena.”

Tattha yasmā upekkhāvasena ñāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “tathāpaggahitaṃ cittaṃ sādhukaṃ ajjhupekkhati, upekkhāvasena paññāvasena paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti, upekkhāvasena nānattakilesehi cittaṃ vimuccati, vimokkhavasena paññāvasena paññindriyaṃ adhimattaṃ hoti. Vimuttattā te dhammā ekarasā honti. Ekarasaṭṭhena bhāvanā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.201). Tasmā ñāṇakiccabhūtā sampahaṃsanā pariyosānanti vuttā.

Therein, knowledge becomes evident by way of equanimity. As it is said: “One regards well with equanimity the mind thus well-exerted. By way of equanimity and by way of wisdom, the wisdom faculty becomes predominant. By way of equanimity, the mind is liberated from various defilements. By way of liberation and by way of wisdom, the wisdom faculty becomes predominant. Because of being liberated, those states become of one taste. Development is by way of the single taste.” Therefore, elation, being the function of knowledge, is called the culmination.

Idāni paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇanti ettha gaṇanānupubbatā paṭhamaṃ, paṭhamaṃ uppannantipi paṭhamaṃ. Ārammaṇūpanijjhānato paccanīkajhāpanato vā jhānaṃ. Pathavīmaṇḍalaṃ pana sakalaṭṭhena pathavīkasiṇanti vuccati, taṃ nissāya paṭiladdhanimittampi, pathavīkasiṇanimitte paṭiladdhajhānampi. Tatra imasmiṃ atthe jhānaṃ pathavīkasiṇanti veditabbaṃ. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇa”nti.

Now, regarding the phrase “the first jhāna is attained, the earth kasiṇa”: herein, “first” is due to the sequence of enumeration, and it is also “first” because it arises first. It is “jhāna” either from closely contemplating the object or from burning up the opposing factors. The earth disk, however, is called “earth kasiṇa” in the sense of “the whole.” Also the counterpart sign obtained by relying on it is called “earth kasiṇa,” and also the jhāna obtained in the earth kasiṇa counterpart sign. Therein, in this context, the jhāna should be understood as the “earth kasiṇa.” Referring to that, it was said: “the first jhāna is attained, the earth kasiṇa.”

Ciraṭṭhitisampādanaṃ

Accomplishing Long-Lasting Stability

76. Evamadhigate [V 1.0145] pana etasmiṃ tena yoginā vālavedhinā viya, sūdena viya ca ākārā pariggahetabbā. Yathā hi sukusalo dhanuggaho vālavedhāya kammaṃ kurumāno yasmiṃ vāre vālaṃ vijjhati, tasmiṃ vāre akkantapadānañca dhanudaṇḍassa ca jiyāya ca sarassa ca ākāraṃ pariggaṇheyya. “Evaṃ me ṭhitena evaṃ dhanudaṇḍaṃ evaṃ jiyaṃ evaṃ saraṃ gahetvā vālo viddho”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya tatheva te ākāre sampādento avirādhetvā vālaṃ vijjheyya. Evameva yogināpi “imaṃ nāma me bhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā evarūpaṃ puggalaṃ sevamānena evarūpe senāsane iminā nāma iriyāpathena imasmiṃ kāle idaṃ adhigata”nti ete bhojanasappāyādayo ākārā pariggahetabbā. Evañhi so naṭṭhe [M 1.0146] vā tasmiṃ te ākāre sampādetvā puna uppādetuṃ, appaguṇaṃ vā paguṇaṃ karonto punappunaṃ appetuṃ sakkhissati.

76. Furthermore, when this has been thus attained, the yogi, like a hair-piercing archer and like a cook, should grasp the conditions. For just as a highly skilled archer, while performing the task of piercing a hair, should grasp the aspect of the placement of his feet, the bow-staff, the string, and the arrow at the very moment he pierces the hair, thinking: 'By me, standing thus, having taken up the bow-staff thus, the string thus, and the arrow thus, the hair was pierced.' Then, from that point onwards, by accomplishing those same conditions in that very way, he would pierce the hair without fail. In this very way, the yogi, too, should grasp these conditions, such as suitable food and so on, thinking: 'By me, having eaten this particular food, while associating with such a person, in such a lodging, with this particular posture, at this time, this was attained.' For in this way, should that concentration be lost, he will be able to produce it again by accomplishing those conditions; or, by making what is not yet proficient, proficient, he will be able to attain absorption again and again.

Yathā ca kusalo sūdo bhattāraṃ parivisanto tassa yaṃ yaṃ ruciyā bhuñjati, taṃ taṃ sallakkhetvā tato paṭṭhāya tādisameva upanāmento lābhassa bhāgī hoti, evamayampi adhigatakkhaṇe bhojanādayo ākāre gahetvā te sampādento naṭṭhe naṭṭhe punappunaṃ appanāya lābhī hoti. Tasmā tena vālavedhinā viya sūdena viya ca ākārā pariggahetabbā. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

And just as a skilled cook, while serving his master, having noted whatever food the master eats with relish, from then on presents that very same kind of food and thus becomes a sharer of gain; so too this yogi, having grasped the conditions such as food at the moment of attainment, by accomplishing them, becomes a gainer of absorption again and again whenever it is lost. Therefore, the conditions should be grasped by him like the hair-piercing archer and like the cook. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo rājānaṃ vā rājamahāmattaṃ vā nānaccayehi sūpehi paccupaṭṭhito assa ambilaggehipi tittakaggehipi kaṭukaggehipi madhuraggehipi khārikehipi akhārikehipi loṇikehipi aloṇikehipi. Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo sakassa bhattu nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti ‘idaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati, imassa vā abhiharati, imassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, imassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, ambilaggaṃ vā me ajja bhattu sūpeyyaṃ ruccati, ambilaggassa vā abhiharati, ambilaggassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, ambilaggassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati…pe… aloṇikassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī’ti. Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo lābhī ceva hoti acchādanassa, lābhī vetanassa, lābhī abhihārānaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito [V 1.0146] byatto kusalo sūdo sakassa bhattu nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… vedanāsu vedanā… citte cittā… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa dhammesu dhammānupassino viharato cittaṃ samādhiyati, upakkilesā pahīyanti, so taṃ nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti. Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu lābhī ceva hoti diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ, lābhī satisampajaññassa. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā [M 1.0147] hi so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu sakassa cittassa nimittaṃ uggaṇhātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.374).

“Bhikkhus, it is as if a wise, competent, and skilled cook were to attend upon a king or a great minister of the king with various kinds of curries: sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and unsalted. That wise, competent, and skilled cook, bhikkhus, grasps the sign of his master: ‘Today this curry is pleasing to my master, or he extends his hand toward this one, or he takes much of this one, or he praises this one. Perhaps today the sour curry is pleasing to my master, or he extends his hand toward the sour one, or he takes much of the sour one, or he praises the sour one… or he praises the unsalted one.’ That wise, competent, and skilled cook, bhikkhus, is a receiver of clothing, a receiver of wages, and a receiver of gifts. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that wise, competent, and skilled cook grasps the sign of his master. In this very same way, bhikkhus, some wise, competent, and skilled bhikkhu here dwells contemplating the body in the body… feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… dhammas in dhammas—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, his mind becomes concentrated and his defilements are abandoned; he grasps that sign. That wise, competent, and skilled bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is a receiver of pleasant abidings in this very life and a receiver of mindfulness and clear comprehension. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that wise, competent, and skilled bhikkhu grasps the sign of his own mind.”

Nimittaggahaṇena cassa puna te ākāre sampādayato appanāmattameva ijjhati, na ciraṭṭhānaṃ. Ciraṭṭhānaṃ pana samādhiparibandhānaṃ dhammānaṃ suvisodhitattā hoti. Yo hi bhikkhu kāmādīnavapaccavekkhaṇādīhi kāmacchandaṃ na suṭṭhu vikkhambhetvā, kāyapassaddhivasena kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ na suppaṭipassaddhaṃ katvā, ārambhadhātumanasikārādivasena thinamiddhaṃ na suṭṭhu paṭivinodetvā, samathanimittamanasikārādivasena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ na susamūhataṃ katvā, aññepi samādhiparibandhe dhamme na suṭṭhu visodhetvā jhānaṃ samāpajjati, so avisodhitaṃ āsayaṃ paviṭṭhabhamaro viya avisuddhaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭharājā viya ca khippameva nikkhamati. Yo pana samādhiparibandhe dhamme suṭṭhu visodhetvā jhānaṃ samāpajjati, so suvisodhitaṃ āsayaṃ paviṭṭhabhamaro viya suparisuddhaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭharājā viya ca sakalampi divasabhāgaṃ antosamāpattiyaṃyeva hoti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Furthermore, for a yogi who, by grasping the sign, again accomplishes those features, only absorption is achieved, not long-lasting stability. Long-lasting stability, however, comes about through the thorough purification of the states that are obstacles to concentration. Indeed, a bhikkhu who enters jhāna without having properly suppressed sensual desire by reflecting on the danger in sensual pleasures, etc.; without having fully calmed the body's distress by means of bodily tranquility; without having properly dispelled sloth and torpor by means of attending to the element of exertion, etc.; without having thoroughly removed restlessness and remorse by means of attending to the sign of serenity, etc.; and without having properly purified other states that are obstacles to concentration—he quickly emerges, like a bee entering an uncleaned hive or a king entering an unpurified garden. But a bhikkhu who enters jhāna after having thoroughly purified the states that are obstacles to concentration remains within the attainment for the entire portion of the day, like a bee entering a well-cleaned hive or a king entering a perfectly pure garden. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Kāmesu chandaṃ paṭighaṃ vinodaye,

Uddhaccamiddhaṃ vicikicchapañcamaṃ;

Vivekapāmojjakarena cetasā,

Rājāva suddhantagato tahiṃ rame”ti.

“One should dispel desire for sensual pleasures, ill will, restlessness and remorse, sloth and torpor, and doubt as the fifth. With a mind that produces joy born of seclusion, one should delight therein, like a king who has gone to a perfectly pure garden.”

Tasmā ciraṭṭhitikāmena paribandhakadhamme visodhetvā jhānaṃ samāpajjitabbaṃ. Cittabhāvanāvepullatthañca yathāladdhaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tassa dve vaḍḍhanābhūmiyo upacāraṃ vā [V 1.0147] appanaṃ vā. Upacāraṃ patvāpi hi taṃ vaḍḍhetuṃ vaṭṭati appanaṃ patvāpi. Ekasmiṃ pana ṭhāne avassaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “yathāladdhaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ vaḍḍhetabba”nti.

Therefore, one who desires long-lasting stability should enter jhāna after purifying the obstructing states. And for the sake of the flourishing of the development of concentration, the counterpart sign, as it has been acquired, should be developed. There are two grounds for its development: either access or absorption. For it is suitable to develop it having reached access, and it is also suitable to develop it having reached absorption. However, in one or the other stage, it must certainly be developed. Therefore, it was said: “The counterpart sign, as it has been acquired, should be developed.”

Nimittavaḍḍhananayo

The Method of Developing the Sign

77. Tatrāyaṃ vaḍḍhananayo, tena yoginā taṃ nimittaṃ pattavaḍḍhanapūvavaḍḍhanabhattavaḍḍhanalatāvaḍḍhanadussavaḍḍhanayogena avaḍḍhetvā yathā nāma kassako kasitabbaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0148] naṅgalena paricchinditvā paricchedabbhantare kasati, yathā vā pana bhikkhū sīmaṃ bandhantā paṭhamaṃ nimittāni sallakkhetvā pacchā bandhanti, evameva tassa yathāladdhassa nimittassa anukkamena ekaṅguladvaṅgulativaṅgulacaturaṅgulamattaṃ manasā paricchinditvā yathāparicchedaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Aparicchinditvā pana na vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Tato vidatthiratanapamukhapariveṇavihārasīmānaṃ gāmanigamajanapadarajjasamuddasīmānañca paricchedavasena vaḍḍhayantena cakkavāḷaparicchedena vā tato vāpi uttari paricchinditvā vaḍḍhetabbaṃ.

77. Herein is the method of expansion. That yogī should not expand that sign by the method of expanding a bowl, a cake, rice, a creeper, or a cloth. Just as a farmer, having delimited the place to be plowed with a plow, plows within the delimited area; or just as monks, when establishing a boundary, first mark the landmarks and afterwards establish it; in the very same way, one should mentally delimit that sign as it has been obtained, and it should be expanded gradually by the measure of one, two, three, or four finger-breadths, according to the delimitation. But it should not be expanded without having delimited it. Then, expanding by way of delimiting the boundaries of monastic residences and monasteries—beginning with a span and a cubit—and the boundaries of villages, towns, districts, kingdoms, and oceans, one should expand it, having delimited it up to the boundary of the world-system, or even beyond that.

Yathā hi haṃsapotakā pakkhānaṃ uṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya parittaṃ parittaṃ padesaṃ uppatantā paricayaṃ katvā anukkamena candimasūriyasantikaṃ gacchanti, evameva bhikkhu vuttanayena nimittaṃ paricchinditvā vaḍḍhento yāva cakkavāḷaparicchedā tato vā uttari vaḍḍheti. Athassa taṃ nimittaṃ vaḍḍhitavaḍḍhitaṭṭhāne pathaviyā ukkūlavikūlanadīviduggapabbatavisamesu saṅkusatasamabbhāhataṃ usabhacammaṃ viya hoti.

For just as young haṃsas, from the time their wings have grown, flying up to a very small region and gaining familiarity, gradually go to the vicinity of the moon and sun; in the very same way, a monk, having delimited the sign by the aforesaid method and expanding it, expands it up to the boundary of the world-system, or even beyond that. Then, for that yogī, that sign, in the place where it has been repeatedly expanded, becomes like the hide of a great bull struck by a hundred pegs on the high places, low places, river-chasms, and uneven mountains of the earth.

Tasmiṃ pana nimitte pattapaṭhamajjhānena ādikammikena samāpajjanabahulena bhavitabbaṃ, na paccavekkhaṇabahulena. Paccavekkhaṇabahulassa hi jhānaṅgāni thūlāni dubbalāni hutvā upaṭṭhahanti. Athassa tāni evaṃ upaṭṭhitattā upari ussukkanāya paccayataṃ āpajjanti. So appaguṇe jhāne ussukkamāno pattapaṭhamajjhānā ca parihāyati, na ca sakkoti dutiyaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Tenāha bhagavā –

Furthermore, with regard to that sign, a beginner who has attained the first jhāna should be one who frequently enters it, not one who frequently reviews it. For, in one who frequently reviews, the jhāna factors appear, having become coarse and weak. Then, because they appear thus, they become a condition for striving for what is higher. Striving when the jhāna is undeveloped, that yogī falls away from the first jhāna that has been attained and is not able to attain the second. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gāvī pabbateyyā bālā abyattā akhettaññū akusalā visame pabbate carituṃ. Tassā evamassa ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ agatapubbañceva disaṃ gaccheyyaṃ, akhāditapubbāni ca tiṇāni khādeyyaṃ, apītapubbāni ca pānīyāni piveyya’nti. Sā [V 1.0148] purimaṃ pādaṃ na supatiṭṭhitaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā pacchimaṃ pādaṃ uddhareyya, sā na ceva agatapubbaṃ disaṃ gaccheyya, na ca akhāditapubbāni tiṇāni khādeyya, na ca apītapubbāni pānīyāni piveyya. Yasmiñcassā padese ṭhitāya evamassa ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ agatapubbañceva…pe… piveyya’nti. Tañca padesaṃ na sotthinā paccāgaccheyya. Taṃ kissa hetu[M 1.0149]? Tathā hi sā, bhikkhave, gāvī pabbateyyā bālā abyattā akhettaññū akusalā visame pabbate carituṃ, evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu bālo abyatto akhettaññū akusalo vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. So taṃ nimittaṃ nāsevati, na bhāveti, na bahulīkaroti, na svādhiṭṭhitaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, tassa evaṃ hoti ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti. So na sakkoti vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. Tassevaṃ hoti ‘yaṃnūnāhaṃ vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja vihareyya’nti. So na sakkoti vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharituṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ubhato bhaṭṭho ubhato parihīno, seyyathāpi sā gāvī pabbateyyā bālā abyattā akhettaññū akusalā visame pabbate caritu”nti (a. ni. 9.35).

“Monks, suppose there is a mountain cow—foolish, inexperienced, ignorant of the terrain, and unskillful at roaming on uneven mountains. She might think: ‘Let me go to a direction I have not gone before, eat grasses I have not eaten before, and drink waters I have not drunk before.’ But without having established her front foot firmly, she would lift her hind foot. She would not go to a direction she had not gone before, nor eat grasses she had not eaten before, nor drink waters she had not drunk before. And from whatever place she stood, she would think: ‘Let me go to a direction I have not gone before… and drink.’ Yet she would not return safely to that place. For what reason? Because, monks, that mountain cow is foolish, inexperienced, ignorant of the terrain, and unskillful at roaming on uneven mountains. In the same way, monks, some monk here is foolish, inexperienced, ignorant of the terrain, and unskillful at entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures… He does not resort to that sign, does not develop it, does not make much of it, and does not firmly establish it. He thinks: ‘Let me, with the stilling of thought and examination… enter and dwell in the second jhāna.’ He is unable to enter and dwell in the second jhāna with the stilling of thought and examination… Then he thinks: ‘Let me, secluded from sensual pleasures… enter and dwell in the first jhāna.’ He is unable to enter and dwell in the first jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures… This, monks, is called a monk who has fallen away on both sides, who has declined on both sides—just like that foolish, inexperienced, ignorant of the terrain, and unskillful mountain cow, unskillful at roaming on uneven mountains.”

Tasmānena tasmiṃyeva tāva paṭhamajjhāne pañcahākārehi ciṇṇavasinā bhavitabbaṃ.

Therefore, one should first become one who has practiced mastery in the five aspects of that very first jhāna.

Pañcavasīkathā

The Account of the Five Masteries

78. Tatrimā pañca vasiyo āvajjanavasī, samāpajjanavasī, adhiṭṭhānavasī, vuṭṭhānavasī, paccavekkhaṇavasīti. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ yatthicchakaṃ yadicchakaṃ yāvadicchakaṃ āvajjeti, āvajjanāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti āvajjanavasī. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ yatthicchakaṃ…pe… samāpajjati, samāpajjanāya dandhāyitattaṃ natthīti samāpajjanavasī. Evaṃ sesāpi vitthāretabbā.

78. Herein are these five masteries: mastery of adverting, mastery of attainment, mastery of resolution, mastery of emerging, and mastery of reviewing. One adverts to the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, for as long as one wishes; there is no sluggishness in adverting: this is mastery of adverting. One attains the first jhāna wherever one wishes… there is no sluggishness in attaining: this is mastery of attainment. Thus the remaining ones should also be elaborated.

Ayaṃ panettha atthappakāsanā, paṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya paṭhamaṃ vitakkaṃ āvajjayato bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā uppannāvajjanānantaraṃ vitakkārammaṇāneva cattāri pañca vā javanāni javanti. Tato dve bhavaṅgāni, tato puna vicārārammaṇaṃ āvajjanaṃ, vuttanayāneva javanānīti evaṃ pañcasu [V 1.0149] jhānaṅgesu yadā nirantaraṃ cittaṃ pesetuṃ sakkoti, athassa āvajjanavasī siddhā hoti. Ayaṃ pana matthakappattā vasī bhagavato yamakapāṭihāriye labbhati[M 1.0150], aññesaṃ vā evarūpe kāle. Ito paraṃ sīghatarā āvajjanavasī nāma natthi.

Herein is the exposition of the meaning: When one emerges from the first jhāna and first adverts to initial thought, the life-continuum is interrupted, and immediately after the arising of that adverting, four or five impulsions having only initial thought as their object arise. After that, two life-continuum moments arise, and after that, an adverting with sustained thought as its object arises again, and impulsions occur in the very way that was stated. Thus, when one is able to direct the mind uninterruptedly to the five jhāna factors, then one's mastery in adverting is accomplished. This mastery, however, which has reached its peak, is obtained by the Blessed One at the time of the Twin Miracle, or by others on such an occasion. Beyond this, there is no mastery in adverting that is quicker.

Āyasmato pana mahāmoggallānassa nandopanandanāgarājadamane viya sīghaṃ samāpajjanasamatthatā samāpajjanavasī nāma.

Furthermore, the ability to attain quickly, like that of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the taming of the Nāga king Nandopananda, is called mastery of attainment.

Accharāmattaṃ vā dasaccharāmattaṃ vā khaṇaṃ ṭhapetuṃ samatthatā adhiṭṭhānavasī nāma. Tatheva lahuṃ vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthatā vuṭṭhānavasī nāma. Tadubhayadassanatthaṃ buddharakkhitattherassa vatthuṃ kathetuṃ vaṭṭati.

The ability to maintain it for the duration of a finger-snap or ten finger-snaps is called mastery of resolution. Similarly, the ability to emerge quickly is called mastery of emerging. To show both of these, it is fitting to tell the story of the Elder Buddharakkhita.

So hāyasmā upasampadāya aṭṭhavassiko hutvā therambatthale mahārohaṇaguttattherassa gilānupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatānaṃ tiṃsamattānaṃ iddhimantasahassānaṃ majjhe nisinno therassa yāguṃ paṭiggāhayamānaṃ upaṭṭhākanāgarājānaṃ gahessāmīti ākāsato pakkhandantaṃ supaṇṇarājānaṃ disvā tāvadeva pabbataṃ nimminitvā nāgarājānaṃ bāhāyaṃ gahetvā tattha pāvisi. Supaṇṇarājā pabbate pahāraṃ datvā palāyi. Mahāthero āha – “sace, āvuso, buddharakkhito nābhavissa, sabbeva gārayhā assāmā”ti.

That venerable one, having been eight years since his higher ordination, was sitting in Therambatthala among thirty thousand powerful ones who had come to attend to the Great Elder Mahārohaṇagutta. He saw the Supaṇṇa king swooping down from the sky, intending to seize the Nāga king who was serving gruel to the elder. Instantly, having created a mountain, he took the Nāga king by the arm and entered there. The Supaṇṇa king struck the mountain and fled. The Great Elder said: 'Friends, if Buddharakkhita had not been here, we all would have been blameworthy.'

Paccavekkhaṇavasī pana āvajjanavasiyā eva vuttā. Paccavekkhaṇajavanāneva hi tattha āvajjanānantarānīti.

The mastery of reviewing, however, is spoken of in terms of the mastery of adverting itself. For, in that case, the reviewing impulsions are immediately subsequent to the adverting.

Dutiyajjhānakathā

Discourse on the Second Jhāna

79. Imāsu pana pañcasu vasīsu ciṇṇavasinā paguṇapaṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ayaṃ samāpatti āsannanīvaraṇapaccatthikā, vitakkavicārānaṃ oḷārikattā aṅgadubbalā”ti ca tattha dosaṃ disvā dutiyajjhānaṃ santato manasikatvā paṭhamajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādāya dutiyādhigamāya yogo kātabbo. Athassa yadā paṭhamajjhānā vuṭṭhāya satassa sampajānassa jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhato vitakkavicārā oḷārikato upaṭṭhahanti, pītisukhañceva cittekaggatā ca santato upaṭṭhāti, tadāssa oḷārikaṅgaṃ pahānāya santaaṅgapaṭilābhāya ca tadeva [V 1.0150] nimittaṃ “pathavī pathavī”ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto “idāni dutiyajjhānaṃ uppajjissatī”ti bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā tadeva pathavīkasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati[M 1.0151]. Tato tasmiṃyevārammaṇe cattāri pañca vā javanāni javanti, yesamavasāne ekaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ dutiyajjhānikaṃ. Sesāni vuttappakārāneva kāmāvacarānīti.

79. Furthermore, in these five masteries, a yogi with practiced mastery, emerging from the proficient first jhāna and seeing the fault in it that 'this attainment has the hindrances as a near enemy, and its factors are weak due to the coarseness of initial and sustained thought,' should attend to the second jhāna as peaceful, abandon delight in the first jhāna, and make an effort to attain the second. Then, when emerging from the first jhāna, being mindful and clearly comprehending, one reviews the jhāna factors, and initial and sustained thought appear as coarse, while rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind appear as peaceful. At that time, for the abandoning of the coarse factor and for the acquisition of the peaceful factor, one should repeatedly attend to that same sign, thinking 'earth, earth.' When it is known, 'Now the second jhāna will arise,' the life-continuum is interrupted, and mind-door adverting arises, taking that very earth kasiṇa as its object. Then, on that same object, four or five impulsions run their course, at the end of which is a single fine-material second jhāna consciousness. The remaining impulsions are of the sense-sphere, as previously described.

Ettāvatā cesa vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evamanena dvaṅgavippahīnaṃ tivaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇaṃ.

By this much, this yogi, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, enters and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, and has rapture and bliss born of concentration. Thus, by this yogi, the second jhāna related to the earth kasiṇa is attained, which has abandoned two factors, is endowed with three factors, possesses threefold excellence, and is endowed with ten characteristics.

80. Tattha vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti vitakkassa ca vicārassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ vūpasamā samatikkamā, dutiyajjhānakkhaṇe apātubhāvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha kiñcāpi dutiyajjhāne sabbepi paṭhamajjhānadhammā na santi. Aññeyeva hi paṭhamajjhāne phassādayo, aññe idha. Oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ adhigamo hotīti dīpanatthaṃ “vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā”ti evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

80. Herein, 'with the stilling of initial and sustained thought' means the stilling, the transcending, and the non-manifestation of these two—initial thought and sustained thought—at the moment of the second jhāna. Although in the second jhāna none of the states of the first jhāna are present—for the states such as contact in the first jhāna are different, and those here are different—it should be understood that the phrase 'with the stilling of initial and sustained thought' is stated in order to clarify that the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, beyond the first jhāna, occurs by transcending the grosser and grosser factor.

Ajjhattanti idha niyakajjhattamadhippetaṃ. Vibhaṅge pana “ajjhattaṃ paccatta”nti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Yasmā ca niyakajjhattamadhippetaṃ, tasmā attani jātaṃ attano santāne nibbattanti ayamettha attho. Sampasādananti sampasādanaṃ vuccati saddhā. Sampasādanayogato jhānampi sampasādanaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇayogato nīlavatthaṃ viya. Yasmā vā taṃ jhānaṃ sampasādanasamannāgatattā vitakkavicārakkhobhavūpasamanena ca cetaso sampasādayati, tasmāpi sampasādananti vuttaṃ. Imasmiñca atthavikappe sampasādanaṃ cetasoti evaṃ padasambandho veditabbo. Purimasmiṃ pana atthavikappe cetasoti etaṃ ekodibhāvena saddhiṃ yojetabbaṃ.

'Internal': here, one's own internality is intended. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only this much is said: 'internal, personal.' And since one's own internality is intended, therefore the meaning here is this: born in oneself, arisen in one's own continuum. 'Confidence': faith is called confidence. Due to its connection with confidence, the jhāna is also called 'confidence,' just as a blue cloth is called 'blue' due to its connection with the color blue. Or, because that jhāna—being endowed with confidence and through the stilling of the disturbance caused by initial and sustained thought—makes the mind confident, it is therefore also called 'confidence.' And in this alternative meaning, the connection of the words should be understood as 'that which makes the mind confident.' But in the former alternative meaning, 'of the mind' should be connected with 'unification.'

Tatrāyamatthayojanā, eko udetīti ekodi, vitakkavicārehi anajjhārūḷhattā aggo seṭṭho hutvā udetīti attho. Seṭṭhopi hi loke ekoti vuccati. Vitakkavicāravirahato vā eko asahāyo hutvā itipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha vā sampayuttadhamme udāyatīti udi, uṭṭhāpetīti [V 1.0151] attho. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena eko ca so udi cāti ekodi, samādhissetaṃ [M 1.0152] adhivacanaṃ. Iti imaṃ ekodiṃ bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti idaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ ekodibhāvaṃ. So panāyaṃ ekodi yasmā cetaso, na sattassa, na jīvassa, tasmā etaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvanti vuttaṃ.

Herein is the explanation of the meaning. It is excellent (`eko`) and it arises (`udeti`), thus it is `ekodi`. The meaning is: because it is not overwhelmed by initial and sustained thought, it arises as supreme (`aggo`) and excellent (`seṭṭho`). Indeed, in the world, even the supreme is called `eka`. Alternatively, it is also suitable to say thus: due to the absence of initial and sustained thought, it arises as one (`eko`), without a companion (`asahāyo`). Or alternatively, because it causes associated states to arise (`udāyati`), it is `udi`; 'it raises them up' is the meaning. In the sense of 'supreme,' it is `eka`, and it is also that `udi`; thus, it is `ekodi`. This is a designation for concentration. Thus, because one develops and increases this `ekodi`, this second jhāna is called `ekodibhāva`. Now, because this `ekodi` is of the mind—not of a being, not of a life-principle—therefore it is called `cetaso ekodibhāva`.

Nanu cāyaṃ saddhā paṭhamajjhānepi atthi, ayañca ekodināmako samādhi, atha kasmā idameva “sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvañcā”ti vuttanti. Vuccate, aduñhi paṭhamajjhānaṃ vitakkavicārakkhobhena vīcitaraṅgasamākulamiva jalaṃ na suppasannaṃ hoti, tasmā satiyāpi saddhāya “sampasādana”nti na vuttaṃ. Na suppasannattāyeva cettha samādhipi na suṭṭhu pākaṭo, tasmā “ekodibhāva”ntipi na vuttaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana jhāne vitakkavicārapalibodhābhāvena laddhokāsā balavatī saddhā, balavasaddhāsahāyapaṭilābheneva ca samādhipi pākaṭo, tasmā idameva evaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Vibhaṅge pana “sampasādananti yā saddhā saddahanā okappanā abhippasādo. Cetaso ekodibhāvanti yā cittassa ṭhiti…pe… sammāsamādhī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vuttena pana tena saddhiṃ ayamatthavaṇṇanā yathā na virujjhati, aññadatthu saṃsandati ceva sameti ca, evaṃ veditabbā.

Is it not so that this faith is also present in the first jhāna, and this concentration named ‘ekodi’ as well? If so, why is only this second jhāna called ‘serenity and unification of mind’? The reply is given: because that first jhāna, due to the agitation of initial and sustained thought, is like water turbulent with ripples and waves and is not well-serene. Therefore, even though faith is present, it is not called ‘sampasādana’ (serenity). And because it is not well-serene, the concentration herein is also not very evident; therefore, it is also not called ‘ekodibhāva’. In this jhāna, however, due to the absence of the obstruction of initial and sustained thought, faith gains its opportunity and becomes strong. And precisely by gaining the assistance of strong faith, concentration also becomes evident. Therefore, it should be understood that only this jhāna is spoken of thus. In the Vibhaṅga, however, only this much is said: ‘“Sampasādana” is that which is faith, believing, commitment, confidence. “Cetaso ekodibhāva” is that which is the stability of mind… right concentration.’ It should be understood that this explanation of the meaning does not contradict what was stated there; on the contrary, it is consistent and in agreement with it.

81. Avitakkaṃ avicāranti bhāvanāya pahīnattā etasmiṃ, etassa vā vitakko natthīti avitakkaṃ. Imināva nayena avicāraṃ. Vibhaṅgepi vuttaṃ “iti ayañca vitakko ayañca vicāro santā honti samitā vūpasantā atthaṅgatā abbhatthaṅgatā appitā byappitā sositā visositā byantikatā, tena vuccati avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti (vibha. 576).

81. “Without initial thought, without sustained thought” means that because initial thought has been abandoned by means of development, in this jhāna, or for this jhāna, there is no initial thought—thus it is called “without initial thought.” In this same way, it is “without sustained thought.” As it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “Thus, this initial thought and this sustained thought are calmed, are quieted, are stilled, have ceased, have utterly ceased, are made to cease, are thoroughly made to cease, are dried up, are utterly dried up, are made to be without remainder; therefore it is called ‘without initial thought, without sustained thought.’”

Etthāha “nanu ca ‘vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā’ti imināpi ayamattho siddho, atha kasmā puna vuttaṃ ‘avitakkaṃ avicāra’nti”. Vuccate, evametaṃ siddhovāyamattho, na panetaṃ tadatthadīpakaṃ. Nanu avocumha “oḷārikassa pana oḷārikassa aṅgassa samatikkamā paṭhamajjhānato paresaṃ dutiyajjhānādīnaṃ samadhigamo hotīti dassanatthaṃ vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamāti evaṃ vutta”nti.

Here one asks: “But is this meaning not already established by ‘from the stilling of initial and sustained thought’? Why then is it said again, ‘without initial thought, without sustained thought’?” It is replied: It is so; this meaning is indeed established. However, that phrase does not illuminate that meaning. Have we not said previously: “It is said thus, ‘from the stilling of initial and sustained thought,’ in order to show that by transcending the grosser factor, the attainment of the second jhāna and so on, which are beyond the first jhāna, occurs”?

Apica vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ sampasādanaṃ, na kilesakālussiyassa. Vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā ekodibhāvaṃ, na upacārajjhānamiva nīvaraṇappahānā[M 1.0153], paṭhamajjhānamiva [V 1.0152] ca na aṅgapātubhāvāti evaṃ sampasādanaekodibhāvānaṃ hetuparidīpakamidaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathā vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā idaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ, na tatiyacatutthajjhānāni viya cakkhuviññāṇādīni viya ca abhāvāti evaṃ avitakkaavicārabhāvassa hetuparidīpakañca, na vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakaṃ. Vitakkavicārābhāvamattaparidīpakameva pana “avitakkaṃ avicāra”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ. Tasmā purimaṃ vatvāpi vattabbamevāti.

Furthermore, it is because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought that this second jhāna is serene, not because of the stilling of the turbidity of defilements. And it is because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought that there is unification of mind; not, as in access concentration, because of the abandoning of the hindrances, nor, as in the first jhāna, because of the manifestation of the factors. Thus, this phrase, ‘from the stilling of initial and sustained thought,’ illuminates the cause for serenity and unification of mind. Similarly, it is because of the stilling of initial and sustained thought that this jhāna is without initial thought and without sustained thought; it is not so because of their natural absence, as in the third and fourth jhānas or as in eye-consciousness and so on. Thus, this phrase also illuminates the cause for the state of being without initial and sustained thought, and does not merely illuminate their absence. This phrase, ‘without initial thought, without sustained thought,’ however, only illuminates the mere absence of initial and sustained thought. Therefore, even after stating the former, the latter should indeed be said.

Samādhijanti paṭhamajjhānasamādhito sampayuttasamādhito vā jātanti attho. Tattha kiñcāpi paṭhamampi sampayuttasamādhito jātaṃ, atha kho ayameva samādhi “samādhī”ti vattabbataṃ arahati vitakkavicārakkhobhavirahena ativiya acalattā, suppasannattā ca, tasmā imassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ idameva “samādhija”nti vuttaṃ. Pītisukhanti idaṃ vuttanayameva.

“Born of concentration” means born from the concentration of the first jhāna or from associated concentration. Although the first jhāna is also born from associated concentration, yet this concentration alone deserves to be called “concentration” because it is exceedingly steady due to the absence of agitation from initial and sustained thought, and because it is very serene. Therefore, to speak of its excellence, only this is called “born of concentration.” “Rapture and bliss”—this is just as has been explained.

Dutiyanti gaṇanānupubbatā dutiyaṃ. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ samāpajjatītipi dutiyaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “dvaṅgavippahīnaṃ tivaṅgasamannāgata”nti, tattha vitakkavicārānaṃ pahānavasena dvaṅgavippahīnatā veditabbā. Yathā ca paṭhamajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇe nīvaraṇāni pahīyanti, na tathā imassa vitakkavicārā. Appanākkhaṇeyeva ca panetaṃ vinā tehi uppajjati. Tenassa te “pahānaṅga”nti vuccanti. Pīti sukhaṃ cittekaggatāti imesaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ uppattivasena tivaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. Tasmā yaṃ vibhaṅge “jhānanti sampasādo pīti sukhaṃ cittassa ekaggatā”ti (vibha. 580) vuttaṃ, taṃ saparikkhāraṃ jhānaṃ dassetuṃ pariyāyena vuttaṃ. Ṭhapetvā pana sampasādanaṃ nippariyāyena upanijjhānalakkhaṇappattānaṃ aṅgānaṃ vasena tivaṅgikameva etaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye tivaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti, pīti sukhaṃ cittassa ekaggatā”ti (dha. sa. 161; vibha. 628). Sesaṃ paṭhamajjhāne vuttanayameva.

“Second”: by way of the sequence of counting, it is the second. It is also “second” because one attains this for a second time. As for what was stated, “with two factors abandoned, possessed of three factors,” therein, the state of having two factors abandoned should be understood by way of the abandoning of initial and sustained thought. And just as the hindrances are abandoned at the moment of access of the first jhāna, initial and sustained thought are not abandoned in the same way for this jhāna. However, this jhāna arises without them only at the moment of absorption. Therefore, they are called its “factors of abandonment.” The state of being possessed of three factors, however, should be understood by way of the arising of these three: rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind. Therefore, what is stated in the Vibhaṅga—“Jhāna is confidence, rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind”—is stated figuratively to show the jhāna together with its accessories. However, setting aside confidence, in the direct sense, by way of the factors that have reached the characteristic of close contemplation, this jhāna is only threefold. As it is said: “What at that time is the threefold jhāna? Rapture, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.” The rest is just as explained in the first jhāna.

Tatiyajjhānakathā

The Explanation of the Third Jhāna

82. Evamadhigate pana tasmimpi vuttanayeneva pañcahākārehi ciṇṇavasinā hutvā paguṇadutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ayaṃ samāpatti āsannavitakkavicārapaccatthikā, ‘yadeva tattha pītigataṃ cetaso uppilāvitaṃ, etenetaṃ [M 1.0154] oḷārikaṃ akkhāyatī’ti (dī. ni. 1.96) vuttāya pītiyā oḷārikattā aṅgadubbalā”ti ca tattha dosaṃ disvā tatiyajjhānaṃ santato manasikaritvā [V 1.0153] dutiyajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādāya tatiyādhigamāya yogo kātabbo. Athassa yadā dutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya satassa sampajānassa jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhato pīti oḷārikato upaṭṭhāti, sukhañceva ekaggatā ca santato upaṭṭhāti.
