Tadāssa oḷārikaṅgappahānāya santaaṅgapaṭilābhāya ca tadeva nimittaṃ “pathavī pathavī”ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto “idāni tatiyajjhānaṃ uppajjissatī”ti bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā tadeva pathavīkasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati. Tato tasmiṃyevārammaṇe cattāri pañca vā javanāni javanti, yesaṃ avasāne ekaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ tatiyajjhānikaṃ, sesāni vuttanayeneva kāmāvacarānīti. Ettāvatā ca panesa pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti, tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti (dī. ni. 1.230; dha. sa. 163). Evamanena ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ duvaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇaṃ.

82. Furthermore, when the second jhāna has been thus attained and one has become proficient in it through the fivefold method as previously described, one emerges from the proficient second jhāna and reflects: "This attainment has initial and sustained thought as its near enemies, and its factors are weak due to the grossness of the aforesaid rapture, of which it is said: ‘Whatever rapture of mind is present there, that is called gross’ (Dī. Ni. 1.96)." Seeing this fault therein, one should attend to the third jhāna as tranquil, exhaust attachment to the second jhāna, and make effort for the attainment of the third. Then, when one emerges from the second jhāna, mindful and clearly comprehending, and reviews the jhāna factors, rapture appears as gross, while pleasure and one-pointedness appear as tranquil. At that time, for the abandoning of the gross factor and the acquisition of the tranquil factors, one should repeatedly attend to that same sign, thinking, "Earth, earth." As one does so, at the point when it can be said, "Now the third jhāna will arise," the life-continuum is interrupted, and the mind-door adverting consciousness arises, taking that very earth kasiṇa as its object. Following this, four or five impulsions occur on that same object, the last of which is a single form-sphere impulsion belonging to the third jhāna, while the rest are sense-sphere impulsions as previously described. And by this much, with the fading away of rapture, one dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing pleasure with the body—that which the noble ones declare: 'equanimous, mindful, dwelling pleasantly'—thus entering and abiding in the third jhāna (Dī. Ni. 1.230; Dha. Sa. 163). In this way, the third jhāna of the earth kasiṇa, which is devoid of one factor, endowed with two factors, threefold in its excellence, and complete with ten characteristics, is attained by this person.

83. Tattha pītiyā ca virāgāti virāgo nāma vuttappakārāya pītiyā jigucchanaṃ vā samatikkamo vā. Ubhinnaṃ pana antarā casaddo sampiṇḍanattho, so vūpasamaṃ vā sampiṇḍeti vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamaṃ vā. Tattha yadā vūpasamameva sampiṇḍeti, tadā “pītiyā ca virāgā kiñca bhiyyo vūpasamā cā”ti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāya virāgo jigucchanattho hoti, tasmā “pītiyā jigucchanā ca vūpasamā cā”ti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo. Yadā pana vitakkavicāravūpasamaṃ sampiṇḍeti, tadā “pītiyā ca virāgā, kiñca bhiyyo vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā”ti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Imissā ca yojanāya virāgo samatikkamanattho hoti, tasmā “pītiyā ca samatikkamā vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā”ti ayamattho daṭṭhabbo.

83. Herein, in the phrase 'pītiyā ca virāgā' (and through the fading away of rapture), the term `virāga` means either disgust with or transcendence of rapture of the kind described. The particle `ca` between the two, however, has the meaning of combination; it combines either with 'quiescence' or with 'the quiescence of initial and sustained thought'. Therein, when it combines only with 'quiescence', the construction should be understood thus: 'and through the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, through its quiescence.' And in this construction, `virāga` has the meaning of disgust; therefore, the meaning should be seen as: 'through disgust with rapture and through its quiescence.' But when it combines with 'the quiescence of initial and sustained thought', the construction should be understood thus: 'and through the fading away of rapture, and furthermore, through the quiescence of initial and sustained thought.' And in this construction, `virāga` has the meaning of transcendence; therefore, the meaning should be seen as: 'through the transcendence of rapture and through the quiescence of initial and sustained thought.'

Kāmañcete vitakkavicārā dutiyajjhāneyeva vūpasantā, imassa pana jhānassa maggaparidīpanatthaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthañcetaṃ vuttaṃ. Vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamāti hi vutte idaṃ paññāyati, nūna vitakkavicāravūpasamo maggo imassa [M 1.0155] jhānassāti. Yathā ca tatiye ariyamagge appahīnānampi sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ “pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ pahānā”ti (dī. ni. 1.373; ma. ni. 2.133; saṃ. ni. 5.184; a. ni. 3.88) evaṃ [V 1.0154] pahānaṃ vuccamānaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti, tadadhigamāya ussukkānaṃ ussāhajanakaṃ, evameva idha avūpasantānampi vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamo vuccamāno vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ hoti. Tenāyamattho vutto “pītiyā ca samatikkamā vitakkavicārānañca vūpasamā”ti.

Although these initial and sustained thoughts have indeed ceased in the second jhāna, this is stated for this jhāna for the purpose of clarifying the path and for the purpose of praise. For when it is said, 'and the quiescence of initial and sustained thought,' this becomes apparent: 'Surely, the quiescence of initial and sustained thought is the path to this jhāna.' Just as in the case of the third noble path, the abandoning of the five lower fetters is spoken of—even though fetters such as identity view are not abandoned by it, having already been abandoned—which is a form of praise that generates enthusiasm in those striving for its attainment; even so here, speaking of the quiescence of initial and sustained thought—although they are not quelled in this jhāna—is a form of praise. Therefore, this meaning is stated: 'through the transcendence of rapture and through the quiescence of initial and sustained thought.'

84. Upekkhako ca viharatīti ettha upapattito ikkhatīti upekkhā. Samaṃ passati, apakkhapatitā hutvā passatīti attho. Tāya visadāya vipulāya thāmagatāya samannāgatattā tatiyajjhānasamaṅgī upekkhakoti vuccati.

84. Herein, regarding the phrase 'and he dwells equanimous,' it is called upekkhā because it looks on (ikkhati) fittingly (upapattito). The meaning is that it sees evenly (samaṃ passati); it sees having become impartial. Because one is endowed with that equanimity which is clear, extensive, and has attained steadfastness, one who is possessed of the third jhāna is called 'equanimous'.

Upekkhā pana dasavidhā hoti chaḷaṅgupekkhā, brahmavihārupekkhā, bojjhaṅgupekkhā, vīriyupekkhā, saṅkhārupekkhā, vedanupekkhā, vipassanupekkhā, tatramajjhattupekkhā, jhānupekkhā, pārisuddhupekkhāti.

Equanimity, however, is of ten kinds: six-factored equanimity, divine abiding equanimity, enlightenment factor equanimity, energy equanimity, formation equanimity, feeling equanimity, insight equanimity, equanimity as neutrality, jhāna equanimity, and purity equanimity.

Tattha yā “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti, na dummano, upekkhako ca viharati sato sampajāno”ti (a. ni. 6.1) evamāgatā khīṇāsavassa chasu dvāresu iṭṭhāniṭṭhachaḷārammaṇāpāthe parisuddhapakatibhāvāvijahanākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ chaḷaṅgupekkhā nāma.

Among these, the equanimity described as: "Here, monks, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither pleased nor displeased but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending"—this equanimity, which arises in the six sense-doors of one whose taints are destroyed, being characterized by not abandoning its pure natural state in the presence of the six kinds of desirable and undesirable objects, is called six-factored equanimity.

Yā pana “upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.556; ma. ni. 1.77) evamāgatā sattesu majjhattākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ brahmavihārupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: "With a mind accompanied by equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction"—this equanimity, which is characterized by neutrality towards beings, is called divine abiding equanimity.

Yā “upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissita”nti (ma. ni. 1.27) evamāgatā sahajātadhammānaṃ majjhattākārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ bojjhaṅgupekkhā nāma.

The equanimity described as: "He develops the equanimity enlightenment factor, which is based on seclusion"—this equanimity, which is characterized by neutrality towards co-arisen states, is called enlightenment factor equanimity.

Yā [M 1.0156] pana “kālenakālaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasikarotī”ti (a. ni. 3.103) evamāgatā anaccāraddhanātisithilavīriyasaṅkhātā upekkhā, ayaṃ vīriyupekkhā nāma.

That which is described as "from time to time directing attention to the sign of equanimity"—this equanimity, reckoned as energy that is neither too strenuous nor too slack, is called energy equanimity.

Yā “kati saṅkhārupekkhā samathavasena uppajjanti, kati saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjanti[V 1.0155]. Aṭṭha saṅkhārupekkhā samathavasena uppajjanti. Dasa saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanāvasena uppajjantī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.57) evamāgatā nīvaraṇādipaṭisaṅkhāsantiṭṭhanā gahaṇe majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā nāma.

That equanimity which is described thus: 'How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity? How many kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight? Eight kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of serenity. Ten kinds of equanimity regarding formations arise by way of insight' (Paṭis. M. 1.57)—this equanimity, which is well-established through contemplation of the hindrances and so forth and is neutral in grasping, is called equanimity regarding formations.

Yā pana “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti upekkhāsahagata”nti (dha. sa. 150) evamāgatā adukkhamasukhasaññitā upekkhā, ayaṃ vedanupekkhā nāma.

Furthermore, that equanimity which is described thus: 'At the time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen, accompanied by equanimity' (Dhs. 150), and is designated as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, this is called equanimity as feeling.

Yā “yadatthi yaṃ bhūtaṃ, taṃ pajahati, upekkhaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.71; a. ni. 7.55) evamāgatā vicinane majjhattabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ vipassanupekkhā nāma.

That equanimity which is described thus: 'Whatever exists, whatever has come to be, that one abandons and attains equanimity' (M. 3.71; A. 7.55), being neutral in investigation, this is called equanimity of insight.

Yā pana chandādīsu yevāpanakesu āgatā sahajātānaṃ samavāhitabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhā nāma.

Furthermore, that equanimity which is found among the miscellaneous factors such as desire, and which balances the co-nascent states, this is called specific neutrality.

Yā “upekkhako ca viharatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.230; dha. sa. 163) evamāgatā aggasukhepi tasmiṃ apakkhapātajananī upekkhā, ayaṃ jhānupekkhā nāma.

That equanimity which is described thus: 'And one dwells equanimous' (D. 1.75; Dhs. 163), which does not give rise to partiality even towards that supreme pleasure, this is called equanimity of jhāna.

Yā pana “upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.232; dha. sa. 165) evamāgatā sabbapaccanīkaparisuddhā paccanīkavūpasamanepi abyāpārabhūtā upekkhā, ayaṃ pārisuddhupekkhā nāma.

Furthermore, that equanimity which is described thus: 'The fourth jhāna, which has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity' (D. 1.75; Dhs. 167), which is purified of all opposing factors and is without exertion even in the pacification of opposing factors, this is called equanimity of purity.

Tatra chaḷaṅgupekkhā ca brahmavihārupekkhā ca bojjhaṅgupekkhā ca tatramajjhattupekkhā ca jhānupekkhā ca pārisuddhupekkhā ca atthato ekā, tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti. Tena tena avatthābhedena panassā ayaṃ bhedo. Ekassāpi sato sattassa kumārayuvatherasenāpatirājādivasena bhedo viya. Tasmā tāsu yattha chaḷaṅgupekkhā, na tattha bojjhaṅgupekkhādayo. Yattha vā pana bojjhaṅgupekkhā, na tattha chaḷaṅgupekkhādayo hontīti veditabbā.

Among these, six-limbed equanimity, equanimity of the divine abidings, equanimity as an enlightenment factor, specific neutrality, equanimity of jhāna, and equanimity of purity are one in essence; they are simply specific neutrality. However, this distinction arises for it due to this or that difference in state, just as for one and the same being there is the distinction by way of being a boy, a youth, an elder, a general, or a king. Therefore, among them, it should be understood that where there is six-limbed equanimity, equanimity as an enlightenment factor and the others are not present; or where there is equanimity as an enlightenment factor, six-limbed equanimity and the others are not present.

Yathā [M 1.0157] cetāsamatthato ekībhāvo, evaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā vipassanupekkhānampi. Paññā eva hi sā kiccavasena dvidhā bhinnā. Yathā hi purisassa sāyaṃ gehaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ sappaṃ ajapadadaṇḍaṃ gahetvā [V 1.0156] pariyesamānassa taṃ thusakoṭṭhake nipannaṃ disvā “sappo nu kho, no”ti avalokentassa sovattikattayaṃ disvā nibbematikassa “sappo, na sappo”ti vicinane majjhattatā hoti, evameva yā āraddhavipassakassa vipassanāñāṇena lakkhaṇattaye diṭṭhe saṅkhārānaṃ aniccabhāvādivicinane majjhattatā uppajjati, ayaṃ vipassanupekkhā nāma. Yathā pana tassa purisassa ajapadadaṇḍena gāḷhaṃ sappaṃ gahetvā “kiṃ tāhaṃ imaṃ sappaṃ aviheṭhento attānañca iminā aḍaṃsāpento muñceyya”nti muñcanākārameva pariyesato gahaṇe majjhattatā hoti. Evameva yā lakkhaṇattayassa diṭṭhattā āditte viya tayo bhave passato saṅkhāraggahaṇe majjhattatā, ayaṃ saṅkhārupekkhā nāma. Iti vipassanupekkhāya siddhāya saṅkhārupekkhāpi siddhāva hoti. Iminā panesā vicinanaggahaṇesu majjhattasaṅkhātena kiccena dvidhā bhinnāti. Vīriyupekkhā pana vedanupekkhā ca aññamaññañca avasesāhi ca atthato bhinnā evāti.

Just as these are one in essence, so too are equanimity regarding formations and equanimity of insight. For it is wisdom itself that is divided into two by way of function. It is as when a man, searching for a snake that entered his house in the evening, takes a forked staff and, seeing it lying in a chaff-bin, looks on thinking, 'Is this a snake or not?' Upon seeing its three hood-markings and becoming free of doubt, he has neutrality in investigating 'Is it a snake or not?' In the same way, for a practitioner who has begun insight, when the three characteristics have been seen with the knowledge of insight, the neutrality that arises in investigating the impermanent nature of formations is called equanimity of insight. Furthermore, it is as when that man, having firmly pinned the snake with the forked staff, seeks only a way to release it, thinking, 'How can I release this snake without harming it, and without being bitten by it?' In this, there is neutrality in the act of grasping. In the same way, because the three characteristics have been seen, for one who sees the three realms of existence as if ablaze, the neutrality in grasping at formations is called equanimity regarding formations. Thus, when equanimity of insight is accomplished, equanimity regarding formations is also accomplished. Yet this wisdom is divided in two by this function, which is designated as neutrality in investigation and in grasping. As for equanimity of energy and equanimity as feeling, they are distinct in essence both from each other and from the remaining eight.

Iti imāsu upekkhāsu jhānupekkhā idhādhippetā. Sā majjhattalakkhaṇā, anābhogarasā, abyāpārapaccupaṭṭhānā, pītivirāgapadaṭṭhānāti. Etthāha, nanu cāyamatthato tatramajjhattupekkhāva hoti, sā ca paṭhamadutiyajjhānesupi atthi. Tasmā tatrāpi upekkhako ca viharatīti evamayaṃ vattabbā siyā, sā kasmā na vuttāti. Aparibyattakiccato. Aparibyattañhi tassā tattha kiccaṃ vitakkādīhi abhibhūtattā. Idha panāyaṃ vitakkavicārapītīhi anabhibhūtattā ukkhittasirā viya hutvā paribyattakiccā jātā, tasmā vuttāti.

Thus, among these kinds of equanimity, it is the equanimity of jhāna that is intended here. It has the characteristic of neutrality, the function of non-application, the manifestation of non-exertion, and its proximate cause is dispassion for rapture. Here it is asked: 'Is this not, in essence, simply specific neutrality, which also exists in the first and second jhānas? Therefore, in those states too, it should be said, "and one dwells equanimous." Why is this not stated?' Because its function is not manifest. For in those states its function is not manifest, since it is overwhelmed by initial application and so on. But here, not being overwhelmed by initial application, sustained application, and rapture, it becomes like one with head held high, and its function becomes manifest; therefore, it is stated.

Niṭṭhitā upekkhako ca viharatīti etassa

The commentary on 'and one dwells equanimous' is concluded.

Sabbaso atthavaṇṇanā.

The explanation of the meaning in its entirety.

85. Idāni sato ca sampajānoti ettha saratīti sato. Sampajānātīti sampajāno. Puggalena sati ca sampajaññañca vuttaṃ. Tattha saraṇalakkhaṇā sati, asammussanarasā, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā. Asammohalakkhaṇaṃ sampajaññaṃ, tīraṇarasaṃ, pavicayapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

85. Now, regarding 'mindful and clearly comprehending': one is 'mindful' (sato) because one remembers (sarati). One is 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāno) because one comprehends clearly (sampajānāti). Thus, mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña) are spoken of by way of the person. Therein, mindfulness has the characteristic of remembering, its function is not-forgetting, and its manifestation is guarding. Clear comprehension has the characteristic of non-delusion, its function is judgment, and its manifestation is investigation.

Tattha [M 1.0158] kiñcāpi idaṃ satisampajaññaṃ purimajjhānesupi atthi. Muṭṭhasatissa hi asampajānassa upacāramattampi na sampajjati, pageva appanā. Oḷārikattā pana tesaṃ jhānānaṃ bhūmiyaṃ viya purisassa cittassa gati sukhā hoti, abyattaṃ tattha satisampajaññakiccaṃ. Oḷārikaṅgappahānena pana sukhumattā imassa jhānassa purisassa khuradhārāyaṃ viya satisampajaññakiccapariggahitā [V 1.0157] eva cittassa gati icchitabbāti idheva vuttaṃ. Kiñca bhiyyo, yathā dhenupago vaccho dhenuto apanīto arakkhiyamāno punadeva dhenuṃ upagacchati, evamidaṃ tatiyajjhānasukhaṃ pītito apanītaṃ, taṃ satisampajaññārakkhena arakkhiyamānaṃ punadeva pītiṃ upagaccheyya, pītisampayuttameva siyā. Sukhe vāpi sattā sārajjanti, idañca atimadhuraṃ sukhaṃ, tato paraṃ sukhābhāvā. Satisampajaññānubhāvena panettha sukhe asārajjanā hoti, no aññathāti imampi atthavisesaṃ dassetuṃ idamidheva vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Herein, although this mindfulness and clear comprehension exist even in the preceding jhānas, indeed, for one with lapsed mindfulness and without clear comprehension, not even access concentration is accomplished, let alone absorption. However, due to the grossness of those jhānas, the movement of the mind is easy, like that of a person on the ground, and the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension is not manifest there. But, due to the abandoning of the gross factors and the subtlety of this jhāna, the movement of the mind should be desired as being solely grasped by the function of mindfulness and clear comprehension, like that of a person on a razor's edge; therefore, this was stated right here. Furthermore, just as a suckling calf, removed from its mother cow and left unguarded, approaches the mother cow once again, so too this happiness of the third jhāna is removed from rapture. If it is left unguarded by the protection of mindfulness and clear comprehension, it would approach rapture once again; it would become conjoined with rapture. Moreover, beings become attached to happiness, and this happiness is exceedingly sweet, for there is no happiness beyond it. Through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension, there is non-attachment to this happiness here, and not otherwise. It should be known that this was stated right here in order to show this special meaning as well.

Idāni sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti ettha kiñcāpi tatiyajjhānasamaṅgino sukhapaṭisaṃvedanābhogo natthi. Evaṃ santepi yasmā tassa nāmakāyena sampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ. Yaṃ vā taṃ nāmakāyasampayuttaṃ sukhaṃ, taṃsamuṭṭhānenassa yasmā atipaṇītena rūpena rūpakāyo phuṭo, yassa phuṭattā jhānā vuṭṭhitopi sukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedeyya. Tasmā etamatthaṃ dassento sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedetīti āha.

Now, regarding the statement 'and he experiences happiness with the body': although one endowed with the third jhāna has no intention to experience happiness, even so, there is happiness associated with his mental body. Or, because of that happiness associated with the mental body, his physical body is pervaded by extremely subtle matter arisen therefrom; due to which pervasion, even having emerged from the jhāna, he would experience happiness. Therefore, showing this meaning, He said, 'and he experiences happiness with the body'.

86. Idāni yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti ettha yaṃjhānahetu yaṃjhānakāraṇā taṃ tatiyajjhānasamaṅgipuggalaṃ buddhādayo ariyā ācikkhanti desenti paññapenti paṭṭhapenti vivaranti vibhajanti uttānīkaronti pakāsenti, pasaṃsantīti adhippāyo. Kinti? Upekkhako satimā sukhavihārīti. Taṃ tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatīti evamettha yojanā veditabbā.

86. Now, regarding the passage 'That which the noble ones declare: “He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous”': here, the intention is that on account of that jhāna, the noble ones, beginning with the Buddhas, declare, teach, make known, establish, disclose, analyze, make plain, reveal, and praise that person endowed with the third jhāna. How so? As 'equanimous, mindful, a dweller in happiness.' The construction here should be understood thus: 'Having attained that third jhāna, one dwells.'

Kasmā pana taṃ te evaṃ pasaṃsantīti? Pasaṃsārahato. Ayañhi yasmā atimadhurasukhe sukhapāramippattepi tatiyajjhāne upekkhako, na tattha sukhābhisaṅgena ākaḍḍhiyati. Yathā ca pīti na uppajjati, evaṃ upaṭṭhitasatitāya satimā. Yasmā ca ariyakantaṃ ariyajanasevitameva ca asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ nāmakāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, tasmā pasaṃsāraho hoti[M 1.0159]. Iti pasaṃsārahato naṃ ariyā te evaṃ pasaṃsāhetubhūte guṇe pakāsento “upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī”ti evaṃ pasaṃsantīti veditabbaṃ.

But why do they praise him thus? Because he is worthy of praise. For this person, being equanimous even in the third jhāna with its exceedingly sweet happiness that has reached the pinnacle of happiness, is not drawn by attachment to that happiness. And he is mindful, with mindfulness so well-established that rapture does not arise. Furthermore, because he experiences with the mental body the undefiled happiness that is pleasing to the noble ones and frequented only by noble persons, he is therefore worthy of praise. Thus, it should be understood that because he is worthy of praise, the noble ones praise him in this way, revealing the qualities that are the cause for praise: 'equanimous, mindful, a dweller in happiness.'

Tatiyanti gaṇanānupubbatā tatiyaṃ, idaṃ tatiyaṃ samāpajjatītipi tatiyaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ duvaṅgasamannāgata”nti, ettha pītiyā pahānavasena ekaṅgavippahīnatā veditabbā[V 1.0158]. Sā panesā dutiyajjhānassa vitakkavicārā viya appanākkhaṇeyeva pahīyati. Tena nassa sā pahānaṅganti vuccati. Sukhaṃ cittekaggatāti imesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ uppattivasena duvaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. Tasmā yaṃ vibhaṅge “jhānanti upekkhā sati sampajaññaṃ sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti (vibha. 591) vuttaṃ, taṃ saparikkhāraṃ jhānaṃ dassetuṃ pariyāyena vuttaṃ. Ṭhapetvā pana upekkhāsatisampajaññāni nippariyāyena upanijjhānalakkhaṇappattānaṃ aṅgānaṃ vasena duvaṅgikamevetaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “katamaṃ tasmiṃ samaye duvaṅgikaṃ jhānaṃ hoti, sukhaṃ cittassekaggatā”ti (dha. sa. 163; vibha. 624). Sesaṃ paṭhamajjhāne vuttanayameva.

It is the third by sequence of counting; it is also the third because one attains this as the third. As for what was said, 'having abandoned one factor, it is endowed with two factors,' here the state of having abandoned one factor is to be understood by way of abandoning rapture. But this rapture is abandoned at the very moment of absorption, just as applied and sustained thought are for the second jhāna. Therefore, it is called the factor to be abandoned for this jhāna. The endowment with two factors is to be understood by way of the arising of these two: happiness and one-pointedness of mind. Therefore, what was stated in the Vibhaṅga—'jhāna is equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind'—was said indirectly to show the jhāna with its accessories. But setting aside equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, in the direct sense, by way of the factors that have attained the characteristic of close contemplation, this jhāna is indeed two-factored. As it is said: 'What at that time is the two-factored jhāna? Happiness and one-pointedness of mind.' The rest is just as was explained in the section on the first jhāna.

Catutthajjhānakathā

Exposition of the Fourth Jhāna

87. Evamadhigate pana tasmiṃpi vuttanayeneva pañcahākārehi ciṇṇavasinā hutvā paguṇatatiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ayaṃ samāpatti āsannapītipaccatthikā, ‘yadeva tattha sukhamiti cetaso ābhogo, etenetaṃ oḷārikaṃ akkhāyatī’ti (dī. ni. 1.96) evaṃ vuttassa sukhassa oḷārikattā aṅgadubbalā”ti ca tattha dosaṃ disvā catutthaṃ jhānaṃ santato manasikatvā tatiyajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādāya catutthādhigamāya yogo kātabbo. Athassa yadā tatiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya satassa sampajānassa jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhato cetasikasomanassasaṅkhātaṃ sukhaṃ oḷārikato upaṭṭhāti, upekkhāvedanā ceva cittekaggatā ca santato upaṭṭhāti, tadāssa oḷārikaṅgappahānāya santaaṅgapaṭilābhāya ca tadeva nimittaṃ “pathavī pathavī”ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto “idāni catutthaṃ jhānaṃ uppajjissatī”ti bhavaṅgaṃ upacchinditvā tadeva pathavīkasiṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā manodvārāvajjanaṃ uppajjati. Tato tasmiṃyevārammaṇe cattāri pañca vā javanāni uppajjanti[M 1.0160], yesaṃ avasāne ekaṃ rūpāvacaraṃ catutthajjhānikaṃ, sesāni vuttappakārāneva kāmāvacarāni. Ayaṃ pana viseso, yasmā sukhavedanā adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya āsevanapaccayena paccayo na hoti, catutthajjhāne ca adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya uppajjitabbaṃ, tasmā tāni upekkhāvedanāsampayuttāni honti. Upekkhāsampayuttattāyeva cettha pītipi parihāyatīti. Ettāvatā cesa sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati (dī. ni. 1.232; dha. sa. 165). Evamanena ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ duvaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ adhigataṃ hoti pathavīkasiṇaṃ.

87. Furthermore, when that third jhāna has also been attained, and having become skilled in the five ways as previously described, emerging from the proficient third jhāna, one sees the fault in it thus: “This attainment has rapture as its near enemy; and, because of the grossness of the happiness spoken of thus, ‘Whatever happiness is there in it is an advertence of the mind; by this it is called gross,’ its factors are weak.” Having seen this fault, having attended to the fourth jhāna as peaceful, and having overcome delight in the third jhāna, effort should be made to attain the fourth. Then, for one who has emerged from the third jhāna, who is mindful and clearly comprehending, and who is reviewing the jhāna factors, happiness appears as gross, while the feeling of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind appear as peaceful. At that time, for the abandoning of the gross factor and for the acquisition of the peaceful factors, as one repeatedly attends to that same sign as “earth, earth,” the mind-door adverting arises, having interrupted the life-continuum and having taken that very earth kasiṇa as its object, with the thought “Now the fourth jhāna will arise.” Following that, four or five impulsions arise on that very same object, at the end of which one is a fourth-jhāna impulsion of the fine-material sphere, while the rest are sense-sphere impulsions of the kind already described. This, however, is the difference: since pleasant feeling is not a condition for neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling by way of repetition condition, and since a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling must arise in the fourth jhāna, therefore those impulsions are associated with the feeling of equanimity. And it is because of being associated with equanimity that rapture also disappears here. By this much, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, one enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and is the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. Thus, by this yogī, the fourth jhāna on the earth kasiṇa is attained, which is abandoned in one factor, endowed with two factors, threefold in excellence, and possessed of ten characteristics.

88. Tattha [V 1.0159] sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānāti kāyikasukhassa ca kāyikadukkhassa ca pahānā. Pubbevāti tañca kho pubbeva, na catutthajjhānakkhaṇe. Somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cetasikasukhassa ca cetasikadukkhassa cāti imesampi dvinnaṃ pubbeva atthaṅgamā, pahānā icceva vuttaṃ hoti.

88. Herein, “by the abandoning of pleasure and by the abandoning of pain” means by the abandoning of bodily pleasure and bodily pain. And “previously” means that this occurs indeed previously, not at the moment of the fourth jhāna. “With the disappearance of joy and sorrow” means that because of the disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain—that is, of these two—indeed previously, it is thus stated as “by the abandoning.”

Kadā pana nesaṃ pahānaṃ hotīti. Catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇe. Somanassañhi catutthajjhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyati. Dukkhadomanassasukhāni paṭhamadutiyatatiyajjhānānaṃ upacārakkhaṇesu. Evametesaṃ pahānakkamena avuttānampi indriyavibhaṅge pana indriyānaṃ uddesakkameneva idhāpi vuttānaṃ sukhadukkhasomanassadomanassānaṃ pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ.

But when does their abandoning occur? At the access moment of the four jhānas. For joy is abandoned at the access moment of the fourth jhāna itself. Pain, displeasure, and pleasure are abandoned at the access moments of the first, second, and third jhānas respectively. Thus, even though the order of abandoning these has not been stated, the abandoning of pleasure, pain, joy, and displeasure, which are mentioned here, should be understood according to the order of exposition of the faculties in the Analysis of the Faculties.

Yadi panetāni tassa tassa jhānassa upacārakkhaṇeyeva pahīyanti, atha kasmā “kattha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati, idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehipi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ettha cuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati. Kattha cuppannaṃ domanassindriyaṃ sukhindriyaṃ somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhati, idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati, ettha cuppannaṃ somanassindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.510) evaṃ jhānesveva nirodho vuttoti? Atisayanirodhattā. Atisayanirodho hi nesaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīsu, na nirodhoyeva. Nirodhoyeva pana upacārakkhaṇe, nātisayanirodho.

If, however, these are abandoned only at the access moment of their respective jhānas, then why is it said: “And where does the arisen faculty of pain cease without remainder? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, secluded from sensual pleasures… enters and dwells in the first jhāna. It is here that the arisen faculty of pain ceases without remainder. And where do the arisen faculty of displeasure, faculty of pleasure, and faculty of joy cease without remainder? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. It is here that the arisen faculty of joy ceases without remainder”? Thus, why is their cessation spoken of as being in the jhānas themselves? It is because of the surpassing cessation. For their surpassing cessation occurs in the first jhāna and so on, not merely cessation. Mere cessation, however, occurs at the access moment, not surpassing cessation.

Tathā [M 1.0161] hi nānāvajjane paṭhamajjhānupacāre niruddhassāpi dukkhindriyassa ḍaṃsamakasādisamphassena vā visamāsanupatāpena vā siyā uppatti, na tveva antoappanāyaṃ. Upacāre vā niruddhampetaṃ na suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti, paṭipakkhena avihatattā. Antoappanāyaṃ pana pītipharaṇena sabbo kāyo sukhokkanto hoti, sukhokkantakāyassa ca suṭṭhu niruddhaṃ hoti dukkhindriyaṃ, paṭipakkhena vihatattā. Nānāvajjaneyeva ca dutiyajjhānupacāre pahīnassa domanassindriyassa yasmā etaṃ vitakkavicārapaccayepi kāyakilamathe cittupaghāte ca sati uppajjati. Vitakkavicārābhāve ca neva uppajjati. Yattha pana uppajjati, tattha vitakkavicārabhāve, appahīnā eva ca dutiyajjhānupacāre vitakkavicārāti tatthassa siyā uppatti, na tveva dutiyajjhāne, pahīnapaccayattā. Tathā tatiyajjhānupacāre pahīnassāpi sukhindriyassa pītisamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpaphuṭakāyassa [V 1.0160] siyā uppatti, na tveva tatiyajjhāne. Tatiyajjhāne hi sukhassa paccayabhūtā pīti sabbaso niruddhāti. Tathā catutthajjhānupacāre pahīnassāpi somanassindriyassa āsannattā appanāppattāya upekkhāya abhāvena sammā anatikkantattā ca siyā uppatti, na tveva catutthajjhāne. Tasmā eva ca etthuppannaṃ dukkhindriyaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjhatīti tattha tattha aparisesaggahaṇaṃ katanti.

For in the access concentration of the first jhāna, which has various advertings, even though the faculty of pain has ceased, it may arise due to contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or due to the discomfort of an uneven seat—but not within absorption. Or, even if it has ceased in the access stage, it is not thoroughly ceased, because it has not been overcome by its opponent. Within absorption, however, the whole body is suffused with pleasure by the pervasion of rapture, and for one whose body is suffused with pleasure, the faculty of pain is thoroughly ceased, because it has been overcome by its opponent. And in the access concentration of the second jhāna, which has various advertings, though the faculty of displeasure has been abandoned, it may arise; for this faculty arises when there is bodily fatigue and mental affliction, which are conditioned by initial and sustained thought. And when initial and sustained thought are absent, it does not arise at all. But where it arises, there initial and sustained thought are present; and in the access of the second jhāna, initial and sustained thought are not abandoned. Therefore, it may arise there—but not in the second jhāna itself, because its conditions have been abandoned. Likewise, in the access of the third jhāna, even though the faculty of pleasure has been abandoned, it may arise for one whose body is pervaded by refined matter born of rapture—but not in the third jhāna itself. For in the third jhāna, rapture, which is the condition for pleasure, has completely ceased. Similarly, in the access of the fourth jhāna, even though the faculty of joy has been abandoned, it may arise due to its nearness, the absence of equanimity that has reached absorption, and its not having been thoroughly overcome—but not in the fourth jhāna itself. And for this very reason, in those respective places, the inclusion of 'without remainder' is made in the statement, 'The faculty of pain that has arisen here... ceases without remainder'.

Etthāha “athevaṃ tassa tassa jhānassupacāre pahīnāpi etā vedanā idha kasmā samāhaṭā”ti? Sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ. Yā hi ayaṃ adukkhamasukhanti ettha adukkhamasukhā vedanā vuttā, sā sukhumā duviññeyyā na sakkā sukhena gahetuṃ, tasmā yathā nāma duṭṭhassa yathā vā tathā vā upasaṅkamitvā gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyassa goṇassa sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ gopo ekasmiṃ vaje sabbā gāvo samāharati, athekekaṃ nīharanto paṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ “ayaṃ so gaṇhatha na”nti tampi gāhayati, evameva bhagavā sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ sabbā etā samāhari. Evañhi samāhaṭā etā dassetvā yaṃ neva sukhaṃ na dukkhaṃ na somanassaṃ na domanassaṃ, ayaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanāti sakkā hoti esā gāhayituṃ.

Here it is said: “If so, these feelings being abandoned even in the access of each respective jhāna, why are they gathered together here?” For the sake of easy grasping. Indeed, this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, which is spoken of in the phrase ‘neither-painful-nor-pleasant,’ is subtle and difficult to discern; it cannot be easily grasped. Therefore, just as a cowherd, for the sake of easily catching an unruly bull that cannot be caught by approaching it in any which way, gathers all the cows into one enclosure, and then, while leading them out one by one, when the one he wants comes along in its turn, he has it caught, saying, “This is that one, catch it!”; in this very way, the Blessed One gathered all these feelings for the sake of easy grasping. For, having shown these feelings thus gathered, it is possible to make one grasp: “That which is neither pleasure nor pain, nor joy nor displeasure, this is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”

Apica adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā paccayadassanatthañcāpi etā vuttāti veditabbā. Dukkhappahānādayo hi tassā paccayā. Yathāha – “cattāro [M 1.0162] kho, āvuso, paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ime khvāvuso, cattāro paccayā adukkhamasukhāya cetovimuttiyā samāpattiyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.458).

Furthermore, it should be understood that these are also stated for the purpose of showing the conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. For the abandoning of pain and so on are its conditions. As it was said: “Friends, there are indeed four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind. Here, friends, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure… enters and abides in the fourth jhāna. These, friends, are indeed the four conditions for the attainment of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant liberation of mind.”

Yathā vā aññattha pahīnāpi sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo tatiyamaggassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ tattha pahīnāti vuttā, evaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthampetassa jhānassetā idha vuttātipi veditabbā.

Or, just as elsewhere self-identity view and so on, though already abandoned, are said to be abandoned there for the purpose of extolling the third path, so too, it should be understood that these feelings are stated here for the purpose of extolling this jhāna.

Paccayaghātena vā ettha rāgadosānamatidūrabhāvaṃ dassetumpetā vuttāti veditabbā. Etāsu hi sukhaṃ somanassassa paccayo, somanassaṃ rāgassa. Dukkhaṃ domanassassa paccayo, domanassaṃ dosassa. Sukhādighātena cassa sappaccayā rāgadosā hatāti atidūre hontīti.

Or, it should be understood that these are stated here to show the extreme distance of lust and hatred through the destruction of their conditions. For among these, pleasure is a condition for joy, and joy is a condition for lust. Pain is a condition for displeasure, and displeasure is a condition for hatred. And by the destruction of pleasure and so on, its lust and hatred, together with their conditions, are destroyed—thus, they become extremely distant.

Adukkhamasukhanti dukkhābhāvena adukkhaṃ. Sukhābhāvena asukhaṃ. Etenettha dukkhasukhapaṭipakkhabhūtaṃ tatiyavedanaṃ dīpeti, na dukkhasukhābhāvamattaṃ. Tatiyavedanā nāma adukkhamasukhā[V 1.0161], upekkhātipi vuccati. Sā iṭṭhāniṭṭhaviparītānubhavanalakkhaṇā, majjhattarasā, avibhūtapaccupaṭṭhānā, sukhadukkhanirodhapadaṭṭhānāti veditabbā.

Neither-painful-nor-pleasant means not painful due to the absence of pain, and not pleasant due to the absence of pleasure. By this, it indicates the third feeling, which is the opposite of pain and pleasure, not merely the absence of pain and pleasure. The third feeling is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and is also termed equanimity. It should be understood as having the characteristic of experiencing what is contrary to the desirable and undesirable, having the function of neutrality, having an indistinct manifestation, and having the cessation of pleasure and pain as its proximate cause.

89. Upekkhāsatipārisuddhinti upekkhāya janitasatiyā pārisuddhiṃ. Imasmiñhi jhāne suparisuddhā sati, yā ca tassā satiyā pārisuddhi, sā upekkhāya katā, na aññena. Tasmā etaṃ “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti vuccati. Vibhaṅgepi vuttaṃ “ayaṃ sati imāya upekkhāya visadā hoti parisuddhā pariyodātā. Tena vuccati upekkhāsatipārisuddhī”ti (vibha. 597). Yāya ca upekkhāya ettha satiyā pārisuddhi hoti, sā atthato tatramajjhattatātiveditabbā. Na kevalañcettha tāya satiyeva parisuddhā, apica kho sabbepi sampayuttadhammā, satisīsena pana desanā vuttā.

89. “Purity of mindfulness due to equanimity”: For in this jhāna, mindfulness is very pure, and the purity of that mindfulness is accomplished by equanimity, not by anything else. Therefore, this is called “purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.” In the Vibhaṅga it is also said: “This mindfulness becomes clear, purified, and bright through this equanimity. Hence, it is called ‘purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.’” The equanimity by which the purity of mindfulness is effected here should be understood as, in essence, neutrality. And not only is mindfulness purified here by it, but indeed all associated states are as well; however, the teaching is given with mindfulness as the principal factor.

Tattha kiñcāpi ayaṃ upekkhā heṭṭhāpi tīsu jhānesu vijjati. Yathā pana divā sūriyappabhābhibhavā sommabhāvena ca attano upakārakattena vā [M 1.0163] sabhāgāya rattiyā alābhā divā vijjamānāpi candalekhā aparisuddhā hoti apariyodātā, evamayampi tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā appaṭilābhā vijjamānāpi paṭhamādijjhānabhedesu aparisuddhā hoti. Tassā ca aparisuddhāya divā aparisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo aparisuddhāva honti. Tasmā tesu ekampi “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti na vuttaṃ. Idha pana vitakkādipaccanīkadhammatejābhibhavābhāvā sabhāgāya ca upekkhāvedanārattiyā paṭilābhā ayaṃ tatramajjhattupekkhācandalekhā ativiya parisuddhā. Tassā parisuddhattā parisuddhacandalekhāya pabhā viya sahajātāpi satiādayo parisuddhā honti pariyodātā. Tasmā idameva “upekkhāsatipārisuddhi”nti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Among these, although this equanimity also exists in the three lower jhānas, just as the crescent moon, though present during the day, is not pure or bright because it is overpowered by the sun’s radiance and because it lacks its kindred night, which is gentle and beneficial to it—so too, this crescent moon of equanimity that is specific neutrality, though present in the various lower jhānas beginning with the first, is not pure, because it is overpowered by the force of opposing states such as applied thought, and because it does not obtain its kindred night of equanimity-feeling. And due to its impurity, like the radiance of an impure crescent moon during the day, the co-arisen states such as mindfulness are also impure. Therefore, not one of those jhānas is called 'the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.' Here, however, due to the absence of being overpowered by the force of opposing states such as applied thought, and due to obtaining its kindred night of equanimity-feeling, this crescent moon of equanimity that is specific neutrality becomes exceedingly pure. Due to its purity, like the radiance of a pure crescent moon, the co-arisen states such as mindfulness also become pure and bright. Therefore, it should be understood that only this jhāna is called 'the purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.'

Catutthanti gaṇanānupubbatā catutthaṃ. Idaṃ catutthaṃ samāpajjatītipi catutthaṃ. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “ekaṅgavippahīnaṃ duvaṅgasamannāgata”nti, tattha somanassassa pahānavasena ekaṅgavippahīnatā veditabbā. Tañca pana somanassaṃ ekavīthiyaṃ purimajavanesuyeva pahīyati. Tenassa taṃ pahānaṅganti vuccati. Upekkhāvedanā cittassekaggatāti imesaṃ pana dvinnaṃ uppattivasena duvaṅgasamannāgatatā veditabbā. Sesaṃ paṭhamajjhāne vuttanayameva. Esa tāva catukkajjhāne nayo.

'Fourth' means the fourth in numerical sequence. It is also called 'fourth' because one attains this as the fourth. As for what was said, 'with one factor abandoned and possessing two factors,' the abandonment of one factor should be understood as the abandonment of joy. And that joy is abandoned in the earlier javanas of a single cognitive process; therefore, that is called its factor of abandonment. The possession of two factors should be understood by way of the arising of these two: equanimous feeling and one-pointedness of mind. The rest is as explained in the first jhāna. This, for now, is the method in the fourfold jhāna system.

Pañcakajjhānakathā

Discourse on the Fivefold Jhāna

90. Pañcakajjhānaṃ [V 1.0162] pana nibbattentena paguṇapaṭhamajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ayaṃ samāpatti āsannanīvaraṇapaccatthikā, vitakkassa oḷārikattā aṅgadubbalā”ti ca tattha dosaṃ disvā dutiyajjhānaṃ santato manasikaritvā paṭhamajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādāya dutiyādhigamāya yogo kātabbo. Athassa yadā paṭhamajjhānā vuṭṭhāya satassa sampajānassa jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhato vitakkamattaṃ oḷārikato upaṭṭhāti, vicārādayo santato. Tadāssa oḷārikaṅgappahānāya santaṅgapaṭilābhāya ca tadeva nimittaṃ “pathavī pathavī”ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto vuttanayeneva dutiyajjhānaṃ uppajjati. Tassa vitakkamattameva pahānaṅgaṃ. Vicārādīni cattāri samannāgataṅgāni. Sesaṃ vuttappakārameva.

90. Furthermore, one who would produce the fivefold jhānas, having emerged from the proficient first jhāna, and having seen the fault in it thus: “This attainment has the near enemy of the hindrances, and because of the coarseness of applied thought, its factors are weak,” should attend to the second jhāna as peaceful, overcome delight in the first jhāna, and make an effort for the attainment of the second. Then, when, having emerged from the first jhāna, while being mindful and clearly comprehending, one reviews the jhāna factors, only applied thought presents itself as coarse, while sustained thought and the other factors present themselves as peaceful. At that time, for that yogi who, for the sake of abandoning the coarse factor and attaining the peaceful factors, repeatedly attends to that very sign as “earth, earth,” the second jhāna arises in the very manner already described. Its abandoned factor is only applied thought. The four factors, sustained thought and the others, are the associated factors. The rest is just as has been described.

Evamadhigate [M 1.0164] pana tasmimpi vuttanayeneva pañcahākārehi ciṇṇavasinā hutvā paguṇadutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ayaṃ samāpatti āsannavitakkapaccatthikā, vicārassa oḷārikattā aṅgadubbalā”ti ca tattha dosaṃ disvā tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ santato manasikaritvā dutiyajjhāne nikantiṃ pariyādāya tatiyādhigamāya yogo kātabbo. Athassa yadā dutiyajjhānato vuṭṭhāya satassa sampajānassa jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhato vicāramattaṃ oḷārikato upaṭṭhāti, pītiādīni santato. Tadāssa oḷārikaṅgappahānāya santaṅgapaṭilābhāya ca tadeva nimittaṃ “pathavī pathavī”ti punappunaṃ manasikaroto vuttanayeneva tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ uppajjati. Tassa vicāramattameva pahānaṅgaṃ catukkanayassa dutiyajjhāne viya pītiādīni tīṇi samannāgataṅgāni. Sesaṃ vuttappakārameva.

Furthermore, even when that jhāna has been attained, having become one who has gained mastery through practice in the five ways in the very manner described, and having emerged from the proficient second jhāna, one sees the fault in it thus: “This attainment has the near enemy of applied thought, and because of the coarseness of sustained thought, its factors are weak.” Then, having attended to the third jhāna as peaceful, and having overcome delight in the second jhāna, effort should be made for the attainment of the third. Then, when, having emerged from the second jhāna, while being mindful and clearly comprehending, one reviews the jhāna factors, only sustained thought presents itself as coarse, while rapture and the other factors present themselves as peaceful. At that time, for that yogi who, for the sake of abandoning the coarse factor and attaining the peaceful factors, repeatedly attends to that very sign as “earth, earth,” the third jhāna arises in the very manner described. Its abandoned factor is only sustained thought. Just as in the second jhāna of the fourfold method, the three factors, rapture and the others, are the associated factors. The rest is just as has been described.

Iti yaṃ catukkanaye dutiyaṃ, taṃ dvidhā bhinditvā pañcakanaye dutiyañceva tatiyañca hoti. Yāni ca tattha tatiyacatutthāni, tāni ca catutthapañcamāni honti. Paṭhamaṃ paṭhamamevāti.

Thus, that which is the second jhāna in the fourfold method, when divided in two, becomes the second and the third in the fivefold method. And those that are the third and fourth jhānas there, become the fourth and fifth. The first remains the first.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Path of Purification, composed for the sake of the delight of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the Section on the Development of Concentration,

Pathavīkasiṇaniddeso nāma

named the Description of the Earth Kasiṇa,

Catuttho paricchedo.

the Fourth Chapter.

5. Sesakasiṇaniddeso

5. Description of the Remaining Kasiṇas

Āpokasiṇakathā

Discourse on the Water Kasiṇa

91. Idāni [M 1.0165][V 1.0163] pathavīkasiṇānantare āpokasiṇe vitthārakathā hoti. Yatheva hi pathavīkasiṇaṃ, evaṃ āpokasiṇampi bhāvetukāmena sukhanisinnena āpasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ, kate vā akate vāti sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ sabbattha. Ito parañhi ettakampi avatvā visesamattameva vakkhāma.

91. Now, following the earth kasiṇa, there is the detailed discourse on the water kasiṇa. For just as with the earth kasiṇa, so too should one who wishes to develop the water kasiṇa sit comfortably and apprehend the sign in water. The entire method, beginning with 'whether prepared or unprepared,' should be elaborated. And as it is here, so it is in all cases. From this point on, without stating even this much, we shall speak only of the specific details.

Idhāpi pubbekatādhikārassa puññavato akate āpasmiṃ pokkharaṇiyā vā taḷāke vā loṇiyaṃ vā samudde vā nimittaṃ uppajjati cūḷasivattherassa viya. Tassa kirāyasmato lābhasakkāraṃ pahāya vivittavāsaṃ vasissāmīti mahātitthe nāvamārūhitvā jambudīpaṃ gacchato antarā mahāsamuddaṃ olokayato tappaṭibhāgaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ udapādi.

Here also, for a person of merit who has made a foundation in the past, the sign arises in unprepared water—in a lotus pond, a lake, a salt-pan, or the ocean—just as it did for the Elder Cūḷasīva. It is said that for this venerable one, as he was abandoning gain and honor with the thought, 'I will live in seclusion,' and had boarded a ship at Mahātittha to go to Jambudīpa, a counterpart kasiṇa sign arose while he was looking upon the great ocean along the way.

Akatādhikārena cattāro kasiṇadose pariharantena nīlapītalohitodātavaṇṇānamaññataravaṇṇaṃ āpaṃ agahetvā yaṃ pana bhūmiṃ asampattameva ākāse suddhavatthena gahitaṃ udakaṃ, aññaṃ vā tathārūpaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ, tena pattaṃ vā kuṇḍikaṃ vā samatittikaṃ pūretvā vihārapaccante vuttappakāre paṭicchanne okāse ṭhapetvā sukhanisinnena na vaṇṇo paccavekkhitabbo. Na lakkhaṇaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ. Nissayasavaṇṇameva katvā ussadavasena paṇṇattidhamme cittaṃ ṭhapetvā ambu, udakaṃ, vāri, salilantiādīsu āponāmesu pākaṭanāmavaseneva “āpo āpo”ti bhāvetabbaṃ.

One who has not made a foundation in the past should, while avoiding the four kasiṇa faults, not take water that has any of the colors blue, yellow, red, or white. Rather, one should take rainwater that has been caught with a clean cloth in the sky before it has reached the ground, or other such water that is clear and limpid. With that water, having filled a bowl or a water pot to the brim and placed it in a secluded location at the edge of the monastery as previously described, one should sit comfortably. The color should not be reflected upon, nor should the characteristic be attended to. Taking the support itself along with its color, and by way of its predominance, having established the mind on the concept, one should develop it by way of a common name from among the names for water—such as ambu, udaka, vāri, salila—repeating 'āpo, āpo'.

Tassevaṃ bhāvayato anukkamena vuttanayeneva nimittadvayaṃ uppajjati. Idha pana uggahanimittaṃ calamānaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti, sace pheṇapupphuḷakamissaṃ udakaṃ hoti, tādisameva upaṭṭhāti, kasiṇadoso [V 1.0164] paññāyati. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana nipparipphandaṃ ākāse ṭhapitamaṇitālavaṇṭaṃ viya maṇimayādāsamaṇḍalamiva ca hutvā upaṭṭhāti. So tassa saha upaṭṭhāneneva [M 1.0166] upacārajjhānaṃ, vuttanayeneva catukkapañcakajjhānāni ca pāpuṇātīti. Āpokasiṇaṃ.

For one thus developing, the two signs gradually arise by the very method already described. Here, however, the learning sign appears as if moving. If the water is mixed with foam and bubbles, it appears just so, and the defect of the kasiṇa is discerned. The counterpart sign, however, being motionless, appears like a jeweled fan-disc placed in the sky and like a jeweled mirror-disc. Together with its very appearance, one attains access concentration and, by the very method already described, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. The Water Kasiṇa.

Tejokasiṇakathā

The Explanation of the Fire Kasiṇa

92. Tejokasiṇaṃ bhāvetukāmenāpi tejasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ. Tattha katādhikārassa puññavato akate nimittaṃ gaṇhantassa dīpasikhāya vā uddhane vā pattapacanaṭṭhāne vā davadāhe vā yattha katthaci aggijālaṃ olokentassa nimittaṃ uppajjati cittaguttattherassa viya. Tassa hāyasmato dhammassavanadivase uposathāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa dīpasikhaṃ olokentasseva nimittaṃ uppajji.

92. By one who wishes to develop the fire kasiṇa, the sign should be apprehended in fire. Therein, for a meritorious person who has made the necessary foundation, while apprehending the sign in an unprepared object, the sign arises when looking at a flame anywhere whatsoever—in a lamp flame, in a stove, in a place for baking bowls, or in a forest fire—as it did for the Elder Cittagutta. Indeed, for that venerable one, the sign arose just from looking at a lamp flame upon entering the Uposatha hall on the day of hearing the Dhamma.

Itarena pana kātabbaṃ. Tatridaṃ karaṇavidhānaṃ, siniddhāni sāradārūni phāletvā sukkhāpetvā ghaṭikaṃ ghaṭikaṃ katvā patirūpaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ vā maṇḍapaṃ vā gantvā pattapacanākārena rāsiṃ katvā ālimpetvā kaṭasārake vā camme vā paṭe vā vidatthicaturaṅgulappamāṇaṃ chiddaṃ kātabbaṃ. Taṃ purato ṭhapetvā vuttanayeneva nisīditvā heṭṭhā tiṇakaṭṭhaṃ vā upari dhūmasikhaṃ vā amanasikaritvā vemajjhe ghanajālāya nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ, nīlanti vā pītanti vātiādivasena vaṇṇo na paccavekkhitabbo, uṇhattavasena lakkhaṇaṃ na manasi kātabbaṃ. Nissayasavaṇṇameva katvā ussadavasena paṇṇattidhamme cittaṃ ṭhapetvā pāvako, kaṇhavattanī, jātavedo, hutāsanotiādīsu aggināmesu pākaṭanāmavaseneva “tejo tejo”ti bhāvetabbaṃ.

For the other, however, it must be prepared. Herein, this is the method of preparation: split resinous heartwood, dry it, and cut it into pieces. Then, go to a suitable tree root or a pavilion, arrange the wood in a pile in the manner of firing an alms-bowl, and set it alight. Make a hole of a span and four fingers in measure in a straw mat, a hide, or a cloth. Place this in front, sit as previously described, and without attending to the grass or wood below or the plume of smoke above, apprehend the sign in the dense flame in the middle. The color should not be reflected upon as 'blue' or 'yellow,' etc., nor should the characteristic be attended to by way of its hotness. Taking the support itself along with its color, and establishing the mind on the concept by way of predominance, one should develop it by way of a well-known name among the names for fire—such as Pāvaka, Kaṇhavattanī, Jātavedo, and Hutāsana—as 'tejo, tejo'.

Tassevaṃ bhāvayato anukkamena vuttanayeneva nimittadvayaṃ uppajjati. Tattha uggahanimittaṃ jālaṃ chijjitvā chijjitvā patanasadisaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Akate gaṇhantassa pana kasiṇadoso paññāyati, alātakhaṇḍaṃ vā aṅgārapiṇḍo vā chārikā vā dhūmo vā upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ niccalaṃ ākāse ṭhapitarattakambalakkhaṇḍaṃ viya suvaṇṇatālavaṇṭaṃ viya kañcanatthambho viya ca upaṭṭhāti. So tassa saha upaṭṭhāneneva upacārajjhānaṃ, vuttanayeneva catukkapañcakajjhānāni ca pāpuṇātīti. Tejokasiṇaṃ.

As he develops it in this way, the pair of signs arises in due course in the way already described. Therein, the learning sign appears like a flame breaking up repeatedly and falling. But for one who apprehends it in an unprepared object, a fault of the kasiṇa appears: a piece of firebrand, or a mass of embers, or ash, or smoke appears. The counterpart sign appears motionless, like a piece of red blanket placed in the sky, like a golden fan, or like a golden pillar. Simultaneously with its appearance, he attains access concentration and, in the way already described, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas. The Fire Kasiṇa.

Vāyokasiṇakathā

The Explanation of the Wind Kasiṇa

93. Vāyokasiṇaṃ [M 1.0167][V 1.0165] bhāvetukāmenāpi vāyusmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ. Tañca kho diṭṭhavasena vā phuṭṭhavasena vā. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu “vāyokasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto vāyusmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti, ucchaggaṃ vā eritaṃ sameritaṃ upalakkheti, veḷaggaṃ vā…pe… rukkhaggaṃ vā kesaggaṃ vā eritaṃ sameritaṃ upalakkheti, kāyasmiṃ vā phuṭṭhaṃ upalakkhetī”ti. Tasmā samasīsaṭṭhitaṃ ghanapattaṃ ucchuṃ vā veḷuṃ vā rukkhaṃ vā caturaṅgulappamāṇaṃ ghanakesassa purisassa sīsaṃ vā vātena pahariyamānaṃ disvā “ayaṃ vāto etasmiṃ ṭhāne paharatī”ti satiṃ ṭhapetvā, yaṃ vā panassa vātapānantarikāya vā bhittichiddena vā pavisitvā vāto kāyappadesaṃ paharati, tattha satiṃ ṭhapetvā vātamālutaanilādīsu vāyunāmesu pākaṭanāmavaseneva “vāto vāto”ti bhāvetabbaṃ. Idha uggahanimittavaḍḍhanato otāritamattassa pāyāsassa usumavaṭṭisadisaṃ calaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ sannisinnaṃ hoti niccalaṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti. Vāyokasiṇaṃ.

93. One who wishes to develop the wind kasiṇa should grasp the sign in the wind, either by sight or by touch. For it is stated in the commentaries: 'When learning the wind kasiṇa, one grasps the sign in the wind. One observes the tip of a sugarcane swaying back and forth, the tip of a bamboo... the top of a tree, or the tip of hair swaying back and forth; or one observes the touch of wind on the body.' Therefore, having seen a dense-leaved sugarcane, bamboo, or tree standing with a level top, or the head of a man with thick hair about four finger-breadths long being struck by the wind, one should establish mindfulness, thinking, 'This wind strikes in this place.' Or else, when wind enters through a window opening or a crack in the wall and strikes a part of one's body, one should establish mindfulness there and, by means of a common name for wind—such as vāta, māluta, and anila—develop the meditation by repeating, 'wind, wind.' Here, the learning sign appears as something moving, like a wisp of steam from rice porridge just taken off the fire. The counterpart sign becomes settled and motionless. The rest should be understood in the way already explained. The Wind Kasiṇa.

Nīlakasiṇakathā

The Explanation of the Blue Kasiṇa

94. Tadanantaraṃ pana nīlakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto nīlakasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vāti vacanato katādhikārassa puññavato tāva tathārūpaṃ mālāgacchaṃ vā pūjāṭhānesu pupphasantharaṃ vā nīlavatthamaṇīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ disvāva nimittaṃ uppajjati. Itarena nīluppalagirikaṇṇikādīni pupphāni gahetvā yathā kesaraṃ vā vaṇṭaṃ vā na paññāyati, evaṃ caṅgoṭakaṃ vā karaṇḍapaṭalaṃ vā pattehiyeva samatittikaṃ pūretvā santharitabbaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇena vā vatthena bhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā pūretabbaṃ. Mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ vā assa bheritalamiva bandhitabbaṃ. Kaṃsanīlapalāsanīlaañjananīlānaṃ vā aññatarena dhātunā pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayena saṃhārimaṃ vā bhittiyaṃyeva vā kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ katvā visabhāgavaṇṇena paricchinditabbaṃ. Tato pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayena “nīlaṃ nīla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Idhāpi uggahanimitte kasiṇadoso paññāyati, kesaradaṇḍakapattantarikādīni upaṭṭhahanti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ kasiṇamaṇḍalato muñcitvā ākāse [M 1.0168] maṇitālavaṇṭasadisaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbanti. Nīlakasiṇaṃ.

94. Next, one who undertakes the blue kasiṇa grasps the sign in what is blue—whether in a flower, in a cloth, or in a color-element. Because it is said thus, for a meritorious person who has done the preparatory work, the sign arises just by seeing such a thing as a bush of blue flowers, a carpet of flowers in a place of worship, or one among blue cloths and gems. For another person, having taken flowers such as blue water lilies or Girikaṇṇikā, a basket or the lid of a casket should be filled level to the brim with only the petals and arranged well, in such a way that no stamen or stalk is visible. Alternatively, having tied a bundle with a blue cloth, it should be filled. Or, on its rim, it should be tied taut like a drum-skin. Or, with one of the elements—bronze-blue, leaf-blue, or collyrium-blue—a portable kasiṇa-disk or one right on a wall should be made by the method stated in the earth kasiṇa, and it should be demarcated with a dissimilar color. Thereafter, by the method stated in the earth kasiṇa, attention should be applied thus: “Blue, blue.” Here also, in the learning sign, a kasiṇa-fault appears: stamens, stalks, gaps between petals, and so on, appear. The counterpart sign, having been released from the kasiṇa-disk, appears in space like a fan made of jewels. The rest should be understood by the method already stated. The Blue Kasiṇa.

Pītakasiṇakathā

The Discourse on the Yellow Kasiṇa

95. Pītakasiṇepi [V 1.0166] eseva nayo. Vuttañhetaṃ pītakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto pītakasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vāti. Tasmā idhāpi katādhikārassa puññavato tathārūpaṃ mālāgacchaṃ vā pupphasantharaṃ vā pītavatthadhātūnaṃ vā aññataraṃ disvāva nimittaṃ uppajjati cittaguttattherassa viya. Tassa kirāyasmato cittalapabbate pattaṅgapupphehi kataṃ āsanapūjaṃ passato saha dassaneneva āsanappamāṇaṃ nimittaṃ udapādi. Itarena kaṇikārapupphādinā vā pītavatthena vā dhātunā vā nīlakasiṇe vuttanayeneva kasiṇaṃ katvā “pītakaṃ pītaka”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti. Pītakasiṇaṃ.

95. This same method should be understood for the yellow kasiṇa as well. For it is said: “One learning the yellow kasiṇa apprehends the sign in something yellow—whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color-element.” Therefore, here too, for a meritorious person who has done the preparatory work, upon seeing such a flower bush, a spread of flowers, or any one among yellow cloths and color-elements, the sign arises—just as it did for the Elder Cittagutta. It is said that for that venerable one, while looking at a seat-offering made with pattaṅga flowers on Mount Cittalapabbata, a sign the size of the seat arose simultaneously with the seeing of it. For another person, having prepared the kasiṇa with kaṇikāra flowers and so on, or with a yellow cloth, or with a color-element, by the same method stated in the blue kasiṇa section, attention should be directed to it as “yellow, yellow.” The rest is just the same. The Yellow Kasiṇa.

Lohitakasiṇakathā

The Discourse on the Red Kasiṇa

96. Lohitakasiṇepi eseva nayo. Vuttañhetaṃ lohitakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto lohitakasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vāti. Tasmā idhāpi katādhikārassa puññavato tathārūpaṃ bandhujīvakādimālāgacchaṃ vā pupphasantharaṃ vā lohitakavatthamaṇidhātūnaṃ vā aññataraṃ disvāva nimittaṃ uppajjati. Itarena jayasumanabandhujīvakarattakoraṇḍakādipupphehi vā rattavatthena vā dhātunā vā nīlakasiṇe vuttanayeneva kasiṇaṃ katvā “lohitakaṃ lohitaka”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti. Lohitakasiṇaṃ.

96. This same method should be understood for the red kasiṇa as well. For it is said: “One learning the red kasiṇa apprehends the sign in something red—whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color-element.” Therefore, here too, for a meritorious person who has done the preparatory work, upon seeing such a flower bush of bandhujīvaka and so on, a spread of flowers, or any one among red cloths, gems, and color-elements, the sign arises. For another person, having prepared the kasiṇa with flowers such as jayasumana, bandhujīvaka, rattakoraṇḍaka, and so on, or with a red cloth, or with a color-element, by the same method stated in the blue kasiṇa section, attention should be directed to it as “red, red.” The rest is just the same. The Red Kasiṇa.

Odātakasiṇakathā

The Discourse on the White Kasiṇa

97. Odātakasiṇepi odātakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto odātasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti pupphasmiṃ vā vatthasmiṃ vā vaṇṇadhātuyā vāti vacanato katādhikārassa tāva puññavato tathārūpaṃ mālāgacchaṃ vā vassikasumanādipupphasantharaṃ vā kumudapadumarāsiṃ vā odātavatthadhātūnaṃ vā aññataraṃ disvāva nimittaṃ uppajjati, tipumaṇḍalarajatamaṇḍalacandamaṇḍalesupi uppajjatiyeva. Itarena [M 1.0169] vuttappakārehi odātapupphehi vā odātavatthena vā dhātunā vā nīlakasiṇe vuttanayeneva kasiṇaṃ katvā “odātaṃ odāta”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti. Odātakasiṇaṃ.

97. In the white kasiṇa also, one learning the white kasiṇa takes the sign in something white—whether in a flower, a cloth, or a color element. Thus, for a meritorious person who has done the preparatory work, the sign arises just upon seeing such a garland-bush, a spread of vassika jasmine or other flowers, a heap of kumuda water lilies or paduma lotuses, or any one among white cloths or elements. It also arises in a disc of lead, a disc of silver, and the moon-disc. For another person, using the aforementioned white flowers, white cloth, or element, the kasiṇa should be prepared by the very method described for the blue kasiṇa, and attention should be directed with the thought, “white, white.” The rest is just the same. The White Kasiṇa.

Ālokakasiṇakathā

The Discourse on the Light Kasiṇa

98. Ālokakasiṇe [V 1.0167] pana ālokakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto ālokasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti bhittichidde vā tāḷacchidde vā vātapānantarikāya vāti vacanato katādhikārassa tāva puññavato yaṃ bhittichiddādīnaṃ aññatarena sūriyāloko vā candāloko vā pavisitvā bhittiyaṃ vā bhūmiyaṃ vā maṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, ghanapaṇṇarukkhasākhantarena vā ghanasākhāmaṇḍapantarena vā nikkhamitvā bhūmiyameva maṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, taṃ disvāva nimittaṃ uppajjati. Itarenāpi tadeva vuttappakāramobhāsamaṇḍalaṃ “obhāso obhāso”ti vā “āloko āloko”ti vā bhāvetabbaṃ. Tathā asakkontena ghaṭe dīpaṃ jāletvā ghaṭamukhaṃ pidahitvā ghaṭe chiddaṃ katvā bhittimukhaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Tena chiddena dīpāloko nikkhamitvā bhittiyaṃ maṇḍalaṃ karoti, taṃ āloko ālokoti bhāvetabbaṃ. Idamitarehi ciraṭṭhitikaṃ hoti. Idha uggahanimittaṃ bhittiyaṃ vā bhūmiyaṃ vā uṭṭhitamaṇḍalasadisameva hoti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ ghanavippasannaālokapuñjasadisaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti. Ālokakasiṇaṃ.

98. Now, regarding the light kasiṇa, one learning the light kasiṇa takes the sign in the light entering through a hole in a wall, a keyhole, or an interstice of a window. Thus, for a meritorious person who has done the preparatory work, when sunlight or moonlight enters through one of these and forms a circle on a wall or the ground; or when it emerges through the dense foliage of a tree or a thick canopy of branches and forms a circle on the ground, upon seeing that, the sign arises. For another person, that same kind of luminous circle should be developed with the thought, “radiance, radiance” or “light, light.” If unable to do so, one should light a lamp inside a pot, cover the mouth of the pot, make a hole in the pot, and place it facing a wall. The light from the lamp passes through the hole and forms a circle on the wall, which should then be developed as “light, light.” This is more long-lasting than the others. Here, the learning sign is just like the circle that appears on the wall or ground. The counterpart sign resembles a mass of dense and very clear light. The rest is just the same. The Light Kasiṇa.

Paricchinnākāsakasiṇakathā

The Discourse on the Bounded Space Kasiṇa

99. Paricchinnākāsakasiṇepi ākāsakasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto ākāsasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhāti bhittichidde vā tāḷacchidde vā vātapānantarikāya vāti vacanato katādhikārassa tāva puññavato bhittichiddādīsu aññataraṃ disvāva nimittaṃ uppajjati. Itarena succhannamaṇḍape vā cammakaṭasārakādīnaṃ vā aññatarasmiṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulappamāṇaṃ chiddaṃ katvā tadeva vā bhittichiddādibhedaṃ chiddaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti bhāvetabbaṃ. Idha uggahanimittaṃ saddhiṃ bhittipariyantādīhi chiddasadisameva hoti, vaḍḍhiyamānampi na vaḍḍhati. Paṭibhāganimittamākāsamaṇḍalameva hutvā upaṭṭhāti, vaḍḍhiyamānañca vaḍḍhati. Sesaṃ pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbanti. Paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ.

99. In the bounded space kasiṇa also, it is said: 'One who is apprehending the space kasiṇa takes the sign in space, such as in a hole in a wall, a keyhole, or the gap of a window.' Therefore, for a fortunate person who has made the requisite preparations, the sign arises simply upon seeing one among such things as a hole in a wall. For another, in a well-covered pavilion or on one among such things as a leather mat, a hole measuring a span and four fingers should be made, or that very hole, being one of the various kinds such as a hole in a wall, should be developed as “space, space.” Here, the learning sign is just like the hole itself, together with the edges of the wall and so on; even when one tries to expand it, it does not expand. The counterpart sign appears, having become a mere circle of space; and when one tries to expand it, it expands. The rest should be understood in the very way spoken of in the earth kasiṇa. The Bounded Space Kasiṇa.

Iti [M 1.0170] kasiṇāni dasabalo,

Dasa yāni avoca sabbadhammadaso;

Rūpāvacaramhi catukkapañcakajjhānahetūni.

Thus, the Ten-Powered One, the Seer of all things, taught the ten kasiṇas which are the causes of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas in the form sphere.

Evaṃ [V 1.0168] tāni ca tesañca,

Bhāvanānayamimaṃ viditvāna;

Tesveva ayaṃ bhiyyo,

Pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

Thus, having known those kasiṇas and this method for their development, this miscellaneous discourse concerning them should also be further understood.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse

100. Imesu hi pathavīkasiṇavasena ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotītiādibhāvo, ākāse vā udake vā pathaviṃ nimminitvā padasā gamanaṃ, ṭhānanisajjādikappanaṃ vā, parittaappamāṇanayena abhibhāyatanapaṭilābhoti evamādīni ijjhanti.

100. Indeed, among these kasiṇas, by means of the earth kasiṇa, such things as the state of 'having been one, he becomes many'; creating earth in the sky or on water and walking on foot; or the arranging of postures such as standing and sitting; and the attainment of the spheres of mastery by the method of the limited and the unlimited—these and other such things are accomplished.

Āpokasiṇavasena pathaviyaṃ ummujjananimmujjanaṃ, udakavuṭṭhisamuppādanaṃ, nadīsamuddādinimmānaṃ, pathavīpabbatapāsādādīnaṃ kampananti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the water kasiṇa, emerging from and diving into the earth, causing a shower of water to arise, creating rivers and oceans, and causing the earth, mountains, palaces, and so forth to shake—these and other such things are accomplished.

Tejokasiṇavasena dhūmāyanā, pajjalanā, aṅgāravuṭṭhisamuppādanaṃ, tejasā tejopariyādānaṃ, yadeva so icchati tassa ḍahanasamatthatā, dibbena cakkhunā rūpadassanatthāya ālokakaraṇaṃ, parinibbānasamaye tejodhātuyā sarīrajjhāpananti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the fire kasiṇa, emitting smoke, emitting flames, causing a shower of embers to arise, overpowering another's heat with one's own heat, the ability to burn whatsoever one wishes, creating light for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye, and the burning of the body by means of the fire element at the time of final Nibbāna—these and other such things are accomplished.

Vāyokasiṇavasena vāyugatigamanaṃ, vātavuṭṭhisamuppādananti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the air kasiṇa, traveling with the speed of wind and producing a great wind—these and other such things are accomplished.

Nīlakasiṇavasena nīlarūpanimmānaṃ, andhakārakaraṇaṃ, suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇanayena abhibhāyatanapaṭilābho, subhavimokkhādhigamoti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the blue kasiṇa, creating blue forms, producing darkness, the attainment of the spheres of mastery by the method of pure and impure colors, and the attainment of the beautiful liberation—these and other such things are accomplished.

Pītakasiṇavasena pītakarūpanimmānaṃ, suvaṇṇanti adhimuccanā, vuttanayeneva abhibhāyatanapaṭilābho, subhavimokkhādhigamo cāti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the yellow kasiṇa, creating yellow forms, the determination 'let it be gold,' the attainment of the spheres of mastery by the method already described, and the attainment of the beautiful liberation—these and other such things are accomplished.

Lohitakasiṇavasena lohitakarūpanimmānaṃ, vuttanayeneva abhibhāyatanapaṭilābho, subhavimokkhādhigamoti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the red kasiṇa, creating red forms, the attainment of the spheres of mastery by the method already described, and the attainment of the beautiful liberation—these and other such things are accomplished.

Odātakasiṇavasena [M 1.0171][V 1.0169] odātarūpanimmānaṃ, thinamiddhassa dūrabhāvakaraṇaṃ, andhakāravidhamanaṃ, dibbena cakkhunā rūpadassanatthāya ālokakaraṇanti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the white kasiṇa, creating white forms, making sloth and torpor far away, dispelling darkness, and producing light for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye—these and other such things are accomplished.

Ālokakasiṇavasena sappabhārūpanimmānaṃ, thinamiddhassa dūrabhāvakaraṇaṃ, andhakāravidhamanaṃ, dibbena cakkhunā rūpadassanatthaṃ ālokakaraṇanti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the light kasiṇa, creating radiant forms, making sloth and torpor far away, dispelling darkness, and producing light for the purpose of seeing forms with the divine eye—these and other such things are accomplished.

Ākāsakasiṇavasena paṭicchannānaṃ vivaṭakaraṇaṃ, antopathavīpabbatādīsupi ākāsaṃ nimminitvā iriyāpathakappanaṃ, tirokuḍḍādīsu asajjamānagamananti evamādīni ijjhanti.

By means of the space kasiṇa, uncovering what is concealed, creating space even within earth, mountains, and so forth to establish a posture, and passing unhindered through walls and so forth—these and other such things are accomplished.

Sabbāneva uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇanti imaṃ pabhedaṃ labhanti. Vuttañhetaṃ “pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānāti. Uddhamadhotiriyaṃ advayamappamāṇa”ntiādi.

All ten kasiṇas indeed attain this distinction: 'above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable.' For it was said: 'One perceives the earth kasiṇa: above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable,' and so forth.

Tattha uddhanti uparigaganatalābhimukhaṃ. Adhoti heṭṭhābhūmitalābhimukhaṃ. Tiriyanti khettamaṇḍalamiva samantā paricchinditaṃ. Ekacco hi uddhameva kasiṇaṃ vaḍḍheti, ekacco adho, ekacco samantato. Tena tena vā kāraṇena evaṃ pasāreti. Ālokamiva dibbacakkhunā rūpadassanakāmo. Tena vuttaṃ uddhamadhotiriyanti. Advayanti idaṃ pana ekassa aññabhāvānupagamanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Yathā hi udakaṃ paviṭṭhassa sabbadisāsu udakameva hoti, na aññaṃ, evameva pathavīkasiṇaṃ pathavīkasiṇameva hoti, natthi tassa añño kasiṇasambhedoti. Eseva nayo sabbattha. Appamāṇanti idaṃ tassa pharaṇaappamāṇavasena vuttaṃ. Tañhi cetasā pharanto sakalameva pharati. Na ayamassa ādi idaṃ majjhanti pamāṇaṃ gaṇhātīti.

Therein, 'above' means facing upwards towards the surface of the sky. 'Below' means facing downwards towards the surface of the earth. 'Across' means bounded on all sides, like the perimeter of a field. For indeed, a certain person develops the kasiṇa only upwards, another downwards, and another all around. For this or that reason, one extends it thus, just as one who desires to see forms with the divine eye extends the light. Therefore, it is said: 'above, below, across.' Now, the term 'non-dual' is said to indicate that one kasiṇa does not pass into the state of another. For just as for one who has entered water there is only water in all directions and nothing else, so too the earth kasiṇa is only the earth kasiṇa; there is no intermixture with another kasiṇa. This same method should be understood in all cases. The term 'immeasurable' is said with reference to the immeasurability of its pervasion. For in pervading it with the mind, one pervades it completely. One does not take a measure, thinking, 'This is its beginning, this is the middle.'

101. Ye ca te sattā kammāvaraṇena vā samannāgatā kilesāvaraṇena vā samannāgatā vipākāvaraṇena vā samannāgatā asaddhā acchandikā duppaññā abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti vuttā, tesamekassāpekakasiṇepi bhāvanā na ijjhati. Tattha kammāvaraṇena samannāgatāti ānantariyakammasamaṅgino. Kilesāvaraṇena samannāgatāti niyatamicchādiṭṭhikā ceva ubhatobyañjanakapaṇḍakā ca. Vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatāti ahetukadvihetukapaṭisandhikā. Asaddhāti buddhādīsu saddhāvirahitā. Acchandikāti apaccanīkapaṭipadāyaṃ chandavirahitā[M 1.0172]. Duppaññāti lokiyalokuttarasammādiṭṭhiyā virahitā. Abhabbā [V 1.0170] niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattanti kusalesu dhammesu niyāmasaṅkhātaṃ sammattasaṅkhātañca ariyamaggaṃ okkamituṃ abhabbāti attho. Na kevalañca kasiṇeyeva, aññesupi kammaṭṭhānesu etesamekassapi bhāvanā na ijjhati. Tasmā vigatavipākāvaraṇenapi kulaputtena kammāvaraṇañca kilesāvaraṇañca ārakā parivajjetvā saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayādīhi saddhañca chandañca paññañca vaḍḍhetvā kammaṭṭhānānuyoge yogo karaṇīyoti.

101. And for those beings who are said to be endowed with the obstruction of kamma, or endowed with the obstruction of defilements, or endowed with the obstruction of result; who are faithless, lacking in zeal, unwise, and incapable of entering the fixed state, the right state, in wholesome dhammas—for not even one of them does the development succeed, even in a single kasiṇa. Therein, 'endowed with the obstruction of kamma' refers to those who possess a deed with immediate result. 'Endowed with the obstruction of defilements' refers to those with fixed wrong views and also to hermaphrodites and eunuchs. 'Endowed with the obstruction of result' refers to those with a rootless or two-rooted relinking-consciousness. 'Faithless' means devoid of faith in the Buddha and so on. 'Lacking in zeal' means devoid of zeal for the practice that is not contrary to the path. 'Unwise' means devoid of mundane and supramundane right view. 'Incapable of entering the fixed state, the right state, in wholesome dhammas' means incapable of entering the noble path, which is designated as the fixed state and the right state, in wholesome dhammas. And not only in the kasiṇas, but also in other meditation subjects, development does not succeed for even one of these persons. Therefore, a son of good family who is free from the obstruction of result, having avoided from afar the obstruction of kamma and the obstruction of defilements, and having developed faith, zeal, and wisdom through such means as listening to the true Dhamma and associating with good persons, should make an exertion in the application to the meditation subject.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Visuddhimagga, made for the delight of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

In the Division on the Development of Concentration,

Sesakasiṇaniddeso nāma

The Description of the Remaining Kasiṇas,

Pañcamo paricchedo.

The Fifth Chapter.

6. Asubhakammaṭṭhānaniddeso

6. The Exposition of the Asubha Meditation Subject

Uddhumātakādipadatthavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Meaning of the Words 'Uddhumātaka' and So On

102.
