Kasiṇānantaramuddiṭṭhesu [M 1.0173][V 1.0171] pana uddhumātakaṃ, vinīlakaṃ, vipubbakaṃ, vicchiddakaṃ, vikkhāyitakaṃ, vikkhittakaṃ, hatavikkhittakaṃ, lohitakaṃ, puḷavakaṃ, aṭṭhikanti dasasu aviññāṇakāsubhesu bhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātaṃ, uddhumātameva uddhumātakaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ uddhumātanti uddhumātakaṃ. Tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

102. Now, as for the section on the ten inanimate foul objects enumerated after the kasiṇas—the bloated (uddhumātaka), the livid (vinīlaka), the festering (vipubbaka), the cut-up (vicchiddaka), the gnawed (vikkhāyitaka), the scattered (vikkhittaka), the hacked and scattered (hatavikkhittaka), the bloody (lohitaka), the worm-infested (puḷavaka), and the skeletal (aṭṭhika)—it is called 'bloated' (uddhumāta) because, like a leather bag inflated with air, it is bloated due to the swollen state that arises in due course after the cessation of life. 'Uddhumāta' itself is 'uddhumātaka'. Or, because it is repulsive, it is a contemptible bloated thing (kucchitaṃ uddhumātaṃ); therefore, it is 'uddhumātaka'. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature.

Vinīlaṃ vuccati viparibhinnanīlavaṇṇaṃ, vinīlameva vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nīlaṭṭhāne nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

A corpse that is of a discolored dark blue color is called 'livid' (vinīla). 'Vinīla' itself is 'vinīlaka'. Or, because it is repulsive, it is a contemptible livid thing; therefore, it is 'vinīlaka'. This is a designation for a corpse that is of a red color in places with much flesh, of a white color in places where pus has collected, and is predominantly of a dark blue color, appearing as if wrapped in a blue cloth in the dark blue areas.

Paribhinnaṭṭhānesu vissandamānaṃ pubbaṃ vipubbaṃ, vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ. Tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

A corpse with pus oozing in places torn apart is called 'festering' (vipubba). 'Vipubba' itself is 'vipubbaka'. Or, because it is repulsive, it is a contemptible festering thing; therefore, it is 'vipubbaka'. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature.

Vicchiddaṃ vuccati dvidhā chindanena apadhāritaṃ, vicchiddameva vicchiddakaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vicchiddanti vicchiddakaṃ. Vemajjhe chinnassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

A corpse that has been split by being cut in two is called 'cut-up' (vicchidda). 'Vicchidda' itself is 'vicchiddaka'. Or, because it is repulsive, it is a contemptible cut-up thing; therefore, it is 'vicchiddaka'. This is a designation for a corpse cut in the middle.

Ito ca etto ca vividhākārena soṇasiṅgālādīhi khāditanti vikkhāyitaṃ, vikkhāyitameva vikkhāyitakaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vikkhāyitanti vikkhāyitakaṃ. Tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

It is called 'gnawed' (vikkhāyita) because it is a corpse eaten from here and there in various ways by dogs, jackals, and so on. 'Vikkhāyita' itself is 'vikkhāyitaka'. Or, because it is repulsive, it is a contemptible gnawed thing; therefore, it is 'vikkhāyitaka'. This is a designation for a corpse of such a nature.

Vividhaṃ [V 1.0172] khittaṃ vikkhittaṃ, vikkhittameva vikkhittakaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vikkhittanti vikkhittakaṃ. Aññena hatthaṃ aññena pādaṃ aññena sīsanti evaṃ tato tato khittassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

Scattered in various ways, it is 'scattered' (vikkhitta). 'Vikkhitta' itself is 'vikkhittaka'. Or, because it is repulsive, it is a contemptible scattered thing; therefore, it is 'vikkhittaka'. This is a designation for a corpse scattered about, with a hand in one place, a foot in another, and the head in yet another.

Hatañca taṃ purimanayeneva vikkhittakañcāti hatavikkhittakaṃ. Kākapadākārena aṅgapaccaṅgesu satthena hanitvā vuttanayena vikkhittassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

It is both hacked and scattered in the aforementioned manner; therefore, it is called 'hacked and scattered' (hatavikkhittaka). This is a designation for a corpse whose major and minor limbs have been hacked with a weapon in the shape of a crow's foot and scattered in the manner previously stated.

Lohitaṃ [M 1.0174] kirati vikkhipati ito cito ca paggharatīti lohitakaṃ. Paggharitalohitamakkhitassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

It is 'lohitaka' because it sheds and scatters blood, and it oozes from here and there. This is a designation for a corpse smeared with blood that has oozed from it.

Puḷavā vuccanti kimayo, puḷave kiratīti puḷavakaṃ. Kimiparipuṇṇassa chavasarīrassetamadhivacanaṃ.

Worms are called 'puḷavā'; it is 'puḷavaka' because it discharges worms. This is a designation for a corpse full of worms.

Aṭṭhiyeva aṭṭhikaṃ. Paṭikkūlattā vā kucchitaṃ aṭṭhīti aṭṭhikaṃ. Aṭṭhisaṅkhalikāyapi ekaṭṭhikassapetamadhivacanaṃ. Imāni ca pana uddhumātakādīni nissāya uppannanimittānampi nimittesu paṭiladdhajjhānānampetāneva nāmāni.

The bone itself is 'aṭṭhika'. Or, because of its repulsiveness, it is a loathsome bone; therefore, it is called 'aṭṭhika'. This is a designation for both a chain of bones (a skeleton) and for a single bone. Furthermore, these very names, 'bloated corpse' and so on, are also the names for the learning signs that have arisen depending on these foul objects, and for the jhānas that have been attained in the counterpart signs.

Uddhumātakakammaṭṭhānaṃ

The Meditation Subject of the Bloated Corpse

103. Tattha uddhumātakasarīre uddhumātakanimittaṃ uppādetvā uddhumātakasaṅkhātaṃ jhānaṃ bhāvetukāmena yoginā pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva vuttappakāraṃ ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Tenassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathentena asubhanimittatthāya gamanavidhānaṃ, samantā nimittupalakkhaṇaṃ, ekādasavidhena nimittaggāho, gatāgatamaggapaccavekkhaṇanti evaṃ appanāvidhānapariyosānaṃ sabbaṃ kathetabbaṃ. Tenāpi sabbaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahetvā pubbe vuttappakāraṃ senāsanaṃ upagantvā uddhumātakanimittaṃ pariyesantena vihātabbaṃ.

103. Herein, a yogī who wishes to develop the jhāna known as 'bloated' by producing the sign of the bloated corpse on a bloated body should, in the very manner described in the case of the earth kasiṇa, approach a teacher of the kind described and properly learn the meditation subject. That teacher, when explaining this meditation subject to the yogī, should explain the entire procedure, ending with the procedure for absorption: namely, the procedure for going for the purpose of taking the foul sign, the marking of the learning sign all around, the grasping of the sign in eleven ways, and the reviewing of the path gone and returned. That yogī, too, having properly learned everything, should go to a dwelling of the kind previously described and should dwell while searching for the sign of a bloated corpse.

104. Evaṃ viharantena ca asukasmiṃ nāma gāmadvāre vā aṭavimukhe vā panthe vā pabbatapāde vā rukkhamūle vā susāne vā uddhumātakasarīraṃ nikkhittanti kathentānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvāpi [V 1.0173] na tāvadeva atitthena pakkhandantena viya gantabbaṃ. Kasmā? Asubhaṃ hi nāmetaṃ vāḷamigādhiṭṭhitampi amanussādhiṭṭhitampi hoti. Tatrassa jīvitantarāyopi siyā. Gamanamaggo vā panettha gāmadvārena vā nahānatitthena vā kedārakoṭiyā vā hoti. Tattha visabhāgarūpaṃ āpāthamāgacchati, tadeva vā sarīraṃ visabhāgaṃ hoti. Purisassa hi itthisarīraṃ itthiyā ca purisasarīraṃ visabhāgaṃ, tadetaṃ adhunāmataṃ subhatopi upaṭṭhāti, tenassa brahmacariyantarāyopi siyā. Sace pana “nayidaṃ mādisassa bhāriya”nti attānaṃ takkayati, evaṃ takkayamānena gantabbaṃ.

104. And for one dwelling thus, even having heard the words of those who say, 'A bloated corpse has been discarded at such-and-such a village gate, or at the entrance of a forest, or on a path, or at the foot of a mountain, or at the root of a tree, or in a charnel ground,' one should not go at that very moment, like one descending hastily by an improper landing-place. Why? For this foul object may be guarded by wild beasts or guarded by non-human beings. There, a danger to one's life might also arise. Or else, the path to it may be through a village gate, or by a bathing ford, or by the edge of a paddy field. There, an incompatible form comes into the range of vision, or that very corpse itself is incompatible. Indeed, for a man, a woman's body is incompatible, and for a woman, a man's body is incompatible. That incompatible body, being recently dead, can also appear as beautiful. Thereby, a danger to one's holy life might also arise. But if one considers oneself, thinking, 'This is not a heavy matter for one like me,' then one who considers thus should go.

105. Gacchantena [M 1.0175] ca saṅghattherassa vā aññatarassa vā abhiññātassa bhikkhuno kathetvā gantabbaṃ. Kasmā? Sace hissa susāne amanussasīhabyagghādīnaṃ rūpasaddādianiṭṭhārammaṇābhibhūtassa aṅgapaccaṅgāni vā pavedhenti, bhuttaṃ vā na parisaṇṭhāti, añño vā ābādho hoti. Athassa so vihāre pattacīvaraṃ surakkhitaṃ karissati. Dahare vā sāmaṇere vā pahiṇitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭijaggissati. Apica susānaṃ nāma nirāsaṅkaṭṭhānanti maññamānā katakammāpi akatakammāpi corā samosaranti. Te manussehi anubaddhā bhikkhussa samīpe bhaṇḍakaṃ chaḍḍetvāpi palāyanti. Manussā “sahoḍḍhaṃ coraṃ addasāmā”ti bhikkhuṃ gahetvā viheṭhenti. Athassa so “mā imaṃ viheṭhayittha, mamāyaṃ kathetvā iminā nāma kammena gato”ti te manusse saññāpetvā sotthibhāvaṃ karissati. Ayaṃ ānisaṃso kathetvā gamane. Tasmā vuttappakārassa bhikkhuno kathetvā asubhanimittadassane sañjātābhilāsena yathānāma khattiyo abhisekaṭṭhānaṃ, yajamāno yaññasālaṃ, adhano vā pana nidhiṭṭhānaṃ pītisomanassajāto gacchati, evaṃ pītisomanassaṃ uppādetvā aṭṭhakathāsu vuttena vidhinā gantabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

105. When going, one should inform the Sangha elder or any other well-known bhikkhu before going. Why? Because if, while in the charnel ground, one is overwhelmed by unpleasant objects such as the sights and sounds of non-human beings, lions, tigers, and so on, causing one's limbs to tremble, or if the food one has eaten does not settle, or if some other illness arises, then that bhikkhu will ensure the bowl and robe are well-protected in the monastery. Or he may send young bhikkhus or novices to attend to that bhikkhu. Moreover, thieves—both those who have committed theft and those who wish to do so—may gather there, considering the charnel ground to be a place free from suspicion. Pursued by people, they might drop stolen goods near the bhikkhu and flee. People, thinking, 'We saw the thief together with the stolen goods,' may seize and harass the bhikkhu. Then, that bhikkhu who was informed can explain, 'Do not harass him; he informed me before he went to perform such-and-such an action,' and thus make the people understand, ensuring his safety. This is the benefit of informing someone before going. Therefore, having informed a bhikkhu of the kind described, one should go with the desire to see the sign of foulness, filled with joy and happiness—just as a khattiya goes to the place of consecration, a sacrificer to the sacrificial hall, or a poor person to a place of hidden treasure—generating such joy and happiness, following the method explained in the commentaries. For it is said:

“Uddhumātakaṃ asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhanto eko adutiyo gacchati upaṭṭhitāya satiyā asammuṭṭhāya antogatehi indriyehi abahigatena mānasena gatāgatamaggaṃ paccavekkhamāno. Yasmiṃ padese uddhumātakaṃ asubhanimittaṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ padese pāsāṇaṃ vā vammikaṃ vā rukkhaṃ vā gacchaṃ vā lataṃ vā sanimittaṃ karoti, sārammaṇaṃ karoti. Sanimittaṃ katvā sārammaṇaṃ katvā uddhumātakaṃ asubhanimittaṃ sabhāvabhāvato upalakkheti, vaṇṇatopi liṅgatopi saṇṭhānatopi disatopi okāsatopi paricchedatopi sandhito vivarato ninnato thalato samantato. So taṃ nimittaṃ suggahitaṃ karoti[V 1.0174], sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāreti, suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapeti. So taṃ nimittaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāretvā suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetvā eko adutiyo gacchati upaṭṭhitāya satiyā [M 1.0176] asammuṭṭhāya antogatehi indriyehi abahigatena mānasena gatāgatamaggaṃ paccavekkhamāno. So caṅkamantopi tabbhāgiyaññeva caṅkamaṃ adhiṭṭhāti. Nisīdantopi tabbhāgiyaññeva āsanaṃ paññapeti.

One who is grasping the foul sign of a bloated corpse goes alone, without a companion, with established and unconfused mindfulness, with inwardly directed faculties, with a mind not gone abroad, reflecting on the path gone and returned. In whatever place the foul sign of a bloated corpse is laid down, in that place he makes a mark of a stone, or an anthill, or a tree, or a bush, or a creeper; he makes it an object. Having made a mark, having made it an object, he discerns the foul sign of a bloated corpse by its own nature: by color, by characteristic, by shape, by direction, by location, by delimitation, by joint, by opening, by depression, by elevation, and from all around. He makes that sign well-grasped, bears it well in mind, and establishes it well. Having made that sign well-grasped, having borne it well in mind, and having established it well, he goes alone, without a companion, with established and unconfused mindfulness, with inwardly directed faculties, with a mind not gone abroad, reflecting on the path gone and returned. When walking, he resolves upon only a walking path related to that. When sitting, he prepares only a seat related to that.

“Samantā nimittupalakkhaṇā kimatthiyā kimānisaṃsāti? Samantā nimittupalakkhaṇā asammohatthā asammohānisaṃsā. Ekādasavidhena nimittaggāho kimatthiyo kimānisaṃsoti? Ekādasavidhena nimittaggāho upanibandhanattho upanibandhanānisaṃso. Gatāgatamaggapaccavekkhaṇā kimatthiyā kimānisaṃsāti? Gatāgatamaggapaccavekkhaṇā vīthisampaṭipādanatthā vīthisampaṭipādanānisaṃsā.

What is the purpose, what is the benefit of marking the sign from all around? Marking the sign from all around is for the purpose of non-confusion and has the benefit of non-confusion. What is the purpose, what is the benefit of grasping the sign in eleven ways? Grasping the sign in eleven ways is for the purpose of binding the mind and has the benefit of binding the mind. What is the purpose, what is the benefit of reflecting on the path gone and returned? Reflecting on the path gone and returned is for the purpose of establishing the course and has the benefit of establishing the course.

“So ānisaṃsadassāvī ratanasaññī hutvā cittīkāraṃ upaṭṭhapetvā sampiyāyamāno tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ upanibandhati ‘addhā imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇamhā parimuccissāmī’ti. So vivicceva kāmehi…pe… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Tassādhigataṃ hoti rūpāvacaraṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ dibbo ca vihāro bhāvanāmayañca puññakiriyavatthu”nti.

That yogi, seeing the benefit and perceiving it as a jewel, having established reverence and greatly cherishing it, binds his mind to that object, thinking, ‘Surely, by this practice I shall be liberated from aging and death.’ He, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and abides in the first jhāna. He has attained the first jhāna of the form realm, a divine abiding, and a basis of meritorious action consisting of development.

106. Tasmā yo cittasaññattatthāya sivathikadassanaṃ gacchati, so ghaṇḍiṃ paharitvā gaṇaṃ sannipātetvāpi gacchatu. Kammaṭṭhānasīsena pana gacchantena ekakena adutiyena mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ avissajjetvā taṃ manasikaronteneva susāne soṇādiparissayavinodanatthaṃ kattaradaṇḍaṃ vā yaṭṭhiṃ vā gahetvā, sūpaṭṭhita bhāvasampādanena asammuṭṭhaṃ satiṃ katvā, manacchaṭṭhānañca indriyānaṃ antogatabhāvasampādanato abahigatamanena hutvā gantabbaṃ.

106. Therefore, a bhikkhu who goes to see a charnel ground for the purpose of training the mind may go even after striking the gong and assembling the community of monks. However, one going with the meditation subject as primary should go alone, without a companion. Not abandoning the root meditation subject and keeping it in mind, one should go having taken a walking stick or a staff to dispel dangers such as dogs in the charnel ground, having established unconfused mindfulness by accomplishing a well-established state, and having become one with a mind not directed outwards by bringing the six sense faculties to an inward-directed state.

Vihārato nikkhamanteneva asukadisāya asukadvārena nikkhantomhīti dvāraṃ sallakkhetabbaṃ. Tato yena maggena gacchati, so maggo vavatthapetabbo, ayaṃ maggo pācinadisābhimukho vā gacchati, pacchimauttaradakkhiṇadisābhimukho vā vidisābhimukhovāti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne vāmato gacchati, imasmiṃ ṭhāne dakkhiṇato, imasmiṃ cassa ṭhāne pāsāṇo[M 1.0177][V 1.0175], imasmiṃ vammiko, imasmiṃ rukkho, imasmiṃ gaccho, imasmiṃ latāti. Evaṃ gamanamaggaṃ vavatthapentena nimittaṭṭhānaṃ gantabbaṃ. No ca kho paṭivātaṃ. Paṭivātaṃ gacchantassa hi kuṇapagandho ghānaṃ paharitvā matthaluṅgaṃ vā saṅkhobheyya, āhāraṃ vā chaḍḍāpeyya, vippaṭisāraṃ vā janeyya “īdisaṃ nāma kuṇapaṭṭhānaṃ āgatomhī”ti. Tasmā paṭivātaṃ vajjetvā anuvātaṃ gantabbaṃ. Sace anuvātamaggena na sakkā hoti gantuṃ, antarā pabbato vā papāto vā pāsāṇo vā vati vā kaṇṭakaṭṭhānaṃ vā udakaṃ vā cikkhallaṃ vā hoti, cīvarakaṇṇena nāsaṃ pidahitvā gantabbaṃ. Idamassa gamanavattaṃ.

Upon the very act of leaving the monastery, one should note the door, thinking, 'I am exiting in such-and-such a direction, through such-and-such a door.' Then, the path by which one goes should be determined: 'This path goes facing eastward,' or 'facing westward, northward, or southward,' or 'facing an intermediate direction.' Furthermore, 'In this place, the path goes to the left; in this place, to the right. And in this place on the path there is a rock; in this place, an anthill; in this place, a tree; in this place, a bush; in this place, a vine.' Thus, while determining the path of travel, one should go to the location of the sign. But one should not go upwind. For one who goes upwind, the stench of a corpse might strike the nose and agitate the brain, or cause one to vomit food, or give rise to remorse, thinking, 'Alas, I have come to such a place of corpses!' Therefore, having avoided the upwind direction, one should go downwind. If it is not possible to go by the downwind path because there is a mountain, a precipice, a rock, a fence, a thorny place, water, or mud in the way, one should cover the nose with the corner of the robe and go. This is the duty concerning going.

107. Evaṃ gatena pana na tāva asubhanimittaṃ oloketabbaṃ. Disā vavatthapetabbā. Ekasmiṃ hi disābhāge ṭhitassa ārammaṇañca na vibhūtaṃ hutvā khāyati, cittañca na kammaniyaṃ hoti. Tasmā taṃ vajjetvā yattha ṭhitassa ārammaṇañca vibhūtaṃ hutvā khāyati, cittañca kammaniyaṃ hoti, tattha ṭhātabbaṃ. Paṭivātānuvātañca pahātabbaṃ. Paṭivāte ṭhitassa hi kuṇapagandhena ubbāḷhassa cittaṃ vidhāvati. Anuvāte ṭhitassa sace tattha adhivatthā amanussā honti, te kujjhitvā anatthaṃ karonti. Tasmā īsakaṃ ukkamma nātianuvāte ṭhātabbaṃ. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamānenāpi nātidūre nāccāsanne nānupādaṃ nānusīsaṃ ṭhātabbaṃ. Atidūre ṭhitassa hi ārammaṇaṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti. Accāsanne bhayamuppajjati. Anupādaṃ vā anusīsaṃ vā ṭhitassa sabbaṃ asubhaṃ samaṃ na paññāyati. Tasmā nātidūre nāccāsanne olokentassa phāsukaṭṭhāne sarīravemajjhabhāge ṭhātabbaṃ.

107. Having gone thus, one should not yet look at the sign of foulness. The directions should be determined. For, when standing in one direction, the object may not appear distinctly, and the mind may not be workable. Therefore, avoiding that place, one should stand where the object does appear distinctly and the mind is workable. Both upwind and downwind positions should be abandoned. For when standing upwind, the mind of one oppressed by the stench of the corpse is scattered. When standing downwind, if there are non-human beings dwelling there, they may become angry and cause harm. Therefore, having moved slightly aside, one should stand in a place that is not excessively downwind. Even when standing thus, one should stand neither too far nor too near, not at the foot-end nor at the head-end. For if one stands too far, the object is indistinct. If one stands too near, fear arises. If one stands at the foot-end or the head-end, the entire foul object is not perceived equally. Therefore, one should stand neither too far nor too near, at a comfortable place for viewing, in line with the middle part of the body.

108. Evaṃ ṭhitena “tasmiṃ padese pāsāṇaṃ vā…pe… lataṃ vā sanimittaṃ karotī”ti evaṃ vuttāni samantā nimittāni upalakkhetabbāni. Tatridaṃ upalakkhaṇavidhānaṃ, sace tassa nimittassa samantā cakkhupathe pāsāṇo hoti, so “ayaṃ pāsāṇo ucco vā nīco vā khuddako vā mahanto vā tambo vā kāḷo vā seto vā dīgho vā parimaṇḍalo vā”ti vavatthapetabbo. Tato “imasmiṃ nāma okāse ayaṃ pāsāṇo idaṃ asubhanimittaṃ, idaṃ asubhanimittaṃ ayaṃ pāsāṇo”ti sallakkhetabbaṃ. Sace vammiko hoti, sopi “ucco vā nīco vā khuddako [M 1.0178] vā mahanto vā tambo vā kāḷo vā seto vā dīgho vā parimaṇḍalo vā”ti vavatthapetabbo. Tato “imasmiṃ nāma okāse ayaṃ vammiko idaṃ asubhanimitta”nti sallakkhetabbaṃ. Sace rukkho hoti, sopi “assattho vā nigrodho vā kacchako vā kapītano vā ucco vā nīco vā khuddako [V 1.0176] vā mahanto vā tambo vā kāḷo vā seto vā”ti vavatthapetabbo. Tato “imasmiṃ nāma okāse ayaṃ rukkho idaṃ asubhanimitta”nti sallakkhetabbaṃ. Sace gaccho hoti, sopi “sindivā karamando vā kaṇavīro vā kuraṇḍako vā ucco vā nīco vā khuddako vā mahanto vā”ti vavatthapetabbo. Tato “imasmiṃ nāma okāse ayaṃ gaccho idaṃ asubhanimitta”nti sallakkhetabbaṃ. Sace latā hoti, sāpi “lābu vā kumbhaṇḍī vā sāmā vā kāḷavalli vā pūtilatā vā”ti vavatthapetabbā. Tato “imasmiṃ nāma okāse ayaṃ latā idaṃ asubhanimittaṃ, idaṃ asubhanimittaṃ ayaṃ latā”ti sallakkhetabbaṃ.

108. Having stood thus, the surrounding signs should be noted, in accordance with what was said: 'In that place, one makes a stone… or a creeper into a sign.' Herein, this is the method for noting: If, within the range of vision around that sign, there is a stone, it should be determined thus: 'This stone is high or low, small or large, red or black or white, long or round.' Then it should be well noted: 'In this particular spot, this is the stone, this is the sign of foulness; this is the sign of foulness, this is the stone.' If there is an anthill, it too should be determined thus: 'high or low, small or large, red or black or white, long or round.' Then it should be well noted: 'In this particular spot, this is the anthill, this is the sign of foulness.' If there is a tree, it too should be determined thus: 'an assattha or a nigrodha or a kacchaka or a kapītana; high or low, small or large, red or black or white.' Then it should be well noted: 'In this particular spot, this is the tree, this is the sign of foulness.' If there is a bush, it too should be determined thus: 'a sindi or a karamanda or a kaṇavīra or a kuraṇḍaka; high or low, small or large.' Then it should be well noted: 'In this particular spot, this is the bush, this is the sign of foulness.' If there is a creeper, it too should be determined thus: 'a lābu or a kumbhaṇḍī or a sāmā or a kāḷavalli or a pūtilatā.' Then it should be well noted: 'In this particular spot, this is the creeper, this is the sign of foulness; this is the sign of foulness, this is the creeper.'

109. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ sanimittaṃ karoti sārammaṇaṃ karotīti, taṃ idheva antogadhaṃ. Punappunaṃ vavatthapento hi sanimittaṃ karoti nāma. Ayaṃ pāsāṇo idaṃ asubhanimittaṃ, idaṃ asubhanimittaṃ ayaṃ pāsāṇoti evaṃ dve dve samāsetvā samāsetvā vavatthapento sārammaṇaṃ karoti nāma.

109. As for what was said—'one makes it with its sign, one makes it with its object'—that is included right here. For one who determines this again and again is said to 'make it with its sign.' By combining the two again and again and determining them thus—'This is the stone, this is the sign of foulness; this is the sign of foulness, this is the stone'—one is said to 'make it with its object.'

Evaṃ sanimittaṃ sārammaṇañca katvā pana sabhāvabhāvato vavatthapetīti vuttattā yvāssa sabhāvabhāvo anaññasādhāraṇo attaniyo uddhumātakabhāvo, tena manasikātabbaṃ. Vaṇitaṃ uddhumātakanti evaṃ sabhāvena sarasena vavatthapetabbanti attho.

Furthermore, having thus made it with its sign and with its object, since it is said, 'One determines it according to its intrinsic state,' one should attend to it by means of that intrinsic state which is its own, not shared with others—the state of being bloated. The meaning is that it should be determined by its intrinsic nature and its essential characteristic thus: 'The bloated is like a boil.'

110. Evaṃ vavatthapetvā vaṇṇatopi liṅgatopi saṇṭhānatopi disatopi okāsatopi paricchedatopīti chabbidhena nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Tena hi yoginā idaṃ sarīraṃ kāḷassa vā odātassa vā maṅguracchavino vāti vaṇṇato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Liṅgato pana itthiliṅgaṃ vā purisaliṅgaṃ vāti avavatthapetvā paṭhamavaye vā majjhimavaye vā pacchimavaye vā ṭhitassa idaṃ sarīranti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Saṇṭhānato uddhumātakassa [M 1.0179] saṇṭhānavaseneva idamassa sīsasaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ gīvāsaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ hatthasaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ udarasaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ nābhisaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ kaṭisaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ ūrusaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ jaṅghāsaṇṭhānaṃ, idaṃ pādasaṇṭhānanti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Disato pana imasmiṃ sarīre dve disā nābhiyā adho heṭṭhimadisā uddhaṃ uparimadisāti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Atha vā ahaṃ imissā disāya ṭhito asubhanimittaṃ imissāti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Okāsato pana imasmiṃ nāma okāse hatthā, imasmiṃ pādā, imasmiṃ sīsaṃ, imasmiṃ majjhimakāyo ṭhitoti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Atha vā ahaṃ imasmiṃ okāse ṭhito asubhanimittaṃ imasminti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Paricchedato idaṃ [V 1.0177] sarīraṃ adho pādatalena upari kesamatthakena tiriyaṃ tacena paricchinnaṃ, yathāparicchinne ca ṭhāne dvattiṃsakuṇapabharitamevāti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Atha vā ayamassa hatthaparicchedo, ayaṃ pādaparicchedo, ayaṃ sīsaparicchedo, ayaṃ majjhimakāyaparicchedoti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Yattakaṃ vā pana ṭhānaṃ gaṇhati, tattakameva idaṃ īdisaṃ uddhumātakanti paricchinditabbaṃ. Purisassa pana itthisarīraṃ itthiyā vā purisasarīraṃ na vaṭṭati. Visabhāge sarīre ārammaṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, vipphandanasseva paccayo hoti. “Ugghāṭitāpi hi itthī purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī”ti (a. ni. 5.55) majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tasmā sabhāgasarīreyeva evaṃ chabbidhena nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ.

110. Having thus determined, the sign should be grasped in six ways: by color, by characteristic, by shape, by direction, by location, and by delimitation. How? That yogi should determine this body by color, as: 'It is the body of a dark person,' or 'of a fair person,' or 'of one with a dusky complexion.' By characteristic: without determining it as 'a female characteristic' or 'a male characteristic,' it should be determined by age: 'This is the body of one who was in the first stage of life,' or 'in the middle stage of life,' or 'in the final stage of life.' By shape, in accordance with the shape of the bloated corpse itself, one should determine: 'This is the shape of its head, this is the shape of its neck, this is the shape of its hands, this is the shape of its belly, this is the shape of its navel, this is the shape of its waist, this is the shape of its thighs, this is the shape of its calves, this is the shape of its feet.' By direction, one should determine: 'In this body, there are two directions—below the navel is the lower direction, and above is the upper direction.' Alternatively, one should determine: 'I am standing in this direction, and the sign of foulness is situated in this direction.' By location, one should determine: 'In this particular location are the hands, in this the feet, in this the head, in this the middle part of the body.' Alternatively, one should determine: 'I am standing in this location, and the sign of foulness is situated in this location.' By delimitation, one should determine: 'This body is delimited below by the soles of the feet, above by the tips of the hair, and across by the skin; and in the place thus delimited, it is simply filled with thirty-two kinds of impurities.' Alternatively, one should determine: 'This is the delimitation of its hand, this is the delimitation of its foot, this is the delimitation of its head, this is the delimitation of the middle part of its body.' Or, whatever part one apprehends, just that much should be delimited thus: 'This bloated corpse is of such a nature.' However, a woman's body is not suitable for a man, nor is a man's body for a woman. In a dissimilar body, the meditation object does not become manifest; it is only a condition for the agitation of defilements. For it is said in the Majjhimaṭṭhakathā: 'Indeed, a woman, even when bloated, seizes and overcomes a man’s mind.' Therefore, the sign should be grasped in these six ways only in a body of the same sex.

111. Yo pana purimabuddhānaṃ santike āsevitakammaṭṭhāno parihatadhutaṅgo parimadditamahābhūto pariggahitasaṅkhāro vavatthāpitanāmarūpo ugghāṭitasattasañño katasamaṇadhammo vāsitavāsano bhāvitabhāvano sabījo ñāṇuttaro appakileso kulaputto, tassa olokitolokitaṭṭhāneyeva paṭibhāganimittaṃ upaṭṭhāti. No ce evaṃ upaṭṭhāti, athevaṃ chabbidhena nimittaṃ gaṇhato upaṭṭhāti. Yassa pana evampi na upaṭṭhāti, tena sandhito vivarato ninnato thalato samantatoti punapi pañcavidhena nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

111. Moreover, for a noble son who, in the presence of former Buddhas, has practiced the meditation subject, has undertaken the ascetic practices, has subdued the great elements, has comprehended the formations, has determined mind-and-matter, has removed the perception of a being, has fulfilled the duty of a recluse, whose dispositions have been perfumed, whose development has been cultivated, who possesses the seed, who has superior knowledge, and who has few defilements—for him the counterpart sign appears in the very place he looks. If it does not appear thus, then it appears for one who grasps the sign in six ways. But for one for whom it does not appear even in this way, the sign should be grasped by him again in five ways: by the joints, by the openings, by the depressions, by the elevations, and all around.

112. Tattha sandhitoti asītisatasandhito. Uddhumātake pana kathaṃ asītisatasandhayo vavatthapessati. Tasmānena tayo dakkhiṇahatthasandhī, tayo vāmahatthasandhī, tayo dakkhiṇapādasandhī, tayo vāmapādasandhī[M 1.0180], eko gīvasandhi, eko kaṭisandhīti evaṃ cuddasamahāsandhivasena sandhito vavatthapetabbaṃ. Vivaratoti vivaraṃ nāma hatthantaraṃ pādantaraṃ udarantaraṃ kaṇṇantaranti evaṃ vivarato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Akkhīnampi nimmīlitabhāvo vā ummīlitabhāvo vā mukhassa ca pihitabhāvo vā vivaṭabhāvo vā vavatthapetabbo. Ninnatoti yaṃ sarīre ninnaṭṭhānaṃ akkhikūpo vā antomukhaṃ vā galavāṭako vā, taṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Atha vā ahaṃ ninne ṭhito sarīraṃ unnateti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Thalatoti yaṃ sarīre unnataṭṭhānaṃ jaṇṇukaṃ vā uro vā nalāṭaṃ vā, taṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Atha vā ahaṃ thale ṭhito sarīraṃ ninneti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Samantatoti sabbaṃ sarīraṃ samantato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Sakalasarīre ñāṇaṃ cāretvā yaṃ ṭhānaṃ vibhūtaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, tattha “uddhumātakaṃ uddhumātaka”nti cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace evampi na upaṭṭhāti, udarapariyosānaṃ atirekaṃ uddhumātakaṃ hoti, tattha “uddhumātakaṃ uddhumātaka”nti cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ.

112. Herein, 'by the joints' refers to the one hundred and eighty joints. However, in a bloated corpse, how will one determine the one hundred and eighty joints? Therefore, it should be determined 'by the joints' by means of the fourteen great joints thus: three joints in the right hand, three joints in the left hand, three joints in the right foot, three joints in the left foot, one joint in the neck, and one joint in the waist. 'By the openings' means that an opening is namely the space between the hands, the space between the feet, the space within the belly, and the ear canals; thus it should be determined by the openings. The state of the eyes being closed or open, and of the mouth being shut or open, should also be determined. 'By the depressions' means that whatever depressed place exists in the body—such as the eye sockets, the inside of the mouth, or the gullet—that should be determined. Alternatively, one should determine, 'I am standing in a low place, the body is in a high place.' 'By the elevations' means that whatever elevated place exists in the body—such as the knee, the chest, or the forehead—that should be determined. Alternatively, one should determine, 'I am standing on high ground, the body is in a low place.' 'All around' means the entire body should be determined from all sides. Having made awareness circulate over the whole body, in whatever place the bloated state becomes manifest and appears, there the mind should be fixed, thinking, 'A bloated corpse, a bloated corpse.' If even in this way it does not appear, the upper body ending at the belly is exceedingly bloated; there the mind should be fixed, thinking, 'A bloated corpse, a bloated corpse.'

113. Idāni [V 1.0178] “so taṃ nimittaṃ suggahitaṃ karotī”tiādīsu ayaṃ vinicchayakathā –

113. Now, in the passages beginning with, 'He makes that sign well grasped,' this is the detailed explanation:

Tena yoginā tasmiṃ sarīre yathāvuttanimittaggāhavasena suṭṭhu nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ. Satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā āvajjitabbaṃ. Evaṃ punappunaṃ karontena sādhukaṃ upadhāretabbañceva vavatthapetabbañca. Sarīrato nātidūre nāccāsanne padese ṭhitena vā nisinnena vā cakkhuṃ ummīletvā oloketvā nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbaṃ. “Uddhumātakapaṭikkūlaṃ uddhumātakapaṭikkūla”nti satakkhattuṃ sahassakkhattuṃ ummīletvā oloketabbaṃ, nimmīletvā āvajjitabbaṃ. Evaṃ punappunaṃ karontassa uggahanimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti. Kadā suggahitaṃ hoti? Yadā ummīletvā olokentassa nimmīletvā āvajjentassa ca ekasadisaṃ hutvā āpāthamāgacchati, tadā suggahitaṃ nāma hoti.

By that yogi, the sign in that body should be thoroughly grasped by means of apprehending the sign in the way described. Having well-established mindfulness, he should advert to it. By doing so again and again, it should be well noted and well determined. Standing or sitting in a place not too far from nor too close to the body, having opened the eyes and looked, the sign should be grasped. As “Bloated and repulsive, bloated and repulsive,” having opened the eyes, he should look a hundred times, a thousand times; having closed them, he should advert to it. For one doing so again and again, the learning sign becomes well-grasped. When does it become well-grasped? When, for one looking with eyes open and for one adverting with eyes closed, it appears as one and the same, then it is called well-grasped.

So taṃ nimittaṃ evaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā sūpadhāritaṃ upadhāretvā suvavatthitaṃ vavatthapetvā sace tattheva bhāvanāpariyosānaṃ pattuṃ na sakkoti, athānena āgamanakāle vuttanayeneva ekakena adutiyena tadeva kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontena sūpaṭṭhitaṃ satiṃ katvā antogatehi [M 1.0181] indriyehi abahigatena mānasena attano senāsanameva gantabbaṃ.

Having thus made that sign well-grasped, having well-noted it, and having well-determined it, if he cannot reach the culmination of the meditation right there, then he should go to his own dwelling place by the method already stated at the time of his coming: alone, without a companion, attending to that very meditation subject, having established mindfulness well, with faculties turned inward and with a mind not directed outward.

Susānā nikkhamanteneva ca āgamanamaggo vavatthapetabbo, yena maggena nikkhantosmi, ayaṃ maggo pācīnadisābhimukho vā gacchati, pacchimauttaradakkhiṇadisābhimukho vā gacchati, vidisābhimukho vā gacchati. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne vāmato gacchati, imasmiṃ dakkhiṇato, imasmiṃ cassa ṭhāne pāsāṇo, imasmiṃ vammiko, imasmiṃ rukkho, imasmiṃ gaccho, imasmiṃ latāti evaṃ āgamanamaggaṃ vavatthapetvā āgatena caṅkamantenāpi tabbhāgiyova caṅkamo adhiṭṭhātabbo, asubhanimittadisābhimukhe bhūmippadese caṅkamitabbanti attho. Nisīdantena āsanampi tabbhāgiyameva paññapetabbaṃ. Sace pana tassaṃ disāyaṃ sobbho vā papāto vā rukkho vā vati vā kalalaṃ vā hoti, na sakkā taṃdisābhimukhe bhūmippadese caṅkamituṃ, āsanampi anokāsattā na sakkā paññapetuṃ. Taṃ disaṃ anapalokentenāpi okāsānurūpe ṭhāne caṅkamitabbañceva nisīditabbañca. Cittaṃ pana taṃdisābhimukhaṃyeva kātabbaṃ.

Furthermore, just upon leaving the charnel ground, the path of return should be determined: 'The path by which I have departed goes facing the eastern direction, or it goes facing the western, northern, or southern direction, or it goes facing an intermediate direction. Furthermore, in this place it goes to the left, in this place to the right. And in this place on the path there is a stone, in this place an anthill, in this place a tree, in this place a thicket, in this place a creeper.' Having thus determined the path of return, the yogi who has returned, even when practicing walking meditation, should resolve upon a walking path that is related to that sign. The meaning is that one should walk on a plot of ground facing the direction of the repulsive sign. When sitting, a seat related to that very sign should also be prepared. But if in that direction there is a pit, a precipice, a tree, a fence, or mud, and it is not possible to walk on a plot of ground facing that direction, and it is not possible to prepare a seat due to lack of space, then even without looking at that direction, one should both walk and sit in a suitable place. However, the mind should be directed towards that very direction.

114. Idāni “samantā nimittupalakkhaṇā kimatthiyā”tiādipañhānaṃ “asammohatthā”tiādivissajjane [V 1.0179] ayaṃ adhippāyo. Yassa hi avelāyaṃ uddhumātakanimittaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā samantā nimittupalakkhaṇaṃ katvā nimittaggahaṇatthaṃ cakkhuṃ ummīletvā olokentasseva taṃ matasarīraṃ uṭṭhahitvā ṭhitaṃ viya ajjhottharamānaṃ viya anubandhamānaṃ viya ca hutvā upaṭṭhāti, so taṃ bībhacchaṃ bheravārammaṇaṃ disvā vikkhittacitto ummattako viya hoti, bhayaṃ chambhitattaṃ lomahaṃsaṃ pāpuṇāti. Pāḷiyaṃ hi vibhattaaṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu aññaṃ evarūpaṃ bheravārammaṇaṃ nāma natthi. Imasmiṃ hi kammaṭṭhāne jhānavibbhantako nāma hoti. Kasmā? Atibheravattā kammaṭṭhānassa. Tasmā tena yoginā santhambhetvā satiṃ sūpaṭṭhitaṃ katvā matasarīraṃ uṭṭhahitvā anubandhanakaṃ nāma natthi. Sace hi so “etassa samīpe ṭhito pāsāṇo vā latā vā āgaccheyya, sarīrampi āgaccheyya. Yathā pana so pāsāṇo vā latā vā nāgacchati, evaṃ sarīrampi nāgacchati. Ayaṃ pana tuyhaṃ upaṭṭhānākāro saññajo saññāsambhavo, kammaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0182] te ajja upaṭṭhitaṃ, mā bhāyi bhikkhū”ti tāsaṃ vinodetvā hāsaṃ uppādetvā tasmiṃ nimitte cittaṃ sañcarāpetabbaṃ. Evaṃ visesamadhigacchati. Idametaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “samantā nimittupalakkhaṇā asammohatthā”ti.

114. Now, the intention behind the questions such as, “What is the purpose of marking the signs all around?” and the answers such as, “for the sake of non-bewilderment,” is this: For when a certain meditator, at an unsuitable time, goes to a place where there is the sign of a bloated corpse, marks the signs all around, and opens his eyes to look in order to grasp the sign—if that very dead body appears to him as if it has risen up, as if it is rushing upon him, or as if it is pursuing him—then, seeing that repulsive and terrifying object, his mind becomes scattered, he becomes as if insane, and he experiences fear, stiffness, and horripilation. Indeed, in the Pāḷi, among the thirty-eight analyzed objects of meditation, there is no other so-called object that is as terrifying as this. In this meditation subject, one can become what is called a “jhāna-deviator.” Why? Because the meditation subject is extremely terrifying. Therefore, that meditator should compose himself, establish mindfulness well, and reflect thus: “There is no such thing as a dead body rising up and pursuing. For if a rock or a vine standing near it were to come, the body too would come. But just as that rock or vine does not come, so too the body does not come. This mode of appearance to you, however, is born of perception, has its origin in perception. The meditation subject has appeared to you today. Do not be afraid, monk!”—thus dispelling that terror and arousing joy, he should direct his mind to that sign. In this way, he attains a special state. It is with reference to this that it is said, “Marking the signs all around is for the sake of non-bewilderment.”

Ekādasavidhena pana nimittaggāhaṃ sampādento kammaṭṭhānaṃ upanibandhati. Tassa hi cakkhūni ummīletvā olokanapaccayā uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati. Tasmiṃ mānasaṃ cārentassa paṭibhāganimittaṃ uppajjati. Tattha mānasaṃ cārento appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Appanāyaṃ ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento arahattaṃ sacchikaroti. Tena vuttaṃ “ekādasavidhena nimittaggāho upanibandhanattho”ti.

Furthermore, one who accomplishes the grasping of the sign in eleven ways binds the meditation subject. Indeed, for that yogi, the learning sign arises conditioned by opening the eyes and looking. For one repeatedly applying the mind to that learning sign, the counterpart sign arises. Repeatedly applying the mind to that counterpart sign, one attains absorption. Having stood firm in absorption and developing insight, one realizes Arahantship. Therefore, it was said: 'The grasping of the sign in eleven ways has the purpose of binding.'

115. Gatāgatamaggapaccavekkhaṇā vīthisampaṭipādanatthāti ettha pana yā gatamaggassa ca āgatamaggassa ca paccavekkhaṇā vuttā, sā kammaṭṭhānavīthiyā sampaṭipādanatthāti attho. Sace hi imaṃ bhikkhuṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā āgacchantaṃ antarāmagge keci ajja, bhante, katimīti divasaṃ vā pucchanti, pañhaṃ vā pucchanti, paṭisanthāraṃ vā karonti, ahaṃ kammaṭṭhānikoti tuṇhībhūtena gantuṃ na vaṭṭati. Divaso kathetabbo, pañho vissajjetabbo. Sace na jānāti, na jānāmīti vattabbaṃ. Dhammiko paṭisanthāro kātabbo. Tassevaṃ karontassa uggahitaṃ taruṇanimittaṃ nassati. Tasmiṃ nassantepi divasaṃ puṭṭhena kathetabbameva. Pañhaṃ ajānantena na jānāmīti vattabbaṃ. Jānantena ekadesena kathetumpi vaṭṭati, paṭisanthāropi kātabbo. Āgantukaṃ [V 1.0180] pana bhikkhuṃ disvā āgantukapaṭisanthāro kātabbova. Avasesānipi cetiyaṅgaṇavattabodhiyaṅgaṇavattauposathāgāravattabhojanasālājantāgharaācariyupajjhāyaāgantukagamikavattādīni sabbāni khandhakavattāni pūretabbāneva. Tassa tāni pūrentassāpi taṃ taruṇanimittaṃ nassati, puna gantvā nimittaṃ gaṇhissāmīti gantukāmassāpi amanussehi vā vāḷamigehi vā adhiṭṭhitattā susānampi gantuṃ na sakkā hoti, nimittaṃ vā antaradhāyati. Uddhumātakaṃ hi ekameva vā dve vā divase ṭhatvā vinīlakādibhāvaṃ gacchati. Sabbakammaṭṭhānesu etena samaṃ dullabhaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā evaṃ naṭṭhe nimitte tena bhikkhunā rattiṭṭhāne vā divāṭhāne vā nisīditvā ahaṃ iminā nāma dvārena vihārā nikkhamitvā asukadisābhimukhaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā asukasmiṃ [M 1.0183] nāma ṭhāne vāmaṃ gaṇhi, asukasmiṃ dakkhiṇaṃ. Tassa asukasmiṃ ṭhāne pāsāṇo, asukasmiṃ vammikarukkhagacchalatānamaññataraṃ. Sohaṃ tena maggena gantvā asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne asubhaṃ addasaṃ. Tattha asukadisābhimukho ṭhatvā evañcevañca samantā nimittāni sallakkhetvā evaṃ asubhanimittaṃ uggahetvā asukadisāya susānato nikkhamitvā evarūpena nāma maggena idañcidañca karonto āgantvā idha nisinnoti evaṃ yāva pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ, tāva gatāgatamaggo paccavekkhitabbo. Tassevaṃ paccavekkhato taṃ nimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, purato nikkhittaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ purimākāreneva vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “gatāgatamaggapaccavekkhaṇā vīthisampaṭipādanatthā”ti.

115. Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'the reflection on the path of going and returning is for the purpose of setting the meditation subject on its course,' the meaning is this: the reflection on the path gone and the path returned, which was mentioned, is for the purpose of properly setting the meditation subject on its course. For if, while this monk is returning after having apprehended a meditation subject, some people on the way ask him about the day, saying, 'Venerable sir, what day of the month is it today?', or ask him a question, or offer a friendly greeting, it is not proper for him to go on in silence, thinking, 'I am a meditator.' The day should be told; the question should be answered. If he does not know, he should say, 'I do not know.' A righteous friendly greeting should be made. For him, while doing so, the tender sign that had been apprehended is lost. Even when it is lost, when asked about the day, it must indeed be told. Not knowing the answer to a question, he should say, 'I do not know.' Knowing it, it is proper to speak of it in part; a friendly greeting should also be made. Furthermore, upon seeing a visiting monk, the friendly greeting due to a visitor must certainly be made. And all the remaining duties of the Khandhakas—such as the duties for the stupa-courtyard, the Bodhi-tree-courtyard, the Uposatha hall, the dining hall, the steam-bath, for one's teacher, preceptor, for visitors, for those departing, etc.—must certainly be fulfilled. For him, while fulfilling those duties, that tender sign is also lost. And even if he wishes to go again and apprehend the sign, thinking, 'I will go and apprehend the sign,' it may not be possible to go to the charnel ground due to it being guarded by non-human beings or by savage beasts, or the sign itself may disappear. Indeed, a bloated corpse, having remained for just one or two days, reaches a state of being discolored, and so on. Among all meditation subjects, there is none so difficult to obtain as this one. Therefore, when the sign is lost in this way, that monk, having sat down in his night-time place or his day-time place, should reflect: 'I, having left the monastery by such-and-such a gate, having taken the path facing such-and-such a direction, at such-and-such a place I turned left, at such-and-such a place I turned right. At such-and-such a place on that path there was a stone; at such-and-such a place there was one among a termite-mound, tree, shrub, or creeper. I, having gone by that path, saw the unlovely object at such-and-such a place. There, having stood facing such-and-such a direction and having marked the signs all around in this and that way, I thus apprehended the sign of the unlovely. Having left the charnel ground in such-and-such a direction, and having come by such-and-such a path while doing this and that, I am now seated here.' In this way, up to the very place where he is seated with his legs crossed, the path of going and returning should be reflected upon. For him who is reflecting thus, that sign becomes manifest; it appears as if placed in front of him. The meditation subject proceeds onto its course in just the same way as before. Therefore, it was said: 'The reflection on the path of going and returning is for the purpose of setting the meditation subject on its course.'

116. Idāni ānisaṃsadassāvī ratanasaññī hutvā cittīkāraṃ upaṭṭhapetvā sampiyāyamāno tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittaṃ upanibandhatīti ettha uddhumātakapaṭikkūle mānasaṃ cāretvā jhānaṃ nibbattetvā jhānapadaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento “addhā imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇamhā parimuccissāmī”ti evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinā bhavitabbaṃ.

116. Now, regarding the statement: 'Seeing the benefits, perceiving it as a jewel, establishing respect, and cherishing it, one binds the mind to that object.' Herein, having directed the mind to a bloated and repulsive corpse and produced jhāna, one who is developing insight that has jhāna as its proximate cause should become one who sees the benefits in this way, thinking: 'Surely, by this practice, I will be liberated from aging and death.'

Yathā pana duggato puriso mahagghaṃ maṇiratanaṃ labhitvā dullabhaṃ vata me laddhanti tasmiṃ ratanasaññī hutvā gāravaṃ janetvā vipulena pemena sampiyāyamāno taṃ rakkheyya, evameva “dullabhaṃ me idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ laddhaṃ duggatassa mahagghamaṇiratanasadisaṃ. Catudhātukammaṭṭhāniko hi attano cattāro mahābhūte pariggaṇhāti, ānāpānakammaṭṭhāniko attano nāsikavātaṃ pariggaṇhāti, kasiṇakammaṭṭhāniko kasiṇaṃ katvā yathāsukhaṃ bhāveti, evaṃ itarāni kammaṭṭhānāni [V 1.0181] sulabhāni. ‘Idaṃ pana ekameva vā dve vā divase tiṭṭhati, tato paraṃ vinīlakādibhāvaṃ pāpuṇātī’ti natthi ito dullabhatara”nti tasmiṃ ratanasaññinā hutvā cittīkāraṃ upaṭṭhapetvā sampiyāyamānena taṃ nimittaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ. Rattiṭṭhāne ca divāṭhāne ca “uddhumātakapaṭikkūlaṃ uddhumātakapaṭikkūla”nti tattha punappunaṃ cittaṃ upanibandhitabbaṃ. Punappunaṃ taṃ nimittaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ, manasikātabbaṃ. Takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ kātabbaṃ.

Just as a poor man, having obtained a priceless gem, would think, 'Rare indeed is what I have obtained!', and perceiving it as a treasure, generating respect, and cherishing it with great affection, would guard it; in the very same way, one should think: 'Rare indeed is this meditation subject I have obtained, like a priceless gem for a poor person. For one who practices the four-elements meditation comprehends their own four great elements; one who practices mindfulness of breathing comprehends their own breath at the nose; one who practices the kasiṇa meditation, having made a kasiṇa, develops it as they please. Thus, other meditation subjects are easy to obtain. But this one lasts for only one or two days, after which it reaches the state of becoming blue-black and so forth. There is nothing rarer than this.' Perceiving that sign as a treasure, having established respect and cherishing it, that sign should be guarded. At one's place for the night and one's place for the day, the mind should be repeatedly bound to it with the thought, 'The bloated corpse is repulsive, the bloated corpse is repulsive.' Again and again, that sign should be adverted to and attended to. It should be struck by reflection, struck by initial application.

117. Tassevaṃ karoto paṭibhāganimittaṃ uppajjati. Tatridaṃ nimittadvayassa nānākaraṇaṃ, uggahanimittaṃ virūpaṃ bībhacchaṃ bheravadassanaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti[M 1.0184]. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā nipanno thūlaṅgapaccaṅgapuriso viya. Tassa paṭibhāganimittapaṭilābhasamakālameva bahiddhā kāmānaṃ amanasikārā vikkhambhanavasena kāmacchando pahīyati. Anunayappahāneneva cassa lohitappahānena pubbo viya byāpādopi pahīyati. Tathā āraddhavīriyatāya thinamiddhaṃ, avippaṭisārakarasantadhammānuyogavasena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ, adhigatavisesassa paccakkhatāya paṭipattidesake satthari paṭipattiyaṃ paṭipattiphale ca vicikicchā pahīyatīti pañca nīvaraṇāni pahīyanti. Tasmiññeva ca nimitte cetaso abhiniropanalakkhaṇo vitakko, nimittānumajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamāno vicāro, paṭiladdhavisesādhigamapaccayā pīti, pītimanassa passaddhisambhavato passaddhi, tannimittaṃ sukhaṃ, sukhitassa cittasamādhisambhavato sukhanimittā ekaggatā cāti jhānaṅgāni pātubhavanti. Evamassa paṭhamajjhānapaṭibimbabhūtaṃ upacārajjhānampi taṅkhaṇaññeva nibbattati. Ito paraṃ yāva paṭhamajjhānassa appanā ceva vasippatti ca, tāva sabbaṃ pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

117. For one who practices thus, the counterpart sign arises. Herein is the distinction between the two signs: the learning sign appears distorted, repulsive, and frightful to behold. The counterpart sign, however, appears like a man with stout major and minor limbs who, having eaten to his heart's content, is lying down. For him, at the very same time as the acquisition of the counterpart sign, sensual desire is abandoned by way of suppression due to non-attention to external sensual pleasures. And for him, just by the abandonment of attachment, ill will is also abandoned, like pus is removed by the removal of blood. Likewise, due to having aroused energy, sloth and torpor are abandoned; by way of application to peaceful states that cause no remorse, restlessness and remorse are abandoned; and due to the direct experience of the distinction that has been attained, doubt is abandoned regarding the Teacher who teaches the practice, the practice, and the fruit of the practice. In this way, the five hindrances are abandoned. And on that very sign, the absorption factors become manifest: initial application, characterized by directing the mind onto the object; sustained application, accomplishing the task of repeatedly examining the sign; joy, caused by attaining the acquired distinction; and since tranquility arises for one with a joyful mind, there is happiness, which has that tranquility as its cause; and since concentration of mind arises for one who is happy, there is one-pointedness, which has happiness as its cause. Thus, for him, access concentration, which is a reflection of the first absorption, also arises at that very moment. Hereafter, up to the full absorption and mastery of the first absorption, everything should be understood by the same method as was stated in the section on the earth kasiṇa.

Vinīlakādikammaṭṭhānāni

The Meditation Subjects Beginning with the Livid One

118. Ito paresu pana vinīlakādīsupi yaṃ taṃ “uddhumātakaṃ asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhanto eko adutiyo gacchati upaṭṭhitāya satiyā”tiādinā nayena gamanaṃ ādiṃ katvā lakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ “vinīlakaṃ asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhanto, vipubbakaṃ asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhanto”ti evaṃ tassa tassa vasena tattha tattha uddhumātakapadamattaṃ parivattetvā vuttanayeneva savinicchayādhippāyaṃ veditabbaṃ.

118. Furthermore, in the subsequent meditation subjects, such as the livid one and so on, whatever characteristic has been stated—beginning with the going [to the charnel ground] in the manner of 'apprehending the sign of the foulness of a bloated corpse, one goes alone, without a companion, with mindfulness established,' and so on—all that should be understood, with its analysis and meaning, by the same method as was stated, by replacing just the term 'bloated' in each respective case according to each respective type of foulness, thus: 'apprehending the sign of the foulness of a livid corpse,' 'apprehending the sign of the foulness of a festering corpse.'

Ayaṃ [V 1.0182] pana viseso – vinīlake “vinīlakapaṭikkūlaṃ vinīlakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Uggahanimittañcettha kabarakabaravaṇṇaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana ussadavasena upaṭṭhāti.

This, however, is the distinction: In the case of the livid one, attention should be directed thus: 'Livid and repulsive, livid and repulsive.' And here, the learning sign appears having a variegated, mottled color. The counterpart sign, however, appears by way of the predominant color.

Vipubbake “vipubbakapaṭikkūlaṃ vipubbakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Uggahanimittaṃ panettha paggharantamiva upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ niccalaṃ sannisinnaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

In the case of the festering one, attention should be directed thus: 'Festering and repulsive, festering and repulsive.' Here, the learning sign appears as if oozing. The counterpart sign appears motionless and settled.

Vicchiddakaṃ yuddhamaṇḍale vā corāṭaviyaṃ vā susāne vā yattha rājāno [M 1.0185] core chindāpenti. Araññe vā pana sīhabyagghehi chinnapurisaṭṭhāne labbhati. Tasmā tathārūpaṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā sace nānādisāyaṃ patitampi ekāvajjanena āpāthamāgacchati iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce āgacchati, sayaṃ hatthena na parāmasitabbaṃ. Parāmasanto hi vissāsaṃ āpajjati. Tasmā ārāmikena vā samaṇuddesena vā aññena vā kenaci ekaṭṭhāne kāretabbaṃ. Alabhantena kattarayaṭṭhiyā vā daṇḍakena vā ekaṅgulantaraṃ katvā upanāmetabbaṃ. Evaṃ upanāmetvā “vicchiddakapaṭikkūlaṃ vicchiddakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Tattha uggahanimittaṃ majjhe chiddaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana paripuṇṇaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

The dismembered one is found on a battlefield, or in a robber-infested forest, or in a charnel ground where kings have thieves executed. Or, in the wilderness, it is found in a place where a person has been torn apart by lions and tigers. Therefore, having gone to such a place, if the parts of the corpse, though fallen in various directions, come into range with a single advertence of mind, this is skillful. If they do not come into range, one should not touch them with one’s own hand. For in touching them, one might attain familiarity. Therefore, they should be caused to be put in one place by a monastery attendant, or a novice, or by some other person. If one cannot obtain such a person, one should bring them near with a walking stick or a staff, leaving a one-finger-breadth gap. Having brought them near in this way, attention should be directed thus: 'Dismembered and repulsive, dismembered and repulsive.' There, the learning sign appears as if with a gap in the middle. The counterpart sign, however, appears as complete.

Vikkhāyitake vikkhāyitakapaṭikkūlaṃ vikkhāyitakapaṭikkūlanti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Uggahanimittaṃ panettha tahiṃ tahiṃ khāyitasadisameva upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ paripuṇṇaṃva hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

In the case of the gnawed-at one, attention should be directed thus: 'The gnawed-at one is repulsive, the gnawed-at one is repulsive.' Herein, the learning sign appears just like the object gnawed in various places. The counterpart sign appears as if complete.

Vikkhittakampi vicchiddake vuttanayeneva aṅgulaṅgulantaraṃ kāretvā vā katvā vā “vikkhittakapaṭikkūlaṃ vikkhittakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Ettha uggahanimittaṃ pākaṭantaraṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana paripuṇṇaṃva hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

For the scattered one as well, in the same way as stated for the dismembered one, having either made or caused to be made a finger's breadth interval, attention should be directed thus: 'The scattered one is repulsive, the scattered one is repulsive.' Herein, the learning sign appears with clear intervals. The counterpart sign, however, appears as if complete.

Hatavikkhittakampi vicchiddake vuttappakāresuyeva ṭhānesu labbhati. Tasmā tattha gantvā vuttanayeneva aṅgulaṅgulantaraṃ kāretvā vā katvā vā “hatavikkhittakapaṭikkūlaṃ hatavikkhittakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Uggahanimittaṃ panettha paññāyamānaṃ pahāramukhaṃ viya hoti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ paripuṇṇameva hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

The hacked and scattered one is also found in the very same kinds of places as mentioned for the dismembered one. Therefore, having gone there and, in the same way as stated, having either made or caused to be made a finger's breadth interval, attention should be directed thus: 'The hacked and scattered one is repulsive, the hacked and scattered one is repulsive.' Herein, the learning sign is like a visible opening of a wound. The counterpart sign appears as truly complete.

Lohitakaṃ [V 1.0183] yuddhamaṇḍalādīsu laddhappahārānaṃ hatthapādādīsu vā chinnesu bhinnagaṇḍapīḷakādīnaṃ vā mukhato paggharamānakāle labbhati. Tasmā taṃ disvā “lohitakapaṭikkūlaṃ lohitakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Ettha uggahanimittaṃ vātappahatā viya rattapaṭākā calamānākāraṃ upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ pana sannisinnaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

The bloody one is found on battlefields and so on, at the time when blood is gushing from the opening of wounds of those who have received blows, or when their hands, feet, and so on, are severed, or from broken boils, pustules, and the like. Therefore, having seen it, attention should be directed thus: 'The bloody one is repulsive, the bloody one is repulsive.' Herein, the learning sign appears in a state of motion, like a red banner struck by the wind. The counterpart sign, however, appears as still.

Puḷavakaṃ dvīhatīhaccayena kuṇapassa navahi vaṇamukhehi kimirāsipaggharaṇakāle hoti. Apica taṃ soṇasiṅgālamanussagomahiṃsahatthiassaajagarādīnaṃ sarīrappamāṇameva hutvā sālibhattarāsi viya tiṭṭhati[M 1.0186]. Tesu yattha katthaci “puḷavakapaṭikkūlaṃ puḷavakapaṭikkūla”nti manasikāro pavattetabbo. Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissattherassa hi kāḷadīghavāpiyā anto hatthikuṇape nimittaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. Uggahanimittaṃ panettha calamānaṃ viya upaṭṭhāti. Paṭibhāganimittaṃ sālibhattapiṇḍo viya sannisinnaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti.

The worm-infested foulness occurs when, after two or three days, a mass of worms oozes out from the nine openings of a corpse. Moreover, being of the same size as the bodies of dogs, jackals, humans, cattle, buffaloes, elephants, horses, pythons, and so on, it remains like a heap of fine rice. In any of these bodies, one should direct one's attention thus: 'The worm-infested is repulsive, the worm-infested is repulsive.' Indeed, for the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa, the sign appeared in an elephant's corpse inside the Kāḷadīghavāpī pond. Herein, the learning sign appears as if stirring. The counterpart sign appears still, like a lump of fine rice.

Aṭṭhikaṃ “seyyathāpi passeyya sarīraṃ sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ aṭṭhisaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nahārusambandha”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.154) nayena nānappakārato vuttaṃ. Tattha yattha taṃ nikkhittaṃ hoti, tattha purimanayeneva gantvā samantā pāsāṇādīnaṃ vasena sanimittaṃ sārammaṇaṃ katvā idaṃ aṭṭhikanti sabhāvabhāvato upalakkhetvā vaṇṇādivasena ekādasahākārehi nimittaṃ uggahetabbaṃ.

The skeleton foulness is described in various ways by the method beginning: 'Just as one might see a body cast away in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by tendons...' There, wherever it has been discarded, one should go to that place by the very same method as before and, by means of rocks and so on from all around, establish the object together with its landmarks. Having firmly noted by its intrinsic nature, 'This is a skeleton,' the sign should be grasped by means of the eleven aspects, such as color and so on.

119. Taṃ pana vaṇṇato setanti olokentassa na upaṭṭhāti, odātakasiṇasambhedo hoti. Tasmā aṭṭhikanti paṭikkūlavaseneva oloketabbaṃ. Liṅganti idha hatthādīnaṃ nāmaṃ. Tasmā hatthapādasīsaurabāhukaṭiūrujaṅghānaṃ vasena liṅgato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Dīgharassavaṭṭacaturassakhuddakamahantavasena pana saṇṭhānato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Disokāsā vuttanayā eva. Tassa tassa aṭṭhino pariyantavasena paricchedato vavatthapetvā yadevettha pākaṭaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti, taṃ gahetvā appanā pāpuṇitabbā. Tassa tassa aṭṭhino ninnaṭṭhānathalaṭṭhānavasena pana ninnato ca thalato ca vavatthapetabbaṃ. Padesavasenāpi ahaṃ ninne ṭhito, aṭṭhi thale, ahaṃ thale, aṭṭhi ninnetipi vavatthapetabbaṃ. Dvinnaṃ pana aṭṭhikānaṃ ghaṭitaghaṭitaṭṭhānavasena sandhito vavatthapetabbaṃ. Aṭṭhikānaṃyeva antaravasena vivarato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Sabbattheva pana ñāṇaṃ cāretvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne idamaṭṭhīti samantato vavatthapetabbaṃ. Evampi nimitte anupaṭṭhahante nalāṭaṭṭhimhi cittaṃ saṇṭhapetabbaṃ.

119. Furthermore, for one who looks at it by way of color as 'white,' it does not appear as a repulsive object; it becomes mingled with the white kasiṇa. Therefore, it should be looked at only by way of repulsiveness as 'a bone.' Here, 'feature' is the name for the hand and so on. Therefore, it should be determined by feature by way of the hand, foot, head, chest, arm, hip, thigh, and shin. Furthermore, by shape, it should be determined by way of being long, short, round, square, small, or large. Direction and location are just as has been stated. Having determined the boundary of each and every bone by way of its limits, and having taken up whichever bone among them becomes manifest and appears, one should attain absorption. Furthermore, by way of the low-lying places and high places of each and every bone, it should be determined by what is low-lying and what is high. Also by way of location, it should be determined thus: 'I am standing in a low-lying place, the bone is on high ground,' or 'I am on high ground, the bone is in a low-lying place.' Furthermore, by way of the place where two bones are joined, it should be determined by the joint. By way of the interval between the bones themselves, it should be determined by the opening. Furthermore, having made one's knowledge range over the entire skeleton, it should be determined all around thus: 'In this place is this bone.' Even so, if the sign does not appear, the mind should be established on the forehead bone.

120. Yathā [V 1.0184] cettha, evaṃ idaṃ ekādasavidhena nimittaggahaṇaṃ ito purimesu puḷavakādīsupi yujjamānavasena sallakkhetabbaṃ. Idañca pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ sakalāyapi aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāya ekasmimpi aṭṭhike sampajjati. Tasmā tesu yatthakatthaci ekādasavidhena nimittaṃ uggahetvā “aṭṭhikapaṭikkūlaṃ aṭṭhikapaṭikkūla”nti [M 1.0187] manasikāro pavattetabbo. Idha uggahanimittampi paṭibhāganimittampi ekasadisameva hotīti vuttaṃ, taṃ ekasmiṃ aṭṭhike yuttaṃ. Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāya pana uggahanimitte paññāyamāne vivaratā. Paṭibhāganimitte paripuṇṇabhāvo yujjati. Ekaṭṭhikepi ca uggahanimittena bībhacchena bhayānakena bhavitabbaṃ. Paṭibhāganimittena pītisomanassajanakena, upacārāvahattā.

120. Just as in this case, so too this elevenfold taking up of the sign should be understood as applicable in the previous cases beginning with the worm-infested. Furthermore, this meditation subject is accomplished both with a complete skeleton and with a single bone. Therefore, in any of these cases, having taken up the sign in the elevenfold way, attention should be directed thus: 'The bone is repulsive, the bone is repulsive.' Here it is said that both the learning sign and the counterpart sign are just the same; that is suitable for a single bone. In the case of a skeleton, however, the learning sign has apparent gaps, whereas the counterpart sign is suitably complete. And even in the case of a single bone, the learning sign should be disgusting and frightening, while the counterpart sign should produce joy and gladness, as it leads to access concentration.

Imasmiṃ hi okāse yaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, taṃ dvāraṃ datvāva vuttaṃ. Tathā hi tattha “catūsu brahmavihāresu dasasu ca asubhesu paṭibhāganimittaṃ natthi. Brahmavihāresu hi sīmasambhedoyeva nimittaṃ. Dasasu ca asubhesu nibbikappaṃ katvā paṭikkūlabhāveyeva diṭṭhe nimittaṃ nāma hotī”ti vatvāpi puna anantarameva “duvidhaṃ idha nimittaṃ uggahanimittaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Uggahanimittaṃ virūpaṃ bībhacchaṃ bhayānakaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhātī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tasmā yaṃ vicāretvā avocumha, idamevettha yuttaṃ.

For in this context, what is said in the commentaries is stated by way of giving an opening. For there, even after saying: 'In the four divine abidings and in the ten foulnesses, there is no counterpart sign. For in the divine abidings, the very breaking of boundaries is the sign. And in the ten foulnesses, when the repulsive nature itself is seen without conceptualization, it is called the sign,' it is then stated immediately after: 'Here the sign is twofold: the learning sign and the counterpart sign. The learning sign appears, being deformed, disgusting, and frightening,' and so on. Therefore, what we have said after investigation, that very thing is suitable here.

Apica mahātissattherassa dantaṭṭhikamattāvalokanena sakalitthisarīrassa aṭṭhisaṅghātabhāvena upaṭṭhānādīni cettha nidassanānīti.

Moreover, the appearance of the entire woman's body as a heap of bones to the Elder Mahātissa through the mere sight of a tooth-bone, and so on, are examples here.

Iti asubhāni subhaguṇo, dasasatalocanena thutakitti;

Yāni avoca dasabalo, ekekajjhānahetunīti.

Thus, the Ten-Powered One—He of excellent qualities, whose fame is praised by the thousand-eyed one—declared those foulnesses, each of which is a cause for the first jhāna.

Evaṃ tāni ca tesañca, bhāvanānayamimaṃ viditvāna;

Tesveva ayaṃ bhiyyo, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

Thus, having known both those ten foulnesses and this method of their development, this miscellaneous talk concerning them should be further understood.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse

121. Etesu hi yattha katthaci adhigatajjhāno suvikkhambhitarāgattā vītarāgo viya nilloluppacāro [V 1.0185] hoti. Evaṃ santepi yvāyaṃ asubhappabhedo vutto, so sarīrasabhāvappattivasena ca rāgacaritabhedavasena cāti veditabbo. Chavasarīraṃ hi paṭikkūlabhāvaṃ āpajjamānaṃ uddhumātakasabhāvappattaṃ vā siyā, vinīlakādīnaṃ vā aññatarasabhāvappattaṃ. Iti yādisaṃ yādisaṃ sakkā hoti laddhuṃ, tādise tādise uddhumātakapaṭikkūlaṃ vinīlakapaṭikkūlanti evaṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhitabbamevāti sarīrasabhāvappattivasena dasadhā asubhappabhedo vuttoti veditabbo.

121. Indeed, among these, in any one whatsoever, a yogi who has attained jhāna, due to the thorough suppression of lust, is free from fickle behavior, like one who is free from lust. Even so, it should be understood that this division of foulness that has been taught is by way of the state the corpse has reached and by way of the different types of lustful temperament. For a corpse, on becoming repulsive, might reach the state of a bloated one, or it might reach the state of one of the others, such as the livid. Therefore, whatever kind of corpse it is possible to obtain, in that very kind the sign should be grasped thus: 'the foulness of the bloated,' 'the foulness of the livid.' Thus, it should be understood that the tenfold division of foulness is taught by way of the state the corpse has reached.

Visesato [M 1.0188] cettha uddhumātakaṃ sarīrasaṇṭhānavipattippakāsanato saṇṭhānarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vinīlakaṃ chavirāgavipattippakāsanato sarīravaṇṇarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vipubbakaṃ kāyavaṇapaṭibaddhassa duggandhabhāvassa pakāsanato mālāgandhādivasena samuṭṭhāpitasarīragandharāgino sappāyaṃ. Vicchiddakaṃ antosusirabhāvappakāsanato sarīre ghanabhāvarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vikkhāyitakaṃ maṃsupacayasampattivināsappakāsanato thanādīsu sarīrappadesesu maṃsupacayarāgino sappāyaṃ. Vikkhittakaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ vikkhepappakāsanato aṅgapaccaṅgalīlārāgino sappāyaṃ. Hatavikkhittakaṃ sarīrasaṅghātabhedavikārappakāsanato sarīrasaṅghātasampattirāgino sappāyaṃ. Lohitakaṃ lohitamakkhitapaṭikkūlabhāvappakāsanato alaṅkārajanitasobharāgino sappāyaṃ. Puḷavakaṃ kāyassa anekakimikulasādhāraṇabhāvappakāsanato kāye mamattarāgino sappāyaṃ. Aṭṭhikaṃ sarīraṭṭhīnaṃ paṭikkūlabhāvappakāsanato dantasampattirāgino sappāyanti evaṃ rāgacaritabhedavasenāpi dasadhā asubhappabhedo vuttoti veditabbo.

Here, especially, the bloated corpse is suitable for one with lust for form, as it reveals the destruction of the body’s form. The livid corpse is suitable for one with lust for the body’s complexion, as it reveals the corruption of the skin’s beauty. The festering corpse is suitable for one with lust for bodily scents produced by means of garlands, perfumes, and so on, as it reveals the state of foul smell connected with the body as a wound. The cut-up corpse is suitable for one with lust for the body’s solidity, as it reveals the state of being hollow inside. The gnawed corpse is suitable for one with lust for the accumulation of flesh in regions of the body such as the breasts, as it reveals the destruction of the fullness of the accumulation of flesh. The scattered corpse is suitable for one with lust for the gracefulness of the major and minor limbs, as it reveals the scattering of the limbs. The hacked and scattered corpse is suitable for one with lust for the perfection of the body’s cohesion, as it reveals the alteration which is the breaking of the body’s cohesion. The bloody corpse is suitable for one with lust for beauty produced by adornments, as it reveals the repulsive state of being smeared with blood. The worm-infested corpse is suitable for one with lust for ‘mineness’ regarding the body, as it reveals the state of being common to many families of worms. The skeleton is suitable for one with lust for the perfection of the teeth, as it reveals the repulsive state of the body’s bones. Thus, it should be understood that the tenfold division of foulness is also taught by way of the different types of lustful temperament.

Yasmā pana dasavidhepi etasmiṃ asubhe seyyathāpi nāma aparisaṇṭhitajalāya sīghasotāya nadiyā arittabaleneva nāvā tiṭṭhati, vinā arittena na sakkā ṭhapetuṃ, evameva dubbalattā ārammaṇassa vitakkabaleneva cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, vinā vitakkena na sakkā ṭhapetuṃ, tasmā paṭhamajjhānamevettha hoti, na dutiyādīni.

Furthermore, in this tenfold foulness, just as in a swiftly flowing river with unsettled waters a boat is held steady only by the strength of a steering-pole, and without a steering-pole it cannot be made to stay, even so, due to the weakness of the object, the mind becomes one-pointed and stays only by the strength of initial thought. Without initial thought, it cannot be made to stay. Therefore, only the first jhāna occurs here, not the second and so on.

Paṭikkūlepi ca etasmiṃ ārammaṇe “addhā imāya paṭipadāya jarāmaraṇamhā parimuccissāmī”ti evamānisaṃsadassāvitāya ceva nīvaraṇasantāpappahānena ca pītisomanassaṃ uppajjati, “bahuṃ dāni vetanaṃ labhissāmī”ti ānisaṃsadassāvino pupphachaḍḍakassa gūtharāsimhi viya, ussannabyādhidukkhassa rogino vamanavirecanappavattiyaṃ viya ca.

And although this object is repulsive, joy and mental happiness arise both from seeing the benefit—thinking, “Surely, by this practice, I will be freed from aging and death”—and from the abandoning of the torment of the hindrances; just as for a scavenger who, seeing the benefit, thinks, “Now I will get a great wage” in regard to a heap of filth, and just as for a sick person afflicted with intense suffering from illness during the occurrence of vomiting and purging.

122. Dasavidhampi [V 1.0186] cetaṃ asubhaṃ lakkhaṇato ekameva hoti. Dasavidhassāpi hetassa asuciduggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlabhāvo eva lakkhaṇaṃ. Tadetaṃ iminā lakkhaṇena na kevalaṃ matasarīre, dantaṭṭhikadassāvino pana cetiyapabbatavāsino mahātissattherassa viya, hatthikkhandhagataṃ rājānaṃ olokentassa saṅgharakkhitattherūpaṭṭhākasāmaṇerassa viya ca jīvamānakasarīrepi [M 1.0189] upaṭṭhāti. Yatheva hi matasarīraṃ, evaṃ jīvamānakampi asubhameva. Asubhalakkhaṇaṃ panettha āgantukena alaṅkārena paṭicchannattā na paññāyati. Pakatiyā pana idaṃ sarīraṃ nāma atirekatisataaṭṭhikasamussayaṃ asītisatasandhisaṅghaṭitaṃ navanhārusatanibandhanaṃ navamaṃsapesisatānulittaṃ allacammapariyonaddhaṃ chaviyā paṭicchannaṃ chiddāvachiddaṃ medakathālikā viya niccuggharitapaggharitaṃ kimisaṅghanisevitaṃ rogānaṃ āyatanaṃ dukkhadhammānaṃ vatthu paribhinnapurāṇagaṇḍo viya navahi vaṇamukhehi satatavissandanaṃ. Yassa ubhohi akkhīhi akkhigūthako paggharati, kaṇṇabilehi kaṇṇagūthako, nāsāpuṭehi siṅghāṇikā, mukhato āhārapittasemharudhirāni, adhodvārehi uccārapassāvā, navanavutiyā lomakūpasahassehi asucisedayūso paggharati. Nīlamakkhikādayo samparivārenti. Yaṃ dantakaṭṭhamukhadhovanasīsamakkhananahānanivāsanapārupanādīhi appaṭijaggitvā yathājātova pharusavippakiṇṇakeso hutvā gāmena gāmaṃ vicaranto rājāpi pupphachaḍḍakacaṇḍālādīsu aññataropi samasarīrapaṭikkūlatāya nibbiseso hoti, evaṃ asuciduggandhajegucchapaṭikkūlatāya rañño vā caṇḍālassa vā sarīre vemattaṃ nāma natthi. Dantakaṭṭhamukhadhovanādīhi panettha dantamalādīni pamajjitvā nānāvatthehi hirikopīnaṃ paṭicchādetvā nānāvaṇṇena surabhivilepanena vilimpitvā pupphābharaṇādīhi alaṅkaritvā “ahaṃ mama”nti gahetabbākārappattaṃ karonti. Tato iminā āgantukena alaṅkārena paṭicchannattā tadassa yāthāvasarasaṃ asubhalakkhaṇaṃ asañjānantā purisā itthīsu, itthiyo ca purisesu ratiṃ karonti. Paramatthato panettha rajjitabbakayuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma aṇumattampi natthi. Tathā hi kesalomanakhadantakheḷasiṅghāṇikauccārapassāvādīsu ekakoṭṭhāsampi sarīrato bahi patitaṃ sattā hatthena chupitumpi na icchanti, aṭṭīyanti harāyanti jigucchanti. Yaṃ yaṃ panettha avasesaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ evaṃ paṭikkūlampi samānaṃ avijjandhakārapariyonaddhā attasineharāgarattā “iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā”ti gaṇhanti. Te evaṃ gaṇhantā aṭaviyaṃ kiṃsukarukkhaṃ disvā rukkhato apatitapupphaṃ “ayaṃ maṃsapesī”ti vihaññamānena jarasiṅgālena samānataṃ āpajjanti. Tasmā –

122. And this tenfold foulness is indeed one in characteristic. For the characteristic of this tenfold foulness is simply the state of being impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive. And this foulness, with this characteristic, appears not only in a dead body, but indeed it also appears in a living body, just as it appeared to the Elder Mahātissa, a resident of Cetiyapabbata, who saw the bones in a woman's teeth as she smiled, and just as it appeared to the novice attendant of the Elder Saṅgharakkhita, who was looking at the king seated on the back of an elephant. For just as a dead body is foul, so too a living body is simply foul. However, in this living body, the characteristic of foulness is not apparent because it is concealed by adventitious adornment. For by nature, this body is built up of over three hundred bones, connected by one hundred and eighty joints, bound by nine hundred sinews, plastered with nine hundred pieces of flesh, wrapped in moist hide, covered by skin, with holes and crevices, constantly oozing and trickling like a pot of fat, frequented by hosts of worms, a resort for diseases, a basis for states of suffering, and like an old, burst boil, it constantly discharges from its nine orifices. From both its eyes flows eye-filth, from its ear-holes ear-filth, from its nostrils snot, from its mouth food, bile, phlegm, and blood, and from its lower openings excrement and urine. From its ninety-nine thousand hair pores oozes impure, sweaty fluid. Bluebottles and the like swarm around it. If this body, not being tended to with things like tooth-sticks, mouth-washing, anointing the head, bathing, dressing, and covering, wanders from village to village just as it was born, with rough and dishevelled hair, then even a king is no different from one such as a scavenger or an outcaste, due to the equal repulsiveness of the body. Thus, in terms of being impure, foul-smelling, disgusting, and repulsive, there is no difference whatsoever between the body of a king and that of an outcaste. Yet people, by cleaning off things like tooth-grime with tooth-sticks, washing their mouths, concealing the shameful parts of the body with various clothes, anointing themselves with fragrant ointments of various colors, and adorning themselves with flowers, jewelry, and so on, make it reach a state to be grasped as 'I' and 'mine.' Therefore, because it is concealed by this adventitious adornment, not understanding its foul characteristic which is its actual nature, men take delight in women, and women in men. In ultimate reality, there is not even an atom's measure of a place in this body that is fit to be lusted after. For it is so: if even one part—such as head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, saliva, snot, excrement, or urine—falls away from the body, beings do not wish even to touch it with their hand; they are distressed, ashamed, and disgusted. And yet, whatever part remains in this body, though it is equally repulsive, beings who are enveloped in the darkness of ignorance and dyed with the dye of lust and affection for the self, grasp it as 'desirable, pleasant, permanent, happiness, and self.' Thus grasping, they become like a tormented old jackal that, seeing a flame-of-the-forest tree in the forest, mistakes a flower that has not fallen from the tree for a piece of flesh. Therefore—

Yathāpi [M 1.0190][V 1.0187] pupphitaṃ disvā, siṅgālo kiṃsukaṃ vane;

Maṃsarukkho mayā laddho, iti gantvāna vegasā.

Just as a jackal in the forest, seeing a blossoming flame-of-the-forest tree, thinks, 'I have found a meat tree,' and rushes there in haste.

Patitaṃ patitaṃ pupphaṃ, ḍaṃsitvā atilolupo;

Nayidaṃ maṃsaṃ aduṃ maṃsaṃ, yaṃ rukkhasminti gaṇhati.

Exceedingly greedy, he bites each and every fallen flower, thinking, 'This is not meat; that which is on the tree is meat,' so he perceives.

Koṭṭhāsaṃ patitaṃyeva, asubhanti tathā budho;

Aggahetvāna gaṇheyya, sarīraṭṭhampi naṃ tathā.

Likewise, a wise person, not taking only a fallen portion of the body as foul, should regard that same portion remaining in the body as likewise foul.

Imañhi subhato kāyaṃ, gahetvā tattha mucchitā;

Bālā karontā pāpāni, dukkhā na parimuccare.

For fools, having taken this body to be beautiful and being infatuated with it, commit evil deeds and are not freed from suffering.

Tasmā passeyya medhāvī, jīvato vā matassa vā;

Sabhāvaṃ pūtikāyassa, subhabhāvena vajjitaṃ.

Therefore the wise should see, whether of the living or of the dead, the nature of this putrid body, which is devoid of beauty.

Vuttañhetaṃ –

For this has been said:

Duggandho asuci kāyo, kuṇapo ukkarūpamo;

Nindito cakkhubhūtehi, kāyo bālābhinandito.

Foul-smelling and unclean is this body, a corpse, like a dung-pit; censured by those with the eye of wisdom, it is a body delighted in by fools.

Allacammapaṭicchanno, navadvāro mahāvaṇo;

Samantato paggharati, asuci pūtigandhiyo.
