Covered with moist skin, with nine openings, a great wound; from all around it oozes that which is impure and of putrid smell.

Sace imassa kāyassa, anto bāhirako siyā;

Daṇḍaṃ nūna gahetvāna, kāke soṇe nivārayeti.

If the inside of this body were on the outside, one would surely take a stick to ward off the crows and dogs.

Tasmā dabbajātikena bhikkhunā jīvamānasarīraṃ vā hotu

Therefore, by a monk of capable nature, whether it be a living body,

Matasarīraṃ [V 1.0188] vā yattha yattha asubhākāro paññāyati, tattha tattheva nimittaṃ gahetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ appanaṃ pāpetabbanti.

or a dead body, wherever an aspect of foulness is perceived, right there the sign should be taken and the meditation subject brought to absorption.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Path of Purification, composed for the delight of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the Development of Concentration,

Asubhakammaṭṭhānaniddeso nāma

the Exposition of the Foulness Meditation Subject, so named,

Chaṭṭho paricchedo.

is the Sixth Chapter.

7. Chaanussatiniddeso

7. The Exposition of the Six Recollections

1. Buddhānussatikathā

1. The Discourse on the Recollection of the Buddha

123. Asubhānantaraṃ [M 1.0191][V 1.0189] uddiṭṭhāsu pana dasasu anussatīsu punappunaṃ uppajjanato satiyeva anussati, pavattitabbaṭṭhānamhiyeva vā pavattattā saddhāpabbajitassa kulaputtassa anurūpā satītipi anussati, buddhaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati buddhānussati, buddhaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Dhammaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati dhammānussati, svākkhātatādidhammaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Saṅghaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati saṅghānussati, suppaṭipannatādisaṅghaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Sīlaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati sīlānussati, akhaṇḍatādisīlaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Cāgaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati cāgānussati, muttacāgatādicāgaguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Devatā ārabbha uppannā anussati devatānussati, devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā attano saddhādiguṇārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Maraṇaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati maraṇānussati, jīvitindriyupacchedārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Kesādibhedaṃ rūpakāyaṃ gatā, kāye vā gatāti kāyagatā, kāyagatā ca sā sati cāti kāyagatasatīti vattabbe rassaṃ akatvā kāyagatāsatīti vuttā, kesādikāyakoṭṭhāsanimittārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Ānāpāne ārabbha uppannā sati ānāpānassati, assāsapassāsanimittārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ. Upasamaṃ ārabbha uppannā anussati upasamānussati, sabbadukkhūpasamārammaṇāya satiyā etamadhivacanaṃ.

123. Now, among the ten recollections enumerated after the meditations on foulness, mindfulness itself is recollection (anussati) because it arises again and again. Or, because it occurs only in a suitable place, it is mindfulness appropriate for a clansman who has gone forth out of faith; for this reason also, it is recollection. The recollection that arises with the Buddha as its object is recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object. The recollection that arises with the Dhamma as its object is recollection of the Dhamma (dhammānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of the Dhamma, beginning with its being well-proclaimed. The recollection that arises with the Sangha as its object is recollection of the Sangha (saṅghānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of the Sangha, beginning with their practicing the good way. The recollection that arises with virtue (sīla) as its object is recollection of virtue (sīlānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of one's own virtue, beginning with its being unbroken. The recollection that arises with generosity (cāga) as its object is recollection of generosity (cāgānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the qualities of one's own generosity, beginning with open-handed generosity. The recollection that arises with the deities as its object is recollection of the deities (devatānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object one's own qualities, beginning with faith, having placed the deities in the position of a witness. The recollection that arises with death as its object is recollection of death (maraṇānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has the cutting off of the life faculty as its object. Mindfulness that has gone to the material body, which is divided into parts beginning with the hair of the head, or has gone into the body, is called kāyagatā (gone to the body). And since that mindfulness is kāyagatā, it should be called kāyagatasati; but without shortening the vowel, it is called kāyagatāsati. This is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the sign in the bodily parts, beginning with the hair of the head. The mindfulness that arises with the in-breaths and out-breaths as its object is mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has the sign of in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. The recollection that arises with peace (upasama) as its object is recollection of peace (upasamānussati); this is a designation for mindfulness that has as its object the stilling of all suffering.

124. Iti imāsu dasasu anussatīsu buddhānussatiṃ tāva bhāvetukāmena aveccappasādasamannāgatena yoginā patirūpasenāsane rahogatena paṭisallīnena “itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi [M 1.0192] satthā [V 1.0190] devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā”ti (a. ni. 6.10) evaṃ buddhassa bhagavato guṇā anussaritabbā.

124. Thus, among these ten recollections, a yogī who wishes to develop the recollection of the Buddha, endowed with unwavering confidence, should first of all, in a suitable dwelling, having gone to a secluded place and being in solitude, recollect the qualities of the Buddha, the Blessed One, in this way: 'For this reason, the Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a Knower of the World, an Unexcelled Trainer of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, an Enlightened One, a Blessed One.'

Tatrāyaṃ anussaraṇanayo – so bhagavā itipi arahaṃ, itipi sammāsambuddho…pe… itipi bhagavāti anussarati. Iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, this is the method of recollection: one recollects, 'That Blessed One is an Arahant for this reason; a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One for this reason; ... a Blessed One for this reason.' This is to say, 'For this reason and for that reason.'

125. Tattha ārakattā arīnaṃ arānañca hatattā paccayādīnaṃ arahattā pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvāti imehi tāva kāraṇehi so bhagavā arahanti anussarati. Ārakā hi so sabbakilesehi suvidūravidūre ṭhito maggena savāsanānaṃ kilesānaṃ viddhaṃsitattāti ārakattā arahaṃ.

125. Therein, one first of all recollects that the Blessed One is an Arahant for these reasons: because of being far, because of having destroyed the enemies, because of having destroyed the spokes, because of being worthy of requisites and so on, and because of the absence of a secret place for doing evil. Indeed, He is far from all defilements; He stands very, very far away, because the defilements together with their latent tendencies have been destroyed by the path. Thus, because of being far, He is an Arahant.

So tato ārakā nāma, yassa yenāsamaṅgitā;

Asamaṅgī ca dosehi, nātho tenārahaṃ matoti.

He is called 'far' from that with which He has no association; and since the Protector is unassociated with faults, for that reason He is considered an Arahant.

126. Te cānena kilesārayo maggena hatāti arīnaṃ hatattāpi arahaṃ.

126. Furthermore, since those enemies, the defilements, have been destroyed by Him with the path, He is also an Arahant because of having destroyed the enemies.

Yasmā rāgādisaṅkhātā, sabbepi arayo hatā;

Paññāsatthena nāthena, tasmāpi arahaṃ matoti.

Since all enemies, known as lust and so on, have been destroyed by the Protector with the sword of wisdom, for that reason also He is considered an Arahant.

127. Yañcetaṃ avijjābhavataṇhāmayanābhi puññādiabhisaṅkhārāraṃ jarāmaraṇanemi āsavasamudayamayena akkhena vijjhitvā tibhavarathe samāyojitaṃ anādikālappavattaṃ saṃsāracakkaṃ, tassānena bodhimaṇḍe vīriyapādehi sīlapathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya saddhāhatthena kammakkhayakaraṃ ñāṇapharasuṃ gahetvā sabbe arā hatāti arānaṃ hatattāpi arahaṃ.

127. Furthermore, of that wheel of saṃsāra—which has turned since beginningless time, is yoked to the chariot of the three existences, has a hub made of ignorance, existence, and craving, spokes of meritorious and other formations, a rim of aging and death, and is pierced by an axle made of the arising of taints—all the spokes were destroyed by Him. At the seat of enlightenment, standing firmly on the ground of virtue with the feet of energy, and taking up with the hand of faith the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma, He destroyed all the spokes. Thus, also because of having destroyed the spokes, He is an Arahant.

128. Atha vā saṃsāracakkanti anamataggaṃ saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ vuccati. Tassa ca avijjā nābhi, mūlattā. Jarāmaraṇaṃ nemi, pariyosānattā. Sesā dasa dhammā arā, avijjāmūlakattā jarāmaraṇapariyantattā ca, tattha dukkhādīsu aññāṇaṃ avijjā. Kāmabhave ca avijjā kāmabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti, rūpabhave avijjā rūpabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti, arūpabhave [V 1.0191] avijjā [M 1.0193] arūpabhave saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave saṅkhārā kāmabhave paṭisandhiviññāṇassa paccayā honti, esa nayo itaresu. Kāmabhave paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ kāmabhave nāmarūpassa paccayo hoti, tathā rūpabhave. Arūpabhave nāmasseva paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave nāmarūpaṃ kāmabhave saḷāyatanassa paccayo hoti, rūpabhave nāmarūpaṃ rūpabhave tiṇṇaṃ āyatanānaṃ paccayo hoti, arūpabhave nāmaṃ arūpabhave ekassa āyatanassa paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave saḷāyatanaṃ kāmabhave chabbidhassa phassassa paccayo hoti, rūpabhave tīṇi āyatanāni rūpabhave tiṇṇaṃ phassānaṃ paccayā honti, arūpabhave ekaṃ āyatanaṃ arūpabhave ekassa phassassa paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave cha phassā kāmabhave channaṃ vedanānaṃ paccayā honti, rūpabhave tayo phassā tattheva tissannaṃ, arūpabhave eko tattheva ekissā vedanāya paccayo hoti. Kāmabhave cha vedanā kāmabhave channaṃ taṇhākāyānaṃ paccayā honti, rūpabhave tisso tattheva tiṇṇaṃ, arūpabhave ekā vedanā arūpabhave ekassa taṇhākāyassa paccayo hoti. Tattha tattha sā sā taṇhā tassa tassa upādānassa, upādānādayo bhavādīnaṃ.

128. Alternatively, the beginningless round of saṃsāra is called the wheel of saṃsāra. And of this, ignorance is the hub, because it is the root. Aging and death are the rim, because they are the end. The remaining ten factors are the spokes, because they are rooted in ignorance and have aging-and-death as their end. Therein, ignorance is not knowing the truths of suffering and so on. And in the sensual realm, ignorance is a condition for formations in the sensual realm; in the form realm, ignorance is a condition for formations in the form realm; in the formless realm, ignorance is a condition for formations in the formless realm. In the sensual realm, formations are conditions for rebirth-consciousness in the sensual realm; this method applies to the others. In the sensual realm, rebirth-consciousness is a condition for name-and-form in the sensual realm, and likewise in the form realm. In the formless realm, it is a condition for name alone. In the sensual realm, name-and-form is a condition for the six sense bases in the sensual realm; in the form realm, name-and-form is a condition for three sense bases in the form realm; in the formless realm, name is a condition for one sense base in the formless realm. In the sensual realm, the six sense bases are a condition for sixfold contact in the sensual realm; in the form realm, three sense bases are conditions for three contacts in the form realm; in the formless realm, one sense base is a condition for one contact in the formless realm. In the sensual realm, six contacts are conditions for six feelings in the sensual realm; in the form realm, three contacts are conditions for three feelings right there; in the formless realm, one contact is a condition for one feeling right there. In the sensual realm, six feelings are conditions for six bodies of craving in the sensual realm; in the form realm, three feelings are conditions for three right there; in the formless realm, one feeling is a condition for one body of craving in the formless realm. In each respective case, that respective craving is a condition for that respective clinging; clinging and so on are conditions for becoming and so on.

Kathaṃ? Idhekacco kāme paribhuñjissāmīti kāmupādānapaccayā kāyena duccaritaṃ carati, vācāya duccaritaṃ carati, manasā duccaritaṃ carati, duccaritapāripūriyā apāye upapajjati. Tatthassa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammanibbattā khandhā upapattibhavo, khandhānaṃ nibbatti jāti, paripāko jarā, bhedo maraṇaṃ.

How? Here, a certain person, thinking, 'I will enjoy sensual pleasures,' with clinging to sensual pleasures as the condition, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind. Due to the fulfillment of misconduct, they are reborn in a state of deprivation. Therein, the kamma that is the cause of their rebirth is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming; the arising of the aggregates is birth; their maturation is aging; and their breaking up is death.

Aparo saggasampattiṃ anubhavissāmīti tatheva sucaritaṃ carati, sucaritapāripūriyā sagge upapajjati. Tatthassa upapattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavoti so eva nayo.

Another, thinking, 'I will experience heavenly prosperity,' in the same way engages in good conduct. Through the fulfillment of good conduct, they are reborn in heaven. Therein, the kamma that is the cause of their rebirth is kamma-becoming; this is the same method.

Aparo pana brahmalokasampattiṃ anubhavissāmīti kāmupādānapaccayāeva mettaṃ bhāveti, karuṇaṃ, muditaṃ, upekkhaṃ bhāveti, bhāvanāpāripūriyā brahmaloke nibbattati. Tatthassa nibbattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavoti so eva nayo.

Furthermore, another, thinking, 'I will experience the prosperity of the Brahma world,' with clinging to sensual pleasures as the very condition, develops loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity. Through the fulfillment of this development, they are reborn in the Brahma world. Therein, the kamma that is the cause of their rebirth is kamma-becoming; this is the same method.

Aparo [M 1.0194] arūpabhave sampattiṃ anubhavissāmīti tatheva ākāsānañcāyatanādisamāpattiyo bhāveti, bhāvanāpāripūriyā tattha tattha nibbattati. Tatthassa nibbattihetubhūtaṃ kammaṃ kammabhavo, kammanibbattā [V 1.0192] khandhā upapattibhavo, khandhānaṃ nibbatti jāti, paripāko jarā, bhedo maraṇanti. Esa nayo sesupādānamūlikāsupi yojanāsu.

Another, thinking, 'I will experience the prosperity of the formless existence,' in the same way develops the attainments such as the base of infinite space. Through the fulfillment of this development, they are reborn in those respective realms. Therein, the kamma that is the cause of their rebirth is kamma-becoming; the aggregates produced by kamma are rebirth-becoming; the arising of the aggregates is birth; their maturation is aging; and their breaking up is death. This method also applies to the applications rooted in the remaining types of clinging.

Evaṃ ayaṃ avijjā hetu, saṅkhārā hetusamuppannā, ubhopete hetusamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ. Atītampi addhānaṃ anāgatampi addhānaṃ avijjā hetu, saṅkhārā hetusamuppannā, ubhopete hetusamuppannāti paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti eteneva nayena sabbapadāni vitthāretabbāni.

Thus: 'This ignorance is a cause; formations are causally arisen; both these are causally arisen.' In this way, the wisdom in the grasping of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma. In the past time and in the future time as well: 'Ignorance is a cause; formations are causally arisen; both these are causally arisen.' In this way, the wisdom in the grasping of conditions is the knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma. By this same method, all terms should be expanded.

Tattha avijjāsaṅkhārā eko saṅkhepo, viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā eko, taṇhupādānabhavā eko, jātijarāmaraṇaṃ eko. Purimasaṅkhepo cettha atīto addhā, dve majjhimā paccuppanno, jātijarāmaraṇaṃ anāgato. Avijjāsaṅkhāraggahaṇena cettha taṇhupādānabhavā gahitāva hontīti ime pañca dhammā atīte kammavaṭṭaṃ, viññāṇādayo pañca etarahi vipākavaṭṭaṃ, taṇhupādānabhavaggahaṇena avijjāsaṅkhārā gahitāva hontīti ime pañca dhammā etarahi kammavaṭṭaṃ, jātijarāmaraṇāpadesena viññāṇādīnaṃ niddiṭṭhattā ime pañca dhammā āyatiṃ vipākavaṭṭaṃ. Te ākārato vīsatividhā honti. Saṅkhāraviññāṇānañcettha antarā eko sandhi, vedanātaṇhānamantarā eko, bhavajātīnamantarā ekoti, iti bhagavā etaṃ catusaṅkhepaṃ tiyaddhaṃ vīsatākāraṃ tisandhiṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sabbākārato jānāti passati aññāti paṭivijjhati. Taṃ ñātaṭṭhena ñāṇaṃ, pajānanaṭṭhena paññā, tena vuccati paccayapariggahe paññā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti. Iminā dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇena bhagavā te dhamme yathābhūtaṃ ñatvā tesu nibbindanto virajjanto vimuccanto vuttappakārassa imassa saṃsāracakkassa are hani vihani viddhaṃsesi. Evampi arānaṃ hatattā arahaṃ.

Therein, ignorance and volitional formations are one section; consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are one section; craving, clinging, and becoming are one section; and birth, aging, and death are one section. Herein, the first section is the past period; the two middle ones are the present; and birth, aging, and death are the future. And herein, by the taking up of ignorance and volitional formations, craving, clinging, and becoming are also taken up. Thus, these five phenomena in the past are the round of kamma. The five beginning with consciousness are now the round of result. By the taking up of craving, clinging, and becoming, ignorance and volitional formations are also taken up. Thus, these five phenomena are now the round of kamma. Because those beginning with consciousness are indicated by the designation of birth, aging, and death, these five phenomena are the round of result in the future. They are twentyfold in their aspects. And herein, there is one connection between volitional formations and consciousness, one between feeling and craving, and one between becoming and birth. Thus, the Blessed One knows, sees, understands, and penetrates this dependent origination—with its four sections, three periods, twenty aspects, and three connections—in all its modes. That is knowledge in the sense of knowing, wisdom in the sense of thorough understanding; hence it is called 'the wisdom in the comprehension of conditions, the knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma.' With this knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma, the Blessed One, having known those phenomena as they truly are, and becoming disenchanted with them, dispassionate towards them, and liberated from them, destroyed, demolished, and shattered the spokes of this wheel of saṃsāra as described. In this way too, because of having destroyed the spokes, he is an Arahant.

Arā saṃsāracakkassa, hatā ñāṇāsinā yato;

Lokanāthena tenesa, arahanti pavuccati.

Because the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed by the Lord of the World with the sword of wisdom, therefore he is called an 'Arahant'.

129. Aggadakkhiṇeyyattā [M 1.0195] ca cīvarādipaccaye arahati pūjāvisesañca. Teneva ca uppanne tathāgate yekeci mahesakkhā devamanussā, na te aññattha pūjaṃ karonti. Tathā hi brahmā sahampati sinerumattena ratanadāmena tathāgataṃ pūjesi. Yathābalañca aññe devā manussā ca [V 1.0193] bimbisārakosalarājādayo. Parinibbutampi ca bhagavantaṃ uddissa channavutikoṭidhanaṃ vissajjetvā asokamahārājā sakalajambudīpe caturāsītivihārasahassāni patiṭṭhāpesi. Ko pana vādo aññesaṃ pūjāvisesānanti paccayādīnaṃ arahattāpi arahaṃ.

129. And because of being worthy of the highest offerings, He is worthy of the requisites such as robes and so forth, and of special veneration. For that very reason, when a Tathāgata has arisen, whatever deities and humans of great power there are, they do not make offerings elsewhere. Indeed, Brahmā Sahampati venerated the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland the size of Mount Sineru. And according to their ability, other deities and humans, such as King Bimbisāra and the King of Kosala, also venerate Him. Furthermore, even after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, the great King Asoka, having spent ninety-six crores of wealth in dedication to Him, established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout all of Jambudīpa. What need is there to speak of His worthiness of other special venerations? Thus, also because of being worthy of requisites and so forth, He is an Arahant.

Pūjāvisesaṃ saha paccayehi,

Yasmā ayaṃ arahati lokanātho;

Atthānurūpaṃ arahanti loke,

Tasmā jino arahati nāmametaṃ.

Because this Lord of the World is worthy of special veneration together with the requisites, therefore, in the world, that Conqueror is worthy of this name 'Arahant', which is in accordance with its meaning.

130. Yathā ca loke yekeci paṇḍitamānino bālā asilokabhayena raho pāpaṃ karonti, evamesa na kadāci karotīti pāpakaraṇe rahābhāvatopi arahaṃ.

130. Furthermore, just as in the world some fools who fancy themselves wise commit evil in secret out of fear of ill-repute, so this Blessed One never does so. Thus, also because of the absence of a secret place for committing evil, He is an Arahant.

Yasmā natthi raho nāma, pāpakammesu tādino;

Rahābhāvena tenesa, arahaṃ iti vissuto.

Because for one such as He (Tādin), there is no such thing as a secret place for evil deeds, by that absence of a secret place, this Blessed One is renowned as 'Arahant'.

Evaṃ sabbathāpi –

Thus, in all ways—

Ārakattā hatattā ca, kilesārīna so muni;

Hatasaṃsāracakkāro, paccayādīna cāraho;

Na raho karoti pāpāni, arahaṃ tena vuccatīti.

Because He is far from defilements, because He has destroyed the enemies that are defilements, because He has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because He is worthy of requisites and such, and because He does no evil in secret, the Sage is called 'Arahant'.

131. Sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā pana sammāsambuddho. Tathāhi esa sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho, abhiññeyye dhamme abhiññeyyato buddho, pariññeyye dhamme pariññeyyato, pahātabbe dhamme pahātabbato, sacchikātabbe dhamme sacchikātabbato, bhāvetabbe dhamme bhāvetabbato. Teneva cāha –

131. Furthermore, He is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) because He has rightly and by Himself awakened to all dhammas. Indeed, this Blessed One has awakened to all dhammas rightly and by Himself: He has awakened to the dhammas that are to be known by direct knowledge as things to be known by direct knowledge; to the dhammas that are to be fully understood as things to be fully understood; to the dhammas that are to be abandoned as things to be abandoned; to the dhammas that are to be realized as things to be realized; and to the dhammas that are to be developed as things to be developed. For that very reason, He said—

Abhiññeyyaṃ abhiññātaṃ, bhāvetabbañca bhāvitaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ pahīnaṃ me, tasmā buddhosmi brāhmaṇāti. (ma. ni. 2.399; su. ni. 563);

What is to be known by direct knowledge has been directly known by me; what is to be developed has been developed; and what is to be abandoned has been abandoned. Therefore, O brahmin, I am the Buddha.

132. Apica [M 1.0196][V 1.0194] cakkhuṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, tassa mūlakāraṇabhāvena samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccanti evaṃ ekekapaduddhārenāpi sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho, esa nayo sotaghānajivhākāyamanesu. Eteneva nayena rūpādīni cha āyatanāni, cakkhuviññāṇādayo chaviññāṇakāyā, cakkhusamphassādayo cha phassā, cakkhusamphassajādayo cha vedanā, rūpasaññādayo cha saññā, rūpasañcetanādayo cha cetanā, rūpataṇhādayo cha taṇhākāyā, rūpavitakkādayo cha vitakkā, rūpavicārādayo cha vicārā, rūpakkhandhādayo pañcakkhandhā, dasa kasiṇāni, dasa anussatiyo, uddhumātakasaññādivasena dasa saññā, kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, dvādasāyatanāni, aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo, kāmabhavādayo nava bhavā, paṭhamādīni cattāri jhānāni, mettābhāvanādayo catasso appamaññā, catasso arūpasamāpattiyo, paṭilomato jarāmaraṇādīni, anulomato avijjādīni paṭiccasamuppādaṅgāni ca yojetabbāni.

132. Moreover, the eye is the Truth of Suffering; the preceding craving which produces it by being its root cause is the Truth of the Origin; the non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation; and the practice for the thorough knowledge of cessation is the Truth of the Path. Thus, even by the extraction of each single term, He has rightly and by Himself understood all phenomena. This same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. By this very method, the six sense bases beginning with form, the six classes of consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness, the six contacts beginning with eye-contact, the six feelings born of eye-contact and so forth, the six perceptions beginning with perception of form, the six volitions beginning with volition regarding form, the six groups of craving beginning with craving for form, the six initial thoughts beginning with initial thought about form, the six sustained thoughts beginning with sustained thought on form, the five aggregates beginning with the form-aggregate, the ten kasiṇas, the ten recollections, the ten perceptions by way of the perception of a bloated corpse and so forth, the thirty-two parts of the body beginning with hair of the head, the twelve sense bases, the eighteen elements, the nine types of existence beginning with sensual existence, the four jhānas beginning with the first, the four immeasurables beginning with the development of loving-kindness, the four formless attainments, and the factors of dependent origination—in reverse order beginning with aging-and-death, and in forward order beginning with ignorance—should be applied.

Tatrāyaṃ ekapadayojanā, jarāmaraṇaṃ dukkhasaccaṃ, jāti samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnampi nissaraṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhapajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccanti evamekekapaduddhārena sabbadhamme sammā sāmañca buddho anubuddho paṭibuddho. Tena vuttaṃ – “sammā sāmañca sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā pana sammāsambuddho”ti.

Herein is the application of a single term: aging-and-death is the Truth of Suffering; birth is the Truth of the Origin; the escape from both is the Truth of Cessation; and the practice for the thorough knowledge of cessation is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by the extraction of each single term, He has rightly and by Himself awakened, subsequently awakened, and penetratively awakened to all phenomena. Therefore it is said: “Because of having rightly and by Himself awakened to all phenomena, He is the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”

133. Vijjāhi pana caraṇena ca sampannattā vijjācaraṇasampanno. Tattha vijjāti tissopi vijjā aṭṭhapi vijjā. Tisso vijjā bhayabheravasutte (ma. ni. 1.52 ādayo) vuttanayeneva veditabbā, aṭṭha ambaṭṭhasutte (dī. ni. 1.278 ādayo). Tatra hi vipassanāñāṇena manomayiddhiyā ca saha cha abhiññā pariggahetvā aṭṭha vijjā vuttā. Caraṇanti sīlasaṃvaro, indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, satta saddhammā, cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānānīti ime pannarasa dhammā veditabbā. Imeyeva hi pannarasa dhammā yasmā etehi carati ariyasāvako gacchati amataṃ disaṃ, tasmā caraṇanti vuttā. Yathāha – “idha, mahānāma, ariyasāvako sīlavā hotī”ti (ma. ni. 2.24) sabbaṃ majjhimapaṇṇāsake vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Bhagavā imāhi vijjāhi iminā ca caraṇena samannāgato. Tena vuccati vijjācaraṇasampannoti.

133. Moreover, because He is endowed with knowledge and conduct, He is called 'Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct.' Herein, by 'knowledge' is meant both the threefold knowledge and the eightfold knowledge. The threefold knowledge should be understood as explained in the Bhayabherava Sutta, and the eightfold knowledge as in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. There, indeed, the eight knowledges are stated, having included the six higher knowledges together with insight-knowledge and the mind-made psychic power. By 'conduct,' these fifteen factors should be understood: moral restraint, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the seven qualities of a good person, and the four form-sphere jhānas. For it is by these very fifteen factors that the noble disciple fares on and goes to the deathless realm; therefore, they are called 'conduct.' As it is said: 'Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple is virtuous...' All of this should be understood in the way stated in the Majjhimapaṇṇāsaka. The Blessed One is endowed with these knowledges and with this conduct. Therefore, He is called 'Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct.'

Tattha [M 1.0197][V 1.0195] vijjāsampadā bhagavato sabbaññutaṃ pūretvā ṭhitā. Caraṇasampadā mahākāruṇikataṃ. So sabbaññutāya sabbasattānaṃ atthānatthaṃ ñatvā mahākāruṇikatāya anatthaṃ parivajjetvā atthe niyojeti. Yathā taṃ vijjācaraṇasampanno. Tenassa sāvakā suppaṭipannā honti, no duppaṭipannā vijjācaraṇavipannānaṃ sāvakā attantapādayo viya.

Therein, the accomplishment of knowledge, having fulfilled the Blessed One's omniscience, stands. The accomplishment of conduct, in turn, fulfills His great compassion. Through omniscience, knowing the benefit and harm for all beings, and through great compassion, avoiding what is harmful, He engages them in what is beneficial. This is characteristic of one accomplished in knowledge and conduct. Therefore, His disciples are of good practice, not of wrong practice—unlike the disciples of those deficient in knowledge and conduct, such as the practitioners of self-mortification and the like.

134. Sobhanagamanattā, sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattā, sammā gatattā, sammā ca gadattā sugato. Gamanampi hi gatanti vuccati. Tañca bhagavato sobhanaṃ parisuddhamanavajjaṃ. Kiṃ pana tanti? Ariyamaggo. Tena hesa gamanena khemaṃ disaṃ asajjamāno gatoti sobhanagamanattā sugato. Sundarañcesa ṭhānaṃ gato amataṃ nibbānanti sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ gatattāpi sugato. Sammā ca gato tena tena maggena pahīne kilese puna apaccāgacchanto. Vuttañhetaṃ – “sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato…pe… arahattamaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato”ti, sammā vā gato dīpaṅkarapādamūlato pabhuti yāva bodhimaṇḍā tāva samatiṃsapāramīpūrikāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sabbalokassa hitasukhameva karonto sassataṃ, ucchedaṃ, kāmasukhaṃ, attakilamathanti ime ca ante anupagacchanto gatoti sammā gatattāpi sugato. Sammā cesa gadati yuttaṭṭhāne yuttameva vācaṃ bhāsatīti sammā gadattāpi sugato. Tatridaṃ sādhakasuttaṃ “yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasañhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasañhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasañhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ appiyā amanāpā, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāya. Yaṃ tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasañhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, na taṃ tathāgato vācaṃ bhāsati. Yampi tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasañhitaṃ, sā ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, tampi tathāgato vācaṃ na bhāsati. Yañca kho tathāgato vācaṃ jānāti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasañhitaṃ, sā [M 1.0198] ca paresaṃ piyā manāpā, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassā vācāya veyyākaraṇāyā”ti (ma. ni. 2.86). Evaṃ sammā gadattāpi sugatoti veditabbo.

134. He is the Sugata because of His beautiful going, because of His going to a beautiful place, because of His going rightly, and because of His speaking rightly. For the going itself is also called ‘gata’ (gone). And that going of the Blessed One is beautiful, utterly pure, and blameless. What, then, is that? The Noble Path. For by that going, He has gone to the safe direction without getting stuck; thus, He is the Sugata because of His beautiful going. And He has gone to the beautiful place, the deathless Nibbāna; thus, He is also the Sugata because of His going to a beautiful place. And He has gone rightly, not returning again to the defilements abandoned by this or that path. And this has been said: ‘Whatever defilements are abandoned by the path of stream-entry, He does not return to those defilements, does not go back, does not come back; thus, He is the Sugata… and so on… Whatever defilements are abandoned by the path of Arahantship, He does not return to those defilements, does not go back, does not come back; thus, He is the Sugata.’ Or, He has gone rightly from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara up to the seat of Awakening, by the right practice of fulfilling the thirty perfections, working only for the welfare and happiness of the whole world, not approaching these extremes of eternalism, annihilationism, indulgence in sensual pleasure, and self-mortification; thus, He is also the Sugata because of His going rightly. And He speaks rightly, uttering only fitting speech in a fitting place; thus, He is also the Sugata because of speaking rightly. In this regard, there is this supporting sutta: ‘Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unpleasant to others, the Tathāgata does not speak that speech. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, but unbeneficial, and which is also disagreeable and unpleasant to others, that speech the Tathāgata also does not speak. And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, but which is disagreeable and unpleasant to others, the Tathāgata is a knower of the right time for the speaking of that speech. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, but which is agreeable and pleasant to others, the Tathāgata does not speak that speech. Whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, but unbeneficial, and which is also agreeable and pleasant to others, that speech the Tathāgata also does not speak. And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, correct, and beneficial, and which is also agreeable and pleasant to others, the Tathāgata is a knower of the right time for the speaking of that speech’ (MN 58). Thus, He is to be understood as the Sugata also because of speaking rightly.

135. Sabbathāpi viditalokattā pana lokavidū. So hi bhagavā sabhāvato samudayato nirodhato [V 1.0196] nirodhūpāyatoti sabbathā lokaṃ avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi. Yathāha – “yattha kho, āvuso, na jāyati na jīyati na mīyati na cavati na upapajjati, nāhaṃ taṃ gamanena lokassa antaṃ ñāteyyaṃ daṭṭheyyaṃ patteyyanti vadāmi, na cāhaṃ, āvuso, apatvāva lokassa antaṃ dukkhassa antakiriyaṃ vadāmi. Api cāhaṃ, āvuso, imasmiññeva byāmamatte kaḷevare sasaññimhi samanake lokañca paññapemi lokasamudayañca lokanirodhañca lokanirodhagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ.

135. Furthermore, because He has known the world in every way, He is the Lokavidū, the Knower of the World. For that Blessed One knew, understood, and penetrated the world in every way: by way of its nature, its origin, its cessation, and the way to its cessation. As was said: ‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn—I do not say that by going one can know, see, or reach that end of the world. And I do not say, friend, that without having reached the end of the world, one can make an end of suffering. Yet, friend, in this very fathom-long body, with its perception and mind, I declare the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the practice leading to the cessation of the world.’

Gamanena na pattabbo, lokassanto kudācanaṃ;

Na ca apatvā lokantaṃ, dukkhā atthi pamocanaṃ.

By going, the end of the world is never to be reached; and without having reached the end of the world, there is no release from suffering.

Tasmā have lokavidū sumedho,

Lokantagū vūsitabrahmacariyo;

Lokassa antaṃ samitāvi ñatvā,

Nāsīsati lokamimaṃ parañcāti. (saṃ. ni. 1.107; a. ni. 4.45);

Therefore, indeed, the wise one, the knower of the world, who has gone to the world's end and lived the holy life; having known the end of the world, the pacified one does not long for this world or the next.

136. Apica tayo lokā saṅkhāraloko sattaloko okāsalokoti. Tattha eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikāti (paṭi. ma. 1.112) āgataṭṭhāne saṅkhāraloko veditabbo. Sassato lokoti vā asassato lokoti vāti (dī. ni. 1.421) āgataṭṭhāne sattaloko.

136. Furthermore, there are three worlds: the world of formations, the world of beings, and the world of location. Therein, in the passage where it is stated, ‘One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment,’ the world of formations is to be understood. In the passage where it is stated, ‘The world is eternal’ or ‘The world is not eternal,’ the world of beings is to be understood.

Yāvatā candimasūriyā pariharanti, disā bhanti virocamānā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko, ettha te vattatī vasoti. (ma. ni. 1.503) –

As far as the moon and sun revolve, lighting up the regions with their radiance, so far extends the thousandfold world; here your power prevails.

Āgataṭṭhāne okāsaloko. Tampi bhagavā sabbathā avedi. Tathā hissa “eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Dve lokā nāmañca rūpañca. Tayo lokā tisso vedanā. Cattāro lokā [M 1.0199] cattāro āhārā. Pañca lokā pañcupādānakkhandhā. Cha lokā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni. Satta lokā satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Aṭṭha lokā aṭṭha lokadhammā. Nava lokā nava [V 1.0197] sattāvāsā. Dasa lokā dasāyatanāni. Dvādasa lokā dvādasāyatanāni. Aṭṭhārasa lokā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.112) ayaṃ saṅkhāralokopi sabbathā vidito.

In the passage cited, the world of location is to be understood. The Blessed One knew this threefold world also in every way. For thus it is said of Him: ‘One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds: the three feelings. Four worlds: the four kinds of nutriment. Five worlds: the five aggregates subject to clinging. Six worlds: the six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: the ten sense bases. Twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements.’ In this way, this world of formations was also known to Him in every way.

Yasmā panesa sabbesampi sattānaṃ āsayaṃ jānāti, anusayaṃ jānāti, caritaṃ jānāti, adhimuttiṃ jānāti, apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe, tikkhindriye mudindriye, svākāre dvākāre, suviññāpaye duviññāpaye, bhabbe abhabbe satte jānāti. Tasmāssa sattalokopi sabbathā vidito.

Furthermore, because He knows the inclination of all beings, knows their underlying tendency, knows their conduct, knows their disposition; because He knows beings with little dust in their eyes and with much, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, of good character and of bad character, those who are easy to teach and those who are difficult to teach, those who are capable and those who are incapable—therefore, the world of beings was also known to Him in every way.

137. Yathā ca sattaloko, evaṃ okāsalokopi. Tathā hesa ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ āyāmato ca vitthārato ca yojanānaṃ dvādasasatasahassāni catutiṃsasatāni ca paññāsañca yojanāni. Parikkhepato pana –

137. And just as the world of beings, so too the world of location was known to Him. For this single world-system is one million, two hundred and three thousand, four hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth. In circumference, however—

Sabbaṃ satasahassāni, chattiṃsaparimaṇḍalaṃ;

Dasa ceva sahassāni, aḍḍhuḍḍhāni satāni ca.

The entire circumference is thirty-six hundred-thousand, and ten thousand, and three hundred and fifty.

Tattha –

Therein—

Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharā.

Two hundred thousand and forty thousand yojanas; this earth is reckoned to be of such a thickness.

Tassāyeva sandhārakaṃ –

That which supports that very earth—

Cattāri satasahassāni, aṭṭheva nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, jalaṃ vāte patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Four hundred thousand and eighty thousand yojanas; of such a thickness, the water is established on the wind.

Tassāpi sandhārako –

And that which supports it—

Nava satasahassāni, māluto nabhamuggato;

Saṭṭhiñceva sahassāni, esā lokassa saṇṭhiti.

Nine hundred thousand and sixty thousand more, the wind extends into the space below; this is the foundation of the world.

Evaṃ saṇṭhite cettha yojanānaṃ –

It being thus established, here in this world-system—

Caturāsīti [M 1.0200][V 1.0198] sahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato tāvadeva, sineru pabbatuttamo.

Eighty-four thousand yojanas submerged in the great ocean; just as high, towering aloft, is the excellent Mount Sineru.

Tato upaḍḍhupaḍḍhena, pamāṇena yathākkamaṃ;

Ajjhogāḷhuggatā dibbā, nānāratanacittitā.

Thence, by half and half in measure, in due order, are mountains submerged and risen, divine, and variegated with various jewels.

Yugandharo īsadharo, karavīko sudassano;

Nemindharo vinatako, assakaṇṇo giri brahā.

Yugandhara, Īsadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara, Vinataka, and Assakaṇṇa—these are the great mountains.

Ete satta mahāselā, sinerussa samantato;

Mahārājānamāvāsā, devayakkhanisevitā.

These seven great mountains are all around Sineru, abodes of the Great Kings, frequented by devas and yakkhas.

Yojanānaṃ satānucco, himavā pañca pabbato;

Yojanānaṃ sahassāni, tīṇi āyatavitthato.

The Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high and extends three thousand yojanas in length and breadth.

Caturāsītisahassehi, kūṭehi paṭimaṇḍito;

Tipañcayojanakkhandha-parikkhepā nagavhayā.

It is adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks. The Jambu tree, called Naga, has a trunk-circumference of fifteen yojanas.

Paññāsayojanakkhandha-sākhāyāmā samantato;

Satayojanavitthiṇṇā, tāvadeva ca uggatā;

Jambū yassānubhāvena, jambudīpo pakāsito.

The Jambu tree has a trunk and branches fifty yojanas in length; it is one hundred yojanas wide all around and just as high. By its power, Jambudīpa is proclaimed.

Yañcetaṃ jambuyā pamāṇaṃ, etadeva asurānaṃ citrapāṭaliyā, garuḷānaṃ simbalirukkhassa, aparagoyāne kadambassa, uttarakurūsu kapparukkhassa, pubbavidehe sirīsassa, tāvatiṃsesu pāricchattakassāti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

And this measure of the Jambu tree is the same for the Citrapāṭali of the asuras, the Simbali tree of the garuḷas, the Kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna, the Kapparukkha in Uttarakuru, the Sirīsa tree in Pubbavideha, and the Pāricchattaka in Tāvatiṃsa. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Pāṭalī simbalī jambū, devānaṃ pāricchattako;

Kadambo kapparukkho ca, sirīsena bhavati sattamanti.

“Pāṭalī, Simbalī, Jambu, the Pāricchattaka of the devas; Kadamba and Kapparukkha, with Sirīsa as the seventh.”

“Dveasīti [V 1.0199] sahassāni, ajjhogāḷho mahaṇṇave;

Accuggato tāvadeva, cakkavāḷasiluccayo;

Parikkhipitvā taṃ sabbaṃ, lokadhātumayaṃ ṭhito”ti.

The Cakkavāḷa mountain range, submerged eighty-two thousand yojanas in the great ocean and risen up just as high, stands encircling that entire world-system.

Tattha candamaṇḍalaṃ ekūnapaññāsayojanaṃ. Sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ paññāsayojanaṃ. Tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ dasasahassayojanaṃ. Tathā asurabhavanaṃ avīcimahānirayo jambudīpo ca. Aparagoyānaṃ sattasahassayojanaṃ. Tathā [M 1.0201] pubbavidehaṃ. Uttarakuru aṭṭhasahassayojanaṃ. Ekameko cettha mahādīpo pañcasatapañcasataparittadīpaparivāro. Taṃ sabbampi ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ ekā lokadhātu. Tadantaresu lokantarikanirayā.

Therein, the moon's disk is forty-nine yojanas. The sun's disk is fifty yojanas. The Tāvatiṃsa realm is ten thousand yojanas. Likewise are the asura realm, the Avīci great hell, and Jambudīpa. Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas. Likewise is Pubbavideha. Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas. Each great continent here is surrounded by five hundred lesser islands. All this is one Cakkavāḷa, one world-system. In the interstices between them are the Lokantarika hells.

Evaṃ anantāni cakkavāḷāni anantā lokadhātuyo bhagavā anantena buddhañāṇena avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi. Evamassa okāsalokopi sabbathā vidito. Evampi sabbathā viditalokattā lokavidū.

Thus, with infinite Buddha-knowledge, the Blessed One knew, understood, and penetratively understood the endless world-systems and infinite world-elements. In this way, the world of location was also known to him in every way. Thus also, because the world is known to him in every way, he is the Knower of the World (Lokavidū).

138. Attanā pana guṇehi visiṭṭhatarassa kassaci abhāvato natthi etassa uttaroti anuttaro. Tathā hesa sīlaguṇenāpi sabbaṃ lokamabhibhavati, samādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanaguṇenāpi. Sīlaguṇenāpi asamo asamasamo appaṭimo appaṭibhāgo appaṭipuggalo…pe… vimuttiñāṇadassanaguṇenāpi. Yathāha – “na kho panāhaṃ samanupassāmi sadevake loke samārake…pe… sadevamanussāya pajāya attanā sīlasampannatara”nti vitthāro. Evaṃ aggapasādasuttādīni (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) “na me ācariyo atthī”tiādikā (ma. ni. 1.285; mahāva. 11) gāthāyo ca vitthāretabbā.

138. Furthermore, because there is no one more distinguished than himself in virtues, 'there is no superior to him,' thus he is the Unsurpassed (Anuttara). Indeed, he surpasses the entire world by the virtue of morality, and also by the virtues of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. By the virtue of morality, he is without equal, equal to the unequalled, without a peer, without a counterpart, and without a rival person... and so on... and also by the virtue of the knowledge and vision of liberation. As it is said: “I do not see anyone in this world with its devas, its Māra... and so on... in this generation with its devas and humans, who is more accomplished in morality than myself.” This should be elaborated. In this way, the Aggappasāda Sutta and others, and the verses beginning, “There is no teacher for me,” should also be elaborated.

139. Purisadamme sāretīti purisadammasārathi. Dameti vinetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha purisadammāti adantā dametuṃ yuttā tiracchānapurisāpi manussapurisāpi amanussapurisāpi. Tathā hi bhagavatā tiracchānapurisāpi apalālo nāgarājā, cūḷodaro, mahodaro, aggisikho, dhūmasikho, aravāḷo nāgarājā, dhanapālako hatthīti evamādayo damitā nibbisā katā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpitā, manussapurisāpi saccakanigaṇṭhaputtaambaṭṭhamāṇavapokkharasāti soṇadantakūṭadantādayo, amanussapurisāpi āḷavakasūcilomakharalomayakkhasakkadevarājādayo [V 1.0200] damitā vinītā vicitrehi vinayanūpāyehi. “Ahaṃ kho, kesi, purisadamme saṇhenapi vinemi, pharusenapi vinemi, saṇhapharusenapi vinemī”ti (a. ni. 4.11) idañcettha suttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

139. He trains persons who are to be tamed (purisadamme), thus he is the Trainer of Persons to be Tamed (Purisadammasārathi). This means, it is said, 'He tames, he disciplines.' Therein, 'persons to be tamed' (purisadammā) are the untamed who are fit to be tamed, whether they be animal-persons, human-persons, or non-human-persons. Indeed, by the Blessed One, animal-persons such as the nāga king Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, the nāga king Aravāḷa, the elephant Dhanapālaka, and others were tamed, made free from venom, and established in the refuges and precepts. Human-persons such as Saccaka son of the Nigaṇṭhas, the youth Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others were also tamed. Non-human-persons such as the yakkhas Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma, Sakka king of the devas, and others were tamed and disciplined by various skillful means of discipline. And this sutta should be elaborated here: “I, Kesi, discipline persons who are to be tamed sometimes gently, sometimes harshly, and sometimes both gently and harshly.”

Apica bhagavā visuddhasīlādīnaṃ paṭhamajjhānādīni sotāpannādīnañca uttari maggapaṭipadaṃ ācikkhanto dantepi dametiyeva.

Furthermore, the Blessed One, while explaining the first jhāna and so forth to those of purified virtue and so forth, and the higher path of practice to stream-enterers and so forth, indeed tames even those who are already tamed.

Atha [M 1.0202] vā anuttaro purisadammasārathīti ekamevidaṃ atthapadaṃ. Bhagavā hi tathā purisadamme sāreti, yathā ekapallaṅkeneva nisinnā aṭṭha disā asajjamānā dhāvanti. Tasmā anuttaro purisadammasārathīti vuccati. “Hatthidamakena, bhikkhave, hatthidammo sārito ekaṃyeva disaṃ dhāvatī”ti idañcettha suttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.312) vitthāretabbaṃ.

Alternatively, 'unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed' is a single term expressing the meaning. For the Blessed One trains persons to be tamed in such a way that, while seated in a single cross-legged posture, they run unimpeded towards the eight directions of the eight attainments. Therefore, he is called 'the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed'. Here, this discourse should be elaborated: “Monks, an elephant to be tamed, when guided by an elephant trainer, runs in only one direction.”

140. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ anusāsatīti satthā. Apica satthā viyāti satthā, bhagavā satthavāho. Yathā satthavāho satthe kantāraṃ tāreti corakantāraṃ tāreti vāḷakantāraṃ tāreti dubbhikkhakantāraṃ tāreti nirudakakantāraṃ tāreti uttāreti nittāreti patāreti khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpeti, evameva bhagavā satthā satthavāho satte kantāraṃ tāreti, jātikantāraṃ tāretītiādinā niddesanayenapettha attho veditabbo. Devamanussānanti devānañca manussānañca. Ukkaṭṭhaparicchedavasena, bhabbapuggalaparicchedavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Bhagavā pana tiracchānagatānampi anusāsanippadānena satthāyeva. Tepi hi bhagavato dhammassavanena upanissayasampattiṃ patvā tāya eva upanissayasampattiyā dutiye vā tatiye vā attabhāve maggaphalabhāgino honti. Maṇḍūkadevaputtādayo cettha nidassanaṃ.

140. He is the Teacher (Satthā) because he instructs appropriately with the benefits in this present life, the benefits in the life to come, and the ultimate benefit. Furthermore, he is the Teacher (Satthā) because he is like a caravan leader (satthavāha); the Blessed One is a caravan leader. Just as a caravan leader guides a caravan across a wilderness—guides them across a wilderness of thieves, guides them across a wilderness of wild beasts, guides them across a wilderness of famine, guides them across a waterless wilderness; leads them across, leads them out, leads them over, and brings them to a place of safety—even so, the Blessed One, the Teacher, the caravan leader, guides beings across the wilderness, guides them across the wilderness of birth, and so forth. Here, the meaning of the term Satthā should also be understood according to the method of the Niddesa. The phrase 'of devas and humans' refers to both devas and humans. This is stated by way of distinguishing superior beings and by way of distinguishing capable individuals. However, the Blessed One is indeed the Teacher even for those born in the animal realm by his giving of instruction. For even they, by hearing the Dhamma from the Blessed One, attain the accomplishment of a supporting condition, and through that very accomplishment of a supporting condition, in their second or third existence, they become partakers of the path and fruit. The frog-deva and others are an example here.

Bhagavati kira gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre campānagaravāsīnaṃ dhammaṃ desiyamāne eko maṇḍūko bhagavato sare nimittaṃ aggahesi, taṃ eko vacchapālako daṇḍaṃ olubbha tiṭṭhanto sīse sannirumbhitvā aṭṭhāsi. So tāvadeva kālaṅkatvā tāvatiṃsabhavane dvādasayojanike kanakavimāne nibbatti. Suttappabuddho viya ca tattha accharāsaṅghaparivutaṃ attānaṃ disvā “are ahampi nāma idha nibbatto, kiṃ nu kho kammamakāsi”nti āvajjento na aññaṃ kiñci addasa [V 1.0201] aññatra bhagavato sare nimittaggāhā. So tāvadeva saha vimānena āgantvā bhagavato pāde sirasā vandi. Bhagavā jānantova pucchi –

It is said that while the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the residents of the city of Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, a certain frog grasped the sign in the Blessed One’s voice. A certain cowherd, while standing leaning on a stick, pressed down on its head with the stick and stood there. That frog, having died at that very moment, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa abode in a golden celestial mansion twelve yojanas in extent. And there, as if awakening from sleep, seeing himself surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, he reflected, 'Oh! I have indeed been reborn here. What kamma, I wonder, have I done?' Reflecting, he saw no other cause whatsoever apart from grasping the sign in the Blessed One's voice. At that very moment, he came together with his celestial mansion and worshipped the Blessed One’s feet with his head. The Blessed One, although knowing, asked:

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti.

“Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with power and glory, with a most pleasing complexion, illuminating all directions?”

Maṇḍūkohaṃ [M 1.0203] pure āsiṃ, udake vārigocaro;

Tava dhammaṃ suṇantassa, avadhi vacchapālakoti.

“In a former existence, I was a frog, an aquatic creature living in the water. While I was listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me.”

Bhagavā tassa dhammaṃ desesi. Caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Devaputtopi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya sitaṃ katvā pakkamīti.

The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to him. There was a penetration of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand beings. The devaputta, too, having been established in the fruit of stream-entry, smiled and departed.

141. Yaṃ pana kiñci atthi ñeyyaṃ nāma, sabbasseva buddhattā vimokkhantikaññāṇavasena buddho. Yasmā vā cattāri saccāni attanāpi bujjhi, aññepi satte bodhesi, tasmā evamādīhipi kāraṇehi buddho. Imassa ca panatthassa viññāpanatthaṃ “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho. Bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”ti evaṃ pavatto sabbopi niddesanayo (mahāni. 192) paṭisambhidānayo (paṭi. ma. 1.162) vā vitthāretabbo.

141. Furthermore, whatever is called knowable, because he has understood all of it by means of the knowledge that culminates in final liberation, he is the Buddha. Or, because he himself understood the Four Truths and he causes other beings to understand them, for these and similar reasons he is the Buddha. And furthermore, to make this meaning known, this entire method of exposition from the Niddesa or the Paṭisambhidāmagga should be elaborated: 'Because he is one who has understood the truths, he is the Buddha. Because he is one who causes the populace to understand, he is the Buddha.'

142. Bhagavāti idaṃ panassa guṇavisiṭṭhasabbasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanaṃ. Tenāhu porāṇā –

142. Furthermore, this term 'Bhagavā' is an appellation of honor and respect for him, who is distinguished by virtues, supreme among all beings, and a master worthy of esteem and reverence. Therefore the ancients have said:

“Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garugāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“'Bhagavā' is an excellent term; 'Bhagavā' is a supreme term. He is endowed with the qualities of being esteemed and revered; therefore, he is called 'Bhagavā'.”

Catubbidhaṃ vā nāmaṃ āvatthikaṃ liṅgikaṃ nemittikaṃ adhiccasamuppannanti. Adhiccasamuppannaṃ nāma lokiyavohārena yadicchakanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha vaccho dammo balībaddoti evamādi āvatthikaṃ. Daṇḍī chattī sikhī karīti evamādi liṅgikaṃ. Tevijjo chaḷabhiññoti evamādi nemittikaṃ. Sirivaḍḍhako dhanavaḍḍhakoti evamādi vacanatthaṃ anapekkhitvā pavattaṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ. Idaṃ [V 1.0202] pana bhagavāti nāmaṃ nemittikaṃ, na mahāmāyāya, na suddhodanamahārājena, na asītiyā ñātisahassehi kataṃ, na sakkasantusitādīhi devatāvisesehi. Vuttampi cetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ…pe… vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ bhagavā”ti (mahāni. 84).

Alternatively, a name is of four kinds: a name based on a temporary state, a name based on a characteristic sign, a name based on a quality, and an adventitious name. An adventitious name is what is called, in worldly usage, an arbitrary name. Among these, names such as 'calf,' 'a bullock fit for taming,' and 'a draught ox' are names based on a temporary state. Names such as 'one with a staff,' 'one with an umbrella,' 'one with a top-knot,' and 'one with a trunk' are names based on a characteristic sign. Names such as 'one with the three knowledges' and 'one with the six supernormal knowledges' are names based on a quality. Names such as 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' and 'Dhanavaḍḍhaka,' which arise without regard to the meaning of the word, are adventitious names. This name 'Bhagavā,' however, is a name based on a quality. It was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana, nor by the eighty thousand relatives, nor by distinguished deities such as Sakka and Santusita. And this was stated by the General of the Dhamma: 'This name, “Bhagavā,” was not given by his mother… this is a term of final liberation for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, a designation personally realized at the root of the Bodhi tree along with the attainment of omniscience—that is, “Bhagavā”'.

143. Yaṃguṇanemittikañcetaṃ nāmaṃ, tesaṃ guṇānaṃ pakāsanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ vadanti –

143. And since this name is one based on qualities as its cause, to show those qualities, they recite this verse:

“Bhagī [M 1.0204] bhajī bhāgi vibhattavā iti,

Akāsi bhagganti garūti bhāgyavā;

Bahūhi ñāyehi subhāvitattano,

Bhavantago so bhagavāti vuccatī”ti. –

“He possessed glory (bhagī), he resorted (bhajī), he had a share (bhāgi), he analyzed (vibhattavā); He accomplished the breaking (bhaggaṃ akāsi), he is revered (garū), he is fortunate (bhāgyavā); His being is well-developed by many methods, He has gone to the end of existence (bhavantago), thus he is called Bhagavā.”

Niddese (mahāni. 84) vuttanayeneva cettha tesaṃ tesaṃ padānaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, the meaning of those respective words should be understood in the very manner explained in the Niddesa.

144. Ayaṃ pana aparo nayo.

144. This, however, is another method.

Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tatoti.

“He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), has broken (bhaggavā), is endowed with the glories (yutto bhagehi), and has analyzed (vibhattavā); He has frequented (bhattavā), and has relinquished the going in existences (vantagamano bhavesu); therefore (tato) he is Bhagavā.”

Tattha vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyayotiādikaṃ niruttilakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā saddanayena vā pisodarādipakkhepalakkhaṇaṃ gahetvā yasmā lokiyalokuttarasukhābhinibbattakaṃ dānasīlādipārappattaṃ bhāgyamassa atthi, tasmā bhāgyavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccatīti ñātabbaṃ.

Therein, by employing the characteristics of etymology such as letter augmentation and letter transposition, or by the method of grammar, employing the characteristic of inclusion in the pisodara group and so on, it should be understood thus: because he possesses that fortune (bhāgya) which generates worldly and supramundane happiness and has reached the perfection of giving, virtue, and so on, therefore, although he should be called 'Bhāgyavā,' he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā pana ahirikānottappakodhūpanāhamakkhapaḷāsaissāmacchariyamāyāsāṭheyyathambhasārambhamānātimānamadapamādataṇhāavijjā- tividhākusalamūladuccaritasaṃkilesamalavisamasaññāvitakkapapañcacatubbidhavipariyesa- āsavaganthaoghayogaagatitaṇhuppādupādānapañcacetokhīlavinibandhanīvaraṇābhinandanā- chavivādamūlataṇhākāyasattānusayaaṭṭhamicchattanavataṇhāmūlakadasākusalakammapathadvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigata- aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritappabhedasabbadarathapariḷāhakilesasatasahassāni[V 1.0203], saṅkhepato vā pañca kilesakhandhaabhisaṅkhāradevaputtamaccumāre abhañji. Tasmā bhaggattā etesaṃ parissayānaṃ bhaggavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati. Āha cettha –

Moreover, because he has broken hundreds of thousands of varieties of all defilements that cause torment and feverish heat—namely: shamelessness and lack of conscience; anger and enmity; denigration and rivalry; envy and stinginess; deceit and hypocrisy; obstinacy and presumption; pride and arrogance; intoxication and heedlessness; craving and ignorance; the three unwholesome roots; the three kinds of misconduct; the three kinds of defilements; the three kinds of stains; the three kinds of crookedness; the three kinds of wrong perceptions; the three kinds of wrong thoughts; the three kinds of proliferation; the four perversions; the four taints; the four bonds; the four floods; the four yokes; the four wrong courses; the four arisings of craving; the four kinds of clinging; the five mental barrennesses; the five mental bondages; the five hindrances; the five kinds of delight; the six roots of dispute; the six bodies of craving; the seven underlying tendencies; the eight wrongnesses; the nine roots of craving; the ten unwholesome courses of action; the sixty-two wrong views; and the one hundred and eight kinds of craving-impelled conduct—or, in brief, because he has broken the five Māras, namely, the Māras of defilements, aggregates, formations, the deity, and death; therefore, because of having broken these dangers, although he should be called 'Bhaggavā', he is called 'Bhagavā'. And in this regard, it is said:

“Bhaggarāgo bhaggadoso, bhaggamoho anāsavo;

Bhaggāssa pāpakā dhammā, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

His passion is broken, his hatred is broken, his delusion is broken; he is without taints. His evil states have been broken; for that reason, he is called 'Bhagavā'.

Bhāgyavatāya cassa satapuññalakkhaṇadharassa rūpakāyasampatti dīpitā hoti. Bhaggadosatāya dhammakāyasampatti. Tathā lokiyasarikkhakānaṃ bahumatabhāvo, gahaṭṭhapabbajitehi abhigamanīyatā, abhigatānañca nesaṃ kāyacittadukkhāpanayane [M 1.0205] paṭibalabhāvo, āmisadānadhammadānehi upakāritā, lokiyalokuttarasukhehi ca saṃyojanasamatthatā dīpitā hoti.

And through his good fortune (bhāgyavatā), the perfection of the physical body of him who bears the marks resulting from innumerable merits is revealed. Through his having broken the faults (bhaggadosatā), the perfection of his Dhamma-body is revealed. Likewise, the following are also revealed: his state of being highly esteemed by worldly people and investigators; his approachability by householders and renunciants; for those who have approached him, his capability in dispelling their bodily and mental suffering; his helpfulness through the gift of material things and the gift of the Dhamma; and his ability to unite them with worldly and supramundane happiness.

Yasmā ca loke issariyadhammayasasirikāmapayattesu chasu dhammesu bhagasaddo pavattati, paramañcassa sakacitte issariyaṃ, aṇimālaṅghimādikaṃ vā lokiyasammataṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ atthi. Tathā lokuttaro dhammo. Lokattayabyāpako yathābhuccaguṇādhigato ativiya parisuddho yaso. Rūpakāyadassanabyāvaṭajananayanappasādajananasamatthā sabbākāraparipūrā sabbaṅgapaccaṅgasirī. Yaṃ yaṃ etena icchitaṃ patthitaṃ attahitaṃ parahitaṃ vā, tassa tassa tatheva abhinipphannattā icchitatthanibbattisaññito kāmo. Sabbalokagarubhāvappattihetubhūto sammāvāyāmasaṅkhāto payatto ca atthi. Tasmā imehi bhagehi yuttattāpi bhagā assa santīti iminā atthena bhagavāti vuccati.

Furthermore, because in the world the term 'bhaga' is applied to six things—sovereignty, Dhamma, fame, glory, desire, and effort—and because for Him there exists supreme sovereignty in His own mind, or the worldly-esteemed sovereignty complete in all aspects, such as Aṇimā, Laghimā, and so on. Likewise, there is the supramundane Dhamma. There is fame, exceedingly pure, pervading the three worlds, and acquired through true qualities. There is the glory of all major and minor limbs, complete in all aspects, capable of producing delight in the eyes of the people who strive to see the form-body. There is desire, known as the accomplishment of what is wished for, because whatever benefit for Himself or for others is wished for or aspired to by Him, that very thing is accomplished just so. And there is effort, known as right effort, which is the cause for attaining the state of being the venerable one for the entire world. Therefore, because He is endowed with these glories (bhagas), and because the glories are His, for this reason He is called Bhagavā.

Yasmā pana kusalādīhi bhedehi sabbadhamme, khandhāyatanadhātusaccaindriyapaṭiccasamuppādādīhi vā kusalādidhamme, pīḷanasaṅkhatasantāpavipariṇāmaṭṭhena vā dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, āyūhananidānasaṃyogapalibodhaṭṭhena samudayaṃ, nissaraṇavivekāsaṅkhataamataṭṭhena nirodhaṃ, niyyānikahetudassanādhipateyyaṭṭhena maggaṃ vibhattavā, vibhajitvā vivaritvā desitavāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tasmā vibhattavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati.

Furthermore, because He has analyzed all dhammas by way of divisions such as wholesome, etc., or wholesome and other dhammas by way of the aggregates, sense bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so on; or because He has analyzed the Noble Truth of Suffering in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, torment, and change; the Noble Truth of the Origin in the sense of accumulation, source, bondage, and obstruction; the Noble Truth of Cessation in the sense of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless; and the Noble Truth of the Path in the sense of leading out, cause, vision, and dominion—it is said that having analyzed, explained, and taught them. Therefore, when 'Vibhattavā' (He who has analyzed) should be said, He is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā ca esa dibbabrahmaariyavihāre kāyacittaupadhiviveke suññatappaṇihitānimittavimokkhe aññe ca lokiyalokuttare uttarimanussadhamme bhaji sevi bahulaṃ akāsi, tasmā bhattavāti vattabbe bhagavāti vuccati.

And because this Supreme Person frequented, cultivated, and abundantly practiced the divine, Brahma, and noble abidings; seclusion from the body, mind, and substrates of existence; the liberations of emptiness, the desireless, and the signless; and other mundane and supramundane states that are beyond the human, therefore, when 'Bhattavā' (He who has frequented) should be said, He is called 'Bhagavā'.

Yasmā [V 1.0204] pana tīsu bhavesu taṇhāsaṅkhātaṃ gamanaṃ anena vantaṃ, tasmā bhavesu vantagamanoti vattabbe bhavasaddato bhakāraṃ gamanasaddato gakāraṃ vantasaddato vakārañca dīghaṃ katvā ādāya bhagavāti vuccati yathā loke mehanassa khassa mālāti vattabbe mekhalāti.

Furthermore, because in the three existences the going, designated as craving, has been abandoned by him, therefore, instead of saying 'bhavesu vantagamano' (one who has abandoned going in the existences), he is called 'Bhagavā' by taking the syllable 'bha' from the word 'bhava,' 'ga' from the word 'gamana,' and 'va' from the word 'vanta,' and lengthening the vowel. This is just as in the world, 'mekhalā' is said when 'mehanassa khassa mālā' should be said.

145. Tassevaṃ iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇena so bhagavā arahaṃ…pe… iminā ca iminā ca kāraṇena bhagavāti buddhaguṇe anussarato neva tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosapariyuṭṭhitaṃ, na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ [M 1.0206] cittaṃ hoti. Ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgatamārabbha (a. ni. 6.10). Iccassa evaṃ rāgādipariyuṭṭhānābhāvena vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa kammaṭṭhānābhimukhatāya ujugatacittassa buddhaguṇapoṇā vitakkavicārā pavattanti. Buddhaguṇe anuvitakkayato anuvicārayato pīti uppajjati. Pītimanassa pītipadaṭṭhānāya passaddhiyā kāyacittadarathā paṭippassambhanti. Passaddhadarathassa kāyikampi cetasikampi sukhaṃ uppajjati. Sukhino buddhaguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā cittaṃ samādhiyatīti anukkamena ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Buddhaguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāraguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ buddhaguṇānussaraṇavasena uppannattā buddhānussaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

145. For one who thus recollects the virtues of the Buddha—'For this reason and that, the Blessed One is an Arahant... for this reason and that, he is the Blessed One'—at that time the mind is not overcome by lust, nor by aversion, nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is indeed upright, directed toward the Tathāgata. Thus, for him, due to the absence of being overcome by lust and so on, with the hindrances subdued, and with the mind upright and inclined towards the meditation subject, initial and sustained thoughts inclining towards the virtues of the Buddha arise. For one who repeatedly applies initial and sustained thought to the virtues of the Buddha, joy arises. For one with a joyful mind, bodily and mental distresses are tranquilized by means of tranquility, which has joy as its proximate cause. For one whose distress has been tranquilized, bodily and mental happiness arises. For one who is happy, the mind, having the virtues of the Buddha as its object, becomes concentrated; thus, the factors of absorption arise successively in a single moment. However, due to the profundity of the Buddha’s virtues or due to the disposition to recollect their diverse qualities, absorption is not attained, and the jhāna only reaches the level of access concentration. Because this arises through the recollection of the Buddha’s virtues, it is reckoned as 'recollection of the Buddha'.

Imañca pana buddhānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu satthari sagāravo hoti sappatisso, saddhāvepullaṃ sativepullaṃ paññāvepullaṃ puññavepullañca adhigacchati, pītipāmojjabahulo hoti, bhayabheravasaho dukkhādhivāsanasamattho, satthārā saṃvāsasaññaṃ paṭilabhati. Buddhaguṇānussatiyā ajjhāvutthañcassa sarīrampi cetiyagharamiva pūjārahaṃ hoti. Buddhabhūmiyaṃ cittaṃ namati. Vītikkamitabbavatthusamāyoge cassa sammukhā satthāraṃ passato viya hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāti. Uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

Furthermore, to speak of the benefits: a monk who is devoted to this recollection of the Buddha is respectful and deferential toward the Teacher. He attains an abundance of faith, an abundance of mindfulness, an abundance of wisdom, and an abundance of merit. He is full of joy and gladness, able to overcome fear and dread, and capable of enduring suffering. He gains the perception of dwelling with the Teacher. Even his body, being pervaded by the recollection of the Buddha’s qualities, becomes worthy of veneration like a shrine-house. His mind inclines toward the Buddha-ground. When an occasion for transgression is encountered, shame and moral dread are present in him as if he were beholding the Teacher in person. And if he does not penetrate further to the higher paths and fruitions, he is at least destined for a happy bourn.

Tasmā have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, buddhānussatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, indeed, the wise one should always practice diligence in this recollection of the Buddha, which is of such great power.

Idaṃ tāva buddhānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This, for now, is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the recollection of the Buddha.

2. Dhammānussatikathā

2. 2. The Exposition on the Recollection of the Dhamma

146. Dhammānussatiṃ [V 1.0205] bhāvetukāmenāpi rahogatena paṭisallīnena “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo sandiṭṭhiko akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti (a. ni. 6.10) evaṃ pariyattidhammassa ceva navavidhassa ca lokuttaradhammassa guṇā anussaritabbā.

146. By one who wishes to develop the recollection of the Dhamma, having gone to a secluded place and being in solitude, the qualities of both the scriptural Dhamma and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma should be recollected thus: 'Well-proclaimed is the Dhamma by the Blessed One, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be experienced by the wise for themselves.'

147. Svākkhātoti imasmiṃ hi pade pariyattidhammopi saṅgahaṃ gacchati, itaresu lokuttaradhammova. Tattha pariyattidhammo tāva svākkhāto ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇattā [M 1.0207] sātthasabyañjanakevalaparipuṇṇaparisuddhabrahmacariyappakāsanattā ca. Yañhi bhagavā ekagāthampi deseti, sā samantabhaddakattā dhammassa paṭhamapādena ādikalyāṇā, dutiyatatiyapādehi majjhekalyāṇā, pacchimapādena pariyosānakalyāṇā. Ekānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ nidānena ādikalyāṇaṃ, nigamanena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ, sesena majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Nānānusandhikaṃ suttaṃ paṭhamānusandhinā ādikalyāṇaṃ, pacchimena pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ, sesehi majjhekalyāṇaṃ. Apica sanidānasauppattikattā ādikalyāṇaṃ, veneyyānaṃ anurūpato atthassa aviparītatāya ca hetudāharaṇayuttato ca majjhekalyāṇaṃ, sotūnaṃ saddhāpaṭilābhajananena nigamanena ca pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ.

147. Indeed, in this term 'well-proclaimed', the scriptural Dhamma is also included, whereas in the others, only the supramundane Dhamma is included. Therein, the scriptural Dhamma is 'well-proclaimed' because it is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, and because it proclaims the holy life which is complete with meaning and phrasing, entirely complete, and utterly pure. For whatever single verse the Blessed One teaches, that verse—because the Dhamma is good in all its parts—is excellent in the beginning with the first line, excellent in the middle with the second and third lines, and excellent in the end with the final line. A discourse with a single connection is excellent in the beginning with its introduction, excellent in the end with its conclusion, and excellent in the middle with the remainder. A discourse with various connections is excellent in the beginning with the first connection, excellent in the end with the last, and excellent in the middle with the remaining ones. Furthermore, it is excellent in the beginning because it has an introduction and an origin story; excellent in the middle because of its suitability for the disciples, the non-perversion of its meaning, and its endowment with reason and example; and excellent in the end because it generates the acquisition of faith in the listeners and because of its conclusion.

Sakalopi sāsanadhammo attano atthabhūtena sīlena ādikalyāṇo, samathavipassanāmaggaphalehi majjhekalyāṇo, nibbānena pariyosānakalyāṇo. Sīlasamādhīhi vā ādikalyāṇo, vipassanāmaggehi majjhekalyāṇo, phalanibbānehi pariyosānakalyāṇo. Buddhasubodhitāya vā ādikalyāṇo, dhammasudhammatāya majjhekalyāṇo, saṅghasuppaṭippattiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo. Taṃ sutvā tathatthāya paṭipannena adhigantabbāya abhisambodhiyā vā ādikalyāṇo, paccekabodhiyā majjhekalyāṇo, sāvakabodhiyā pariyosānakalyāṇo.

The entire teaching-Dhamma is excellent in the beginning with virtue, which is its own meaning; excellent in the middle with serenity, insight, the paths, and the fruits; and excellent in the end with Nibbāna. Or, it is excellent in the beginning with virtue and concentration; excellent in the middle with insight and the paths; and excellent in the end with the fruits and Nibbāna. Or, it is excellent in the beginning because of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment; excellent in the middle because of the excellent nature of the Dhamma; and excellent in the end because of the Sangha's good practice. Or, for one who, having heard it, practices for that purpose, it is excellent in the beginning with the perfect self-enlightenment to be attained, excellent in the middle with the enlightenment of a Private Buddha, and excellent in the end with the enlightenment of a disciple.

Suyyamāno cesa nīvaraṇavikkhambhanato savanenapi kalyāṇameva āvahatīti ādikalyāṇo, paṭipajjiyamāno samathavipassanāsukhāvahanato paṭipattiyāpi kalyāṇaṃ āvahatīti majjhekalyāṇo, tathāpaṭipanno ca paṭipattiphale niṭṭhite tādibhāvāvahanato paṭipattiphalenapi [V 1.0206] kalyāṇaṃ āvahatīti pariyosānakalyāṇoti evaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇattā svākkhāto.

Furthermore, this Dhamma, when being heard, brings only well-being even by the mere act of hearing, due to the suppression of the hindrances; thus, it is excellent in the beginning. When being practiced, it brings well-being also through practice, due to its bringing the happiness of serenity and insight; thus, it is excellent in the middle. And when one has practiced accordingly and the fruit of the practice is accomplished, it brings well-being also through the fruit of the practice, due to its bringing about the 'tādi' state; thus, it is excellent in the end. In this way, because of being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, it is 'well-proclaimed'.

Yaṃ panesa bhagavā dhammaṃ desento sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ maggabrahmacariyañca pakāseti nānānayehi dīpeti, taṃ yathānurūpaṃ atthasampattiyā sātthaṃ, byañjanasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattiatthapadasamāyogato sātthaṃ, akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesasampattiyā sabyañjanaṃ. Atthagambhīratāpaṭivedhagambhīratāhi sātthaṃ, dhammagambhīratādesanāgambhīratāhi [M 1.0208] sabyañjanaṃ. Atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāvisayato sātthaṃ, dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāvisayato sabyañjanaṃ. Paṇḍitavedanīyato parikkhakajanappasādakanti sātthaṃ, saddheyyato lokiyajanappasādakanti sabyañjanaṃ. Gambhīrādhippāyato sātthaṃ, uttānapadato sabyañjanaṃ. Upanetabbassa abhāvato sakalaparipuṇṇabhāvena kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ. Apanetabbassa abhāvato niddosabhāvena parisuddhaṃ.

Moreover, when the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, he proclaims and clarifies in various ways the holy life of the teaching and the holy life of the path. That holy life is, in accordance with its nature, with meaning due to its accomplishment in meaning, and with expression due to its accomplishment in phrasing. It is with meaning due to its connection with the components of meaning: concise exposition, initial exposition, detailed explanation, analysis, making plain, and designation. It is with expression due to its accomplishment in the components of phrasing: letters, words, sentences, methodology, etymology, and exposition. It is with meaning due to the profundity of meaning and the profundity of penetration; it is with expression due to the profundity of the Dhamma and the profundity of the teaching. It is with meaning as it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of meaning and of discernment; it is with expression as it is the domain of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language. It is with meaning as it is to be understood by the wise and inspires confidence in discerning people; it is with expression as it is to be believed and inspires confidence in worldly people. It is with meaning due to its profound intention; it is with expression due to its plain wording. Because there is nothing to be added, it is entirely complete, being perfect in all its parts. Because there is nothing to be removed, it is utterly pure, being flawless.

Apica paṭipattiyā adhigamabyattito sātthaṃ, pariyattiyā āgamabyattito sabyañjanaṃ, sīlādipañcadhammakkhandhayuttato kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ, nirupakkilesato nittaraṇatthāya pavattito lokāmisanirapekkhato ca parisuddhanti evaṃ sātthasabyañjanakevalaparipuṇṇaparisuddhabrahmacariyappakāsanato svākkhāto.

Furthermore, it is with meaning due to the manifestation of attainment through practice, and with expression due to the manifestation of the scriptural tradition through study. It is entirely complete due to being endowed with the five aggregates of the Dhamma beginning with virtue. It is utterly pure due to being without defilements, because it proceeds for the purpose of crossing over, and because it is without regard for worldly allurements. Thus, because it proclaims a holy life that is with meaning, with expression, entirely complete, and utterly pure, it is 'well-proclaimed'.

Atthavipallāsābhāvato vā suṭṭhu akkhātoti svākkhāto. Yathā hi aññatitthiyānaṃ dhammassa attho vipallāsamāpajjati, antarāyikāti vuttadhammānaṃ antarāyikattābhāvato, niyyānikāti vuttadhammānaṃ niyyānikattābhāvato. Tena te durakkhātadhammāyeva honti, na tathā bhagavato dhammassa attho vipallāsamāpajjati. Ime dhammā antarāyikā, ime dhammā niyyānikāti evaṃ vuttadhammānaṃ tathābhāvānatikkamanatoti.
