Evaṃ tāva pariyattidhammo svākkhāto.

Alternatively, it is 'well-proclaimed' because of the absence of distortion in its meaning. For, just as the meaning of the doctrine of other sectarians becomes distorted—because the things they have declared as 'obstructive' lack the quality of being obstructive, and the things they have declared as 'leading out' lack the quality of leading out—and thereby they are indeed those with a poorly proclaimed doctrine, not so does the meaning of the Blessed One's Dhamma become distorted. This is because the things declared thus, 'These dhammas are obstructive,' and 'These dhammas are leading out,' do not transgress that very state. In this way, first, the Dhamma as scripture is well-proclaimed.

Lokuttaradhammo pana nibbānānurūpāya paṭipattiyā paṭipadānurūpassa ca nibbānassa akkhātattā svākkhāto. Yathāha – “supaññattā kho pana tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ nibbānagāminī paṭipadā saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā ca. Seyyathāpi nāma gaṅgodakaṃ yamunodakena saṃsandati sameti, evameva supaññattā (dī. ni. 2.296) tena bhagavatā sāvakānaṃ [V 1.0207] nibbānagāminī paṭipadā saṃsandati nibbānañca paṭipadā cā”ti. Ariyamaggo cettha antadvayaṃ anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadābhūtova “majjhimā paṭipadā”ti akkhātattā svākkhāto. Sāmaññaphalāni paṭipassaddhakilesāneva “paṭipassaddhakilesānī”ti akkhātattā svākkhātāni. Nibbānaṃ sassatāmatatāṇaleṇādisabhāvameva sassatādisabhāvavasena akkhātattā svākkhātanti evaṃ lokuttaradhammopi svākkhāto.

The supramundane Dhamma, however, is well-proclaimed because it is proclaimed as the practice that is in conformity with Nibbāna, and as the Nibbāna that is in conformity with the practice. As it is said: 'Well-proclaimed indeed by that Blessed One for the disciples is the practice leading to Nibbāna; Nibbāna and the practice converge. Just as the water of the Ganges converges and meets with the water of the Yamunā, even so is the practice leading to Nibbāna well-proclaimed by that Blessed One for the disciples; Nibbāna and the practice converge.' And here, the Noble Path, by not approaching the two extremes and being the Middle Way itself, is well-proclaimed because it is proclaimed as the 'Middle Way.' The fruits of recluseship, being themselves states where defilements are allayed, are well-proclaimed because they are proclaimed as 'states where defilements are allayed.' Nibbāna, being itself of the nature of the permanent, the deathless, the shelter, the refuge, and so on, is well-proclaimed because it is proclaimed by way of its nature as permanent, and so on. Thus, the supramundane Dhamma is also well-proclaimed.

148. Sandiṭṭhikoti [M 1.0209] ettha pana ariyamaggo tāva attano santāne rāgādīnaṃ abhāvaṃ karontena ariyapuggalena sāmaṃ daṭṭhabboti sandiṭṭhiko. Yathāha –“ratto kho, brāhmaṇa, rāgena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto attabyābādhāyapi ceteti, parabyābādhāyapi ceteti, ubhayabyābādhāyapi ceteti. Cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Rāge pahīne neva attabyābādhāya ceteti, na parabyābādhāya ceteti, na ubhayabyābādhāya ceteti, na cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedeti. Evampi kho, brāhmaṇa, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hotī”ti(a. ni. 3.54). Apica navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo yena yena adhigato hoti, tena tena parasaddhāya gantabbataṃ hitvā paccavekkhaṇañāṇena sayaṃ daṭṭhabboti sandiṭṭhiko. Atha vā pasatthā diṭṭhi sandiṭṭhi, sandiṭṭhiyā jayatīti sandiṭṭhiko. Tathā hettha ariyamaggo sampayuttāya, ariyaphalaṃ kāraṇabhūtāya, nibbānaṃ visayibhūtāya sandiṭṭhiyā kilese jayati. Tasmā yathā rathena jayatīti rathiko, evaṃ navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo sandiṭṭhiyā jayatīti sandiṭṭhiko.

148. Regarding `sandiṭṭhiko` (visible here and now): Herein, first, the Noble Path is to be seen by the noble person themselves by bringing about the absence of lust and other defilements in their own continuum; thus, it is `sandiṭṭhiko`. As it is said: "Brahmin, a lustful person, overcome by lust, with a mind obsessed, intends for their own affliction, for the affliction of others, and for the affliction of both. They experience mental suffering and displeasure. When lust is abandoned, they intend neither for their own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both. They do not experience mental suffering and displeasure. In this way, Brahmin, the Dhamma is `sandiṭṭhiko` (visible here and now)." Furthermore, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, by whichever noble disciple it is attained, is to be seen by that noble disciple themselves through the knowledge of reviewing, having abandoned the need to proceed by faith in others; thus, it is `sandiṭṭhiko`. Alternatively, an excellent view (`pasatthā diṭṭhi`) is `sandiṭṭhi`. One conquers by `sandiṭṭhi`; thus, it is `sandiṭṭhiko`. Indeed, herein, the Noble Path conquers the defilements by the excellent view associated with it; the Noble Fruit, by the excellent view which was its cause; and Nibbāna, by the excellent view which took it as an object. Therefore, just as one who conquers by a chariot (`rathena`) is called a charioteer (`rathiko`), so too the ninefold supramundane Dhamma conquers by an excellent view (`sandiṭṭhiyā`); thus, it is `sandiṭṭhiko`.

Atha vā diṭṭhanti dassanaṃ vuccati. Diṭṭhameva sandiṭṭhaṃ, dassananti attho. Sandiṭṭhaṃ arahatīti sandiṭṭhiko. Lokuttaradhammo hi bhāvanābhisamayavasena sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena ca dissamānoyeva vaṭṭabhayaṃ nivatteti. Tasmā yathā vatthaṃ arahatīti vatthiko, evaṃ sandiṭṭhaṃ arahatīti sandiṭṭhiko.

Alternatively, `diṭṭha` is said to mean seeing (`dassanaṃ`). `Diṭṭha` itself is `sandiṭṭhaṃ`, meaning 'seeing.' It is worthy of `sandiṭṭhaṃ` (seeing); thus, it is `sandiṭṭhiko`. Indeed, the supramundane Dhamma turns back the danger of the round of rebirth only when it is being seen through the full understanding by means of development and the full understanding by means of realization. Therefore, just as one who is worthy of cloth (`vatthaṃ`) is called `vatthiko`, so too, it is worthy of seeing (`sandiṭṭhaṃ`); thus, it is `sandiṭṭhiko`.

149. Attano phaladānaṃ sandhāya nāssa kāloti akālo. Akāloyeva akāliko. Na pañcāhasattāhādibhedaṃ kālaṃ khepetvā phalaṃ deti, attano pana pavattisamanantarameva phaladoti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā attano phaladāne pakaṭṭho kālo patto assāti kāliko. Ko so? Lokiyo [V 1.0208] kusaladhammo. Ayaṃ pana samanantaraphalattā na kālikoti akāliko. Idaṃ maggameva sandhāya vuttaṃ.

149. With reference to the giving of its own fruit, for this there is no time; therefore, it is `akālo` (timeless). `Akālo` itself is `akāliko` (not subject to time). It does not give its fruit after a period of time, such as five or seven days, has passed; rather, it is said that it gives its fruit immediately after its own arising. Alternatively, that for which, in the giving of its own fruit, there is a remote time that has been reached, is `kāliko` (subject to time). What is that? The worldly wholesome dhamma. But this, because it has an immediate fruit, is not `kāliko`; therefore, it is `akāliko`. This is said with reference to the path alone.

150. “Ehi passa imaṃ dhamma”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko. Kasmā panesa taṃ vidhiṃ arahatīti? Vijjamānattā parisuddhattā ca[M 1.0210]. Rittamuṭṭhiyaṃ hi hiraññaṃ vā suvaṇṇaṃ vā atthīti vatvāpi “ehi passa ima”nti na sakkā vattuṃ. Kasmā? Avijjamānattā. Vijjamānampi ca gūthaṃ vā muttaṃ vā manuññabhāvappakāsanena cittasampahaṃsanatthaṃ “ehi passa ima”nti na sakkā vattuṃ. Apica kho pana tiṇehi vā paṇṇehi vā paṭicchādetabbameva hoti. Kasmā? Aparisuddhattā. Ayaṃ pana navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo sabhāvatova vijjamāno vigatavalāhake ākāse sampuṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ viya paṇḍukambale nikkhittajātimaṇi viya ca parisuddho. Tasmā vijjamānattā parisuddhattā ca ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko.

150. It is worthy of the exhortation that proceeds as, 'Come, see this Dhamma'; therefore, it is `ehipassiko`. But why is it worthy of that exhortation? Because of its actual existence and its purity. Indeed, even after saying, 'There is silver or gold in this empty fist,' it is not possible to say, 'Come, see this.' Why? Because of its non-existence. And even though it exists, it is not possible to say, 'Come, see this' regarding feces or urine for the purpose of gladdening the mind by showing its pleasant nature. To the contrary, it should only be covered with grass or leaves. Why? Because of its impurity. But this ninefold supramundane Dhamma, existing by its own intrinsic nature, is thoroughly pure, like the full moon disc in a cloudless sky and like a genuine jewel placed on a pale woolen blanket. Therefore, because of its actual existence and its purity, it is worthy of the exhortation 'come and see'; thus, it is `ehipassiko`.

151. Upanetabboti opaneyyiko. Ayaṃ panettha vinicchayo, upanayanaṃ upanayo, ādittaṃ celaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā ajjhupekkhitvāpi bhāvanāvasena attano citte upanayanaṃ arahatīti opanayiko. Opanayikova opaneyyiko. Idaṃ saṅkhate lokuttaradhamme yujjati. Asaṅkhate pana attano cittena upanayanaṃ arahatīti opaneyyiko. Sacchikiriyāvasena allīyanaṃ arahatīti attho.

151. It is fit to be led up to; therefore, it is `opaneyyiko`. Herein is the analysis: `upanayanaṃ` is `upanayo` (leading up to). Even while disregarding a blazing cloth or head, by means of cultivation, it is worthy of being led up to in one's own mind; therefore, it is `opanayiko`. `Opanayiko` itself is `opaneyyiko`. This is applicable to the conditioned supramundane dhamma. But regarding the unconditioned, it is worthy of being led up to by one's own mind; therefore, it is `opaneyyiko`. The meaning is this: by means of realization, it is worthy of being adhered to.

Atha vā nibbānaṃ upanetīti ariyamaggo upaneyyo. Sacchikātabbataṃ upanetabboti phalanibbānadhammo upaneyyo. Upaneyyo eva opaneyyiko.

Alternatively, because the Noble Path leads to Nibbāna, it is `upaneyyo`. Because it is to be brought to the state of being realized, the Dhamma of fruit and Nibbāna is `upaneyyo`. `Upaneyyo` itself is `opaneyyiko`.

152. Paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhīti sabbehipi ugghaṭitaññūādīhi viññūhi attani attani veditabbo “bhāvito me maggo, adhigataṃ phalaṃ, sacchikato nirodho”ti. Na hi upajjhāyena bhāvitena maggena saddhivihārikassa kilesā pahīyanti, na so tassa phalasamāpattiyā phāsuviharati, na tena sacchikataṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikaroti. Tasmā na esa parassa sīse ābharaṇaṃ viya daṭṭhabbo, attano pana citteyeva daṭṭhabbo, anubhavitabbo viññūhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bālānaṃ pana avisayo cesa.

152. ‘To be known personally by the wise’ means: it is to be known in oneself by all wise ones—such as the ugghaṭitaññū, vipañcitaññū, and neyya individuals who have penetrated the Four Truths—thus: ‘The path has been developed by me, the fruit has been attained, and cessation has been realized.’ Indeed, the defilements of a co-resident are not abandoned by the path developed by his preceptor; he does not dwell at ease through that preceptor's attainment of fruition; he does not realize the Nibbāna that was realized by that preceptor. Therefore, this supramundane Dhamma should not be seen like an ornament on another’s head; rather, it is said, it is to be seen and experienced only in one’s own mind by the wise. But for fools, this is not their domain at all.

Apica [M 1.0211][V 1.0209] svākkhāto ayaṃ dhammo. Kasmā? Sandiṭṭhikattā. Sandiṭṭhiko, akālikattā. Akāliko, ehipassikattā. Yo ca ehipassiko, so nāma opaneyyiko hotīti.

Furthermore, this Dhamma is well-proclaimed. Why? Because it is to be seen for oneself. It is to be seen for oneself because it is timeless. It is timeless because it is worthy of the invitation 'come and see'. And that which is worthy of the invitation 'come and see' is indeed leading onward.

153. Tassevaṃ svākkhātatādibhede dhammaguṇe anussarato neva tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti dhammaṃ ārabbhāti (a. ni. 6.10) purimanayeneva vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Dhammaguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāraguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ dhammaguṇānussaraṇavasena uppannattā dhammānussaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

153. When one recollects in this way the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-proclaimed, at that time the mind is not overcome by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time his mind is quite upright, based on the Dhamma. Just as explained before, with the hindrances suppressed, the factors of absorption arise in a single moment. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of the Dhamma or due to the strong inclination towards recollecting the various diverse qualities, the jhāna does not reach absorption but only attains access. Because it arises by way of recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma, this is designated as 'recollection of the Dhamma'.

Imañca pana dhammānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu evaṃ opaneyyikassa dhammassa desetāraṃ imināpaṅgena samannāgataṃ satthāraṃ neva atītaṃse samanupassāmi, na panetarahi aññatra tena bhagavatāti evaṃ dhammaguṇadassaneneva satthari sagāravo hoti sappatisso. Dhamme garucittīkāro saddhādivepullaṃ adhigacchati, pītipāmojjabahulo hoti, bhayabheravasaho, dukkhādhivāsanasamattho, dhammena saṃvāsasaññaṃ paṭilabhati, dhammaguṇānussatiyā ajjhāvutthañcassa sarīrampi cetiyagharamiva pūjārahaṃ hoti, anuttaradhammādhigamāya cittaṃ namati, vītikkamitabbavatthusamāyoge cassa dhammasudhammataṃ samanussarato hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāti. Uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of the Dhamma reflects thus: 'I do not see, either in the past or at present, a teacher endowed with this quality as an expounder of a Dhamma that leads inwards, other than that Blessed One.' In this way, just by seeing the qualities of the Dhamma, he becomes respectful and deferential toward the Teacher. He has profound regard for the Dhamma, attains an abundance of faith and the like, abounds in joy and gladness, is able to overcome fear and dread, and is capable of enduring suffering. He obtains the perception of living together with the Dhamma. His body, steeped in the recollection of the Dhamma's qualities, becomes worthy of veneration like a shrine-house. His mind inclines toward the attainment of the unsurpassed Dhamma. And when he is confronted with an occasion for transgression, as he recollects the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, conscience and shame are present in him. If he does not penetrate further, he is nevertheless destined for a fortunate bourn.

Tasmā have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, dhammānussatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, the wise should indeed always be heedful in this recollection of the Dhamma, which is so greatly powerful.

Idaṃ dhammānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed explanation on the recollection of the Dhamma.

3. Saṅghānussatikathā

3. The Exposition on the Recollection of the Sangha

154. Saṅghānussatiṃ bhāvetukāmenāpi rahogatena paṭisallīnena “suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, ujuppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, ñāyappaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, sāmīcippaṭipanno [V 1.0210] bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā[M 1.0212], esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho āhuneyyo, pāhuneyyo, dakkhiṇeyyo, añjalikaraṇīyo, anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā”ti (a. ni. 6.10) evaṃ ariyasaṅghaguṇā anussaritabbā.

154. One who wishes to develop the recollection of the Sangha should, having gone to a solitary place and being in seclusion, recollect the qualities of the noble Sangha thus: "The Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the way to Nibbāna, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world."

155. Tattha suppaṭipannoti suṭṭhu paṭipanno, sammāpaṭipadaṃ anivattipaṭipadaṃ anulomapaṭipadaṃ apaccanīkapaṭipadaṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannoti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavato ovādānusāsaniṃ sakkaccaṃ suṇantīti sāvakā. Sāvakānaṃ saṅgho sāvakasaṅgho, sīladiṭṭhisāmaññatāya saṅghātabhāvamāpanno sāvakasamūhoti attho. Yasmā pana sā sammāpaṭipadā uju avaṅkā akuṭilā ajimhā, ariyo ca ñāyotipi vuccati, anucchavikattā ca sāmīcītipi saṅkhaṃ gatā. Tasmā tampaṭipanno ariyasaṅgho ujuppaṭipanno ñāyappaṭipanno sāmīcippaṭipannotipi vutto.

155. Herein, regarding `suppaṭipanno`, it means one who has practiced well. It is said that one has practiced the right practice, the non-reverting practice, the conforming practice, the non-opposing practice, and the practice in accordance with the Dhamma. They are called `sāvakā` (disciples) because they listen respectfully to the Blessed One's advice and instruction. The community of disciples is the `sāvakasaṅgho`; the meaning is an assembly of disciples that has reached a state of being bound together due to the commonality of noble virtue and noble view. Furthermore, because that right practice is `uju` (straight), being not crooked, not bent, and not curved; and is also called `ariyo ñāyo` (the noble methodical way); and has also come to be designated as `sāmīci` (proper) on account of its suitability, therefore the noble Saṅgha that has practiced it is also called `ujuppaṭipanno` (one who has practiced the straight way), `ñāyappaṭipanno` (one who has practiced the methodical way), and `sāmīcippaṭipanno` (one who has practiced properly).

Ettha ca ye maggaṭṭhā, te sammāpaṭipattisamaṅgitāya suppaṭipannā. Ye phalaṭṭhā, te sammāpaṭipadāya adhigantabbassa adhigatattā atītaṃ paṭipadaṃ sandhāya suppaṭipannāti veditabbā.

And herein, those who are established in the path are `suppaṭipannā` (well-practiced) because they are endowed with the right practice. Those who are established in the fruit should be understood as `suppaṭipannā` (well-practiced) with reference to the past practice, because they have already attained that which is to be attained by the right practice.

Apica svākkhāte dhammavinaye yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipannattāpi apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannattāpi suppaṭipanno.

Moreover, one is `suppaṭipanno` (well-practiced) both because of having practiced in the well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya according to how it was taught, and also because of having practiced the unerring practice.

Majjhimāya paṭipadāya antadvayamanupagamma paṭipannattā kāyavacīmanovaṅkakuṭilajimhadosappahānāya paṭipannattā ca ujuppaṭipannattā ca ujuppaṭipanno.

One is `ujuppaṭipanno` (practicing the straight way) because of having practiced by way of the Middle Path without approaching the two extremes, and because of having practiced for the abandoning of the faults of crookedness, bent-ness, and curved-ness of body, speech, and mind.

Ñāyo vuccati nibbānaṃ. Tadatthāya paṭipannattā ñāyappaṭipanno.

Nibbāna is called the `ñāya` (methodical way). Because of having practiced for its sake, one is `ñāyappaṭipanno` (one who has practiced the methodical way).

Yathā paṭipannā sāmīcippaṭipannārahā honti, tathā paṭipannattā sāmīcippaṭipanno.

Because one has practiced in such a way as to be worthy of respectful acts, one is `sāmīcippaṭipanno` (one who has practiced properly).

156. Yadidanti yāni imāni. Cattāri purisayugānīti yugaḷavasena paṭhamamaggaṭṭho phalaṭṭhoti idamekaṃ yugaḷanti evaṃ cattāri purisayugaḷāni honti. Aṭṭha purisapuggalāti purisapuggalavasena eko paṭhamamaggaṭṭho eko phalaṭṭhoti iminā nayena aṭṭheva purisapuggalā honti[V 1.0211]. Ettha ca purisoti vā puggaloti vā ekatthāni etāni padāni. Veneyyavasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅghoti yānimāni yugavasena [M 1.0213] cattāri purisayugāni, pāṭiekkato aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, āhuneyyotiādīsu ānetvā hunitabbanti āhunaṃ, dūratopi ānetvā sīlavantesu dātabbanti attho. Catunnaṃ paccayānametamadhivacanaṃ. Taṃ āhunaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto tassa mahapphalakaraṇatoti āhuneyyo. Atha vā dūratopi āgantvā sabbasāpateyyampi ettha hunitabbanti āhavanīyo. Sakkādīnampi vā āhavanaṃ arahatīti āhavanīyo. Yo cāyaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ āhavanīyo nāma aggi, yattha hutaṃ mahapphalanti tesaṃ laddhi. Sace hutassa mahapphalatāya āhavanīyo, saṅghova āhavanīyo. Saṅghe hutañhi mahapphalaṃ hoti. Yathāha –

156. The phrase `yadidaṃ` means: these which are. As to 'four pairs of persons': by way of pairs, the person established in the first path and the person established in its fruit—this is one pair. In this way, there are four pairs of persons. As to 'eight individual persons': by way of individual persons, the one established in the first path is one, and the one established in its fruit is one—by this method, there are indeed eight individual persons. And here, the words 'person' (`purisa`) and 'individual' (`puggala`) have the same meaning. But this was stated for the sake of those to be trained. As to 'This is the Blessed One's community of disciples': these four pairs of persons by way of pairs, and eight individual persons taken one by one—this is the Blessed One's community of disciples. In 'worthy of gifts' (`āhuneyyo`), etc., that which is to be brought and offered is a gift (`āhunaṃ`); the meaning is that it is to be brought even from afar and given to those endowed with virtue. This is a designation for the four requisites. One is 'worthy of gifts' because one is fit to receive that gift, making it of great fruit. Alternatively, because even coming from afar, all of one's wealth should be offered here, one is 'worthy of oblations' (`āhavanīyo`). Or, because one is worthy of the offering of Sakka and others, one is 'worthy of oblations'. And there is this fire of the brahmins named 'āhavanīya', in which what is offered is of great fruit—this is their belief. If something is 'worthy of oblations' because what is offered has great fruit, then the Sangha alone is 'worthy of oblations'. For indeed, what is offered to the Sangha is of great fruit. As it is said:

“Yo ca vassasataṃ jantu, aggiṃ paricare vane;

Ekañca bhāvitattānaṃ, muhuttamapi pūjaye;

Sāyeva pūjanā seyyo, yañce vassasataṃ huta”nti. (dha. pa. 107);

“And should a person tend the fire in the forest for a hundred years; and should one honor a person of developed self for even a moment; that honoring is indeed better than what is sacrificed for a hundred years.”

Tadetaṃ nikāyantare āhavanīyoti padaṃ idha āhuneyyoti iminā padena atthato ekaṃ. Byañjanato panettha kiñcimattameva nānaṃ. Iti āhuneyyo.

This term, which is `āhavanīyo` (worthy of oblations) in another school, is here the same in meaning as this term `āhuneyyo` (worthy of gifts). In wording, however, there is only a slight difference. Thus, `āhuneyyo`.

Pāhuneyyoti ettha pana pāhunaṃ vuccati disāvidisato āgatānaṃ piyamanāpānaṃ ñātimittānamatthāya sakkārena paṭiyattaṃ āgantukadānaṃ. Tampi ṭhapetvā te tathārūpe pāhunake saṅghasseva dātuṃ yuttaṃ, saṅghova taṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto. Saṅghasadiso hi pāhunako natthi. Tathā hesa ekabuddhantare ca dissati, abbokiṇṇañca piyamanāpattakarehi dhammehi samannāgatoti. Evaṃ pāhunamassa dātuṃ yuttaṃ pāhunañca paṭiggahetuṃ yuttoti pāhuneyyo. Yesaṃ pana pāhavanīyoti pāḷi, tesaṃ yasmā saṅgho pubbakāramarahati, tasmā sabbapaṭhamaṃ ānetvā ettha hunitabbanti pāhavanīyo. Sabbappakārena vā āhavanamarahatīti pāhavanīyo. Svāyamidha teneva atthena pāhuneyyoti vuccati.

Herein, `pāhuna` is said to be a gift for guests, prepared with honor for the sake of beloved and dear relatives and friends who have come from various directions. Setting aside such guests, it is fitting to give even that gift only to the Sangha, and the Sangha alone is worthy to receive it. For indeed, there is no guest comparable to the Sangha. Thus, this Sangha is seen even in the interval between Buddhas, and is unmixed and endowed with qualities that make one beloved and dear. In this way, because it is fitting to give a guest-offering to the Sangha, and it is worthy to receive a guest-offering, it is called `pāhuneyyo`. For those, however, whose text reads `pāhavanīyo`, their explanation is: because the Sangha is worthy of the first honor, it should be brought before all others and offered here; hence, `pāhavanīyo`. Or, because the Sangha is worthy of an offering in every way, it is called `pāhavanīyo`. This very word is here called `pāhuneyyo` with that same meaning.

Dakkhiṇāti pana paralokaṃ saddahitvā dātabbadānaṃ vuccati. Taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ arahati, dakkhiṇāya vā hito yasmā naṃ mahapphalakaraṇatāya visodhetīti dakkhiṇeyyo.

Furthermore, `dakkhiṇā` is said to be a gift that should be given with faith in the next world. One is called `dakkhiṇeyyo` because one is worthy of that `dakkhiṇā`, or is beneficial to the `dakkhiṇā`, for one purifies it by making it highly fruitful.

Ubho [M 1.0214][V 1.0212] hatthe sirasmiṃ patiṭṭhapetvā sabbalokena kayiramānaṃ añjalikammaṃ arahatīti añjalikaraṇīyo.

Because one is worthy of the act of reverential salutation (`añjalikamma`)—performed by the whole world by placing both hands on the head—one is therefore called `añjalikaraṇīyo`.

Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassāti sabbalokassa asadisaṃ puññavirūhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Yathā hi rañño vā amaccassa vā sālīnaṃ vā yavānaṃ vā virūhanaṭṭhānaṃ rañño sālikkhettaṃ rañño yavakkhettanti vuccati, evaṃ saṅgho sabbalokassa puññānaṃ virūhanaṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅghaṃ nissāya hi lokassa nānappakārahitasukhasaṃvattanikāni puññāni virūhanti. Tasmā saṅgho anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassāti.

`Anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassa` (the unsurpassed field of merit for the world) means it is the incomparable place for the growth of merit for the entire world. For just as a place for the growth of rice or barley belonging to a king or a minister is called 'the king's rice field' or 'the king's barley field,' so too the Sangha is the place for the growth of merit for the entire world. For, by depending on the Sangha, merits of various kinds that bring about welfare and happiness for the world do grow. Therefore, the Sangha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

157. Evaṃ suppaṭipannatādibhede saṅghaguṇe anussarato neva tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti saṅghaṃ ārabbhāti (a. ni. 6.10) purimanayeneva vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Saṅghaguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāraguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ saṅghaguṇānussaraṇavasena uppannattā saṅghānussaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

157. When one recollects the virtues of the Sangha in this way—as being of good practice and so forth—at that time, the mind is not overcome by lust, hatred, or delusion. At that moment, with the Sangha as its object, one's mind becomes upright. As in the previous method, with the hindrances suppressed, the jhāna factors arise in a single moment. However, due to the profundity of the Sangha’s virtues or due to the inclination to recollect their various kinds of virtues, absorption is not reached, and only access jhāna is attained. Because this arises by way of recollecting the virtues of the Sangha, it is reckoned simply as 'recollection of the Sangha.'

Imañca pana saṅghānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu saṅghe sagāravo hoti sappatisso. Saddhādivepullaṃ adhigacchati, pītipāmojjabahulo hoti, bhayabheravasaho, dukkhādhivāsanasamattho, saṅghena saṃvāsasaññaṃ paṭilabhati. Saṅghaguṇānussatiyā ajjhāvutthañcassa sarīraṃ sannipatitasaṅghamiva uposathāgāraṃ pūjārahaṃ hoti, saṅghaguṇādhigamāya cittaṃ namati, vītikkamitabbavatthusamāyoge cassa sammukhā saṅghaṃ passato viya hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāti, uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of the Sangha becomes respectful and deferential towards the Sangha. He attains an abundance of faith and other virtues, becomes full of rapture and joy, is an endurer of fear and terror, and becomes capable of enduring pain. He obtains the perception of living together with the Sangha. And his body, being dwelt in by the recollection of the Sangha's virtues, becomes worthy of veneration like an Uposatha hall where the Sangha has assembled. His mind inclines towards the attainment of the Sangha's virtues. And when he encounters an occasion for transgression, moral shame and moral dread are present to him as if he were seeing the Sangha in his presence. Moreover, while not penetrating further, he is bound for a happy destination.

Tasmā have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, saṅghānussatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, indeed, the wise should practice diligence

and constantly cultivate the recollection of the Sangha,

which is so greatly efficacious.

Idaṃ saṅghānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed discourse on the recollection of the Sangha.

4. Sīlānussatikathā

4. The Discourse on the Recollection of Virtue

158. Sīlānussatiṃ [M 1.0215][V 1.0213] bhāvetukāmena pana rahogatena paṭisallīnena “aho vata me sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikānī”ti (a. ni. 6.10) evaṃ akhaṇḍatādiguṇavasena attano sīlāni anussaritabbāni. Tāni ca gahaṭṭhena gahaṭṭhasīlāni, pabbajitena pabbajitasīlāni.

158. Furthermore, one who wishes to develop the recollection of virtue should, having gone to a solitary place and being in seclusion, recollect one's own virtues by way of their qualities, beginning with being unbroken, thus: 'Oh, indeed my virtues are unbroken, without holes, unvariegated, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unmisappropriated, and conducive to concentration.' And those virtues should be recollected by a householder as the householder's virtues, and by one who has gone forth as the virtues of one who has gone forth.

Gahaṭṭhasīlāni vā hontu pabbajitasīlāni vā, yesaṃ ādimhi vā ante vā ekampi na bhinnaṃ, tāni pariyante chinnasāṭako viya na khaṇḍānīti akhaṇḍāni. Yesaṃ vemajjhe ekampi na bhinnaṃ, tāni majjhe vinividdhasāṭako viya na chiddānīti acchiddāni. Yesaṃ paṭipāṭiyā dve vā tīṇi vā na bhinnāni, tāni piṭṭhiyā vā kucchiyā vā uṭṭhitena dīghavaṭṭādisaṇṭhānena visabhāgavaṇṇena kāḷarattādīnaṃ aññatarasarīravaṇṇā gāvī viya na sabalānīti asabalāni. Yāni antarantarā na bhinnāni, tāni visabhāgabinduvicitrā gāvī viya na kammāsānīti akammāsāni. Avisesena vā sabbānipi sattavidhena methunasaṃyogena kodhupanāhādīhi ca pāpadhammehi anupahatattā akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni. Tāniyeva taṇhādāsabyato mocetvā bhujissabhāvakaraṇena bhujissāni. Buddhādīhi viññūhi pasatthattā viññuppasatthāni. Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi aparāmaṭṭhatāya kenaci vā ayaṃ te sīlesu dosoti evaṃ parāmaṭṭhuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya aparāmaṭṭhāni. Upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiṃ vā, atha vā pana maggasamādhiṃ phalasamādhiñcāpi saṃvattentīti samādhisaṃvattanikāni.

Whether they are the virtues of a householder or the virtues of one gone forth, those in which not even one is broken at the beginning or at the end are unbroken (akhaṇḍāni), like a cloth not torn at its edges. Those in which not even one is broken in the middle are unperforated (acchiddāni), like a cloth not pierced in the middle. Those in which two or three are not broken in sequence are unspotted (asabalāni), like a cow whose body is not marked with patches of a dissimilar color—such as black or dark red—of a long or round shape appearing on its back or belly. Those which are not broken here and there are undappled (akammāsāni), like a cow not variegated with spots of a dissimilar color. Alternatively, all of them, without distinction, are unbroken, unperforated, unspotted, and undappled because they are undamaged by the seven kinds of sexual union and by evil states such as anger and resentment. These same virtues are liberating (bhujissāni) because they free one from the slavery of craving and make one a free person. They are praised by the wise (viññuppasatthāni) because they are praised by the wise, such as the Buddhas. They are untouched (aparāmaṭṭhāni) because they are not grasped by craving and wrong view, or because no one can find fault with them by saying, “This is a fault in your virtues.” They are conducive to concentration (samādhisaṃvattanikāni) because they lead to access concentration or absorption concentration, or even to path concentration and fruition concentration.

159. Evaṃ akhaṇḍatādiguṇavasena attano sīlāni anussarato nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti, sīlaṃ ārabbhāti purimanayeneva vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Sīlaguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāraguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ [M 1.0216] sīlaguṇānussaraṇavasena uppannattā sīlānussaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

159. Thus, when one recollects one’s own virtues by way of their qualities of being unbroken and so forth, at that time one's mind is not beset by lust, nor beset by hatred... nor beset by delusion. At that time, taking virtue as its object, one's mind becomes truly upright. Thus, in the way previously explained, for one whose hindrances are suppressed, the jhāna factors arise in a single moment. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of virtue or to the strong inclination to recollect their diverse qualities, without reaching absorption, the jhāna attained is only that which has reached access. This, having arisen by way of recollecting the qualities of virtue, is reckoned as the 'recollection of virtue'.

Imañca [V 1.0214] pana sīlānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu sikkhāya sagāravo hoti sabhāgavutti, paṭisanthāre appamatto, attānuvādādibhayavirahito, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī, saddhādivepullaṃ adhigacchati, pītipāmojjabahulo hoti. Uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

Moreover, a bhikkhu who cultivates this recollection of virtue is respectful towards the training, lives harmoniously with his fellows, is diligent in exchanging courtesies, is free from the fear of self-reproach and the like, and sees danger in the slightest faults. He attains to an abundance of faith and so on, and is full of joy and gladness. If he does not penetrate further, he is destined for a good bourn.

Tasmā have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, sīlānussatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, let the wise indeed always practice diligence in this recollection of virtue, which is of such great power.

Idaṃ sīlānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the recollection of virtue.

5. Cāgānussatikathā

5. The Exposition on the Recollection of Generosity

160. Cāgānussatiṃ bhāvetukāmena pana pakatiyā cāgādhimuttena niccappavattadānasaṃvibhāgena bhavitabbaṃ. Atha vā pana bhāvanaṃ ārabhantena ito dāni pabhuti sati paṭiggāhake antamaso ekālopamattampi dānaṃ adatvā na bhuñjissāmīti samādānaṃ katvā taṃdivasaṃ guṇavisiṭṭhesu paṭiggāhakesu yathāsatti yathābalaṃ dānaṃ datvā tattha nimittaṃ gaṇhitvā rahogatena paṭisallīnena “lābhā vata me suladdhaṃ vata me, yohaṃ maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitāya pajāya vigatamalamaccherena cetasā viharāmi muttacāgo payatapāṇi vossaggarato yācayogo dānasaṃvibhāgarato”ti evaṃ vigatamalamaccheratādiguṇavasena attano cāgo anussaritabbo.

160. One who wishes to develop the recollection of generosity should, by nature, be inclined towards generosity, constantly engaged in giving and sharing. Alternatively, when beginning the development, one should make the resolution: “From this day forward, if there is a recipient, I will not eat without first giving a gift of at least a small morsel.” On that day, one should give according to one’s capacity and strength to recipients distinguished by virtue, then take that as the object for recollection. Having gone into solitude and seclusion, one should recollect one’s own generosity by way of its qualities, such as being free from the stain of stinginess, thus: “Truly, it is a gain for me, truly it is well-gained by me, that I, among a populace overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess, dwell with a mind free from the stain of stinginess—with liberated generosity, with hands ready to give, delighting in relinquishment, fit to be requested, and rejoicing in giving and sharing.”

Tattha lābhā vata meti mayhaṃ vata lābhā, ye ime “āyuṃ kho pana datvā āyussa bhāgī hoti dibbassa vā mānusassa vā” iti (a. ni. 5.37) ca, “dadaṃ piyo hoti bhajanti naṃ bahū” iti (a. ni. 5.34) ca, “dadamāno piyo hoti, sataṃ dhammaṃ anukkamaṃ” iti (a. ni. 5.35) ca evamādīhi nayehi bhagavatā dāyakassa lābhā saṃvaṇṇitā, te mayhaṃ avassaṃ bhāginoti adhippāyo. Suladdhaṃ vata meti yaṃ mayā idaṃ sāsanaṃ manussattaṃ vā laddhaṃ, taṃ suladdhaṃ vata me. Kasmā[M 1.0217]? Yohaṃ maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitāya pajāya…pe… dānasaṃvibhāgaratoti.

Here, “Truly, it is a gain for me” means: “Indeed, these are gains for me.” The gains for a donor have been praised by the Blessed One through various methods, such as: “Indeed, having given longevity, one becomes a partaker of longevity, whether divine or human” (AN 5.37); and, “A giver is dear; many associate with him” (AN 5.34); and, “A giver is dear, following the tradition of the good” (AN 5.35). The intended meaning is: “Those gains will certainly be my portion.” “Truly, it is well-gained by me” means: “This Dispensation or this human existence that was gained by me is indeed well-gained by me.” Why? “Because I, among a populace overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess… delight in giving and sharing.”

Tattha [V 1.0215] maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitāyāti maccheramalena abhibhūtāya. Pajāyāti pajāyanavasena sattā vuccanti. Tasmā attano sampattīnaṃ parasādhāraṇabhāvamasahanalakkhaṇena cittassa pabhassarabhāvadūsakānaṃ kaṇhadhammānaṃ aññatarena maccheramalena abhibhūtesu sattesūti ayamettha attho. Vigatamalamaccherenāti aññesampi rāgadosādimalānañceva maccherassa ca vigatattā vigatamalamaccherena. Cetasā viharāmīti yathāvuttappakāracitto hutvā vasāmīti attho. Suttesu pana mahānāmasakkassa sotāpannassa sato nissayavihāraṃ pucchato nissayavihāravasena desitattā agāraṃ ajjhāvasāmīti vuttaṃ. Tattha abhibhavitvā vasāmīti attho.

Here, ‘overwhelmed by the stain of stinginess’ means overpowered by the stain of stinginess. ‘Populace’ refers to beings in the sense of being generated. Thus, the meaning here is: among beings who are overpowered by the stain of stinginess—one of the dark qualities that corrupts the mind’s luminous nature, characterized by the inability to endure one’s own possessions being common to others. ‘Free from the stain of stinginess’ means free from the stain of stinginess, as well as from other stains like greed and hatred. ‘I dwell with a mind’ means: “I abide having a mind of the described nature.” However, in the suttas, when Mahānāma the Sakyan, a stream-enterer, asked about a supportive dwelling, it was taught in terms of a supportive dwelling: “I inhabit the home.” There, the meaning is: “I abide having mastered it.”

Muttacāgoti vissaṭṭhacāgo. Payatapāṇīti parisuddhahattho. Sakkaccaṃ sahatthā deyyadhammaṃ dātuṃ sadā dhotahatthoyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vossaggaratoti vossajjanaṃ vossaggo, pariccāgoti attho. Tasmiṃ vossagge satatābhiyogavasena ratoti vossaggarato. Yācayogoti yaṃ yaṃ pare yācanti, tassa tassa dānato yācanayogoti attho. Yājayogotipi pāṭho. Yajanasaṅkhātena yājena yuttoti attho. Dānasaṃvibhāgaratoti dāne ca saṃvibhāge ca rato. Ahañhi dānañca demi, attanā paribhuñjitabbatopi ca saṃvibhāgaṃ karomi, ettheva casmi ubhaye ratoti evaṃ anussaratīti attho.

‘Freely generous’ means having unhesitating generosity. ‘With a prepared hand’ means with a purified hand. It is said thus: ‘Always with a clean hand, one is ready to give a gift respectfully with one’s own hand.’ ‘Delighting in relinquishment’: Relinquishment is letting go, renunciation; this is the meaning. One who delights in that relinquishment through constant application is ‘one who delights in relinquishment.’ ‘Amenable to requests’: Because one gives whatever others ask for, one is suitable to be asked; this is the meaning. There is also the reading ‘amenable to offerings,’ which means endowed with the gift known as an offering. ‘Delighting in giving and sharing’: Delighting in both giving and sharing. The meaning is that one recollects thus: ‘Indeed, I give gifts, and I also share from what is to be used by myself. I delight in both of these.’

161. Tassevaṃ vigatamalamaccheratādiguṇavasena attano cāgaṃ anussarato neva tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti cāgaṃ ārabbhāti (a. ni. 5.10) purimanayeneva vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Cāgaguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāracāgaguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ cāgaguṇānussaraṇavasena uppannattā cāgānussaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

161. When one recollects one’s own generosity in terms of its qualities of being free from the stain of stinginess and so forth, at that time his mind is not beset by lust. It is not beset by hatred… nor by delusion. At that time his mind is simply upright, focused on generosity. As explained before, in that single moment when the hindrances are suppressed, the factors of jhāna arise. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of generosity or the strong inclination to recollect their diverse qualities, without reaching full absorption, only access concentration is attained. This is called the recollection of generosity because it arises from recollecting the qualities of generosity.

Imañca [M 1.0218] pana cāgānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu bhiyyoso mattāya cāgādhimutto hoti, alobhajjhāsayo, mettāya anulomakārī, visārado, pītipāmojjabahulo, uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

A bhikkhu who is devoted to this recollection of generosity becomes further inclined toward generosity, with a disposition for non-greed, acting in conformity with loving-kindness, confident, and abundant in joy and gladness. But even if he does not penetrate further, he is destined for a good bourn.

Tasmā [V 1.0216] have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, cāgānussatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, let the wise verily and always practice heedfulness in this recollection of generosity, which is of such great power.

Idaṃ cāgānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the recollection of generosity.

6. Devatānussatikathā

6. The Exposition on the Recollection of the Devas

162. Devatānussatiṃ bhāvetukāmena pana ariyamaggavasena samudāgatehi saddhādīhi guṇehi samannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ. Tato rahogatena paṭisallīnena “santi devā cātumahārājikā, santi devā tāvatiṃsā, yāmā, tusitā, nimmānaratino, paranimmitavasavattino, santi devā brahmakāyikā, santi devā tatuttari, yathārūpāya saddhāya samannāgatā tā devatā ito cutā tattha upapannā, mayhampi tathārūpā saddhā saṃvijjati. Yathārūpena sīlena. Yathārūpena sutena. Yathārūpena cāgena. Yathārūpāya paññāya samannāgatā tā devatā ito cutā tattha upapannā, mayhampi tathārūpā paññā saṃvijjatī”ti (a. ni. 6.10) evaṃ devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā attano saddhādiguṇā anussaritabbā.

162. Now, one who wishes to develop the recollection of devas should be endowed with the qualities beginning with faith, which have arisen by means of the noble path. Then, having gone to a secluded place and being withdrawn, one should recollect: 'There are the Cātumahārājika devas, there are the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the Yāma devas, the Tusita devas, the Nimmānaratī devas, the Paranimmitavasavattī devas, the Brahmakāyika devas, and devas beyond them. Those devas, endowed with faith of such a nature, having passed away from here, were reborn there; for me too, faith of such a nature exists. Those devas, endowed with virtue of such a nature, with learning of such a nature, with generosity of such a nature, and with wisdom of such a nature, having passed away from here, were reborn there; for me too, wisdom of such a nature exists.' Thus, having placed the devas in the position of a witness, one's own qualities beginning with faith should be recollected.

Sutte pana yasmiṃ mahānāma samaye ariyasāvako attano ca tāsañca devatānaṃ saddhañca sīlañca sutañca cāgañca paññañca anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hotīti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi vuttaṃ, atha kho taṃ sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetabbadevatānaṃ attano saddhādīhi samānaguṇadīpanatthaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyañhi devatā sakkhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā attano guṇe anussaratīti daḷhaṃ katvā vuttaṃ.

However, in the Sutta it is said: 'Mahānāma, at whatever time a noble disciple recollects his own faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom, and also those of the devas, at that time his mind is not assailed by lust.' Although it is said thus, it should be known that this was said for the purpose of illuminating the similarity of one's own qualities beginning with faith with those of the devas who are to be placed in the position of a witness. For indeed, in the commentary it is firmly stated: 'Having placed the devas in the position of a witness, one recollects one's own qualities.'

163. Tasmā pubbabhāge devatānaṃ guṇe anussaritvā aparabhāge attano saṃvijjamāne saddhādiguṇe anussarato cassa neva tasmiṃ samaye [M 1.0219] rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti devatā ārabbhāti (a. ni. 6.10) purimanayeneva vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Saddhādiguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāraguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ [V 1.0217] appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ devatānaṃ guṇasadisasaddhādiguṇānussaraṇavasena devatānussaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

163. Therefore, when one recollects the qualities of the devas in the preliminary stage, and in the subsequent stage recollects one's own existing qualities of faith and so forth, his mind is not overwhelmed by lust at that time. Nor by hatred... nor by delusion. At that time, his mind is quite upright, focused on the devas. Just as before, with the hindrances suppressed, the factors of jhāna arise for a moment. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of faith and so forth, or the strong inclination to recollect their various aspects, full absorption (appanā) is not reached; only access concentration (upacāra) is attained. This jhāna, by means of recollecting one's own qualities of faith and so forth that are similar to the qualities of the devas, is indeed reckoned as the recollection of the devas.

Imañca pana devatānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu devatānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo, bhiyyoso mattāya saddhādivepullaṃ adhigacchati, pītipāmojjabahulo viharati. Uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

Moreover, a bhikkhu who is devoted to this recollection of the devas becomes dear and pleasing to the devas. He attains an even greater abundance of faith and other qualities, and dwells experiencing abundant rapture and gladness. But even if he does not penetrate further, he is destined for a good destination.

Tasmā have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, devatānussatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, let the wise verily and always practice heedfulness in this recollection of the devas, which is of such great power.

Idaṃ devatānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed exposition on the recollection of devas.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse

164. Yaṃ pana etāsaṃ vitthāradesanāyaṃ “ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgataṃ ārabbhā”tiādīni vatvā “ujugatacitto kho pana, mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”ti (a. ni. 6.10) vuttaṃ, tattha itipi so bhagavātiādīnaṃ atthaṃ nissāya uppannaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ sandhāya labhati atthavedanti vuttaṃ. Pāḷiṃ nissāya uppannaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ sandhāya labhati dhammavedaṃ. Ubhayavasena labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjanti vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

164. In the detailed exposition where it is said, "At that time, his mind is quite upright towards the Tathāgata," and further, "The noble disciple with an upright mind, Mahānāma, gains understanding of the meaning, gains understanding of the Dhamma, gains joy associated with the Dhamma, and for one who is joyful, rapture arises"—here, 'gains understanding of the meaning' is said with reference to the satisfaction arising in dependence on the meaning of phrases such as 'Indeed, the Blessed One...' 'Gains understanding of the Dhamma' refers to the satisfaction arising in dependence on the Pali text. 'Gains joy associated with the Dhamma' should be understood as being said as arising from both aspects.

Yañca devatānussatiyaṃ devatā ārabbhāti vuttaṃ, taṃ pubbabhāge devatā ārabbha pavattacittavasena devatāguṇasadise vā devatābhāvanipphādake guṇe ārabbha pavattacittavasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

And as to what was said in the recollection of devas, 'one takes the devas as the object,' this should be understood as said either by way of a mind that has arisen in the preliminary stage taking the devas as its object, or by way of a mind that has arisen taking as its object one's own qualities that are similar to the qualities of the devas or that bring about the state of being a deva.

165. Imā [M 1.0220] pana cha anussatiyo ariyasāvakānaññeva ijjhanti. Tesaṃ hi buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇā pākaṭā honti. Te ca akhaṇḍatādiguṇehi sīlehi, vigatamalamaccherena cāgena, mahānubhāvānaṃ devatānaṃ guṇasadisehi saddhādiguṇehi samannāgatā. Mahānāmasutte (a. ni. 6.10) ca [V 1.0218] sotāpannassa nissayavihāraṃ puṭṭhena bhagavatā sotāpannassa nissayavihāradassanatthameva etā vitthārato kathitā.

165. These six recollections, however, are successful only for noble disciples. For them, the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha are manifest. And they are endowed with virtues possessing qualities such as being unbroken, with generosity devoid of the stain of stinginess, and with qualities such as faith, which are similar to the qualities of devas of great power. And in the Mahānāma Sutta, these were taught in detail by the Blessed One, when asked about the dependent abiding of a stream-enterer, only for the sake of showing the dependent abiding of a stream-enterer.

Gedhasuttepi “idha, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, itipi so bhagavā…pe… ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti nikkhantaṃ muttaṃ vuṭṭhitaṃ gedhamhā. Gedhoti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānamadhivacanaṃ. Idampi kho, bhikkhave, ārammaṇaṃ karitvā evamidhekacce sattā visujjhantī”ti (a. ni. 6.25) evaṃ ariyasāvakassa anussativasena cittaṃ visodhetvā uttari paramatthavisuddhiadhigamatthāya kathitā.

In the Gedha Sutta, it is said: "Here, monks, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata... And at that time, his mind is quite upright, released, freed, and risen above greed. 'Greed,' monks, is a designation for these five cords of sensual pleasure. By making this an object, some beings here are purified." Thus, these recollections were taught for a noble disciple to purify the mind by means of recollection, and for the sake of subsequently attaining ultimate purification.

Āyasmatā mahākaccānena desite sambādhokāsasuttepi “acchariyaṃ, āvuso, abbhutaṃ, āvuso, yāvañcidaṃ tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sambādhe okāsādhigamo anubuddho sattānaṃ visuddhiyā…pe… nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya yadidaṃ cha anussatiṭṭhānāni. Katamāni cha? Idhāvuso, ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati…pe… evamidhekacce sattā visuddhidhammā bhavantī”ti (a. ni. 6.26) evaṃ ariyasāvakasseva paramatthavisuddhidhammatāya okāsādhigamavasena kathitā.

In the Sambādhokāsa Sutta, taught by the Venerable Mahākaccāna, it is said: "It is wonderful, friends, it is amazing, friends, how the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, has awakened to the attainment of an opening in confinement for the purification of beings... for the realization of Nibbāna, namely, these six grounds for recollection. What six? Here, friends, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata... Thus, some beings here are of a purified nature." Thus, they were taught for the noble disciple only, by way of the attainment of an opening, for the sake of his state of ultimate purification.

Uposathasuttepi “kathañca, visākhe, ariyūposatho hoti? Upakkiliṭṭhassa, visākhe, cittassa upakkamena pariyodapanā hoti. Kathañca, visākhe, upakkiliṭṭhassa cittassa upakkamena pariyodapanā hoti? Idha, visākhe, ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussaratī”ti (a. ni. 3.71) evaṃ ariyasāvakasseva uposathaṃ upavasato cittavisodhanakammaṭṭhānavasena uposathassa mahapphalabhāvadassanatthaṃ kathitā.

In the Uposatha Sutta too, it is said: “And how, Visākha, is there the noble Uposatha? There is the cleansing, Visākha, by effort, of a defiled mind. And how, Visākha, is there the cleansing, by effort, of a defiled mind? Here, Visākha, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata.” Thus, it was taught in order to show the great fruitfulness of the Uposatha for a noble disciple only who observes the Uposatha, by way of the meditation subject for purifying the mind.

Ekādasanipātepi “saddho kho, mahānāma, ārādhako hoti, no assaddho. Āraddhavīriyo, upaṭṭhitasati, samāhito, paññavā, mahānāma[M 1.0221], ārādhako hoti, no duppañño. Imesu kho tvaṃ, mahānāma, pañcasu dhammesu patiṭṭhāya cha dhamme uttari bhāveyyāsi. Idha tvaṃ, mahānāma, tathāgataṃ anussareyyāsi itipi so bhagavā”ti (a. ni. 11.11) evaṃ ariyasāvakasseva “tesaṃ no, bhante, nānāvihārena viharataṃ kenassa vihārena viharitabba”nti pucchato vihāradassanatthaṃ kathitā.

In the Eleventh Nipāta, it is also said: “Faithful, Mahānāma, one is capable, not faithless. One with aroused energy, established mindfulness, concentrated, and wise, Mahānāma, is capable, not unwise. Established in these five qualities, Mahānāma, you should further develop six qualities. Here, Mahānāma, you should recollect the Tathāgata: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One…’” Thus, it was spoken to show the proper dwelling for a noble disciple only who asks, “For us, venerable sir, who are dwelling in various ways, by which dwelling should we dwell?”

166. Evaṃ [V 1.0219] santepi parisuddhasīlādiguṇasamannāgatena puthujjanenāpi manasi kātabbā. Anussavavasenāpi hi buddhādīnaṃ guṇe anussarato cittaṃ pasīdatiyeva. Yassānubhāvena nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhetvā uḷārapāmojjo vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā arahattaṃyeva sacchikareyya kaṭaandhakāravāsī phussadevatthero viya.

166. Even so, these recollections should be borne in mind even by an ordinary person who is endowed with such qualities as purified virtue. For even by way of hearsay, the mind of one who recollects the qualities of the Buddha and others certainly becomes serene. By the power of that serenity, having suppressed the hindrances and become possessed of great joy, he might begin insight and realize arahantship itself, like the Elder Phussadeva, who lived in Kaṭaandhakāra.

So kirāyasmā mārena nimmitaṃ buddharūpaṃ disvā “ayaṃ tāva sarāgadosamoho evaṃ sobhati, kathaṃ nu kho bhagavā na sobhati, so hi sabbaso vītarāgadosamoho”ti buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ paṭilabhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti.

Reportedly, that venerable one, seeing a Buddha-form created by Māra, thought: ‘If this one, who is still with lust, hatred, and delusion, shines so, how then would the Blessed One not shine, who is in every way free from lust, hatred, and delusion!’ Having gained rapture with the Buddha as its object, he developed insight and attained arahantship.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus, in the Path of Purification, composed for the joy of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the development of concentration,

Chaanussatiniddeso nāma

named the Exposition of the Six Recollections,

Sattamo paricchedo.

the Seventh Chapter.

8. Anussatikammaṭṭhānaniddeso

8. Exposition of the Recollection Meditation Subjects

Maraṇassatikathā

The Discourse on Mindfulness of Death

167. Idāni [M 1.0222][V 1.0220] ito anantarāya maraṇassatiyā bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto. Tattha maraṇanti ekabhavapariyāpannassa jīvitindriyassa upacchedo. Yaṃ panetaṃ arahantānaṃ vaṭṭadukkhasamucchedasaṅkhātaṃ samucchedamaraṇaṃ, saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ khaṇikamaraṇaṃ, rukkho mato lohaṃ matantiādīsu sammutimaraṇañca, na taṃ idha adhippetaṃ.

167. Now, immediately following this, the explanation of the development of mindfulness of death is taken up. Therein, “death” is the cutting off of the life faculty that is included within a single existence. However, that which is the “death by cutting off” of the arahants, reckoned as the complete cutting off of the suffering of the round of existence; that which is the “momentary death,” reckoned as the dissolution of formations at every moment; and that which is “conventional death” in expressions such as “the tree is dead,” “the metal is dead,” and so on—these are not intended here.

Yampi cetaṃ adhippetaṃ, taṃ kālamaraṇaṃ akālamaraṇanti duvidhaṃ hoti. Tattha kālamaraṇaṃ puññakkhayena vā āyukkhayena vā ubhayakkhayena vā hoti. Akālamaraṇaṃ kammupacchedakakammavasena.

And this death which is intended is of two kinds: timely death and untimely death. Therein, timely death occurs through the exhaustion of merit, through the exhaustion of lifespan, or through the exhaustion of both. Untimely death occurs by the force of kamma that cuts off kamma.

Tattha yaṃ vijjamānāyapi āyusantānajanakapaccayasampattiyā kevalaṃ paṭisandhijanakassa kammassa vipakkavipākattā maraṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ puññakkhayena maraṇaṃ nāma. Yaṃ gatikālāhārādisampattiyā abhāvena ajjatanakālapurisānaṃ viya vassasatamattaparimāṇassa āyuno khayavasena maraṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ āyukkhayena maraṇaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana dūsīmārakalāburājādīnaṃ viya taṅkhaṇaññeva ṭhānācāvanasamatthena kammunā upacchinnasantānānaṃ, purimakammavasena vā satthaharaṇādīhi upakkamehi upacchijjamānasantānānaṃ maraṇaṃ hoti, idaṃ akālamaraṇaṃ nāma. Taṃ sabbampi vuttappakārena jīvitindriyupacchedena saṅgahitaṃ. Iti jīvitindriyupacchedasaṅkhātassa maraṇassa saraṇaṃ maraṇassati.

Herein, that death which occurs, even while there is a sufficiency of conditions that generate the continuity of life, solely because the rebirth-generating kamma has its result ripened, is called “death by the exhaustion of merit.” That death which occurs by the force of the exhaustion of a lifespan of a measure of about one hundred years, like that of people of the present time, due to the absence of favorable conditions of destination, time, nutriment, and so on, is called “death by the exhaustion of lifespan.” Furthermore, that death of those whose continuity is cut off by kamma capable of dislodging them from their place in that very moment, like that of Dūsī Māra, King Kalābu, and others, or the death of beings whose continuity is being cut off by the force of past kamma through assault with weapons and other such violent means, is called “untimely death.” All of this is included by the cutting off of the life faculty in the manner described. Thus, mindfulness of death is the recollection of death, which is reckoned as the cutting off of the life faculty.

168. Taṃ bhāvetukāmena rahogatena paṭisallīnena “maraṇaṃ bhavissati, jīvitindriyaṃ upacchijjissatī”ti vā, “maraṇaṃ maraṇa”nti vā yoniso manasikāro pavattetabbo. Ayoniso [V 1.0221] pavattayato hi iṭṭhajanamaraṇānussaraṇe soko uppajjati vijātamātuyā piyaputtamaraṇānussaraṇe viya. Aniṭṭhajanamaraṇānussaraṇe pāmojjaṃ uppajjati verīnaṃ verimaraṇānussaraṇe viya. Majjhattajanamaraṇānussaraṇe saṃvego na uppajjati matakaḷevaradassane chavaḍāhakassa viya. Attano maraṇānussaraṇe santāso uppajjati ukkhittāsikaṃ vadhakaṃ disvā bhīrukajātikassa [M 1.0223] viya. Tadetaṃ sabbampi satisaṃvegañāṇavirahato hoti. Tasmā tattha tattha hatamatasatte oloketvā diṭṭhapubbasampattīnaṃ sattānaṃ matānaṃ maraṇaṃ āvajjetvā satiñca saṃvegañca ñāṇañca yojetvā “maraṇaṃ bhavissatī”tiādinā nayena manasikāro pavattetabbo. Evaṃ pavattento hi yoniso pavatteti, upāyena pavattetīti attho. Evaṃ pavattayatoyeva hi ekaccassa nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, maraṇārammaṇā sati saṇṭhāti, upacārappattameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti.

168. By one who wishes to develop this, having gone to a secluded place and being in solitude, attention should be wisely aroused thus: 'Death will be, the life-faculty will be cut off,' or 'Death, death.' For if one arouses it unwisely, sorrow arises when recollecting the death of a loved one, like a mother recollecting the death of her beloved son. Joy arises when recollecting the death of an unloved person, like recollecting the death of an enemy. A sense of urgency does not arise when recollecting the death of a neutral person, like a corpse-burner seeing a dead body. Terror arises when recollecting one's own death, like a timid person seeing an executioner with an upraised sword. All this occurs due to the absence of mindfulness, sense of urgency, and knowledge. Therefore, having observed here and there beings who have been killed or have died, and having reflected upon the death of beings formerly seen in possession of prosperity, one should combine mindfulness, sense of urgency, and knowledge, and arouse attention by the method beginning with, 'Death will be.' Indeed, one who proceeds in this way, proceeds wisely; the meaning is that one proceeds by a suitable method. For a certain person who proceeds in this way, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness with death as its object is established, and the meditation subject reaches access concentration.

169. Yassa pana ettāvatā na hoti, tena vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānato, sampattivipattito, upasaṃharaṇato, kāyabahusādhāraṇato, āyudubbalato, animittato, addhānaparicchedato, khaṇaparittatoti imehi aṭṭhahākārehi maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

169. But for one for whom this has not yet come about, death should be recollected by these eight aspects: as an executioner ever-present, by the ruin of prosperity, by comparison, by the body being common to many, by the weakness of life, by its signlessness, by the limitation of the life-span, and by the brevity of the moment.

Tattha vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānatoti vadhakassa viya paccupaṭṭhānato. Yathā hi imassa sīsaṃ chindissāmīti asiṃ gahetvā gīvāya cārayamāno vadhako paccupaṭṭhitova hoti, evaṃ maraṇampi paccupaṭṭhitamevāti anussaritabbaṃ. Kasmā? Saha jātiyā āgatato, jīvitaharaṇato ca. Yathā hi ahicchattakamakuḷaṃ matthakena paṃsuṃ gahetvāva uggacchati, evaṃ sattā jarāmaraṇaṃ gahetvāva nibbattanti. Tathā hi nesaṃ paṭisandhicittaṃ uppādānantarameva jaraṃ patvā pabbatasikharato patitasilā viya bhijjati saddhiṃ sampayuttakhandhehi. Evaṃ khaṇikamaraṇaṃ tāva saha jātiyā āgataṃ. Jātassa pana avassaṃ maraṇato idhādhippetamaraṇampi saha jātiyā āgataṃ. Tasmā esa satto jātakālato paṭṭhāya yathā nāma uṭṭhito sūriyo atthābhimukho gacchateva, gatagataṭṭhānato īsakampi na nivattati. Yathā vā nadī pabbateyyā sīghasotā hārahārinī sandateva vattateva īsakampi na nivattati, evaṃ īsakampi anivattamāno maraṇābhimukhova yāti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Herein, 'as an executioner ever-present' means like the presence of an executioner. Just as an executioner, taking a sword and brandishing it at the neck, thinking, 'I will cut off this person's head,' is ever-present, so too should death be recollected as ever-present. Why? Because it comes together with birth and because it takes away life. Just as a mushroom sprout emerges from the soil already carrying dust on its head, so too beings are born carrying aging and death. Indeed, their rebirth-linking consciousness, immediately after arising, reaches aging and shatters like a stone falling from a mountain peak, along with its associated aggregates. Thus, momentary death comes with birth itself. Moreover, since death is inevitable for one who is born, the death intended here also comes with birth. Therefore, this being, from the moment of birth, is like the rising sun moving toward its setting, never turning back even slightly from the place it has reached. Or like a swift mountain river, carrying all before it, flowing and rolling on, never turning back even a little, it moves inexorably toward death. Hence it is said:

“Yamekarattiṃ [V 1.0222] paṭhamaṃ, gabbhe vasati māṇavo;

Abbhuṭṭhitova so yāti, sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī”ti. (jā. 1.15.363);

“From the first night a being dwells in the womb, having set out, it journeys on, never turning back.”

Evaṃ gacchato cassa gimhābhitattānaṃ kunnadīnaṃ khayo viya, pāto āporasānugatabandhanānaṃ dumapphalānaṃ patanaṃ viya, muggarābhitāḷitānaṃ mattikabhājanānaṃ bhedo [M 1.0224] viya, sūriyarasmisamphuṭṭhānaṃ ussāvabindūnaṃ viddhaṃsanaṃ viya ca maraṇameva āsannaṃ hoti. Tenāha –

And for one thus proceeding, death alone is ever near: like the drying up of small rivers scorched by summer heat; like the falling at dawn of tree-fruits with stems weakened by sap; like the shattering of clay pots struck by a hammer; and like the vanishing of dewdrops touched by the sun’s rays. Therefore, it was said:

“Accayanti ahorattā, jīvitamuparujjhati;

Āyu khīyati maccānaṃ, kunnadīnaṃva odakaṃ. (saṃ. ni. 1.146);

“Days and nights pass by, life is brought to an end; the lifespan of mortals wastes away, like the water of small rivers.”

“Phalānamiva pakkānaṃ, pāto papatato bhayaṃ;

Evaṃ jātāna maccānaṃ, niccaṃ maraṇato bhayaṃ.

“Just as for ripe fruits, there is fear of falling at dawn, so for mortals who are born, there is constant fear of death.”

“Yathāpi kumbhakārassa, kataṃ mattikabhājanaṃ;

Khuddakañca mahantañca, yaṃ pakkaṃ yañca āmakaṃ;

Sabbaṃ bhedanapariyantaṃ, evaṃ maccāna jīvitaṃ’. (su. ni. 581-582);

Just as any earthen vessel made by a potter, whether small or great, whether baked or raw, all have shattering as their end; so too is the life of mortals.

“Ussāvova tiṇaggamhi, sūriyuggamanaṃ pati;

Evamāyu manussānaṃ, mā maṃ amma nivārayā”ti. (jā. 1.11.79);

“Just as a dewdrop on a blade of grass at sunrise, so is the life of humans. Mother, do not hinder me.”

Evaṃ ukkhittāsiko vadhako viya saha jātiyā āgataṃ panetaṃ maraṇaṃ gīvāya asiṃ cārayamāno so vadhako viya jīvitaṃ haratiyeva, na aharitvā nivattati. Tasmā saha jātiyā āgatato, jīvitaharaṇato ca ukkhittāsiko vadhako viya maraṇampi paccupaṭṭhitamevāti evaṃ vadhakapaccupaṭṭhānato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, like an executioner with a raised sword, this death, which comes together with birth, surely takes away life, just like that executioner who circles the sword at the neck; it does not turn back without having taken it. Therefore, because it comes together with birth and because it takes away life, death is indeed ever-present, like an executioner with a raised sword. In this way, death should be recollected by way of its being ever-present like an executioner.

170. Sampattivipattitoti idha sampatti nāma tāvadeva sobhati, yāva naṃ vipatti nābhibhavati, na ca sā sampatti nāma atthi, yā vipattiṃ atikkamma tiṭṭheyya. Tathā hi –

170. As for prosperity and adversity: Here, that which is called prosperity shines only so long as adversity does not overwhelm it. And there is no such thing as a prosperity that could stand, having overcome adversity. For indeed—

“Sakalaṃ [V 1.0223] mediniṃ bhutvā, datvā koṭisataṃ sukhī;

Aḍḍhāmalakamattassa, ante issarataṃ gato.

The happy one, having ruled over the entire earth and having given a hundred koṭis, in the end, arrived at a state of mastery over a mere half of a myrobalan fruit.

“Teneva dehabandhena, puññamhi khayamāgate;

Maraṇābhimukho sopi, asoko sokamāgato”ti.

With that very same body, when his merit came to be exhausted, facing death, even he, Asoka, the sorrowless one, came to sorrow.

Apica [M 1.0225] sabbaṃ ārogyaṃ byādhipariyosānaṃ, sabbaṃ yobbanaṃ jarāpariyosānaṃ, sabbaṃ jīvitaṃ maraṇapariyosānaṃ, sabboyeva lokasannivāso jātiyā anugato, jarāya anusaṭo, byādhinā abhibhūto, maraṇena abbhāhato. Tenāha –

Furthermore, all health has illness as its end, all youth has old age as its end, and all life has death as its end. Every inhabitant of the world is pursued by birth, pervaded by old age, overwhelmed by sickness, and struck down by death. Therefore, it was said:

“Yathāpi selā vipulā, nabhaṃ āhacca pabbatā;

Samantā anupariyeyyuṃ, nippothentā catuddisā.

Just as massive mountains of rock, reaching up to the sky, might advance from all around, from the four directions, grinding everything to powder.

“Evaṃ jarā ca maccu ca, adhivattanti pāṇine;

Khattiye brāhmaṇe vesse, sudde caṇḍālapukkuse;

Na kiñci parivajjeti, sabbamevābhimaddati.

Thus old age and death overwhelm beings—Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, Suddas, Caṇḍālas, and Pukkusas. They spare nothing at all; they crush everything completely.

“Na tattha hatthīnaṃ bhūmi, na rathānaṃ na pattiyā;

Na cāpi mantayuddhena, sakkā jetuṃ dhanena vā”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.136);

There, there is no ground for elephants, no ground for chariots, no ground for infantry. Nor is it possible to conquer by warfare of incantations, or by wealth.

Evaṃ jīvitasampattiyā maraṇavipattipariyosānataṃ vavatthapentena sampattivipattito maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, by determining that the prosperity of life has the adversity that is death as its end, death should be recollected by way of prosperity and adversity.

171. Upasaṃharaṇatoti parehi saddhiṃ attano upasaṃharaṇato. Tattha sattahākārehi upasaṃharaṇato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ, yasamahattato, puññamahattato, thāmamahattato, iddhimahattato, paññāmahattato, paccekabuddhato, sammāsambuddhatoti. Kathaṃ? Idaṃ maraṇaṃ nāma mahāyasānaṃ mahāparivārānaṃ [V 1.0224] sampannadhanavāhanānaṃ mahāsammatamandhātumahāsudassana daḷhanemi nimippabhutīnampi upari nirāsaṅkameva patitaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayhaṃ upari na patissati?

171. By way of comparison means by comparing oneself with others. Therein, death should be recollected by way of comparison in seven aspects: by greatness of fame, by greatness of merit, by greatness of strength, by greatness of psychic power, by greatness of wisdom, by being a Paccekabuddha, and by being a Sammāsambuddha. How? This thing called death has fallen without hesitation even upon those of great fame and large retinues, endowed with wealth and vehicles, such as Mahāsammata, Mandhātu, Mahāsudassana, Daḷhanemi, Nimi, and others. For what reason, then, will it not fall upon me?

Mahāyasā rājavarā, mahāsammataādayo;

Tepi maccuvasaṃ pattā, mādisesu kathāva kāti.

Excellent kings of great fame, Mahāsammata and others—even they have come under the power of death. What is there to say of those like me?

Evaṃ tāva yasamahattato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, first, it should be recollected by way of greatness of fame.

Kathaṃ puññamahattato?

How by way of greatness of merit?

Jotiko jaṭilo uggo, meṇḍako atha puṇṇako;

Ete caññe ca ye loke, mahāpuññāti vissutā;

Sabbe maraṇamāpannā, mādisesu kathāva kāti.

Jotika, Jaṭila, Ugga, Meṇḍaka, and then Puṇṇaka; these and others in the world who are renowned as being of great merit—all have met with death. What is there to say of those like me?

Evaṃ puññamahattato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be recollected by way of greatness of merit.

Kathaṃ [M 1.0226] thāmamahattato?

How by way of greatness of strength?

Vāsudevo baladevo, bhīmaseno yudhiṭṭhilo;

Cānuro yo mahāmallo, antakassa vasaṃ gatā.

Vāsudeva, Baladeva, Bhīmasena, Yudhiṭṭhila, and Cāṇura the great wrestler have gone under the power of the Ender.

Evaṃ thāmabalūpetā, iti lokamhi vissutā;

Etepi maraṇaṃ yātā, mādisesu kathāva kāti.

Those endowed with strength and power, thus renowned in the world—even they have gone to death. What is there to say of those like me?

Evaṃ thāmamahattato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be recollected by way of greatness of strength.

Kathaṃ iddhimahattato?

How by way of greatness of psychic power?

Pādaṅguṭṭhakamattena[V 1.0225], vejayantamakampayi;

Yo nāmiddhimataṃ seṭṭho, dutiyo aggasāvako.

He who is the best of those with psychic power, the second chief disciple, shook the Vejayanta palace with just his big toe.

Sopi maccumukhaṃ ghoraṃ, migo sīhamukhaṃ viya;

Paviṭṭho saha iddhīhi, mādisesu kathāva kāti.

Even he, together with his psychic powers, entered the dreadful mouth of death, like a deer into the mouth of a lion. What is there to say of those like me?

Evaṃ iddhimahattato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be recollected by way of greatness of psychic power.

Kathaṃ paññāmahattato?

How by way of greatness of wisdom?

Lokanāthaṃ ṭhapetvāna, ye caññe atthi pāṇino;

Paññāya sāriputtassa, kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ.

Setting aside the Lord of the World, whatever other beings there are, their wisdom is not worth the sixteenth part of Sāriputta’s wisdom.

Evaṃ nāma mahāpañño, paṭhamo aggasāvako;

Maraṇassa vasaṃ patto, mādisesu kathāva kāti.

Even he of such great wisdom, the first chief disciple, has come under the power of death. What is there to say of those like me?

Evaṃ paññāmahattato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be recollected by way of greatness of wisdom.

Kathaṃ paccekabuddhato? Yepi te attano ñāṇavīriyabalena sabbakilesasattunimmathanaṃ katvā paccekabodhiṃ pattā khaggavisāṇakappā sayambhuno, tepi maraṇato na muttā, kuto panāhaṃ muccissāmīti.

How by way of the Paccekabuddhas? Even those who, by the power of their own energy guided by wisdom, having crushed all the enemies that are the defilements and having attained Paccekabodhi, are like the single horn of a rhinoceros and are self-become—even those Paccekabuddhas are not freed from death. How then could I be freed?

Taṃ taṃ nimittamāgamma, vīmaṃsantā mahesayo;

Sayambhuññāṇatejena, ye pattā āsavakkhayaṃ.

Relying on this or that sign, the great seers, investigating, attained the destruction of the taints by the power of their self-become knowledge.

Ekacariyanivāsena, khaggasiṅgasamūpamā;

Tepi nātigatā maccuṃ, mādisesu kathāva kāti.

Through their solitary practice and dwelling, they are comparable to a rhinoceros's horn; even they have not overcome Death. For beings like me, what is there to say?

Evaṃ [M 1.0227][V 1.0226] paccekabuddhato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be recollected by way of the Paccekabuddhas.

Kathaṃ sammāsambuddhato? Yopi so bhagavā asītianubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavicitrarūpakāyo sabbākāraparisuddhasīlakkhandhādiguṇaratanasamiddhadhammakāyo yasamahattapuññamahattathāmamahattaiddhimahattapaññāmahattānaṃ pāraṃ gato asamo asamasamo appaṭipuggalo arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, sopi salilavuṭṭhinipātena mahāaggikkhandho viya maraṇavuṭṭhinipātena ṭhānaso vūpasanto.

How by way of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One? Even that Blessed One—whose physical body was made wonderful by the thirty-two major marks of a great man and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics; whose Dhamma-body was complete with the jewels of qualities such as the aggregate of virtue, utterly pure in all aspects; who had gone to the furthest shore of greatness in fame, greatness in merit, greatness in strength, greatness in psychic power, and greatness in wisdom; who is unequaled, equal to the unequaled, and without a rival person; the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—even he, like a great mass of fire extinguished by a downpour of rain, was quenched in an instant by the downpour of death.

Evaṃ mahānubhāvassa, yaṃ nāmetaṃ mahesino;

Na bhayena na lajjāya, maraṇaṃ vasamāgataṃ.

This death did not submit to the power of the great seer of such great majesty, neither out of fear nor out of shame.

Nillajjaṃ vītasārajjaṃ, sabbasattābhimaddanaṃ;

Tayidaṃ mādisaṃ sattaṃ, kathaṃ nābhibhavissatīti.

Shameless, devoid of hesitation, crushing all beings—how will that very death not overwhelm a being such as me?

Evaṃ sammāsambuddhato anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be recollected by way of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Tassevaṃ yasamahattatādisampannehi parehi saddhiṃ maraṇasāmaññatāya attānaṃ upasaṃharitvā tesaṃ viya sattavisesānaṃ mayhampi maraṇaṃ bhavissatīti anussarato upacārappattaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ hotīti. Evaṃ upasaṃharaṇato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

For one who, having thus compared oneself with others endowed with qualities such as greatness of fame by way of the commonality of death, recollects, 'Just as for those special beings, for me too there will be death,' the meditation subject reaches access concentration. Thus, by way of comparison, death should be recollected.

172. Kāyabahusādhāraṇatoti ayaṃ kāyo bahusādhāraṇo. Asītiyā tāva kimikulānaṃ sādhāraṇo, tattha chavinissitā pāṇā chaviṃ khādanti, cammanissitā cammaṃ khādanti, maṃsanissitā maṃsaṃ khādanti, nhārunissitā nhāruṃ khādanti, aṭṭhinissitā aṭṭhiṃ khādanti, miñjanissitā miñjaṃ khādanti. Tattheva jāyanti jīyanti mīyanti, uccārapassāvaṃ karonti. Kāyova nesaṃ sūtigharañceva gilānasālā ca susānañca vaccakuṭi ca passāvadoṇikā ca. Svāyaṃ tesampi kimikulānaṃ pakopena maraṇaṃ nigacchatiyeva. Yathā ca asītiyā kimikulānaṃ, evaṃ ajjhattikānaṃyeva anekasatānaṃ rogānaṃ bāhirānañca ahivicchikādīnaṃ maraṇassa paccayānaṃ sādhāraṇo.

172. This body is common to many. Firstly, it is common to eighty families of worms. Among them, creatures that dwell depending on the outer skin eat the outer skin; those that dwell depending on the inner skin eat the inner skin; those that dwell depending on the flesh eat the flesh; those that dwell depending on the sinews eat the sinews; those that dwell depending on the bones eat the bones; those that dwell depending on the marrow eat the marrow. Right there they are born, grow old, and die; they produce feces and urine. The body itself is for them a maternity home, a hospital, a charnel ground, a toilet, and a urinal. This very body certainly goes to death even by the affliction of those families of worms. And just as it is common to the eighty families of worms, so too it is common to the many hundreds of internal diseases and to external causes of death such as snakes, scorpions, and so on.

Yathā [V 1.0227] hi catumahāpathe ṭhapite lakkhamhi sabbadisāhi āgatā sarasattitomarapāsāṇādayo nipatanti, evaṃ kāyepi sabbupaddavā nipatanti[M 1.0228]. Svāyaṃ tesampi upaddavānaṃ nipātena maraṇaṃ nigacchatiyeva. Tenāha bhagavā – “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu divase nikkhante rattiyā paṭihitāya iti paṭisañcikkhati, bahukā kho me paccayā maraṇassa, ahi vā maṃ ḍaṃseyya, vicchiko vā maṃ ḍaṃseyya, satapadī vā maṃ ḍaṃseyya, tena me assa kālaṅkiriyā, so mamassa antarāyo, upakkhalitvā vā papateyyaṃ, bhattaṃ vā me bhuttaṃ byāpajjeyya, pittaṃ vā me kuppeyya, semhaṃ vā me kuppeyya, satthakā vā me vātā kuppeyyuṃ, tena me assa kālaṅkiriyā, so mamassa antarāyo”ti. Evaṃ (a. ni. 6.20) kāyabahusādhāraṇato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

For just as at a great crossroads where a target is set up, arrows, spears, javelins, bricks, stones, and so on, coming from all directions, fall upon it, so too do all dangers fall upon the body. This very body certainly goes to death by the falling of those dangers. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘Here, monks, when the day has passed and night has arrived, a monk reflects thus: “Indeed, the causes of my death are many. A snake might bite me, a scorpion might sting me, or a centipede might bite me. By that, my death could occur; that would be an obstacle for me. Or I might stumble and fall; or the food I have eaten might become disturbed; or my bile might be provoked; or my phlegm might be provoked; or the cutting winds in me might be provoked. By that, my death could occur; that would be an obstacle for me.”’ Thus, death should be recollected by way of the body being common to many.

173. Āyudubbalatoti āyu nāmetaṃ abalaṃ dubbalaṃ. Tathā hi sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ assāsapassāsūpanibaddhañceva iriyāpathūpanibaddhañca sītuṇhūpanibaddhañca mahābhūtūpanibaddhañca āhārūpanibaddhañca. Tadetaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva pavattati. Bahi nikkhantanāsikavāte pana anto apavisante, paviṭṭhe vā anikkhamante mato nāma hoti. Catunnaṃ iriyāpathānampi samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva pavattati. Aññataraññatarassa pana adhimattatāya āyusaṅkhārā upacchijjanti. Sītuṇhānampi samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva pavattati. Atisītena pana atiuṇhena vā abhibhūtassa vipajjati. Mahābhūtānampi samavuttitaṃ labhamānameva pavattati.
