Pathavīdhātuyā pana āpodhātuādīnaṃ vā aññataraññatarassa pakopena balasampannopi puggalo patthaddhakāyo vā atisārādivasena kilinnapūtikāyo vā mahāḍāhapareto vā sambhijjamānasandhibandhano vā hutvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇāti. Kabaḷīkārāhārampi yuttakāle labhantasseva jīvitaṃ pavattati, āhāraṃ alabhamānassa pana parikkhayaṃ gacchatīti. Evaṃ āyudubbalato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

173. By way of the weakness of life: this which is called life is without strength and is feeble. For the life of beings is dependent upon the in-breath and out-breath, the postures, cold and heat, the great elements, and food. This life continues only when it obtains a balanced occurrence of the in-breaths and out-breaths. But when the nasal breath that has gone out does not enter within, or when the breath that has entered does not go out, one is called dead. It continues only when obtaining a balanced occurrence of the four postures as well. But through the excess of any one of them, the life-formations are cut off. It continues only when obtaining a balanced occurrence of cold and heat as well. But for one who is overcome by extreme cold or extreme heat, it perishes. It continues only when obtaining a balanced occurrence of the great elements as well. But through the disturbance of the earth element, or of one or another of the water element and so on, even a person endowed with strength reaches the destruction of life, having become one with a stiff body, or one with a moist and putrid body due to diarrhea and so on, or one overcome by a great burning fever. Life continues only for one who obtains physical food at the proper time; but for one not obtaining food, it goes to destruction. Thus, death should be recollected by way of the weakness of life.

174. Animittatoti avavatthānato, paricchedābhāvatoti attho. Sattānaṃ hi –

174. By way of being without a sign: this means because of non-determination, that is, because of the absence of limitation. For of beings—

Jīvitaṃ byādhi kālo ca, dehanikkhepanaṃ gati;

Pañcete jīvalokasmiṃ, animittā na nāyare.

Life, sickness, and the time of death, the place of casting off the body, and the destination—these five in the world of living beings are without a sign; they cannot be known.

Tattha [M 1.0229] jīvitaṃ tāva “ettakameva jīvitabbaṃ, na ito para”nti vavatthānābhāvato animittaṃ[V 1.0228]. Kalalakālepi hi sattā maranti, abbudapesighanamāsikadvemāsatemāsacatumāsapañcamāsadasamāsakālepi. Kucchito nikkhantasamayepi. Tato paraṃ vassasatassa antopi bahipi marantiyeva. Byādhipi “imināva byādhinā sattā maranti, nāññenā”ti vavatthānābhāvato animitto. Cakkhurogenāpi hi sattā maranti, sotarogādīnaṃ aññatarenāpi. Kālopi “imasmiṃyeva kāle maritabbaṃ, nāññasmi”nti evaṃ vavatthānābhāvato animitto. Pubbaṇhepi hi sattā maranti, majjhanhikādīnaṃ aññatarasmimpi. Dehanikkhepanampi “idheva mīyamānānaṃ dehena patitabbaṃ, nāññatrā”ti evaṃ vavatthānābhāvato animittaṃ. Antogāme jātānaṃ hi bahigāmepi attabhāvo patati. Bahigāme jātānampi antogāme. Tathā thalajānaṃ vā jale, jalajānaṃ vā thaleti anekappakārato vitthāretabbaṃ. Gatipi “ito cutena idha nibbattitabba”nti evaṃ vavatthānābhāvato animittā. Devalokato hi cutā manussesupi nibbattanti, manussalokato cutā devalokādīnampi yattha katthaci nibbattantīti evaṃ yantayuttagoṇo viya gatipañcake loko samparivattatīti evaṃ animittato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Herein, life is uncertain because there is no established limit such as: “One should live only this long, and no longer.” For beings die even at the kalala stage, the abbuda stage, the pesi stage, the ghana stage, and also at one month, two months, three months, four months, five months, and ten months. They also die at the moment of emerging from the womb. Beyond that, they die even within a hundred years and beyond it. Illness is also uncertain, for there is no established limit such as: “Beings die only from this illness, not from any other.” For beings die from eye diseases, and also from one or another of such ailments as ear diseases. The time of death is also uncertain, as there is no established limit such as: “One must die only at this time, not at any other.” For beings die in the morning, and also at some other time such as midday. The place where the body is cast off is also uncertain, for there is no established limit such as: “The bodies of those dying must fall only in this place, not elsewhere.” For the body of one born within a village may fall outside it, and the body of one born outside may fall within. Similarly, the body of a land-dweller may fall in the water, and that of a water-dweller on land—this should be elaborated in many ways. The destination is also uncertain, as there is no established limit such as: “One who has passed away from here must be reborn there.” For those who pass away from the deva world are reborn among humans, and those who pass away from the human world are reborn anywhere in the deva worlds and so on. Thus, like an ox yoked to a mill, the world revolves through the five destinations. In this way, one should recollect death as being uncertain.

175. Addhānaparicchedatoti manussānaṃ jīvitassa nāma etarahi paritto addhā. Yo ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ, appaṃ vā bhiyyo. Tenāha bhagavā – “appamidaṃ, bhikkhave, manussānaṃ āyu, gamanīyo samparāyo, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ, caritabbaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, natthi jātassa amaraṇaṃ. Yo, bhikkhave, ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ, appaṃ vā bhiyyoti.

175. By way of the limited span of life: for humans, the length of life at present is indeed short. One who lives long lives a hundred years or a little more. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Brief, bhikkhus, is the life of humans—the next world is to be gone to. What is wholesome should be done, the holy life should be lived, for there is no not-dying for one who is born. One who lives long, bhikkhus, lives a hundred years or a little more.”

Appamāyumanussānaṃ, hīḷeyya naṃ suporiso;

Careyyādittasīsova, natthi maccussa nāgamoti. (saṃ. ni. 1.145);

The life of humans is short; a virtuous person should scorn it. One should practice as if one's head were on fire, for there is no non-coming of death.

Aparampi āha – “bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, arako nāma satthā ahosī”ti sabbampi sattahi upamāhi alaṅkataṃ suttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Furthermore, he said: "Monks, formerly there was a teacher named Araka." The entire discourse, adorned with seven similes, should be elaborated.

Aparampi āha – “yocāyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāveti, aho vatāhaṃ rattindivaṃ jīveyyaṃ, bhagavato sāsanaṃ manasikareyyaṃ, bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti. Yocāyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāveti[M 1.0230], aho vatāhaṃ divasaṃ jīveyyaṃ, bhagavato sāsanaṃ manasikareyyaṃ, bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti. Yo cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ [V 1.0229] maraṇassatiṃ bhāveti, aho vatāhaṃ tadantaraṃ jīveyyaṃ, yadantaraṃ ekaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjāmi, bhagavato sāsanaṃ manasikareyyaṃ, bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti. Yo cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāveti, aho vatāhaṃ tadantaraṃ jīveyyaṃ, yadantaraṃ cattāro pañca ālope saṅkhāditvā ajjhoharāmi, bhagavato sāsanaṃ manasikareyyaṃ, bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, bhikkhū pamattā viharanti, dandhaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāventi āsavānaṃ khayāya. Yo ca khvāyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāveti, aho vatāhaṃ tadantaraṃ jīveyyaṃ, yadantaraṃ ekaṃ ālopaṃ saṅkhāditvā ajjhoharāmi, bhagavato sāsanaṃ manasikareyyaṃ, bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti. Yo cāyaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāveti, aho vatāhaṃ tadantaraṃ jīveyyaṃ, yadantaraṃ assasitvā vā passasāmi, passasitvā vā assasāmi, bhagavato sāsanaṃ manasikareyyaṃ, bahuṃ vata me kataṃ assāti. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, bhikkhū appamattā viharanti, tikkhaṃ maraṇassatiṃ bhāventi āsavānaṃ khayāyā”ti (a. ni. 6.19). Evaṃ catupañcālopasaṅkhādanamattaṃ avissāsiyo paritto jīvitassa addhāti evaṃ addhānaparicchedato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Furthermore, it is said: "Monks, a monk who develops mindfulness of death thus: 'Oh, that I might live for a night and a day, that I might attend to the Blessed One's teaching—much indeed would be done by me!' Monks, a monk who develops mindfulness of death thus: 'Oh, that I might live for a day, that I might attend to the Blessed One's teaching—much indeed would be done by me!' Monks, a monk who develops mindfulness of death thus: 'Oh, that I might live for the interval it takes to eat a single alms-meal, that I might attend to the Blessed One's teaching—much indeed would be done by me!' Monks, a monk who develops mindfulness of death thus: 'Oh, that I might live for the interval it takes to chew and swallow four or five morsels, that I might attend to the Blessed One's teaching—much indeed would be done by me!' These, monks, are called monks who dwell heedlessly, who develop mindfulness of death slowly for the destruction of the taints. But monks, a monk who develops mindfulness of death thus: 'Oh, that I might live for the interval it takes to chew and swallow a single morsel, that I might attend to the Blessed One's teaching—much indeed would be done by me!' Monks, a monk who develops mindfulness of death thus: 'Oh, that I might live for the interval it takes to breathe in after breathing out, or to breathe out after breathing in, that I might attend to the Blessed One's teaching—much indeed would be done by me!' These, monks, are called monks who dwell heedfully, who develop mindfulness of death keenly for the destruction of the taints." Thus, death should be recollected by way of determining the duration, realizing that the span of life is unreliable and brief, lasting only as long as the time it takes to chew four or five morsels.

176. Khaṇaparittatoti paramatthato hi atiparitto sattānaṃ jīvitakkhaṇo ekacittappavattimattoyeva. Yathā nāma rathacakkaṃ pavattamānampi ekeneva nemippadesena pavattati, tiṭṭhamānampi ekeneva tiṭṭhati, evameva ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ. Tasmiṃ citte niruddhamatte satto niruddhoti vuccati. Yathāha – “atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvittha, na jīvati, na jīvissati. Anāgate cittakkhaṇe na jīvittha, na jīvati, jīvissati. Paccuppanne cittakkhaṇe na jīvittha, jīvati, na jīvissati.

176. Regarding the brevity of the moment: indeed, in the ultimate sense, the life-moment of beings is exceedingly brief; it is merely the duration of the occurrence of a single mind-moment. Just as a chariot wheel, even when rolling, rolls on only one point of its rim, and even when standing still, stands on only one point, even so, the life of beings has the duration of a single mind-moment. When that mind has just ceased, the being is said to have ceased. As it is said: 'In a past mind-moment, one lived; one does not live, nor will one live. In a future mind-moment, one did not live, nor does one live; one will live. In the present mind-moment, one did not live; one lives, but one will not live.'

“Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca, sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā, lahu so vattate khaṇo.

'Life-faculty, individual existence, and feelings of pleasure and pain are purely phenomenal, conjoined with a single mind-moment; that moment proceeds swiftly.'

“Ye niruddhā marantassa, tiṭṭhamānassa vā idha;

Sabbepi sadisā khandhā, gatā appaṭisandhikā.

'The aggregates that have ceased for one who is dying, or for one who is still existing here—all those aggregates are similar: they are gone, without relinking.'

“Anibbattena [M 1.0231][V 1.0230] na jāto, paccuppannena jīvati;

Cittabhaṅgā mato loko, paññatti paramatthiyā”ti. (mahāni. 39);

'By that which has not arisen, one is not born; by that which is present, one lives. Due to the breaking of the mind, the world is dead in the ultimate sense; the conventional designation, however, is based on ultimate reality.'

Evaṃ khaṇaparittato maraṇaṃ anussaritabbaṃ.

Thus, death should be recollected by way of the brevity of the moment.

177. Iti imesaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ ākārānaṃ aññataraññatarena anussaratopi punappunaṃ manasikāravasena cittaṃ āsevanaṃ labhati, maraṇārammaṇā sati santiṭṭhati, nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, jhānaṅgāni pātubhavanti. Sabhāvadhammattā pana saṃvejanīyattā ca ārammaṇassa appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Lokuttarajjhānaṃ pana dutiyacatutthāni ca āruppajjhānāni sabhāvadhammepi bhāvanāvisesena appanaṃ pāpuṇanti. Visuddhibhāvanānukkamavasena hi lokuttaraṃ appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ārammaṇātikkamabhāvanāvasena āruppaṃ. Appanāpattasseva hi jhānassa ārammaṇasamatikkamanamattaṃ tattha hoti. Idha pana tadubhayampi natthi. Tasmā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti. Tadetaṃ maraṇassatibalena uppannattā maraṇassaticceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

177. Thus, by recollecting through one or another of these eight aspects, the mind, by way of repeated attention, obtains familiarity. Mindfulness with death as its object becomes established, the hindrances are suppressed, and the jhāna factors arise. However, because the object is a conditioned phenomenon and a basis for spiritual urgency, the jhāna does not reach absorption, being only that which has reached access concentration. On the other hand, supramundane jhāna, as well as the second and fourth immaterial jhānas, reach absorption even with a conditioned phenomenon as an object, by means of a special development of meditation. For, the supramundane reaches absorption by way of the sequence of development of the purifications. The immaterial jhāna does so by way of the development of transcending the object. For in that case, there is merely the transcending of the object of the preceding jhāna that has already reached absorption. Here, in mindfulness of death, however, neither of those two is present. Therefore, the jhāna is only that which has reached access concentration. And since this has arisen through the power of mindfulness of death, it goes by the designation 'mindfulness of death'.

Imañca pana maraṇassatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu satataṃ appamatto hoti, sabbabhavesu anabhiratisaññaṃ paṭilabhati, jīvitanikantiṃ jahāti, pāpagarahī hoti, asannidhibahulo parikkhāresu vigatamalamacchero, aniccasaññā cassa paricayaṃ gacchati, tadanusāreneva dukkhasaññā anattasaññā ca upaṭṭhāti. Yathā abhāvitamaraṇā sattā sahasā vāḷamigayakkhasappacoravadhakābhibhūtā viya maraṇasamaye bhayaṃ santāsaṃ sammohaṃ āpajjanti, evaṃ anāpajjitvā abhayo asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti. Sace diṭṭheva dhamme amataṃ nārādheti, kāyassa bhedā sugatiparāyano hoti.

Furthermore, a monk who is devoted to this mindfulness of death is constantly heedful. He obtains the perception of non-delight in all forms of existence, abandons craving for life, becomes a reproacher of evil, does not make much accumulation of requisites, and is free from the stain of stinginess. The perception of impermanence becomes familiar to him, and in conformity with it, the perceptions of suffering and non-self are also established. Just as beings who have not developed mindfulness of death, when suddenly overcome by beasts of prey, yakkhas, serpents, thieves, or murderers, fall into fear, terror, and confusion at the time of death, so he, not falling into such states, passes away fearless and unconfused. If he does not attain the deathless in this very life, upon the breakup of the body, he is bound for a happy destination.

Tasmā have appamādaṃ, kayirātha sumedhaso;

Evaṃ mahānubhāvāya, maraṇassatiyā sadāti.

Therefore, let the wise indeed always practice heedfulness in this mindfulness of death of such great power.

Idaṃ maraṇassatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed discourse on mindfulness of death.

Kāyagatāsatikathā

Discourse on Mindfulness Directed to the Body

178. Idāni [M 1.0232][V 1.0231] yaṃ taṃ aññatra buddhuppādā appavattapubbaṃ sabbatitthiyānaṃ avisayabhūtaṃ tesu tesu suttantesu “ekadhammo, bhikkhave, bhāvito bahulīkato mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati. Mahato atthāya saṃvattati. Mahato yogakkhemāya saṃvattati. Mahato satisampajaññāya saṃvattati. Ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati. Vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya saṃvattati. Katamo ekadhammo? Kāyagatā sati… (a. ni. 1.563 ādayo). Amataṃ te, bhikkhave, paribhuñjanti, ye kāyagatāsatiṃ paribhuñjanti. Amataṃ te, bhikkhave, na paribhuñjanti, ye kāyagatāsatiṃ na paribhuñjanti. Amataṃ tesaṃ, bhikkhave, paribhuttaṃ… aparibhuttaṃ… parihīnaṃ… aparihīnaṃ… viraddhaṃ… aviraddhaṃ, yesaṃ kāyagatāsati āraddhāti (a. ni. 1.603) evaṃ bhagavatā anekehi ākārehi pasaṃsitvā “kathaṃ bhāvitā, bhikkhave, kāyagatāsati kathaṃ bahulīkatā mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.154) nayena ānāpānapabbaṃ, iriyāpathapabbaṃ, catusampajaññapabbaṃ, paṭikkūlamanasikārapabbaṃ, dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ, navasivathikapabbānīti imesaṃ cuddasannaṃ pabbānaṃ vasena kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ, tassa bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto.

178. Now, that which was previously unarisen outside the appearance of a Buddha, beyond the scope of all sectarians, is found in various discourses: "Monks, one thing, when developed and cultivated, leads to great urgency, to great benefit, to great security from bondage, to great mindfulness and clear comprehension, to the attainment of knowledge and vision, to a pleasant dwelling in this very life, and to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. What is that one thing? Mindfulness directed to the body... Monks, those who partake of mindfulness directed to the body partake of the Deathless. Those who do not partake of mindfulness directed to the body do not partake of the Deathless. For them, monks, the Deathless is partaken of... not partaken of... lost... not lost... missed... not missed. For those by whom mindfulness directed to the body is undertaken, for them the Deathless is undertaken." Thus, having been praised by the Blessed One in many ways, it is said: "How, monks, is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it becomes of great fruit and great benefit? Here, monks, a monk gone to the forest..." and so on. By this method, the meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body is specified by means of these fourteen sections: the section on mindfulness of breathing, the section on postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, the section on reflection on repulsiveness, the section on reflection on the elements, and the nine sections on charnel grounds. The exposition on its development has now arrived in due course.

Tattha yasmā iriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ dhātumanasikārapabbanti imāni tīṇi vipassanāvasena vuttāni. Nava sivathikapabbāni vipassanāñāṇesuyeva ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttāni. Yāpi cettha uddhumātakādīsu samādhibhāvanā ijjheyya, sā asubhaniddese pakāsitāyeva. Ānāpānapabbaṃ pana paṭikkūlamanasikārapabbañca imānevettha dve samādhivasena vuttāni. Tesu ānāpānapabbaṃ ānāpānassativasena visuṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃyeva. Yaṃ panetaṃ “puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati. Atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… mutta”nti (ma. ni. 3.154) evaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ aṭṭhimiñjena saṅgahetvā paṭikkūlamanasikāravasena desitaṃ dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ, idamidha kāyagatāsatīti adhippetaṃ.

Herein, the section on postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the section on reflection on the elements—these three are spoken of by way of insight. The nine charnel ground sections are spoken of by way of the contemplation of danger within the insight knowledges themselves. And whatever development of concentration might be accomplished here in regard to the bloated corpse and so on, that has already been explained in the exposition on foulness. However, the section on mindfulness of breathing and the section on reflection on repulsiveness—only these two are spoken of here by way of concentration. Among them, the section on mindfulness of breathing is a separate meditation subject in itself by way of mindfulness of breathing. But as for that thirty-two-part meditation subject taught by way of reflection on repulsiveness, including the brain with the bone marrow, thus: “Furthermore, monks, a monk reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by skin, and full of many kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs… urine,’” this is what is intended here as ‘mindfulness directed to the body.’

179. Tatthāyaṃ [M 1.0233] pāḷivaṇṇanāpubbaṅgamo bhāvanāniddeso. Imameva kāyanti imaṃ catumahābhūtikaṃ [V 1.0232] pūtikāyaṃ. Uddhaṃ pādatalāti pādatalato upari. Adho kesamatthakāti kesaggato heṭṭhā. Tacapariyantanti tiriyaṃ tacaparicchinnaṃ. Pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhatīti nānappakārakesādiasucibharito ayaṃ kāyoti passati. Kathaṃ? Atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā…pe… muttanti.

179. Therein, this is the exposition on development, which is preceded by the explanation of the Pali. 'This very body' means this foul body which is based on the four great elements. 'Upwards from the soles of the feet' means above from the soles of the feet. 'Downwards from the crown of the head' means below from the tips of the hair. 'Bounded by skin' means enclosed horizontally by skin. 'Reviews as full of many kinds of impurity' means one sees that this body is filled with various kinds of impurities beginning with head-hairs. How? “In this body there are head-hairs… urine.”

Tattha atthīti saṃvijjanti. Imasminti yvāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyanto pūro nānappakārassa asucinoti vuccati, tasmiṃ. Kāyeti sarīre. Sarīraṃ hi asucisañcayato kucchitānaṃ kesādīnañceva cakkhurogādīnañca rogasatānaṃ āyabhūtato kāyoti vuccati. Kesā lomāti ete kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā. Tattha atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā, atthi imasmiṃ kāye lomāti evaṃ sambandho veditabbo.

Herein, 'there are' (atthi) means they exist (saṃvijjanti). 'In this' (imasmiṃ) refers to that which is spoken of as being upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by skin, and full of various kinds of impurities. 'Body' (kāye) refers to the physical form (sarīre). Indeed, the physical form (sarīraṃ) is called 'kāya' because it is a collection of impurities, and a place of origin for foul things such as head-hairs and for hundreds of diseases such as eye diseases. 'Head-hairs, body-hairs' (kesā lomā) refers to these thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs. Herein, the connection should be understood thus: 'In this body, there are head-hairs; in this body, there are body-hairs.'

Imasmiṃ hi pādatalā paṭṭhāya upari, kesamatthakā paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, tacato paṭṭhāya paritoti ettake byāmamatte kaḷevare sabbākārenapi vicinanto na koci kiñci muttaṃ vā maṇiṃ vā veḷuriyaṃ vā agaruṃ vā kuṅkumaṃ vā kappūraṃ vā vāsacuṇṇādiṃ vā aṇumattampi sucibhāvaṃ passati, atha kho paramaduggandhajegucchaṃ asirikadassanaṃ nānappakāraṃ kesalomādibhedaṃ asuciṃyeva passati. Tena vuttaṃ “atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… mutta”nti. Ayamettha padasambandhato vaṇṇanā.

For in this mere fathom-long carcass—starting upwards from the soles of the feet, downwards from the crown of the head, and around from the skin—if anyone were to investigate in every way, they would not see even an atom's measure of purity, be it a pearl, a jewel, lapis lazuli, agarwood, saffron, camphor, or scented powders and the like. Instead, one sees only what is utterly foul-smelling and repulsive, an unlovely sight, and various kinds of impurities divided into head-hairs, body-hairs, and so on. Therefore, it is said: 'In this body, there are head-hairs, body-hairs… up to urine.' This here is the explanation according to the connection of the words.

180. Imaṃ pana kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetukāmena ādikammikena kulaputtena vuttappakāraṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Tenāpissa kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathentena sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ dasadhā ca manasikārakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Tattha vacasā manasā vaṇṇato saṇṭhānato disato okāsato paricchedatoti evaṃ sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ.

180. Now, a clansman who is a beginner and wishes to develop this meditation subject should approach a good friend of the type described and take up this meditation subject. And when that teacher explains the meditation subject to him, the sevenfold skill in apprehension and the tenfold skill in attention should be taught. Therein, the sevenfold skill in apprehension should be taught thus: by word, by mind, by color, by shape, by direction, by location, and by delimitation.

Imasmiṃ hi paṭikkūlamanasikārakammaṭṭhāne yopi tipiṭako hoti, tenāpi manasikārakāle paṭhamaṃ vācāya sajjhāyo kātabbo. Ekaccassa hi sajjhāyaṃ karontasseva kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti malayavāsī mahādevattherassa santike uggahitakammaṭṭhānānaṃ dvinnaṃ therānaṃ viya. Thero [M 1.0234] kira tehi kammaṭṭhānaṃ yācito cattāro māse imaṃyeva sajjhāyaṃ karothāti dvattiṃsākārapāḷiṃ adāsi. Te kiñcāpi nesaṃ dve tayo nikāyā paguṇā, padakkhiṇaggāhitāya [V 1.0233] pana cattāro māse dvattiṃsākāraṃ sajjhāyantāva sotāpannā ahesuṃ. Tasmā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathentena ācariyena antevāsiko vattabbo “paṭhamaṃ tāva vācāya sajjhāyaṃ karohī”ti.

Indeed, in this meditation subject of attention to the repulsive, even one who is a master of the Tipiṭaka should first make the recitation verbally at the time of applying the mind. For, to a certain one, the meditation subject becomes clear even while making the recitation, as it did for the two elders who had learned the meditation subject in the presence of the Elder Mahādeva, the resident of Malaya. It is said that the Elder, having been requested for the meditation subject by them, gave the Pāli text on the thirty-two parts, saying, 'For four months, practice this very recitation.' Although they were proficient in two or three Nikāyas, nevertheless, due to their reverential acceptance, they became stream-enterers even while reciting the thirty-two parts for four months. Therefore, a teacher explaining the meditation subject should tell the resident pupil, 'First of all, make the recitation verbally.'

Karontena ca tacapañcakādīni paricchinditvā anulomapaṭilomavasena sajjhāyo kātabbo. Kesā lomā nakhā dantā tacoti hi vatvā puna paṭilomato taco dantā nakhā lomā kesāti vattabbaṃ.

And when reciting, one should demarcate the skin-pentad and other such groups, and the recitation should be done in forward and reverse order. Indeed, having said, 'head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin,' it should be said again in reverse order: 'skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.'

Tadanantaraṃ vakkapañcake maṃsaṃ nhāru aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ vakkanti vatvā puna paṭilomato vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ, taco dantā nakhā lomā kesāti vattabbaṃ.

Immediately after that, in the kidney-pentad, having said, 'flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys,' it should be said again in reverse order: 'kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.'

Tato papphāsapañcake hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsanti vatvā puna paṭilomato papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ, vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ, taco dantā nakhā lomā kesāti vattabbaṃ.

Then, in the lung-pentad, having said, 'heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs,' it should be said again in reverse order: 'lungs, spleen, pleura, liver, heart; kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.'

Tato matthaluṅgapañcake antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ karīsaṃ matthaluṅganti vatvā puna paṭilomato matthaluṅgaṃ karīsaṃ udariyaṃ antaguṇaṃ antaṃ, papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ, vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ, taco dantā nakhā lomā kesāti vattabbaṃ.

Then, in the brain-pentad, having said, 'intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, feces, brain,' it should be said again in reverse order: 'brain, feces, stomach contents, mesentery, intestines; lungs, spleen, pleura, liver, heart; kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.'

Tato medachakke pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medoti vatvā puna paṭilomato medo sedo lohitaṃ pubbo semhaṃ pittaṃ, matthaluṅgaṃ karīsaṃ udariyaṃ antaguṇaṃ antaṃ, papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ, vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ, taco dantā nakhā lomā kesāti vattabbaṃ.

Then, in the fat-hexad, having said, 'bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat,' it should be said again in reverse order: 'fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile; brain, feces, stomach contents, mesentery, intestines; lungs, spleen, pleura, liver, heart; kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.'

Tato muttachakke assu vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā muttanti vatvā puna paṭilomato muttaṃ lasikā siṅghāṇikā kheḷo vasā assu, medo sedo lohitaṃ pubbo semhaṃ pittaṃ, matthaluṅgaṃ karīsaṃ udariyaṃ antaguṇaṃ antaṃ, papphāsaṃ pihakaṃ kilomakaṃ yakanaṃ hadayaṃ, vakkaṃ aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhi nhāru maṃsaṃ, taco dantā nakhā lomā kesāti vattabbaṃ.

Then, in the urine-hexad, having said, 'tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine,' it should be said again in reverse order: 'urine, synovial fluid, snot, saliva, grease, tears; fat, sweat, blood, pus, phlegm, bile; brain, feces, stomach contents, mesentery, intestines; lungs, spleen, pleura, liver, heart; kidneys, bone marrow, bones, sinews, flesh; skin, teeth, nails, body hairs, head hairs.'

Evaṃ [M 1.0235][V 1.0234] kālasataṃ kālasahassaṃ kālasatasahassampi vācāya sajjhāyo kātabbo. Vacasā sajjhāyena hi kammaṭṭhānatanti paguṇā hoti, na ito cito ca cittaṃ vidhāvati. Koṭṭhāsā pākaṭā honti, hatthasaṅkhalikā viya vatipādapanti viya ca khāyanti.

In this way, recitation should be done verbally a hundred times, a thousand times, or even a hundred thousand times. For by verbal recitation, the text of the meditation subject becomes fluent, and the mind does not run here and there. The parts become manifest; they appear like a chain of hand-bones and like a row of fence posts.

Yathā pana vacasā, tatheva manasāpi sajjhāyo kātabbo. Vacasā sajjhāyo hi manasā sajjhāyassa paccayo hoti. Manasā sajjhāyo lakkhaṇapaṭivedhassa paccayo hoti.

Moreover, just as recitation should be done verbally, so too should it be done mentally. For verbal recitation is a condition for mental recitation. Mental recitation is a condition for the penetration of the characteristics.

Vaṇṇatoti kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇo vavatthapetabbo.

As to color: the color of the head hairs and so on should be determined.

Saṇṭhānatoti tesaññeva saṇṭhānaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ.

As to shape: the shape of those very parts should be determined.

Disatoti imasmiṃ hi sarīre nābhito uddhaṃ uparimadisā, adho heṭṭhimadisā, tasmā ayaṃ koṭṭhāso imissā nāma disāyāti disā vavatthapetabbā.

As to direction: for in this body, above the navel is the upper direction, and below is the lower direction. Therefore, the direction should be determined thus: 'This part is in such-and-such a direction.'

Okāsatoti ayaṃ koṭṭhāso imasmiṃ nāma okāse patiṭṭhitoti evaṃ tassa tassa okāso vavatthapetabbo.

As to location: the location of each and every part should be determined thus: 'This part is established in such-and-such a location.'

Paricchedatoti sabhāgaparicchedo visabhāgaparicchedoti dve paricchedā. Tattha ayaṃ koṭṭhāso heṭṭhā ca upari ca tiriyañca iminā nāma paricchinnoti evaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo veditabbo. Kesā na lomā, lomāpi na kesāti evaṃ amissakatāvasena visabhāgaparicchedo veditabbo.

As to delimitation: there are two delimitations, namely, delimitation by its own part and delimitation by what is not its own part. Therein, delimitation by its own part should be understood thus: 'This part is delimited below, above, and across by such-and-such.' Delimitation by what is not its own part should be understood by way of being unmixed, thus: 'Hairs of the head are not body hairs, and body hairs are not hairs of the head.'

Evaṃ sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ ācikkhantena pana idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ asukasmiṃ sutte paṭikkūlavasena kathitaṃ, asukasmiṃ dhātuvasenāti ñatvā ācikkhitabbaṃ. Idañhi mahāsatipaṭṭhāne (dī. ni. 2.377) paṭikkūlavaseneva kathitaṃ. Mahāhatthipadopama(ma. ni. 1.300 ādayo) mahārāhulovāda(ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) dhātuvibhaṅgesu(ma. ni. 3.342 ādayo) dhātuvasena kathitaṃ. Kāyagatāsatisutte (ma. ni. 3.153) pana yassa vaṇṇato upaṭṭhāti, taṃ sandhāya cattāri jhānāni vibhattāni. Tattha dhātuvasena kathitaṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0235] hoti. Paṭikkūlavasena kathitaṃ samathakammaṭṭhānaṃ. Tadetaṃ idha samathakammaṭṭhānamevāti.

Furthermore, one who explains the skill in grasping in seven ways should explain this meditation subject after knowing that 'in such-and-such a sutta it is taught by way of repulsiveness, and in such-and-such a sutta by way of the elements.' Indeed, in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta it is taught only by way of repulsiveness. In the Mahāhatthipadopama, Mahārāhulovāda, and Dhātuvibhaṅga Suttas, it is taught by way of the elements. However, in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, with reference to the person to whom a part appears by way of color, the four jhānas are distinguished. Therein, what is taught by way of the elements is an insight meditation subject. What is taught by way of repulsiveness is a serenity meditation subject. This meditation subject here is solely a serenity meditation subject.

181. Evaṃ [M 1.0236] sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ ācikkhitvā anupubbato, nātisīghato, nātisaṇikato, vikkhepapaṭibāhanato, paṇṇattisamatikkamanato, anupubbamuñcanato, appanāto, tayo ca suttantāti evaṃ dasadhā manasikārakosallaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Tattha anupubbatoti idañhi sajjhāyakaraṇato paṭṭhāya anupaṭipāṭiyā manasikātabbaṃ, na ekantarikāya. Ekantarikāya hi manasikaronto yathā nāma akusalo puriso dvattiṃsapadaṃ nisseṇiṃ ekantarikāya ārohanto kilantakāyo patati, na ārohanaṃ sampādeti, evameva bhāvanāsampattivasena adhigantabbassa assādassa anadhigamā kilantacitto patati, na bhāvanaṃ sampādeti.

181. Having thus explained the skill in grasping in seven ways, the skill in attention should be explained in ten ways: sequentially, not too quickly, not too slowly, by warding off distraction, by transcending concepts, by sequentially letting go, by absorption, and the three suttas. Therein, regarding 'sequentially': starting from the act of recitation, this meditation subject should be attended to in sequential order, not by skipping. For one who attends by skipping, just as an unskilled man climbing a thirty-two-rung ladder by skipping rungs becomes weary in body and falls, and does not complete the ascent; even so, due to not attaining the delightful state that is to be obtained through the accomplishment of the development, he falls away with a weary mind and does not complete the development.

Anupubbato manasikarontenāpi ca nātisīghato manasikātabbaṃ. Atisīghato manasikaroto hi yathā nāma tiyojanamaggaṃ paṭipajjitvā okkamanavissajjanaṃ asallakkhetvā sīghena javena satakkhattumpi gamanāgamanaṃ karoto purisassa kiñcāpi addhānaṃ parikkhayaṃ gacchati, atha kho pucchitvāva gantabbaṃ hoti, evameva kevalaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ pāpuṇāti, avibhūtaṃ pana hoti, na visesaṃ āvahati, tasmā nātisīghato manasikātabbaṃ.

And even when attending sequentially, one should not attend too quickly. For if one attends too quickly, it is just as with a man traveling a three-yojana road: without taking note of the features of the path, though he may go back and forth a hundred times with great speed, his journey comes to an end, yet he must still proceed by asking. So too, the meditation subject merely reaches its conclusion, but it remains unclear and does not bring about a special attainment. Therefore, one should not attend too quickly.

Yathā ca nātisīghato, evaṃ nātisaṇikatopi. Atisaṇikato manasikaroto hi yathā nāma tadaheva tiyojanamaggaṃ gantukāmassa purisassa antarāmagge rukkhapabbatataḷākādīsu vilambamānassa maggo parikkhayaṃ na gacchati, dvīhatīhena pariyosāpetabbo hoti, evameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariyosānaṃ na gacchati, visesādhigamassa paccayo na hoti.

And just as one should not attend too quickly, so too one should not attend too slowly. For if one attends too slowly, it is just as with a man who wishes to travel a three-yojana road on that very day: if he lingers along the way among trees, mountains, ponds, and so on, the journey does not come to an end and must be completed in two or three days. Just so, the meditation subject does not reach its conclusion and does not become a condition for the attainment of a special state.

Vikkhepapaṭibāhanatoti kammaṭṭhānaṃ vissajjetvā bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cetaso vikkhepo paṭibāhitabbo. Appaṭibāhato hi yathā nāma ekapadikaṃ papātamaggaṃ paṭipannassa purisassa akkamanapadaṃ asallakkhetvā ito cito ca vilokayato padavāro virajjhati, tato sataporise papāte patitabbaṃ hoti, evameva bahiddhā vikkhepe sati kammaṭṭhānaṃ parihāyati paridhaṃsati. Tasmā vikkhepapaṭibāhanato manasikātabbaṃ.

By 'warding off distraction' is meant that the distraction of the mind, which abandons the meditation subject for diverse external objects, should be warded off. For if it is not warded off, it is just as with a man who has taken to a one-foot-wide cliff path: if, without taking note of his stepping place, he looks here and there, his footstep fails, and consequently he must fall into a precipice a hundred men deep. Just so, when there is external distraction, the meditation subject deteriorates and is destroyed. Therefore, one should attend by warding off distraction.

Paṇṇattisamatikkamanatoti [M 1.0237][V 1.0236] yāyaṃ kesā lomātiādikā paṇṇatti, taṃ atikkamitvā paṭikkūlanti cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Yathā hi udakadullabhakāle manussā araññe udapānaṃ disvā tattha tālapaṇṇādikaṃ kiñcideva saññāṇaṃ bandhitvā tena saññāṇena āgantvā nhāyanti ceva pivanti ca. Yadā pana nesaṃ abhiṇhasañcārena āgatāgatapadaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tadā saññāṇena kiccaṃ na hoti, icchiticchitakkhaṇe gantvā nhāyanti ceva pivanti ca, evameva pubbabhāge kesā lomātipaṇṇattivasena manasikaroto paṭikkūlabhāvo pākaṭo hoti. Atha kesā lomātipaṇṇattiṃ samatikkamitvā paṭikkūlabhāveyeva cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ.

'By transcending the designation' means that, having gone beyond the designation such as 'head hair, body hair,' the mind should be established on repulsiveness. For instance, in a time when water is scarce, people, having seen a well in the forest, tie some kind of sign there, such as a palm leaf, and by means of that sign, they come to both bathe and drink. But when the track of their coming and going becomes clear due to their frequent traversing, then there is no need for the sign; going whenever they wish, they both bathe and drink. Just so, in the preliminary stage, for one attending by means of the designation 'head hair, body hair,' the state of repulsiveness becomes clear. Then, having transcended the designation 'head hair, body hair,' the mind should be established on the state of repulsiveness itself.

Anupubbamuñcanatoti yo yo koṭṭhāso na upaṭṭhāti, taṃ taṃ muñcantena anupubbamuñcanato manasikātabbaṃ. Ādikammikassa hi kesāti manasikaroto manasikāro gantvā muttanti imaṃ pariyosānakoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhati. Muttanti ca manasikaroto manasikāro gantvā kesāti imaṃ ādikoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhati. Athassa manasikaroto manasikaroto keci koṭṭhāsā upaṭṭhahanti, keci na upaṭṭhahanti. Tena ye ye upaṭṭhahanti, tesu tesu tāva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Yāva dvīsu upaṭṭhitesu tesampi eko suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhahati, evaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ pana tameva punappunaṃ manasikarontena appanā uppādetabbā.

'By sequentially letting go' means that one should attend by letting go of whichever part does not appear. For a beginner, when attending as 'head hair,' the attention goes and stops only at this final part, 'urine.' And when attending as 'urine,' the attention goes and stops only at this first part, 'head hair.' Then, for him, as he attends again and again, some parts appear, and some do not. Therefore, he should first work on whichever parts appear, until, when two parts have appeared, one of them appears much more clearly. Then, by repeatedly attending to that very part which has thus appeared clearly, absorption should be produced.

Tatrāyaṃ upamā – yathā hi dvattiṃsatālake tālavane vasantaṃ makkaṭaṃ gahetukāmo luddo ādimhi ṭhitatālassa paṇṇaṃ sarena vijjhitvā ukkuṭṭhiṃ kareyya, atha kho so makkaṭo paṭipāṭiyā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ tāle patitvā pariyantatālameva gaccheyya, tatthapi gantvā luddena tatheva kate puna teneva nayena āditālaṃ āgaccheyya, so evaṃ punappunaṃ paripātiyamāno ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhiṭṭhāneyeva uṭṭhahitvā anukkamena ekasmiṃ tāle nipatitvā tassa vemajjhe makuḷatālapaṇṇasūciṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā vijjhiyamānopi na uṭṭhaheyya, evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein is a simile. Just as a hunter, wishing to catch a monkey living in a palm grove with thirty-two palms, might shoot with an arrow the leaf of the palm tree standing at the beginning and make a shout; then that monkey, leaping in sequence to this and that palm tree, would go only to the final palm tree. Having gone there also, when the hunter does the same, it would again, by that same method, come to the first palm tree. That monkey, being thus chased again and again, rising up from the very palm tree where the shout was made, would in due course leap down onto one palm tree, and in its middle, having firmly grasped the spike of a budding palm leaf, would not rise up even while being shot. This accomplishment should be seen thus.

Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – yathā hi tālavane dvattiṃsatālā, evaṃ imasmiṃ kāye dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsā. Makkaṭo viya cittaṃ. Luddo viya yogāvacaro. Makkaṭassa dvattiṃsatālake tālavane nivāso viya yogino [M 1.0238] cittassa dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsake kāye ārammaṇavasena anusañcaraṇaṃ. Luddena ādimhi ṭhitatālassa paṇṇaṃ sarena vijjhitvā ukkuṭṭhiyā katāya makkaṭassa tasmiṃ tasmiṃ tāle patitvā pariyantatālagamanaṃ viya yogino kesāti manasikāre āraddhe [V 1.0237] paṭipāṭiyā gantvā pariyosānakoṭṭhāseyeva cittassa saṇṭhānaṃ. Puna paccāgamanepi eseva nayo. Punappunaṃ paripātiyamānassa makkaṭassa ukkuṭṭhukkuṭṭhiṭṭhāne uṭṭhānaṃ viya punappunaṃ manasikaroto kesuci kesuci upaṭṭhitesu anupaṭṭhahante vissajjetvā upaṭṭhitesu parikammakaraṇaṃ. Anukkamena ekasmiṃ tāle nipatitvā tassa majjhe makuḷatālapaṇṇasūciṃ daḷhaṃ gahetvā vijjhiyamānassapi anuṭṭhānaṃ viya avasāne dvīsu upaṭṭhitesu yo suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhāti, tameva punappunaṃ manasikaritvā appanāya uppādanaṃ.

Herein is the comparison of the simile. Just as there are thirty-two palms in the palm grove, so in this body there are thirty-two parts. The mind is like the monkey. The yogāvacara is like the hunter. Like the monkey's dwelling in the palm grove with thirty-two palms, is the repeated traversing of the yogī's mind among the thirty-two parts in the body by way of taking them as an object. Like the monkey's leaping to this and that palm tree and going to the final palm tree when the hunter has shot the leaf of the palm tree standing at the beginning with an arrow and made a shout, is the settling of the yogī's mind only on the final part, having gone in sequence, when the attention 'hair,' etc., has been undertaken. Again, in returning, this is the very same method. Like the rising of the monkey, being chased again and again, from the place where the shout was made, is the performing of preliminary work on the manifest parts, having abandoned the non-manifest ones, for one who attends again and again when some parts have become manifest. Like the not rising up of the monkey even while being shot, having leaped in sequence onto one palm tree and firmly grasped in its middle the spike of a budding palm leaf, is the producing of absorption at the end, by attending again and again to whichever of two manifest parts appears more clearly.

Aparāpi upamā – yathā nāma piṇḍapātiko bhikkhu dvattiṃsakulaṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya vasanto paṭhamageheyeva dve bhikkhā labhitvā parato ekaṃ vissajjeyya. Punadivase tisso labhitvā parato dve vissajjeyya. Tatiyadivase ādimhiyeva pattapūraṃ labhitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā paribhuñjeyya. Evaṃsampadamidaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Dvattiṃsakulagāmo viya hi dvattiṃsākāro. Piṇḍapātiko viya yogāvacaro. Tassa taṃ gāmaṃ upanissāya vāso viya yogino dvattiṃsākāre parikammakaraṇaṃ. Paṭhamagehe dve bhikkhā labhitvā parato ekissā vissajjanaṃ viya dutiyadivase tisso labhitvā parato dvinnaṃ vissajjanaṃ viya ca manasikaroto manasikaroto anupaṭṭhahante vissajjetvā upaṭṭhitesu yāva koṭṭhāsadvaye parikammakaraṇaṃ. Tatiyadivase ādimhiyeva pattapūraṃ labhitvā āsanasālāyaṃ nisīditvā paribhogo viya dvīsu yo suṭṭhutaraṃ upaṭṭhāti, tameva punappunaṃ manasikaritvā appanāya uppādanaṃ.

Another simile is to be seen. Just as an alms-gathering bhikkhu, dwelling in dependence on a village of thirty-two families, having received two alms-portions at the very first house, might leave aside one house beyond that. On the next day, having received three alms-portions, he might leave aside two houses beyond that. On the third day, having received a bowl-full at the very beginning, he might go to the eating hall and partake of it. This state of affairs should be seen thus. For the thirty-two parts are like the village of thirty-two families. The meditator is like the alms-gatherer. The meditator's preliminary work on the thirty-two parts is like that bhikkhu's dwelling in dependence on that village. The preliminary work on up to two sections among those that have appeared—having abandoned those that do not appear while attending again and again—is like leaving aside one house beyond after receiving two alms-portions at the first house, and on the second day, like leaving aside two houses beyond after receiving three. The production of absorption by repeatedly attending to that very one of the two sections which appears most clearly is like the partaking of food after sitting down in the eating hall, having received a bowl-full at the very beginning on the third day.

Appanātoti appanākoṭṭhāsato kesādīsu ekekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse appanā hotīti veditabbāti ayamevettha adhippāyo.

Regarding `appanāto`, this is the intended meaning here: it is to be known that absorption occurs in each and every section among those beginning with head hair, by means of the section that is the basis for absorption.

Tayo ca suttantāti adhicittaṃ, sītibhāvo, bojjhaṅgakosallanti ime tayo suttantā vīriyasamādhiyojanatthaṃ veditabbāti ayamettha adhippāyo. Tattha –

Regarding 'And the three suttantas,' the intended meaning here is this: these three suttantas—on the higher mind, on becoming cool, and on skill in the enlightenment factors—are to be understood as being for the purpose of yoking energy and concentration. Therein—

“Adhicittamanuyuttena[M 1.0239], bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tīṇi nimittāni kālenakālaṃ manasikātabbāni. Kālenakālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Kālenakālaṃ paggahanimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Kālenakālaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasikātabbaṃ. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ samādhinimittaññeva manasikareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ [V 1.0238] cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ paggahanimittaññeva manasikareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvatteyya. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ upekkhānimittaññeva manasikareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ na sammā samādhiyeyya āsavānaṃ khayāya. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu kālenakālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ paggahanimittaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasikaroti, taṃ hoti cittaṃ muduñca kammaññañca pabhassarañca, na ca pabhaṅgu, sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind is to attend to three signs from time to time. From time to time, he is to attend to the sign of concentration. From time to time, he is to attend to the sign of exertion. From time to time, he is to attend to the sign of equanimity. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend only to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind would lead to laziness. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend only to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind would lead to restlessness. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind were to attend only to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind would not be rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind attends from time to time to the sign of concentration, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity, his mind becomes pliant, workable, radiant, and not brittle, and it is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā ukkaṃ bandhati, ukkaṃ bandhitvā ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpeti, ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpetvā saṇḍāsena jātarūpaṃ gahetvā ukkāmukhe pakkhipitvā kālenakālaṃ abhidhamati, kālenakālaṃ udakena paripphoseti, kālenakālaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ abhidhameyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ ḍaheyya. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ udakena paripphoseyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ nibbāyeyya. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ ajjhupekkheyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ na sammā paripākaṃ gaccheyya. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ kālenakālaṃ abhidhamati, kālenakālaṃ udakena paripphoseti, kālenakālaṃ ajjhupekkhati, taṃ hoti jātarūpaṃ muduñca kammaññañca pabhassarañca, na ca pabhaṅgu, sammā upeti kammāya. Yassā yassā ca piḷandhanavikatiyā ākaṅkhati yadi paṭikāya yadi kuṇḍalāya yadi [M 1.0240] gīveyyāya yadi suvaṇṇamālāya, tañcassa atthaṃ anubhoti.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a goldsmith or a goldsmith's apprentice sets up a crucible, and having set up the crucible, lights the mouth of the crucible, and having lit the mouth of the crucible, takes gold with tongs, places it in the mouth of the crucible, and from time to time blows on it, from time to time sprinkles water on it, and from time to time looks on. If, bhikkhus, the goldsmith or the goldsmith's apprentice were to blow on that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would be burnt. If, bhikkhus, the goldsmith or the goldsmith's apprentice were to sprinkle water on that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would be cooled. If, bhikkhus, the goldsmith or the goldsmith's apprentice were to look on at that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would not reach proper refinement. But since, bhikkhus, the goldsmith or the goldsmith's apprentice blows on that gold from time to time, sprinkles water on it from time to time, and looks on from time to time, that gold becomes soft, workable, and radiant, and it is not brittle; it is properly fit for work. For whatever kind of ornament he desires—whether a girdle, an earring, a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves that purpose for him.”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyuttena…pe… samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya. Yassa yassa ca abhiññā sacchi karaṇīyassa dhammassa cittaṃ abhininnāmeti abhiññā sacchi kiriyāya, tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati sati āyatane”ti (a. ni. 3.103).

In this very way, O monks, for one devoted to the higher mind... the mind becomes concentrated for the destruction of the taints. And for whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he directs his mind for the purpose of realizing it by direct knowledge, in that very state he attains the capability of realization, when the supporting condition is present.

Idaṃ [V 1.0239] suttaṃ adhicittanti veditabbaṃ.

This sutta should be known as 'The Higher Mind'.

“Chahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu bhabbo anuttaraṃ sītibhāvaṃ sacchikātuṃ. Katamehi chahi? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ niggaṇhāti. Yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paggaṇhāti. Yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃsitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ sampahaṃseti. Yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbaṃ, tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Paṇītādhimuttiko ca hoti nibbānābhirato. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, chahi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu bhabbo anuttaraṃ sītibhāvaṃ sacchikātu”nti (a. ni. 6.85).

“O monks, a monk endowed with six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed coolness. What six? Here, O monks, a monk restrains the mind when it should be restrained, uplifts the mind when it should be uplifted, gladdens the mind when it should be gladdened, and regards the mind with equanimity when it should be regarded with equanimity. And he is one with a disposition towards the sublime, delighting in Nibbāna. O monks, a monk endowed with these six qualities is indeed capable of realizing the unsurpassed coolness.”

Idaṃ suttaṃ anuttaraṃ sītibhāvoti veditabbaṃ.

This sutta should be known as 'The Unsurpassed Coolness'.

Bojjhaṅgakosallaṃ “pana evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, akālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234) appanākosallakathāyaṃ dassitameva.

Skill in the enlightenment factors has indeed been shown in the discourse on skill in absorption thus: “Just so, O monks, when the mind is sluggish, that is the wrong time for developing the tranquility-enlightenment-factor.”

Iti idaṃ sattavidhaṃ uggahakosallaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā idañca dasavidhaṃ manasikārakosallaṃ suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā tena yoginā ubhayakosallavasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahetabbaṃ. Sace panassa ācariyena saddhiṃ ekavihāreyeva phāsu hoti, evaṃ vitthārena akathāpetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyujjantena visesaṃ labhitvā uparūpari kathāpetabbaṃ. Aññattha vasitukāmena yathāvuttena vidhinā vitthārato kathāpetvā punappunaṃ parivattetvā sabbaṃ gaṇṭhiṭṭhānaṃ chinditvā pathavīkasiṇaniddese vuttanayeneva ananurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ pahāya anurūpe [M 1.0241] vihāre vasantena khuddakapalibodhupacchedaṃ katvā paṭikkūlamanasikāre parikammaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Thus, having well grasped this sevenfold skill in learning and having thoroughly established this tenfold skill in attention, that yogī should properly take up the meditation subject by means of skill in both. If, however, it is comfortable for him to dwell in the very same monastery with his teacher, then without having the meditation subject explained in detail, he should thoroughly establish it and, while applying himself to the meditation subject, upon attaining a distinction, he should have the progressively higher stages explained. One who wishes to dwell elsewhere should have it explained in detail according to the aforesaid method, review it again and again, cut through all knotty points, and—by the very method stated in the Earth Kasiṇa Exposition—abandon an unsuitable lodging and, while dwelling in a suitable monastery, cut off the minor impediments. The preliminary work on the attention to the repulsive should then be done.

Karontena pana kesesu tāva nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ekaṃ vā dve vā kese luñcitvā hatthatale ṭhapetvā vaṇṇo tāva vavatthapetabbo. Chinnaṭṭhānepi kese oloketuṃ vaṭṭati. Udakapatte vā yāgupatte vā oloketumpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Kāḷakakāle disvā kāḷakāti manasikātabbā[V 1.0240]. Setakāle setāti. Missakakāle pana ussadavasena manasikātabbā honti. Yathā ca kesesu, evaṃ sakalepi tacapañcake disvāva nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

When doing so, a practitioner should first take up the sign in the hairs of the head. How? Having plucked one or two hairs and placed them on the palm of the hand, the color should first be determined. It is also proper to look at the hairs at the place of shaving. It is indeed proper to look at them in a bowl of water or a bowl of rice-gruel. At a time when they are black, having seen them, they should be attended to as 'black.' At a time when they are white, as 'white.' But at a time when they are mixed, they should be attended to by way of the predominant aspect. And just as with the hairs of the head, so too in the entire skin-pentad, the sign should be taken up only after seeing.

Koṭṭhāsavavatthāpanakathā

The Discourse on the Determination of the Parts

182. Evaṃ nimittaṃ gahetvā sabbakoṭṭhāse vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena vavatthapetvā vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhaāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlato vavatthapetabbā.

182. Thus, having taken up the sign and having determined all the parts by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, their repulsiveness should be determined in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, basis, and location.

Tatrāyaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsesu anupubbakathā. Kesā tāva pakativaṇṇena kāḷakā addāriṭṭhakavaṇṇā. Saṇṭhānato dīghavaṭṭalikā tulādaṇḍasaṇṭhānā. Disato uparimadisāya jātā. Okāsato ubhosu passesu kaṇṇacūḷikāhi, purato nalāṭantena, pacchato galavāṭakena paricchinnā. Sīsakaṭāhaveṭhanaṃ allacammaṃ kesānaṃ okāso. Paricchedato kesā sīsaveṭhanacamme vīhaggamattaṃ pavisitvā patiṭṭhitena heṭṭhā attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā, dve kesā ekato natthīti ayaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Kesā na lomā, lomā na kesāti evaṃ avasesaekatiṃsakoṭṭhāsehi amissīkatā kesā nāma pāṭiyekko ekakoṭṭhāsoti ayaṃ visabhāgaparicchedo. Idaṃ kesānaṃ vaṇṇādito vavatthāpanaṃ.

Herein is the sequential discourse concerning all the parts. First, the hairs of the head: by natural color, they are black, the color of moist, black ariṭṭhaka berries. By way of shape, they are long and round, having the shape of a balance-rod. By way of direction, they are grown in the upper direction. By way of location, they are delimited on both sides by the tufts of hair near the ears, in front by the edge of the forehead, and behind by the nape of the neck. The moist skin covering the skull is the location for the hairs of the head. By way of delimitation, the hairs of the head—established in the skin covering the head, having penetrated to the extent of the tip of a paddy grain—are delimited below by their own root-base, above by space, and laterally by one another. Thus, 'no two hairs are in one place'—this is the delimitation by common part. 'Hairs of the head are not body-hairs, and body-hairs are not hairs of the head'—thus, being unmixed with the remaining thirty-one parts, the so-called hairs of the head are a separate, single part. This is the delimitation by dissimilar part. This is the determination of the hairs of the head by way of color and so forth.

183. Idaṃ pana nesaṃ vaṇṇādivasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlato vavatthāpanaṃ. Kesā nāmete vaṇṇatopi paṭikkūlā. Saṇṭhānatopi gandhatopi āsayatopi okāsatopi paṭikkūlā.

183. Now, this is the fivefold determination of their repulsiveness by way of color and so forth. These so-called hairs of the head are repulsive by way of color, and also by way of shape, smell, basis, and location.

Manuññepi [M 1.0242] hi yāgupatte vā bhattapatte vā kesavaṇṇaṃ kiñci disvā kesamissakamidaṃ haratha nanti jigucchanti. Evaṃ kesā vaṇṇato paṭikkūlā. Rattiṃ bhuñjantāpi kesasaṇṭhānaṃ akkavākaṃ vā makacivākaṃ vā chupitvāpi tatheva jigucchanti. Evaṃ saṇṭhānato paṭikkūlā.

For even in a pleasing bowl of gruel or a bowl of rice, if they see something of hair-color, they are disgusted, saying, 'Take this away, it is mixed with hair!' Thus, hairs of the head are repulsive by way of color. Even while eating at night, if they touch something with the shape of a hair—such as a strand of akkavāka fiber or a strand of makacivāka fiber—they are disgusted in the same way. Thus, they are repulsive by way of shape.

Telamakkhanapupphadhūpādi saṅkhāravirahitānañca kesānaṃ gandho paramajeguccho hoti. Tato jegucchataro aggimhi pakkhittānaṃ. Kesā hi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikkūlāpi siyuṃ, gandhena pana paṭikkūlāyeva. Yathā hi daharassa kumārassa vaccaṃ vaṇṇato haliddivaṇṇaṃ, saṇṭhānatopi haliddipiṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍitañca uddhumātakakāḷasunakhasarīraṃ vaṇṇato tālapakkavaṇṇaṃ[V 1.0241]. Saṇṭhānato vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamudiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ. Dāṭhāpissa sumanamakuḷasadisāti ubhayampi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato siyā appaṭikkūlaṃ gandhena pana paṭikkūlameva. Evaṃ kesāpi siyuṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānato appaṭikkūlā gandhena pana paṭikkūlāyevāti.

And the smell of hairs devoid of preparations such as anointing with oil, flowers, incense, and so on, is extremely repulsive. More repulsive than that is the smell of those thrown into a fire. For hairs may not be repulsive by way of color and shape, but by way of smell they are indeed repulsive. Just as the excrement of a young child, by way of color, has the color of turmeric, and by way of shape, has the shape of a lump of turmeric; and the bloated corpse of a black dog discarded in a refuse pile, by way of color, has the color of a ripe palm fruit, and by way of shape, has the shape of a fashioned mudiṅga drum that has been rolled, and its fangs are like jasmine buds—thus both may not be repulsive by way of color and shape, but by way of smell they are indeed repulsive. Similarly, hairs too may not be repulsive by way of color and shape, but by way of smell they are indeed repulsive.

Yathā pana asuciṭṭhāne gāmanissandena jātāni sūpeyyapaṇṇāni nāgarikamanussānaṃ jegucchāni honti aparibhogāni, evaṃ kesāpi pubbalohitamuttakarīsapittasemhādinissandena jātattā jegucchāti idaṃ nesaṃ āsayato pāṭikkulyaṃ.

Furthermore, just as vegetables suitable for curry that have grown in an unclean place from the drainage of a village are repulsive and unfit for use by city-dwellers, so too, hairs are repulsive because they are born from the outflow of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so on. This is their repulsiveness by way of dependence.

Ime ca kesā nāma gūtharāsimhi uṭṭhitakaṇṇikaṃ viya ekatiṃsakoṭṭhāsarāsimhi jātā. Te susānasaṅkāraṭṭhānādīsu jātasākaṃ viya parikkhādīsu jātakamalakuvalayādipupphaṃ viya ca asuciṭṭhāne jātattā paramajegucchāti idaṃ nesaṃ okāsato pāṭikkulyaṃ.

And these things called hairs, like a mushroom that has sprung up on a heap of excrement, are born in the mass of the thirty-one parts. And like vegetables grown in charnel grounds, refuse heaps, and so on, and like flowers such as lotuses and water lilies grown in moats and so on, because they are born in an unclean place, they are extremely repulsive. This is their repulsiveness by way of location.

Yathā ca kesānaṃ, evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlatā veditabbā. Vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena pana sabbepi visuṃ visuṃ vavatthapetabbā.

Just as for the hairs of the head, so too for all the other parts, repulsiveness is to be determined in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, dependence, and location. Furthermore, all of them are to be determined separately by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.

184. Tattha lomā tāva pakativaṇṇato na kesā viya asambhinnakāḷakā, kāḷapiṅgalā pana honti. Saṇṭhānato onataggā tālamūlasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato ṭhapetvā kesānaṃ patiṭṭhitokāsañca hatthapādatalāni ca yebhuyyena avasesasarīraveṭhanacamme jātā. Paricchedato sarīraveṭhanacamme likhāmattaṃ pavisitvā [M 1.0243] patiṭṭhitena heṭṭhā attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā, dve lomā ekato natthi, ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

184. Herein, the body-hairs, by way of their natural color, are not unmixedly black like the hairs of the head, but are rather blackish-brown. By way of shape, they have bent tips and the shape of a palm root. By way of direction, they grow in two directions. By way of location, except for the place where the hairs of the head are established and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, they mostly grow on the skin that wraps the rest of the body. By way of delimitation, being established by penetrating the skin that wraps the body to the extent of a nit, they are delimited below by their own root-base, above by space, and laterally by one another; two body-hairs are not together. This is their delimitation by like parts. Their delimitation by unlike parts, however, is just like that of the hairs of the head.

185. Nakhāti vīsatiyā nakhapattānaṃ nāmaṃ. Te sabbepi vaṇṇato setā. Saṇṭhānato macchasakalikasaṇṭhānā. Disato pādanakhā heṭṭhimadisāya, hatthanakhā uparimadisāyāti dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato aṅgulīnaṃ aggapiṭṭhesu patiṭṭhitā. Paricchedato dvīsu disāsu aṅgulikoṭimaṃsehi, anto aṅgulipiṭṭhimaṃsena, bahi ceva agge ca ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena [V 1.0242] paricchinnā, dve nakhā ekato natthi, ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

185. 'Nails' is the name for the twenty nail-plates. All of them are white by way of color. By way of shape, they have the shape of fish scales. By way of direction, the toenails grow in the lower direction and the fingernails in the upper direction; thus they grow in two directions. By way of location, they are established on the top surfaces of the tips of the digits. By way of delimitation, they are delimited below and above by the flesh at the tips of the digits, internally by the flesh on the top surface of the digits, externally and at the tip by space, and laterally by one another; two nails are not together. This is their delimitation by like parts. Their delimitation by unlike parts, however, is just like that of the hairs of the head.

186. Dantāti paripuṇṇadantassa dvattiṃsa dantaṭṭhikāni. Tepi vaṇṇato setā. Saṇṭhānato anekasaṇṭhānā. Tesaṃ hi heṭṭhimāya tāva dantapāḷiyā majjhe cattāro dantā mattikāpiṇḍe paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitaalābubījasaṇṭhānā. Tesaṃ ubhosu passesu ekeko ekamūlako ekakoṭiko mallikamakuḷasaṇṭhāno. Tato ekeko dvimūlako dvikoṭiko yānakaupatthambhinisaṇṭhāno. Tato dve dve timūlā tikoṭikā. Tato dve dve catumūlā catukoṭikāti. Uparimapāḷiyāpi eseva nayo. Disato uparimadisāya jātā. Okāsato dvīsu hanukaṭṭhikesu patiṭṭhitā. Paricchedato heṭṭhā hanukaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitena attano mūlatalena, upari ākāsena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā, dve dantā ekato natthi, ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

186. "Teeth" refers to the thirty-two tooth-bones of one with a full set of teeth. They too are white by way of color. By way of shape, they are of various shapes. Among them, in the lower row of teeth, the four middle teeth are like gourd seeds placed in a row in a lump of clay. On both sides of these, each single-rooted, single-pointed tooth is like a jasmine bud. Next to them, each tooth is double-rooted, double-pointed, and like a chariot's prop. Then two each are triple-rooted and triple-pointed. Then two each are quadruple-rooted and quadruple-pointed. The same method applies to the upper row too. By way of direction, they arise in the upper direction. By way of location, they are fixed in the two jaw-bones. By way of delimitation, they are bounded below by their own root-base fixed in the jaw-bone, above by space, and laterally by each other. No two teeth are together—this is their delimitation by like parts. Their delimitation by unlike parts is just like that of the hairs of the head.

187. Tacoti sakalasarīraṃ veṭhetvā ṭhitacammaṃ. Tassa upari kāḷasāmapītādivaṇṇā chavi nāma yā sakalasarīratopi saṅkaḍḍhiyamānā badaraṭṭhimattā hoti. Taco pana vaṇṇato setoyeva. So cassa setabhāvo aggijālābhighātapaharaṇappahārādīhi viddhaṃsitāya chaviyā pākaṭo hoti. Saṇṭhānato sarīrasaṇṭhānova hoti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo.

187. "Skin" is the thick skin that envelops the entire body. Above that is the epidermis, called chavi, which has colors such as black, dark, and yellow, and which, when peeled off from the entire body and rolled up, is about the size of a jujube stone. But the skin itself is only white by way of color. And its whiteness becomes apparent when the epidermis is destroyed by the impact of fire-flames, blows, and other assaults. By way of shape, it is just the shape of the body. This is the summary here.

Vitthārato [M 1.0244] pana pādaṅgulittaco kosakārakakosasaṇṭhāno. Piṭṭhipādattaco puṭabandhaupāhanasaṇṭhāno. Jaṅghattaco bhattapuṭakatālapaṇṇasaṇṭhāno. Ūruttaco taṇḍulabharitadīghatthavikasaṇṭhāno. Ānisadattaco udakapūritapaṭaparissāvanasaṇṭhāno. Piṭṭhittaco phalakonaddhacammasaṇṭhāno. Kucchittaco vīṇādoṇikonaddhacammasaṇṭhāno. Urattaco yebhuyyena caturassasaṇṭhāno. Ubhayabāhuttaco tūṇironaddhacammasaṇṭhāno. Piṭṭhihatthattaco khurakosasaṇṭhāno, phaṇakatthavikasaṇṭhāno vā. Hatthaṅgulittaco kuñcikākosakasaṇṭhāno. Gīvattaco galakañcukasaṇṭhāno. Mukhattaco chiddāvachiddo kīṭakulāvakasaṇṭhāno. Sīsattaco pattatthavikasaṇṭhānoti.

But in detail: The skin of the toes is shaped like a silk-worm's cocoon. The skin of the top of the feet is shaped like a shoe with an instep-cover. The skin of the shins is shaped like a palm-leaf rice-packet. The skin of the thighs is shaped like a long bag filled with rice. The skin of the buttocks is shaped like a cloth water-strainer filled with water. The skin of the back is shaped like a hide stretched on a board. The skin of the belly is shaped like a hide stretched on the body of a lute. The skin of the chest is mostly square in shape. The skin of both arms is shaped like a hide stretched over a quiver. The skin of the back of the hands is shaped like a razor case or a case for a small knife. The skin of the fingers is shaped like a key-case. The skin of the neck is shaped like a neck-covering tunic. The skin of the face, being full of holes, is shaped like an insect's nest. The skin of the head is shaped like a bowl-bag.

Tacapariggaṇhakena ca yogāvacarena uttaroṭṭhato paṭṭhāya uparimukhaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesetvā paṭhamaṃ tāva [V 1.0243] mukhaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitacammaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tato nalāṭaṭṭhicammaṃ. Tato thavikāya pakkhittapattassa ca thavikāya ca antarena hatthamiva sīsaṭṭhikassa ca sīsacammassa ca antarena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā aṭṭhikena saddhiṃ cammassa ekābaddhabhāvaṃ viyojentena sīsacammaṃ vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tato khandhacammaṃ. Tato anulomena paṭilomena ca dakkhiṇahatthacammaṃ. Atha teneva nayena vāmahatthacammaṃ. Tato piṭṭhicammaṃ taṃ vavatthapetvā anulomena paṭilomena ca dakkhiṇapādacammaṃ. Atha teneva nayena vāmapādacammaṃ. Tato anukkameneva vatthiudarahadayagīvacammāni vavatthapetabbāni. Atha gīvacammānantaraṃ heṭṭhimahanucammaṃ vavatthapetvā adharoṭṭhapariyosānaṃ pāpetvā niṭṭhapetabbaṃ. Evaṃ oḷārikoḷārikaṃ pariggaṇhantassa sukhumampi pākaṭaṃ hoti. Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhito. Paricchedato heṭṭhā patiṭṭhitatalena, upari ākāsena paricchinno, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

And the yogi who apprehends the skin, beginning from the upper lip, should send forth knowledge towards the upper part of the face and, having first enclosed the face, should determine the skin situated there. Then, the skin of the forehead. Then, like inserting a hand between a bowl placed in a bag and the bag itself, having sent forth knowledge between the skull bone and the scalp-skin, and separating the state of the skin's single attachment with the bone, the scalp-skin should be determined. Then, the skin of the shoulders. Then, forwards and backwards, the skin of the right hand. Then, in the same way, the skin of the left hand. Then, the skin of the back; having determined that, forwards and backwards, the skin of the right foot. Then, in the same way, the skin of the left foot. Then, successively, the skins of the bladder, belly, chest, and neck should be determined. Then, immediately after the skin of the neck, having determined the skin of the lower jaw, and having brought it to the end of the lower lip, it should be concluded. Thus, for one who apprehends the grosser and grosser parts, even the subtle becomes manifest. By way of direction, it is produced in two directions. By way of location, it stands enclosing the entire body. By way of delimitation, it is delimited below by the surface on which it is established, and above by space; this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

188. Maṃsanti nava maṃsapesisatāni. Taṃ sabbampi vaṇṇato rattaṃ kiṃsukapupphasadisaṃ. Saṇṭhānato jaṅghapiṇḍikamaṃsaṃ tālapaṇṇapuṭabhattasaṇṭhānaṃ. Ūrumaṃsaṃ nisadapotasaṇṭhānaṃ. Ānisadamaṃsaṃ uddhanakoṭisaṇṭhānaṃ. Piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ tālaguḷapaṭalasaṇṭhānaṃ. Phāsukadvayamaṃsaṃ koṭṭhalikāya kucchiyaṃ tanumattikālepasaṇṭhānaṃ. Thanamaṃsaṃ vaṭṭetvā avakkhittamattikāpiṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Bāhudvayamaṃsaṃ [M 1.0245] dviguṇaṃ katvā ṭhapitaniccammamahāmūsikasaṇṭhānaṃ. Evaṃ oḷārikoḷārikaṃ pariggaṇhantassa sukhumampi pākaṭaṃ hoti. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato vīsādhikāni tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni anulimpitvā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato heṭṭhā aṭṭhisaṅghāte patiṭṭhitatalena, upari tacena, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

188. Flesh consists of nine hundred pieces of flesh. All of it is red in color, like a kiṃsuka flower. By way of shape: the flesh of the calf has the shape of a packet of rice wrapped in a palm leaf. The thigh flesh has the shape of a young grinding stone. The buttock flesh has the shape of the corner of an oven. The back flesh has the shape of a layer of ripe palmyra fruit pulp. The flesh on the two sides of the ribs has the shape of a thin plaster of fine clay on the inside of a granary. The breast flesh has the shape of a lump of clay that has been rolled and thrown down upside down. The flesh of the two arms has the shape of a large, skinless mouse placed doubled up. Thus, for one who apprehends the grosser and grosser parts, even the subtle becomes manifest. By way of direction, it is produced in two directions. By way of location, it stands smeared over the three hundred and twenty bones. By way of delimitation: below, it is delimited by the surface established on the collection of bones; above, by the skin; and laterally, by each other. This is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

189. Nhārūti nava nhārusatāni. Vaṇṇato sabbepi nhārū setā. Saṇṭhānato nānāsaṇṭhānā. Etesu hi gīvāya uparimabhāgato paṭṭhāya pañca mahānhārū sarīraṃ vinandhamānā purimapassena otiṇṇā. Pañca pacchimapassena. Pañca dakkhiṇapassena. Pañca vāmapassena. Dakkhiṇahatthaṃ vinandhamānāpi hatthassa purimapassena pañca. Pacchimapassena pañca. Tathā vāmahatthaṃ vinandhamānā. Dakkhiṇapādaṃ vinandhamānāpi pādassa purimapassena pañca. Pacchimapassena pañca. Tathā vāmapādaṃ vinandhamānāpīti evaṃ sarīradhārakā nāma saṭṭhimahānhārū kāyaṃ vinandhamānā otiṇṇā[V 1.0244]. Ye kaṇḍarātipi vuccanti. Te sabbepi kandalamakuḷasaṇṭhānā. Aññe pana taṃ taṃ padesaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitā. Tato sukhumatarā suttarajjukasaṇṭhānā. Aññe tato sukhumatarā pūtilatāsaṇṭhānā, aññe tato sukhumatarā mahāvīṇātantisaṇṭhānā. Aññe thūlasuttakasaṇṭhānā. Hatthapādapiṭṭhīsu nhārū sakuṇapādasaṇṭhānā. Sīse nhārū dārakānaṃ sīsajālakasaṇṭhānā. Piṭṭhiyaṃ nhārū ātape pasāritaallajālasaṇṭhānā. Avasesā taṃtaṃaṅgapaccaṅgānugatā nhārū sarīre paṭimukkajālakañcukasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato sakalasarīre aṭṭhīni ābandhitvā ṭhitā. Paricchedato heṭṭhā tiṇṇaṃ aṭṭhisatānaṃ upari patiṭṭhitatalehi, upari maṃsacammāni āhacca ṭhitappadesehi, tiriyaṃ aññamaññena paricchinnā, ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

189. Tendons consist of nine hundred tendons. By way of color, all the tendons are white. By way of shape, they are of various shapes. Indeed, among these, starting from the upper part of the neck, five major tendons, binding the body, descend along the front side. Five descend along the back side. Five along the right side. Five along the left side. Binding the right hand, five descend along its front side and five along its back side. Likewise for those binding the left hand. Binding the right foot, five descend along its front side and five along its back side. Likewise for those binding the left foot. Thus, sixty major tendons, called 'the body's supporters', descend, binding the body. These are also called sinews. All of them have the shape of a plantain bud. The other tendons, however, are situated having pervaded their respective areas. Finer than these have the shape of a thread-rope. Others, finer than these, have the shape of a pūtilatā creeper. Others, finer still, have the shape of the string of a great lute. Others have the shape of a coarse thread. On the backs of the hands and feet, the tendons have the shape of a bird's foot. In the head, the tendons have the shape of a children's hairnet. In the back, the tendons have the shape of a wet fishing net spread out in the sun. The remaining tendons, which follow their respective major and minor limbs, have the shape of a worn mail coat with meshes. By way of direction, they are produced in two directions. By way of location, they are situated throughout the entire body, binding the bones. By way of delimitation: below, they are delimited by the surfaces established upon the three hundred bones; above, by the places situated touching the flesh and skin; and sideways, by one another. This is their homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

190. Aṭṭhīti ṭhapetvā dvattiṃsa dantaṭṭhīni avasesāni catusaṭṭhi hatthaṭṭhīni, catusaṭṭhi pādaṭṭhīni, catusaṭṭhi maṃsanissitāni muduaṭṭhīni, dve paṇhikaṭṭhīni, ekekasmiṃ pāde dve dve gopphakaṭṭhīni, dve jaṅghaṭṭhīni, ekaṃ jaṇṇukaṭṭhi, ekaṃ ūruṭṭhi, dve kaṭiṭṭhīni, aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīni, catuvīsati phāsukaṭṭhīni, cuddasa uraṭṭhīni[M 1.0246], ekaṃ hadayaṭṭhi, dve akkhakaṭṭhīni, dve koṭṭaṭṭhīni, dve bāhuṭṭhīni, dve dve aggabāhuṭṭhīni, satta gīvaṭṭhīni, dve hanukaṭṭhīni, ekaṃ nāsikaṭṭhi, dve akkhiṭṭhīni, dve kaṇṇaṭṭhīni, ekaṃ nalāṭaṭṭhi. Ekaṃ muddhaṭṭhi, nava sīsakapālaṭṭhīnīti evaṃ timattāni aṭṭhisatāni, tāni sabbānipi vaṇṇato setāni. Saṇṭhānato nānāsaṇṭhānāni.

190. Bones: setting aside the thirty-two tooth-bones, the remainder are sixty-four hand-bones, sixty-four foot-bones, sixty-four soft bones dependent on flesh, two heel-bones, two ankle-bones in each foot, two shin-bones, one knee-bone, one thigh-bone, two hip-bones, eighteen spinal vertebrae, twenty-four rib-bones, fourteen chest-bones, one heart-bone, two collar-bones, two shoulder-blades, two upper-arm-bones, two forearm-bones in each arm, seven neck-bones, two jaw-bones, one nose-bone, two eye-socket-bones, two ear-bones, one forehead-bone, one crown-bone, and nine cranial-bones. Thus, there are three hundred bones in measure. All of them are white by color. By way of shape, they are of various shapes.

Tattha hi aggapādaṅguliaṭṭhīni katakabījasaṇṭhānāni. Tadanantarāni majjhapabbaṭṭhīni panasaṭṭhisaṇṭhānāni. Mūlapabbaṭṭhīni paṇavasaṇṭhānāni. Piṭṭhipādaṭṭhīni koṭṭitakandalakandarāsisaṇṭhānāni. Paṇhikaṭṭhi ekaṭṭhitālaphalabījasaṇṭhānaṃ. Gopphakaṭṭhīni baddhakīḷāgoḷakasaṇṭhānāni. Jaṅghaṭṭhīnaṃ gopphakaṭṭhīsu patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ apanītatacasindikaḷīrasaṇṭhānaṃ. Khuddakajaṅghaṭṭhikaṃ dhanukadaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Mahantaṃ milātasappapiṭṭhisaṇṭhānaṃ. Jaṇṇukaṭṭhi ekato parikkhīṇapheṇakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Tattha jaṅghaṭṭhikassa patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ atikhiṇaggagosiṅgasaṇṭhānaṃ. Ūruṭṭhi duttacchitavāsiparasudaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Tassa kaṭiṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ kīḷāgoḷakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Tena kaṭiṭṭhino patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ aggacchinnamahāpunnāgaphalasaṇṭhānaṃ.

Therein, the bones of the tips of the toe joints have the shape of kataka seeds. Next to them, the middle-joint-bones have the shape of jackfruit seeds. The root-joint-bones have the shape of a paṇava drum. The bones of the top of the foot have the shape of a mass of pounded sinews of the kandala plant. The heel-bone has the shape of the seed of a single-seeded palmyra fruit. The ankle-bones have the shape of tied playing-balls. The place where the shin-bones are established on the ankle-bones has the shape of a date palm shoot with its sheath removed. The small shin-bone has the shape of a bow-stave. The large one has the shape of the back of a withered snake. The knee-bone has the shape of a lump of froth worn away on one side. Therein, the place where the shin-bone is established has the shape of a cow's horn with a blunt tip. The thigh-bone has the shape of a badly planed handle of an adze or axe. The place where it is established in the hip-bone has the shape of a playing-top. The place in the hip-bone established by it has the shape of a large punnāga fruit cut at its tip.
