Kaṭiṭṭhīni [V 1.0245] dvepi ekābaddhāni hutvā kumbhakārikauddhanasaṇṭhānāni. Pāṭiyekkaṃ kammārakūṭayottakasaṇṭhānāni. Koṭiyaṃ ṭhitaṃ ānisadaṭṭhi adhomukhaṃ katvā gahitasappaphaṇasaṇṭhānaṃ, sattaṭṭhaṭṭhānesu chiddāvachiddaṃ. Piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīni abbhantarato uparūpari ṭhapitasīsapaṭṭaveṭhakasaṇṭhānāni. Bāhirato vaṭṭanāvaḷisaṇṭhānāni. Tesaṃ antarantarā kakacadantasadisā dve tayo kaṇṭakā honti. Catuvīsatiyā phāsukaṭṭhīsu aparipuṇṇāni aparipuṇṇaasisaṇṭhānāni. Paripuṇṇāni paripuṇṇaasisaṇṭhānāni. Sabbānipi odātakukkuṭassa pasāritapakkhasaṇṭhānāni. Cuddasa uraṭṭhīni jiṇṇasandamānikapañjarasaṇṭhānāni. Hadayaṭṭhi dabbiphaṇasaṇṭhānaṃ.

The two hip bones, when joined together, resemble a potter’s oven. Individually, they resemble the strap of a blacksmith's anvil. The sacrum bone, situated at the end and held with its face downwards, resembles a grasped cobra’s hood, perforated in seven or eight places. The spinal bones, from the inside, resemble coiled lead plates placed one upon another. From the outside, they resemble a row of spools of thread. Between them are two or three thorn-like bones resembling saw teeth. Among the twenty-four ribs, the incomplete ones resemble incomplete swords, and the complete ones resemble complete swords. All of them resemble the outstretched wings of a white rooster. The fourteen breastbones resemble a dilapidated carrying-frame. The sternum has the shape of the bowl of a ladle.

Akkhakaṭṭhīni khuddakalohavāsidaṇḍasaṇṭhānāni. Koṭṭaṭṭhīni ekato parikkhīṇasīhaḷakuddālasaṇṭhānāni. Bāhuṭṭhīni ādāsadaṇḍakasaṇṭhānāni. Aggabāhuṭṭhīni yamakatālakandasaṇṭhānāni. Maṇibandhaṭṭhīni ekato alliyāpetvā ṭhapitasīsakapaṭṭaveṭhakasaṇṭhānāni. Piṭṭhihatthaṭṭhīni koṭṭitakandalakandarāsisaṇṭhānāni[M 1.0247]. Hatthaṅgulīsu mūlapabbaṭṭhīni paṇavasaṇṭhānāni. Majjhapabbaṭṭhīni aparipuṇṇapanasaṭṭhisaṇṭhānāni. Aggapabbaṭṭhīni katakabījasaṇṭhānāni.

The collarbones resemble the handle of a small iron adze. The shoulder blades resemble a Sinhala hoe worn away on one side. The upper arm bones resemble mirror handles. The forearm bones resemble twin palmyra bulbs. The wrist bones, stuck together, resemble placed and coiled lead plates. The bones of the back of the hand resemble a mass of sinews from a pounded kandala plant. In the fingers, the bones of the basal joints are shaped like small drums, the bones of the middle joints like incomplete jackfruit seeds, and the bones of the tip joints like kataka seeds.

Satta gīvaṭṭhīni daṇḍena vijjhitvā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitavaṃsakaḷīracakkalakasaṇṭhānāni. Heṭṭhimahanukaṭṭhi kammārānaṃ ayokūṭayottakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Uparimaṃ avalekhanasatthakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Akkhikūpanāsakūpaṭṭhīni apanītamiñjataruṇatālaṭṭhisaṇṭhānāni. Nalāṭaṭṭhi adhomukhaṭṭhapitasaṅkhathālakakapālasaṇṭhānaṃ. Kaṇṇacūḷikaṭṭhīni nhāpitakhurakosasaṇṭhānāni. Nalāṭakaṇṇacūḷikānaṃ upari paṭṭabandhanokāse aṭṭhisaṅkuṭitaghaṭapuṇṇapaṭalakhaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Muddhaṭṭhi mukhacchinnavaṅkanāḷikerasaṇṭhānaṃ. Sīsaṭṭhīni sibbetvā ṭhapitajajjaralābukaṭāhasaṇṭhānāni.

The seven neck bones have the shape of bamboo shoot slices pierced by a stick and placed in order. The lower jawbone has the shape of a blacksmith's iron tongs. The upper jawbone has the shape of a small knife for peeling sugarcane. The bones of the eye sockets and nasal cavities have the shape of a young palm seed from which the kernel has been removed. The forehead bone has the shape of a fragment of a conch-shell bowl placed face down. The temporal bones have the shape of a barber's razor case. Above the forehead and temporal bones, at the place for tying a headband, the bone has the shape of a piece of a curled layer of ghee overflowing from a full pot. The bone at the crown of the head has the shape of a crooked coconut shell ladle with its opening cut. The head bones, sewn together, have the shape of a placed, decaying gourd bowl.

Disato dvīsu disāsu jātāni. Okāsato avisesena sakalasarīre ṭhitāni. Visesena panettha sīsaṭṭhīni givaṭṭhīsu patiṭṭhitāni. Gīvaṭṭhīni piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīsu. Piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṭṭhīni kaṭiṭṭhīsu. Kaṭiṭṭhīni ūruṭṭhīsu. Ūruṭṭhīni jaṇṇukaṭṭhīsu. Jaṇṇukaṭṭhīni jaṅghaṭṭhīsu. Jaṅghaṭṭhīni gopphakaṭṭhīsu. Gopphakaṭṭhīni piṭṭhipādaṭṭhīsu patiṭṭhitāni. Paricchedato anto aṭṭhimiñjena, uparito maṃsena, agge mūle ca aññamaññena paricchinnāni, ayaṃ nesaṃ sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

By way of direction, they arise in two directions. By way of location, they are situated generally throughout the entire body. Specifically here, the head bones are established on the neck bones. The neck bones are established on the spinal vertebrae. The spinal vertebrae are established on the hip bones. The hip bones are established on the thigh bones. The thigh bones are established on the knee bones. The knee bones are established on the shin bones. The shin bones are established on the ankle bones. The ankle bones are established on the bones of the top of the foot. By way of delimitation, they are delimited internally by marrow, externally by flesh, and at the ends and roots by one another—this is their homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

191. Aṭṭhimiñjanti [V 1.0246] tesaṃ tesaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantaragataṃ miñjaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ. Saṇṭhānato mahantamahantānaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantaragataṃ veḷunāḷiyaṃ pakkhittaseditamahāvettaggasaṇṭhānaṃ. Khuddānukhuddakānaṃ abbhantaragataṃ veḷuyaṭṭhipabbesu pakkhittaseditatanuvettaggasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantare patiṭṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantaratalehi paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

191. Bone marrow is the marrow found inside those various bones. By way of color, it is white. By way of shape, the marrow inside very large bones has the shape of a large rattan shoot that has been steamed and placed in a bamboo tube. The marrow inside very small bones has the shape of a thin rattan shoot tip that has been steamed and placed in the nodes of a bamboo stick. By way of direction, it arises in two directions. By way of location, it is established inside the bones. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the inner surfaces of the bones; this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

192. Vakkanti ekabandhanā dve maṃsapiṇḍikā. Taṃ vaṇṇato mandarattaṃ pāḷibhaddakaṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato dārakānaṃ yamakakīḷāgoḷakasaṇṭhānaṃ, ekavaṇṭapaṭibaddhaambaphaladvayasaṇṭhānaṃ vā. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato galavāṭakā nikkhantena ekamūlena thokaṃ gantvā dvidhā [M 1.0248] bhinnena thūlanhārunā vinibaddhaṃ hutvā hadayamaṃsaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato vakkaṃ vakkabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

192. The kidneys are two fleshy masses bound together by a single band. In color, they are faintly red, resembling the color of a coral tree seed. In shape, they resemble a pair of play-balls for children or two mango fruits connected by a single stalk. In terms of direction, they arise from the upper direction. In terms of location, they emerge from the throat-passage through a single root, extend a short distance, then split into two and are bound by a thick sinew, situated surrounding the heart-flesh. In terms of delimitation, the kidney is delimited by its own kidney portion—this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

193. Hadayanti hadayamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato rattapadumapattapiṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato bāhirapattāni apanetvā adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitapadumamakuḷasaṇṭhānaṃ. Bahi maṭṭhaṃ, anto kosātakīphalassa abbhantarasadisaṃ. Paññavantānaṃ thokaṃ vikasitaṃ, mandapaññānaṃ makuḷitameva. Anto cassa punnāgaṭṭhipatiṭṭhānamatto āvāṭako hoti, yattha addhapasatamattaṃ lohitaṃ saṇṭhāti, yaṃ nissāya manodhātu ca manoviññāṇadhātu ca vattanti. Taṃ panetaṃ rāgacaritassa rattaṃ hoti, dosacaritassa kāḷakaṃ, mohacaritassa maṃsadhovanaudakasadisaṃ, vitakkacaritassa kulatthayūsavaṇṇaṃ, saddhācaritassa kaṇikārapupphavaṇṇaṃ, paññācaritassa acchaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ paṇḍaraṃ parisuddhaṃ niddhotajātimaṇi viya jutimantaṃ khāyati. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato sarīrabbhantare dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ majjhe patiṭṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato hadayaṃ hadayabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

193. The heart is the heart-flesh. By color, it resembles the back of a red lotus petal. By shape, it resembles a lotus bud placed upside down after removing the outer petals. The exterior is smooth, while the interior resembles the inside of a smooth gourd. For the wise, it is slightly open; for the dull-witted, it remains closed like a bud. Inside, there is a cavity the size of the space occupied by a punnāga seed, where about half a handful of blood resides, upon which the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element depend. Furthermore, this blood is red for one of lustful temperament; dark for one of hateful temperament; like water used to wash meat for one of deluded temperament; like the color of horse-gram soup for one of speculative temperament; like the color of a kaṇikāra flower for one of faithful temperament. For one of wise temperament, it appears clear, very clear, untroubled, white, pure, and radiant like a well-polished, high-quality gem. By direction, it arises from the upper direction. By location, it is established inside the body, between the two breasts. By delimitation, the heart is delimited by its own heart-flesh portion—this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

194. Yakananti yamakamaṃsapaṭalaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato rattaṃ paṇḍukadhātukaṃ nātirattakumudassa pattapiṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato mūle ekaṃ agge yamakaṃ koviḷārapattasaṇṭhānaṃ. Tañca dandhānaṃ ekameva hoti mahantaṃ, paññavantānaṃ dve vā tīṇi vā khuddakāni. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ, okāsato dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ abbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato yakanaṃ [V 1.0247] yakanabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

194. The liver is a double layer of flesh. By color, it is red and of a pale nature; it is not overly red, having the color of the back of a white water lily petal. By shape, at its base it is single and at its tip double, having the shape of a koviḷāra leaf. For the dull-witted, it is single and large, whereas for the wise, there are two or three that are small. By direction, it has arisen in the upper direction. By location, it is situated inside, between the two breasts, resting on the right side. By delimitation, the liver is delimited by its own liver portion—this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

195. Kilomakanti paṭicchannāpaṭicchannabhedato duvidhaṃ pariyonahanamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ duvidhampi vaṇṇato setaṃ dukūlapilotikavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato attano okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato paṭicchannakilomakaṃ uparimāya disāya. Itaraṃ dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato paṭicchannakilomakaṃ [M 1.0249] hadayañca vakkañca paṭicchādetvā, appaṭicchannakilomakaṃ sakalasarīre cammassa heṭṭhato maṃsaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato heṭṭhā maṃsena, upari cammena, tiriyaṃ kilomakabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

195. The fascia is the enveloping flesh, of two kinds by the division into concealed and unconcealed. Both kinds are white in color, like a worn, fine cloth. By shape, it conforms to the shape of its location. By direction, the concealed fascia has arisen from the upper direction; the other has arisen from two directions. By location, the concealed fascia is situated covering the heart and the kidneys, while the unconcealed fascia is situated enveloping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body. By delimitation, it is delimited below by flesh, above by skin, and transversely by its own fascial portion—this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

196. Pihakanti udarajivhāmaṃsaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato nīlaṃ nigguṇḍipupphavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato sattaṅgulappamāṇaṃ abandhanaṃ kāḷavacchakajivhāsaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato hadayassa vāmapasse udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ, yasmiṃ paharaṇappahārena bahinikkhante sattānaṃ jīvitakkhayo hoti. Paricchedato pihakabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

196. The spleen is the flesh of the stomach-tongue. By color, it is blue, having the color of the nigguṇḍi flower. By shape, it is seven finger-breadths in measure, unattached, and has the shape of a black calf's tongue. By direction, it has arisen from the upper direction. By location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, resting on the upper side of the stomach lining; when this is forced out by a blow, the life of beings is destroyed. By delimitation, it is delimited by its own splenic portion—this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

197. Papphāsanti dvattiṃsamaṃsakhaṇḍappabhedaṃ papphāsamaṃsaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato rattaṃ nātipakkaudumbaraphalavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato visamacchinnabahalapūvakhaṇḍasaṇṭhānaṃ. Abbhantare asitapītānaṃ abhāve uggatena kammajatejusmānā abbhāhatattā saṃkhāditapalālapiṇḍamiva nirasaṃ nirojaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato sarīrabbhantare dvinnaṃ thanānaṃ antare hadayañca yakanañca upari chādetvā olambantaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato papphāsabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

197. The lungs are the flesh of the lungs, divided into thirty-two sections. By color, they are red, like a not-too-ripe fig. By shape, they have the shape of a thick piece of cake unevenly cut. Inside, due to the absence of what has been eaten and drunk, and being afflicted by the arisen kamma-born heat, they are without sap and without nutritive essence, like a lump of well-chewed straw. By direction, they arise from the upper direction. By location, they are situated inside the body between the two breasts, hanging down and covering the heart and the liver from above. By delimitation, they are delimited by the portion of the lungs themselves; this is their homogeneous delimitation. Their heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

198. Antanti purisassa dvattiṃsahatthā itthiyā aṭṭhavīsatihatthā ekavīsatiyā ṭhānesu obhaggā antavaṭṭi. Tadetaṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ sakkharasudhāvaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato lohitadoṇiyaṃ ābhujitvā ṭhapitasīsacchinnasappasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato upari galavāṭake heṭṭhā ca karīsamagge vinibandhattā galavāṭakakarīsamaggapariyante sarīrabbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato [V 1.0248] antabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

198. The intestines are the intestinal coil, which for a man is thirty-two cubits and for a woman twenty-eight cubits, and is bent in twenty-one places. By color, it is white, the color of plaster made with gravel. By shape, it has the shape of a snake with its head cut off, placed coiled in a trough of blood. By direction, it arises from two directions. By location, being bound to the throat-pipe above and to the feces-passage below, it is situated inside the body between the throat-pipe and the feces-passage as its two ends. By delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of the intestines themselves; this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

199. Antaguṇanti [M 1.0250] antabhogaṭṭhānesu bandhanaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ dakasītalikamūlavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato dakasītalikamūlasaṇṭhānameva. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato kuddālapharasukammādīni karontānaṃ yantākaḍḍhanakāle yantasuttakamiva yantaphalakāni antabhoge ekato agaḷante ābandhitvā pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakassa antarā saṃsibbitvā ṭhitarajjukā viya ekavīsatiyā antabhogānaṃ antarā ṭhitaṃ. Paricchedato antaguṇabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

199. The mesentery is the binding in the places of the intestinal coils. By color, it is white, the color of the root of the water-moss plant. By shape, it has the very shape of the root of the water-moss plant. By direction, it arises from two directions. By location, it is situated between the twenty-one intestinal coils, binding them together so that the intestinal coils of those doing work with hoes, axes, and so on, do not slip, just as a machine-rope binds the machine-boards when a machine is pulled, and like a small rope sewn and fixed within the circle of a foot-wiping rope. By delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of the mesentery itself; this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

200. Udariyanti udare bhavaṃ asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato ajjhohaṭāhāravaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato parissāvane sithilabaddhataṇḍulasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato udare ṭhitaṃ.

200. Undigested food is what is in the stomach: the food that has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. By color, it has the color of ingested food. By shape, it has the shape of loosely tied rice in a cloth filter. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, it is situated in the stomach.

Udaraṃ nāma ubhato nippīḷiyamānassa allasāṭakassa majjhe sañjātaphoṭakasadisaṃ antapaṭalaṃ, bahi maṭṭhaṃ, anto maṃsakasambupaliveṭhanakiliṭṭhapāvārakapupphakasadisaṃ, kuthitapanasatacassa abbhantarasadisantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati, yattha takkoṭakā gaṇḍuppādakā tālahīrakā sūcimukhakā paṭatantasuttakā iccevamādidvattiṃsakulappabhedā kimayo ākulabyākulā saṇḍasaṇḍacārino hutvā nivasanti, ye pānabhojanādimhi avijjamāne ullaṅghitvā viravantā hadayamaṃsaṃ abhihananti, pānabhojanādiajjhoharaṇavelāyañca uddhaṃmukhā hutvā paṭhamajjhohaṭe dve tayo ālope turitaturitā viluppanti, yaṃ tesaṃ kimīnaṃ sūtigharaṃ vaccakuṭi gilānasālā susānañca hoti. Yattha seyyathāpi nāma caṇḍālagāmadvāre candanikāya nidāghasamaye thūlaphusitake deve vassante udakena vuyhamānaṃ muttakarīsacammaaṭṭhinhārukhaṇḍakheḷasiṅghāṇikālohitappabhutinānākuṇapajātaṃ nipatitvā kaddamodakāluḷitaṃ dvīhatīhaccayena sañjātakimikulaṃ sūriyātapasantāpavegakuthitaṃ upari pheṇapupphuḷake muñcantaṃ abhinīlavaṇṇaṃ paramaduggandhajegucchaṃ neva upagantuṃ, na daṭṭhuṃ araharūpataṃ āpajjitvā tiṭṭhati, pageva [M 1.0251] ghāyituṃ vā sāyituṃ vā, evameva nānappakāraṃ pānabhojanādidantamusalasañcuṇṇitaṃ jivhāhatthaparivattitakheḷalālāpalibuddhaṃ [V 1.0249] taṅkhaṇavigatavaṇṇagandharasādisampadaṃ tantavāyakhalisuvānavamathusadisaṃ nipatitvā pittasemhavātapaliveṭhitaṃ hutvā udaraggisantāpavegakuthitaṃ kimikulākulaṃ uparūpari pheṇapupphuḷakāni muñcantaṃ paramakasambuduggandhajegucchabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā tiṭṭhati. Yaṃ sutvāpi pānabhojanādīsu amanuññatā saṇṭhāti, pageva paññācakkhunā avaloketvā. Yattha ca patitaṃ pānabhojanādi pañcadhā vivekaṃ gacchati, ekaṃ bhāgaṃ pāṇakā khādanti, ekaṃ bhāgaṃ udaraggi jhāpeti, eko bhāgo muttaṃ hoti, eko bhāgo karīsaṃ, eko bhāgo rasabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā soṇitamaṃsādīni upabrūhayati.

The stomach, it is said, is the inner lining, like a blister formed in the middle of a wet cloth being squeezed from both sides. On the outside, it is smooth; on the inside, it is like the fringe of a soiled rug wrapped around putrid meat and carrion. It is also fitting to say it is like the inside of a rotten jackfruit rind. Therein dwell thirty-two families of worms, such as roundworms, boil-producing worms, tapeworms, pinworms, and threadworms, moving about tangled and intertwined in swarms. When there is no food or drink, they leap up, crying out, and strike the flesh of the heart. And at the time of swallowing food and drink, facing upwards, they hastily plunder the first two or three morsels swallowed. For these worms, that stomach is a delivery house, a latrine, a sick-ward, and a charnel ground. Just as, at the gate of an outcaste village, in a cesspool during the hot season when rain with large drops is falling, various kinds of carrion—such as urine, feces, skin, bones, pieces of sinew, spittle, snot, and blood—are carried along by the water, fall in, and are stirred up with mud and water. After two or three days, it has worms that have arisen, is seething with the force of the heat from the sun's rays, releasing foam and bubbles on its surface, is of a deep blue-black color, and is extremely disgusting with a foul smell. It stands, having reached a state unfit to be approached or seen, let alone to be smelled or tasted. Just so, various kinds of food and drink, ground to a powder by the pestle of the teeth, turned over by the hand that is the tongue and smeared with spittle and saliva, are in that very moment bereft of their endowment of color, smell, and taste. Like a weaver's starch-paste and dog's vomit, it falls in, becomes enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind, seethes with the force of the heat of the stomach-fire, becomes infested with families of worms, releasing foam and bubbles ever higher, and reaches a state of being extremely disgusting with a foul smell like carrion, and there it remains. Merely upon hearing of this, revulsion towards food and drink is established; how much more so when observing it with the eye of wisdom? And it is in this stomach that the food and drink which has fallen in undergoes a fivefold division: one part the worms eat; one part the stomach-fire cooks; one part becomes urine; one part becomes feces; and one part, having reached the state of nutrient essence, nourishes the blood, flesh, and so on.

Paricchedato udarapaṭalena ceva udariyabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ. Ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the stomach lining and by the final part of the undigested food. This is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

201. Karīsanti vaccaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato yebhuyyena ajjhohaṭāhāravaṇṇameva hoti. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato heṭṭhimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato pakkāsaye ṭhitaṃ. Pakkāsayo nāma heṭṭhānābhi-piṭṭhikaṇṭakamūlānaṃ antare antāvasāne ubbedhena aṭṭhaṅgulamatto veḷunāḷikasadiso, yattha seyyathāpi nāma upari bhūmibhāge patitaṃ vassodakaṃ ogaḷitvā heṭṭhā bhūmibhāgaṃ pūretvā tiṭṭhati, evameva yaṃkiñci āmāsaye patitaṃ pānabhojanādikaṃ udaragginā pheṇuddehakaṃ pakkaṃ pakkaṃ nisadāya pisitamiva saṇhabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā antabilena ogaḷitvā ogaḷitvā omadditvā veḷupabbe pakkhipamānapaṇḍumattikā viya sannicitaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato pakkāsayapaṭalena ceva karīsabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

201. Feces is excrement. As to color, it generally has the very color of the ingested food. As to shape, it has the shape of its location. As to direction, it is produced in the lower direction. As to location, it is situated in the receptacle for digested food. The receptacle for digested food is a place about eight finger-breadths in height, resembling a hollow bamboo tube, located at the end of the intestines between the area below the navel and the base of the spine. Therein, just as rainwater that has fallen on the upper ground flows down, fills the lower ground, and remains, even so, whatever drink, food, and so on, that has fallen into the receptacle for undigested food, being repeatedly cooked by the stomach-fire, gives off froth, and having attained a state of fineness as if ground on a grinding stone, trickles down again and again through the intestinal passage, is pressed down, and remains accumulated like pale clay being placed in a bamboo joint. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the lining of the receptacle for digested food and by the final part of the feces. This is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

202. Matthaluṅganti sīsakaṭāhabbhantare ṭhitamiñjarāsi. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ ahicchattakapiṇḍavaṇṇaṃ. Dadhibhāvaṃ asampattaṃ duṭṭhakhīravaṇṇantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato sīsakaṭāhabbhantare cattāro sibbinimagge nissāya samodhānetvā ṭhapitā cattāro piṭṭhapiṇḍā viya samohitaṃ tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato sīsakaṭāhassa abbhantaratalehi ceva matthaluṅgabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ[M 1.0252], ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

202. The brain is the mass of marrow situated inside the skull-pan. As to color, it is white, with the color of a lump of an umbrella mushroom. It is also fit to say it has the color of spoiled milk that has not yet reached the state of curd. As to shape, it has the shape of its location. As to direction, it is produced in the upper direction. As to location, it is situated inside the skull-pan, collected together like four lumps of flour-dough placed together, brought together depending on the four suture lines. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the inner surfaces of the skull-pan and by the final part of the brain. This is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

203. Pittanti [V 1.0250] dve pittāni baddhapittañca abaddhapittañca. Tattha baddhapittaṃ vaṇṇato bahalamadhukatelavaṇṇaṃ. Abaddhapittaṃ milātaākulipupphavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato ubhayampi okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato baddhapittaṃ uparimāya disāya jātaṃ, itaraṃ dvīsu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato abaddhapittaṃ ṭhapetvā kesalomadantanakhānaṃ maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānañceva thaddhasukkhacammañca udakamiva telabindu avasesasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ, yamhi kupite akkhīni pītakāni honti, bhamanti, gattaṃ kampati, kaṇḍūyati. Baddhapittaṃ hadayapapphāsānaṃ antare yakanamaṃsaṃ nissāya patiṭṭhite mahākosātakīkosakasadise pittakosake ṭhitaṃ, yamhi kupite sattā ummattakā honti, vipallatthacittā hirottappaṃ chaḍḍetvā akātabbaṃ karonti, abhāsitabbaṃ bhāsanti, acintitabbaṃ cintenti. Paricchedato pittabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

203. Bile refers to two kinds of bile: bound bile and unbound bile. Among them, bound bile, by way of color, has the color of thick madhuka oil. Unbound bile has the color of a faded ākuli flower. As to shape, both have the shape of their location. As to direction, bound bile is produced in the upper direction, while the other is produced in two directions. As to location, unbound bile—excluding the places free of flesh of the head-hair, body-hair, teeth, and nails, and the hard, dry skin—pervades the rest of the body like a drop of oil spreading through water. When it is aggravated, the eyes turn yellow, dizziness occurs, the body trembles, and itching arises. Bound bile is located in the gall bladder, which is situated between the heart and lungs, relying on the liver, and resembles the fruit of the great kosātakī gourd. When it is aggravated, beings become insane, their minds deranged; they abandon moral shame and moral fear, do what should not be done, say what should not be said, and think what should not be thought. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the bile part. This is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

204. Semhanti sarīrabbhantare ekapatthapūrappamāṇaṃ semhaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato setaṃ nāgabalāpaṇṇarasavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato udarapaṭale ṭhitaṃ. Yaṃ pānabhojanādiajjhoharaṇakāle seyyathāpi nāma udake sevālapaṇakaṃ kaṭṭhe vā kathale vā patante chijjitvā dvidhā hutvā puna ajjhottharitvā tiṭṭhati, evameva pānabhojanādimhi nipatante chijjitvā dvidhā hutvā puna ajjhottharitvā tiṭṭhati, yamhi ca mandībhūte pakkagaṇḍo viya pūtikukkuṭaṇḍamiva ca udaraṃ paramajegucchaṃ kuṇapagandhaṃ hoti, tato uggatena ca gandhena uddekopi mukhampi duggandhaṃ pūtikuṇapasadisaṃ hoti. So ca puriso apehi duggandhaṃ vāyasīti vattabbataṃ āpajjati, yañca vaḍḍhitvā bahalattamāpannaṃ pidhānaphalakamiva vaccakuṭiyaṃ udarapaṭalassa abbhantareyeva kuṇapagandhaṃ sannirumbhitvā tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato semhabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

204. Phlegm is the phlegm inside the body, amounting to about one bowlful. As to color, it is white, the color of the juice of nāgabalā leaves. As to shape, it has the shape of the space it occupies. As to direction, it is produced in the upper direction. As to location, it is situated in the lining of the stomach. When food and drink are being swallowed, just as, in water, when a piece of wood or a potsherd falls, the algae and duckweed break apart, become twofold, and then cover over again, even so, when food and drink fall upon it, it breaks apart, becomes twofold, and then covers over again. And when this phlegm becomes weakened, the stomach becomes extremely disgusting and has the smell of a corpse, like a ripe boil or a rotten chicken egg. And by the smell rising from that, both the belch and the mouth become foul-smelling, like a putrid corpse. And that person becomes liable to be told, 'Go away! You smell foul!' And when it has increased and become thick, it remains blocking the corpse-smell within the lining of the stomach, like a covering-plank in a latrine. As to delimitation, it is delimited by the phlegm-part. This is its delimitation by what is homogeneous. The delimitation by what is heterogeneous, however, is just like that of the hair.

205. Pubboti [M 1.0253] pūtilohitavasena pavattapubbaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇo. Matasarīre pana pūtibahalācāmavaṇṇo hoti. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhāno. Disato dvīsu disāsu hoti. Okāsato pana pubbassa okāso nāma nibaddho natthi, yattha so sannicito tiṭṭheyya, yatra yatra khāṇukaṇṭakapaharaṇaggijālādīhi abhihate sarīrappadese lohitaṃ saṇṭhahitvā paccati, gaṇḍapīḷakādayo vā uppajjanti, tatra tatra tiṭṭhati. Paricchedato pubbabhāgena paricchinno, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

205. Pus is that which has arisen by way of putrid blood. As to color, it has the color of a pale, withered leaf. In a dead body, however, it has the color of putrid, thick rice-gruel. As to shape, it has the shape of the space it occupies. As to direction, it is in the two directions. As to location, however, there is no fixed location for pus where it might be accumulated; wherever a region of the body is struck by such things as stumps, thorns, weapons, or flames of fire, and the blood, having coagulated, putrefies, or where boils, abscesses, and so on, arise, there it is situated. As to delimitation, it is delimited by the pus-part. This is its delimitation by what is homogeneous. The delimitation by what is heterogeneous, however, is just like that of the hair.

206. Lohitanti [V 1.0251] dve lohitāni sannicitalohitañca saṃsaraṇalohitañca. Tattha sannicitalohitaṃ vaṇṇato nipakkabahalalākhārasavaṇṇaṃ. Saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ acchalākhārasavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato ubhayampi okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato sannicitalohitaṃ uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Itaraṃ dvisu disāsu jātaṃ. Okāsato saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ ṭhapetvā kesalomadantanakhānaṃ maṃsavinimuttaṭṭhānañceva thaddhasukkhacammañca dhamanijālānusārena sabbaṃ upādiṇṇasarīraṃ pharitvā ṭhitaṃ. Sannicitalohitaṃ yakanaṭṭhānassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā ekapatthapūramattaṃ hadayavakkapapphāsānaṃ upari thokaṃ thokaṃ paggharantaṃ vakkahadayayakanapapphāse temayamānaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Tasmiṃ hi vakkahadayādīni atemente sattā pipāsitā honti. Paricchedato lohitabhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

206. Blood: there are two kinds of blood, accumulated blood and circulating blood. Of these, accumulated blood, as to color, has the color of cooked, thick lac-juice. Circulating blood has the color of clear lac-juice. As to shape, both have the shape of the space they occupy. As to direction, accumulated blood is produced in the upper direction. The other is produced in the two directions. As to location, circulating blood—excepting the places of the hair of the head, body hair, teeth, and nails that are devoid of flesh, as well as hard, dry skin—pervades and remains in the entire karmically-acquired body, following the network of vessels. Accumulated blood, filling the lower part of the liver's location to the measure of one bowlful, dripping little by little over the heart, kidneys, and lungs, remains moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. Indeed, when that blood does not moisten the kidneys, heart, and so on, beings become thirsty. As to delimitation, it is delimited by the blood-part; this is its delimitation by what is homogeneous. The delimitation by what is heterogeneous, however, is just like that of the hair.

207. Sedoti lomakūpādīhi paggharaṇakaāpodhātu. So vaṇṇato vippasannatilatelavaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhāno. Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato sedassokāso nāma nibaddho natthi, yattha so lohitaṃ viya sadā tiṭṭheyya. Yadā pana aggisantāpasūriyasantāpautuvikārādīhi sarīraṃ santapati, tadā udakato abbūḷhamattavisamacchinnabhisamuḷālakumudanāḷakalāpo viya sabbakesalomakūpavivarehi paggharati, tasmā tassa saṇṭhānampi kesalomakūpavivarānaññeva vasena veditabbaṃ. Sedapariggaṇhakena ca yoginā kesalomakūpavivare pūretvā ṭhitavaseneva sedo manasi kātabbo. Paricchedato [M 1.0254] sedabhāgena paricchinno, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

207. Sweat is the water element that flows out from the pores of the body hair and so on. As to color, it has the color of very clear sesame oil. As to shape, it has the shape of the space it occupies. As to direction, it is produced in the two directions. As to location, there is no fixed location for sweat where it would always remain, like the accumulated blood. But when the body is heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, changes in season, and so on, it flows out from all the openings of the pores of the hair of the head and body hair, like a bundle of lotus fibers, lotus roots, and water-lily stems just pulled from the water and unevenly cut. Therefore, its shape should be known only by way of the openings of the pores of the hair of the head and body hair. And the yogi who apprehends sweat should attend to it mentally only as filling and remaining in the openings of the pores of the hair of the head and body hair. As to delimitation, it is delimited by the sweat-part; this is its delimitation by what is homogeneous. The delimitation by what is heterogeneous, however, is just like that of the hair.

Medoti thinasineho. So vaṇṇato phālitahaliddivaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānato thūlasarīrassa tāva cammamaṃsantare ṭhapitahaliddivaṇṇadukūlapilotikasaṇṭhāno hoti. Kisasarīrassa jaṅghamaṃsaṃ ūrumaṃsaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakanissitaṃ piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ udaravaṭṭimaṃsanti etāni nissāya diguṇatiguṇaṃ katvā ṭhapitahaliddivaṇṇadukūlapilotikasaṇṭhāno. Disato dvīsu disāsu jāto. Okāsato thūlassa sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā kisassa jaṅghamaṃsādīni nissāya ṭhito, yaṃ sinehasaṅkhaṃ gatampi paramajegucchattā neva muddhani telatthāya, na nāsatelādīnamatthāya gaṇhanti. Paricchedato heṭṭhā maṃsena, upari cammena, tiriyaṃ medabhāgena paricchinno, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

Fat is thick grease. As to color, it has the color of split turmeric. As to shape, for a stout person, it has the shape of a worn-out, fine, turmeric-colored cloth placed between the skin and flesh. For a lean person, it has the shape of a worn-out, fine, turmeric-colored cloth placed in two or three layers, adhering to these: the flesh of the calves, the flesh of the thighs, the flesh of the back attached to the spine, and the flesh of the abdominal wall. As to direction, it is produced in the two directions. As to location, in a stout person, it pervades the entire body, while in a lean person, it is situated adhering to the flesh of the calves and so on. Although it is counted as grease, due to its extreme loathsomeness, it is not taken for oiling the head, nor for nasal oil and the like. As to delimitation, it is delimited below by flesh, above by skin, and across by the fat-part; this is its delimitation by what is homogeneous. The delimitation by what is heterogeneous, however, is just like that of the hair.

208. Assūti [V 1.0252] akkhīhi paggharaṇakaāpodhātu. Taṃ vaṇṇato vippasannatilatelavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato uparimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato akkhikūpakesu ṭhitaṃ. Na cetaṃ pittakosake pittamiva akkhikūpakesu sadā sannicitaṃ tiṭṭhati. Yadā pana sattā somanassajātā mahāhasitaṃ hasanti, domanassajātā rodanti paridevanti, tathārūpaṃ vā visamāhāraṃ āhārenti, yadā ca nesaṃ akkhīni dhūmarajapaṃsukādīhi abhihaññanti. Tadā etehi somanassadomanassavisabhāgāhārautūhi samuṭṭhahitvā akkhikūpake pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Assupariggaṇhakena ca yoginā akkhikūpake pūretvā ṭhitavaseneva pariggaṇhitabbaṃ. Paricchedato assubhāgena paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

208. Tears are the water element, oozing from the eyes. By color, they are like very clear sesame oil. By shape, they take the shape of their space. By direction, they originate from the upward direction. By location, they reside in the eye sockets. And they do not always remain accumulated in the eye sockets like bile in the gallbladder. However, when beings experience joy and laugh heartily, or experience sorrow and weep and lament, or consume such unsuitable food, or when their eyes are afflicted by smoke, dust, or dirt—then, arising from this joy, sorrow, unsuitable food, and seasonal conditions, tears fill the eye sockets and either remain or flow out. And a yogī who comprehends tears should comprehend them only by way of their state of having filled the eye sockets and remaining there. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of tears; this is its homogeneous delimitation. Its heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

209. Vasāti vilīnasineho. Sā vaṇṇato nāḷikeratelavaṇṇā. Ācāme āsittatelavaṇṇātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Saṇṭhānato nhānakāle pasannaudakassa upari paribbhamantasinehabinduvisaṭasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato yebhuyyena hatthatalahatthapiṭṭhipādatalapādapiṭṭhināsapuṭanalāṭaaṃsakūṭesu ṭhitā. Na cesā etesu okāsesu sadā vilīnāva hutvā tiṭṭhati. Yadā pana aggisantāpasūriyasantāpautuvisabhāgadhātuvisabhāgehi te padesā usmājātā [M 1.0255] honti, tadā tattha nhānakāle pasannaudakūpari sinehabinduvisaṭo viya ito cito ca sañcarati. Paricchedato vasābhāgena paricchinnā, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisoyeva.

209. Fat is liquefied grease. By color, it has the color of coconut oil. It can also be said to have the color of oil poured into rice gruel. By shape, it has the shape of a spreading drop of oil floating on the surface of clear water during a bath. By direction, it is produced in two directions. By location, it is mostly situated on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the shoulder-peaks. And it does not always remain liquefied in these locations. But when those areas become heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, an unsuitable season, or unsuitable elements, then it moves about here and there, like a spreading drop of oil on the surface of clear water during a bath. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of fat; this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

210. Kheḷoti antomukhe pheṇamissā āpodhātu. So vaṇṇato seto pheṇavaṇṇo. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhāno. Pheṇasaṇṭhānotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Disato uparimāya disāya jāto. Okāsato ubhohi kapolapassehi oruyha jivhāya ṭhito. Na cesa ettha sadā sannicito hutvā tiṭṭhati. Yadā pana sattā tathārūpamāhāraṃ passanti vā saranti vā, uṇhatittakaṭukaloṇambilānaṃ vā kiñci mukhe ṭhapenti, yadā vā nesaṃ hadayaṃ āgilāyati, kismiñci deva vā jigucchā uppajjati, tadā kheḷo uppajjitvā ubhohi kapolapassehi oruyha jivhāya saṇṭhāti. Aggajivhāya cesa tanuko hoti, mūlajivhāya bahalo, mukhe pakkhittañca puthukaṃ vā taṇḍulaṃ vā aññaṃ vā kiñci khādanīyaṃ nadīpuline khatakūpakasalilaṃ viya [V 1.0253] parikkhayaṃ agacchantova temetuṃ samattho hoti. Paricchedato kheḷabhāgena paricchinno, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

210. Saliva is the water element mixed with foam inside the mouth. By color, it is white, having the color of foam. By shape, it has the shape of its location; it can also be said to have the shape of foam. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, it is situated on the tongue. And it does not always remain accumulated there. But when beings see or remember such food, or place in the mouth some food item that is hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour, or when their heart is afflicted, or when disgust towards anything whatsoever arises, then saliva, having arisen, descends from both sides of the cheeks and settles on the tongue. It is thin at the tip of the tongue and thick at the root of the tongue. It is able to moisten what is placed in the mouth—be it flattened rice, uncooked rice, or any other edible food—without becoming exhausted, like the water of a well dug in a river's sandbank. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of saliva; this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

211. Siṅghāṇikāti matthaluṅgato paggharaṇakaasuci. Sā vaṇṇato taruṇatālaṭṭhimiñjavaṇṇā. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānā. Disato uparimāya disāya jātā. Okāsato nāsāpuṭe pūretvā ṭhitā. Na cesā ettha sadā sannicitā hutvā tiṭṭhati, atha kho yathā nāma puriso paduminipatte dadhiṃ bandhitvā heṭṭhā kaṇṭakena vijjheyya, athānena chiddena dadhimuttaṃ gaḷitvā bahi pateyya, evameva yadā sattā rodanti, visabhāgāhārautuvasena vā sañjātadhātukhobhā honti, tadā anto sīsato pūtisemhabhāvamāpannaṃ matthaluṅgaṃ gaḷitvā tālumatthakavivarena otaritvā nāsāpuṭe pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Siṅghāṇikā pariggaṇhakena ca yoginā nāsāpuṭe pūretvā ṭhitavaseneva pariggaṇhitabbā. Paricchedato siṅghāṇikābhāgena paricchinnā, ayamassā sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

211. Nasal mucus is an impurity that flows from the brain. By color, it has the color of the kernel of a young palm seed. By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is produced in the upper direction. By location, it is situated, having filled the nostrils. And it does not always remain accumulated there. But rather, it is as when a man might tie up curd in a lotus leaf and pierce it from below with a thorn, and then the whey from the curd would trickle out through this hole and fall outside. In this very way, when beings cry, or when a disturbance of the elements arises due to unsuitable food or climate, then from within the head, the brain, having reached the state of putrid phlegm, flows down, descends through the opening at the top of the palate, and fills the nostrils, either remaining there or dripping out. And by the yogī who apprehends nasal mucus, it is to be apprehended simply by way of its state of filling the nostrils. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of nasal mucus; this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

212. Lasikāti [M 1.0256] sarīrasandhīnaṃ abbhantare picchilakuṇapaṃ. Sā vaṇṇato kaṇikāraniyyāsavaṇṇā. Saṇṭhānato okāsasaṇṭhānā. Disato dvīsu disāsu jātā. Okāsato aṭṭhisandhīnaṃ abbhañjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā asītisatasandhīnaṃ abbhantare ṭhitā. Yassa cesā mandā hoti, tassa uṭṭhahantassa nisīdantassa abhikkamantassa paṭikkamantassa samiñjantassa pasārentassa aṭṭhikāni kaṭakaṭāyanti, accharāsaddaṃ karonto viya sañcarati. Ekayojanadviyojanamattaṃ addhānaṃ gatassa vāyodhātu kuppati, gattāni dukkhanti. Yassa pana bahukā honti, tassa uṭṭhānanisajjādīsu na aṭṭhīni kaṭakaṭāyanti, dīghampi addhānaṃ gatassa na vāyodhātu kuppati, na gattāni dukkhanti. Paricchedato lasikābhāgena paricchinnā, ayamassā sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

212. Synovial fluid is the slimy, putrid substance inside the body's joints. By color, it has the color of the sap of the kaṇikāra tree. By shape, it has the shape of the space it occupies. By direction, it arises in two directions. By location, accomplishing the function of lubricating the joints, it is situated within the one hundred and eighty joints. For whomever this is deficient, their bones creak when standing, sitting, walking forward, walking backward, bending, or stretching; they move about as if making a snapping sound. After traveling a distance of one or two yojanas, their wind element becomes disturbed, and their limbs ache. But for whomever it is abundant, their bones do not creak during standing, sitting, and so on; even after traveling a long distance, their wind element does not become disturbed, and their limbs do not ache. By way of delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of synovial fluid—this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of hair.

213. Muttanti muttarasaṃ. Taṃ vaṇṇato māsakhārodakavaṇṇaṃ. Saṇṭhānato adhomukhaṭṭhapitaudakakumbhaabbhantaragataudakasaṇṭhānaṃ. Disato heṭṭhimāya disāya jātaṃ. Okāsato vatthissa abbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Vatthi nāma vatthi puṭo vuccati. Yattha seyyathāpi candanikāya pakkhitte amukhe ravaṇaghaṭe candanikāraso pavisati, na cassa pavisanamaggo paññāyati[V 1.0254], evameva sarīrato muttaṃ pavisati, na cassa pavisanamaggo paññāyati, nikkhamanamaggo pana pākaṭo hoti. Yamhi ca muttassa bharite passāvaṃ karomāti sattānaṃ āyūhanaṃ hoti. Paricchedato vatthiabbhantarena ceva muttabhāgena ca paricchinnaṃ, ayamassa sabhāgaparicchedo. Visabhāgaparicchedo pana kesasadisova.

213. Urine is the fluid of urine. By color, it has the color of water with lye from black gram. By shape, it has the shape of water contained within an inverted water pot. By direction, it arises from the lower direction. By location, it is situated within the bladder. The bladder is called the 'bladder-pouch'. Wherein, just as when a small, mouthless clay pot is placed in a drain, the drain water enters, and its path of entry is not discerned; even so, urine from the body enters it, and its path of entry is not discerned, but its path of exit is evident. And when it is filled with urine, the exertion of beings occurs, thinking, 'We will urinate.' By delimitation, it is delimited by the interior of the bladder and by the portion of urine; this is its homogeneous delimitation. The heterogeneous delimitation, however, is just like that of the hair.

214. Evañhi kesādike koṭṭhāse vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena vavatthapetvā anupubbato nātisīghatotiādinā nayena vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena pañcadhā paṭikkūlā paṭikkūlāti manasikaroto paṇṇattisamatikkamāvasāne seyyathāpi cakkhumato purisassa dvattiṃsavaṇṇānaṃ kusumānaṃ ekasuttakaganthitaṃ mālaṃ olokentassa sabbapupphāni apubbāpariyamiva pākaṭāni honti, evameva atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesāti imaṃ kāyaṃ olokentassa sabbe te dhammā [M 1.0257] apubbāpariyāva pākaṭā honti. Tena vuttaṃ manasikārakosallakathāyaṃ “ādikammikassa hi kesāti manasikaroto manasikāro gantvā muttanti imaṃ pariyosānakoṭṭhāsameva āhacca tiṭṭhatī”ti.

214. For thus, for one who has determined the constituents beginning with hair by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and who attends to them as ‘repulsive, repulsive’ in five ways—by way of color, shape, smell, abode, and location—according to the method of ‘gradually, not too quickly,’ etc., at the end of the meditation that transcends conceptualization, it is just as for a person with good eyesight looking at a garland of flowers of thirty-two kinds of colors strung on a single thread, all the flowers become manifest as if without prior or subsequent order; even so, for one looking at this body, thinking, ‘There are hairs in this body,’ all those constituents become manifest as if without prior or subsequent order. Therefore, it was said in the discourse on skill in attention: ‘For a beginner, when attending to “hairs,” the attention proceeds and, reaching the final constituent, “urine,” it stops.’”

Sace pana bahiddhāpi manasikāraṃ upasaṃharati, athassa evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsesu pākaṭībhūtesu āhiṇḍantā manussatiracchānādayo sattākāraṃ vijahitvā koṭṭhāsarāsivaseneva upaṭṭhahanti, tehi ca ajjhohariyamānaṃ pānabhojanādi koṭṭhāsarāsimhi pakkhipamānamiva upaṭṭhāti.

But if one directs attention externally as well, then for that yogī, when all the constituents have thus become manifest, wandering humans, animals, and so on, having abandoned their aspect as beings, appear only by way of being a heap of constituents. And the drinks, food, etc., being consumed by them appear as if being placed into that heap of constituents.

Athassa anupubbamuñcanādivasena paṭikkūlā paṭikkūlāti punappunaṃ manasikaroto anukkamena appanā uppajjati. Tattha kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ uggahanimittaṃ. Sabbākārato paṭikkūlavasena upaṭṭhānaṃ paṭibhāganimittaṃ. Taṃ āsevato bhāvayato vuttanayena asubhakammaṭṭhānesu viya paṭhamajjhānavaseneva appanā uppajjati.

Then, for that yogī who repeatedly attends to it as ‘repulsive, repulsive’ by way of gradually letting go, etc., absorption arises in due course. Therein, the appearance of hair, etc., by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation is the learning sign. The appearance as repulsive in all aspects is the counterpart sign. For one who resorts to and develops that sign, absorption arises by way of the first jhāna only, in the aforesaid manner, just as in the foulness meditation subjects.

Sā yassa ekova koṭṭhāso pākaṭo hoti, ekasmiṃ vā koṭṭhāse appanaṃ patvā puna aññasmiṃ yogaṃ na karoti, tassa ekāva uppajjati. Yassa pana aneke koṭṭhāsā pākaṭā honti, ekasmiṃ vā jhānaṃ patvā puna aññasmiṃpi yogaṃ karoti, tassa mallakattherassa viya koṭṭhāsagaṇanāya paṭhamajjhānāni nibbattanti.

If only one constituent becomes evident to someone, or if, having attained absorption in one constituent, he does not apply himself to another, then only one absorption arises for him. But if many constituents become evident to someone, or if, having attained jhāna in one constituent, he also applies himself to another, then first jhānas arise for him corresponding to the number of constituents, like those of the Elder Mallaka.

So [V 1.0255] kirāyasmā dīghabhāṇakaabhayattheraṃ hatthe gahetvā “āvuso abhaya, imaṃ tāva pañhaṃ uggaṇhāhī”ti vatvā āha – “mallakatthero dvattiṃsakoṭṭhāsesu dvattiṃsāya paṭhamajjhānānaṃ lābhī. Sace rattiṃ ekaṃ, divā ekaṃ samāpajjati, atirekaddhamāsena puna sampajjati, sace pana devasikaṃ ekaṃ samāpajjati, atirekamāsena puna sampajjatī”ti.

It is said that that venerable one, taking the Elder Abhaya the Dīgha-reciter by the hand, said, 'Friend Abhaya, first learn this question,' and then said: 'The Elder Mallaka was an attainer of thirty-two first jhānas in the thirty-two constituents. If he attains one at night and one during the day, he completes the cycle again in more than half a month. But if he attains one daily, he completes the cycle again in more than a month.'

Evaṃ paṭhamajjhānavasena ijjhamānampi cetaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādīsu satibalena ijjhanato kāyagatāsatīti vuccati.

And though this meditation subject is thus accomplished by way of the first jhāna, because it is accomplished by the power of mindfulness regarding color, shape, and so on, it is called 'mindfulness directed to the body'.

Imañca kāyagatāsatimanuyutto bhikkhu aratiratisaho hoti, na ca naṃ arati sahati, uppannaṃ aratiṃ abhibhuyya abhibhuyya viharati. Bhayabheravasaho hoti, na ca naṃ bhayabheravaṃ sahati, uppannaṃ bhayabheravaṃ abhibhuyya abhibhuyya viharati. Khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassa [M 1.0258] …pe… pāṇaharānaṃ adhivāsakajātiko hoti (ma. ni. 3.159). Kesādīnaṃ vaṇṇabhedaṃ nissāya catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ lābhī hoti. Cha abhiññā paṭivijjhati (ma. ni. 3.159).

And a bhikkhu devoted to this mindfulness directed to the body is able to endure non-delight and delight; non-delight does not overcome him; he dwells having repeatedly overcome arisen non-delight. He is able to endure fear and dread; fear and dread do not overcome him; he dwells having repeatedly overcome arisen fear and dread. He is patient of cold and heat… and is of a nature to endure feelings that can take one's life. Relying on the distinctions in color of the hair and so on, he is an attainer of the four jhānas. He penetrates the six direct knowledges.

Tasmā have appamatto, anuyuñjetha paṇḍito;

Evaṃ anekānisaṃsaṃ, imaṃ kāyagatāsatinti.

Therefore, a wise person, being unremitting, should indeed cultivate this mindfulness directed to the body, which has such manifold benefits.

Idaṃ kāyagatāsatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed discourse on mindfulness directed to the body.

Ānāpānassatikathā

The Discourse on Mindfulness of Breathing

215. Idāni yaṃ taṃ bhagavatā “ayampi kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhi bhāvito bahulīkato santo ceva paṇīto ca asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro, uppannuppanne ca pāpake akusale dhamme ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasametī”ti evaṃ pasaṃsitvā –

215. Now, that concentration through mindfulness of breathing which the Blessed One praised thus: 'Bhikkhus, when this concentration through mindfulness of breathing is developed and much cultivated, it is peaceful and sublime, unadulterated and a blissful abiding; and it instantly causes arisen evil, unwholesome states to disappear and be calmed'—

“Kathaṃ bhāvito ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhi kathaṃ bahulīkato santo ceva paṇīto ca asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro, uppannuppanne ca pāpake akusale dhamme ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti vūpasameti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā rukkhamūlagato [V 1.0256] vā suññāgāragato vā nisīdati pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā, so satova assasati sato passasati. Dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti. Dīghaṃ vā passasanto…pe… rassaṃ vā assasanto…pe… rassaṃ vā passasanto rassaṃ passasāmīti pajānāti. Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmīti sikkhati. Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī passasissāmīti sikkhati. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti sikkhati. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhati. Pītipaṭisaṃvedī… sukhapaṭisaṃvedī… cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃvedī… passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāraṃ… cittapaṭisaṃvedī… abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ… samādahaṃ cittaṃ… vimocayaṃ cittaṃ [M 1.0259] … aniccānupassī… virāgānupassī… nirodhānupassī. Paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmīti sikkhati. Paṭinissaggānupassī passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti –

‘How, bhikkhus, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so that it is peaceful and sublime, unadulterated, and a pleasant abiding, and on the spot causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to disappear and be stilled? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest or to the root of a tree or to an empty dwelling, sits down, folds his legs crosswise, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him. Mindful he breathes in, mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands, “I breathe in long.” Breathing out long… and so on… breathing in short… breathing out short, he understands, “I breathe out short.” He trains himself, “I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.” He trains himself, “I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.” He trains himself, “I will breathe in calming the bodily formation.” He trains himself, “I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.” He trains himself, “I will breathe in experiencing rapture”… “experiencing pleasure”… “experiencing the mental formation”… “calming the mental formation”… “experiencing the mind”… “gladdening the mind”… “concentrating the mind”… “liberating the mind”… “contemplating impermanence”… “contemplating fading away”… “contemplating cessation.” He trains himself, “I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment.” He trains himself, “I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.”’

Evaṃ soḷasavatthukaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tassa bhāvanānayo anuppatto. So pana yasmā pāḷivaṇṇanānusāreneva vuccamāno sabbākāraparipūro hoti. Tasmā ayamettha pāḷivaṇṇanāpubbaṅgamo niddeso.

Thus, the sixteen-faceted meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing has been indicated. The method of its development is next in sequence. However, since that method becomes complete in all aspects only when explained in accordance with the Pāḷi commentary, this exposition here is therefore preceded by the Pāḷi commentary.

216. Kathaṃ bhāvito ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati samādhīti ettha tāva kathanti ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanaṃ nānappakārato vitthāretukamyatāpucchā. Bhāvito ca bhikkhave ānāpānassatisamādhīti nānappakārato vitthāretukamyatāya puṭṭhadhammanidassanaṃ. Kathaṃ bahulīkato…pe… vūpasametīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tattha bhāvitoti uppādito vaḍḍhito vā. Ānāpānassatisamādhīti ānāpānapariggāhikāya satiyā saddhiṃ sampayutto samādhi. Ānāpānassatiyaṃ vā samādhi ānāpānassatisamādhi. Bahulīkatoti punappunaṃ kato. Santoceva paṇīto cāti santo ceva paṇīto ceva. Ubhayattha eva saddena niyamo veditabbo. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Ayañhi yathā asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ kevalaṃ paṭivedhavasena santañca paṇītañca, oḷārikārammaṇattā pana paṭikkūlārammaṇattā ca ārammaṇavasena neva santaṃ na paṇītaṃ, na evaṃ kenaci pariyāyena asanto vā apaṇīto vā, atha kho ārammaṇasantatāyapi santo vūpasanto nibbuto, paṭivedhasaṅkhātaaṅgasantatāyapi. Ārammaṇapaṇītatāyapi paṇīto atittikaro, aṅgapaṇītatāyapīti. Tena vuttaṃ “santo ceva paṇīto cā”ti.

216. Regarding the passage, ‘How, bhikkhus, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed?’: here, first, ‘how’ is a question prompted by the desire to explain in detail and in various ways the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. The statement, ‘Developed, bhikkhus, is concentration through mindfulness of breathing,’ is a demonstration of the teaching that was asked to be explained in detail and in various ways. For the passage beginning, ‘How is it cultivated… and stills,’ this same method applies.

Therein, ‘developed’ means produced or increased. ‘Concentration through mindfulness of breathing’ is concentration associated with mindfulness that comprehends the in-breath and out-breath. Or, it is the concentration that arises on account of mindfulness of breathing. ‘Cultivated’ means done again and again. ‘Peaceful and sublime’ means both peaceful and sublime. In both cases, the particle ‘eva’ should be understood as restrictive.

What is meant by this? This concentration, unlike the meditation subject of unattractiveness—which is peaceful and sublime only by way of penetration, but on account of its gross and repulsive object is, by way of its object, neither peaceful nor sublime—is in no way unpeaceful or unsublime. Rather, it is peaceful, stilled, and extinguished on account of the peacefulness of its object, and also on account of the peacefulness of its factors, which are reckoned as penetration. It is sublime and brings no satiety on account of the sublimity of its object, and also on account of the sublimity of its factors. Therefore, it was said, ‘peaceful and sublime.’

Asecanako [V 1.0257] ca sukho ca vihāroti ettha pana nāssa secananti asecanako, anāsittako abbokiṇṇo pāṭiyekko āveṇiko. Natthi ettha parikammena vā upacārena vā santatā. Ādisamannāhārato pabhuti attano sabhāveneva santo ca paṇīto cāti attho. Keci pana asecanakoti anāsittako ojavanto sabhāveneva [M 1.0260] madhuroti vadanti. Evaṃ ayaṃ asecanako ca, appitappitakkhaṇe kāyikacetasikasukhapaṭilābhāya saṃvattanato sukho ca vihāroti veditabbo. Uppannuppanneti avikkhambhite avikkhambhite. Pāpaketi lāmake. Akusale dhammeti akosallasambhūte dhamme. Ṭhānaso antaradhāpetīti khaṇeneva antaradhāpeti vikkhambheti. Vūpasametīti suṭṭhu upasameti. Nibbedhabhāgiyattā vā anupubbena ariyamaggavuddhippatto samucchindati, paṭippassambhetīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, regarding ‘unadulterated and a pleasant abiding’: ‘unadulterated’ (asecanako) means there is no adding to it; it is unadulterated, unmixed, separate, and distinct. Herein, its peacefulness is not achieved by means of preliminary work or access concentration. From the initial application of mind, by its own nature it is both peaceful and sublime—this is the meaning. Some, however, say that ‘unadulterated’ (asecanako) means unadulterated, possessing savor, and naturally sweet. Thus, this should be known as ‘unadulterated,’ and because it conduces to the attainment of bodily and mental happiness at every moment of absorption, it is also a ‘pleasant abiding’ (sukho vihāro). Regarding ‘that have arisen’ (uppannuppanne): this refers to those states that have not been suppressed. Regarding ‘evil’ (pāpake): this means base. Regarding ‘unwholesome states’ (akusale dhamme): this means states born of unskillfulness. Regarding ‘it makes them disappear on the spot’ (ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti): it makes them disappear and suppresses them at that very moment. Regarding ‘it stills’ (vūpasameti): it thoroughly calms. Or, because it is conducive to penetration, having gradually attained the growth of the noble path, it eradicates and stills them—so it is said.

Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho. Bhikkhave, kena pakārena kenākārena kena vidhinā bhāvito ānāpānassatisamādhi kena pakārena bahulīkato santo ceva…pe… vūpasametīti.

Herein is the concise meaning: Bhikkhus, in what manner, in what mode, by what method is the concentration of mindfulness of breathing developed, and in what manner is it cultivated, so that it is peaceful and… stills?

217. Idāni tamatthaṃ vitthārento “idha, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha idha bhikkhave bhikkhūti bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhi ettha idhasaddo sabbappakāraānāpānassatisamādhinibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ – idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139). Tena vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti.

217. Now, elaborating on that meaning, the Blessed One said, ‘Here, bhikkhus,’ and so on. Therein, ‘Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’ means: ‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu in this Dispensation.’ For in this context, the word ‘here’ illuminates the Dispensation as the foundation for an individual who gives rise to the concentration of mindfulness of breathing in all its aspects, and it also denies that another dispensation has such a quality. As it is said: ‘Here alone, bhikkhus, is there an ascetic… empty are the doctrines of others of other ascetics’ (MN 1.71). Therefore, it was said, ‘a bhikkhu in this Dispensation.’

Araññagato vā…pe… suññāgāragato vāti idamassa ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu anuvisaṭaṃ cittaṃ ānāpānassatisamādhiārammaṇaṃ abhiruhituṃ na icchati, kūṭagoṇayuttaratho viya uppathameva dhāvati. Tasmā seyyathāpi nāma gopo kūṭadhenuyā sabbaṃ khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhitaṃ kūṭavacchaṃ dametukāmo dhenuto apanetvā ekamante mahantaṃ thambhaṃ nikhaṇitvā tattha yottena bandheyya, athassa so vaccho ito cito ca vipphanditvā palāyituṃ asakkonto tameva thambhaṃ upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, evameva imināpi bhikkhunā dīgharattaṃ rūpārammaṇādirasapānavaḍḍhitaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ dametukāmena rūpādiārammaṇato apanetvā araññaṃ vā…pe… suññāgāraṃ vā pavesetvā tattha assāsapassāsathambhe satiyottena bandhitabbaṃ. Evamassa [V 1.0258] taṃ cittaṃ ito cito ca vipphanditvāpi pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇaṃ alabhamānaṃ satiyottaṃ chinditvā palāyituṃ [M 1.0261] asakkontaṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ upacārappanāvasena upanisīdati ceva upanipajjati ca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Whether he has gone to the forest... or to an empty dwelling—this is the explanation of the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing. For this bhikkhu's mind, which for a long time has run about among objects such as forms, does not wish to ascend to the object of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; like a cart yoked to a crooked ox, it runs only along the wrong path. Therefore, just as a cowherd wishing to tame a crooked calf—one that has grown by drinking all the milk of a crooked cow—would take it away from its mother, drive a large post into the ground in a secluded spot, and tie it there with a rope; and then that calf, after struggling here and there, unable to escape, would sit down or lie down by that very post; even so, this bhikkhu, wishing to tame his unruly mind—one that has grown for a long time by drinking the flavor of objects such as forms—should take it away from objects like forms, make it enter the forest... or an empty dwelling, and there bind it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of in-and-out breathing. Thus his mind, though struggling here and there, not obtaining its formerly habitual object and being unable to escape by breaking the rope of mindfulness, settles down and rests upon that very object by way of access and absorption. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yathā thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ damaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha”nti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 3.374; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.107);

“Just as a man wishing to tame a calf would bind it to a post, even so, here, one should firmly bind one's own mind to the object with mindfulness.”

Evamassetaṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanānurūpaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “idamassa ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpana”nti.

Thus, this dwelling is suitable for the development of meditation. Therefore, it was said: “This is the explanation of the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.”

Atha vā yasmā idaṃ kammaṭṭhānappabhede muddhabhūtaṃ sabbaññubuddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ itthipurisahatthiassādisaddasamākulaṃ gāmantaṃ apariccajitvā na sukaraṃ bhāvetuṃ, saddakaṇṭakattā jhānassa. Agāmake pana araññe sukaraṃ yogāvacarena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ sampāpuṇituṃ. Tasmāssa anurūpasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha.

Alternatively, because this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing—which is pre-eminent among the varieties of meditation subjects and is the proximate cause for the attainment of special qualities and for a pleasant abiding in this present existence for all Buddhas, certain Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—is not easy to develop without abandoning a monastery in the vicinity of a village, which is teeming with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so on, due to sound being a thorn to jhāna. However, in a forest without a village, it is easy for a yogi to undertake this meditation subject, produce the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, and then, having made that very jhāna the foundation, to contemplate conditioned phenomena and attain the supreme fruit, Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing this bhikkhu a suitable dwelling, said, “gone to the forest,” and so on.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya hi bhagavā, so yathā vatthuvijjācariyo nagarabhūmiṃ passitvā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā “ettha nagaraṃ māpethā”ti upadisati, sotthinā ca nagare niṭṭhite rājakulato mahāsakkāraṃ labhati, evameva yogāvacarassa anurūpasenāsanaṃ upaparikkhitvā “ettha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitabba”nti upadisati, tato tattha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuttena yoginā kamena arahatte patte “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā”ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhati.

Indeed, the Blessed One is like a master of site-knowledge. Just as a master of site-knowledge, having seen a city site and thoroughly examined it, instructs, “Establish the city here,” and when the city is successfully completed, he receives great honor from the royal family; even so, the Blessed One, having examined a suitable dwelling for the yogi, instructs, “Here, the meditation subject should be diligently practiced.” Thereafter, when the yogi who diligently practices the meditation subject there gradually attains Arahantship, that Blessed One receives great honor, with the thought, “Oh, that Blessed One is truly a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One!”

Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu dīpisadisoti vuccati. Yathā hi mahādīpirājā araññe tiṇagahanaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pabbatagahanaṃ vā nissāya nilīyitvā vanamahiṃsagokaṇṇasūkarādayo mige gaṇhāti, evameva ayaṃ araññādīsu kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto bhikkhu yathākkamena sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiarahattamagge ceva ariyaphalañca gaṇhatīti veditabbo. Tenāhu porāṇā –

This bhikkhu, however, is said to be like a leopard. For just as a great leopard-king, relying on a thicket of grass, a thicket of woods, or a mountain thicket in the forest, lies in wait and captures animals such as wild buffalo, gokaṇṇa deer, and boars; even so, it should be understood that this bhikkhu, applying himself to the meditation subject in the forest and other such places, gradually attains the paths of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and Arahantship, as well as the noble fruits. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Yathāpi [M 1.0262][V 1.0259] dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhatī mige;

Tathevāyaṃ buddhaputto, yuttayogo vipassako;

Araññaṃ pavisitvāna, gaṇhāti phalamuttama”nti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.374; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.107);

“Just as a leopard, lying in wait, captures game; even so, this son of the Buddha, one who has applied himself to the practice, an insight meditator, having entered the forest, attains the supreme fruit.”

Tenassa parakkamajavayoggabhūmiṃ araññasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha.

Therefore, the Blessed One, pointing out the forest dwelling as a suitable ground for the power of exertion, said the passage beginning with, “gone to the forest, or...”

218. Tattha araññagatoti “araññanti nikkhamitvā bahi indakhīlā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti (vibha. 529) ca, “āraññakaṃ nāma senāsanaṃ pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti (pārā. 654) ca evaṃ vuttalakkhaṇesu araññesu yaṃkiñci pavivekasukhaṃ araññaṃ gato. Rukkhamūlagatoti rukkhasamīpaṃ gato. Suññāgāragatoti suññaṃ vivittokāsaṃ gato. Ettha ca ṭhapetvā araññañca rukkhamūlañca avasesasattavidhasenāsanagatopi suññāgāragatoti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

218. Herein, ‘gone to the forest’ means having gone to any forest that provides the pleasure of seclusion, among those defined by characteristics stated in such texts as the Vibhaṅga: “Having gone out beyond the city boundary post, all that is forest,” and the Pārājika: “A forest dwelling is at a minimum distance of five hundred bow-lengths.” ‘Gone to the root of a tree’ means having gone near a tree. ‘Gone to an empty dwelling’ means having gone to an empty, secluded place. And here, setting aside the forest and the root of a tree, one who has gone to any of the remaining seven kinds of dwellings may also be called ‘one gone to an empty dwelling.’”

Evamassa ututtayānukūlaṃ dhātucariyānukūlañca ānāpānassatibhāvanānurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ upadisitvā alīnānuddhaccapakkhikaṃ santaṃ iriyāpathaṃ upadisanto nisīdatīti āha. Athassa nisajjāya daḷhabhāvaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ pavattanasukhataṃ ārammaṇapariggahūpāyañca dassento pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvātiādimāha. Tattha pallaṅkanti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Ābhujitvāti bandhitvā. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimasarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā. Aṭṭhārasapiṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Evañhi nisīdantassa cammamaṃsanhārūni na paṇamanti. Athassa yā tesaṃ paṇamanappaccayā khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā na uppajjanti. Tāsu anuppajjamānāsu cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ na paripatati, vuddhiṃ phātiṃ upagacchati. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā. Atha vā parīti pariggahaṭṭho. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho. Satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho. Tena vuccati “parimukhaṃ sati”nti evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vuttanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepo, pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ katvāti.

Having thus advised a dwelling suitable for the three seasons, conducive to the elements and temperaments, and appropriate for the development of mindfulness of breathing, and while instructing on a calm posture that is on the side of neither sluggishness nor restlessness, he said, 'he sits down.' Then, to show the firmness of the sitting, the ease with which the in-breaths and out-breaths occur, and the means for grasping the meditation object, he spoke the passage beginning with, 'having folded his legs crosswise.' Therein, 'crosswise' means the sitting posture with the thighs bound all around. 'Having folded' means having bound. 'Having set the body upright' means having placed the upper body straight, causing the eighteen vertebrae to meet end to end. For when one sits in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Then, for him, the feelings that would arise moment by moment because of their bending do not arise. When those feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject does not fall away, and it attains growth and expansion. 'Having established mindfulness at the forefront' means having placed mindfulness facing the meditation subject. Alternatively, 'pari' has the meaning of encompassing, 'mukha' has the meaning of outlet, and 'sati' has the meaning of establishment. Therefore, it is called 'parimukhaṃ satiṃ'. In this way, the meaning here should also be understood according to the method spoken in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Therein, this is the summary: having made mindfulness the encompassed outlet.

219. So [M 1.0263] satova assasati sato passasatīti so bhikkhu evaṃ nisīditvā evañca satiṃ [V 1.0260] upaṭṭhapetvā taṃ satiṃ avijahanto sato eva assasati sato passasati, satokārī hotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Idāni yehākārehi satokārī hoti, te dassetuṃ dīghaṃ vā assasantotiādimāha. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ “so satova assasati sato passasatī”ti etasseva vibhaṅge –

219. Regarding 'Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out': that monk, having sat down in this manner and established mindfulness in this way, not abandoning that mindfulness, breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully; thus, it is said he acts mindfully. Now, to show the ways in which he acts mindfully, he spoke the passage beginning with, 'Breathing in long...' For this has been stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga in the analysis of this very passage, 'Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out':

“Bāttiṃsāya ākārehi sato kārī hoti. Dīghaṃ assāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sato kārī hoti. Dīghaṃ passāsavasena…pe… paṭinissaggānupassī assāsavasena. Paṭinissaggānupassī passāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sato kārī hotī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.165).

One acts with mindfulness in thirty-two aspects. When one knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by means of a long in-breath, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, one acts with mindfulness. By means of a long out-breath... and so on... contemplating relinquishment by means of the in-breath. When one, contemplating relinquishment by means of the out-breath, knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, one acts with mindfulness.

Tattha dīghaṃ vā assasantoti dīghaṃ vā assāsaṃ pavattayanto. Assāsoti bahi nikkhamanavāto. Passāsoti anto pavisanavātoti vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Suttantaṭṭhakathāsu pana uppaṭipāṭiyā āgataṃ. Tattha sabbesampi gabbhaseyyakānaṃ mātukucchito nikkhamanakāle paṭhamaṃ abbhantaravāto bahi nikkhamati. Pacchā bāhiravāto sukhumarajaṃ gahetvā abbhantaraṃ pavisanto tāluṃ āhacca nibbāyati. Evaṃ tāva assāsapassāsā veditabbā.

Herein, 'breathing in long' means producing a long in-breath. 'In-breath' is the wind going out, and 'out-breath' is the wind coming in; so it is said in the Vinaya commentary. In the Sutta commentaries, however, it is given in the opposite order. There, for all beings lying in the womb, at the time of emerging from the mother’s womb, first the internal wind goes out; then the external wind, carrying subtle dust, enters inside and, striking the palate, ceases. Thus, in the first place, are the in-breaths and out-breaths to be understood.

Yā pana tesaṃ dīgharassatā, sā addhānavasena veditabbā. Yathā hi okāsaddhānaṃ pharitvā ṭhitaṃ udakaṃ vā vālikā vā “dīghamudakaṃ dīghā vālikā, rassamudakaṃ rassā vālikā”ti vuccati, evaṃ cuṇṇavicuṇṇāpi assāsapassāsā hatthisarīre ca ahisarīre ca tesaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ dīghaṃ addhānaṃ saṇikaṃ pūretvā saṇikameva nikkhamanti. Tasmā dīghāti vuccanti. Sunakhasasādīnaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ rassaṃ addhānaṃ sīghaṃ pūretvā sīghameva nikkhamanti, tasmā rassāti vuccanti. Manussesu pana keci hatthiahiādayo viya kāladdhānavasena dīghaṃ assasanti ca passasanti ca. Keci sunakhasasādayo viya rassaṃ, tasmā tesaṃ kālavasena dīghamaddhānaṃ [M 1.0264] nikkhamantā ca pavisantā ca te “dīghā” ittaramaddhānaṃ nikkhamantā ca pavisantā ca “rassā”ti veditabbā.

However, their quality of being long or short is to be understood by way of duration. For just as water or sand that has spread over an extent of space is called 'long water' or 'long sand,' and 'short water' or 'short sand,' so too, even though they are fine and subtle, the in-breaths and out-breaths in the bodies of elephants and snakes slowly fill the long extent designated as their individual existence and exit just as slowly. Therefore, they are called 'long.' They quickly fill the short extent designated as the individual existence of dogs, rabbits, and the like, and exit just as quickly; therefore, they are called 'short.' Among humans, however, some, like elephants, snakes, and so on, breathe in and out for a long duration by way of time. Some, like dogs, rabbits, and so on, breathe for a short duration. Therefore, for these beings, by way of time, those breaths that exit and enter over a long duration are to be known as 'long,' and those that exit and enter over a shorter duration are to be known as 'short.'

Tatrāyaṃ [V 1.0261] bhikkhu navahākārehi dīghaṃ assasanto passasanto ca “dīghaṃ assasāmi, passasāmī”ti pajānāti. Evaṃ pajānato cassa ekenākārena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā sampajjatīti veditabbā. Yathāha paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.166) –

Therein, this monk, breathing in long and breathing out long, knows by nine modes: 'I breathe in long; I breathe out long.' It should be known that for one who knows in this way, the development of the foundation of mindfulness as contemplation of the body is accomplished by one of these modes. As it was said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Kathaṃ dīghaṃ assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti. Dīghaṃ passasanto dīghaṃ passasāmīti pajānāti. Dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasati. Dīghaṃ passāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte passasati. Dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatipi passasatipi. Dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatopi passasatopi chando uppajjati. Chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasati. Chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ passāsaṃ…pe… dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatipi passasatipi. Chandavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatopi passasatopi pāmojjaṃ uppajjati. Pāmojjavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasati. Pāmojjavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ passāsaṃ…pe… dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatipi passasatipi. Pāmojjavasena tato sukhumataraṃ dīghaṃ assāsapassāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte assasatopi passasatopi dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā cittaṃ vivattati, upekkhā saṇṭhāti. Imehi navahi ākārehi dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā kāyo. Upaṭṭhānaṃ sati. Anupassanā ñāṇaṃ. Kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ, no sati. Sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati ca. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena taṃ kāyaṃ anupassati. Tena vuccati kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā”ti.
