How does one, when breathing in long, know: ‘I am breathing in long’? When breathing out long, know: ‘I am breathing out long’? One breathes in a long in-breath in a long duration. One breathes out a long out-breath in a long duration. One breathes in and breathes out a long in-and-out-breath in a long duration. For one breathing in and for one breathing out a long in-and-out-breath in a long duration, desire arises. By the power of desire, one thereupon breathes in a subtler long in-breath in a long duration. By the power of desire, one thereupon breathes out a subtler long out-breath… and so on… one breathes in and breathes out a subtler long in-and-out-breath in a long duration. By the power of desire, for one breathing in and for one breathing out a subtler long in-and-out-breath in a long duration, nascent joy arises. By the power of nascent joy, one thereupon breathes in a subtler long in-breath in a long duration. By the power of nascent joy, one thereupon breathes out a subtler long out-breath… and so on… one breathes in and breathes out a subtler long in-and-out-breath in a long duration. By the power of nascent joy, for one breathing in and for one breathing out a subtler long in-and-out-breath in a long duration, the mind turns away from the long in-and-out-breaths; equanimity is established. By these nine modes, the long in-and-out-breaths are the body. Establishment is mindfulness. Contemplation is knowledge. The body is establishment, not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both establishment and mindfulness. With that mindfulness and with that knowledge, one contemplates that body. Therefore, it is called the development of the establishment of mindfulness through contemplation of the body in the body.

Esa [M 1.0265] nayo rassapadepi. Ayaṃ pana viseso, yathā ettha “dīghaṃ assāsaṃ addhānasaṅkhāte”ti vuttaṃ, evamidha “rassaṃ assāsaṃ ittarasaṅkhāte assasatī”ti āgataṃ. Tasmā rassavasena yāva “tena vuccati kāye kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānabhāvanā”ti, tāva yojetabbaṃ.

This same method should be known in the section on the short breath as well. This, however, is the difference: just as here it was said, ‘a long in-breath in a long duration,’ so here it is stated, ‘one breathes in a short in-breath in a short duration.’ Therefore, by way of the short breath, the text should be connected as far as: ‘Therefore, it is called the development of the establishment of mindfulness through contemplation of the body in the body.’

Evaṃ ayaṃ addhānavasena ittaravasena ca imehākārehi assāsapassāse pajānanto dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti…pe… rassaṃ vā passasanto rassaṃ passasāmīti pajānātīti veditabbo. Evaṃ pajānato cassa –

Thus, it should be understood that a practitioner who knows the in-breaths and out-breaths by these modes, by way of duration and by way of brevity, when breathing in long knows, ‘I breathe in long,’… and so on… when breathing out short knows, ‘I breathe out short.’ And for one who knows thus:

Dīgho [V 1.0262] rasso ca assāso,

Passāsopi ca tādiso;

Cattāro vaṇṇā vattanti,

Nāsikaggeva bhikkhunoti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165);

The in-breath is long and short, and the out-breath is likewise; for a bhikkhu, these four kinds occur at the very tip of the nose.

220. Sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatīti sakalassa assāsakāyassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ viditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto assasissāmīti sikkhati. Sakalassa passāsakāyassa ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ viditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto passasissāmīti sikkhati. Evaṃ viditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto ñāṇasampayuttacittena assasati ceva passasati ca. Tasmā “assasissāmi passasissāmī”ti sikkhatīti vuccati. Ekassa hi bhikkhuno cuṇṇavicuṇṇavisaṭe assāsakāye passāsakāye vā ādi pākaṭo hoti, na majjhapariyosānaṃ. So ādimeva pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, majjhapariyosāne kilamati. Ekassa majjhaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, na ādipariyosānaṃ. Ekassa pariyosānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, na ādimajjhaṃ. So pariyosānaṃyeva pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, ādimajjhe kilamati. Ekassa sabbampi pākaṭaṃ hoti, so sabbampi pariggahetuṃ sakkoti, na katthaci kilamati, tādisena bhavitabbanti dassento āha – “sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmīti…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti.

220. ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body… and so on… I will breathe out experiencing the whole body,’ thus he trains. He trains thus: ‘I will breathe in,’ making known and making manifest the beginning, middle, and end of the entire in-breath body. He trains thus: ‘I will breathe out,’ making known and making manifest the beginning, middle, and end of the entire out-breath body. Thus making them known and manifest, he breathes in and out with a mind conjoined with knowledge. Therefore, he is said to be one who trains thus: ‘I will breathe in, I will breathe out.’ For one bhikkhu, with an in-breath body or out-breath body that is broken up and dispersed, the beginning is manifest, but not the middle and end. He is able to grasp only the beginning; he struggles with the middle and end. For another, the middle is manifest, but not the beginning and end. For another, the end is manifest, but not the beginning and middle. He is able to grasp only the end; he struggles with the beginning and middle. For another, the whole of it is manifest; he is able to grasp the whole of it and does not struggle anywhere. To show that one should become like this, it is said: ‘He trains, “I will breathe in experiencing the whole body… and so on… I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.”’

Tattha [M 1.0266] sikkhatīti evaṃ ghaṭati vāyamati. Yo vā tathābhūtassa saṃvaro, ayamettha adhisīlasikkhā. Yo tathābhūtassa samādhi, ayaṃ adhicittasikkhā. Yā tathābhūtassa paññā, ayaṃ adhipaññāsikkhāti imā tisso sikkhāyo tasmiṃ ārammaṇe tāya satiyā tena manasikārena sikkhati āsevati bhāveti bahulīkarotīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Herein, ‘he trains’ means he strives and makes an effort thus. Or, the restraint of one who is thus constituted—this is the training in higher virtue here. The concentration of one who is thus constituted—this is the training in higher mind. The wisdom of one who is thus constituted—this is the training in higher wisdom. The meaning here should be understood thus: with that object, with that mindfulness, and with that attention, he trains in, resorts to, develops, and makes much of these three trainings.

Tattha yasmā purimanaye kevalaṃ assasitabbaṃ passasitabbameva, na ca aññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ. Ito paṭṭhāya pana ñāṇuppādanādīsu yogo karaṇīyo. Tasmā tattha assasāmīti pajānāti passasāmīti pajānāticceva vattamānakālavasena pāḷiṃ vatvā ito paṭṭhāya kattabbassa ñāṇuppādanādino ākārassa dassanatthaṃ sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assasissāmītiādinā nayena anāgatavacanavasena pāḷi āropitāti veditabbā.

Herein, since in the previous method there was only breathing in and breathing out to be done, and nothing else was to be done, but from this point onward application should be made to the production of knowledge and so on, therefore, it should be understood that after stating the Pāli text there in the present tense—‘he knows, “I am breathing in”; he knows, “I am breathing out”’—from this point onward, to show the mode of what is to be done, such as the production of knowledge, the Pāli text is set down in the future tense with the method beginning, ‘I will breathe in experiencing the whole body,’ and so on.

Passambhayaṃ [V 1.0263] kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhatīti oḷārikaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento paṭippassambhento nirodhento vūpasamento assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati. Tatra evaṃ oḷārikasukhumatā ca passaddhi ca veditabbā. Imassa hi bhikkhuno pubbe apariggahitakāle kāyo ca cittañca sadarathā honti oḷārikā. Kāyacittānaṃ oḷārikatte avūpasante assāsapassāsāpi oḷārikā honti, balavatarā hutvā pavattanti, nāsikā nappahoti, mukhena assasantopi passasantopi tiṭṭhati. Yadā panassa kāyopi cittampi pariggahitā honti, tadā te santā honti vūpasantā. Tesu vūpasantesu assāsapassāsā sukhumā hutvā pavattanti, “atthi nu kho natthī”ti vicetabbatākārappattā honti.

'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation... I will breathe out calming the bodily formation,' thus he trains. He trains thus: 'I will breathe in... I will breathe out,' while calming, tranquillizing, causing to cease, and pacifying the gross bodily formation. Herein, grossness, subtlety, and tranquillity should be understood thus. For before this bhikkhu has apprehended the meditation subject, his body and mind are agitated and gross. When the grossness of body and mind is unpacified, the in-breaths and out-breaths are also gross; they occur with great force. The nose is not sufficient, and he stands breathing in and out through the mouth. But when his body and mind are apprehended, they become peaceful and especially pacified. When they are pacified, the in-breaths and out-breaths occur subtly, reaching a state where one must investigate whether they exist or not.

Seyyathāpi purisassa dhāvitvā, pabbatā vā orohitvā, mahābhāraṃ vā sīsato oropetvā ṭhitassa oḷārikā assāsapassāsā honti, nāsikā nappahoti, mukhena assasantopi passasantopi tiṭṭhati. Yadā panesa taṃ parissamaṃ vinodetvā nhatvā ca pivitvā ca allasāṭakaṃ hadaye katvā sītāya chāyāya nipanno hoti, athassa te assāsapassāsā [M 1.0267] sukhumā honti “atthi nu kho natthī”ti vicetabbatākārappattā, evameva imassa bhikkhuno pubbe apariggahitakāle kāyo ca…pe… vicetabbatākārappattā honti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hissa pubbe apariggahitakāle “oḷārikoḷārike kāyasaṅkhāre passambhemī”ti ābhogasamannāhāramanasikārapaccavekkhaṇā natthi, pariggahitakāle pana atthi. Tenassa apariggahitakālato pariggahitakāle kāyasaṅkhāro sukhumo hoti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

Just as for a man who has been running, or has descended from a mountain, or has stood up after putting down a heavy load from his head, his in-breaths and out-breaths are gross. His nose is not sufficient; he stands breathing in and out through his mouth. But when this man has dispelled that fatigue, has bathed and drunk, has placed a wet cloth over his heart, and is lying down in a cool shade, then his in-breaths and out-breaths become subtle, having reached a state where it must be investigated, 'Do they exist or not?' Even so, for this bhikkhu, previously at the time of non-apprehension, the body... they reach a state where they must be investigated. What is the reason for that? Because for him, previously at the time of non-apprehension, there is no adverting, applying, attending, or reviewing with the thought, 'I shall calm the gross bodily formations.' But at the time of apprehension, there is. Therefore, the bodily formation at the time of apprehension is subtler than at the time of non-apprehension. Hence the ancients have said:

“Sāraddhe kāye citte ca, adhimattaṃ pavattati;

Asāraddhamhi kāyamhi, sukhumaṃ sampavattatī”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165);

When body and mind are agitated, the bodily formation proceeds excessively; when the body is unagitated, it proceeds subtly.

221. Pariggahepi oḷāriko, paṭhamajjhānupacāre sukhumo. Tasmimpi oḷāriko, paṭhamajjhāne sukhumo. Paṭhamajjhāne ca dutiyajjhānupacāre ca oḷāriko, dutiyajjhāne sukhumo. Dutiyajjhāne ca tatiyajjhānupacāre ca oḷāriko, tatiyajjhāne sukhumo. Tatiyajjhāne ca catutthajjhānupacāre ca oḷāriko, catutthajjhāne atisukhumo appavattimeva pāpuṇātīti. Idaṃ tāva dīghabhāṇakasaṃyuttabhāṇakānaṃ mataṃ.

221. Even during apprehension, it is gross; in the access to the first jhāna, it is subtle. In that same access, it is gross; in the first jhāna, it is subtle. In the first jhāna and in the access to the second jhāna, it is gross; in the second jhāna, it is subtle. In the second jhāna and in the access to the third jhāna, it is gross; in the third jhāna, it is subtle. In the third jhāna and in the access to the fourth jhāna, it is gross; in the fourth jhāna, it is extremely subtle, reaching a state of non-occurrence. This, for now, is the view of the reciters of the Dīgha Nikāya and the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Majjhimabhāṇakā [V 1.0264] pana paṭhamajjhāne oḷāriko, dutiyajjhānupacāre sukhumoti evaṃ heṭṭhimaheṭṭhimajjhānato uparūparijjhānupacārepi sukhumataramicchanti. Sabbesaññeva pana matena apariggahitakāle pavattakāyasaṅkhāro pariggahitakāle paṭippassambhati. Pariggahitakāle pavattakāyasaṅkhāro paṭhamajjhānupacāre…pe… catutthajjhānupacāre pavattakāyasaṅkhāro catutthajjhāne paṭippassambhati. Ayaṃ tāva samathe nayo.

The reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, however, hold that it is gross in the first jhāna and subtle in the access to the second jhāna. Thus they maintain that it becomes progressively more subtle in the access to each higher jhāna than in the lower jhānas themselves. But according to the view of all, the bodily formation that occurs at the time of non-apprehension is tranquillized at the time of apprehension. The bodily formation that occurs at the time of apprehension is tranquillized in the access to the first jhāna... the bodily formation that occurs in the access to the fourth jhāna is tranquillized in the fourth jhāna. This, for now, is the method in regard to serenity.

Vipassanāyaṃ pana apariggahe pavatto kāyasaṅkhāro oḷāriko, mahābhūtapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, upādārūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, sakalarūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, arūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, rūpārūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, paccayapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, sappaccayanāmarūpapariggahe sukhumo. Sopi oḷāriko, lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāya sukhumo. Sopi dubbalavipassanāya oḷāriko, balavavipassanāya sukhumo. Tattha pubbe vuttanayeneva purimassa purimassa pacchimena [M 1.0268] pacchimena paṭippassaddhi veditabbā. Evamettha oḷārikasukhumatā ca passaddhi ca veditabbā.

In the case of insight, however, the bodily formation that occurs during non-apprehension is gross; at the apprehension of the great elements, it is subtle. That too is gross; at the apprehension of derived materiality, it is subtle. That too is gross; at the apprehension of all materiality, it is subtle. That too is gross; at the apprehension of immateriality, it is subtle. That too is gross; at the apprehension of materiality and immateriality, it is subtle. That too is gross; at the apprehension of conditions, it is subtle. That too is gross; at the apprehension of name-and-form with its conditions, it is subtle. That too is gross; in insight that takes the characteristics as its object, it is subtle. That too is gross in the case of weak insight, but subtle in the case of strong insight. Therein, the tranquillization of each preceding one by each succeeding one should be understood in the way stated before. Thus herein, grossness and subtlety, and tranquillity, should be understood.

Paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.171) panassa saddhiṃ codanāsodhanāhi evamattho vutto –

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however, its meaning has been stated together with objections and clarifications in the following manner:

“Kathaṃ passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmi…pe… passasissāmīti sikkhati? Katame kāyasaṅkhārā? Dīghaṃ assāsapassāsā kāyikā ete dhammā kāyapaṭibaddhā kāyasaṅkhārā. Te kāyasaṅkhāre passambhento nirodhento vūpasamento sikkhati…pe… yathārūpehi kāyasaṅkhārehi kāyassa ānamanā, vinamanā, sannamanā, paṇamanā, iñjanā, phandanā, calanā, kampanā passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti sikkhati, passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhati. Yathārūpehi kāyasaṅkhārehi kāyassa na ānamanā, na vinamanā, na sannamanā, na paṇamanā, aniñjanā, aphandanā, acalanā, akampanā santaṃ sukhumaṃ passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati.

How does one train, 'Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in... calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out'? What are the bodily formations? Long in-breaths and out-breaths are bodily; these phenomena, being bound to the body, are bodily formations. He trains calming, causing to cease, and pacifying these bodily formations... With whatever kind of bodily formations there is bending forward, bending sideways, bending all around, bending backward, stirring, throbbing, shaking, and trembling of the body, he trains, 'Calming that bodily formation, I shall breathe in'; he trains, 'Calming that bodily formation, I shall breathe out.' With whatever kind of bodily formations there is no bending forward, no bending sideways, no bending all around, no bending backward of the body, but there is non-stirring, non-throbbing, non-shaking, and non-trembling, he trains, 'Calming that calm and subtle bodily formation, I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out.'

“Iti kira passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmīti sikkhati. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ [V 1.0265] passasissāmīti sikkhati. Evaṃ sante vātūpaladdhiyā ca pabhāvanā na hoti. Assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā na hoti. Ānāpānassatiyā ca pabhāvanā na hoti, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā na hoti, na ca naṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā samāpajjantipi vuṭṭhahantipi.

If, it is said, one trains thus: 'Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in,' and one trains: 'Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out,' this being so, there is no development of the apprehension of the wind, there is no development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, there is no development of mindfulness of breathing, and there is no development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; and the wise can neither enter upon nor emerge from that attainment.

“Iti kira passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati. Evaṃ sante vātūpaladdhiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā hoti, tañca naṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā samāpajjantipi vuṭṭhahantipi. Yathā kathaṃ viya?

If one trains thus: 'Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in and I shall breathe out,' this being so, there is development of the apprehension of the wind, there is development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, there is development of mindfulness of breathing, and there is development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; and the wise can both enter upon and emerge from that attainment. How so?

“Seyyathāpi kaṃse ākoṭite paṭhamaṃ oḷārikā saddā pavattanti. Oḷārikānaṃ saddānaṃ nimittaṃ sugahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi oḷārike sadde atha pacchā sukhumakā [M 1.0269] saddā pavattanti. Sukhumakānaṃ saddānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi sukhumake sadde atha pacchā sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇatāpi cittaṃ pavattati, evameva paṭhamaṃ oḷārikā assāsapassāsā pavattanti. Oḷārikānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi oḷārike assāsapassāse atha pacchā sukhumakā assāsapassāsā pavattanti. Sukhumakānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ nimittaṃ suggahitattā sumanasikatattā sūpadhāritattā niruddhepi sukhumake assāsapassāse atha pacchā sukhumaassāsapassāsanimittārammaṇatāpi cittaṃ na vikkhepaṃ gacchati.

Just as when a bronze gong is struck, at first coarse sounds occur. Because the sign of the coarse sounds has been well grasped, well attended to, and well considered, even after the coarse sounds have ceased, then afterwards subtle sounds occur. Because the sign of the subtle sounds has been well grasped, well attended to, and well considered, even after the subtle sounds have ceased, then afterwards the mind proceeds with the subtle sound-sign as its object. So too, at first coarse in-breaths and out-breaths occur. Because the sign of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths has been well grasped, well attended to, and well considered, even after the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, then afterwards subtle in-breaths and out-breaths occur. Because the sign of the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths has been well grasped, well attended to, and well considered, even after the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, then afterwards the mind, having the sign of the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths as its object, does not go to distraction.

“Evaṃ sante vātūpaladdhiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, assāsapassāsānañca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatiyā ca pabhāvanā hoti, ānāpānassatisamādhissa ca pabhāvanā hoti, tañca naṃ samāpattiṃ paṇḍitā samāpajjantipi vuṭṭhahantipi. Passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assāsapassāsā kāyo, upaṭṭhānaṃ sati, anupassanā ñāṇaṃ, kāyo upaṭṭhānaṃ, no sati, sati upaṭṭhānañceva sati ca, tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena taṃ kāyaṃ anupassati. Tena vuccati kāye kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā”ti.

When this is so, there is development of the apprehension of the wind, there is development of in-breaths and out-breaths, there is development of mindfulness of breathing, and there is development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing; and the wise both enter upon and emerge from that attainment. In the phrase ‘calming the bodily formation’: the in-breaths and out-breaths are the ‘body’; mindfulness is the ‘establishment’; contemplation is ‘knowledge.’ The body is the establishment, not mindfulness. But mindfulness is both establishment and mindfulness. With that mindfulness, with that knowledge, one contemplates that body. Therefore this is called ‘the development of the establishment of mindfulness by contemplating the body in the body.’

Ayaṃ [V 1.0266] tāvettha kāyānupassanāvasena vuttassa paṭhamacatukkassa anupubbapadavaṇṇanā.

This, in the first place, is the sequential explanation of the words of the first tetrad spoken by way of the contemplation of the body.

222. Yasmā panettha idameva catukkaṃ ādikammikassa kammaṭṭhānavasena vuttaṃ. Itarāni pana tīṇi catukkāni ettha pattajjhānassa vedanācittadhammānupassanāvasena vuttāni. Tasmā idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānapadaṭṭhānāya vipassanāya saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitukāmena ādikammikena kulaputtena pubbe vuttanayeneva sīlaparisodhanādīni sabbakiccāni katvā vuttappakārassa ācariyassa santike pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetabbaṃ.

222. Because herein this very tetrad is spoken of by way of the meditation subject for a beginner, while the other three tetrads are spoken of for one who has attained jhāna by way of the contemplation of feelings, mind, and dhammas; therefore, a clansman who is a beginner and wishes to attain Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges by developing this meditation subject with insight that has the fourth Ānāpāna-jhāna as its basis, should first fulfill all duties beginning with the purification of virtue in the way already described, and then learn the five-limbed meditation subject from a teacher of the kind mentioned.

Tatrime [M 1.0270] pañca sandhayo uggaho, paripucchā, upaṭṭhānaṃ, appanā, lakkhaṇanti. Tattha uggaho nāma kammaṭṭhānassa uggaṇhanaṃ. Paripucchā nāma kammaṭṭhānassa paripucchanā. Upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma kammaṭṭhānassa upaṭṭhānaṃ. Appanā nāma kammaṭṭhānassa appanā. Lakkhaṇaṃ nāma kammaṭṭhānassa lakkhaṇaṃ. “Evaṃlakkhaṇamidaṃ kammaṭṭhāna”nti kammaṭṭhānasabhāvūpadhāraṇanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, these are the five limbs: learning, inquiry, appearance, absorption, and characteristic. Therein, learning is the learning of the meditation subject. Inquiry is the questioning concerning the meditation subject. Appearance is the noting of the sign's appearance. Absorption is the attainment of absorption. Characteristic is the discerning of the characteristic. This is said to be the determination of the intrinsic nature of the meditation subject, as in: ‘This meditation subject has such a characteristic.’

Evaṃ pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhanto attanāpi na kilamati, ācariyampi na viheseti. Tasmā thokaṃ uddisāpetvā bahukālaṃ sajjhāyitvā evaṃ pañcasandhikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā ācariyassa santike vā aññatra vā pubbe vuttappakāre senāsane vasantena upacchinnakhuddakapalibodhena katabhattakiccena bhattasammadaṃ paṭivinodetvā sukhanisinnena ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena cittaṃ sampahaṃsetvā ācariyuggahato ekapadampi asammuyhantena idaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ manasikāravidhi –

One who learns this five-limbed meditation subject in this way neither tires himself nor vexes his teacher. Therefore, having had a little pointed out and having recited it for a long time, having thus learned the five-limbed meditation subject, dwelling either in the presence of the teacher or elsewhere in a lodging of the kind already described, having cut off the minor impediments, having finished his meal and dispelled his drowsiness from the food, seated comfortably, having gladdened his mind by recollecting the qualities of the Three Jewels, and without becoming confused about a single phrase of what he learned from the teacher, he should apply his mind to this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing. Herein, this is the method of application:

223.

223.

Gaṇanā anubandhanā, phusanā ṭhapanā sallakkhaṇā;

Vivaṭṭanā pārisuddhi, tesañca paṭipassanāti.

Counting and following, touching and fixing, observing, turning away, purification, and the reviewing of them.

Tattha gaṇanāti gaṇanāyeva. Anubandhanāti anuvahanā. Phusanāti phuṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ. Ṭhapanāti appanā. Sallakkhaṇāti vipassanā. Vivaṭṭanāti maggo. Pārisuddhīti phalaṃ. Tesañca paṭipassanāti paccavekkhaṇā.

Herein, counting is just counting. Following is continuous application. Touching is the place of contact. Fixing is absorption. Observing is insight. Turning away is the path. Purification is the fruit. And the reviewing of them is reviewing.

Tattha iminā ādikammikena kulaputtena paṭhamaṃ gaṇanāya idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ[V 1.0267]. Gaṇentena ca pañcannaṃ heṭṭhā na ṭhapetabbaṃ. Dasannaṃ upari na netabbaṃ. Antarā khaṇḍaṃ na dassetabbaṃ. Pañcannaṃ heṭṭhā ṭhapentassa hi sambādhe okāse cittuppādo vipphandati sambādhe vaje sanniruddhagogaṇo viya. Dasannampi upari nentassa gaṇananissitako cittuppādo hoti. Antarā khaṇḍaṃ dassentassa “sikhāppattaṃ nu kho me kammaṭṭhānaṃ, no”ti cittaṃ vikampati. Tasmā ete dose vajjetvā gaṇetabbaṃ.

Here, this clansman who is a beginner should first apply his mind to this meditation subject by means of counting. When counting, he should not stop below five and should not go beyond ten. He should not show a break in the middle. For one who stops below five, the mind flutters in the confined space like a herd of cattle shut up in a narrow pen. For one who goes beyond ten, the mind becomes dependent on the counting. For one who shows a break in the middle, his mind wavers, wondering: ‘Has my meditation subject reached its culmination or not?’ Therefore, one should count avoiding these faults.

Gaṇentena ca paṭhamaṃ dandhagaṇanāya dhaññamāpakagaṇanāya gaṇetabbaṃ. Dhaññamāpako hi nāḷiṃ pūretvā “eka”nti vatvā okirati. Puna pūrento kiñci kacavaraṃ disvā taṃ chaḍḍento “ekaṃ eka”nti vadati. Esa nayo dve dvetiādīsu. Evameva imināpi assāsapassāsesu yo upaṭṭhāti, taṃ [M 1.0271] gahetvā “ekaṃ eka”nti ādiṃ katvā yāva “dasa dasā”ti pavattamānaṃ pavattamānaṃ upalakkhetvāva gaṇetabbaṃ. Tassa evaṃ gaṇayato nikkhamantā ca pavisantā ca assāsapassāsā pākaṭā honti.

When counting, one should first count with the slow counting, the counting of a grain-measurer. For a grain-measurer, having filled his measure, says ‘one’ and empties it. Then, while filling it again, if he sees some rubbish, he removes it and says, ‘one, one.’ This same method applies to ‘two, two,’ and so on. In the same way, this meditator too should count by taking up whichever in-breath or out-breath presents itself, beginning with ‘one, one,’ and marking them as they occur continuously up to ‘ten, ten.’ For one who counts in this way, the outgoing and incoming breaths become manifest.

Athānena taṃ dandhagaṇanaṃ dhaññamāpakagaṇanaṃ pahāya sīghagaṇanāya gopālakagaṇanāya gaṇetabbaṃ. Cheko hi gopālako sakkharādayo ucchaṅgena gahetvā rajjudaṇḍahattho pātova vajaṃ gantvā gāvo piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā palighatthambhamatthake nisinno dvārappattaṃ dvārappattaṃyeva gāviṃ ekā dveti sakkharaṃ khipitvā gaṇeti. Tiyāmarattiṃ sambādhe okāse dukkhaṃ vutthagogaṇo nikkhamanto nikkhamanto aññamaññaṃ upanighaṃsanto vegena vegena puñjapuñjo hutvā nikkhamati. So vegena vegena “tīṇi cattāri pañca dasā”ti gaṇetiyeva, evamimassāpi purimanayena gaṇayato assāsapassāsā pākaṭā hutvā sīghaṃ sīghaṃ punappunaṃ sañcaranti. Tatonena “punappunaṃ sañcarantī”ti ñatvā anto ca bahi ca agahetvā dvārappattaṃ dvārappattaṃyeva gahetvā “eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañca cha. Eko dve tīṇi cattāri pañca cha satta…pe… aṭṭha, nava, dasā”ti sīghaṃ sīyaṃ gaṇetabbameva. Gaṇanapaṭibaddhe hi kammaṭṭhāne gaṇanabaleneva cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, arittupatthambhanavasena caṇḍasote nāvāṭṭhapanamiva.

Then, abandoning that slow counting, the counting of the grain-measurer, he should count with the quick counting, the counting of a cowherd. For a clever cowherd, taking pebbles or the like in his lap, with a rope and stick in his hand, goes to the pen in the morning, and striking the cows on their backs, he sits on top of the gate-post and counts each cow just as it reaches the gate, throwing down a pebble for each, saying, ‘One, two.’ The herd of cattle, having passed the three watches of the night uncomfortably in a confined space, comes out in a great rush, in bunches, rubbing against one another. He counts them very quickly: ‘Three, four, five… ten.’ Similarly, for this meditator counting in the former way, the in-breaths and out-breaths become manifest and move back and forth very quickly and repeatedly. Then, having understood, ‘They move repeatedly,’ without grasping them inside or outside, he should count swiftly just as each reaches the nostril-door: ‘One, two, three, four, five, six; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven… eight, nine, ten.’ For in a meditation subject that is connected with counting, the mind becomes one-pointed by the power of counting alone, like the stationing of a boat in a fierce current by means of a pole.

Tassevaṃ sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gaṇayato kammaṭṭhānaṃ nirantaraṃ pavattaṃ viya hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Atha nirantaraṃ pavattatīti ñatvā anto ca bahi ca vātaṃ apariggahetvā purimanayeneva vegena vegena gaṇetabbaṃ. Anto pavisanavātena hi saddhiṃ cittaṃ pavesayato abbhantaraṃ vātabbhāhataṃ medapūritaṃ [V 1.0268] viya hoti. Bahi nikkhamanavātena saddhiṃ cittaṃ nīharato bahiddhā puthuttārammaṇe cittaṃ vikkhipati. Phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhokāse pana satiṃ ṭhapetvā bhāventasseva bhāvanā sampajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “anto ca bahi ca vātaṃ apariggahetvā purimanayeneva vegena vegena gaṇetabba”nti.

For one who counts thus swiftly, the meditation subject presents itself as if occurring without interruption. Then, knowing that it occurs without interruption, he should count swiftly in the same manner as before, without grasping the breath inside or outside. For when one directs the mind along with the incoming breath, the inside of the body feels as if struck by wind and filled with fat. When one leads the mind out along with the outgoing breath, the mind becomes distracted by various external objects. But the development of meditation succeeds only for one who establishes mindfulness on the very spot of contact and develops it. Therefore it was said: ‘Without grasping the breath inside or outside, one should count swiftly in the same manner as before.’

Kīvaciraṃ panetaṃ gaṇetabbanti? Yāva vinā gaṇanāya assāsapassāsārammaṇe sati santiṭṭhati. Bahivisaṭavitakkavicchedaṃ katvā assāsapassāsārammaṇe satisaṇṭhāpanatthaṃyeva hi gaṇanāti.

For how long should one count? Until mindfulness is established on the in-and-out breath as its object without counting. For counting is for the purpose of cutting off externally scattered thoughts and establishing mindfulness on the in-and-out breath.

224. Evaṃ [M 1.0272] gaṇanāya manasi katvā anubandhanāya manasi kātabbaṃ. Anubandhanā nāma gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā satiyā nirantaraṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ anugamanaṃ. Tañca kho na ādimajjhapariyosānānugamanavasena. Bahinikkhamanavātassa hi nābhi ādi, hadayaṃ majjhaṃ, nāsikaggaṃ pariyosānaṃ. Abbhantaraṃ pavisanavātassa nāsikaggaṃ ādi, hadayaṃ majjhaṃ nābhi pariyosānaṃ. Tañcassa anugacchato vikkhepagataṃ cittaṃ sāraddhāya ceva hoti iñjanāya ca. Yathāha –

224. Having thus attended by way of counting, one should then attend by way of following. Following means withdrawing the counting and continuously pursuing the in-breaths and out-breaths with mindfulness. And this is not by way of following them to their beginning, middle, and end. For the outgoing breath, the navel is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the tip of the nose is the end. For the incoming breath, the tip of the nose is the beginning, the heart is the middle, and the navel is the end. For one who follows it thus, his scattered mind becomes agitated and stirred. As it is said:

“Assāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato ajjhattaṃ vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā ca. Passāsādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchato bahiddhā vikkhepagatena cittena kāyopi cittampi sāraddhā ca honti iñjitā ca phanditā cā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.157).

‘When one follows the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath with mindfulness, with a mind scattered internally, both body and mind become agitated, stirred, and tremble. When one follows the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath with mindfulness, with a mind scattered externally, both body and mind become agitated, stirred, and tremble.’

Tasmā anubandhanāya manasikarontena ādimajjhapariyosānavasena na manasi kātabbaṃ. Apica kho phusanāvasena ca ṭhapanāvasena ca manasi kātabbaṃ. Gaṇanānubandhanāvasena viya hi phusanāṭhapanāvasena visuṃ manasikāro natthi. Phuṭṭhaphuṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva pana gaṇento gaṇanāya ca phusanāya ca manasi karoti. Tattheva gaṇanaṃ paṭisaṃharitvā te satiyā anubandhanto, appanāvasena ca cittaṃ ṭhapento anubandhanāya ca phusanāya ca ṭhapanāya ca manasi karotīti vuccati. Svāyamattho aṭṭhakathāsu vuttapaṅguḷadovārikūpamāhi paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttakakacūpamāya ca veditabbo.

Therefore, when attending by way of following, one should not attend by way of the beginning, middle, and end. Rather, one should attend by way of touching and by way of fixing. For, unlike by way of counting and following, there is not a separate act of attention by way of touching and fixing. Instead, while counting at the very spot of contact, one attends by way of counting and by way of touching. When, having withdrawn the counting at that very spot, one follows them with mindfulness while fixing the mind by way of absorption, one is said to attend by way of following, touching, and fixing. This meaning should be understood through the similes of the lame man and the gatekeeper stated in the commentaries, and through the simile of the saw stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

225. Tatrāyaṃ paṅguḷopamā – seyyathāpi paṅguḷo dolāya kīḷataṃ mātāputtānaṃ dolaṃ khipitvā [V 1.0269] tattheva dolāthambhamūle nisinno kamena āgacchantassa ca gacchantassa ca dolāphalakassa ubho koṭiyo majjhañca passati, na ca ubhokoṭimajjhānaṃ dassanatthaṃ byāvaṭo hoti, evamevāyaṃ bhikkhu sativasena upanibandhanathambhamūle ṭhatvā assāsapassāsadolaṃ khipitvā tattheva nimitte satiyā nisīdanto kamena āgacchantānañca gacchantānañca phuṭṭhaṭṭhāne assāsapassāsānaṃ ādimajjhapariyosānaṃ satiyā anugacchanto tattha ca cittaṃ ṭhapento passati, na ca tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ byāvaṭo hoti, ayaṃ paṅguḷopamā.

225. Herein, this is the simile of the lame man: Just as a lame man, having pushed the swing for a mother and son playing on it, sits right there at the base of the swing post and sees both ends and the middle of the swing plank as it comes and goes in sequence, and is not occupied with seeing its two ends and middle; so too this bhikkhu, standing by means of mindfulness at the base of the tying-post, having set in motion the swing of the in-and-out breaths, sitting with mindfulness at that very sign, sees the beginning, middle, and end of the in-and-out breaths at the point of contact as they come and go in sequence, following them with mindfulness and placing his mind there, and is not occupied with seeing them. This is the simile of the lame man.

226. Ayaṃ [M 1.0273] pana dovārikūpamā – seyyathāpi dovāriko nagarassa anto ca bahi ca purise “ko tvaṃ, kuto vā āgato, kuhiṃ vā gacchasi, kiṃ vā te hatthe”ti na vīmaṃsati. Na hi tassa te bhārā, dvārappattaṃ dvārappattaṃyeva pana vīmaṃsati, evameva imassa bhikkhuno antopaviṭṭhavātā ca bahinikkhantavātā ca na bhārā honti, dvārappattā dvārappattāyeva bhārāti ayaṃ dovārikūpamā.

226. This, however, is the simile of the gatekeeper: Just as a gatekeeper of a city does not investigate people inside or outside the city—asking, 'Who are you? Where have you come from? Where are you going? What is in your hand?'—for they are not his responsibility. He investigates only each and every one who arrives at the gate. So too, for this bhikkhu, the breaths that have entered inside and the breaths that have gone outside are not his responsibility. Only the breaths that arrive at the gate are his responsibility. This is the simile of the gatekeeper.

227. Kakacūpamā pana ādito paṭṭhāya evaṃ veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

227. The simile of the saw, however, should be understood from the beginning thus. For this was said:

“Nimittaṃ assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Ajānato ca tayo dhamme, bhāvanā nupalabbhati.

'The sign, the in-breaths and out-breaths, are not the object of a single consciousness; and for one who does not know these three things, development is not obtained.'

“Nimittaṃ assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Jānato ca tayo dhamme, bhāvanā upalabbhatī”ti. (paṭi. ma. 1.159);

'The sign, the in-breaths and out-breaths, are not the object of a single consciousness; and for one who knows these three things, development is obtained.'

“Kathaṃ ime tayo dhammā ekacittassa ārammaṇā na honti, na cime tayo dhammā aviditā honti, na ca cittaṃ vikkhepaṃ gacchati, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhi gacchati? Seyyathāpi rukkho same bhūmibhāge nikkhitto, tamenaṃ puriso kakacena chindeyya. Rukkhe phuṭṭhakakacadantānaṃ vasena purisassa sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, na āgate vā gate vā [V 1.0270] kakacadante manasi karoti, na āgatā vā gatā vā kakacadantā aviditā honti, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati.

'How is it that these three things are not the objects of a single consciousness, and yet these three things are not unknown, and the mind does not go to distraction, while striving is manifest, application is accomplished, and distinction is attained? Suppose a tree were laid on level ground, and a man were to cut it with a saw. The man’s mindfulness is established by means of the saw’s teeth in contact with the tree. He does not attend to the saw’s teeth that are coming or going, yet the saw’s teeth that are coming or going are not unknown to him; and striving is manifest, application is accomplished, and he attains distinction.'

“Yathā rukkho same bhūmibhāge nikkhitto, evaṃ upanibandhanānimittaṃ. Yathā kakacadantā, evaṃ assāsapassāsā. Yathā rukkhe phuṭṭhakakacadantānaṃ vasena purisassa sati upaṭṭhitā hoti, na āgate vā gate vā kakacadante manasi karoti, na āgatā vā gatā vā kakacadantā aviditā honti, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati, evameva bhikkhu nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā nisinno hoti, na āgate vā gate vā assāsapassāse manasi karoti, na ca āgatā vā gatā vā assāsapassāsā aviditā [M 1.0274] honti, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati.

'As the tree laid on level ground, so is the sign for binding the mind. As the saw’s teeth, so are the in-breaths and out-breaths. Just as the man’s mindfulness is established by means of the saw’s teeth in contact with the tree, and he does not attend to the saw’s teeth that are coming or going, yet the saw’s teeth that are coming or going are not unknown to him, while striving is manifest, application is accomplished, and he attains distinction; so too, a bhikkhu sits having established mindfulness at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth, and he does not attend to the in-breaths and out-breaths that are coming or going, yet the in-breaths and out-breaths that are coming or going are not unknown to him, while striving is manifest, application is accomplished, and he attains distinction.'

“Padhānanti katamaṃ padhānaṃ? Āraddhavīriyassa kāyopi cittampi kammaniyaṃ hoti, idaṃ padhānaṃ. Katamo payogo? Āraddhavīriyassa upakkilesā pahīyanti, vitakkā vūpasamanti, ayaṃ payogo. Katamo viseso? Āraddhavīriyassa saṃyojanā pahīyanti, anusayā byantī honti, ayaṃ viseso. Evaṃ ime tayo dhammā ekacittassa ārammaṇā na honti, na cime tayo dhammā aviditā honti, na ca cittaṃ vikkhepaṃ gacchati, padhānañca paññāyati, payogañca sādheti, visesamadhigacchati (paṭi. ma. 1.159).

'What is striving? For one with energy aroused, both body and mind become workable—this is striving. What is application? For one with energy aroused, defilements are abandoned and thoughts are stilled—this is application. What is distinction? For one with energy aroused, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are brought to an end—this is distinction. Thus these three things are not the objects of a single consciousness, and yet these three things are not unknown, and the mind does not go to distraction; striving is manifest, application is accomplished, and distinction is attained.'

“Ānāpānassati yassa, paripuṇṇā subhāvitā;

Anupubbaṃ paricitā, yathā buddhena desitā;

So imaṃ lokaṃ pabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā”ti. (paṭi. ma. 1.160);

'One for whom mindfulness of breathing is complete and well-developed, cultivated in sequence as taught by the Buddha, illuminates this world like the moon freed from a cloud.'

Ayaṃ kakacūpamā. Idha panassa āgatāgatavasena amanasikāramattameva payojananti veditabbaṃ.

This is the simile of the saw. Here, however, it should be understood that its purpose is simply non-attention to the coming and going.

228. Idaṃ [V 1.0271] kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaroto kassaci na cireneva nimittañca uppajjati, avasesajhānaṅgapaṭimaṇḍitā appanāsaṅkhātā ṭhapanā ca sampajjati. Kassaci pana gaṇanāvaseneva manasikārakālato pabhuti anukkamato oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodhavasena kāyadarathe vūpasante kāyopi cittampi lahukaṃ hoti, sarīraṃ ākāse laṅghanākārappattaṃ viya hoti. Yathā sāraddhakāyassa mañce vā pīṭhe vā nisīdato mañcapīṭhaṃ onamati, vikūjati, paccattharaṇaṃ valiṃ gaṇhāti. Asāraddhakāyassa pana nisīdato neva mañcapīṭhaṃ onamati, na vikūjati, na paccattharaṇaṃ valiṃ gaṇhāti, tūlapicupūritaṃ viya mañcapīṭhaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā asāraddho kāyo lahuko hoti. Evameva gaṇanāvasena manasikārakālato pabhuti anukkamato oḷārikaassāsapassāsanirodhavasena kāyadarathe vūpasante kāyopi cittampi lahukaṃ hoti, sarīraṃ ākāse laṅghanākārappattaṃ viya hoti.

228. For one who attends to this meditation subject, the counterpart sign soon arises, and the establishment of mind known as absorption, adorned with the remaining jhāna factors, is accomplished. But for some, from the time of attending by way of counting, as the bodily distress is calmed through the successive cessation of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths, both body and mind become light, and the body feels as if it were about to leap into the air. Just as when a person with a weary body sits on a bed or chair, the bed or chair bends and creaks, and the covering gathers folds; but when a person with an unweary body sits, the bed or chair does not bend, does not creak, nor does the covering gather folds; it is as if the bed or chair were filled with cotton-wool. Why? Because an unweary body is light. Just so, from the time of attending by way of counting, as the bodily distress is calmed through the successive cessation of the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths, both body and mind become light, and the body feels as if it were about to leap into the air.

Tassa [M 1.0275] oḷārike assāsapassāse niruddhe sukhumassāsapassāsanimittārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ pavattati. Tasmimpi niruddhe aparāparaṃ tato sukhumataraṃ sukhumataraṃ nimittārammaṇaṃ pavattatiyeva. Kathaṃ? Yathā puriso mahatiyā lohasalākāya kaṃsathālaṃ ākoṭeyya, ekappahārena mahāsaddo uppajjeyya, tassa oḷārikasaddārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ pavatteyya. Niruddhe oḷārike sadde atha pacchā sukhumasaddanimittārammaṇaṃ, tasmimpi niruddhe aparāparaṃ tato sukhumataraṃ sukhumataraṃ saddanimittārammaṇaṃ pavattateva, evanti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampicetaṃ – “seyyathāpi kaṃse ākoṭite”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.171) vitthāro.

When his coarse in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, his mind continues with the subtle sign of the in-breaths and out-breaths as its object. When that too has ceased, the mind indeed proceeds with a successively subtler and subtler sign as its object. How so? Suppose a man strikes a bronze bowl with a large iron rod; with a single stroke a loud sound arises, and his mind proceeds with the coarse sound as its object. When the coarse sound has ceased, afterwards the mind proceeds with the subtle sound-sign as its object; when that too has ceased, the mind indeed proceeds with a successively subtler and subtler sound-sign as its object; so it should be understood. And this was also said: 'Just as when a bronze bowl is struck...' (Paṭis I 171)—the detailed account should be known from there.

229. Yathā hi aññāni kammaṭṭhānāni uparūpari vibhūtāni honti, na tathā idaṃ. Idaṃ pana uparūpari bhāventassa sukhumattaṃ gacchati, upaṭṭhānampi na upagacchati, evaṃ anupaṭṭhahante pana tasmiṃ tena bhikkhunā uṭṭhāyāsanā cammakhaṇḍaṃ papphoṭetvā na gantabbaṃ. Kiṃ kātabbaṃ? “Ācariyaṃ pucchissāmī”ti vā, “naṭṭhaṃ dāni me kammaṭṭhāna”nti vā na vuṭṭhātabbaṃ. Iriyāpathaṃ vikopetvā gacchato hi kammaṭṭhānaṃ navanavameva hoti. Tasmā yathānisinneneva desato āharitabbaṃ.

229. For while other meditation subjects become clearer stage by stage, this one does not. Rather, as this one is developed stage by stage, it becomes more subtle and may even fail to appear. Yet when it fails to appear, the bhikkhu should not get up from his seat, shake out his piece of leather, and leave. What is to be done? He should not get up thinking, 'I will ask the teacher,' or, 'My meditation subject is now lost.' For if he goes after breaking his posture, the meditation subject becomes entirely new. Therefore, he should bring it back from its location while remaining seated just as he was.

Tatrāyaṃ āharaṇūpāyo, tena hi bhikkhunā kammaṭṭhānassa anupaṭṭhānabhāvaṃ ñatvā iti paṭisañcikkhitabbaṃ, ime assāsapassāsā nāma kattha atthi, kattha natthi. Kassa vā atthi, kassa [V 1.0272] vā natthīti. Athevaṃ paṭisañcikkhatā ime antomātukucchiyaṃ natthi, udake nimuggānaṃ natthi, tathā asaññībhūtānaṃ, matānaṃ, catutthajjhānasamāpannānaṃ, rūpārūpabhavasamaṅgīnaṃ, nirodhasamāpannānanti ñatvā evaṃ attanāva attā paṭicodetabbo “nanu tvaṃ, paṇḍita, neva mātukucchigato, na udake nimuggo, na asaññībhūto, na mato, na catutthajjhānasamāpanno, na rūpārūpabhavasamaṅgī, na nirodhasamāpanno. Atthiyeva te assāsapassāsā, mandapaññatāya pana pariggahetuṃ na sakkosī”ti. Athānena pakatiphuṭṭhavasena cittaṃ ṭhapetvā manasikāro pavattetabbo. Ime hi dīghanāsikassa nāsāpuṭaṃ ghaṭṭentā pavattanti. Rassanāsikassa uttaroṭṭhaṃ. Tasmānena imaṃ nāma ṭhānaṃ ghaṭṭentīti nimittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ. Imameva hi atthavasaṃ paṭicca vuttaṃ bhagavatā – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, muṭṭhasatissa asampajānassa ānāpānassatibhāvanaṃ vadāmī”ti (ma. ni. 3.149; saṃ. ni. 5.992).

Here is the method for bringing it back: The bhikkhu, knowing that the meditation subject is not appearing, should reflect thus: 'Where do these in-breaths and out-breaths exist, and where do they not exist? For whom do they exist, and for whom do they not?' Reflecting thus, he understands: 'They do not exist for one in the mother’s womb, nor for those submerged in water, nor for unconscious beings, nor for the dead, nor for those attained to the fourth jhāna, nor for beings of the form and formless existences, nor for those attained to cessation.' Knowing this, he should admonish himself thus: 'Surely, you wise one, are not in the mother’s womb, nor submerged in water, nor unconscious, nor dead, nor attained to the fourth jhāna, nor a being of the form or formless existences, nor attained to cessation. You do have in-breaths and out-breaths, but owing to your dull wisdom, you are unable to grasp them.' Then, establishing the mind on the place of natural contact, he should apply attention. For these breaths occur striking the tip of the nose of one with a long nose, and the upper lip of one with a short nose. Therefore, he should establish the sign thus: 'They strike this particular place.' It is for this very reason that the Blessed One said: 'Bhikkhus, I do not say that the development of mindfulness of breathing is for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension' (Majjhima Nikāya 3.149; Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.992).

230. Kiñcāpi [M 1.0276] hi yaṃkiñci kammaṭṭhānaṃ satassa sampajānasseva sampajjati. Ito aññaṃ pana manasikarontassa pākaṭaṃ hoti. Idaṃ pana ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ garukaṃ garukabhāvanaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhaputtānaṃ mahāpurisānaṃyeva manasikārabhūmibhūtaṃ, na ceva ittaraṃ, na ca ittarasattasamāsevitaṃ. Yathā yathā manasi karīyati, tathā tathā santañceva hoti sukhumañca. Tasmā ettha balavatī sati ca paññā ca icchitabbā.

230. Although it is true that any meditation subject succeeds only for one who is mindful and clearly comprehending, a meditation subject other than this one becomes manifest for one who attends to it. This meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing, however, is weighty and of arduous development, being the very ground for the attention of great beings—that is, of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the sons of the Buddha. It is by no means trifling, nor is it practiced by trifling beings. In whatever way attention is given to it, in that same way it becomes both peaceful and subtle. Therefore, for this, strong mindfulness and wisdom are to be desired.

Yathā hi maṭṭhasāṭakassa tunnakaraṇakāle sūcipi sukhumā icchitabbā. Sūcipāsavedhanampi tato sukhumataraṃ, evameva maṭṭhasāṭakasadisassa imassa kammaṭṭhānassa bhāvanākāle sūcipaṭibhāgā satipi, sūcipāsavedhanapaṭibhāgā taṃsampayuttā paññāpi balavatī icchitabbā. Tāhi ca pana satipaññāhi samannāgatena bhikkhunā na te assāsapassāsā aññatra pakatiphuṭṭhokāsā pariyesitabbā.

For just as when mending a fine cloth, a fine needle is to be desired, and the tool for piercing the needle's eye must be even finer; so too, when developing this meditation subject, which is like a fine cloth, strong mindfulness, which is comparable to the needle, and strong wisdom associated with it, which is comparable to the tool for piercing the needle's eye, are to be desired. And a bhikkhu endowed with such mindfulness and wisdom should not seek those in-breaths and out-breaths elsewhere than at their natural point of contact.

Yathā pana kassako kasiṃ kasitvā balībadde muñcitvā gocaramukhe katvā chāyāya nisinno vissameyya, athassa te balībaddā vegena aṭaviṃ paviseyyuṃ. Yo hoti cheko kassako, so puna te gahetvā yojetukāmo na tesaṃ anupadaṃ gantvā aṭaviṃ āhiṇḍahi, atha kho rasmiñca patodañca gahetvā ujukameva tesaṃ nipātanatitthaṃ gantvā nisīdati vā nipajjati vā, atha te goṇe divasabhāgaṃ caritvā nipātanatitthaṃ otaritvā nhatvā ca pivitvā [V 1.0273] ca paccuttaritvā ṭhite disvā rasmiyā bandhitvā patodena vijjhanto ānetvā yojetvā puna kammaṃ karoti, evameva tena bhikkhunā na te assāsapassāsā aññatra pakatiphuṭṭhokāsā pariyesitabbā. Satirasmiṃ pana paññāpatodañca gahetvā pakatiphuṭṭhokāse cittaṃ ṭhapetvā manasikāro pavattetabbo. Evañhissa manasikaroto na cirasseva te upaṭṭhahanti nipātanatitthe viya goṇā. Tatonena satirasmiyā bandhitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne yojetvā paññāpatodena vijjhantena punappunaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitabbaṃ.

Suppose a farmer, having plowed, unyokes his oxen, directs them toward the pasture, and, sitting in the shade, might rest. Those oxen might then quickly enter the forest. A skilled farmer, desiring to catch and yoke them again, does not wander about the forest following their tracks. Instead, taking his rope and goad, he goes straight to their usual watering place and sits or lies down there. When he sees the oxen—after they have roamed for the day, come down to the watering place, bathed and drunk, and climbed back out to stand still—he ties them with the rope, and urging them on with the goad, brings them back, yokes them, and resumes his work. In this very way, that bhikkhu should not seek out the in-breaths and out-breaths anywhere other than their natural place of contact. Rather, taking the rope of mindfulness and the goad of wisdom, he should establish his mind at the natural place of contact and apply attention. For one who attends in this way, the breaths will appear in no long time, just as the oxen appear at the watering place. Then, having tied them with the rope of mindfulness and yoked them in that very place, he should, while urging them on with the goad of wisdom, repeatedly engage with the meditation subject.

231. Tassevamanuyuñjato na cirasseva nimittaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Taṃ panetaṃ na sabbesaṃ ekasadisaṃ hoti. Apica kho kassaci sukhasamphassaṃ uppādayamāno tūlapicu viya kappāsapicu viya vātadhārā viya ca upaṭṭhātīti ekacce āhu.

231. For one who applies himself in this way, the sign appears in no long time. This sign, however, is not the same for everyone. Moreover, some say that for a certain person it appears producing a pleasant contact, like silk-cotton, like cotton, or like a current of wind.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0277] pana aṭṭhakathāsu vinicchayo, idañhi kassaci tārakarūpaṃ viya maṇiguḷikā viya muttāguḷikā viya ca, kassaci kharasamphassaṃ hutvā kappāsaṭṭhi viya dārusārasūci viya ca, kassaci dīghapāmaṅgasuttaṃ viya kusumadāmaṃ viya dhūmasikhā viya ca, kassaci vitthataṃ makkaṭakasuttaṃ viya valāhakapaṭalaṃ viya padumapupphaṃ viya rathacakkaṃ viya candamaṇḍalaṃ viya sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ viya ca upaṭṭhāti. Tañca panetaṃ yathā sambahulesu bhikkhūsu suttantaṃ sajjhāyitvā nisinnesu ekena bhikkhunā “tumhākaṃ kīdisaṃ hutvā idaṃ suttaṃ upaṭṭhātī”ti vutte eko “mayhaṃ mahatī pabbateyyā nadī viya hutvā upaṭṭhātī”ti āha. Aparo “mayhaṃ ekā vanarāji viya”. Añño “mayhaṃ eko sītacchāyo sākhāsampanno phalabhārabharitarukkho viyā”ti. Tesaṃ hi taṃ ekameva suttaṃ saññānānatāya nānato upaṭṭhāti. Evaṃ ekameva kammaṭṭhānaṃ saññānānatāya nānato upaṭṭhāti. Saññajañhi etaṃ saññānidānaṃ saññāpabhavaṃ. Tasmā saññānānatāya nānato upaṭṭhātīti veditabbaṃ.

This, however, is the determination in the commentaries: For this sign appears to some like the form of a star, like a jewel, or like a pearl; to some, having a coarse contact, it appears like a cotton seed or like a splinter of heartwood; to some, it appears like a long carpenter's string, like a garland of flowers, or like a wisp of smoke; to some, it appears spread out like a spider's thread, like a layer of cloud, like a lotus flower, like a chariot wheel, like the moon's disk, or like the sun's disk. It is as when, after many bhikkhus have been sitting and reciting a sutta, one bhikkhu asks, 'To you, what did this sutta seem like?' and one answers, 'To me it seemed like a great mountain river,' another, 'To me, like a line of forest,' and another, 'To me, like a tree with cool shade and spreading branches, laden with the burden of its fruit.' For though the sutta is one and the same, it appears differently to them because of the diversity of their perception. So too, this single meditation subject appears differently because of the diversity of perception. For this sign is born of perception, has perception as its cause, and has perception as its origin. Therefore, it should be understood that it appears differently because of the diversity of perception.

Ettha ca aññameva assāsārammaṇaṃ cittaṃ, aññaṃ passāsārammaṇaṃ, aññaṃ nimittārammaṇaṃ. Yassa hi ime tayo dhammā natthi, tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ neva appanaṃ, na upacāraṃ pāpuṇāti. Yassa pana ime tayo dhammā atthi, tasseva kammaṭṭhānaṃ upacārañca appanañca pāpuṇāti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, the mind with the in-breath as its object is one thing, the mind with the out-breath as its object is another, and the mind with the sign as its object is yet another. For one to whom these three things are not present, their meditation subject attains neither absorption nor access concentration. But for one to whom these three things are present, their meditation subject attains both access concentration and absorption. For this has been said:

“Nimittaṃ [V 1.0274] assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Ajānato tayo dhamme, bhāvanā nupalabbhati.

The sign, the in-breaths, and out-breaths,

Are not the object of a single mind;

For one who does not know these three things,

Development is not found.

“Nimittaṃ assāsapassāsā, anārammaṇamekacittassa;

Jānatova tayo dhamme, bhāvanā upalabbhatī”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165);

The sign, the in-breaths, and out-breaths,

Are not the object of a single mind;

For one who knows these three things,

Development is found.

232. Evaṃ upaṭṭhite pana nimitte tena bhikkhunā ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā ārocetabbaṃ “mayhaṃ, bhante, evarūpaṃ nāma upaṭṭhātī”ti. Ācariyena pana etaṃ nimittanti vā na vā nimittanti na vattabbaṃ. “Evaṃ hoti, āvuso”ti vatvā punappunaṃ manasi karohīti vattabbo. Nimittanti hi vutte vosānaṃ āpajjeyya. Na nimittanti vutte nirāso visīdeyya. Tasmā tadubhayampi avatvā manasikāreyeva niyojetabboti. Evaṃ tāva dīghabhāṇakā.

232. When the sign has appeared in this way, that bhikkhu should go to his teacher and inform him: 'Venerable sir, a sign of such a kind has appeared to me.' The teacher, however, should not say, 'This is the sign,' nor, 'This is not the sign.' Having said, 'Friend, it happens thus,' he should instruct him, saying: 'Apply your mind to it again and again.' For if it were said, 'It is the sign,' he might come to a standstill. If it were said, 'It is not the sign,' he would become hopeless and dejected. Therefore, without saying either of the two, he should be urged only to apply his mind. Thus say the Dīgha Reciters.

Majjhimabhāṇakā panāhu “nimittamidaṃ, āvuso, kammaṭṭhānaṃ punappunaṃ manasi karohi sappurisāti vattabbo”ti. Athānena nimitteyeva cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ[M 1.0278]. Evamassāyaṃ ito pabhuti ṭhapanāvasena bhāvanā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

The Majjhima Reciters, however, say he should be instructed thus: 'Friend, this is the sign. O good man, apply your mind to the meditation subject again and again.' Then, he should fix his mind on that very sign. Thus, for him, from this point onward, this development occurs by way of fixing. For this was said by the ancients:

“Nimitte ṭhapayaṃ cittaṃ, nānākāraṃ vibhāvayaṃ;

Dhīro assāsapassāse, sakaṃ cittaṃ nibandhatī”ti. (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.165);

The wise one, placing the mind on the sign and causing the various characteristics of the in-breaths and out-breaths to disappear, firmly binds their own mind.

Tassevaṃ nimittupaṭṭhānato pabhuti nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhitāneva honti, kilesā sannisinnāva. Sati upaṭṭhitāyeva. Cittaṃ upacārasamādhinā samāhitameva. Athānena taṃ nimittaṃ neva vaṇṇato manasi kātabbaṃ, na lakkhaṇato paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Apica kho khattiyamahesiyā cakkavattigabbho viya kassakena sāliyavagabbho viya ca āvāsādīni satta asappāyāni vajjetvā tāneva satta sappāyāni sevantena sādhukaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ. Atha naṃ evaṃ rakkhitvā punappunaṃ manasikāravasena vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ gamayitvā dasavidhaṃ appanākosallaṃ sampādetabbaṃ, vīriyasamatā [V 1.0275] yojetabbā. Tassevaṃ ghaṭentassa pathavīkasiṇe vuttānukkameneva tasmiṃ nimitte catukkapañcakajjhānāni nibbattanti.

For him, from the appearance of the sign in this way, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, and the defilements are stilled. Mindfulness is indeed established. The mind is indeed concentrated with access concentration. Then, he should neither attend to that sign by its color, nor review it by its characteristics. Rather, just as a chief queen protects the embryo of a wheel-turning monarch, or as a farmer protects the budding rice and barley, so too should he carefully protect it by avoiding the seven unsuitable things and cultivating the seven suitable things. Then, having protected it thus, he should bring it to growth and full development by means of repeated attention. The tenfold skill in absorption should be accomplished, and a balance of energy should be applied. For him who strives in this way, following the very sequence described for the earth kasiṇa, the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise in that sign.

233. Evaṃ nibbattacatukkapañcakajjhāno panettha bhikkhu sallakkhaṇāvivaṭṭanāvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā pārisuddhiṃ pattukāmo tadeva jhānaṃ pañcahākārehi vasippattaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti. Kathaṃ? So hi samāpattito vuṭṭhāya assāsapassāsānaṃ samudayo karajakāyo ca cittañcāti passati. Yathā hi kammāragaggariyā dhamamānāya bhastañca purisassa ca tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicca vāto sañcarati, evameva kāyañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsāti. Tato assāsapassāse ca kāyañca rūpanti cittañca taṃsampayuttadhamme ca arūpanti vavatthapeti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato pana nāmarūpavavatthānaṃ parato āvibhavissati.

233. Thus, a bhikkhu here who has produced the fourfold and fivefold jhānas, wishing to attain purity—that is, the noble fruit—by developing the meditation subject through the power of insight and the path, makes that very jhāna proficient and mastered in five ways, then establishes insight by determining mentality-materiality. How? Having emerged from the attainment, he sees that the origin of the in-breaths and out-breaths is the kamma-born body and the mind. For just as wind moves dependent on the bellows and the person's corresponding effort when a blacksmith's bellows are being pumped, so too, the in-breaths and out-breaths are dependent on the body and the mind. Then he determines the in-breaths and out-breaths and the body as materiality, and the mind and the mental factors associated with it as immateriality. This is the summary here. But in detail, the determination of mentality-materiality will become clear hereafter.

Evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesati. Pariyesanto ca naṃ disvā tīsupi addhāsu nāmarūpassa pavattiṃ ārabbha kaṅkhaṃ vitarati. Vitiṇṇakaṅkho kalāpasammasanavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā udayabbayānupassanāya pubbabhāge uppanne obhāsādayo dasa vipassanupakkilese pahāya [M 1.0279] upakkilesavimuttaṃ paṭipadāñāṇaṃ maggoti vavatthapetvā udayaṃ pahāya bhaṅgānupassanaṃ patvā nirantaraṃ bhaṅgānupassanena vayato upaṭṭhitesu sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindanto virajjanto vimuccanto yathākkamena cattāro ariyamagge pāpuṇitvā arahattaphale patiṭṭhāya ekūnavīsatibhedassa paccavekkhaṇāñāṇassa pariyantaṃ patto sadevakassa lokassa aggadakkhiṇeyyo hoti.

Having thus determined mentality-materiality, he seeks its cause. Having sought and seen it, he overcomes doubt concerning the occurrence of mentality-materiality in the three periods of time. Having overcome doubt, he applies the three characteristics by way of comprehension by groups. He abandons the ten corruptions of insight, such as illumination, that have arisen in the preliminary stage of the contemplation of rise and fall. Having determined that the knowledge of the path of practice, free from corruptions, is the path, he abandons arising and attains the contemplation of dissolution. Through the continuous contemplation of dissolution, as all formations appear to him as perishing, he becomes disenchanted with them, dispassionate towards them, and liberated from them. He then sequentially attains the four noble paths and becomes established in the fruit of arahantship. Having reached the culmination of the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge, he becomes the foremost recipient of offerings in the world with its gods.

Ettāvatā cassa gaṇanaṃ ādiṃ katvā vipassanāpariyosānā ānāpānassatisamādhibhāvanā samattā hotīti ayaṃ sabbākārato paṭhamacatukkavaṇṇanā.

With this, for him, the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing, which begins with counting and culminates in insight, is completed. This is the explanation of the first tetrad in all its aspects.

234. Itaresu pana tīsu catukkesu yasmā visuṃ kammaṭṭhānabhāvanānayo nāma natthi. Tasmā anupadavaṇṇanānayeneva tesaṃ evaṃ attho veditabbo.

234. Furthermore, in the other three tetrads, since there is no separate method for developing the meditation subject, their meaning should be understood by the method of the word-by-word explanation alone.

Pītipaṭisaṃvedīti pītiṃ paṭisaṃviditaṃ karonto pākaṭaṃ karonto assasissāmi passasissāmīti [V 1.0276] sikkhati. Tattha dvīhākārehi pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti ārammaṇato ca asammohato ca.

‘Experiencing rapture’: he trains, ‘I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out,’ making the rapture distinctly known, making it manifest. Herein, rapture is experienced in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion.

Kathaṃ ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjati. Tassa samāpattikkhaṇe jhānapaṭilābhena ārammaṇato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti, ārammaṇassa paṭisaṃviditattā. Kathaṃ asammohato? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttaṃ pītiṃ khayato vayato sammasati. Tassa vipassanākkhaṇe lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena asammohato pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.172) –

How is rapture experienced by way of the object? One attains the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. At the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna, rapture is experienced by way of the object, because the object is experienced. How is it experienced by way of non-delusion? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and emerged from them, one comprehends the rapture associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing. At the moment of insight, through the penetration of its characteristics, rapture is experienced by way of non-delusion. For this was said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Dīghaṃ assāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Dīghaṃ passāsavasena… rassaṃ assāsavasena… rassaṃ passāsavasena… sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī assāsapassāsavasena… passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ assāsapassāsavasena cittassa ekaggataṃ avikkhepaṃ pajānato sati [M 1.0280] upaṭṭhitā hoti. Tāya satiyā tena ñāṇena sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Āvajjato sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Jānato passato paccavekkhato cittaṃ adhiṭṭhahato saddhāya adhimuccato vīriyaṃ paggaṇhato satiṃ upaṭṭhāpayato cittaṃ samādahato paññāya pajānato abhiññeyyaṃ pariññeyyaṃ pahātabbaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ sacchikaroto sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hoti. Evaṃ sā pīti paṭisaṃviditā hotī”ti.

“When one understands the mind’s one-pointedness and non-distraction by way of long in-breaths, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced. When one understands the mind’s one-pointedness and non-distraction by way of long out-breaths… by way of short in-breaths… by way of short out-breaths… by way of experiencing the whole body with the in-and-out breaths… by way of tranquilizing the bodily formation with the in-and-out breaths, mindfulness is established. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced. When one adverts, that rapture is experienced. When one knows, sees, reviews, resolves the mind, becomes decided by faith, exerts energy, establishes mindfulness, concentrates the mind, understands with wisdom, directly knows what should be directly known, fully understands what should be fully understood, abandons what should be abandoned, develops what should be developed, and realizes what should be realized, that rapture is experienced. Thus that rapture is experienced.”

Eteneva nayena avasesapadānipi atthato veditabbāni. Idampanettha visesamattaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena sukhapaṭisaṃveditā, catunnampi vasena cittasaṅkhārapaṭisaṃveditā veditabbā. Cittasaṅkhāroti vedanādayo dve khandhā. Sukhapaṭisaṃvedīpade cettha vipassanābhūmidassanatthaṃ “sukhanti dve sukhāni kāyikañca sukhaṃ cetasikañcā”ti paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.173) vuttaṃ. Passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāranti oḷārikaṃ oḷārikaṃ cittasaṅkhāraṃ passambhento, nirodhentoti attho. So vitthārato kāyasaṅkhāre vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

The remaining terms should also be understood in meaning in the same way. This, however, is the specific point here: ‘experiencing happiness’ should be understood by way of the three jhānas, and ‘experiencing the mental formation’ by way of all four. ‘Mental formation’ means the two aggregates, feeling and perception. And here, in the term ‘experiencing happiness,’ in order to show the plane for insight, it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: ‘“Happiness” means two kinds of happiness: bodily happiness and mental happiness.’ ‘Tranquilizing the mental formation’ means tranquilizing, that is, causing to cease, the grosser mental formation. This should be understood in detail in the same way as was explained for the bodily formation.

Apicettha pītipade pītisīsena vedanā vuttā. Sukhapade sarūpeneva vedanā. Dvīsu cittasaṅkhārapadesu [V 1.0277] “saññā ca vedanā ca cetasikā ete dhammā cittapaṭibaddhā cittasaṅkhārā”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.174; ma. ni. 1.463) vacanato saññāsampayuttā vedanāti evaṃ vedanānupassanānayena idaṃ catukkaṃ bhāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, here in the term on rapture, feeling is mentioned with rapture as the heading. In the term on happiness, feeling is mentioned by its own nature. In the two terms on the mental formation, in accordance with the text, ‘Perception and feeling are mental; these things are bound up with the mind; they are mental formations,’ it is feeling associated with perception that is meant. Thus it should be understood that this tetrad has been taught by way of the contemplation of feeling.

235. Tatiyacatukkepi catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ vasena cittapaṭisaṃveditā veditabbā. Abhippamodayaṃ cittanti cittaṃ modento pamodento hāsento pahāsento assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhati. Tattha dvīhākārehi abhippamodo hoti samādhivasena ca vipassanāvasena ca.

235. In the third tetrad also, ‘experiencing the mind’ should be understood by way of the four jhānas. ‘Gladdening the mind’: he trains, ‘I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out,’ gladdening, delighting, making the mind joyful and elated. Therein, gladdening occurs in two ways: by way of concentration and by way of insight.

Kathaṃ samādhivasena? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjati. So samāpattikkhaṇe sampayuttapītiyā cittaṃ āmodeti pamodeti. Kathaṃ vipassanāvasena? Sappītike dve jhāne samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttapītiṃ khayato vayato sammasati. Evaṃ vipassanākkhaṇe jhānasampayuttaṃ pītiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā cittaṃ āmodeti pamodeti. Evaṃ [M 1.0281] paṭipanno “abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti vuccati.

How by way of concentration? One attains the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. At the moment of attainment, one gladdens and delights the mind with the associated rapture. How by way of insight? Having attained the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and emerged from them, one comprehends the rapture associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing. Thus, at the moment of insight, having made the rapture associated with the jhāna its object, one gladdens and delights the mind. One who is practicing in this way is said to be training thus: ‘I shall breathe in gladdening the mind; I shall breathe out gladdening the mind.’

Samādahaṃ cittanti paṭhamajjhānādivasena ārammaṇe cittaṃ samaṃ ādahanto samaṃ ṭhapento. Tāni vā pana jhānāni samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ khayato vayato sampassato vipassanākkhaṇe lakkhaṇapaṭivedhena uppajjati khaṇikacittekaggatā. Evaṃ uppannāya khaṇikacittekaggatāya vasenapi ārammaṇe cittaṃ samaṃ ādahanto samaṃ ṭhapento “samādahaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti vuccati.

‘Concentrating the mind’: this means placing the mind evenly, setting it evenly, on the object by way of the first jhāna and so on. Or, when one has attained those jhānas and emerged from them and contemplates the mind associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing, at that moment of insight momentary one-pointedness of mind arises through the penetration of the characteristics. By means of that arisen momentary one-pointedness of mind, too, one places the mind evenly, sets it evenly, on the object. Such a one is said to be training thus: ‘I shall breathe in concentrating the mind; I shall breathe out concentrating the mind.’

Vimocayaṃ cittanti paṭhamajjhānena nīvaraṇehi cittaṃ mocento vimocento, dutiyena vitakkavicārehi, tatiyena pītiyā, catutthena sukhadukkhehi cittaṃ mocento vimocento. Tāni vā pana jhānāni samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya jhānasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ khayato vayato sammasati. So vipassanākkhaṇe aniccānupassanāya niccasaññāto cittaṃ mocento, dukkhānupassanāya sukhasaññāto, anattānupassanāya attasaññāto, nibbidānupassanāya nandito, virāgānupassanāya rāgato, nirodhānupassanāya samudayato, paṭinissaggānupassanāya ādānato cittaṃ mocento assasati ceva passasati ca. Tena vuccati “vimocayaṃ cittaṃ assasissāmi [V 1.0278] passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti. Evaṃ cittānupassanāvasena idaṃ catukkaṃ bhāsitanti veditabbaṃ.

‘Liberating the mind’ means liberating the mind from the hindrances with the first jhāna; from thought and examination with the second jhāna; from rapture with the third jhāna; and from pleasure and pain with the fourth jhāna. Alternatively, having attained those jhānas and emerged from them, one contemplates the mind associated with the jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing. At the moment of insight, liberating the mind from the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence; from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering; from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self; from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment; from lust through the contemplation of dispassion; from the origin through the contemplation of cessation; and from grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment, he breathes in and breathes out. For this reason it is said: ‘He trains thus: “I shall breathe in liberating the mind; I shall breathe out liberating the mind.”’ In this way, this tetrad should be understood as spoken by way of the contemplation of the mind.

236. Catutthacatukke pana aniccānupassīti ettha tāva aniccaṃ veditabbaṃ. Aniccatā veditabbā. Aniccānupassanā veditabbā. Aniccānupassī veditabbo.

236. Now, in the fourth tetrad, regarding the words ‘contemplating impermanence,’ first, the impermanent should be understood. Impermanence should be understood. The contemplation of impermanence should be understood. The one who contemplates impermanence should be understood.

Tattha aniccanti pañcakkhandhā. Kasmā? Uppādavayaññathattabhāvā. Aniccatāti tesaṃyeva uppādavayaññathattaṃ, hutvā abhāvo vā, nibbattānaṃ tenevākārena aṭṭhatvā khaṇabhaṅgena bhedoti attho. Aniccānupassanāti tassā aniccatāya vasena rūpādīsu aniccanti anupassanā. Aniccānupassīti tāya anupassanāya samannāgato. Tasmā evaṃbhūto assasanto [M 1.0282] passasanto ca idha “aniccānupassī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti veditabbo.

Herein, ‘the impermanent’ means the five aggregates. Why? Because of their nature of arising, vanishing, and altering. ‘Impermanence’ is just their arising, vanishing, and altering; or their non-existence after having come to be; or the meaning is the breaking up by momentary dissolution of what has been generated, without its remaining in the same state. ‘Contemplation of impermanence’ is the contemplation of form and so on as impermanent by way of that impermanence. ‘One who contemplates impermanence’ is one endowed with that contemplation. Therefore, being such a one, while breathing in and breathing out, one should be understood here as training thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence; I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence.’

Virāgānupassīti ettha pana dve virāgā khayavirāgo ca accantavirāgo ca. Tattha khayavirāgoti saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgo. Accantavirāgoti nibbānaṃ. Virāgānupassanāti tadubhayadassanavasena pavattā vipassanā ca maggo ca. Tāya duvidhāyapi anupassanāya samannāgato hutvā assasanto passasanto ca “virāgānupassī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti veditabbo. Nirodhānupassīpadepi eseva nayo.

Here, regarding ‘contemplating fading away,’ there are two kinds of fading away: the fading away that is destruction and the ultimate fading away. Herein, the fading away that is destruction is the momentary dissolution of formations. The ultimate fading away is Nibbāna. The contemplation of fading away is the insight and the path that proceed by way of seeing both of these. Being endowed with this twofold contemplation, while breathing in and breathing out, one should be understood as training thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating fading away; I shall breathe out contemplating fading away.’ The same method applies to the term ‘contemplating cessation.’

Paṭinissaggānupassīti etthāpi dve paṭinissaggā pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ca pakkhandanapaṭinissaggo ca. Paṭinissaggoyeva anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Vipassanāmaggānaṃ etamadhivacanaṃ.

Here too, regarding ‘contemplating relinquishment,’ there are two kinds of relinquishment: relinquishment as abandoning and relinquishment as entering. Relinquishment itself is the contemplation; hence, ‘contemplation of relinquishment.’ This is a designation for insight and the paths.

Vipassanā hi tadaṅgavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajati, saṅkhatadosadassanena ca tabbiparīte nibbāne tanninnatāya pakkhandatīti pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggoti ca vuccati. Maggo samucchedavasena saddhiṃ khandhābhisaṅkhārehi kilese pariccajati, ārammaṇakaraṇena ca nibbāne pakkhandatīti pariccāgapaṭinissaggo ceva pakkhandanapaṭinissaggoti ca vuccati. Ubhayampi pana purimapurimaññāṇānaṃ anuanupassanato anupassanāti vuccati. Tāya duvidhāyapi paṭinissaggānupassanāya samannāgato hutvā assasanto [V 1.0279] passasanto ca “paṭinissaggānupassī assasissāmi passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti veditabbo.

Indeed, insight, by means of its respective factors, abandons the defilements together with the aggregate-formations; and by seeing the danger in the conditioned, it enters Nibbāna, which is the opposite, through its inclination to that. Thus it is called both relinquishment-as-abandoning and relinquishment-as-entering. The path, by way of eradication, abandons the defilements together with the aggregate-formations; and by making Nibbāna its object, it enters it. Thus it is called both relinquishment-as-abandoning and relinquishment-as-entering. Both, however, are called ‘contemplation’ because they repeatedly contemplate in accordance with the preceding knowledges. It should be understood that, being endowed with this twofold contemplation of relinquishment, while breathing in and breathing out, one trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in, contemplating relinquishment; I shall breathe out, contemplating relinquishment.’

Idaṃ catutthacatukkaṃ suddhavipassanāvaseneva vuttaṃ. Purimāni pana tīṇi samathavipassanāvasena. Evaṃ catunnaṃ catukkānaṃ vasena soḷasavatthukāya ānāpānassatiyā bhāvanā veditabbā. Evaṃ soḷasavatthuvasena ca pana ayaṃ ānāpānassati mahapphalā hoti mahānisaṃsā.

This fourth tetrad is stated by way of pure insight alone. The first three, however, are stated by way of serenity and insight. Thus the development of mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases should be understood by way of the four tetrads. And when this mindfulness of breathing is developed in this way by way of the sixteen bases, it is of great fruit, of great benefit.

237. Tatrassa “ayampi kho, bhikkhave, ānāpānassatisamādhi bhāvito bahulīkato santo ceva paṇīto cā”tiādivacanato santabhāvādivasenāpi mahānisaṃsatā veditabbā, vitakkupacchedasamatthatāyapi. Ayañhi santapaṇītaasecanakasukhavihārattā samādhiantarāyakarānaṃ vitakkānaṃ vasena ito cito ca cittassa vidhāvanaṃ vicchinditvā ānāpānārammaṇābhimukhameva [M 1.0283] cittaṃ karoti. Teneva vuttaṃ “ānāpānassati bhāvetabbā vitakkupacchedāyā”ti (a. ni. 9.1).

237.
