Therein, its great benefit should be understood by way of its peaceful nature and so on, based on such statements as: ‘This concentration due to mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and made much of, is peaceful and sublime…’; and it should also be understood by its ability to cut off thoughts. For since this is a peaceful, sublime, unadulterated, and blissful abiding, it cuts off the mind’s running about here and there on account of thoughts that obstruct concentration and makes the mind face the breathing object alone. Therefore it is said: ‘Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for cutting off thoughts.’

Vijjāvimuttipāripūriyā mūlabhāvenāpi cassā mahānisaṃsatā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “ānāpānassati, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā cattāro satipaṭṭhāne paripūreti, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrenti, satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā vijjāvimuttiṃ paripūrentī”ti (ma. ni. 3.147).

Its great benefit should also be understood from its being the root for the perfecting of knowledge and liberation. For this was said by the Blessed One: ‘Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and made much of, perfects the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and made much of, perfect the seven enlightenment factors. The seven enlightenment factors, when developed and made much of, perfect knowledge and liberation’ (MN 118).

Apica carimakānaṃ assāsapassāsānaṃ viditabhāvakaraṇatopissā mahānisaṃsatā veditabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “evaṃ bhāvitāya kho, rāhula, ānāpānassatiyā evaṃ bahulīkatāya yepi te carimakā assāsapassāsā, tepi viditāva nirujjhanti, no aviditā”ti (ma. ni. 2.121).

Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood from its causing the final in-breaths and out-breaths to be known. For this was said by the Blessed One: ‘When mindfulness of breathing, Rāhula, has been developed and made much of in this way, even the final in-breaths and out-breaths cease while they are known, not while they are unknown’ (MN 62).

238. Tattha nirodhavasena tayo carimakā bhavacarimakā, jhānacarimakā, cuticarimakāti. Bhavesu hi kāmabhave assāsapassāsā pavattanti, rūpārūpabhavesu nappavattanti, tasmā [V 1.0280] te bhavacarimakā. Jhānesu purime jhānattaye pavattanti, catutthe nappavattanti, tasmā te jhānacarimakā. Ye pana cuticittassa purato soḷasamena cittena saddhiṃ uppajjitvā cuticittena saha nirujjhanti, ime cuticarimakā nāma. Ime idha “carimakā”ti adhippetā.

238. Herein, by way of cessation, there are three kinds of final breaths: the final breaths of an existence, the final breaths of a jhāna, and the final breaths of death. For in-breaths and out-breaths occur in the sense-sphere existence but not in the form and formless existences; therefore those are the final breaths of an existence. In the jhānas, they occur in the first three jhānas but not in the fourth; therefore those are the final breaths of a jhāna. But those that arise together with the sixteenth consciousness-moment before the death-consciousness and cease together with the death-consciousness, these are called the final breaths of death. It is these that are intended here by ‘final’.

Imaṃ kira kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuttassa bhikkhuno ānāpānārammaṇassa suṭṭhu pariggahitattā cuticittassa purato soḷasamassa cittassa uppādakkhaṇe uppādaṃ āvajjayato uppādopi nesaṃ pākaṭo hoti. Ṭhitiṃ āvajjayato ṭhitipi nesaṃ pākaṭā hoti. Bhaṅgaṃ āvajjayato ca bhaṅgo nesaṃ pākaṭo hoti.

It is said that for a bhikkhu devoted to this meditation subject, because the breathing object is well grasped, when he adverts to the arising at the arising-moment of the sixteenth consciousness-moment before the death-consciousness, their arising becomes manifest to him. When he adverts to the presence, their presence becomes manifest to him. And when he adverts to the dissolution, their dissolution becomes manifest to him.

Ito aññaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā arahattaṃ pattassa bhikkhuno hi āyuantaraṃ paricchinnaṃ vā hoti aparicchinnaṃ vā. Idaṃ pana soḷasavatthukaṃ ānāpānassatiṃ bhāvetvā arahattaṃ pattassa āyuantaraṃ paricchinnameva hoti. So “ettakaṃ dāni me āyusaṅkhārā pavattissanti, na ito [M 1.0284] para”nti ñatvā attano dhammatāya eva sarīrapaṭijaggananivāsanapārupanādīni sabbakiccāni katvā akkhīni nimīleti koṭapabbatavihāravāsītissatthero viya mahākarañjiyavihāravāsīmahātissatthero viya devaputtamahāraṭṭhe piṇḍapātikatissatthero viya cittalapabbatavihāravāsino dve bhātiyattherā viya ca.

Indeed, for a bhikkhu who attains arahantship by developing a meditation subject other than this one, his remaining life-span may be determined or undetermined. But for one who attains arahantship by developing this mindfulness of breathing with its sixteen bases, his remaining life-span is definitely determined. Knowing, ‘My life-formations will now proceed for only this long, not beyond this,’ he does all his duties, such as looking after his body, putting on his robes, etc., by his own nature, and then closes his eyes, like the Elder Tissa, resident of Koṭapabbata Monastery; the Great Elder Tissa, resident of Mahākarañjiya Monastery; the Elder Tissa the Alms-gatherer in the great country of Devaputta; and the two brother Elders, residents of Cittalapabbata Monastery.

Tatridaṃ ekavatthuparidīpanaṃ. Dvebhātiyattherānaṃ kireko puṇṇamuposathadivase pātimokkhaṃ osāretvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā caṅkame ṭhito candālokaṃ oloketvā attano āyusaṅkhāre upadhāretvā bhikkhusaṅghamāha – “tumhehi kathaṃ parinibbāyantā bhikkhū diṭṭhapubbā”ti. Tatra keci āhaṃsu “amhehi āsane nisinnakāva parinibbāyantā diṭṭhapubbā”ti. Keci “amhehi ākāse pallaṅkamābhujitvā nisinnakā”ti. Thero āha – “ahaṃ dāni vo caṅkamantameva parinibbāyamānaṃ dassessāmī”ti tato caṅkame lekhaṃ katvā “ahaṃ ito caṅkamakoṭito parakoṭiṃ gantvā nivattamāno imaṃ lekhaṃ patvāva parinibbāyissāmī”ti vatvā caṅkamaṃ oruyha parabhāgaṃ gantvā nivattamāno ekena pādena lekhaṃ akkantakkhaṇeyeva parinibbāyi.

Here is an illustration of one case. It is said that on the full-moon observance day, one of the two brother Elders, after reciting the Pātimokkha, surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus, went to his own dwelling. Standing on the cloister walk and looking at the moonlight, he reviewed his life-formations and asked the Sangha of bhikkhus: ‘In what posture have you formerly seen bhikkhus attain final Nibbāna?’ Some said: ‘We have seen them attain final Nibbāna while sitting on their seats.’ Others said: ‘We have seen them sitting cross-legged in the air.’ The Elder said: ‘I shall now show you one attaining final Nibbāna while walking.’ Then, having made a line on the cloister walk, he said: ‘I shall go from this end of the cloister walk to the other end, and on returning, I shall attain final Nibbāna just upon reaching this line.’ He then stepped onto the cloister walk, went to the other end, and on returning, at the very moment one foot had trodden on the line, he attained final Nibbāna.

Tasmā have appamatto, anuyuñjetha paṇḍito;

Evaṃ anekānisaṃsaṃ, ānāpānassatiṃ sadāti.

Therefore, indeed, a wise person, being heedful, should always be devoted to mindfulness of breathing, which thus has manifold benefits.

Idaṃ ānāpānassatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed exposition on mindfulness of breathing.

Upasamānussatikathā

The Exposition on the Recollection of Peace

239. Ānāpānassatiyā [V 1.0281] anantaraṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ pana upasamānussatiṃ bhāvetukāmena rahogatena paṭisallīnena – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyati, yadidaṃ madanimmadano pipāsavinayo ālayasamugghāto vaṭṭupacchedo taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodho nibbāna”nti (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) evaṃ sabbadukkhūpasamasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa guṇā anussaritabbā.

239. Furthermore, by one who wishes to develop the recollection of peace, taught immediately after mindfulness of breathing, having gone into solitude and seclusion, the qualities of Nibbāna, which is designated as the pacification of all suffering, should be recollected thus: “Bhikkhus, of all things, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost; that is, the subduing of intoxication, the elimination of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.34; Itivuttaka 90).

Tattha yāvatāti yattakā. Dhammāti sabhāvā. Saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vāti saṅgamma samāgamma paccayehi katā vā akatā vā. Virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ [M 1.0285] aggamakkhāyatīti tesaṃ saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammānaṃ virāgo aggamakkhāyati seṭṭho uttamoti vuccati. Tattha virāgoti na rāgābhāvamattameva, atha kho yadidaṃ madanimmadano…pe… nibbānanti yo so madanimmadanotiādīni nāmāni asaṅkhatadhammo labhati, so virāgoti paccetabbo. So hi yasmā tamāgamma sabbepi mānamadapurisamadādayo madā nimmadā amadā honti vinassanti, tasmā madanimmadanoti vuccati. Yasmā ca tamāgamma sabbāpi kāmapipāsā vinayaṃ abbhatthaṃ yāti, tasmā pipāsavinayoti vuccati. Yasmā pana tamāgamma pañcakāmaguṇālayā samugghātaṃ gacchanti, tasmā ālayasamugghātoti vuccati. Yasmā ca tamāgamma tebhūmakaṃ vaṭṭaṃ upacchijjati, tasmā vaṭṭupacchedoti vuccati. Yasmā pana tamāgamma sabbaso taṇhā khayaṃ gacchati virajjati nirujjhati ca, tasmā taṇhakkhayo virāgo nirodhoti vuccati. Yasmā panesa catasso yoniyo pañca gatiyo satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo nava ca sattāvāse aparāparabhāvāya vinanato ābandhanato saṃsibbanato vānanti laddhavohārāya taṇhāya nikkhanto nissaṭo visaṃyutto, tasmā nibbānanti vuccatīti.

Here, ‘yāvatā’ means ‘as many as.’ ‘Dhammā’ refers to intrinsic natures. ‘Saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā’ means: having come together and assembled, made or not made by causes. ‘Virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyati’ means: among those conditioned and unconditioned dhammas, dispassion is declared the highest; it is called the most excellent, the supreme. Here, ‘virāgo’ is not merely the absence of lust, but rather, that unconditioned dhamma which obtains such names as ‘the subduing of intoxication’… up to ‘Nibbāna,’ that is to be understood as ‘dispassion.’ For, because by depending on it all intoxications—such as the intoxication of pride, the intoxication of manhood, and others—become devoid of intoxication, without intoxication, and are destroyed, it is therefore called ‘the subduing of intoxication.’ And because by depending on it all thirst for sensual pleasures goes to removal and destruction, it is therefore called ‘the dispelling of thirst.’ Moreover, because by depending on it the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are attachments, go to complete uprooting, it is therefore called ‘the uprooting of attachment.’ And because by depending on it the round of the three planes is cut off, it is therefore called ‘the cutting off of the round.’ Furthermore, because by depending on it craving in every way goes to destruction, fades away, and ceases, it is therefore called ‘the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation.’ And because it has departed from, is released from, and is disjoined from that craving—which has obtained the designation ‘vāna’ because it weaves, binds, and stitches one to a subsequent existence across the four kinds of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings—it is therefore called Nibbāna.

Evametesaṃ madanimmadanatādīnaṃ guṇānaṃ vasena nibbānasaṅkhāto upasamo anussaritabbo. Ye vā panaññepi bhagavatā – “asaṅkhatañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi… saccañca… pārañca… sududdasañca… ajarañca… dhuvañca… nippapañcañca… amatañca… sivañca… khemañca… abbhutañca… anītikañca… abyābajjhañca… visuddhiñca… dīpañca… tāṇañca [V 1.0282]… leṇañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.366) suttesu upasamaguṇā vuttā, tesampi vasena anussaritabboyeva.

Thus, the peace known as Nibbāna should be recollected by way of these qualities, such as the subduing of intoxication. And whatever other qualities of peace have also been spoken by the Blessed One in suttas such as, “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned… the truth… the further shore… the very hard to see… the ageless… the stable… the unproliferated… the deathless… the auspicious… the secure… the wonderful… the unafflicted… the unharassed… purity… the island… the shelter… the refuge…” (cf. Saṃyutta Nikāya 43.12–44), by means of these too, it should indeed be recollected.

Tassevaṃ madanimmadanatādiguṇavasena upasamaṃ anussarato neva tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti upasamaṃ ārabbhāti buddhānussatiādīsu vuttanayeneva vikkhambhitanīvaraṇassa ekakkhaṇe jhānaṅgāni uppajjanti. Upasamaguṇānaṃ pana gambhīratāya nānappakāraguṇānussaraṇādhimuttatāya vā appanaṃ appatvā upacārappattameva jhānaṃ hoti[M 1.0286]. Tadetamupasamaguṇānussaraṇavasena upasamānussaticceva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

When one recollects peace in this way by way of its qualities such as the subduing of intoxication, at that time one’s mind is not obsessed by lust, nor obsessed by hatred, nor obsessed by delusion. At that time one’s mind is directed straight, taking peace as its object. Then, in the way described for the recollection of the Buddha and so on, with the hindrances suppressed, the jhāna factors arise in a single moment. However, because of the profundity of the qualities of peace, or because of one’s inclination to recollect its various qualities, the jhāna does not reach absorption but only access concentration. This, being a recollection of the qualities of peace, is reckoned as the recollection of peace.

Cha anussatiyo viya ca ayampi ariyasāvakasseva ijjhati, evaṃ santepi upasamagarukena puthujjanenāpi manasi kātabbā. Sutavasenāpi hi upasame cittaṃ pasīdati. Imañca pana upasamānussatiṃ anuyutto bhikkhu sukhaṃ supati, sukhaṃ paṭibujjhati, santindriyo hoti santamānaso hirottappasamannāgato pāsādiko paṇītādhimuttiko sabrahmacārīnaṃ garu ca bhāvanīyo ca. Uttari appaṭivijjhanto pana sugatiparāyano hoti.

Like the six recollections, this too succeeds only for a noble disciple. Nevertheless, it should be attended to by a worldling who has respect for peace. For even by way of hearing, the mind finds confidence in peace. Furthermore, a bhikkhu devoted to this recollection of peace sleeps in comfort and wakes in comfort; he has tranquil faculties and a tranquil mind; he is endowed with shame and fear of wrongdoing, is inspiring, is intent on the sublime, and is respected and esteemed by his companions in the holy life. And if he penetrates no higher, he is headed for a happy destination.

Tasmā have appamatto, bhāvayetha vicakkhaṇo;

Evaṃ anekānisaṃsaṃ, ariye upasame satinti.

Therefore, let the discerning one, being diligent, indeed develop mindfulness of the noble peace, which in this way has so many benefits.

Idaṃ upasamānussatiyaṃ vitthārakathāmukhaṃ.

This is the introduction to the detailed explanation on the recollection of peace.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

In the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the division on the development of concentration,

Anussatikammaṭṭhānaniddeso nāma

the Exposition of the Recollection Meditation Subjects, so named,

Aṭṭhamo paricchedo.

is the eighth chapter.

9. Brahmavihāraniddeso

9. Exposition of the Divine Abidings

Mettābhāvanākathā

The Discourse on the Development of Loving-Kindness

240. Anussatikammaṭṭhānānantaraṃ [M 1.0287][V 1.0283] uddiṭṭhesu pana mettā, karuṇā, muditā, upekkhāti imesu catūsu brahmavihāresu mettaṃ bhāvetukāmena tāva ādikammikena yogāvacarena upacchinnapalibodhena gahitakammaṭṭhānena bhattakiccaṃ katvā bhattasammadaṃ paṭivinodetvā vivitte padese supaññatte āsane sukhanisinnena ādito tāva dose ādīnavo, khantiyañca ānisaṃso paccavekkhitabbo.

240. Now, following the recollection meditation subjects that were taught, among these four divine abidings—loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—a beginner yogi who wishes to develop loving-kindness should first, having cut off the impediments and taken up a meditation subject from a teacher, having completed his duties concerning the meal and dispelled his drowsiness from the meal, sit down comfortably in a secluded place on a well-prepared seat. To begin with, the danger in aversion and the benefit in patience should be reviewed.

Kasmā? Imāya hi bhāvanāya doso pahātabbo, khanti adhigantabbā. Na ca sakkā kiñci adiṭṭhādīnavaṃ pahātuṃ, aviditānisaṃsaṃ vā adhigantuṃ. Tasmā “duṭṭho kho, āvuso, dosena abhibhūto pariyādiṇṇacitto pāṇampi hanatī”tiādīnaṃ (a. ni. 3.72) vasena dose ādīnavo daṭṭhabbo.

Why? For by this development, aversion is to be abandoned and patience is to be attained. And it is not possible to abandon anything whose danger has not been seen, or to attain anything whose benefit is not known. Therefore, the danger in aversion should be seen by way of suttas such as: 'Friend, one who is corrupted by aversion, overcome by it, with a mind seized, even kills a living being' (AN 3.72).

“Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā”; (Dī. ni. 2.90; dha. pa. 184);

“Khantibalaṃ balānīkaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ”. (dha. pa. 399; su. ni. 628);

“Patient forbearance is the supreme austerity; Nibbāna is supreme, say the Buddhas” (DN 2.90; Dhp 184); “One who has the strength of patience, an army of strength—that one I call a brahmin” (Dhp 399; Snp 628);

“Khantā bhiyyo na vijjatī”tiādīnaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.250) vasena khantiyaṃ ānisaṃso veditabbo.

By way of suttas such as, “There is nothing greater than patience” (SN 1.250), the benefit in patience should be known.

Athevaṃ diṭṭhādīnavato dosato cittaṃ vivecanatthāya, viditānisaṃsāya ca khantiyā saṃyojanatthāya [V 1.0284] mettābhāvanā ārabhitabbā. Ārabhantena ca āditova puggalabhedo jānitabbo “imesu puggalesu mettā paṭhamaṃ na bhāvetabbā, imesu neva bhāvetabbā”ti.

Then, to disengage the mind from aversion, whose danger has been seen, and to unite it with patience, whose benefit is known, the development of loving-kindness should be undertaken. And when undertaking it, one should from the very beginning know the distinction among persons: 'Loving-kindness should not be developed at first towards these persons, and not at all towards these others.'

Ayañhi mettā appiyapuggale, atippiyasahāyake, majjhatte, verīpuggaleti imesu catūsu paṭhamaṃ na bhāvetabbā. Liṅgavisabhāge odhiso na bhāvetabbā. Kālakate na bhāvetabbāva. Kiṃkāraṇā appiyādīsu paṭhamaṃ na bhāvetabbā? Appiyaṃ hi piyaṭṭhāne ṭhapento kilamati. Atippiyasahāyakaṃ majjhattaṭṭhāne ṭhapento kilamati, appamattakepi cassa dukkhe uppanne ārodanākārappatto viya hoti. Majjhattaṃ [M 1.0288] garuṭṭhāne ca piyaṭṭhāne ca ṭhapento kilamati. Verimanussarato kodho uppajjati, tasmā appiyādīsu paṭhamaṃ na bhāvetabbā.

For this loving-kindness should not be developed at first towards these four types of persons: an unliked person, a very dear friend, a neutral person, and a hostile person. It should not be developed specifically towards one of a different sex. And it should not be developed at all towards a person who has died. For what reason should it not be developed at first towards the unliked person and the others? Because one becomes weary when placing an unliked person in the position of a dear one. One becomes weary when placing a very dear friend in the position of a neutral one; and when even a slight suffering befalls that person, one becomes as if about to weep. One becomes weary when placing a neutral person in the position of a respected one or a dear one. When recalling a hostile person, anger arises. Therefore, loving-kindness should not be developed at first towards the unliked person and the others.

Liṅgavisabhāge pana tameva ārabbha odhiso bhāventassa rāgo uppajjati. Aññataro kira amaccaputto kulūpakattheraṃ pucchi “bhante, kassa mettā bhāvetabbā”ti? Thero “piyapuggale”ti āha. Tassa attano bhariyā piyā hoti. So tassā mettaṃ bhāvento sabbarattiṃ bhittiyuddhamakāsi. Tasmā liṅgavisabhāge odhiso na bhāvetabbā.

Now, in the case of a person of a different sex, if one develops it specifically taking that very person as the object, lust arises. It is said that a certain minister’s son asked an elder who frequented his family, “Venerable sir, towards whom should loving-kindness be developed?” The elder replied, “Towards a dear person.” Now, his own wife was dear to him. So, while developing loving-kindness towards her, he spent the whole night making war with the wall. Therefore, one should not develop it specifically towards a person of a different sex.

Kālakate pana bhāvento neva appanaṃ, na upacāraṃ pāpuṇāti. Aññataro kira daharabhikkhu ācariyaṃ ārabbha mettaṃ ārabhi. Tassa mettā nappavattati. So mahātherassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, paguṇāva me mettājhānasamāpatti, na ca naṃ samāpajjituṃ sakkomi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āha. Thero “nimittaṃ, āvuso, gavesāhī”ti āha. So gavesanto ācariyassa matabhāvaṃ ñatvā aññaṃ ārabbha mettāyanto samāpattiṃ appesi. Tasmā kālakate na bhāvetabbāva.

Now, when one develops loving-kindness towards someone who has died, one attains neither absorption nor access concentration. A certain young bhikkhu, it is said, began developing loving-kindness taking his teacher as his object. His loving-kindness did not proceed. He went to a great elder and said, 'Venerable sir, my attainment of the loving-kindness jhāna is indeed well-practiced, and yet I cannot enter into it. What could be the reason?' The elder replied, 'Friend, investigate the sign.' While investigating, he discovered that his teacher had died. Then, taking another as his object and developing loving-kindness, he attained the absorption. Therefore, one should not develop loving-kindness at all towards someone who has died.

241. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ pana “ahaṃ sukhito homi niddukkho”ti vā, “avero abyāpajjo anīgho sukhī attānaṃ pariharāmī”ti vā evaṃ punappunaṃ attaniyeva bhāvetabbā.

241. First of all, one should repeatedly cultivate within oneself thus: “May I be happy and free from suffering,” or “May I be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress; may I, being happy, maintain myself.”

Evaṃ sante yaṃ vibhaṅge (vibha. 643) vuttaṃ –

This being so, there is what was stated in the Vibhaṅga:

“Kathañca bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati? Seyyathāpi [V 1.0285] nāma ekaṃ puggalaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ disvā mettāyeyya, evameva sabbe satte mettāya pharatī”ti.

“And how does a monk dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness? Just as one might extend loving-kindness to a dear and beloved person upon seeing them, even so, one pervades all beings with loving-kindness.”

“Yañca paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 2.22) –

And in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

“Katamehi pañcahākārehi anodhisopharaṇā mettā cetovimutti bhāvetabbā, sabbe sattā averā hontu” abyāpajjā anīghā sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu. Sabbe pāṇā… sabbe bhūtā… sabbe puggalā… sabbe attabhāvapariyāpannā averā abyāpajjā anīghā sukhī attānaṃ pariharantū”tiādi –

“In what five ways should the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, as an unspecified pervasion, be developed? ‘May all beings be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress; may they, being happy, maintain themselves!’ ‘May all living beings… may all creatures… may all persons… may all who have come into individual existence be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress; may they, being happy, maintain themselves!’ and so on.

Vuttaṃ. Yañca mettasutte (khu. pā. 9.3; su. ni. 145) –

This was said. And in the Mettā Sutta:

“Sukhinova [M 1.0289] khemino hontu,

Sabbasattā bhavantu sukhitattā”tiādi. –

“May they be happy and secure; may all beings have happy hearts,” and so on.

Vuttaṃ, taṃ virujjhati. Na hi tattha attani bhāvanā vuttāti ce. Tañca na virujjhati. Kasmā? Tañhi appanāvasena vuttaṃ. Idaṃ sakkhibhāvavasena.

This was said. That is contradicted. If it is said, “For the development of loving-kindness towards oneself is not stated there,” that too is not contradicted. Why? Because that was stated by way of absorption. This is stated by way of taking oneself as a witness.

Sacepi hi vassasataṃ vassasahassaṃ vā “ahaṃ sukhito homī”tiādinā nayena attani mettaṃ bhāveti, nevassa appanā uppajjati. “Ahaṃ sukhito homī”ti bhāvayato pana yathā ahaṃ sukhakāmo dukkhapaṭikkūlo jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo ca, evaṃ aññepi sattāti attānaṃ sakkhiṃ katvā aññasattesu hitasukhakāmatā uppajjati. Bhagavatāpi –

For even if one were to develop loving-kindness towards oneself for a hundred years or a thousand years in the manner of “May I be happy,” and so on, absorption would never arise for them. But for one who cultivates “May I be happy,” the desire for the welfare and happiness of other beings arises by taking oneself as a witness, thinking: “Just as I desire happiness, am averse to suffering, wish to live, and do not wish to die, so too do other beings.” By the Blessed One also—

“Sabbā disā anuparigamma cetasā,

Nevajjhagā piyataramattanā kvaci;

Evaṃ piyo puthu attā paresaṃ,

Tasmā na hiṃse paramattakāmo”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.119; udā. 41); –

“Having traversed all directions with the mind, one would nowhere find anyone dearer than oneself. In the same way, their own self is dear to each person. Therefore, one who desires their own welfare should not harm another.”

Vadatā [V 1.0286] ayaṃ nayo dassito.

in saying this, this method was shown.

242. Tasmā sakkhibhāvatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ attānaṃ mettāya pharitvā tadanantaraṃ sukhappavattanatthaṃ yvāyaṃ piyo manāpo garu bhāvanīyo ācariyo vā ācariyamatto vā upajjhāyo vā upajjhāyamatto vā tassa dānapiyavacanādīni piyamanāpattakāraṇāni sīlasutādīni garubhāvanīyattakāraṇāni ca anussaritvā “esa sappuriso sukhī hotu niddukkho”tiādinā nayena mettā bhāvetabbā.

242. Therefore, for the sake of being a witness, one should first pervade oneself with loving-kindness. Then, for the sake of its easy progress, toward a person who is dear, agreeable, respected, and venerable—a teacher or one like a teacher, a preceptor or one like a preceptor—one should develop loving-kindness by recalling the reasons for his being dear and agreeable, such as his generosity and kind speech, and the reasons for his being respected and venerable, such as his virtue and learning, by the method beginning: “May this good person be happy and free from suffering.”

Evarūpe ca puggale kāmaṃ appanā sampajjati, iminā pana bhikkhunā tāvatakeneva tuṭṭhiṃ anāpajjitvā sīmāsambhedaṃ kattukāmena tadanantaraṃ atippiyasahāyake, atippiyasahāyakato majjhatte, majjhattato verīpuggale mettā bhāvetabbā. Bhāventena ca ekekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse muduṃ kammaniyaṃ cittaṃ katvā tadanantare tadanantare upasaṃharitabbaṃ.

And toward such a person, absorption may indeed be accomplished. However, this bhikkhu, not being content with just that and wishing to break down the barriers, should then develop loving-kindness toward a very dear friend; from a very dear friend, toward a neutral person; and from a neutral person, toward a hostile person. And while developing it, having made the mind soft and workable in each section, he should apply it to the next in succession.

Yassa [M 1.0290] pana verīpuggalo vā natthi, mahāpurisajātikattā vā anatthaṃ karontepi pare verīsaññāva nuppajjati, tena “majjhatte me mettacittaṃ kammaniyaṃ jātaṃ, idāni naṃ verimhi upasaṃharāmī”ti byāpārova na kātabbo. Yassa pana atthi, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “majjhattato verīpuggale mettā bhāvetabbā”ti.

But for one who has no hostile person, or for whom, due to being of a great man's nature, the perception of an enemy does not arise even when others do him harm, for such a one, the effort, “My mind of loving-kindness toward the neutral person has become workable; now I will apply it to a hostile one,” should not be made. However, it was with reference to one who does have a hostile person that it was said: “Loving-kindness should be developed from the neutral person toward the hostile person.”

243. Sace panassa verimhi cittamupasaṃharato tena katāparādhānussaraṇena paṭighamuppajjati, athānena purimapuggalesu yattha katthaci punappunaṃ mettaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhahitvā punappunaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ mettāyantena paṭighaṃ vinodetabbaṃ. Sace evampi vāyamato na nibbāti, atha –

243. If, however, while directing his mind toward an enemy, resentment arises in him due to recalling the offense done by that person, then he should repeatedly enter upon loving-kindness toward any of the previous persons, emerge from it, and again and again dispel the resentment by suffusing that person with loving-kindness. If, even while striving thus, it does not subside, then—

Kakacūpamaovāda-ādīnaṃ anusārato;

Paṭighassa pahānāya, ghaṭitabbaṃ punappunaṃ.

By following the advice of the Simile of the Saw and other discourses, one must strive again and again for the abandoning of resentment.

Tañca kho iminā ākārena attānaṃ ovadanteneva “are kujjhanapurisa, nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

And this should be done by admonishing oneself in this way: “O man prone to anger, was it not said by the Blessed One—

‘Ubhatodaṇḍakena [V 1.0287] cepi, bhikkhave, kakacena corā ocarakā aṅgamaṅgāni okanteyyuṃ, tatrāpi yo mano padoseyya. Na me so tena sāsanakaro’ti (ma. ni. 1.232) ca,

‘Even if, monks, bandits were to sever your limbs one by one with a two-handled saw, whoever would allow his mind to become hateful on that account would not be following my teaching’ (MN 21), and

‘Tasseva tena pāpiyo, yo kuddhaṃ paṭikujjhati;

Kuddhamappaṭikujjhanto, saṅgāmaṃ jeti dujjayaṃ.

‘He who repays anger with anger is thereby the worse of the two; he who does not repay anger with anger wins a battle hard to win.

“‘Ubhinnamatthaṃ carati, attano ca parassa ca;

Paraṃ saṅkupitaṃ ñatvā, yo sato upasammatī’ti ca. (saṃ. ni. 1.188); –

‘He works for the good of both, his own and the other's, who, knowing the other is provoked, mindfully becomes calm’ (SN 7.2), and

“‘Sattime, bhikkhave, dhammā sapattakantā sapattakaraṇā kodhanaṃ āgacchanti itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā. Katame satta? Idha, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṃ icchati aho vatāyaṃ dubbaṇṇo assāti. Taṃ kissahetu? Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa vaṇṇavatāya nandati. Kodhanāyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto kiñcāpi so hoti sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu odātavatthavasano, atha kho so dubbaṇṇova hoti kodhābhibhūto. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, [M 1.0291] paṭhamo dhammo sapattakanto sapattakaraṇo kodhanaṃ āgacchati itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa evaṃ icchati ahovatāyaṃ dukkhaṃ sayeyyāti…pe… na pacurattho assāti…pe… na bhogavā assāti…pe… na yasavā assāti…pe… na mittavā assāti…pe… na kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjeyyāti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na, bhikkhave, sapatto sapattassa sugatigamanena nandati. Kodhanāyaṃ, bhikkhave, purisapuggalo kodhābhibhūto kodhapareto kāyena duccaritaṃ carati, vācāya manasā duccaritaṃ carati. So kāyena vācāya manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati kodhābhibhūto’ti (a. ni. 7.64) ca,

‘These seven things, monks, desired by an enemy and caused by an enemy, befall an angry man or woman. What seven? Here, monks, an enemy wishes of an enemy: “Oh, may this one be ugly!” For what reason? An enemy, monks, does not delight in the beauty of an enemy. This angry person, monks, overcome by anger, with a mind obsessed by it, even though he may be well-bathed, well-anointed, with trimmed hair and beard, and dressed in white clothes, is still ugly, being overcome by anger. This, monks, is the first thing desired by an enemy and caused by an enemy that befalls an angry man or woman. Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes of an enemy: “Oh, may this one sleep in misery!”… “May he not be prosperous!”… “May he not be wealthy!”… “May he not be famous!”… “May he not have friends!”… “May he, with the breakup of the body, after death, not be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world!” For what reason? An enemy, monks, does not delight in an enemy’s good destination. This angry person, monks, overcome by anger, with a mind obsessed by it, engages in misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the plane of misery, in hell, being overcome by anger.’ (AN 7.64) and

“‘Seyyathāpi[V 1.0288], bhikkhave, chavālātaṃ ubhatopadittaṃ majjhe gūthagataṃ neva gāme kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati, na araññe kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati. Tathūpamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmī’ti ca,

‘Just as, monks, a charnel-ground firebrand burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle serves as fuel neither in the village nor in the forest; I say, monks, that this person is a similar example.’ and,

“So dāni tvaṃ evaṃ kujjhanto na ceva bhagavato sāsanakaro bhavissasi, paṭikujjhanto ca kuddhapurisatopi pāpiyo hutvā na dujjayaṃ saṅgāmaṃ jessasi, sapattakaraṇe ca dhamme attāva attano karissasi, chavālātūpamo ca bhavissasī”ti.

“Now, by being angry in this way, you will not be one who follows the teaching of the Blessed One. And by retaliating with anger, having become more wicked than the person who was first angry, you will not win the battle that is hard to win. You yourself will do to yourself those things that are done by enemies, and you will become like the charnel-ground firebrand.”

244. Tassevaṃ ghaṭayato vāyamato sace taṃ paṭighaṃ vūpasammati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce vūpasammati, atha yo yo dhammo tassa puggalassa vūpasanto hoti parisuddho, anussariyamāno pasādaṃ āvahati, taṃ taṃ anussaritvā āghāto paṭivinetabbo.

244. For one who is striving and making an effort in this way, if that anger subsides, this is good. If it does not subside, then whatever qualities of that person are tranquil and pure, and which, when recollected, bring about clarity of mind—having repeatedly recollected those very qualities, the grudge should be dispelled.

Ekaccassa hi kāyasamācārova upasanto hoti. Upasantabhāvo cassa bahuṃ vattapaṭipattiṃ karontassa sabbajanena ñāyati. Vacīsamācāramanosamācārā pana avūpasantā honti. Tassa te acintetvā kāyasamācāravūpasamoyeva anussaritabbo.

For a certain person, only his bodily conduct is tranquil. And his state of tranquility, as he performs many duties and observances, is known by all people. But his verbal and mental conduct are not tranquil. Without thinking of those, only the tranquility of his bodily conduct should be recollected.

Ekaccassa [M 1.0292] vacīsamācārova upasanto hoti. Upasantabhāvo cassa sabbajanena ñāyati. So hi pakatiyā ca paṭisanthārakusalo hoti sakhilo sukhasambhāso sammodako uttānamukho pubbabhāsī madhurena sarena dhammaṃ osāreti, parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi dhammakathaṃ katheti. Kāyasamācāramanosamācārā pana avūpasantā honti, tassa te acintetvā vacīsamācāravūpasamoyeva anussaritabbo.

For a certain person, only his verbal conduct is tranquil. And his state of tranquility is known by all people. For he, by nature, is skilled in courteous speech, is gentle, is pleasant in conversation, is congenial, has a bright face, and is one who speaks first. He recites the Dhamma with a sweet voice; he gives a Dhamma talk with well-rounded and complete words and phrases. But his bodily and mental conduct are not tranquil. Without thinking of those, only the tranquility of his verbal conduct should be recollected.

Ekaccassa manosamācārova upasanto hoti, upasantabhāvo cassa cetiyavandanādīsu sabbajanassa pākaṭo hoti. Yo hi avūpasantacitto hoti, so cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā there vā vandamāno na sakkaccaṃ vandati, dhammassavanamaṇḍape vikkhittacitto vā pacalāyanto vā nisīdati. Upasantacitto pana okappetvā vandati, ohitasoto aṭṭhiṃkatvā kāyena vā vācāya vā cittappasādaṃ karonto dhammaṃ suṇāti. Iti ekaccassa manosamācārova upasanto hoti, kāyavacīsamācārā avūpasantā honti, tassa te acintetvā manosamācāravūpasamoyeva anussaritabbo.

For a certain person, only his mental conduct is tranquil, and this tranquility becomes evident to all in his acts of reverence at shrines and the like. For one whose mind is not tranquil, when paying reverence to a shrine, a Bodhi tree, or elders, does not do so respectfully; in the hall for listening to the Dhamma, he sits with a distracted mind or while drowsing. But one with a tranquil mind pays reverence with conviction and listens to the Dhamma with an attentive ear, making it his own and generating confidence of mind through body or speech. Thus, for a certain person, only mental conduct is tranquil, while bodily and verbal conduct are not tranquil. For him, without considering the latter, only the tranquility of his mental conduct should be recollected.

Ekaccassa [V 1.0289] pana imesu tīsu dhammesu ekopi avūpasanto hoti, tasmiṃ puggale “kiñcāpi esa idāni manussaloke carati, atha kho katipāhassa accayena aṭṭhamahānirayasoḷasaussadanirayaparipūrako bhavissatī”ti kāruññaṃ upaṭṭhapetabbaṃ. Kāruññampi hi paṭicca āghāto vūpasammati.

For a certain person, however, not even one of these three qualities is tranquil. Regarding such a person, compassion should be established, thinking: ‘Although this person now moves about in the human world, yet after a few days he will become a filler of the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells.’ For, based on compassion, resentment subsides.

Ekaccassa tayopime dhammā vūpasantā honti, tassa yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ anussaritabbaṃ. Tādise hi puggale na dukkarā hoti mettābhāvanāti.

For a certain person, all three of these qualities are tranquil. Of these, one should recollect whichever quality one wishes. For toward such a person, the development of loving-kindness is not difficult.

Imassa ca atthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ – “pañcime, āvuso, āghātapaṭivinayā. Yattha bhikkhuno uppanno āghāto sabbaso paṭivinodetabbo”ti (a. ni. 5.162) idaṃ pañcakanipāte āghātapaṭivinayasuttaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

And to make this meaning clear, this Āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta from the Book of Fives should be elaborated upon: ‘Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment, by which any resentment that has arisen in a bhikkhu should be entirely dispelled.’

245. Sace panassa evampi vāyamato āghāto uppajjatiyeva, athānena evaṃ attā ovaditabbo –

245. But if, despite such effort, resentment still arises, then one should advise oneself thus:

“Attano [M 1.0293] visaye dukkhaṃ, kataṃ te yadi verinā;

Kiṃ tassāvisaye dukkhaṃ, sacitte kattumicchasi.

“If an enemy has caused you suffering in his domain, why do you wish to create suffering in your own mind, which is not his domain?

“Bahūpakāraṃ hitvāna, ñātivaggaṃ rudammukhaṃ;

Mahānatthakaraṃ kodhaṃ, sapattaṃ na jahāsi kiṃ.

“Having left your very helpful relatives with their tearful faces, why do you not abandon anger, your enemy, which causes great harm?

“Yāni rakkhasi sīlāni, tesaṃ mūlanikantanaṃ;

Kodhaṃ nāmupaḷālesi, ko tayā sadiso jaḷo.

“You cherish anger, which cuts at the root of the very virtues that you guard. What fool is there like you?

“Kataṃ anariyaṃ kammaṃ, parena iti kujjhasi;

Kiṃ nu tvaṃ tādisaṃyeva, yo sayaṃ kattumicchasi.

“You are angry that another has done an ignoble deed; why then do you wish to do the very same kind of deed yourself?

“Dosetukāmo [V 1.0290] yadi taṃ, amanāpaṃ paro kari;

Dosuppādena tasseva, kiṃ pūresi manorathaṃ.

If another, wishing to anger you, were to do something disagreeable, why would you fulfill his wish by allowing anger to arise?

“Dukkhaṃ tassa ca nāma tvaṃ, kuddho kāhasi vā navā;

Attānaṃ panidāneva, kodhadukkhena bādhasi.

Whether or not you cause him suffering by your anger, you are right now tormenting yourself with the suffering of anger.

“Kodhaṃ vā ahitaṃ maggaṃ, ārūḷhā yadi verino;

Kasmā tuvampi kujjhanto, tesaṃyevānusikkhasi.

If your enemies have taken to the harmful path of anger, why, by getting angry, do you imitate them?

“Yaṃ dosaṃ tava nissāya, sattunā appiyaṃ kataṃ;

Tameva dosaṃ chindassu, kimaṭṭhāne vihaññasi.

Cut off that very aversion, on account of which your enemy did you an unpleasantness. Why do you torment yourself over what is not the real issue?

“Khaṇikattā ca dhammānaṃ, yehi khandhehi te kataṃ;

Amanāpaṃ niruddhā te, kassa dānīdha kujjhasi.

Because phenomena are momentary, those aggregates by which the unpleasantness was done to you have ceased. At whom, then, are you now angry here?

“Dukkhaṃ karoti yo yassa, taṃ vinā kassa so kare;

Sayampi dukkhahetutta, miti kiṃ tassa kujjhasī”ti.

He who causes suffering to another—without that other, to whom could he cause it? Since you yourself are also a cause of the suffering, why are you angry only at him?

246. Sace panassa evaṃ attānaṃ ovadatopi paṭighaṃ neva vūpasammati, athānena attano ca parassa ca kammassakatā paccavekkhitabbā. Tattha attano tāva evaṃ paccavekkhitabbā “ambho tvaṃ tassa kuddho kiṃ karissasi? Nanu taveva cetaṃ dosanidānaṃ kammaṃ anatthāya saṃvattissati? Kammassako hi tvaṃ kammadāyādo kammayoni kammabandhu kammapaṭisaraṇo, yaṃ kammaṃ karissasi, tassa dāyādo bhavissasi, idañca te kammaṃ neva sammāsambodhiṃ[M 1.0294], na paccekabodhiṃ, na sāvakabhūmiṃ, na brahmattasakkattacakkavattipadesarājādisampattīnaṃ aññataraṃ sampattiṃ sādhetuṃ samatthaṃ, atha kho sāsanato cāvetvā vighāsādādibhāvassa ceva nerayikādidukkhavisesānañca te saṃvattanikamidaṃ kammaṃ. So tvaṃ idaṃ karonto ubhohi hatthehi vītaccite vā aṅgāre, gūthaṃ vā gahetvā paraṃ paharitukāmo puriso viya attānameva paṭhamaṃ dahasi ceva duggandhañca karosī”ti.

246. But if, even after admonishing oneself in this way, one’s resentment does not subside, then one should reflect on the ownership of kamma, both one’s own and the other’s. Regarding one’s own, one should reflect thus: “Hey you, angry at him—what will you do? Surely this kamma of yours, rooted in aversion, will lead to your own harm. For you are the owner of your kamma, heir to your kamma, born of your kamma, related to your kamma, with kamma as your resort; whatever kamma you do, you will be its heir. And this kamma of yours is not capable of achieving perfect enlightenment, private enlightenment, the level of a disciple, or any attainment such as the status of Brahmā, Sakka, a wheel-turning monarch, or a regional king; but rather, having made you fall away from the Teaching, this kamma of yours leads to the state of being an eater of scraps and to various kinds of suffering in hell and other such states. You, in doing this, are like a man who, wishing to strike another, takes hold of glowing coals without flames or of excrement with both hands and thereby first burns himself and makes himself stink.”

Evaṃ [V 1.0291] attano kammassakataṃ paccavekkhitvā parassapi evaṃ paccavekkhitabbā “esopi tava kujjhitvā kiṃ karissati? Nanu etassevetaṃ anatthāya saṃvattissati? Kammassako hi ayamāyasmā kammadāyādo…pe… yaṃ kammaṃ karissati, tassa dāyādo bhavissati. Idañcassa kammaṃ neva sammāsambodhiṃ, na paccekabodhiṃ, na sāvakabhūmiṃ, na brahmattasakkattacakkavattipadesarājādisampattīnaṃ aññataraṃ sampattiṃ sādhetuṃ samatthaṃ, atha kho sāsanato cāvetvā vighāsādādibhāvassa ceva nerayikādidukkhavisesānañcassa saṃvattanikamidaṃ kammaṃ. Svāyaṃ idaṃ karonto paṭivāte ṭhatvā paraṃ rajena okiritukāmo puriso viya attānaṃyeva okirati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Having reflected thus on one’s own ownership of kamma, one should then reflect on the other’s in the same way: “What will this person do by being angry with you? Will this not lead to his own harm? For this venerable one is the owner of his kamma, heir to his kamma… Whatever kamma he does, he will be its heir. And this kamma of his is not capable of accomplishing Perfect Enlightenment, Private Enlightenment, the stage of a disciple, or any attainment such as the state of a Brahmā, Sakka, a wheel-turning monarch, or a regional king; but rather, having caused him to fall away from the Teaching, this kamma of his is conducive to the state of being an eater of scraps and to various kinds of suffering, such as in hell. In doing this, he is like a man who, standing against the wind and wishing to sprinkle dust on another, only sprinkles it on himself.” For this was said by the Blessed One:

“‘Yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati,

Suddhassa posassa anaṅgaṇassa;

Tameva bālaṃ pacceti pāpaṃ,

Sukhumo rajo paṭivātaṃva khitto’”ti. (dha. pa. 125; su. ni. 667);

‘Whoever offends an uncorrupted man, a person pure and stainless, upon that very fool the evil recoils, like fine dust thrown against the wind.’

247. Sace panassa evaṃ kammassakatampi paccavekkhato neva vūpasammati, athānena satthu pubbacariyaguṇā anussaritabbā.

247. But if, while one is reflecting in this way on the ownership of kamma, it still does not subside, then one should recollect the Teacher's virtues from his former conduct.

Tatrāyaṃ paccavekkhaṇānayo – ambho pabbajita, nanu te satthā pubbeva sambodhā anabhisambuddho bodhisattopi samāno cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pāramiyo pūrayamāno tattha tattha vadhakesupi paccatthikesu cittaṃ nappadūsesi. Seyyathidaṃ, sīlavajātake tāva attano deviyā paduṭṭhena pāpaamaccena ānītassa paṭirañño tiyojanasataṃ [M 1.0295] rajjaṃ gaṇhantassa nisedhanatthāya uṭṭhitānaṃ amaccānaṃ āvudhampi chupituṃ na adāsi. Puna saddhiṃ amaccasahassena āmakasusāne galappamāṇaṃ bhūmiṃ khaṇitvā nikhaññamāno cittappadosamattampi akatvā kuṇapakhādanatthaṃ āgatānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ paṃsuviyūhanaṃ nissāya purisakāraṃ katvā paṭiladdhajīvito yakkhānubhāvena attano sirigabbhaṃ oruyha sirisayane sayitaṃ paccatthikaṃ disvā kopaṃ akatvāva aññamaññaṃ sapathaṃ katvā taṃ mittaṭṭhāne ṭhapayitvā āha –

Here is the method of reflection: ‘O recluse, surely your Teacher, even before his enlightenment, while he was still an unenlightened Bodhisatta fulfilling the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, did not defile his mind even toward executioners and enemies in his various births? For instance, in the Sīlava Jātaka, when a rival king—brought by an evil minister who had misconducted himself with the Bodhisatta's own queen—was seizing his kingdom of three hundred yojanas, he did not even allow the ministers who rose up to stop him to touch a weapon. Again, while being buried up to his neck in the earth in a charnel ground for raw corpses along with a thousand ministers, he did not conceive even the slightest ill will. Instead, relying on the dust scattered by jackals that had come to eat the corpses, he made a manly effort. Having regained his life, through the power of a yakkha he descended into his own royal chamber, and seeing the enemy king lying on the royal bed, he felt no anger at all. After they exchanged oaths, he established him in the position of a friend and said:

“Āsīsetheva [V 1.0292] puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohamattānaṃ, yathā icchiṃ tathā ahū”ti. (jā. 1.1.51);

‘A man should indeed hope; a wise person should not become disheartened. I see myself: as I wished, so it has come to be.’

Khantivādījātake dummedhena kāsiraññā “kiṃvādī tvaṃ samaṇā”ti puṭṭho “khantivādī nāmāha”nti vutte sakaṇṭakāhi kasāhi tāḷetvā hatthapādesu chijjamānesu kopamattampi nākāsi.

In the Khantivādī Jātaka, when asked by the foolish king of Kāsī, “What do you profess, recluse?” and he replied, “I am one who professes patience,” the king had him beaten with thorny whips. And while his hands and feet were being severed, he did not show even a trace of anger.

Anacchariyañcetaṃ, yaṃ mahallako pabbajjūpagato evaṃ kareyya. Cūḷadhammapālajātake pana uttānaseyyakopi samāno –

It is not astonishing that an old man who has gone forth would act in this way. But in the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, while still an infant lying on his back—

“Candanarasānulittā, bāhā chijjanti dhammapālassa;

Dāyādassa pathabyā, pāṇā me deva rujjhantī”ti. (jā. 1.5.49);

‘Anointed with sandalwood essence, the arms of Dhammapāla are cut off; O king, heir to the earth, my life is being destroyed!’

Evaṃ vippalapamānāya mātuyā pitarā mahāpatāpena nāma raññā vaṃsakaḷīresu viya catūsu hatthapādesu chedāpitesu tāvatāpi santuṭṭhiṃ anāpajjitvā sīsamassa chindathāti āṇatte “ayaṃ dāni te cittapariggaṇhanakālo, idāni ambho dhammapāla, sīsacchedāṇāpake pitari, sīsacchedake purise, paridevamānāya mātari, attani cāti imesu catūsu samacitto hohī”ti daḷhaṃ samādānamadhiṭṭhāya paduṭṭhākāramattampi nākāsi.

While his mother was lamenting thus, his father, King Mahāpatāpa, had his four hands and feet cut off like tender bamboo shoots. Not satisfied even with that, he commanded, 'Cut off his head!' Then the Bodhisatta made this firm resolution: 'Now is the time for you to properly restrain your mind. Now, O Dhammapāla, be of equanimous mind toward these four: the father who orders your head to be cut off, the man who cuts it off, your lamenting mother, and yourself.' And he did not show even the slightest sign of ill will.

Idañcāpi anacchariyameva, yaṃ manussabhūto evamakāsi. Tiracchānabhūtopi pana chaddanto nāma vāraṇo hutvā visappitena sallena nābhiyaṃ viddhopi tāva anatthakārimhi luddake cittaṃ nappadūsesi. Yathāha –

This, too, is not surprising, that one who was a human being acted thus. But even when born as an animal, as the great elephant named Chaddanta, though struck in the navel by a poisoned arrow, he did not corrupt his mind toward the malevolent hunter. As it is said:

“Samappito [M 1.0296] puthusallena nāgo,

Aduṭṭhacitto luddakaṃ ajjhabhāsi;

Kimatthayaṃ kissa vā samma hetu,

Mamaṃ vadhī kassa vāyaṃ payogo”ti. (jā. 1.16.124);

‘Pierced by a broad arrow, the great elephant, with an uncorrupted mind, addressed the hunter: “For what purpose, friend, or for what reason do you slay me? At whose instigation is this?”’

Evaṃ [V 1.0293] vatvā ca kāsirañño mahesiyā tava dantānamatthāya pesitomhi bhadanteti vutte tassā manorathaṃ pūrento chabbaṇṇarasminiccharaṇasamujjalitacārusobhe attano dante chetvā adāsi.

When the hunter replied, ‘Venerable sir, I have been sent by the chief queen of the king of Kāsī for the sake of your tusks,’ the Bodhisatta, fulfilling her heart's desire, cut off his own tusks—beautifully radiant and resplendent with the emission of six-colored rays—and gave them to him.

Mahākapi hutvā attanāyeva pabbatapapātato uddharitena purisena –

When he was a great ape, a man whom he himself had rescued from a mountain precipice thought:

“Bhakkho ayaṃ manussānaṃ, yathevaññe vane migā;

Yaṃnūnimaṃ vadhitvāna, chāto khādeyya vānaraṃ.

‘This monkey is food for humans, just like other beasts in the forest. Being hungry, why should I not kill this monkey and eat it?

“Āhitova gamissāmi, maṃsamādāya sambalaṃ;

Kantāraṃ nittharissāmi, pātheyyaṃ me bhavissatī”ti. (jā. 1.16.205-206); –

‘Having eaten my fill, I will go on my way, taking its meat as provisions for the journey. I will cross the wilderness; it will be my sustenance.’

Evaṃ cintetvā silaṃ ukkhipitvā matthake sampadālite assupuṇṇehi nettehi taṃ purisaṃ udikkhamāno –

Having thought thus, the man lifted a stone and smashed the Bodhisatta’s head. Then the Bodhisatta, with eyes full of tears, looked up at that man and said:

“Mā ayyosi me bhadante, tvaṃ nāmetādisaṃ kari;

Tvaṃ khosi nāma dīghāvu, aññaṃ vāretumarahasī”ti. (jā. 1.16.209); –

‘My lord, good sir, do not do such a thing! You are indeed long-lived; you ought to be one who prevents others from such acts.’

Vatvā tasmiṃ purise cittaṃ appadūsetvā attano ca dukkhaṃ acintetvā tameva purisaṃ khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpesi.

Having spoken thus, without corrupting his mind toward that man and without considering his own suffering, he led that very man to a place of safety.

Bhūridatto nāma nāgarājā hutvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya vammikamuddhani sayamāno kappuṭṭhānaggisadisena osadhena sakalasarīre siñciyamānopi peḷāya pakkhipitvā sakalajambudīpe kīḷāpiyamānopi tasmiṃ brāhmaṇe manopadosamattampi na akāsi. Yathāha –

When he was Bhūridatta, the Nāga king, he undertook the Uposatha precepts and lay down on an anthill. Though his entire body was sprinkled with a drug like the fire at the world-dissolution, and though he was put into a basket and made to perform all over Jambudīpa, he did not conceive even the slightest ill will toward that brahmin. As it is said:

“Peḷāya pakkhipantepi, maddantepi ca pāṇinā;

Alampāne na kuppāmi, sīlakhaṇḍabhayā mamā”ti. (cariyā. 2.16);

‘Though they put me in a basket and crush me with their hands, I am not angry with the snake charmer, from fear that my virtue would be broken.’

Campeyyopi [M 1.0297][V 1.0294] nāgarājā hutvā ahituṇḍikena viheṭhiyamāno manopadosamattampi nuppādesi. Yathāha –

When he was the Nāga king Campeyya, though he was being tormented by a snake charmer, he did not generate even a trace of ill will. As it is said:

“Tadāpi maṃ dhammacāriṃ, upavutthauposathaṃ;

Ahituṇḍiko gahetvāna, rājadvāramhi kīḷati.

‘Then, while I was living righteously, observing the Uposatha, a snake charmer seized me and made me perform at the king’s gate.

“Yaṃ so vaṇṇaṃ cintayati, nīlaṃ pītaṃ va lohitaṃ;

Tassa cittānuvattanto, homi cintitasannibho.

‘Whatever color he thinks of—blue, yellow, or red—complying with his mind, I become just as he imagined.

“Thalaṃ kareyyaṃ udakaṃ, udakampi thalaṃ kare;

Yadihaṃ tassa kuppeyyaṃ, khaṇena chārikaṃ kare.

‘I could make dry land water, and water dry land. If I were to get angry with him, in an instant I could reduce him to ashes.

“Yadi cittavasī hessaṃ, parihāyissāmi sīlato;

Sīlena parihīnassa, uttamattho na sijjhatī”ti. (cariyā. 2.21-24);

‘But if I were to yield to my mind’s control, I would fall away from my virtue; and for one who has fallen from virtue, the ultimate goal is not achieved.’

Saṅkhapālanāgarājā hutvā tikhiṇāhi sattīhi aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu ovijjhitvā pahāramukhehi sakaṇṭakā latāyo pavesetvā nāsāya daḷhaṃ rajjuṃ pakkhipitvā soḷasahi bhojaputtehi kājenādāya vayhamāno dharaṇītale ghaṃsiyamānasarīro mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ paccanubhonto kujjhitvā olokitamatteneva sabbe bhojaputte bhasmaṃ kātuṃ samatthopi samāno cakkhuṃ ummīletvā paduṭṭhākāramattampi na akāsi.

When he was the Nāga king Saṅkhapāla, he was pierced in eight places with sharp spears, thorny vines were inserted through the wounds, and a strong rope was passed through his nose. He was then carried by sixteen hunters' sons using a carrying pole, and while his body was being scraped along the ground and he was experiencing great suffering, though he was capable of reducing all the hunters' sons to ash with a single angry glance, he opened his eyes but did not show even the slightest sign of ill will.

Yathāha –

As it is said:

“Cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiñcaḷāra,

Uposathaṃ niccamupāvasāmi;

Athāgamuṃ soḷasa bhojaputtā,

Rajjuṃ gahetvāna daḷhañca pāsaṃ.

‘On the fourteenth and the fifteenth, Āḷāra, I always observe the Uposatha. Then sixteen hunters' sons came, taking a rope and a strong noose.

“Bhetvāna [V 1.0295] nāsaṃ atikassa rajjuṃ,

Nayiṃsu maṃ samparigayha luddā;

Etādisaṃ dukkhamahaṃ titikkhaṃ,

Uposathaṃ appaṭikopayanto”ti. (jā. 2.17.180-181);

‘Having pierced my nose and pulled the rope taut, the hunters led me away, having completely surrounded me. I endured such suffering as this so as not to break my Uposatha observance.’

Na [M 1.0298] kevalañca etāneva, aññānipi mātuposakajātakādīsu anekāni acchariyāni akāsi. Tassa te idāni sabbaññutaṃ pattaṃ sadevaloke kenaci appaṭisamakhantiguṇaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ satthāraṃ apadisato paṭighacittaṃ nāma uppādetuṃ ativiya ayuttaṃ appatirūpanti.

And He performed not only these, but also many other wondrous deeds in the Mātuposaka Jātaka and others. For you, who point to that Blessed One as your Teacher—one who has now attained omniscience and possesses a virtue of patience unmatched by anyone in the world with its devas—to give rise to a mind of aversion is utterly unsuitable and inappropriate.

248. Sace panassa evaṃ satthu pubbacaritaguṇaṃ paccavekkhatopi dīgharattaṃ kilesānaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagatassa neva taṃ paṭighaṃ vūpasammati, athānena anamataggiyāni paccavekkhitabbāni. Tatra hi vuttaṃ –

248. But if, for this person who has for a long time come to a state of slavery to the defilements, that aversion does not subside at all even when reflecting in this way on the virtue of the Teacher’s past conduct, then the Anamatagga discourses should be reflected upon by him. For therein it is said:

“Na so, bhikkhave, satto sulabharūpo, yo na mātābhūtapubbo, yo na pitābhūtapubbo, yo na bhātā, yo na bhaginī, yo na putto, yo na dhītābhūtapubbā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.137-142).

“Monks, a being who has not formerly been a mother, who has not formerly been a father, who has not formerly been a brother, who has not formerly been a sister, who has not formerly been a son, who has not formerly been a daughter, is not easy to find.”

Tasmā tasmiṃ puggale evaṃ cittaṃ uppādetabbaṃ, “ayaṃ kira me atīte mātā hutvā dasamāse kucchiyā pariharitvā muttakarīsakheḷasiṅghāṇikādīni haricandanaṃ viya ajigucchamānā apanetvā ure naccāpentī aṅgena pariharamānā posesi, pitā hutvā ajapathasaṅkupathādīni gantvā vāṇijjaṃ payojayamāno mayhamatthāya jīvitampi pariccajitvā ubhatobyūḷhe saṅgāme pavisitvā nāvāya mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhanditvā aññāni ca dukkarāni karitvā ‘puttake posessāmī’ti tehi tehi upāyehi dhanaṃ saṃharitvā maṃ posesi. Bhātā, bhaginī, putto, dhītā ca hutvāpi idañcidañcupakāraṃ akāsīti tatra me nappatirūpaṃ manaṃ padūsetu”nti.

Therefore, regarding that person, a thought should be aroused thus: ‘It seems that in the past this person, having been my mother, carried me in her womb for ten months; not being disgusted, she removed my urine, feces, saliva, and mucus as if they were yellow sandalwood; making me dance upon her breast and carrying me on her hip, she nourished me. It seems that having been my father, he traveled goat-paths and treacherous paths, engaging in trade; for my sake, having given up even his life, having entered a battle arrayed on both sides, having set forth onto the great ocean by boat, and having performed other difficult deeds, thinking, “I will raise my children,” he gathered wealth by those various means and nourished me. And also having been my brother, sister, son, or daughter, this person rendered me this and that service, it seems. Therefore, it is not proper for me to defile my mind towards that person.’”

249. Sace pana evampi cittaṃ nibbāpetuṃ na sakkotiyeva, athānena evaṃ mettānisaṃsā paccavekkhitabbā – “ambho pabbajita, nanu vuttaṃ bhagavatā –

249. But if one is still unable to appease one’s mind even in this way, then the benefits of loving-kindness should be reflected upon by him thus: ‘O, recluse, was it not said by the Blessed One:’

‘Mettāya [V 1.0296] kho, bhikkhave, cetovimuttiyā āsevitāya bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya ekādasānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā[M 1.0299]. Katame ekādasa? Sukhaṃ supati, sukhaṃ paṭibujjhati, na pāpakaṃ supinaṃ passati, manussānaṃ piyo hoti, amanussānaṃ piyo hoti, devatā rakkhanti, nāssa aggi vā visaṃ vā satthaṃ vā kamati, tuvaṭaṃ cittaṃ samādhiyati, mukhavaṇṇo pasīdati, asammūḷho kālaṅkaroti, uttarimappaṭivijjhanto brahmalokūpago hotī’ti (a. ni. 11.15).

“Monks, when the liberation of mind by loving-kindness has been pursued, developed, and cultivated, made a vehicle and a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, eleven benefits can be expected. What are the eleven? One sleeps in comfort, wakes in comfort, and sees no bad dreams; one is dear to human beings and to non-human beings; deities protect one; neither fire nor poison nor a weapon can harm one; one's mind concentrates quickly; one's facial complexion is serene; one dies unconfused; and if one penetrates no higher, one is reborn in the Brahma-world.”

“Sace tvaṃ idaṃ cittaṃ na nibbāpessasi, imehi ānisaṃsehi paribāhiro bhavissasī”ti.

“If you do not quell this mind, you will be deprived of these benefits.”

250. Evampi nibbāpetuṃ asakkontena pana dhātuvinibbhogo kātabbo. Kathaṃ? “Ambho pabbajita, tvaṃ etassa kujjhamāno kassa kujjhasi? Kiṃ kesānaṃ kujjhasi, udāhu lomānaṃ, nakhānaṃ…pe… muttassa kujjhasi? Atha vā pana kesādīsu pathavīdhātuyā kujjhasi, āpodhātuyā, tejodhātuyā, vāyodhātuyā kujjhasi? Ye vā pañcakkhandhe dvādasāyatanāni aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo upādāya ayamāyasmā itthannāmoti vuccati, tesu kiṃ rūpakkhandhassa kujjhasi, udāhu vedanā saññā saṅkhāraviññāṇakkhandhassa kujjhasi? Kiṃ vā cakkhāyatanassa kujjhasi, kiṃ rūpāyatanassa kujjhasi…pe… kiṃ manāyatanassa kujjhasi, kiṃ dhammāyatanassa kujjhasi? Kiṃ vā cakkhudhātuyā kujjhasi, kiṃ rūpadhātuyā, kiṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātuyā…pe… kiṃ manodhātuyā, kiṃ dhammadhātuyā, kiṃ manoviññāṇadhātuyā”ti? Evañhi dhātuvinibbhogaṃ karoto āragge sāsapassa viya ākāse cittakammassa viya ca kodhassa patiṭṭhānaṭṭhānaṃ na hoti.

250. If one is unable to quell it even in this way, then an analysis of the elements should be undertaken. How? ‘O recluse, when you are angry with this person, at what are you angry? Are you angry at the hairs of the head, or the hairs of the body, the nails… or the urine? Or are you angry at the earth element in the hairs, etc., or at the water element, the fire element, or the air element? Or, with reference to the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements, this venerable one is called so-and-so—are you angry with the aggregate of form, or with the aggregate of feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness? Or are you angry with the eye base, or with the form base… or with the mind base, or with the mental-object base? Or are you angry with the eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element… or with the mind element, the mental-object element, or the mind-consciousness element?’ For one who makes an analysis of the elements in this way, anger finds no foothold, just as a mustard seed on the point of an awl or a painting in the sky.

251. Dhātuvinibbhogaṃ pana kātuṃ asakkontena dānasaṃvibhāgo kātabbo. Attano santakaṃ parassa dātabbaṃ, parassa santakaṃ attanā gahetabbaṃ. Sace pana paro bhinnājīvo hoti aparibhogārahaparikkhāro, attano santakameva dātabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ karoto ekanteneva tasmiṃ puggale āghāto vūpasammati. Itarassa ca atītajātito paṭṭhāya anubandhopi kodho taṅkhaṇaññeva vūpasammati, cittalapabbatavihāre tikkhattuṃ vuṭṭhāpitasenāsanena piṇḍapātikattherena “ayaṃ[M 1.0300], bhante, aṭṭhakahāpaṇagghanako patto mama mātarā upāsikāya dinno dhammiyalābho, mahāupāsikāya [V 1.0297] puññalābhaṃ karothā”ti vatvā dinnaṃ pattaṃ laddhamahātherassa viya. Evaṃ mahānubhāvametaṃ dānaṃ nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

251. If one is unable to perform the analysis of elements, then a sharing of gifts should be done. One should give what belongs to oneself to the other, and accept what belongs to the other. However, if the other person is of corrupt livelihood and possesses requisites that are unsuitable for use, one should only give what belongs to oneself. By doing so, one's resentment toward that person completely subsides. And for the other, even anger that has followed from past lives also subsides in that very moment, just as it did for the Great Elder who received the bowl given by the alms-food-eating elder at Cittalapabbata Monastery—the one who was thrice made to vacate his lodging—who said: ‘Venerable sir, this bowl, worth eight kahāpaṇas, was given to me by my mother, a lay devotee, as a righteous gain. Please let the great lay devotee acquire merit.’ This giving is of such great power. And this has been said:

“Adantadamanaṃ dānaṃ, dānaṃ sabbatthasādhakaṃ;

Dānena piyavācāya, unnamanti namanti cā”ti.

“Giving tames the untamed, giving accomplishes all objectives; through giving and kind speech, they rise up and defer.”

252. Tassevaṃ verīpuggale vūpasantapaṭighassa yathā piyātippiyasahāyakamajjhattesu, evaṃ tasmimpi mettāvasena cittaṃ pavattati. Athānena punappunaṃ mettāyantena attani piyapuggale majjhatte verīpuggaleti catūsu janesu samacittataṃ sampādentena sīmāsambhedo kātabbo. Tassidaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ, sace imasmiṃ puggale piyamajjhattaverīhi saddhiṃ attacatutthe ekasmiṃ padese nisinne corā āgantvā “bhante, ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti vatvā “kiṃ kāraṇā”ti vutte “taṃ māretvā galalohitaṃ gahetvā balikaraṇatthāyā”ti vadeyyuṃ, tatra ceso bhikkhu “asukaṃ vā asukaṃ vā gaṇhantū”ti cinteyya, akatova hoti sīmāsambhedo. Sacepi “maṃ gaṇhantu, mā ime tayo”tipi cinteyya, akatova hoti sīmāsambhedo. Kasmā? Yassa yassa hi gahaṇamicchati, tassa tassa ahitesī hoti, itaresaṃyeva hitesī hoti.

252. For that yogi, when aversion towards a hostile person has been pacified in this way, the mind proceeds by way of loving-kindness towards that person just as it does towards a dear person, a very dear person, a companion, and a neutral person. Then, by repeatedly practicing loving-kindness and accomplishing impartiality of mind towards the four persons—oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, and a hostile person—the breaking of the boundaries should be done. This is its characteristic: If, while this person is sitting in one place together with a dear person, a neutral person, and a hostile person, with himself as the fourth, robbers were to come and say, ‘Venerable sir, give one monk to us,’ and when asked, ‘For what reason?’ they should reply, ‘To kill him, take the blood from his throat, and make a sacrificial offering,’ and if that monk among them should think, ‘Let them take so-and-so or so-and-so,’ the breaking of the boundaries has not been done. Even if he should think, ‘Let them take me, but not these three,’ the breaking of the boundaries has not been done. Why? Because for whomever he wishes to be taken, he is one who seeks what is unbeneficial for that one, and one who seeks only what is beneficial for the others.

Yadā pana catunnaṃ janānamantare ekampi corānaṃ dātabbaṃ na passati, attani ca tesu ca tīsu janesu samameva cittaṃ pavatteti, kato hoti sīmāsambhedo. Tenāhu porāṇā –

But when, among the four persons, he does not see even one who should be given to the robbers, and he causes his mind to proceed equally towards himself and towards those three persons, the breaking of the boundaries has been done. Therefore, the ancients said:

“Attani hitamajjhatte, ahite ca catubbidhe;

Yadā passati nānattaṃ, hitacittova pāṇinaṃ.

“When one still sees a distinction in the fourfold group—oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, and a hostile person—one is then said to have merely a beneficial mind towards beings.

“Na nikāmalābhī mettāya, kusalīti pavuccati;

Yadā catasso sīmāyo, sambhinnā honti bhikkhuno.

He is not called one who obtains at will in loving-kindness, or one who is skilled. When, however, the four boundaries are broken for a monk,

“Samaṃ pharati mettāya, sabbalokaṃ sadevakaṃ;

Mahāviseso purimena, yassa sīmā na ñāyatī”ti.

He who pervades the entire world with its devas equally with loving-kindness, for whom a boundary is not known, is greatly superior to the former person.”

253. Evaṃ [M 1.0301][V 1.0298] sīmāsambhedasamakālameva ca iminā bhikkhunā nimittañca upacārañca laddhaṃ hoti. Sīmāsambhede pana kate tameva nimittaṃ āsevanto bhāvento bahulīkaronto appakasireneva pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva appanaṃ pāpuṇāti.

253. At the very same time as the breaking of the boundaries in this way, this monk has obtained both the sign and access concentration. But when the breaking of the boundaries has been done, by attending to, developing, and cultivating that very sign, he reaches absorption with little difficulty, in the very way described for the earth kasiṇa.

Ettāvatānena adhigataṃ hoti pañcaṅgavippahīnaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ tividhakalyāṇaṃ dasalakkhaṇasampannaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ mettāsahagataṃ. Adhigate ca tasmiṃ tadeva nimittaṃ āsevanto bhāvento bahulīkaronto anupubbena catukkanaye dutiyatatiyajjhānāni, pañcakanaye dutiyatatiyacatutthajjhānāni ca pāpuṇāti.

By this much application to meditation, this yogi has attained the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness, which is abandoned of five factors, endowed with five factors, of threefold goodness, and complete with ten characteristics. And when that is attained, by frequenting, developing, and making much of that very sign, one gradually reaches the second and third jhānas in the fourfold system, and the second, third, and fourth jhānas in the fivefold system.

So hi paṭhamajjhānādīnaṃ aññataravasena mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati. Tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati (vibha. 642; dī. ni. 1.556). Paṭhamajjhānādivasena appanāppattacittasseva hi ayaṃ vikubbanā sampajjati.

Truly, that yogi dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, by way of one or another of the first jhāna and so on. Similarly, the second; similarly, the third; similarly, the fourth. Thus, above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world with all its beings with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness that is extensive, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction (Vibh. 642; Dī. Ni. 1.556). For this performance is accomplished only for one whose mind has reached absorption by means of the first jhāna and so on.

254. Ettha ca mettāsahagatenāti mettāya samannāgatena. Cetasāti cittena. Ekaṃ disanti ekamekissā disāya paṭhamapariggahitaṃ sattaṃ upādāya ekadisāpariyāpannasattapharaṇavasena vuttaṃ. Pharitvāti phusitvā ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Viharatīti brahmavihārādhiṭṭhitaṃ iriyāpathavihāraṃ pavatteti. Tathā dutiyanti yathā puratthimādīsu disāsu yaṃkiñci ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tatheva tadanantaraṃ dutiyaṃ tatiyaṃ catutthañcāti attho. Iti uddhanti eteneva nayena uparimaṃ disanti vuttaṃ hoti. Adho tiriyanti adhodisampi tiriyaṃdisampi evameva. Tattha ca adhoti heṭṭhā. Tiriyanti anudisāsu. Evaṃ sabbadisāsu assamaṇḍale assamiva mettāsahagataṃ cittaṃ sāretipi paccāsāretipīti. Ettāvatā ekaṃ disaṃ pariggahetvā odhiso mettāpharaṇaṃ dassitaṃ.

254. Herein, ‘accompanied by loving-kindness’ means endowed with loving-kindness. ‘With a mind’ means with the mind. ‘One direction’ is said by way of pervading the beings included in one direction, taking as basis a being first apprehended in that one direction. ‘Pervading’ means having touched it and made it an object. ‘He dwells’ means he brings about the dwelling in a posture that is founded on the divine abiding. ‘Similarly, the second’ means that just as one dwells pervading any one direction among the eastern and so on, in that very way, immediately afterward, he pervades the second, the third, and the fourth. ‘Thus, above’ means by this same method, ‘the upper direction’ is said to be. ‘Below, across’ means the lower direction and the transverse directions in the same way. And therein, ‘below’ means underneath. ‘Across’ means in the intermediate directions. In this way, in all directions, like a horse in a training ring, he both drives forth and draws back the mind accompanied by loving-kindness. Thus far, the pervasion of loving-kindness with limitation has been shown, by apprehending one direction.

Sabbadhītiādi pana anodhiso dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha sabbadhīti sabbattha. Sabbattatāyāti sabbesu hīnamajjhimukkaṭṭhamittasapattamajjhattādippabhedesu attatāya[M 1.0302]. “Ayaṃ parasatto”ti vibhāgaṃ akatvā attasamatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā sabbattatāyāti sabbena cittabhāgena īsakampi [V 1.0299] bahi avikkhipamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sabbāvantanti sabbasattavantaṃ, sabbasattayuttanti attho. Lokanti sattalokaṃ. Vipulenātievamādipariyāyadassanato panettha puna mettāsahagatenāti vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā ettha odhiso pharaṇe viya puna tathāsaddo itisaddo vā na vutto, tasmā puna mettāsahagatena cetasāti vuttaṃ. Nigamavasena vā etaṃ vuttaṃ. Vipulenāti ettha ca pharaṇavasena vipulatā daṭṭhabbā. Bhūmivasena pana etaṃ mahaggataṃ paguṇavasena ca appamāṇasattārammaṇavasena ca appamāṇaṃ, byāpādapaccatthikappahānena averaṃ, domanassappahānato abyāpajjaṃ, niddukkhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasātiādinā nayena vuttāya vikubbanāya attho.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with 'Sabbadhi' is said to show the unspecified pervasion. Therein, 'sabbadhi' means 'in all places.' 'Sabbattatāya' means with the state of self towards all beings, whether distinguished as inferior, middling, or superior; as friend, enemy, or neutral. That is to say, it means with equality to self, without making the division, 'This is another being.' Alternatively, 'sabbattatāya' means with the entire portion of the mind, not diverting even a little of it outward. 'Sabbāvantaṃ' means possessing all beings, endowed with all beings. 'Lokaṃ' means the world of beings. The phrase 'with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness' is repeated here because of the exposition of terms beginning with 'vast' (vipulena). Or, because here, unlike in the specified pervasion, the words 'tathā' (similarly) or 'iti' (thus) are not stated, the phrase 'with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness' is therefore repeated. Or, this is stated by way of a conclusion. And here, regarding 'vast' (vipulena), the vastness should be understood by way of pervasion. Furthermore, by way of plane, this mind is 'exalted' (mahaggataṃ); by way of proficiency and by way of having immeasurable beings as its object, it is 'immeasurable' (appamāṇaṃ); through the abandoning of ill will and enmity, it is 'without enmity' (averaṃ); through the abandoning of mental pain, it is 'without affliction' (abyāpajjaṃ) and 'without suffering' (niddukkhaṃ). This is the meaning of the performance described by the method beginning, 'With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.'

255. Yathā cāyaṃ appanāppattacittasseva vikubbanā sampajjati, tathā yampi paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 2.22) “pañcahākārehi anodhisopharaṇā mettācetovimutti, sattahākārehi odhisopharaṇā mettā cetovimutti, dasahākārehi disāpharaṇā mettā cetovimuttī”ti vuttaṃ, tampi appanāppattacittasseva sampajjatīti veditabbaṃ.

255. And just as this performance is accomplished only for one whose mind has reached absorption, so too it should be understood that what is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga—'The liberation of mind through loving-kindness with unspecified pervasion in five ways, with specified pervasion in seven ways, and with directional pervasion in ten ways'—is also accomplished only for one whose mind has reached absorption.

Tattha ca sabbe sattā averā abyāpajjā anīghā sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu, sabbe pāṇā, sabbe bhūtā, sabbe puggalā, sabbe attabhāvapariyāpannā averā…pe… pariharantūti imehi pañcahākārehi anodhisopharaṇā mettā cetovimutti veditabbā.

And therein, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness with unspecified pervasion should be understood in these five ways: 'May all beings be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress; may they maintain themselves in happiness. May all breathing things, all creatures, all persons, all who are included in an individual existence be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves in happiness.'

Sabbā itthiyo averā…pe… attānaṃ pariharantu, sabbe purisā, sabbe ariyā, sabbe anariyā, sabbe devā, sabbe manussā, sabbe vinipātikā averā…pe… pariharantūti imehi sattahākārehi odhisopharaṇā mettā cetovimutti veditabbā.

The liberation of mind through loving-kindness with specified pervasion should be understood in these seven ways: 'May all women be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves. May all men, all noble ones, all non-noble ones, all gods, all humans, all those in the states of woe be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves.'

Sabbe puratthimāya disāya sattā averā…pe… attānaṃ pariharantu. Sabbe pacchimāya disāya, sabbe uttarāya disāya, sabbe dakkhiṇāya disāya, sabbe puratthimāya anudisāya, sabbe pacchimāya anudisāya, sabbe [M 1.0303] uttarāya anudisāya, sabbe dakkhiṇāya anudisāya, sabbe heṭṭhimāya disāya, sabbe uparimāya disāya sattā averā…pe… pariharantu. Sabbe puratthimāya disāya pāṇā, bhūtā, puggalā, attabhāvapariyāpannā, averā…pe… pariharantu. Sabbā puratthimāya disāya itthiyo, sabbe purisā, ariyā, anariyā, devā, manussā, vinipātikā [V 1.0300] averā…pe… pariharantu. Sabbā pacchimāya disāya, uttarāya, dakkhiṇāya, puratthimāya anudisāya, pacchimāya, uttarāya, dakkhiṇāya anudisāya, heṭṭhimāya disāya, uparimāya disāya itthiyo…pe… vinipātikā averā abyāpajjā anīghā sukhī attānaṃ pariharantūti imehi dasahākārehi disāpharaṇā mettā cetovimutti veditabbā.

The liberation of mind through loving-kindness with directional pervasion should be understood in these ten ways: 'May all beings in the eastern direction be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves. May all beings in the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, the southeastern direction, the northwestern direction, the northeastern direction, the southwestern direction, the downward direction, and the upward direction be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves. May all breathing things, creatures, persons, and all who are embodied in the eastern direction be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves. May all women in the eastern direction, all men, noble ones, non-noble ones, gods, humans, and all those in the states of woe be free from enmity… may they maintain themselves. In the same way, may all women… and all those in the states of woe in the western direction, the northern, the southern, the southeastern, the northwestern, the northeastern, the southwestern, the downward, and the upward direction be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from distress; may they, being happy, maintain themselves.'

256. Tattha sabbeti anavasesapariyādānametaṃ. Sattāti rūpādīsu khandhesu chandarāgena sattā visattāti sattā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

256. Herein, 'all' means inclusion without remainder. 'Beings' (sattā) are so called because they are attached (sattā) and clung (visattā) to the aggregates such as form through desire and lust. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Rūpe kho, rādha, yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā, tatra satto, tatra visatto, tasmā sattoti vuccati… vedanāya… saññāya… saṅkhāresu… viññāṇe yo chando yo rāgo yā nandī yā taṇhā, tatra satto, tatra visatto, tasmā sattoti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.161).

'Rādha, whatever desire, lust, delight, and craving there is for form, one is attached there, clung there; therefore one is called a 'being' (satta). … Whatever desire, lust, delight, and craving there is for feeling… for perception… for volitional formations… for consciousness, one is attached there, clung there; therefore one is called a 'being' (satta).'

Ruḷhīsaddena pana vītarāgesupi ayaṃ vohāro vattatiyeva, vilīvamayepi bījanivisese tālavaṇṭavohāro viya. Akkharacintakā pana atthaṃ avicāretvā nāmamattametanti icchanti. Yepi atthaṃ vicārenti, te satvayogena sattāti icchanti.

However, by conventional usage, this term is also applied to those who are free from lust, just as the term 'palm-leaf fan' is used for a particular kind of fan even when it is made of rushes. Grammarians, without considering the meaning, hold that it is merely a name. But those who do consider the meaning hold that they are called 'beings' (sattā) because of their connection with fortitude (satva).

Pāṇanatāya pāṇā, assāsapassāsāyattavuttitāyāti attho. Bhūtattā bhūtā, saṃbhūtattā abhinibbattattāti attho. Punti vuccati nirayo. Tasmiṃ galantīti puggalā, gacchantīti attho. Attabhāvo vuccati sarīraṃ. Khandhapañcakameva vā, tamupādāya paññattimattasambhavato. Tasmiṃ attabhāve pariyāpannāti attabhāvapariyāpannā. Pariyāpannāti paricchinnā, antogadhāti attho.

They are 'breathing things' (pāṇā) because of breathing; the meaning is that their life depends on in-breathing and out-breathing. They are 'creatures' (bhūtā) because of having come to be; the meaning is that they are born, have been produced. 'Pun' is said to be hell. They are 'persons' (puggalā) because they fall into it; the meaning is that they go there. 'Individual existence' (attabhāva) is said to be the body, or it is just the five aggregates, since it is a mere concept that arises in dependence on them.
