They are 'those included in an individual existence' (attabhāvapariyāpannā) because they are included (pariyāpannā) in that individual existence. 'Included' (pariyāpannā) means defined, contained within; that is the meaning.

Yathā [M 1.0304] ca sattāti vacanaṃ, evaṃ sesānipi ruḷhīvasena āropetvā sabbānetāni sabbasattavevacanānīti veditabbāni. Kāmañca aññānipi sabbe jantū sabbe jīvātiādīni sabbasattavevacanāni atthi, pākaṭavasena pana imāneva pañca gahetvā “pañcahākārehi anodhisopharaṇā mettā cetovimuttī”ti vuttaṃ.

And just as the word 'beings' (sattā) is applied metaphorically, so too the remaining terms should be understood, by applying them through conventional usage, as all being synonyms for 'all beings.' Although there are indeed other synonyms for 'all beings'—such as 'all creatures' (jantū), 'all living things' (jīvā), and so on—by way of what is prominent only these five have been taken, and it is said: 'The liberation of mind through loving-kindness with unspecified pervasion in five ways.'

Ye pana sattā pāṇātiādīnaṃ na kevalaṃ vacanamattatova, atha kho atthatopi nānattameva [V 1.0301] iccheyyuṃ, tesaṃ anodhisopharaṇā virujjhati, tasmā tathā atthaṃ agahetvā imesu pañcasu ākāresu aññataravasena anodhiso mettā pharitabbā.

But for those who might wish that the terms 'beings,' 'breathing things,' and so on, differ not only merely in wording but also in meaning, for them the unspecified pervasion is contradicted. Therefore, without taking the meaning in that way, loving-kindness should be pervaded without specification by means of any one of these five aspects.

257. Ettha ca sabbe sattā averā hontūti ayamekā appanā. Abyāpajjā hontūti ayamekā appanā. Abyāpajjāti byāpādarahitā. Anīghā hontūti ayamekā appanā. Anīghāti niddukkhā. Sukhī attānaṃ pariharantūti ayamekā appanā. Tasmā imesupi padesu yaṃ yaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, tassa tassa vasena mettā pharitabbā. Iti pañcasu ākāresu catunnaṃ appanānaṃ vasena anodhisopharaṇe vīsati appanā honti.

257. And herein, 'May all beings be free from enmity' is one absorption. 'May they be free from ill will' is one absorption. 'Free from ill will' (abyāpajjā) means free from malice (byāpāda). 'May they be free from distress' is one absorption. 'Free from distress' (anīghā) means without suffering (niddukkhā). 'May they maintain themselves in happiness' is one absorption. Therefore, in these phrases too, loving-kindness should be pervaded by way of whichever phrase becomes prominent. Thus, in the unspecified pervasion, by way of four absorptions for each of the five aspects, there are twenty absorptions.

Odhisopharaṇe pana sattasu ākāresu catunnaṃ vasena aṭṭhavīsati. Ettha ca itthiyo purisāti liṅgavasena vuttaṃ. Ariyā anariyāti ariyaputhujjanavasena. Devā manussā vinipātikāti upapattivasena.

In the specified pervasion, however, by way of the four absorptions for each of the seven aspects, there are twenty-eight. And here, 'women' and 'men' is stated in terms of gender; 'noble ones' and 'non-noble ones' in terms of noble ones and worldlings; 'gods,' 'humans,' and 'those in the states of woe' in terms of rebirth.

Disāpharaṇe pana sabbe puratthimāya disāya sattātiādinā nayena ekamekissā disāya vīsati vīsati katvā dvesatāni, sabbā puratthimāya disāya itthiyotiādinā nayena ekamekissā disāya aṭṭhavīsati aṭṭhavīsati katvā asīti dvesatānīti cattāri satāni asīti ca appanā. Iti sabbānipi paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttāni aṭṭhavīsādhikāni pañca appanāsatānīti.

In the directional pervasion, however, by the method beginning 'all beings in the eastern direction,' making twenty for each single direction, there are two hundred absorptions; and by the method beginning 'all women in the eastern direction,' making twenty-eight for each single direction, there are two hundred and eighty absorptions. Thus, there are four hundred and eighty absorptions. In this way, all the absorptions spoken of in the Paṭisambhidāmagga are five hundred with an excess of twenty-eight.

Iti etāsu appanāsu yassa kassaci vasena mettaṃ cetovimuttiṃ bhāvetvā ayaṃ yogāvacaro “sukhaṃ supatī”tiādinā nayena vutte ekādasānisaṃse paṭilabhati.

Thus, among these absorptions, having developed the liberation of mind through loving-kindness by way of any aspect whatsoever, this meditator obtains the eleven benefits spoken of by the method beginning, 'He sleeps in comfort.'

258. Tattha [M 1.0305] sukhaṃ supatīti yathā sesā janā samparivattamānā kākacchamānā dukkhaṃ supanti, evaṃ asupitvā sukhaṃ supati. Niddaṃ okkantopi samāpattiṃ samāpanno viya hoti.

258. Therein, as for 'He sleeps in comfort': just as other people sleep with difficulty, tossing and turning and snoring, not sleeping thus, he sleeps in comfort. Even when having entered sleep, he is like one who has entered a meditative attainment.

Sukhaṃ paṭibujjhatīti yathā aññe nitthunantā vijambhantā samparivattantā dukkhaṃ paṭibujjhanti, evaṃ appaṭibujjhitvā vikasamānamiva padumaṃ sukhaṃ nibbikāraṃ paṭibujjhati.

As for 'He awakens in comfort': just as others awaken with difficulty—groaning, yawning, and tossing and turning—not awakening thus, he awakens in comfort, without bodily distortion, like a blooming lotus.

Na [V 1.0302] pāpakaṃ supinaṃ passatīti supinaṃ passantopi bhaddakameva supinaṃ passati, cetiyaṃ vandanto viya pūjaṃ karonto viya dhammaṃ suṇanto viya ca hoti. Yathā pana aññe attānaṃ corehi samparivāritaṃ viya vāḷehi upaddutaṃ viya papāte patantaṃ viya ca passanti, evaṃ pāpakaṃ supinaṃ na passati.

As for 'He does not see a bad dream': even when seeing a dream, he sees only a good dream; he is as if paying homage to a cetiya, as if making an offering, and as if listening to the Dhamma. But just as others see themselves as if surrounded by thieves, as if attacked by wild beasts, and as if falling from a cliff, he does not see a bad dream thus.

Manussānaṃ piyo hotīti ure āmuttamuttāhāro viya sīse piḷandhamālā viya ca manussānaṃ piyo hoti manāpo.

As for 'He is dear to human beings': he is dear and beloved to human beings, like a string of pearls worn on the chest and like a garland worn on the head.

Amanussānaṃ piyo hotīti yatheva manussānaṃ, evaṃ amanussānampi piyo hoti visākhatthero viya.

As for 'He is dear to non-human beings': just as he is dear to human beings, so too is he dear to non-human beings, like the Elder Visākha.

So kira pāṭaliputte kuṭumbiyo ahosi. So tattheva vasamāno assosi “tambapaṇṇidīpo kira cetiyamālālaṅkato kāsāvapajjoto icchiticchitaṭṭhāneyeva ettha sakkā nisīdituṃ vā nipajjituṃ vā utusappāyaṃ senāsanasappāyaṃ puggalasappāyaṃ dhammassavanasappāyanti sabbamettha sulabha”nti.

He, it is said, was a householder in Pāṭaliputta. While living there, he heard: 'The island of Tambapaṇṇi, they say, is adorned with a series of shrines and is resplendent with the color of the robes. Here one can sit or lie down in any place one wishes. Suitable climate, suitable lodging, suitable persons, and a suitable opportunity to hear the Dhamma—all this suitability is easy to obtain here.'

So attano bhogakkhandhaṃ puttadārassa niyyādetvā dussante baddhena ekakahāpaṇeneva gharā nikkhamitvā samuddatīre nāvaṃ udikkhamāno ekamāsaṃ vasi. So vohārakusalatāya imasmiṃ ṭhāne bhaṇḍaṃ kiṇitvā asukasmiṃ vikkiṇanto dhammikāya vaṇijjāya tenevantaramāsena sahassaṃ abhisaṃhari. Anupubbena mahāvihāraṃ āgantvā pabbajjaṃ yāci.

Having entrusted his mass of wealth to his wife and children, he left home with only a single kahāpaṇa tied in the hem of his garment. He lived for one month on the seashore, looking for a ship. Due to his skill in trade, buying goods in this place and selling them in another, by means of righteous commerce he accumulated a thousand within that very month. In due course he came to the Mahāvihāra and asked for the going forth.

So [M 1.0306] pabbājanatthāya sīmaṃ nīto taṃ sahassatthavikaṃ ovaṭṭikantarena bhūmiyaṃ pātesi. “Kimeta”nti ca vutte “kahāpaṇasahassaṃ, bhante”ti vatvā “upāsaka, pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya na sakkā vicāretuṃ, idānevetaṃ vicārehī”ti vutte “visākhassa pabbajjaṭṭhānamāgatā mā rittahatthā gamiṃsū”ti muñcitvā sīmāmāḷake vippakiritvā pabbajitvā upasampanno.

When he was led to the boundary for the purpose of the going forth, he dropped the purse with the thousand coins from within his folded upper garment onto the ground. When asked, 'What is this?' he said, 'A thousand kahāpaṇas, venerable sir.' When he was told, 'Lay follower, from the time of the going forth it is not allowable to manage this; dispose of it right now,' he thought, 'May those who have come to the place of Visākha's going forth not depart empty-handed.' Untying the purse, he scattered the coins in the precincts of the boundary hall. Having gone forth, he received the higher ordination.

So pañcavasso hutvā dvemātikā paguṇā katvā pavāretvā attano sappāyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā [V 1.0303] ekekasmiṃ vihāre cattāro māse katvā samappavattavāsaṃ vasamāno cari. Evaṃ caramāno –

Having become of five rains-retreats, having made the two Mātikās fluent, he performed the Pavāraṇā and took up a meditation subject suitable for himself. He spent four months in each monastery, dwelling with an equal distribution of his time. As he was journeying thus—

Vanantare ṭhito thero, visākho gajjamānako;

Attano guṇamesanto, imamatthaṃ abhāsatha.

Standing in the midst of the forest, the elder Visākha, roaring, reflected on his own virtues and spoke this matter:

“Yāvatā upasampanno, yāvatā idha āgato;

Etthantare khalitaṃ natthi, aho lābhā te mārisā”ti.

“From the time I was ordained, for as long as I have been here, in this interval there has been no transgression. Oh, Mārisa, what a gain for you!”

So cittalapabbatavihāraṃ gacchanto dvedhā pathaṃ patvā “ayaṃ nu kho maggo udāhu aya”nti cintayanto aṭṭhāsi. Athassa pabbate adhivatthā devatā hatthaṃ pasāretvā “esa maggo”ti vatvā dasseti. So cittalapabbatavihāraṃ gantvā tattha cattāro māse vasitvā paccūse gamissāmīti cintetvā nipajji. Caṅkamasīse maṇilarukkhe adhivatthā devatā sopānaphalake nisīditvā parodi.

While going to the Cittalapabbata Monastery, he reached a fork in the road and stood there thinking, “Is this the path, or is that one?” Then a deity dwelling on the mountain extended a hand, saying, “This is the path,” and showed him. Having gone to the Cittalapabbata Monastery, he dwelt there for four months. Thinking, “I will go at dawn,” he lay down. A deity dwelling in the Maṇila tree at the head of the walking path sat on a plank of the staircase and wept.

Thero “ko eso”ti āha. Ahaṃ, bhante, maṇiliyāti. Kissa rodasīti? Tumhākaṃ gamanaṃ paṭiccāti. Mayi idha vasante tumhākaṃ ko guṇoti? Tumhesu, bhante, idha vasantesu amanussā aññamaññaṃ mettaṃ paṭilabhanti, te dāni tumhesu gatesu kalahaṃ karissanti, duṭṭhullampi kathayissantīti. Thero “sace mayi idha vasante tumhākaṃ phāsuvihāro hoti, sundara”nti vatvā aññepi cattāro māse tattheva vasitvā puna tatheva gamanacittaṃ uppādesi. Devatāpi puna tatheva parodi. Etenevupāyena thero tattheva vasitvā tattheva parinibbāyīti evaṃ mettāvihārī bhikkhu amanussānaṃ piyo hoti.

The elder asked, “Who is that?” “Venerable sir, I am the Maṇila tree-deity.” “For what reason do you weep?” “On account of your departure.” “While I am dwelling here, what benefit is there for you?” “Venerable sir, while you are dwelling here, the non-human beings obtain loving-kindness for one another. Now, when you have gone, they will quarrel and also speak harsh words.” The elder, saying, “If, while I am dwelling here, there is a comfortable abiding for you, it is good,” dwelt in that very place for another four months and again, just as before, produced the thought of going. The deity also wept again just as before. By this very means, the elder dwelt in that very place and in that very place attained Parinibbāna. Thus, a bhikkhu who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to non-human beings.

Devatā rakkhantīti puttamiva mātāpitaro devatā rakkhanti.

“Deities protect him” means: just as parents protect their son, so do deities protect him.

Nāssa [M 1.0307] aggi vā visaṃ vā satthaṃ vā kamatīti mettāvihārissa kāye uttarāya upāsikāya viya aggi vā, saṃyuttabhāṇakacūḷasivattherasseva visaṃ vā, saṃkiccasāmaṇerasseva satthaṃ vā na kamati, na pavisati. Nāssa kāyaṃ vikopetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhenuvatthumpi cettha kathayanti[V 1.0304]. Ekā kira dhenu vacchakassa khīradhāraṃ muñcamānā aṭṭhāsi. Eko luddako taṃ vijjhissāmīti hatthena samparivattetvā dīghadaṇḍasattiṃ muñci. Sā tassā sarīraṃ āhacca tālapaṇṇaṃ viya pavaṭṭamānā gatā, neva upacārabalena, na appanābalena, kevalaṃ vacchake balavapiyacittatāya. Evaṃ mahānubhāvā mettāti.

“Fire, poison, or a weapon does not affect him” means: For one who dwells in loving-kindness, just as fire did not harm the female lay disciple Uttarā, nor poison the Elder Cūḷasiva, the reciter of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, nor a weapon the novice Saṅkicca, so fire, poison, or a weapon does not take effect on or penetrate his body. This means that his body is not injured. Here, the teachers also relate the story of the cow. It is said that a cow once stood letting a stream of milk flow for her calf. A hunter, thinking, “I will pierce her,” brandished a long-shafted spear with his hand and released it. It struck her body but rolled up like a palm leaf and went away. This was not by the power of access concentration or by the power of absorption, but solely because of her powerful affection for her calf. So powerful is loving-kindness.

Tuvaṭaṃ cittaṃ samādhiyatīti mettāvihārino khippameva cittaṃ samādhiyati, natthi tassa dandhāyitattaṃ.

“His mind is quickly concentrated” means: For one who dwells in loving-kindness, the mind becomes concentrated quickly; there is no sluggishness in him.

Mukhavaṇṇo vippasīdatīti bandhanā pavuttaṃ tālapakkaṃ viya cassa vippasannavaṇṇaṃ mukhaṃ hoti.

“The complexion of his face is bright” means: His face becomes especially clear in complexion, like a ripe palm fruit fallen from its stalk.

Asammūḷho kālaṅkarotīti mettāvihārino sammohamaraṇaṃ nāma natthi, asammūḷhova niddaṃ okkamanto viya kālaṃ karoti.

“He dies unbewildered” means: For one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no such thing as a bewildered death; he passes away unbewildered, as if entering into sleep.

Uttarimappaṭivijjhantoti mettāsamāpattito uttariṃ arahattaṃ adhigantuṃ asakkonto ito cavitvā suttappabuddho viya brahmalokamupapajjatīti.

“If he penetrates no higher” means: Being unable to attain Arahantship, which is higher than the attainment of loving-kindness, when he passes away from here he is reborn in the Brahmā world as if awakening from sleep.

Ayaṃ mettābhāvanāyaṃ vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed exposition on the development of loving-kindness.

Karuṇābhāvanākathā

The Exposition on the Development of Compassion

259. Karuṇaṃ bhāvetukāmena pana nikkaruṇatāya ādīnavaṃ karuṇāya ca ānisaṃsaṃ paccavekkhitvā karuṇābhāvanā ārabhitabbā. Tañca pana ārabhantena paṭhamaṃ piyapuggalādīsu na ārabhitabbā. Piyo hi piyaṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati. Atippiyasahāyako atippiyasahāyakaṭṭhāneyeva. Majjhatto majjhattaṭṭhāneyeva. Appiyo appiyaṭṭhāneyeva. Verī veriṭṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati. Liṅgavisabhāgakālakatā akhettameva.

259. Furthermore, one who wishes to develop compassion should reflect on the danger in cruelty and the benefit of compassion, and then the development of compassion should be begun. And when beginning it, one should not start at first with a dear person and the others. For a dear person remains only in the position of being dear; a very dear friend, only in the position of being a very dear friend; a neutral person, only in the position of being neutral; a disliked person, only in the position of being disliked; and an enemy, only in the position of being an enemy. Persons of the opposite sex and deceased persons are indeed unsuitable fields.

“Kathañca bhikkhu karuṇāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati? Seyyathāpi nāma ekaṃ puggalaṃ duggataṃ durūpetaṃ disvā karuṇāyeyya, evameva [M 1.0308] sabbasatte karuṇāya pharatī”ti [V 1.0305] vibhaṅge (vibha. 653) pana vuttattā sabbapaṭhamaṃ tāva kiñcideva karuṇāyitabbarūpaṃ paramakicchappattaṃ duggataṃ durūpetaṃ kapaṇapurisaṃ chinnāhāraṃ kapālaṃ purato ṭhapetvā anāthasālāya nisinnaṃ hatthapādehi paggharantakimigaṇaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ karontaṃ disvā “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ satto āpanno, appeva nāma imamhā dukkhā mucceyyā”ti karuṇā pavattetabbā. Taṃ alabhantena sukhitopi pāpakārī puggalo vajjhena upametvā karuṇāyitabbo.

“And how does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion? Just as one might feel compassion on seeing an unfortunate and miserable person, so one pervades all beings with compassion.” As it is said thus in the Vibhaṅga, one should first of all see a person who inspires compassion: someone utterly wretched, unfortunate, and miserable, a poor man deprived of food, sitting in a shelter for the destitute with a bowl before him, with swarms of maggots oozing from his hands and feet, uttering cries of pain. Seeing him, one should arouse compassion, thinking: “Alas, this being has fallen into misery! If only he could be freed from this suffering!” If one does not find such a person, one should arouse compassion for a prosperous but evil-doing person, comparing him to one condemned to execution.

Kathaṃ? Seyyathāpi saha bhaṇḍena gahitacoraṃ “vadhetha na”nti rañño āṇāya rājapurisā bandhitvā catukke catukke pahārasatāni dentā āghātanaṃ nenti. Tassa manussā khādanīyampi bhojanīyampi mālāgandhavilepanatambulānipi denti. Kiñcāpi so tāni khādanto ceva paribhuñjanto ca sukhito bhogasamappito viya gacchati, atha kho taṃ neva koci “sukhito ayaṃ mahābhogo”ti maññati, aññadatthu “ayaṃ varāko idāni marissati, yaṃ yadeva hi ayaṃ padaṃ nikkhipati, tena tena santike maraṇassa hotī”ti taṃ jano karuṇāyati. Evameva karuṇākammaṭṭhānikena bhikkhunā sukhitopi puggalo evaṃ karuṇāyitabbo “ayaṃ varāko kiñcāpi idāni sukhito susajjito bhoge paribhuñjati, atha kho tīsu dvāresu ekenāpi katassa kalyāṇakammassa abhāvā idāni apāyesu anappakaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedissatī”ti.

How so? Suppose royal men have caught a thief with the stolen goods. On the king’s order, “Execute him!” they bind him and, giving him hundreds of blows at each crossroads, lead him to the execution ground. People give him food and drink, garlands, perfumes, ointments, and betel. Although he goes along eating and enjoying these things as if he were happy and endowed with possessions, no one thinks, “He is happy, he has great wealth.” On the contrary, people feel compassion for him, thinking: “This poor wretch is about to die. With every step he takes, he draws closer to death.” In the same way, a bhikkhu practicing the compassion meditation should feel compassion even for a prosperous person, thinking: “Though this poor wretch is now happy, well-adorned, and enjoying his possessions, yet because he has not done a single good deed through any of the three doors, he will soon experience immense bodily suffering and mental sorrow in the states of woe.”

Evaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ karuṇāyitvā tato paraṃ eteneva upāyena piyapuggale, tato majjhatte, tato verimhīti anukkamena karuṇā pavattetabbā. Sace panassa pubbe vuttanayeneva verimhi paṭighaṃ uppajjati, taṃ mettāya vuttanayeneva vūpasametabbaṃ. Yopi cettha katakusalo hoti, tampi ñātirogabhogabyasanādīnaṃ aññatarena byasanena samannāgataṃ disvā vā sutvā vā tesaṃ abhāvepi vaṭṭadukkhaṃ anatikkantattā “dukkhitova aya”nti evaṃ sabbathāpi karuṇāyitvā vuttanayeneva attani piyapuggale majjhatte verimhīti catūsu janesu sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā [M 1.0309] taṃ nimittaṃ āsevantena bhāventena bahulīkarontena mettāya vuttanayeneva tikacatukkajjhānavasena appanā vaḍḍhetabbā.

Having thus shown compassion for that person, one should then extend it in sequence to a dear person, then to a neutral person, and then to an enemy. If, however, resentment towards the enemy should arise in him, it should be pacified in the very way described for loving-kindness. And even in the case of one here who has done what is wholesome, on seeing or hearing that they are beset by some misfortune such as the loss of relatives, disease, or loss of wealth, or even in the absence of these, since they have not transcended the suffering of the round of rebirths, one should show compassion in every way, thinking, “This person is indeed suffering.” Then, in the very way described, having broken down the boundaries among the four persons—oneself, a dear person, a neutral person, and an enemy—by practicing, developing, and cultivating that sign, one should increase absorption by way of the triad and tetrad of jhānas, in the very way described for loving-kindness.

Aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana paṭhamaṃ veripuggalo karuṇāyitabbo, tasmiṃ cittaṃ muduṃ katvā duggato, tato piyapuggalo, tato attāti ayaṃ kamo vutto, so “duggataṃ durūpeta”nti pāḷiyā [V 1.0306] na sameti, tasmā vuttanayenevettha bhāvanamārabhitvā sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā appanā vaḍḍhetabbā. Tato paraṃ “pañcahākārehi anodhisopharaṇā sattahākārehi odhisopharaṇā dasahākārehi disāpharaṇā”ti ayaṃ vikubbanā, “sukhaṃ supatī”tiādayo ānisaṃsā ca mettāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbāti.

In the commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya, however, this sequence is given: first, an enemy should be shown compassion; having made the mind tender towards him, then an unfortunate person, then a dear person, and then oneself. That sequence does not agree with the Pāli which says, “an unfortunate person in a bad state.” Therefore, having begun the development here in the very way described and having broken down the boundaries, one should develop absorption. Thereafter, this higher transformation—the unspecified pervasion in five ways, the specified pervasion in seven ways, and the directional pervasion in ten ways—and the benefits, such as “one sleeps in comfort,” should be understood in the very way described for loving-kindness.

Ayaṃ karuṇābhāvanāya vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed exposition of the development of compassion.

Muditābhāvanākathā

Exposition on the Development of Sympathetic Joy

260. Muditābhāvanaṃ ārabhantenāpi na paṭhamaṃ piyapuggalādīsu ārabhitabbā. Na hi piyo piyabhāvamatteneva muditāya padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, pageva majjhattaverino. Liṅgavisabhāgakālakatā akhettameva.

260. Even when beginning the development of sympathetic joy, one should not start first with such persons as a dear one. For a dear person is not a proximate cause for sympathetic joy merely by the fact of being dear, still less a neutral person or an enemy. A person of the opposite sex or a deceased person are an unsuitable field indeed.

Atippiyasahāyako pana siyā padaṭṭhānaṃ, yo aṭṭhakathāyaṃ soṇḍasahāyoti vutto. So hi muditamuditova hoti, paṭhamaṃ hasitvā pacchā katheti, tasmā so vā paṭhamaṃ muditāya pharitabbo. Piyapuggalaṃ vā sukhitaṃ sajjitaṃ modamānaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā “modati vatāyaṃ satto, aho sādhu aho suṭṭhū”ti muditā uppādetabbā. Imameva hi atthavasaṃ paṭicca vibhaṅge (vibha. 663) vuttaṃ “kathañca bhikkhu muditāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati? Seyyathāpi nāma ekaṃ puggalaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ disvā mudito assa, evameva sabbasatte muditāya pharatī”ti.

However, a very dear companion can be a proximate cause; he is called a 'boon companion' in the commentary. For he is indeed very joyful; he laughs first and speaks afterwards. Therefore, he should be the first to be pervaded with sympathetic joy. Or, on seeing or hearing that a dear person is happy, prosperous, and rejoicing, one should arouse sympathetic joy, thinking: 'Indeed, this being is rejoicing! How good! How excellent!' It is with reference to this very matter that it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'And how does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy? Just as he would be joyful on seeing a dear and beloved person, so he pervades all beings with sympathetic joy.'

Sacepissa so soṇḍasahāyo vā piyapuggalo vā atīte sukhito ahosi, sampati pana duggato durūpeto, atītameva cassa sukhitabhāvaṃ anussaritvā “esa atīte evaṃ mahābhogo mahāparivāro niccappamudito ahosī”ti tamevassa muditākāraṃ gahetvā muditā uppādetabbā “anāgate vā pana puna taṃ sampattiṃ labhitvā [M 1.0310] hatthikkhandhaassapiṭṭhisuvaṇṇasivikādīhi vicarissatī”ti anāgatampissa muditākāraṃ gahetvā muditā uppādetabbā.

If that boon companion or dear person was happy in the past but is now unfortunate and of wretched appearance, one should recollect his past state of happiness, thinking, 'In the past this person had great wealth, a great retinue, and was always joyful,' and arouse sympathetic joy by taking that very mode of his joy. Or, thinking, 'In the future, he will again obtain that good fortune and will go about on the backs of elephants and horses, in golden palanquins, and so on,' one should arouse sympathetic joy by taking a mode of his future joy.

Evaṃ piyapuggale muditaṃ uppādetvā atha majjhatte tato verimhīti anukkamena muditā pavattetabbā. Appanā vaḍḍhetabbā. Sace panassa pubbe vuttanayeneva verimhi paṭighaṃ uppajjati, taṃ [V 1.0307] mettāyaṃ vuttanayeneva vūpasametvā “imesu ca tīsu attani cā”ti catūsu janesu samacittatāya sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā taṃ nimittaṃ āsevantena bhāventena bahulīkarontena mettāyaṃ vuttanayeneva tikacatukkajjhānavaseneva appanā vaḍḍhetabbā. Tato paraṃ “pañcahākārehi anodhisopharaṇā sattahākārehi odhisopharaṇā dasahākārehi disāpharaṇā”ti ayaṃ vikubbanā, “sukhaṃ supatī”tiādayo ānisaṃsā ca mettāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbāti.

Having thus aroused sympathetic joy towards a dear person, one should then direct it successively towards a neutral person and then an enemy. Absorption should be developed. If resentment towards the enemy arises in him in the way already described, it should be quieted in the way described for loving-kindness. Then, by making his mind impartial towards the four persons—that is, these three and himself—he should break down the boundaries. By cultivating, developing, and making much of that sign, he should develop absorption by means of the triad and tetrad of jhānas in the way described for loving-kindness. Thereafter, the modes of pervasion—the fivefold unspecified pervasion, the sevenfold specified pervasion, and the tenfold directional pervasion—and the benefits such as 'he sleeps in comfort' should be understood in the very way described for loving-kindness.

Ayaṃ muditābhāvanāya vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed exposition on the development of sympathetic joy.

Upekkhābhāvanākathā

Exposition on the Development of Equanimity

261. Upekkhābhāvanaṃ bhāvetukāmena pana mettādīsu paṭiladdhatikacatukkajjhānena paguṇatatiyajjhānā vuṭṭhāya “sukhitā hontū”tiādivasena sattakelāyanamanasikārayuttattā, paṭighānunayasamīpacārittā, somanassayogena oḷārikattā ca purimāsu ādīnavaṃ, santasabhāvattā upekkhāya ānisaṃsañca disvā yvāssa pakatimajjhatto puggalo, taṃ ajjhupekkhitvā upekkhā uppādetabbā. Tato piyapuggalādīsu. Vuttañhetaṃ “kathañca bhikkhu upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati? Seyyathāpi nāma ekaṃ puggalaṃ neva manāpaṃ na amanāpaṃ disvā upekkhako assa, evameva sabbe satte upekkhāya pharatī”ti (vibha. 673).

261. Furthermore, one who wishes to develop equanimity, who has attained the triple and quadruple jhānas through loving-kindness and so on, should emerge from the third jhāna in which he is proficient. He should see the danger in the preceding states because they are connected with a fond regard for beings expressed as 'May they be happy!', because they verge on approval and resentment, and because they are coarse through their association with joy; and he should see the benefit in equanimity because of its peaceful nature. Then he should arouse equanimity by looking on with equanimity at a person who is naturally neutral to him. Then he should do so towards a dear person, and so on. For it is said: 'And how does a bhikkhu dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity? Just as he might be equanimous on seeing a person who is neither pleasing nor displeasing, so he pervades all beings with equanimity.'

Tasmā vuttanayena majjhattapuggale upekkhaṃ uppādetvā atha piyapuggale, tato soṇḍasahāyake, tato verimhīti evaṃ “imesu ca tīsu attani cā”ti sabbattha majjhattavasena sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā taṃ nimittaṃ āsevitabbaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ bahulīkātabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ karoto pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayeneva catutthajjhānaṃ uppajjati.

Therefore, having aroused equanimity towards a neutral person in the way described, then towards a dear person, then a boon companion, and then a hostile person—thus, having broken down the boundaries everywhere by means of neutrality towards 'these three persons and oneself'—that sign should be cultivated, developed, and made much of. For one who does so, the fourth jhāna arises in the very same way as described in the section on the earth kasiṇa.

Kiṃ [M 1.0311] panetaṃ pathavīkasiṇādīsu uppannatatiyajjhānassāpi uppajjatīti? Nuppajjati. Kasmā? Ārammaṇavisabhāgatāya. Mettādīsu uppannatatiyajjhānasseva pana uppajjati, ārammaṇasabhāgatāyāti. Tato paraṃ pana vikubbanā ca ānisaṃsapaṭilābho ca mettāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabboti.

But does this arise for one who has the third jhāna that arose on an earth kasiṇa, etc.? It does not arise. Why? Because of the dissimilarity of the object. But it arises only for one who has the third jhāna that arose on loving-kindness, etc., because of the similarity of the object. Furthermore, the transformations and the attainment of the benefits should be understood in the very same way as described in the section on loving-kindness.

Ayaṃ [V 1.0308] upekkhābhāvanāya vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation of the development of equanimity.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Exposition

262.

262.

Brahmuttamena kathite, brahmavihāre ime iti viditvā;

Bhiyyo etesu ayaṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

Having known in this way these divine abidings taught by the Buddha, the one supreme among Brahmas, this miscellaneous exposition on them should be further understood.

Etāsu hi mettākaruṇāmuditāupekkhāsu atthato tāva mejjatīti mettā, siniyhatīti attho. Mitte vā bhavā, mittassa vā esā pavattītipi mettā. Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ hadayakampanaṃ karotīti karuṇā. Kiṇāti vā paradukkhaṃ hiṃsati vināsetīti karuṇā. Kiriyati vā dukkhitesu pharaṇavasena pasāriyatīti karuṇā. Modanti tāya taṃsamaṅgino, sayaṃ vā modati, modanamattameva vā tanti muditā. “Averā hontū”tiādibyāpārappahānena majjhattabhāvūpagamanena ca upekkhatīti upekkhā.

For in these—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—first, as to their verbal meaning: it is loving-kindness (mettā) because it is tender (mejjati); that is, it is affectionate (siniyhati). Or it is loving-kindness because it occurs in relation to a friend, or it is the conduct of a friend. It is compassion (karuṇā) because when there is the suffering of others, it causes the hearts of good people to tremble. Or, it is karuṇā because it assails (kiṇāti), that is, it harms and destroys the suffering of others. Or, it is karuṇā because it is spread out (kiriyati) by way of pervading those afflicted with suffering. It is sympathetic joy (muditā) because those endowed with it rejoice by means of it, or one rejoices oneself, or it is simply the act of rejoicing. It is equanimity (upekkhā) because one looks on (upekkhati) by abandoning such activities as, 'May they be free from enmity,' etc., and by arriving at a state of neutrality.

263. Lakkhaṇādito panettha hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā mettā, hitūpasaṃhārarasā, āghātavinayapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ manāpabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Byāpādūpasamo etissā sampatti, sinehasambhavo vipatti. Dukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā karuṇā, paradukkhāsahanarasā, avihiṃsāpaccupaṭṭhānā, dukkhābhibhūtānaṃ anāthabhāvadassanapadaṭṭhānā. Vihiṃsūpasamo tassā sampatti, sokasambhavo vipatti. Pamodanalakkhaṇā muditā, anissāyanarasā, arativighātapaccupaṭṭhānā, sattānaṃ sampattidassanapadaṭṭhānā. Arativūpasamo tassā sampatti, pahāsasambhavo vipatti. Sattesu majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā upekkhā, sattesu samabhāvadassanarasā, paṭighānunayavūpasamapaccupaṭṭhānā, “kammassakā sattā, te kassa [M 1.0312] ruciyā sukhitā vā bhavissanti, dukkhato vā muccissanti, pattasampattito vā na parihāyissantī”ti evaṃ pavattakammassakatādassanapadaṭṭhānā. Paṭighānunayavūpasamo tassā sampatti, gehasitāya aññāṇupekkhāya sambhavo vipatti.

263. Furthermore, as to their characteristics and so on, among these: Loving-kindness has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of welfare, the function of bringing benefit, the manifestation of removing resentment, and the proximate cause of seeing the agreeable aspect of beings. The calming of ill will is its success; the arising of affection is its failure. Compassion has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of wishing to remove suffering, the function of not tolerating the suffering of others, the manifestation of non-harming, and the proximate cause of seeing the helplessness of those overwhelmed by suffering. The calming of cruelty is its success; the arising of sorrow is its failure. Sympathetic joy has the characteristic of gladdening, the function of being without envy, the manifestation of dispelling discontent, and the proximate cause of seeing the success of beings. The calming of discontent is its success; the arising of mirth is its failure. Equanimity has the characteristic of occurring in the mode of neutrality toward beings, the function of seeing beings equally, the manifestation of the calming of aversion and approval, and its proximate cause is seeing that beings are owners of their kamma, thus: 'Beings are owners of their kamma. By whose wish will they become happy, or be freed from suffering, or not decline from the success they have attained?' The calming of aversion and approval is its success; the arising of ignorant equanimity based on the household life is its failure.

264. Catunnampi panetesaṃ brahmavihārānaṃ vipassanāsukhañceva bhavasampatti ca sādhāraṇappayojanaṃ[V 1.0309]. Byāpādādipaṭighāto āveṇikaṃ. Byāpādapaṭighātappayojanā hettha mettā. Vihiṃsāaratirāgapaṭighātappayojanā itarā. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

264. Furthermore, for all four of these divine abodes, the happiness of insight and the success of existence are the common purpose. The counteracting of ill will and so on is the specific purpose. Herein, loving-kindness has the purpose of counteracting ill will. The others have the purpose of counteracting cruelty, discontent, and lust. And this has been said:

“Nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa yadidaṃ mettā cetovimutti. Nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, vihesāya yadidaṃ karuṇā cetovimutti. Nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, aratiyā yadidaṃ muditā cetovimutti. Nissaraṇañhetaṃ, āvuso, rāgassa yadidaṃ upekkhā cetovimuttī”ti (dī. ni. 3.326; a. ni. 6.13).

‘Friends, this is indeed the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness. Friends, this is indeed the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion. Friends, this is indeed the escape from discontent, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy. Friends, this is indeed the escape from lust, namely, the liberation of mind through equanimity.’

265. Ekekassa cettha āsannadūravasena dve dve paccatthikā. Mettābrahmavihārassa hi samīpacāro viya purisassa sapatto guṇadassanasabhāgatāya rāgo āsannapaccatthiko, so lahuṃ otāraṃ labhati, tasmā tato suṭṭhu mettā rakkhitabbā. Pabbatādigahananissito viya purisassa sapatto sabhāgavisabhāgatāya byāpādo dūrapaccatthiko, tasmā tato nibbhayena mettāyitabbaṃ. Mettāyissati ca nāma, kopañca karissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

265. Herein, for each of these divine abidings, there are two enemies each by way of a near one and a far one. For the divine abiding of loving-kindness, lust is the near enemy due to the similarity of seeing good qualities, like a rival of a person who moves about nearby. It finds an opening quickly; therefore, loving-kindness must be well guarded from it. Ill will is the far enemy due to the dissimilarity in nature, like a rival of a person who relies on a difficult place such as a mountain. Therefore, from it, loving-kindness should be developed fearlessly. For it is an impossible case that one would develop loving-kindness and also produce anger.

Karuṇābrahmavihārassa “cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpānaṃ iṭṭhānaṃ kantānaṃ manāpānaṃ manoramānaṃ lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ appaṭilābhaṃ vā appaṭilābhato samanupassato pubbe vā paṭiladdhapubbaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ vipariṇataṃ samanussarato uppajjati domanassaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ domanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati gehasitaṃ domanassa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.307) nayena āgataṃ gehasitaṃ domanassaṃ vipattidassanasabhāgatāya āsannapaccatthikaṃ. Sabhāgavisabhāgatāya vihiṃsā dūrapaccatthikā[M 1.0313]. Tasmā tato nibbhayena karuṇāyitabbaṃ. Karuṇañca nāma karissati, pāṇiādīhi ca viheṭhissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

For the divine abiding of compassion, the near enemy is the grief based on the household life, which is mentioned in the passage beginning: 'When one perceives the non-attainment of forms cognizable by the eye that are pleasant, desirable, agreeable, delightful, and connected with the world's material lures, or when one recollects what was formerly attained but is now past, ceased, and changed, sorrow arises; such sorrow is called grief based on the household life.' This is the near enemy due to the similarity of seeing misfortune. Cruelty is the far enemy due to the dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, fearless of it, compassion should be developed. For it is an impossible case that one would practice compassion and also harm with one's hands and so on.

Muditābrahmavihārassa “cakkhuviññeyyānaṃ rūpānaṃ iṭṭhānaṃ…pe… lokāmisapaṭisaṃyuttānaṃ paṭilābhaṃ vā paṭilābhato samanupassato pubbe vā paṭiladdhapubbaṃ atītaṃ niruddhaṃ vipariṇataṃ samanussarato uppajjati somanassaṃ, yaṃ evarūpaṃ somanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati gehasitaṃ somanassa”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.306) nayena āgataṃ gehasitaṃ somanassaṃ sampattidassanasabhāgatāya āsannapaccatthikaṃ, sabhāgavisabhāgatāya arati dūrapaccatthikā. Tasmā tato [V 1.0310] nibbhayena muditā bhāvetabbā. Mudito ca nāma bhavissati, pantasenāsanesu ca adhikusalesu dhammesu vā ukkaṇṭhissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

For the divine abiding of sympathetic joy, the near enemy is the joy based on the household life, which is mentioned in the passage beginning: 'When one perceives the attainment of forms cognizable by the eye that are pleasant... and connected with the world's material lures, or when one recollects what was formerly attained but is now past, ceased, and changed, joy arises; such joy is called joy based on the household life.' This is the near enemy because it shares the nature of seeing success. Discontent is the far enemy because of the dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, sympathetic joy should be developed fearlessly of it. For it is impossible that one would be sympathetically joyful and also become discontented with remote lodgings or with higher wholesome states.

Upekkhābrahmavihārassa pana “cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjati upekkhā bālassa mūḷhassa puthujjanassa anodhijinassa avipākajinassa anādīnavadassāvino assutavato puthujjanassa yā evarūpā upekkhā, rūpaṃ sā nātivattati. Tasmā sā upekkhā gehasitāti vuccatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.308) nayena āgatā gehasitā aññāṇupekkhā dosaguṇāvicāraṇavasena sabhāgattā āsannapaccatthikā. Sabhāgavisabhāgatāya rāgapaṭighā dūrapaccatthikā. Tasmā tato nibbhayena upekkhitabbaṃ. Upekkhissati ca nāma, rajjissati ca paṭihaññissati cāti aṭṭhānametaṃ.

Furthermore, for the divine abiding of equanimity, the near enemy is the ignorant equanimity based on the household life, which is mentioned in the passage beginning: 'Having seen a form with the eye, equanimity arises in a foolish, deluded, uninstructed ordinary person who has not conquered the confines or the results, and who does not see the danger. Such equanimity does not transcend the form; therefore it is called equanimity based on the household life.' This is the near enemy because it shares the nature of not investigating faults and virtues. Lust and aversion are the far enemies because of the dissimilarity in nature. Therefore, one should be equanimous fearlessly of them. For it is impossible that one would be equanimous and also be lustful and averse.

266. Sabbesampi ca etesaṃ kattukāmatā chando ādi, nīvaraṇādivikkhambhanaṃ majjhaṃ, appanā pariyosānaṃ. Paññattidhammavasena eko vā satto aneke vā sattā ārammaṇaṃ. Upacāre vā appanāya vā pattāya ārammaṇavaḍḍhanaṃ.

266. Furthermore, for all of these, the will to practice is the beginning, the suppression of the hindrances and so on is the middle, and absorption is the culmination. By way of concept, the object is one being or many beings. When access or absorption is reached, there is the extension of the object.

Tatrāyaṃ vaḍḍhanakkamo, yathā hi kusalo kassako kasitabbaṭṭhānaṃ paricchinditvā kasati, evaṃ paṭhamameva ekamāvāsaṃ paricchinditvā tattha sattesu imasmiṃ āvāse sattā averā hontūtiādinā nayena mettā bhāvetabbā. Tattha cittaṃ muduṃ kammaniyaṃ katvā dve āvāsā paricchinditabbā. Tato anukkamena tayo, cattāro, pañca, cha, satta, aṭṭha, nava, dasa, ekā racchā, upaḍḍhagāmo, gāmo, janapado, rajjaṃ, ekā disāti evaṃ yāva ekaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ, tato vā pana bhiyyo tattha tattha sattesu mettā [M 1.0314] bhāvetabbā. Tathā karuṇādayoti ayamettha ārammaṇavaḍḍhanakkamo.

Herein, this is the method of extension. Just as a skilled farmer, having demarcated the area to be plowed, then plows it, so too, at the very first, having demarcated a single dwelling, loving-kindness should be developed towards the beings therein by the method of: 'May the beings in this dwelling be free from enmity,' and so on. There, having made the mind soft and workable, two dwellings should be demarcated. Then, in sequence, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten dwellings, one street, half a village, a village, a district, a kingdom, and one direction should be demarcated. In this way, up to one world-sphere, or even beyond, loving-kindness should be developed towards the beings in each of those respective places. Similarly, compassion and the others are to be developed. This, herein, is the method of extending the object.

267. Yathā pana kasiṇānaṃ nissando āruppā, samādhinissando nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ, vipassanānissando phalasamāpatti, samathavipassanānissando nirodhasamāpatti, evaṃ purimabrahmavihārattayanissando ettha upekkhābrahmavihāro. Yathā hi thambhe anussāpetvā tulāsaṅghāṭaṃ anāropetvā na sakkā ākāse kūṭagopānasiyo ṭhapetuṃ, evaṃ purimesu tatiyajjhānaṃ vinā na sakkā catutthaṃ bhāvetunti.

267. Furthermore, just as the formless attainments are the outflow of the kasiṇas, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the outflow of concentration, the attainment of fruition is the outflow of insight, and the attainment of cessation is the outflow of serenity and insight, so too, herein, the divine abiding of equanimity is the outflow of the preceding triad of divine abidings. For just as it is not possible to place the ridge-pole and rafters in the air without having erected the pillars and placed the tie-beams, so too it is not possible to develop the fourth [divine abiding] without the third jhāna in the preceding ones.

268. Ettha [V 1.0311] siyā, kasmā panetā mettākaruṇāmuditāupekkhā brahmavihārāti vuccanti? Kasmā ca catassova? Ko ca etāsaṃ kamo, abhidhamme ca kasmā appamaññāti vuttāti? Vuccate, seṭṭhaṭṭhena tāva niddosabhāvena cettha brahmavihāratā veditabbā. Sattesu sammāpaṭipattibhāvena hi seṭṭhā ete vihārā. Yathā ca brahmāno niddosacittā viharanti, evaṃ etehi sampayuttā yogino brahmasamā hutvā viharantīti seṭṭhaṭṭhena niddosabhāvena ca brahmavihārāti vuccanti.

268. Herein, this reflection might arise: Why, then, are these—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—called the divine abidings? And why are they said to be only four? And what is their sequence? And in the Abhidhamma, why are they called the 'immeasurables'? It is said: Herein, their nature as divine abidings should be known, firstly, in the sense of being sublime and by their faultless nature. For, because they are the state of right conduct towards beings, these abidings are sublime. And just as brahmās dwell with faultless minds, so too, yogis endowed with these dwell having become like brahmās. Thus, they are called divine abidings in the sense of being sublime and by their faultless nature.

269. Kasmā ca catassovātiādi pañhassa pana idaṃ vissajjanaṃ.

269. As for the question beginning, 'And why only four?' and so on, this is the explanation.

Visuddhimaggādivasā catasso,

Hitādiākāravasā panāsaṃ;

Kamo pavattanti ca appamāṇe,

Tā gocare yena tadappamaññā.

By way of being the path of purification and so on, there are four; furthermore, their sequence is by way of the modes of welfare and so on. And because they proceed within an immeasurable range, for that reason they are called the 'immeasurables'.

Etāsu hi yasmā mettā byāpādabahulassa, karuṇā vihesābahulassa, muditā aratibahulassa, upekkhā rāgabahulassa visuddhimaggo. Yasmā ca hitūpasaṃhāraahitāpanayanasampattimodanaanābhogavasena catubbidhoyeva sattesu manasikāro. Yasmā ca yathā mātā daharagilānayobbanappattasakiccapasutesu catūsu puttesu daharassa abhivuḍḍhikāmā hoti, gilānassa gelaññāpanayanakāmā, yobbanappattassa yobbanasampattiyā ciraṭṭhitikāmā, sakakiccapasutassa kismiñci pariyāye abyāvaṭā hoti, tathā appamaññāvihārikenāpi sabbasattesu mettādivasena bhavitabbaṃ. Tasmā ito visuddhimaggādivasā catassova appamaññā.

Indeed, among these, loving-kindness is the path of purification for one who abounds in ill will; compassion for one who abounds in cruelty; sympathetic joy for one who abounds in discontent; and equanimity for one who abounds in lust. And because attention to beings is of just four kinds: by way of promoting welfare, removing harm, rejoicing in their prosperity, and impartiality. And because, just as a mother with her four sons—a young one, a sick one, one who has reached youth, and one diligent in his own affairs—desires the growth of the young one, the removal of the sick one's illness, the long endurance of the prosperity of the one who has reached youth, and on some occasion is not occupied with the one diligent in his own affairs, so too should one who abides in the immeasurables be disposed towards all beings by way of loving-kindness and so on. Therefore, on account of being paths of purification and so on, there are only these four immeasurables.

Yasmā [M 1.0315] catassopetā bhāvetukāmena paṭhamaṃ hitākārappavattivasena sattesu paṭipajjitabbaṃ, hitākārappavattilakkhaṇā ca mettā. Tato evaṃ patthitahitānaṃ sattānaṃ dukkhābhibhavaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā sambhāvetvā vā dukkhāpanayanākārappavattivasena, dukkhāpanayanākārappavattilakkhaṇā ca karuṇā. Athevaṃ patthitahitānaṃ patthitadukkhāpagamānañca nesaṃ sampattiṃ disvā sampattipamodanavasena, pamodanalakkhaṇā ca muditā. Tato paraṃ pana kattabbābhāvato ajjhupekkhakattasaṅkhātena majjhattākārena paṭipajjitabbaṃ, majjhattākārappavattilakkhaṇā ca upekkhā[V 1.0312]. Tasmā ito hitādiākāravasā panāsaṃ paṭhamaṃ mettā vuttā, atha karuṇā muditā upekkhāti ayaṃ kamo veditabbo.

Because one who wishes to develop these four should first practice towards beings by way of the mode of promoting their welfare, and loving-kindness has the characteristic of the mode of promoting welfare. Then, having seen, heard, or considered that those beings whose welfare has thus been wished for are overcome by suffering, one should practice by way of the mode of removing suffering; and compassion has the characteristic of the mode of removing suffering. Then, having seen the prosperity of those whose welfare has been wished for and whose suffering one has wished to remove, one should practice by way of rejoicing in their prosperity; and gladness has the characteristic of rejoicing. Thereafter, since there is nothing further to be done, one should practice with a neutral mode, which is reckoned as the state of overlooking; and equanimity has the characteristic of proceeding with a neutral mode. Therefore, on account of these modes of promoting welfare and so on, loving-kindness is stated first, then compassion, gladness, and equanimity. This order should be understood.

Yasmā pana sabbāpetā appamāṇe gocare pavattanti. Appamāṇā hi sattā etāsaṃ gocarabhūtā. Ekasattassāpi ca ettake padese mettādayo bhāvetabbāti evaṃ pamāṇaṃ agahetvā sakalapharaṇavaseneva pavattāti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, it is because all of them occur in a boundless field. For boundless are the beings that constitute their object. And even towards a single being, loving-kindness and the others are to be developed not by taking a measure such as 'in just this area,' but by way of pervading the whole. Hence it is said:

Visuddhimaggādivasā catasso,

Hitādiākāravasā panāsaṃ;

Kamo pavattanti ca appamāṇe,

Tā gocare yena tadappamaññāti.

By way of the path of purification and so on, they are four; by way of the modes of promoting welfare and so on is their sequence. And they proceed with a boundless object; that is why they are called the 'immeasurables'.

270. Evaṃ appamāṇagocaratāya ekalakkhaṇāsu cāpi etāsu purimā tisso tikacatukkajjhānikāva honti. Kasmā? Somanassāvippayogato. Kasmā panāyaṃ somanassena avippayogoti? Domanassasamuṭṭhitānaṃ byāpādādīnaṃ nissaraṇattā. Pacchimā pana avasesaekajjhānikāva. Kasmā? Upekkhāvedanāsampayogato. Na hi sattesu majjhattākārappavattā brahmavihārupekkhā upekkhāvedanaṃ vinā vattatīti.

270. Thus, although they have the single characteristic of having a boundless object, among these the first three belong only to the jhānas of the triad and tetrad. Why? Because of their non-dissociation from joy. But why are they not dissociated from joy? Because they are the escape from ill will and other states that arise from displeasure. The last one, however, belongs only to the remaining single jhāna. Why? Because of its association with the feeling of equanimity. For the divine abiding of equanimity, which proceeds with a neutral attitude towards beings, does not occur without the feeling of equanimity.

271. Yo panevaṃ vadeyya “yasmā bhagavatā aṭṭhakanipāte catūsupi appamaññāsu avisesena vuttaṃ ‘tato tvaṃ bhikkhu imaṃ samādhiṃ savitakkampi savicāraṃ bhāveyyāsi, avitakkampi vicāramattaṃ bhāveyyāsi, avitakkampi avicāraṃ bhāveyyāsi, sappītikampi bhāveyyāsi, nippītikampi bhāveyyāsi, sātasahagatampi bhāveyyāsi, upekkhāsahagatampi bhāveyyāsī’ti (a. ni. 8.63), tasmā [M 1.0316] catasso appamaññā catukkapañcakajjhānikā”ti. So māhevantissa vacanīyo. Evañhi sati kāyānupassanādayopi catukkapañcakajjhānikā siyuṃ, vedanādīsu ca paṭhamajjhānampi natthi, pageva dutiyādīni. Tasmā byañjanacchāyāmattaṃ gahetvā mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, gambhīraṃ hi buddhavacanaṃ, taṃ ācariye payirupāsitvā adhippāyato gahetabbaṃ.

271. If someone were to say: 'Because the Blessed One has said in the Book of the Eights, without distinction concerning the four immeasurables: “Then, bhikkhu, you should develop this concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; you should develop it without applied thought but with sustained thought; you should develop it without applied thought and without sustained thought; you should develop it with rapture; you should develop it without rapture; you should develop it accompanied by happiness; you should develop it accompanied by equanimity” (AN 8.63), therefore the four immeasurables belong to the jhānas of the tetrad and pentad,' he should be told: 'Do not say so.' For if that were the case, then contemplation of the body and so on would also belong to the jhānas of the tetrad and pentad; and in the case of feelings and so on, not even the first jhāna exists, let alone the second and the others. Therefore, do not misrepresent the Blessed One by grasping merely the shadow of the letter. For the word of the Buddha is profound; it should be understood according to its intended meaning after having served the teachers.

272. Ayañhi [V 1.0313] tatrādhippāyo – “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti evaṃ āyācitadhammadesanaṃ kira taṃ bhikkhuṃ yasmā so pubbepi dhammaṃ sutvā tattheva vasati, na samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ gacchati, tasmā naṃ bhagavā “evameva panidhekacce moghapurisā mamaññeva ajjhesanti, dhamme ca bhāsite mamaññeva anubandhitabbaṃ maññantī”ti apasādetvā puna yasmā so arahattassa upanissayasampanno, tasmā naṃ ovadanto āha – “tasmātiha te bhikkhu evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ, ajjhattaṃ me cittaṃ ṭhitaṃ bhavissati susaṇṭhitaṃ, na cuppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassantīti. Evañhi te bhikkhu sikkhitabba”nti.

272. For this is the intention there: It is said that a certain bhikkhu requested the teaching of the Dhamma, saying, 'Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.' Because that bhikkhu, even after hearing the Dhamma before, had remained right there and did not go to practice the ascetic's duties, the Blessed One rebuked him, saying: 'In this way some foolish men here entreat only me, and when the Dhamma has been taught, they think they should just follow me around.' Then, because he was endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship, the Blessed One advised him, saying: 'Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train thus: “My mind will be internally steady and well-composed, and arisen evil, unwholesome states will not persist, having overpowered the mind.” Thus, bhikkhu, should you train.'

Iminā panassa ovādena niyakajjhattavasena cittekaggatāmatto mūlasamādhi vutto. Tato “ettakeneva santuṭṭhiṃ anāpajjitvā evaṃ so eva samādhi vaḍḍhetabbo”ti dassetuṃ “yato kho te bhikkhu ajjhattaṃ cittaṃ ṭhitaṃ hoti susaṇṭhitaṃ, na cuppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Tato te bhikkhu evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ mettā me cetovimutti bhāvitā bhavissati bahulīkatā yānikatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhāti. Evañhi te bhikkhu sikkhitabba”nti evamassa mettāvasena bhāvanaṃ vatvā puna “yato kho te bhikkhu ayaṃ samādhi evaṃ bhāvito hoti bahulīkato, tato tvaṃ bhikkhu imaṃ mūlasamādhiṃ savitakkampi savicāraṃ bhāveyyāsi…pe… upekkhāsahagatampi bhāveyyāsī”ti vuttaṃ.

By this instruction, the root concentration was spoken of as mere one-pointedness of mind by way of one's own internal state. Then, to show that 'one should develop that same concentration further without becoming content with just that,' it was said: 'When, bhikkhu, your mind is internally steady and well-composed, and arisen evil, unwholesome states do not persist, having overpowered the mind, then you should train thus: “My liberation of mind through loving-kindness will be developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, familiarized, and well undertaken.” Thus, bhikkhu, should you train.' Having thus spoken of the development by way of loving-kindness, it was further said: 'When, bhikkhu, this concentration is thus developed and cultivated, then you, bhikkhu, should develop this root concentration with applied thought and sustained thought… and accompanied by equanimity.'

Tassattho – yadā te bhikkhu ayaṃ mūlasamādhi evaṃ mettāvasena bhāvito hoti, tadā tvaṃ tāvatakenāpi tuṭṭhiṃ anāpajjitvāva imaṃ mūlasamādhiṃ [M 1.0317] aññesupi ārammaṇesu catukkapañcakajjhānāni pāpayamāno savitakkampi savicārantiādinā nayena bhāveyyāsīti.

The meaning of this is: 'Bhikkhu, when this root concentration has been developed by you in this way by means of loving-kindness, then, without becoming content with just that, you should develop this root concentration, causing it to reach the jhānas of the tetrad and pentad on other objects as well, in accordance with the method beginning “with applied thought and sustained thought…” and so on.'

Evaṃ vatvā ca puna karuṇādiavasesabrahmavihārapubbaṅgamampissa aññesu ārammaṇesu catukkapañcakajjhānavasena bhāvanaṃ kareyyāsīti dassento “yato kho te bhikkhu ayaṃ samādhi evaṃ bhāvito hoti bahulīkato. Tato te bhikkhu evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ karuṇā me cetovimuttī”tiādimāha.

And having spoken thus, again, in order to show, 'You should undertake the development on other objects by way of the jhānas of the tetrad and pentad, a development which is also preceded by the remaining divine abidings beginning with compassion,' He spoke the text beginning: 'When, bhikkhu, this concentration is thus developed and cultivated, then, bhikkhu, you should train thus: “My liberation of mind through compassion…”' and so on.

Evaṃ mettādipubbaṅgamaṃ catukkapañcakajjhānavasena bhāvanaṃ dassetvā puna kāyānupassanādipubbaṅgamaṃ [V 1.0314] dassetuṃ “yato kho te bhikkhu ayaṃ samādhi evaṃ bhāvito hoti bahulīkato, tato te bhikkhu evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ kāye kāyānupassī viharissāmī”ti ādiṃ vatvā “yato kho te bhikkhu ayaṃ samādhi evaṃ bhāvito bhavissati subhāvito, tato tvaṃ bhikkhu yena yeneva gagghasi, phāsuññeva gagghasi, yattha yattheva ṭhassasi, phāsuññeva ṭhassasi, yattha yattheva nisīdissasi, phāsuññeva nisīdissasi, yattha yattheva seyyaṃ kappessasi, phāsuññeva seyyaṃ kappessasī”ti arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ samāpesi. Tasmā tikacatukkajjhānikāva mettādayo, upekkhā pana avasesaekajjhānikāvāti veditabbā. Tatheva ca abhidhamme (dha. sa. 251 ādayo; vibha. 673 ādayo) vibhattāti.

Having thus shown the development by way of the fourfold and fivefold jhānas preceded by loving-kindness and so on, and again, in order to show the development preceded by contemplation of the body and so on, having spoken the text beginning, ‘When, bhikkhu, this concentration is thus developed and cultivated by you, then, bhikkhu, you should train thus: “I will dwell contemplating the body in the body,”’ He concluded the discourse with the peak of Arahantship, saying: ‘When, bhikkhu, this concentration will have been thus developed and well developed by you, then wherever you shall go, you shall go with ease; wherever you shall stand, you shall stand with ease; wherever you shall sit, you shall sit with ease; wherever you shall lie down, you shall lie down with ease.’ Therefore, it should be understood that loving-kindness and the others are attainable only with the three-fold and four-fold jhānas, while equanimity, on the other hand, is attainable only with the remaining single jhāna. And they are classified in the same way in the Abhidhamma.

273. Evaṃ tikacatukkajjhānavasena ceva avasesaekajjhānavasena ca dvidhā ṭhitānampi etāsaṃ subhaparamādivasena aññamaññaṃ asadiso ānubhāvaviseso veditabbo. Haliddavasanasuttasmiṃ hi etā subhaparamādibhāvena visesetvā vuttā. Yathāha – “subhaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, mettaṃ cetovimuttiṃ vadāmi. Ākāsānañcāyatanaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, karuṇaṃ cetovimuttiṃ vadāmi. Viññāṇañcāyatanaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, muditaṃ cetovimuttiṃ vadāmi. Ākiñcaññāyatanaparamāhaṃ, bhikkhave, upekkhaṃ cetovimuttiṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.235).

273. Thus, although they are established in two ways—by way of the three-fold and four-fold jhānas, and by way of the remaining single jhāna—their special power, which is dissimilar from one another, should be understood by way of their having the beautiful as their highest, and so on. For in the Haliddavasana Sutta they are spoken of as distinguished by their state of having the beautiful as their highest, and so on. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, I say that the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness has the beautiful liberation as its highest. Bhikkhus, I say that the liberation of the mind through compassion has the attainment of the base of infinite space as its highest. Bhikkhus, I say that the liberation of the mind through sympathetic joy has the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness as its highest. Bhikkhus, I say that the liberation of the mind through equanimity has the attainment of the base of nothingness as its highest' (SN 46:54).

Kasmā [M 1.0318] panetā evaṃ vuttāti? Tassa tassa upanissayattā. Mettāvihārissa hi sattā appaṭikkūlā honti. Athassa appaṭikkūlaparicayā appaṭikkūlesu parisuddhavaṇṇesu nīlādīsu cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti mettā subhavimokkhassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā subhaparamāti vuttā.

But why are they spoken of thus? Because each is a supporting condition for that respective liberation. For to one who abides in loving-kindness, beings are not repulsive. Then, for him, because of his familiarity with the unrepulsive, when he directs his mind to unrepulsive, pure colors such as blue, his mind enters into it with little difficulty. Thus, loving-kindness is a strong supporting condition for the beautiful liberation, but not beyond that; therefore it is said to have the beautiful liberation as its highest.

Karuṇāvihārissa pana daṇḍābhighātādirūpanimittaṃ pattadukkhaṃ samanupassantassa karuṇāya pavattisambhavato rūpe ādīnavo parividito hoti. Athassa parividitarūpādīnavattā pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññataraṃ ugghāṭetvā rūpanissaraṇe ākāse cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti karuṇā ākāsānañcāyatanassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā ākāsānañcāyatanaparamāti vuttā.

But for one who abides in compassion, who repeatedly observes the suffering experienced which has as its cause form, such as being struck by a stick, the danger in form becomes well discerned, due to the possibility of the arising of compassion. Then, for him, because the danger in form has been well discerned, when he has removed one of the kasiṇas such as the earth kasiṇa and directs his mind to space as the escape from form, his mind enters into it with little difficulty. Thus, compassion is a strong supporting condition for the attainment of the base of infinite space, but not beyond that; therefore it is said to have the attainment of the base of infinite space as its highest.

Muditāvihārissa pana tena tena pāmojjakāraṇena uppannapāmojjasattānaṃ viññāṇaṃ samanupassantassa muditāya pavattisambhavato viññāṇaggahaṇaparicitaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Athassa anukkamādhigataṃ [V 1.0315] ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ atikkamma ākāsanimittagocare viññāṇe cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandatīti muditā viññāṇañcāyatanassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā viññāṇañcāyatanaparamāti vuttā.

Furthermore, for one who abides in sympathetic joy, since sympathetic joy arises as he observes the consciousness of beings in whom gladness has arisen for this or that reason, his mind becomes familiar with apprehending consciousness. Then, for him, when he has successively attained and transcended the base of the infinity of space, and he directs his mind to the consciousness that has the sign of space as its object, his mind enters into it with little difficulty. Thus, sympathetic joy is a strong supporting condition for the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, but not beyond that; therefore it is said to have the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness as its highest.

Upekkhāvihārissa pana “sattā sukhitā vā hontu dukkhato vā vimuccantu, sampattasukhato vā mā vimuccantū”ti ābhogābhāvato sukhadukkhādiparamatthagāhavimukhabhāvato avijjamānaggahaṇadukkhaṃ cittaṃ hoti. Athassa paramatthagāhato vimukhabhāvaparicitacittassa paramatthato avijjamānaggahaṇadukkhacittassa ca anukkamādhigataṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma sabhāvato avijjamāne paramatthabhūtassa viññāṇassa abhāve cittaṃ upasaṃharato appakasireneva tattha cittaṃ pakkhandati. Iti upekkhā ākiñcaññāyatanassa upanissayo hoti, na tato paraṃ, tasmā ākiñcaññāyatanaparamāti vuttāti.

Furthermore, for one who abides in equanimity, since there is no advertence such as, ‘May beings be happy, or be freed from suffering, or not be parted from the good fortune they have acquired!’, and since he is turned away from grasping at the ultimate reality of pleasure, pain, and so on, his mind finds it difficult to apprehend what is non-existent. Then, for one whose mind is familiar with being turned away from grasping at ultimate reality and finds it difficult to apprehend what is non-existent in an ultimate sense, when he has successively attained and transcended the base of the infinity of consciousness and directs his mind to the absence of the ultimately real consciousness, which is non-existent by its intrinsic nature, his mind enters into it with little difficulty. Thus, equanimity is a strong supporting condition for the attainment of the base of nothingness, but not beyond that; therefore it is said to have the attainment of the base of nothingness as its highest.

274. Evaṃ subhaparamādivasena etāsaṃ ānubhāvaṃ viditvā puna sabbāpetā dānādīnaṃ sabbakalyāṇadhammānaṃ paripūrikāti veditabbā. Sattesu [M 1.0319] hi hitajjhāsayatāya sattānaṃ dukkhāsahanatāya, pattasampattivisesānaṃ ciraṭṭhitikāmatāya, sabbasattesu ca pakkhapātābhāvena samappavattacittā mahāsattā “imassa dātabbaṃ, imassa na dātabba”nti vibhāgaṃ akatvā sabbasattānaṃ sukhanidānaṃ dānaṃ denti. Tesaṃ upaghātaṃ parivajjayantā sīlaṃ samādiyanti. Sīlaparipūraṇatthaṃ nekkhammaṃ bhajanti. Sattānaṃ hitāhitesu asammohatthāya paññaṃ pariyodapenti. Sattānaṃ hitasukhatthāya niccaṃ vīriyamārabhanti. Uttamavīriyavasena vīrabhāvaṃ pattāpi ca sattānaṃ nānappakārakaṃ aparādhaṃ khamanti. “Idaṃ vo dassāma karissāmā”ti kataṃ paṭiññaṃ na visaṃvādenti. Tesaṃ hitasukhāya avicalādhiṭṭhānā honti. Tesu avicalāya mettāya pubbakārino honti. Upekkhāya paccupakāraṃ nāsīsantīti evaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā yāva dasabalacatuvesārajjachaasādhāraṇañāṇaaṭṭhārasabuddhadhammappabhede sabbepi kalyāṇadhamme paripūrentīti evaṃ dānādisabbakalyāṇadhammaparipūrikā etāva hontīti.

274. Having thus understood their power by way of being supreme in the beautiful and so on, it should be known that, again, all of them are fulfillers of all wholesome qualities beginning with giving. For, with an intention for the welfare of beings, with an inability to endure the suffering of beings, with a desire for the long-lasting stability of the special success they have attained, and with a mind that proceeds evenly towards all beings without partiality, great beings give gifts—the source of happiness—to all beings without making a distinction, not thinking, “This one should be given to, this one should not be given to.” Avoiding harm to them, they undertake the precepts of virtue. To perfect their virtue, they resort to renunciation. To be undeluded about what is for the welfare and what is for the harm of beings, they purify their wisdom. For the welfare and happiness of beings, they constantly arouse their energy. Though they have attained a state of heroism through supreme energy, they forbear the various kinds of offenses of beings. They do not break a promise they have made, saying, “We will give you this, we will do this for you.” For their welfare and happiness, they are of unshakable resolution. With unshakable loving-kindness, they are benefactors to them. With equanimity, they do not hope for a return of favor. Thus, having fulfilled the perfections, they fulfill all wholesome qualities up to and including the various kinds of Buddha-qualities: the ten powers, the four kinds of fearlessness, the six kinds of knowledge not shared by others, and the eighteen distinctive qualities of a Buddha. In this way, they are indeed the fulfillers of all wholesome qualities beginning with giving.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, made for the gladdening of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the section on the Development of Concentration,

Brahmavihāraniddeso nāma

the chapter named the Exposition of the Divine Abodes,

Navamo paricchedo.

is the Ninth Chapter.

10. Āruppaniddeso

10. The Exposition of the Formless States

Paṭhamāruppavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the First Formless State

275. Brahmavihārānantaraṃ [M 1.0320][V 1.0316] uddiṭṭhesu pana catūsu āruppesu ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ tāva bhāvetukāmo “dissante kho pana rūpādhikaraṇaṃ daṇḍādānasatthādānakalahaviggahavivādā, natthi kho panetaṃ sabbaso āruppeti. So iti paṭisaṅkhāya rūpānaṃyeva nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hotī”ti (ma. ni. 2.103) vacanato etesaṃ daṇḍādānādīnañceva cakkhusotarogādīnañca ābādhasahassānaṃ vasena karajarūpe ādīnavaṃ disvā tassa samatikkamāya ṭhapetvā paricchinnākāsakasiṇaṃ navasu pathavīkasiṇādīsu aññatarasmiṃ catutthajjhānaṃ uppādeti.

275. Now, among the four formless states mentioned after the divine abodes, one who wishes to develop the base of the infinity of space should first, in accordance with the saying, “It is seen that because of form there occur the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, conflicts, and disputes. But this is not found at all in the formless realm. Having reflected thus, he is practicing for disenchantment with, dispassion for, and cessation of form,” see the danger in the physical body in terms of these takings up of sticks, etc., and also in terms of the thousands of afflictions such as diseases of the eye and ear. In order to transcend it, leaving aside the limited-space kasiṇa, he produces the fourth jhāna in one of the nine kasiṇas beginning with the earth kasiṇa.

Tassa kiñcāpi rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānavasena karajarūpaṃ atikkantaṃ hoti, atha kho kasiṇarūpampi yasmā tappaṭibhāgameva, tasmā tampi samatikkamitukāmo hoti. Kathaṃ? Yathā ahibhīruko puriso araññe sappena anubaddho vegena palāyitvā palātaṭṭhāne lekhācittaṃ tālapaṇṇaṃ vā valliṃ vā rajjuṃ vā phalitāya vā pana pathaviyā phalitantaraṃ disvā bhāyateva uttasateva, neva naṃ dakkhitukāmo hoti. Yathā ca anatthakārinā veripurisena saddhiṃ ekagāme vasamāno puriso tena vadhabandhagehajhāpanādīhi upadduto aññaṃ gāmaṃ vasanatthāya gantvā tatrāpi verinā samānarūpasaddasamudācāraṃ purisaṃ disvā bhāyateva uttasateva, neva naṃ dakkhitukāmo hoti.

Although his physical body has been transcended by means of the fourth jhāna of the form sphere, yet since the kasiṇa form is its counterpart, he wishes to transcend that too. How? Just as a man who is afraid of snakes, when pursued by a snake in the forest, flees swiftly, and then at the place to which he has fled he sees a palm leaf adorned with drawings, or a creeper, or a rope, or a crack in the cracked ground, he is still afraid and alarmed and does not want to look at it. And just as a man living in the same village with a hostile enemy, being harassed by him with killing, imprisonment, house-burning, and so on, goes to another village to live, and there too, on seeing a man of similar appearance, voice, and behavior to the enemy, he is still afraid and alarmed and does not want to look at him.

Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – tesaṃ hi purisānaṃ ahinā verinā vā upaddutakālo viya bhikkhuno ārammaṇavasena karajarūpasamaṅgikālo. Tesaṃ vegena palāyanaaññagāmagamanāni viya bhikkhuno rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānavasena karajarūpasamatikkamanakālo. Tesaṃ palātaṭṭhāne ca aññagāme [V 1.0317] ca lekhācittatālapaṇṇādīni ceva verisadisaṃ purisañca disvā bhayasantāsaadassanakāmatā viya bhikkhuno kasiṇarūpampi tappaṭibhāgameva idanti sallakkhetvā tampi samatikkamitukāmatā. Sūkarābhihatasunakhapisācabhīrukādikāpi cettha upamā veditabbā.

Herein is the application of the simile: Indeed, like the time when those men are harassed by a snake or an enemy, so is the time when the bhikkhu is endowed with a physical body by way of it being an object. Like their fleeing and going to another village with speed, so is the time when the bhikkhu transcends the physical body by means of the fourth form-sphere jhāna. Like their seeing intricately drawn palm-leaves and so on, and a man resembling the enemy, in the place they fled to and in the other village, and their consequent fear, terror, and desire not to see, so is the bhikkhu’s wish to transcend that kasiṇa-form also, after having firmly noted, ‘This is just its counterpart.’ And here, similes such as that of a dog attacked by a boar, and one who is afraid of a goblin, should also be understood.

276. Evaṃ [M 1.0321] so tasmā catutthajjhānassa ārammaṇabhūtā kasiṇarūpā nibbijja pakkamitukāmo pañcahākārehi ciṇṇavasī hutvā paguṇarūpāvacaracatutthajjhānato vuṭṭhāya tasmiṃ jhāne “imaṃ mayā nibbiṇṇaṃ rūpaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karotī”ti ca, “āsannasomanassapaccatthika”nti ca, “santavimokkhato oḷārika”nti ca ādīnavaṃ passati. Aṅgoḷārikatā panettha natthi. Yatheva hetaṃ rūpaṃ duvaṅgikaṃ, evaṃ āruppānipīti.

276. So, being disgusted with the kasiṇa-form that is the object of the fourth jhāna and wishing to depart from it, having become a master in five ways and emerged from the proficient fourth form-sphere jhāna, he sees the danger in that jhāna thus: “This jhāna takes as its object the form with which I am disgusted,” and “It has gladness as a near enemy,” and “It is grosser than the peaceful liberation.” There is no grossness of factors here, for just as this form-sphere jhāna has two factors, so too do the formless attainments.

So tattha evaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvā nikantiṃ pariyādāya ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ santato anantato manasikaritvā cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ vā yattakaṃ icchati tattakaṃ vā kasiṇaṃ pattharitvā tena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti vā, “ananto ākāso”ti vā manasikaronto ugghāṭeti kasiṇaṃ. Ugghāṭento hi neva kilañjaṃ viya saṃvelleti, na kapālato pūvaṃ viya uddharati, kevalaṃ pana taṃ neva āvajjeti, na manasi karoti, na paccavekkhati, anāvajjento amanasikaronto apaccavekkhanto ca aññadatthu tena phuṭṭhokāsaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti manasikaronto kasiṇaṃ ugghāṭeti nāma. Kasiṇampi ugghāṭiyamānaṃ neva ubbaṭṭati na vivaṭṭati, kevalaṃ imassa amanasikārañca “ākāso ākāso”ti manasikārañca paṭicca ugghāṭitaṃ nāma hoti, kasiṇugghāṭimākāsamattaṃ paññāyati. Kasiṇugghāṭimākāsanti vā kasiṇaphuṭṭhokāsoti vā kasiṇavivittākāsanti vā sabbametaṃ ekameva.

That yogī, having thus seen the danger therein and brought his craving to an end, attends to the base of the infinity of space as “peaceful” and “infinite.” Having extended the kasiṇa either to the limit of the world-sphere or as far as he wishes, he removes the kasiṇa by attending to the space touched by it as “space, space” or “infinite space.” Indeed, when removing it, he neither rolls it up like a mat nor lifts it out like a cake from a pan. He simply does not advert to it, does not attend to it, and does not review it. By not adverting, not attending, and not reviewing, but instead attending to the space touched by it as “space, space,” he is said to remove the kasiṇa. And when the kasiṇa is being removed, it neither rises up nor recedes; it is only called “removed” in dependence on his non-attention to it and his attention to “space, space.” Only the space from which the kasiṇa has been removed appears. “The space from which the kasiṇa has been removed,” “the space touched by the kasiṇa,” and “the space secluded from the kasiṇa” are all one and the same.

So taṃ kasiṇugghāṭimākāsanimittaṃ “ākāso ākāso”ti punappunaṃ āvajjeti, takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karoti. Tassevaṃ punappunaṃ āvajjayato takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karoto nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, sati santiṭṭhati, upacārena cittaṃ samādhiyati. So taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ āsevati, bhāveti, bahulīkaroti. Tassevaṃ punappunaṃ āvajjayato manasikaroto pathavīkasiṇādīsu rūpāvacaracittaṃ viya ākāse ākāsānañcāyatanacittaṃ appeti. Idhāpi hi purimabhāge [V 1.0318] tīṇi cattāri vā javanāni kāmāvacarāni upekkhāvedanāsampayuttāneva honti. Catutthaṃ pañcamaṃ vā arūpāvacaraṃ. Sesaṃ pathavīkasiṇe vuttanayameva.

He repeatedly adverts to that sign of space from which the kasiṇa was removed as “space, space,” applying thought to it and striking it with thought. For him who repeatedly adverts to it in this way, applying thought to it and striking it with thought, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated through access. He repeatedly cultivates, develops, and practices that sign frequently. For him who repeatedly adverts and attends to it in this way, the mind of the base of the infinity of space attains absorption in space, just as the fine-material-sphere mind does in the earth kasiṇa and others. Here too, indeed, in the preliminary stage, three or four impulsions are of the sense-sphere, associated with equanimous feeling. The fourth or fifth is of the formless sphere. The rest is just as was explained in the earth kasiṇa.

Ayaṃ [M 1.0322] pana viseso, evaṃ uppanne arūpāvacaracitte so bhikkhu yathā nāma yānapputoḷi kumbhimukhādīnaṃ aññataraṃ nīlapilotikāya vā pītalohitodātādīnaṃ vā aññatarāya pilotikāya bandhitvā pekkhamāno puriso vātavegena vā aññena vā kenaci apanītāya pilotikāya ākāsaṃyeva pekkhamāno tiṭṭheyya, evameva pubbe kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ jhānacakkhunā pekkhamāno viharitvā “ākāso ākāso”ti iminā parikammamanasikārena sahasā apanīte tasmiṃ nimitte ākāsaññeva pekkhamāno viharati. Ettāvatā cesa “sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti vuccati (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 2.129).

This, however, is the distinction. When the formless-sphere consciousness has thus arisen, that monk is just as a man who, having covered one of the openings of a vehicle such as a covered palanquin, a small doorway, or a pot-mouth with a blue cloth, or with some other cloth such as a yellow, red, or white one, and while looking at it, if that cloth were removed by the force of the wind or by some other person, he would stand looking only at the space demarcated by that opening. Just so, having previously dwelt looking at the kasiṇa-circle with the jhānic eye, with this preliminary-work attention of 'space, space,' when that sign is suddenly removed, he dwells looking only at the space-object. And by this much, this yogi is said to be one who, 'by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, through not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that "space is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.'

277. Tattha sabbasoti sabbākārena, sabbāsaṃ vā anavasesānanti attho. Rūpasaññānanti saññāsīsena vuttarūpāvacarajjhānānañceva tadārammaṇānañca. Rūpāvacarajjhānampi hi rūpanti vuccati “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.129), tassa ārammaṇampi “bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.173), tasmā idha rūpe saññā rūpasaññāti evaṃ saññāsīsena vuttarūpāvacarajjhānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Rūpaṃ saññā assāti rūpasaññaṃ. Rūpaṃ assa nāmanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pathavīkasiṇādibhedassa tadārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ. Samatikkamāti virāgā nirodhā ca. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Etāsaṃ kusalavipākakiriyavasena pañcadasannaṃ jhānasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ, etesañca pathavīkasiṇādivasena navannaṃ ārammaṇasaṅkhātānaṃ rūpasaññānaṃ sabbākārena anavasesānaṃ vā virāgā ca nirodhā ca virāgahetuñceva nirodhahetuñca ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Na hi sakkā sabbaso anatikkantarūpasaññena etaṃ upasampajja viharitunti.

277. Herein, 'completely' means in every way, or of all, without remainder. 'Perceptions of form' refers to both the form-sphere jhānas—spoken of with 'perception' as the principal term—and their objects. For the form-sphere jhāna is indeed called 'form' in passages such as 'one with form sees forms,' and its object is also called 'form' in passages such as 'one sees external forms, beautiful and ugly.' Therefore, here, 'perception in form is perception of form'; thus, this is a designation for the form-sphere jhāna, spoken of with 'perception' as the principal term. As for the object, it has form as its sign, which is to say, 'Form is its name.' This should be understood as a designation for that object, which is differentiated as the earth-kasiṇa, etc. 'Transcends' means through dispassion and cessation. What is said? Having transcended—either in every way or without remainder—these fifteen perceptions of form reckoned as jhāna (by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional) and these nine perceptions of form reckoned as objects (by way of the earth-kasiṇa, etc.), through dispassion and cessation, and through the cause of dispassion and the cause of cessation, one enters and abides in the base of the infinity of space. For it is not possible for one who has not completely transcended the perceptions of form to enter and abide in this.
