Tattha yasmā ārammaṇe avirattassa saññāsamatikkamo na hoti, samatikkantāsu ca saññāsu ārammaṇaṃ samatikkantameva hoti. Tasmā ārammaṇasamatikkamaṃ avatvā “tattha katamā rūpasaññā[V 1.0319]? Rūpāvacarasamāpattiṃ samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā saññā sañjānanā sañjānitattaṃ[M 1.0323], imā vuccanti rūpasaññāyo. Imā rūpasaññāyo atikkanto hoti vītikkanto samatikkanto. Tena vuccati sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā”ti (vibha. 602) evaṃ vibhaṅge saññānaṃyeva samatikkamo vutto. Yasmā pana ārammaṇasamatikkamena pattabbā etā samāpattiyo, na ekasmiññeva ārammaṇe paṭhamajjhānādīni viya. Tasmā ayaṃ ārammaṇasamatikkamavasenāpi atthavaṇṇanā katāti veditabbā.

Here, because for one not detached from an object, the transcendence of perception does not occur, and when perceptions are transcended, the object itself is also transcended. Therefore, without stating the transcendence of the object, it is said: 'Here, what are the perceptions of form? The perception, perceiving, or state of having perceived, of one who has attained the form-sphere absorption, or of one reborn there, or of one abiding happily in the present life—these are called perceptions of form. These perceptions of form are overcome, surpassed, and transcended. Therefore, it is said: "by completely transcending perceptions of form."' Thus, in the Vibhaṅga, only the transcendence of perceptions is mentioned. However, since these attainments are to be reached by the transcendence of the object, not on a single object as in the first jhāna and so on, it should be understood that this explanation is also given in terms of the transcendence of the object.

278. Paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamāti cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānañca paṭighātena samuppannā saññā paṭighasaññā. Rūpasaññādīnaṃ etamadhivacanaṃ. Yathāha – “tattha katamā paṭighasaññā? Rūpasaññā saddasaññā gandhasaññā rasasaññā phoṭṭhabbasaññā, imā vuccanti paṭighasaññāyo”ti (vibha. 603). Tāsaṃ kusalavipākānaṃ pañcannaṃ, akusalavipākānaṃ pañcannanti sabbaso dasannampi paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā pahānā asamuppādā appavattiṃ katvāti vuttaṃ hoti.

278. The cessation of perceptions of resistance: Perception arising from the impact of the bases, such as the eye, and their objects, such as forms, is called perception of resistance. This is a designation for perceptions of form, etc., as it is said: 'Here, what are perceptions of resistance? Perceptions of form, perceptions of sound, perceptions of smell, perceptions of taste, perceptions of touch—these are called perceptions of resistance.' Of these ten perceptions of resistance—five wholesome-resultant and five unwholesome-resultant—the cessation is said to be brought about by their abandonment, non-arising, and non-occurrence.

Kāmañcetā paṭhamajjhānādīni samāpannassāpi na santi. Na hi tasmiṃ samaye pañcadvāravasena cittaṃ pavattati. Evaṃ santepi aññattha pahīnānaṃ sukhadukkhānaṃ catutthajjhāne viya, sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ tatiyamagge viya ca imasmiṃ jhāne ussāhajananatthaṃ imassa jhānassa pasaṃsāvasena etāsamettha vacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Even though these perceptions of resistance are not present for one who has attained the first jhāna and so forth, for at that time the mind does not function through the five sense doors, still, just as happiness and suffering, which were abandoned elsewhere, are mentioned in the fourth jhāna, and identity view and so forth in the third path, so too the mention of these perceptions here should be understood as being for the purpose of generating effort and in praise of this jhāna.

Atha vā kiñcāpi tā rūpāvacaraṃ samāpannassāpi na santi, atha kho na pahīnattā na santi. Na hi rūpavirāgāya rūpāvacarabhāvanā saṃvattati, rūpāyattā ca etāsaṃ pavatti. Ayaṃ pana bhāvanā rūpavirāgāya saṃvattati. Tasmā tā ettha pahīnāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Na kevalañca vattuṃ, ekaṃseneva evaṃ dhāretumpi vaṭṭati. Tāsañhi ito pubbe appahīnattāyeva paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa saddo “kaṇṭako”ti (a. ni. 10.72) vutto bhagavatā. Idha ca pahīnattāyeva arūpasamāpattīnaṃ āneñjatā (vibha. 226) santavimokkhatā (ma. ni. 1.66) ca vuttā. Āḷāro ca kālāmo arūpasamāpanno pañcamattāni sakaṭasatāni nissāya nissāya atikkamantāni neva addasa, na pana saddaṃ assosīti (dī. ni. 2.192).

Or alternatively, even though these perceptions of resistance are not present for one who has attained the form-sphere, still, they are not absent due to being abandoned. For the development of the form-sphere does not lead to dispassion toward form, and the occurrence of these perceptions depends on form. But this development leads to dispassion toward form. Therefore, it is proper to say that they are abandoned here. Not only is it proper to say so, but it is also fitting to firmly hold this view. For before this, because they were not abandoned, sound was called a 'thorn' by the Blessed One for one who had attained the first jhāna. Here, however, because they are abandoned, the formless attainments are described as 'imperturbable' and as 'peaceful liberation.' Moreover, Āḷāra Kālāma, while absorbed in the formless attainment, did not see five hundred carts passing close by, nor did he hear their sound.

279. Nānattasaññānaṃ [M 1.0324][V 1.0320] amanasikārāti nānatte vā gocare pavattānaṃ saññānaṃ, nānattānaṃ vā saññānaṃ. Yasmā hi etā “tattha katamā nānattasaññā? Asamāpannassa manodhātusamaṅgissa vā manoviññāṇadhātusamaṅgissa vā saññā sañjānanā sañjānitattaṃ, imā vuccanti nānattasaññāyo”ti evaṃ vibhaṅge (vibha. 604) vibhajitvā vuttā idha adhippetā asamāpannassa manodhātumanoviññāṇadhātusaṅgahitā saññā rūpasaddādibhede nānatte nānāsabhāve gocare pavattanti, yasmā cetā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, dvādasākusalasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakusalavipākasaññā, dve akusalavipākasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakiriyasaññāti evaṃ catucattālīsampi saññā nānattā nānāsabhāvā aññamaññaṃ asadisā, tasmā nānattasaññāti vuttā. Tāsaṃ sabbaso nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā anāvajjanā asamannāhārā apaccavekkhaṇā. Yasmā tā nāvajjeti, na manasi karoti, na paccavekkhati, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti.

279. ‘By not attending to perceptions of diversity’ means not attending to perceptions that arise in a diverse field, or to diverse perceptions. For in the Vibhaṅga, these are explained as follows: ‘What are perceptions of diversity? The perception, perceiving, or state of having perceived of one who has not attained jhāna and is endowed with either the mind-element or the mind-consciousness-element—these are called perceptions of diversity.’ Here, the intended meaning is the perceptions included in the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element of one who has not attained jhāna, which arise in a diverse field, in the various distinct natures such as forms, sounds, etc. Since these forty-four perceptions—eight sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven sense-sphere wholesome-resultant perceptions, two unwholesome-resultant perceptions, and eleven sense-sphere functional perceptions—are diverse, of various natures, and dissimilar to one another, they are called ‘perceptions of diversity.’ The non-attention to all these perceptions of diversity is non-adverting, non-consideration, and non-reviewing. Because one does not advert to them, does not attend to them, and does not review them, it is so stated.

Yasmā cettha purimā rūpasaññā paṭighasaññā ca iminā jhānena nibbatte bhavepi na vijjanti. Pageva tasmiṃ bhave imaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharaṇakāle, tasmā tāsaṃ samatikkamā atthaṅgamāti dvedhāpi abhāvoyeva vutto. Nānattasaññāsu pana yasmā aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, nava kiriyasaññā, dasākusalasaññāti imā sattavīsatisaññā iminā jhānena nibbatte bhave vijjanti, tasmā tāsaṃ amanasikārāti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Tatrāpi hi imaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharanto tāsaṃ amanasikārāyeva upasampajja viharati, tā pana manasikaronto asamāpanno hotīti.

Because in this state, the previous perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance do not exist even in the existence produced by this jhāna, let alone at the time of entering and dwelling in this jhāna within that existence. Therefore, their overcoming and cessation is stated as simply their non-existence in both cases. However, regarding diverse perceptions—since these twenty-seven perceptions (eight wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, nine functional perceptions, and ten unwholesome perceptions) exist in the existence produced by this jhāna—it should be understood that their non-attention is stated. For even there, one who enters and dwells in this jhāna does so by not attending to them; but if one attends to them, one is not in attainment.

Saṅkhepato cettha rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamāti iminā sabbarūpāvacaradhammānaṃ pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārāti iminā sabbesaṃ kāmāvacaracittacetasikānaṃ pahānañca amanasikāro ca vuttoti veditabbo.

Briefly, here, by ‘the overcoming of perceptions of form,’ the abandonment of all form-sphere phenomena is stated. By ‘the disappearance of perceptions of resistance’ and ‘the non-attention to perceptions of diversity,’ the abandonment of and non-attention to all sense-sphere consciousness and mental factors are stated—this should be understood.

280. Ananto ākāsoti ettha nāssa uppādanto vā vayanto vā paññāyatīti ananto. Ākāsoti kasiṇugghāṭimākāso vuccati. Manasikāravasenāpi cettha anantatā veditabbā. Teneva [M 1.0325] vibhaṅge vuttaṃ “tasmiṃ ākāse cittaṃ ṭhapeti, saṇṭhapeti, anantaṃ pharati, tena vuccati ananto ākāso”ti (vibha. 605).

280. Herein, regarding ‘infinite space,’ because its limit of arising or limit of passing away is not discerned, it is ‘infinite.’ ‘Space’ refers to the space opened up by removing the kasina. Here, infinity should also be understood by way of attention. Therefore, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “In that space, one places the mind, establishes it, and pervades it as infinite; for that reason, it is called ‘infinite space.’”

Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ [V 1.0321] upasampajja viharatīti ettha pana nāssa antoti anantaṃ, ākāsaṃ anantaṃ ākāsānantaṃ, ākāsānantameva ākāsānañcaṃ, taṃ ākāsānañcaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa devānaṃ devāyatanamivāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ.

Herein, regarding ‘having attained the base of the infinitude of space, he dwells’: because there is no end to it, it is ‘infinite’ (anantaṃ). Space is infinite, thus ‘infinite space’ (ākāsānantaṃ). Infinite space itself is ‘the infinitude of space’ (ākāsānañcaṃ). That infinitude of space, in the sense of a foundation, is a ‘base’ (āyatana) for this jhāna with its associated states, just as the divine abode is for the devas; thus, it is the ‘base of the infinitude of space’ (ākāsānañcāyatana).

Upasampajja viharatīti tamākāsānañcāyatanaṃ patvā nipphādetvā tadanurūpena iriyāpathavihārena viharatīti.

‘He dwells having attained’ means that having reached and produced that base of the infinitude of space, he dwells with a mode of conduct conformable to it.

Ayaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanakammaṭṭhāne vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation on the meditation subject of the base of the infinitude of space.

Viññāṇañcāyatanakathā

The Explanation of the Base of the Infinitude of Consciousness

281. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ bhāvetukāmena pana pañcahākārehi ākāsānañcāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasībhāvena “āsannarūpāvacarajjhānapaccatthikā ayaṃ samāpatti, no ca viññāṇañcāyatanamiva santā”ti ākāsānañcāyatane ādīnavaṃ disvā tattha nikantiṃ pariyādāya viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ santato manasikaritvā taṃ ākāsaṃ pharitvā pavattaviññāṇaṃ “viññāṇaṃ viññāṇa”nti punappunaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ, manasikātabbaṃ, paccavekkhitabbaṃ, takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ kātabbaṃ. “Anantaṃ ananta”nti pana na manasikātabbaṃ.

281. However, one who wishes to develop the base of the infinitude of consciousness, having attained mastery in the attainment of the base of the infinitude of space in five ways, should see the danger in the base of the infinitude of space—namely, “This attainment has the fine-material jhāna as its near enemy, and it is not as peaceful as the base of the infinitude of consciousness”—and having overcome attachment to it, and having attended to the base of the infinitude of consciousness as peaceful, the consciousness that has arisen pervading that space should be repeatedly adverted to, attended to, reviewed, and made to be struck by initial and sustained thought as “consciousness, consciousness.” However, one should not attend to it as “infinite, infinite.”

Tassevaṃ tasmiṃ nimitte punappunaṃ cittaṃ cārentassa nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, sati santiṭṭhati, upacārena cittaṃ samādhiyati. So taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ āsevati, bhāveti, bahulīkaroti. Tassevaṃ karoto ākāse ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ viya ākāsaphuṭe viññāṇe viññāṇañcāyatanacittaṃ appeti. Appanānayo panettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ettāvatā cesa “sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma anantaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 2.129) vuccati.

For him who in this way repeatedly directs his mind to that sign, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated through access. He repeatedly resorts to, develops, and makes much of that sign. For him who does so, the mind of the base of the infinitude of consciousness attains absorption upon the consciousness that pervaded space, just as the base of the infinitude of space attained absorption upon space. The method of absorption here should be understood in the way already stated. And by this much, it is said of him: “By completely transcending the base of the infinitude of space, attending ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters upon and abides in the base of the infinitude of consciousness.”

282. Tattha sabbasoti idaṃ vuttanayameva. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti ettha pana pubbe vuttanayena jhānampi ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, ārammaṇampi[M 1.0326]. Ārammaṇampi hi purimanayeneva ākāsānañcañca taṃ paṭhamassa āruppajjhānassa ārammaṇattā devānaṃ devāyatanaṃ viya adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena [V 1.0322] āyatanañcāti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Tathā ākāsānañcañca taṃ tassa jhānassa sañjātihetuttā “kambojā assānaṃ āyatana”ntiādīni viya sañjātidesaṭṭhena āyatanañcātipi ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ. Evametaṃ jhānañca ārammaṇañcāti ubhayampi appavattikaraṇena ca amanasikaraṇena ca samatikkamitvāva yasmā idaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihātabbaṃ, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā “ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammā”ti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

282. Herein, the word “completely” (sabbaso) is in the manner already stated. In the phrase “having transcended the base of the infinitude of space,” both the jhāna and the object are the base of the infinitude of space, as explained before. For the object, too, in the way previously stated, is the infinitude of space (ākāsānañca); and because it is the object of the first formless jhāna, it is also a base (āyatana) in the sense of a foundation (adhiṭṭhāna), like the divine abode for the devas. Thus, it is the base of the infinitude of space. Likewise, it is the infinitude of space (ākāsānañca); and because it is the cause for the arising of that jhāna, it is also a base (āyatana) in the sense of a place of origin (sañjātidesa)—like “Kamboja is the birthplace of horses,” and so on. Thus, it is the base of the infinitude of space. Since this base of the infinitude of consciousness is to be entered upon and abided in only after having transcended both these—the jhāna and its object—by causing them not to arise and by non-attention, therefore it should be understood that both are grouped together when it is said, “having transcended the base of the infinitude of space.”

Anantaṃ viññāṇanti taṃyeva ananto ākāsoti evaṃ pharitvā pavattaviññāṇaṃ “anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti evaṃ manasikarontoti vuttaṃ hoti. Manasikāravasena vā anantaṃ. So hi tamākāsārammaṇaṃ viññāṇaṃ anavasesato manasikaronto “ananta”nti manasi karoti. Yaṃ pana vibhaṅge vuttaṃ “anantaṃ viññāṇanti, taṃyeva ākāsaṃ viññāṇena phuṭaṃ manasi karoti, anantaṃ pharati, tena vuccati anantaṃ viññāṇa”nti (vibha. 610).

“Consciousness is infinite” means that one attends to the consciousness that has arisen pervading that very infinite space as “consciousness is infinite.” Or, it is infinite by way of attention. For when one attends to that consciousness, which has space as its object, without remainder, one attends to it in one's mind as “infinite.” As it is said in the Vibhaṅga: “‘Consciousness is infinite’—one attends to that very space touched by consciousness, pervades it infinitely; therefore, it is called ‘infinite consciousness.’”

Tattha viññāṇenāti upayogatthe karaṇavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evañhi aṭṭhakathācariyā tassa atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti, anantaṃ pharati taññeva ākāsaṃ phuṭaṃ viññāṇaṃ manasi karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Herein, “by consciousness” (viññāṇena) should be understood as an instrumental case used in the sense of the object. For the commentary teachers explain its meaning thus: it means that having pervaded infinitely, one attends to the consciousness that has pervaded that very space.

Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharatīti ettha pana nāssa antoti anantaṃ. Anantameva ānañcaṃ. Viññāṇaṃ ānañcaṃ viññāṇānañcanti avatvā viññāṇañcanti vuttaṃ. Ayañhettha rūḷhīsaddo. Taṃ viññāṇañcaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa devānaṃ devāyatanamivāti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

In the phrase “one dwells having attained the base of the infinitude of consciousness,” herein, there is no end to it, thus it is infinite (ananta). The infinite itself is infinitude (ānañca). Instead of saying “consciousness is infinitude” (viññāṇaṃ ānañcaṃ) or “the infinitude of consciousness” (viññāṇānañcaṃ), it is said “consciousness-infinitude” (viññāṇañcaṃ). This is the established term here. That infinitude of consciousness, in the sense of a foundation, is a base (āyatana) for this jhāna with its associated states, just as the divine abode is for the devas; thus it is the base of the infinitude of consciousness. The rest is just as the preceding.

Ayaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanakammaṭṭhāne vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed explanation on the meditation subject of the base of the infinitude of consciousness.

Ākiñcaññāyatanakathā

The Explanation of the Base of Nothingness

283. Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ bhāvetukāmena pana pañcahākārehi viññāṇañcāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasībhāvena “āsannaākāsānañcāyatanapaccatthikā ayaṃ samāpatti, no ca ākiñcaññāyatanamiva santā”ti viññāṇañcāyatane [M 1.0327] ādīnavaṃ disvā tattha nikantiṃ pariyādāya [V 1.0323] ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasikaritvā tasseva viññāṇañcāyatanārammaṇabhūtassa ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇassa abhāvo suññatā vivittākāro manasikātabbo. Kathaṃ? Taṃ viññāṇaṃ amanasikaritvā “natthi natthī”ti vā, “suññaṃ suñña”nti vā, “vivittaṃ vivitta”nti vā punappunaṃ āvajjitabbaṃ, manasikātabbaṃ, paccavekkhitabbaṃ, takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ kātabbaṃ.

283. Furthermore, one who wishes to develop the base of nothingness, having achieved mastery in five ways in the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, should see the danger in the base of infinite consciousness thus: 'This attainment has the base of infinite space as a near enemy, and it is not peaceful like the base of nothingness.' Having exhausted craving for it and having attended to the base of nothingness as peaceful, one should attend to the absence, the emptiness, and the secluded aspect of that very consciousness of the base of infinite space which had become the object for the base of infinite consciousness. How? Without attending to that consciousness, one should repeatedly advert to, attend to, and review: 'There is not, there is not,' or 'Empty, empty,' or 'Secluded, secluded.' It should be repeatedly subjected to reasoning and applied thought.

Tassevaṃ tasmiṃ nimitte cittaṃ cārentassa nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, sati santiṭṭhati, upacārena cittaṃ samādhiyati. So taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ āsevati, bhāveti, bahulīkaroti. Tassevaṃ karoto ākāse phuṭe mahaggataviññāṇe viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ viya tasseva ākāsaṃ pharitvā pavattassa mahaggataviññāṇassa suññavivittanatthibhāve ākiñcaññāyatanacittaṃ appeti. Etthāpi ca appanānayo vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

For one who thus directs the mind toward that sign, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration. That person repeatedly resorts to, develops, and makes much of that sign. For one who does so, just as the consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness reaches absorption regarding the sublime consciousness that pervaded space, so too the mind of the base of nothingness reaches absorption in the state of emptiness, seclusion, and non-existence of that very sublime consciousness that had arisen pervading space. And here too, the method of absorption should be understood in the way already stated.

Ayaṃ pana viseso, tasmiṃ hi appanācitte uppanne so bhikkhu yathā nāma puriso maṇḍalamāḷādīsu kenacideva karaṇīyena sannipatitaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ disvā katthaci gantvā sannipātakiccāvasāneva uṭṭhāya pakkantesu bhikkhūsu āgantvā dvāre ṭhatvā puna taṃ ṭhānaṃ olokento suññameva passati, vivittameva passati. Nāssa evaṃ hoti “ettakā nāma bhikkhū kālaṅkatā vā disāpakkantā vā”ti, atha kho suññamidaṃ vivittanti natthibhāvameva passati, evameva pubbe ākāse pavattitaviññāṇaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanajjhānacakkhunā passanto viharitvā “natthi natthī”tiādinā parikammamanasikārena antarahite tasmiṃ viññāṇe tassa apagamasaṅkhātaṃ abhāvameva passanto viharati. Ettāvatā cesa “sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma natthi kiñcīti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 2.129) vuccati.

This, however, is the distinction. Indeed, when that absorption-consciousness has arisen, that bhikkhu is like a man who, having seen a community of bhikkhus assembled in a circular assembly hall or the like for some business, goes somewhere else. When the bhikkhus have risen and departed at the conclusion of the assembly's business, he returns, stands at the door, and looking again at that place, sees only that it is empty, sees only that it is secluded. It does not occur to him, 'Have so many bhikkhus died, or have they departed to another region?' But rather, he sees only the state of non-existence, thinking, 'This place is empty, it is secluded.' In the very same way, having previously dwelt perceiving—with the eye of the jhāna of the base of infinite consciousness—the first formless consciousness that had been made to occur in space, then, when that consciousness has disappeared through the preparatory attention of 'There is nothing, there is nothing,' etc., he dwells perceiving only the concept of its absence, which is reckoned as its departure. To this extent, it is said of this person: 'By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, aware that "There is nothing whatsoever," he attains and dwells in the base of nothingness.'

284. Idhāpi sabbasoti idaṃ vuttanayameva. Viññāṇañcāyatananti etthāpi ca pubbe vuttanayeneva jhānampi viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ ārammaṇampi. Ārammaṇampi hi purimanayeneva viññāṇañcañca taṃ dutiyassa āruppajjhānassa ārammaṇattā devānaṃ devāyatanaṃ viya adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanañcāti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ[M 1.0328]. Tathā viññāṇañcañca taṃ tasseva jhānassa sañjātihetuttā “kambojā assānaṃ āyatana”ntiādīni viya sañjātidesaṭṭhena āyatanañcātipi [V 1.0324] viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ. Evametaṃ jhānañca ārammaṇañcāti ubhayampi appavattikaraṇena ca amanasikaraṇena ca samatikkamitvāva yasmā idaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihātabbaṃ, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

284. Here too, 'entirely' (sabbaso) should be understood in the same way as explained. Regarding 'the base of infinite consciousness,' here too, as previously explained, both the jhāna and the object are the base of infinite consciousness. For the object, just as before, is both infinite consciousness and a base. It is the object of the second formless jhāna, and because it is a base in the sense of being a foundation, like a dwelling place for devas, it is called the 'base of infinite consciousness.' Similarly, that infinite consciousness is also a cause for the arising of that jhāna, and just as in 'Kamboja is the breeding ground of horses,' and other such examples, it is called the 'base of infinite consciousness' in the sense of being the place of origin. Thus, since this base of nothingness is to be attained and dwelled in only after transcending both—the jhāna and its object—by not causing them to arise and by not attending to them, both are combined into one, and it is said, 'having transcended the base of infinite consciousness.' Thus it should be understood.

Natthi kiñcīti natthi natthi, suññaṃ suññaṃ, vivittaṃ vivittanti evaṃ manasikarontoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yampi vibhaṅge vuttaṃ “natthi kiñcīti taññeva viññāṇaṃ abhāveti vibhāveti antaradhāpeti natthi kiñcīti passati, tena vuccati natthi kiñcī”ti, taṃ kiñcāpi khayato sammasanaṃ viya vuttaṃ, atha khvassa evameva attho daṭṭhabbo. Tañhi viññāṇaṃ anāvajjento amanasikaronto apaccavekkhanto kevalamassa natthibhāvaṃ suññabhāvaṃ vivittabhāvameva manasikaronto abhāveti vibhāveti antaradhāpetīti vuccati, na aññathāti.

“There is nothing whatsoever” means “nothing, nothing,” “empty, empty,” “secluded, secluded”—thus it is said that one attends. And as stated in the Vibhaṅga: “Regarding ‘there is nothing whatsoever,’ one makes that very consciousness not appear, causes it to be devoid of appearance, causes it to disappear, and sees ‘there is nothing whatsoever.’ Therefore, it is called ‘there is nothing whatsoever.’” Although this is stated as if it were a contemplation by way of destruction, its meaning should still be understood in just this way. For it is said that by not adverting to, not attending to, and not reviewing that consciousness, but merely attending to its state of non-existence, its state of emptiness, and its state of seclusion, one makes it not appear, causes it to be devoid of appearance, and causes it to disappear—it is said thus, and not otherwise.

Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharatīti ettha pana nāssa kiñcananti akiñcanaṃ, antamaso bhaṅgamattampi assa avasiṭṭhaṃ natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Akiñcanassa bhāvo ākiñcaññaṃ, ākāsānañcāyatanaviññāṇāpagamassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Taṃ ākiñcaññaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanamassa jhānassa devānaṃ devāyatanamivāti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Furthermore, regarding the passage, “Having attained the base of nothingness, one dwells therein”: Herein, because there is nothing for it, it is called “having nothing” (akiñcanaṃ). It is said that not even a remnant the size of a moment of dissolution remains for it. The state of “having nothing” is “nothingness” (ākiñcaññaṃ); this is a designation for the passing away of the consciousness of the base of infinite space. That “nothingness” (ākiñcaññaṃ), in the sense of being a foundation, is a base (āyatana) for this jhāna, just as a divine abode is for the devas; thus, it is the “base of nothingness” (ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ). The rest is just as before.

Ayaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanakammaṭṭhāne vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed exposition on the meditation subject of the base of nothingness.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakathā

The Discourse on the Base of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception

285. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ bhāvetukāmena pana pañcahākārehi ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasībhāvena “āsannaviññāṇañcāyatanapaccatthikā ayaṃ samāpatti, no ca nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ viya santā”ti vā “saññā rogo, saññā gaṇḍo, saññā sallaṃ, etaṃ santaṃ, etaṃ paṇītaṃ yadidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññā”ti vā evaṃ ākiñcaññāyatane ādīnavaṃ, upari ānisaṃsañca disvā ākiñcaññāyatane nikantiṃ pariyādāya nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ santato manasikaritvā “sāva abhāvaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattitā ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpatti [V 1.0325] santā santā”ti [M 1.0329] punappunaṃ āvajjitabbā, manasikātabbā, paccavekkhitabbā, takkāhatā vitakkāhatā kātabbā.

285. Now, one who wishes to develop the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having achieved mastery in the attainment of the base of nothingness in five ways, should see the danger in the base of nothingness and the benefit in what is higher, thus: “This attainment has the base of infinite consciousness as its near enemy, and it is not as peaceful as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,” or, “Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, neither-perception-nor-non-perception.” Having thus overcome delight in the base of nothingness, and having attended to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as peaceful, that very attainment of the base of nothingness which arose by taking non-existence as its object should be repeatedly adverted to, attended to, reviewed, and subjected to thought and reflection, thinking: “Peaceful, peaceful.”

Tassevaṃ tasmiṃ nimitte punappunaṃ mānasaṃ cārentassa nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti, sati santiṭṭhati, upacārena cittaṃ samādhiyati. So taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ āsevati, bhāveti, bahulīkaroti. Tassevaṃ karoto viññāṇāpagame ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ viya ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattisaṅkhātesu catūsu khandhesu nevasaññānāsaññāyatanacittaṃ appeti. Appanānayo panettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Ettāvatā cesa “sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharatī”ti (vibha. 508; dī. ni. 2.129) vuccati.

When he repeatedly directs his mind to that sign, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is established, and the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration. He cultivates, develops, and frequently practices that sign. As he does so, the mind of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception attains absorption in the four aggregates reckoned as the attainment of the base of nothingness, just as the base of nothingness attains absorption upon the departure of consciousness. The method of absorption here should be understood in the same way as stated before. To this extent, it is said of this person: “Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

286. Idhāpi sabbasoti idaṃ vuttanayameva. Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti etthāpi pubbe vuttanayeneva jhānampi ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ ārammaṇampi. Ārammaṇampi hi purimanayeneva ākiñcaññañca taṃ tatiyassa āruppajjhānassa ārammaṇattā devānaṃ devāyatanaṃ viya adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanañcāti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Tathā ākiñcaññañca taṃ tasseva jhānassa sañjātihetuttā kambojā assānaṃ āyatanantiādīni viya sañjātidesaṭṭhena āyatanañcātipi ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ. Evametaṃ jhānañca ārammaṇañcāti ubhayampi appavattikaraṇena ca amanasikaraṇena ca samatikkamitvāva yasmā idaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja vihātabbaṃ, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkammāti idaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

286. Here too, this 'sabbaso' (completely) is in the manner already stated. In the phrase 'having transcended the base of nothingness', here also, in the manner previously stated, both the jhāna is the base of nothingness and its object is also the base of nothingness. For the object, as in the previous method, is called the base of nothingness because it is both nothingness (ākiñcañña) and a base (āyatana) in the sense of being a foundation for the third formless jhāna, like the divine abode for the gods. Similarly, it is also called the base of nothingness because it is both nothingness and a base in the sense of being a place of origin for that very jhāna, like in such phrases as 'Kamboja is the base of horses.' Thus, because this base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is to be attained and abided in only after having transcended both this jhāna and its object by not causing them to arise and by not attending to them, it is for this reason that, taking both of these together, the phrase 'having transcended the base of nothingness' is stated. This should be understood.

Nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti ettha pana yāya saññāya bhāvato taṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti vuccati. Yathā paṭipannassa sā saññā hoti, taṃ tāva dassetuṃ vibhaṅge “nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti uddharitvā “taññeva ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ santato manasi karoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāveti, tena vuccati nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti (vibha. 619) vuttaṃ. Tattha santato manasi karotīti “santā vatāyaṃ samāpatti, yatra hi nāma natthibhāvampi ārammaṇaṃ karitvā ṭhassatī”ti evaṃ santārammaṇatāya taṃ santāti manasi karoti.

Now, in this term 'the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception', it is so called because of the existence of a certain kind of perception. In order to first show how that perception arises for one who is practicing, the Vibhaṅga cites the term 'one with neither perception nor non-perception' and states: 'He attends to that very base of nothingness as peaceful, he develops the attainment that has residual formations; therefore he is called one with neither perception nor non-perception' (Vibh. §619). Therein, 'he attends to it as peaceful' means that because of its peaceful object, he attends to that base of nothingness as 'peaceful,' thinking thus: 'Peaceful indeed is this attainment, that it can abide having made even the state of non-existence its object!'

Santato [M 1.0330] ce manasi karoti, kathaṃ samatikkamo hotīti? Asamāpajjitukāmatāya. So hi [V 1.0326] kiñcāpi taṃ santato manasi karoti, atha khvassa “ahametaṃ āvajjissāmi, samāpajjissāmi, adhiṭṭhahissāmi, vuṭṭhahissāmi, paccavekkhissāmī”ti esa ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro na hoti. Kasmā? Ākiñcaññāyatanato nevasaññānāsaññāyatanassa santatarapaṇītataratāya.

If he attends to it as peaceful, how is there a transcending of it? Through the desire not to enter into attainment. For although he attends to it as peaceful, this engagement, application, and attention: “I will advert to it, I will enter into attainment, I will resolve upon it, I will emerge from it, I will review it,” does not arise for him. Why? Because the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is more peaceful and more sublime than the base of nothingness.

Yathā hi rājā mahacca rājānubhāvena hatthikkhandhavaragato nagaravīthiyaṃ vicaranto dantakārādayo sippike ekaṃ vatthaṃ daḷhaṃ nivāsetvā ekena sīsaṃ veṭhetvā dantacuṇṇādīhi samokiṇṇagatte anekāni dantavikatiādīni sippāni karonte disvā “aho vata re chekā ācariyā īdisānipi nāma sippāni karissantī”ti evaṃ tesaṃ chekatāya tussati, na cassa evaṃ hoti “aho vatāhaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya evarūpo sippiko bhaveyya”nti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Rajjasiriyā mahānisaṃsatāya. So sippino samatikkamitvāva gacchati. Evameva esa kiñcāpi taṃ samāpattiṃ santato manasi karoti, atha khvassa “ahametaṃ samāpattiṃ āvajjissāmi, samāpajjissāmi, adhiṭṭhahissāmi, vuṭṭhahissāmi, paccavekkhissāmī”ti neva esa ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro hoti.

For it is like a king who, with great royal power, situated on the back of a noble elephant while traveling in the city street, sees artisans such as ivory-carvers—who have worn one garment firmly, wrapped their heads with one cloth, and have bodies covered all over with ivory dust and so on—doing many crafts such as special works of ivory. He is pleased with their skill, thinking: “Oh, how skilled these masters are! They can indeed do even such fine crafts.” But it does not occur to him thus: “Oh, how good it would be if I, having abandoned the kingdom, were to become such an artisan!” For what reason is that? Because of the great benefit of the glory of kingship. He goes on, having simply passed beyond the artisans. In the same way, although this yogi attends to that attainment as peaceful, yet for him this engagement, application, and attention: “I will advert to this attainment, I will enter into it, I will resolve upon it, I will emerge from it, I will review it,” does not arise at all.

So taṃ santato manasikaronto pubbe vuttanayena taṃ paramasukhumaṃ appanāppattaṃ saññaṃ pāpuṇāti, yāya nevasaññīnāsaññī nāma hoti, saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattiṃ bhāvetīti vuccati. Saṅkhārāvasesasamāpattinti accantasukhumabhāvappattasaṅkhāraṃ catutthāruppasamāpattiṃ.

By attending to that attainment as peaceful in the manner previously stated, he attains that perception which is extremely subtle and has reached absorption, by which he becomes one who has neither perception nor non-perception, and it is said that he develops the attainment with residual formations. ‘The attainment with residual formations’ means the fourth formless attainment, which consists of formations that have reached a state of extreme subtlety.

287. Idāni yaṃ taṃ evamadhigatāya saññāya vasena nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti vuccati, taṃ atthato dassetuṃ “nevasaññānāsaññāyatananti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa vā upapannassa vā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārissa vā cittacetasikā dhammā”ti (vibha. 620) vuttaṃ. Tesu idha samāpannassa cittacetasikā dhammā adhippetā. Vacanattho panettha oḷārikāya saññāya abhāvato sukhumāya ca bhāvato nevassa sasampayuttadhammassa jhānassa saññā nāsaññanti nevasaññānāsaññaṃ. Nevasaññānāsaññañca taṃ [M 1.0331] manāyatanadhammāyatanapariyāpannattā āyatanañcāti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ. Atha vā yāyamettha saññā, sā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya nevasaññā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā nāsaññāti nevasaññānāsaññā[V 1.0327]. Nevasaññānāsaññā ca sā sesadhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena āyatanañcāti nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ.

287. Now, regarding that which is called the 'base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception' by means of the perception thus attained, to show its meaning it is said: “The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consists of the mind and mental factors of one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or of one who has been reborn there, or of one who is dwelling happily in the present life” (Vibh. §620). Among these, the mind and mental factors of one who has attained it are intended here. As to the meaning of the term: here, because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, for this jhāna with its associated states, there is not perception, nor is it without perception; therefore, it is 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' And since it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is a base due to its inclusion in the mind-base and the mind-object-base, it is the 'base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' Alternatively, whatever perception there is here, it is 'not perception' due to its inability to perform the function of distinct perception; yet, because it exists with the subtle nature of residual formations, it is 'not non-perception.' Thus, it is 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' And since it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception and is a base in the sense of being a foundation for the remaining states, it is the 'base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception'.

Na kevalañcettha saññāva edisī, atha kho vedanāpi nevavedanānāvedanā, cittampi nevacittaṃnācittaṃ, phassopi nevaphassonāphasso. Esa nayo sesasampayuttadhammesu. Saññāsīsena panāyaṃ desanā katāti veditabbā. Pattamakkhanatelappabhutīhi ca upamāhi esa attho vibhāvetabbo.

And here, not only is perception of this kind, but feeling is also neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling, consciousness is neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness, and contact is neither-contact-nor-non-contact. This method should be applied to the remaining associated states. It should be understood, however, that this discourse is given with perception as the heading. And this meaning should be clarified by similes such as that of the oil for smearing a bowl.

Sāmaṇero kira telena pattaṃ makkhetvā ṭhapesi, taṃ yāgupānakāle thero pattamāharāti āha. So “patte telamatthi, bhante”ti āha. Tato “āhara, sāmaṇera, telaṃ, nāḷiṃ pūressāmī”ti vutte “natthi, bhante, tela”nti āha. Tattha yathā antovutthattā yāguyā saddhiṃ akappiyaṭṭhena “telamatthī”ti hoti. Nāḷipūraṇādīnaṃ vasena “natthī”ti hoti. Evaṃ sāpi saññā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya nevasaññā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā nāsaññā hoti.

A novice, it is said, having smeared a bowl with oil, put it aside. At the time for drinking rice-gruel, the elder said to him, “Bring the bowl.” He replied, “Venerable sir, there is oil in the bowl.” Then, when it was said, “Bring the oil, novice, I will fill a nāḷi,” he replied, “Venerable sir, there is no oil.” Therein, just as it is said, 'There is oil,' on account of its being stored inside and its unsuitability to be taken together with the gruel, and it is said, 'There is no oil,' with regard to filling a nāḷi and so on; in the same way, that perception, due to its inability to perform the function of a clear perception, is 'not perception,' and due to its existence in a very subtle state as a remainder of formations, it is 'not non-perception'.

Kiṃ panettha saññākiccanti? Ārammaṇasañjānanañceva vipassanāya ca visayabhāvaṃ upagantvā nibbidājananaṃ. Dahanakiccamiva hi sukhodake tejodhātu sañjānanakiccaṃ pesā paṭuṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Sesasamāpattīsu saññā viya vipassanāya visayabhāvaṃ upagantvā nibbidājananampi kātuṃ na sakkoti. Aññesu hi khandhesu akatābhiniveso bhikkhu nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakkhandhe sammasitvā nibbidaṃ pattuṃ samattho nāma natthi apica āyasmā sāriputto. Pakativipassako pana mahāpañño sāriputtasadisova sakkuṇeyya. Sopi “evaṃ kirime dhammā ahutvā sambhonti, hutvā paṭiventī”ti (ma. ni. 3.95) evaṃ kalāpasammasanavaseneva, no anupadadhammavipassanāvasena. Evaṃ sukhumattaṃ gatā esā samāpatti.

What, then, is the function of perception here? It is the recognition of the object and, by becoming a domain for insight, the generation of disenchantment. For just as the fire element in cool water cannot perform its function of burning, so this perception cannot clearly perform its function of recognition. Unlike perception in the other attainments, it cannot generate disenchantment by becoming a domain for insight. Indeed, a monk who has not directed his mind towards the other aggregates is not able to attain disenchantment by contemplating the aggregates of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the Venerable Sāriputta, however, is able. But one who is a regular practitioner of insight, of great wisdom and like Sāriputta, would be able. Even he would be able only by way of contemplating in groups—‘Indeed, it seems these phenomena arise without having been; having been, they cease’—not by way of insight into phenomena step-by-step. So subtle has this attainment become.

Yathā [M 1.0332] ca pattamakkhanatelūpamāya, evaṃ maggudakūpamāyapi ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Maggappaṭipannassa kira therassa purato gacchanto sāmaṇero thokaṃ udakaṃ disvā “udakaṃ, bhante, upāhanā omuñcathā”ti āha. Tato therena “sace udakamatthi, āhara nhānasāṭikaṃ, nhāyissāmā”ti vutte “natthi, bhante”ti āha. Tattha yathā upāhanatemanamattaṭṭhena “udakamatthī”ti [V 1.0328] hoti, nhāyanaṭṭhena “natthī”ti hoti. Evampi sā paṭusaññākiccaṃ kātuṃ asamatthatāya nevasaññā, saṅkhārāvasesasukhumabhāvena vijjamānattā nāsaññā hoti.

And just as with the simile of the oil for smearing a bowl, so too should this meaning be clarified with the simile of water on the path. It is said that a novice walking ahead of an elder on a journey saw a little water and said, 'Venerable sir, there is water; please remove your sandals.' Then, when the elder said, 'If there is water, bring a bathing cloth; we shall bathe,' the novice replied, 'There is none, venerable sir.' Therein, just as it is said 'there is water' in the sense of it being just enough to wet the sandals, and it is said 'there is none' in the sense of it being enough for bathing, so too, that perception, due to its inability to perform the function of a clear perception, is 'not perception'; and due to its existence as a subtle remainder of formations, it is 'not non-perception'.

Na kevalañca etāheva, aññāhipi anurūpāhi upamāhi esa attho vibhāvetabbo. Upasampajja viharatīti idaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

And this meaning should be clarified not only with these similes, but also with other suitable ones. The phrase 'having attained, he abides' is just as has been explained.

Ayaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakammaṭṭhāne vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed discourse on the meditation subject of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Pakiṇṇakakathā

Miscellaneous Discourse

288. Asadisarūpo nātho, āruppaṃ yaṃ catubbidhaṃ āha.

288. The Protector, of incomparable form, declared the fourfold formless attainment.

Taṃ iti ñatvā tasmiṃ, pakiṇṇakakathāpi viññeyyā.

Having thus known that formless attainment, the miscellaneous discourse concerning it should also be understood.

289. Āruppasamāpattiyo hi –

289. Indeed, the formless attainments:

Ārammaṇātikkamato, catassopi bhavantimā;

Aṅgātikkamametāsaṃ, na icchanti vibhāvino.

These four arise by way of transcending the object; the discerning do not admit the transcending of factors in these.

Etāsu hi rūpanimittātikkamato paṭhamā, ākāsātikkamato dutiyā, ākāse pavattitaviññāṇātikkamato tatiyā. Ākāse pavattitaviññāṇassa apagamātikkamato catutthīti sabbathā ārammaṇātikkamato catassopi bhavantimā āruppasamāpattiyoti veditabbā. Aṅgātikkamaṃ pana etāsaṃ na icchanti paṇḍitā. Na hi rūpāvacarasamāpattīsu viya etāsu aṅgātikkamo atthi. Sabbāsupi hi etāsu upekkhā, cittekaggatāti dve eva jhānaṅgāni honti.

For among these, the first arises by transcending the form-sign; the second, by transcending space; the third, by transcending the consciousness that arose in relation to space; and the fourth, by transcending the absence of the consciousness that arose in relation to space. Thus, it should be understood that all four of these formless attainments arise in every way by transcending the object. However, the wise do not admit the transcending of factors in these. For there is no transcending of factors in these as there is in the fine-material sphere attainments. Indeed, in all of these, there are only two jhāna factors: equanimity and one-pointedness of mind.

290. Evaṃ santepi –

290. Although this is so:

Suppaṇītatarā honti, pacchimā pacchimā idha;

Upamā tattha viññeyyā, pāsādatalasāṭikā.

Here, each succeeding attainment is progressively more sublime. Therein, the similes of the palace terrace and the fine cloth should be understood.

Yathā [M 1.0333][V 1.0329] hi catubhūmikassa pāsādassa heṭṭhimatale dibbanaccagītavāditasurabhigandhamālābhojanasayanacchādanādivasena paṇītā pañcakāmaguṇā paccupaṭṭhitā assu. Dutiye tato paṇītatarā. Tatiye tato paṇītatarā. Catutthe sabbapaṇītatarā. Tattha kiñcāpi tāni cattāripi pāsādatalāneva, natthi nesaṃ pāsādatalabhāvena viseso. Pañcakāmaguṇasamiddhavisesena pana heṭṭhimato heṭṭhimato uparimaṃ uparimaṃ paṇītataraṃ hoti.

For instance, just as in a four-storied palace, on the lowest floor, refined five strands of sensual pleasure—by way of divine dancing, singing, music, fragrant garlands, food, beds, and coverings—might be present. On the second floor, they are more refined than those. On the third, they are more refined still. On the fourth, they are the most refined of all. Therein, although those four are all just palace floors, and there is no difference between them by way of being palace floors, yet due to the distinction in the abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure, each upper floor is more refined than each lower floor.

Yathā ca ekāya itthiyā kantitathūlasaṇhasaṇhatarasaṇhatamasuttānaṃ catupalatipaladvipalaekapalasāṭikā assu āyāmena ca vitthārena ca samappamāṇā. Tattha kiñcāpi tā sāṭikā catassopi āyāmato ca vitthārato ca samappamāṇā, natthi tāsaṃ pamāṇato viseso. Sukhasamphassasukhumabhāvamahagghabhāvehi pana purimāya purimāya pacchimā pacchimā paṇītatarā honti, evameva kiñcāpi catūsu etāsu upekkhā, cittekaggatāti etāni dveyeva aṅgāni honti, atha kho bhāvanāvisesena tesaṃ aṅgāni paṇītapaṇītatarabhāvena suppaṇītatarā honti pacchimā pacchimā idhāti veditabbā.

Furthermore, just as a woman might have cloths of four palas, three palas, two palas, and one pala, made from spun, coarse, fine, finer, and finest threads, all of equal measure in length and width. Therein, although those four cloths are of equal measure in length and width, and there is no difference in their measurement, yet by way of pleasantness of touch, fineness, and great value, each later cloth is more refined than each former one. In this very way, although in these four [formless attainments] there are only these two factors—equanimity and one-pointedness of mind—yet, through the distinction in cultivation, by way of those factors becoming progressively more refined, the later and later attainments become exceedingly refined. Thus it should be understood here.

291. Evaṃ anupubbena paṇītapaṇītā cetā –

291. Thus, successively, these [four attainments] are progressively more refined:

Asucimhi maṇḍape laggo, eko tannissito paro;

Añño bahi anissāya, taṃ taṃ nissāya cāparo.

One is attached to a pavilion in a filthy place, another depends on him; another stands outside, not depending, and yet another depends on that one.

Ṭhito catūhi etehi, purisehi yathākkamaṃ;

Samānatāya ñātabbā, catassopi vibhāvinā.

By the discerning one, these four attainments should be understood as similar to these four men standing in due order.

Tatrāyamatthayojanā – asucimhi kira dese eko maṇḍapo, atheko puriso āgantvā taṃ asuciṃ jigucchamāno taṃ maṇḍapaṃ hatthehi ālambitvā tattha laggo laggito viya aṭṭhāsi. Athāparo āgantvā taṃ maṇḍape laggaṃ purisaṃ nissito. Athañño āgantvā cintesi “yo esa maṇḍapalaggo, yo ca tannissito, ubhopete duṭṭhitā. Dhuvo [M 1.0334] ca nesaṃ maṇḍapapapāte pāto, handāhaṃ bahiyeva tiṭṭhāmī”ti. So tannissitaṃ anissāya bahiyeva aṭṭhāsi. Athāparo āgantvā maṇḍapalaggassa ca tannissitassa ca akhemabhāvaṃ cintetvā bahiṭṭhitañca suṭṭhitoti mantvā [V 1.0330] taṃ nissāya aṭṭhāsi. Tattha asucimhi dese maṇḍapo viya kasiṇugghāṭimākāsaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, asucijigucchāya maṇḍapalaggo puriso viya rūpanimittajigucchāya ākāsārammaṇaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ, maṇḍapalaggaṃ purisaṃ nissito viya ākāsārammaṇaṃ ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ, tesaṃ dvinnampi akhemabhāvaṃ cintetvā anissāya taṃ maṇḍapalaggaṃ bahiṭṭhito viya ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ akatvā tadabhāvārammaṇaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ, maṇḍapalaggassa tannissitassa ca akhemataṃ cintetvā bahiṭṭhitañca suṭṭhitoti mantvā taṃ nissāya ṭhito viya viññāṇābhāvasaṅkhāte bahipadese ṭhitaṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ ārabbha pavattaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, this is the explanation of the meaning. In an impure place, it is said, there was a pavilion. A man came and, being disgusted by the impurity, grasped the pavilion with his hands and stood there as if clinging to it. Then another man came and stood depending on the man clinging to the pavilion. Then another came and thought: 'This one clinging to the pavilion, and the one depending on him, are both badly stood. When the pavilion collapses, their fall is certain. Well now, I shall stand only outside.' So, not depending on the dependent one, he stood only outside. Then another came and, having considered the unsafe state of both the one clinging to the pavilion and the one depending on him, and having thought that the one standing outside was well-stood, stood depending on him. Herein, the space where the kasina is removed should be seen to be like the pavilion in the impure place. The sphere of infinite space, which has space as its object due to disgust for the form-sign, should be seen to be like the man clinging to the pavilion out of disgust for the impurity. The sphere of infinite consciousness, which arises taking as its object the sphere of infinite space, should be seen to be like the man depending on the one clinging to the pavilion. The sphere of nothingness, which, not making the sphere of infinite space its object, has the absence of that first formless consciousness as its object, should be seen to be like the one who stood outside, not depending on the one clinging to the pavilion. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which arises taking as its object the sphere of nothingness established in the external place designated as 'the absence of consciousness,' should be seen to be like the one who stood depending on the one outside.

292. Evaṃ pavattamānañca –

292. And although it proceeds thus—

Ārammaṇaṃ karoteva, aññābhāvena taṃ idaṃ;

Diṭṭhadosampi rājānaṃ, vuttihetu jano yathā.

This [sphere] indeed makes that [sphere] its object, due to the absence of another; just as people, for the sake of their livelihood, depend on even a king whose faults are seen.

Idañhi nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ “āsannaviññāṇañcāyatanapaccatthikā ayaṃ samāpattī”ti evaṃ diṭṭhadosampi taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ aññassa ārammaṇassa abhāvā ārammaṇaṃ karoteva. Yathā kiṃ? Diṭṭhadosampi rājānaṃ vuttihetu yathā jano. Yathā hi asaṃyataṃ pharusakāyavacīmanosamācāraṃ kañci sabbadisampatiṃ rājānaṃ “pharusasamācāro aya”nti evaṃ diṭṭhadosampi aññattha vuttiṃ alabhamāno jano vuttihetu nissāya vattati, evaṃ diṭṭhadosampi taṃ ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ aññaṃ ārammaṇaṃ alabhamānamidaṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoteva.

For this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even though a flaw is seen in that sphere of nothingness—'This attainment has the sphere of infinite consciousness as its near enemy'—it still takes that sphere of nothingness as its object due to the absence of another object. How so? Just as a person depends on a king for livelihood, even though a flaw is seen in him. For just as a person who cannot find a livelihood elsewhere depends for livelihood on some unrestrained king, a lord of all directions with harsh bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, even though seeing the flaw, 'This one has harsh conduct'; so too, this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, unable to find another object, still takes as its object that sphere of nothingness in which a flaw is seen.

293. Evaṃ kurumānañca –

293. And while thus taking it as an object—

Āruḷho dīghanisseṇiṃ, yathā nisseṇibāhukaṃ;

Pabbataggañca āruḷho, yathā pabbatamatthakaṃ.

Just as one who has climbed a long ladder leans on the ladder's side-rail; and just as one who has climbed to a mountain peak leans on the very mountain top.

Yathā [M 1.0335][V 1.0331] vā girimārūḷho, attanoyeva jaṇṇukaṃ;

Olubbhati tathevetaṃ, jhānamolubbha vattatīti.

Or just as one who has climbed a rocky mountain leans on his own knee; so too, this [attainment] proceeds by taking that jhāna as its object.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, made for the delight of good people,

Samādhibhāvanādhikāre

in the Section on the Development of Concentration,

Āruppaniddeso nāma

the Exposition of the Immaterial Attainments by name,

Dasamo paricchedo.

is the Tenth Chapter.

11. Samādhiniddeso

11. The Exposition of Concentration

Āhārepaṭikkūlabhāvanā

The Development of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Nutriment

294. Idāni [M 1.0336][V 1.0332] āruppānantaraṃ ekā saññāti evaṃ uddiṭṭhāya āhāre paṭikkūlasaññāya bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto. Tattha āharatīti āhāro. So catubbidho kabaḷīkārāhāro, phassāhāro, manosañcetanāhāro, viññāṇāhāroti.

294. Now, immediately after the immaterial attainments, the detailed exposition of the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment—which was pointed out in brief as 'one perception'—has come in due course. Therein, 'nutriment' (āhāra) is so called because it brings (āharati) [its fruit]. It is of four kinds: physical nutriment, contact as nutriment, mental volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment.

Ko panettha kimāharatīti? Kabaḷīkārāhāro ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ āharati. Phassāhāro tisso vedanā āharati. Manosañcetanāhāro tīsu bhavesu paṭisandhiṃ āharati. Viññāṇāhāro paṭisandhikkhaṇe nāmarūpaṃ āharati.

Herein, which [nutriment] brings what? Physical nutriment brings material form that has nutritive essence as its eighth component. Contact as nutriment brings the three feelings. Mental volition as nutriment brings rebirth-linking in the three kinds of existence. Consciousness as nutriment brings name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Tesu kabaḷīkārāhāre nikantibhayaṃ. Phassāhāre upagamanabhayaṃ. Manosañcetanāhāre upapattibhayaṃ. Viññāṇāhāre paṭisandhibhayaṃ. Evaṃ sappaṭibhayesu ca tesu kabaḷīkārāhāro puttamaṃsūpamena (saṃ. ni. 2.63) dīpetabbo. Phassāhāro niccammagāvūpamena (saṃ. ni. 2.63). Manosañcetanāhāro aṅgārakāsūpamena (saṃ. ni. 2.63). Viññāṇāhāro sattisatūpamenāti (saṃ. ni. 2.63). Imesu pana catūsu āhāresu asitapītakhāyitasāyitappabhedo kabaḷīkāro āhārova imasmiṃ atthe āhāroti adhippeto. Tasmiṃ āhāre paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇavasena uppannā saññā āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā.

Among these, in edible food, there is the danger of craving. In the nutriment of contact, there is the danger of approach. In the nutriment of mental volition, there is the danger of arising in a new existence. In the nutriment of consciousness, there is the danger of relinking. And so, among these nutriments fraught with danger, the nutriment of edible food should be illustrated by the simile of a son’s flesh; the nutriment of contact, by the simile of a skinless cow; the nutriment of mental volition, by the simile of a pit of embers; and the nutriment of consciousness, by the simile of a hundred spears. Now, among these four nutriments, only edible food—distinguished as that which is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—is intended as ‘nutriment’ in this context. The perception that has arisen by way of grasping the repulsive aspect in that nutriment is the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.

Taṃ āhāre paṭikkūlasaññaṃ bhāvetukāmena kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggahetvā uggahato ekapadampi avirajjhantena rahogatena paṭisallīnena asitapītakhāyitasāyitappabhede kabaḷīkārāhāre dasahākārehi paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā. Seyyathidaṃ, gamanato, pariyesanato, paribhogato, āsayato, nidhānato, aparipakkato, paripakkato, phalato, nissandato, sammakkhanatoti.

One who wishes to develop that perception of repulsiveness in nutriment should, having learned the meditation subject and not deviating even in a single phrase from what was learned, while in seclusion and withdrawn, contemplate the repulsiveness of edible food—distinguished as that which is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—in ten aspects. These are: by way of going, seeking, consuming, receptacle, storage, its undigested state, its digested state, its result, its discharge, and its smearing.

295. Tattha [V 1.0333] gamanatoti evaṃ mahānubhāve nāma sāsane pabbajitena sakalarattiṃ buddhavacanasajjhāyaṃ vā samaṇadhammaṃ vā katvā kālasseva vuṭṭhāya cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ katvā pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā pariveṇaṃ [M 1.0337] sammajjitvā sarīraṃ paṭijaggitvā āsanamārūyha vīsatiṃsa vāre kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaritvā uṭṭhāya pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā nijanasambādhāni pavivekasukhāni chāyūdakasampannāni sucīni sītalāni ramaṇīyabhūmibhāgāni tapovanāni pahāya ariyaṃ vivekaratiṃ anapekkhitvā susānābhimukhena siṅgālena viya āhāratthāya gāmābhimukhena gantabbaṃ.

295. Therein, as to 'by way of going': One who has gone forth into such a truly powerful Dispensation, after spending the entire night reciting the Buddha’s word or practicing the ascetic’s duties, should rise early, perform the duties in the shrine-courtyard and the Bodhi-tree-courtyard, set out drinking water and water for use, sweep the monastery grounds, and attend to the body. Then, having ascended to one's seat and attended to the meditation subject twenty or thirty times, one should rise, take bowl and robe, and—abandoning the ascetic groves which are free from the crowding of people, pleasant with seclusion, endowed with shade and water, clean, cool, and have delightful tracts of land, and not regarding the noble delight in seclusion—one should go facing the village for the sake of nutriment, just like a jackal facing a charnel ground.

Evaṃ gacchatā ca mañcamhā vā pīṭhamhā vā otaraṇato paṭṭhāya pādarajagharagolikavaccādisamparikiṇṇaṃ paccattharaṇaṃ akkamitabbaṃ hoti. Tato appekadā mūsikajatukavaccādīhi upahatattā antogabbhato paṭikkūlataraṃ pamukhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tato ulūkapārāvatādivaccasammakkhitattā uparimatalato paṭikkūlataraṃ heṭṭhimatalaṃ. Tato kadāci kadāci vāteritehi purāṇatiṇapaṇṇehi gilānasāmaṇerānaṃ muttakarīsakheḷasiṅghāṇikāhi vassakāle udakacikkhallādīhi ca saṃkiliṭṭhattā heṭṭhimatalato paṭikkūlataraṃ pariveṇaṃ. Pariveṇato paṭikkūlatarā vihāraracchā daṭṭhabbā hoti.

While going thus, from the moment of descending from the bed or chair, one must tread upon a floor covering strewn with foot-dust, house-lizard excrement, and the like. Then, sometimes, due to being spoiled by rat excrement, bat excrement, and the like, the porch is to be seen as more repulsive than the inner chamber. Then, because it is smeared with the excrement of owls, pigeons, and the like, the lower level is to be seen as more repulsive than the upper level. Then, occasionally, due to being soiled by old grass and leaves scattered by the wind, by the urine, feces, saliva, and mucus of sick novices, and, during the rainy season, by water, mud, and the like, the monastery compound is to be seen as more repulsive than the lower level. The monastery lane is to be seen as more repulsive than the monastery compound.

Anupubbena pana bodhiñca cetiyañca vanditvā vitakkamāḷake ṭhitena muttarāsisadisaṃ cetiyaṃ morapiñchakalāpamanoharaṃ bodhiṃ devavimānasampattisassirīkaṃ senāsanañca anapaloketvā evarūpaṃ nāma ramaṇīyaṃ padesaṃ piṭṭhito katvā āhārahetu gantabbaṃ bhavissatīti pakkamitvā gāmamaggaṃ paṭipannena khāṇukaṇṭakamaggopi udakavegabhinnavisamamaggopi daṭṭhabbo hoti.

But, in due course, after paying homage to the Bodhi tree and the cetiya, while standing on the terrace of reflection, without looking back at the cetiya resembling a heap of pearls, the Bodhi tree captivating like a peacock's tail-feather plume, and the lodging possessing the graceful splendor of a celestial mansion's perfection—having turned one's back on such a delightful place, thinking, 'It will be necessary to go for the sake of food,' and having departed and entered upon the village path, one is to see even a path with stumps and thorns, and even an uneven path broken by the force of water.

Tato gaṇḍaṃ paṭicchādentena viya nivāsanaṃ nivāsetvā vaṇacoḷakaṃ bandhantena viya kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā aṭṭhisaṅghātaṃ paṭicchādentena viya cīvaraṃ pārupitvā bhesajjakapālaṃ nīharantena viya pattaṃ nīharitvā gāmadvārasamīpaṃ pāpuṇantena hatthikuṇapaassakuṇapagokuṇapamahiṃsakuṇapamanussakuṇapaahikuṇapakukkurakuṇapānipi daṭṭhabbāni bhavanti. Na kevalañca daṭṭhabbāni, gandhopi nesaṃ ghānaṃ paṭihanamāno adhivāsetabbo hoti. Tato gāmadvāre ṭhatvā caṇḍahatthiassādiparissayaparivajjanatthaṃ gāmaracchā oloketabbā honti.

Then, one is to put on the lower garment as if covering a sore; fasten the waistband as if tying a bandage; drape the outer robe as if covering a collection of bones; and take out the bowl as if taking out a medicine vessel. Upon arriving near the village gate, even the carcasses of elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, humans, snakes, and dogs are to be seen. And not only are they to be seen, but their stench assailing the nose must also be endured. Then, standing at the village gate, the village lanes are to be surveyed to avoid dangers such as fierce elephants and horses.

Iccetaṃ [M 1.0338][V 1.0334] paccattharaṇādianekakuṇapapariyosānaṃ paṭikkūlaṃ āhārahetu akkamitabbañca daṭṭhabbañca ghāyitabbañca hoti. Aho vata bho paṭikkūlo āhāroti evaṃ gamanato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

Thus, this repulsive matter, beginning with the worn-out floor covering and ending with many carcasses, must be stepped on, seen, and smelled for the sake of food. 'Oh, indeed, how repulsive is nutriment!'—in this way, its repulsiveness should be reflected upon by way of going.

296. Kathaṃ pariyesanato? Evaṃ gamanapaṭikkūlaṃ adhivāsetvāpi gāmaṃ paviṭṭhena saṅghāṭipārutena kapaṇamanussena viya kapālahatthena gharapaṭipāṭiyā gāmavīthīsu caritabbaṃ hoti. Yattha vassakāle akkantaakkantaṭṭhāne yāva piṇḍikamaṃsāpi udakacikkhalle pādā pavisanti, ekena hatthena pattaṃ gahetabbaṃ hoti, ekena cīvaraṃ ukkhipitabbaṃ. Gimhakāle vātavegena samuṭṭhitehi paṃsutiṇarajehi okiṇṇasarīrena caritabbaṃ. Taṃ taṃ gehadvāraṃ patvā macchadhovanamaṃsadhovanataṇḍuladhovanakheḷasiṅghāṇikasunakhasūkaravaccādīhi sammissāni kimikulākulāni nīlamakkhikaparikiṇṇāni oḷigallāni ceva candanikaṭṭhānāni ca daṭṭhabbāni honti akkamitabbānipi. Yato tā makkhikā uṭṭhahitvā saṅghāṭiyampi pattepi sīsepi nilīyanti.

296. How, by way of seeking? Even after having endured the repulsiveness of going, a monk who has entered a village, covered in his patched outer robe, must walk along the village streets from house to house like a solitary beggar with a bowl in his hand. There, during the rainy season, in every place he steps, his feet sink into the watery mud even up to the calf-flesh. With one hand, the bowl must be held; with the other, the robe must be lifted. During the hot season, he must walk with his body covered in dust, bits of grass, and dirt stirred up by the force of the wind. Arriving at this or that house door, cesspools and drains must be seen and also stepped over—places mixed with fish-washing water, meat-washing water, rice-washing water, spittle, snot, dog excrement, pig excrement, and so on, teeming with worms and swarming with blue flies. From there, those flies rise up and settle on his outer robe, on his bowl, and on his head.

Gharaṃ paviṭṭhassāpi keci denti, keci na denti. Dadamānāpi ekacce hiyyo pakkabhattampi purāṇakhajjakampi pūtikummāsapūpādīnipi dadanti. Adadamānāpi kecideva “aticchatha, bhante”ti vadanti, keci pana apassamānā viya tuṇhī honti, keci aññena mukhaṃ karonti, keci “gaccha, re muṇḍakā”tiādīhi pharusavācāhi samudācaranti. Evaṃ kapaṇamanussena viya gāme piṇḍāya caritvā nikkhamitabbanti.

Even for one who has entered a house, some give, and some do not give. Even among those who give, some give rice cooked yesterday, stale hard-food, or rotten barley-cakes and so on. Even among those who do not give, only some say, 'Pass on, venerable sir.' Others, however, are silent as if not seeing. Some turn their faces away. Some address him with harsh words such as, 'Go, you shaveling!' Thus, having wandered for alms in the village like a wretched beggar, he must depart.

Iccetaṃ gāmappavesanato paṭṭhāya yāva nikkhamanā udakacikkhallādipaṭikkūlaṃ āhārahetu akkamitabbañceva daṭṭhabbañca adhivāsetabbañca hoti. Aho vata bho paṭikkūlo āhāroti evaṃ pariyesanato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

Thus, from entering the village up to departing, this repulsive matter such as watery mud must be stepped on, seen, and endured for the sake of food. 'Oh, how truly repulsive food is!'—in this way, its repulsiveness should be reflected upon by means of seeking.

297. Kathaṃ paribhogato? Evaṃ pariyiṭṭhāhārena pana bahigāme phāsukaṭṭhāne sukhanisinnena yāva tattha hatthaṃ na otāreti, tāva tathārūpaṃ garuṭṭhāniyaṃ bhikkhuṃ vā lajjimanussaṃ vā disvā nimantetumpi sakkā hoti. Bhuñjitukāmatāya panettha hatthe otāritamatte [V 1.0335] “gaṇhathā”ti vadantena [M 1.0339] lajjitabbaṃ hoti. Hatthaṃ pana otāretvā maddantassa pañcaṅgulianusārena sedo paggharamāno sukkhathaddhabhattampi temento muduṃ karoti.

297. How by way of consumption? Now, for one who has sought food in this way, while comfortably seated in a suitable place outside the village, as long as he has not yet put his hand into it, it is possible, upon seeing a monk worthy of respect or a conscientious person, to invite them. However, as soon as the hand is put into this food out of a desire to eat, one should be ashamed to say, 'Take some.' Furthermore, for one who, having put in his hand, is kneading the food, sweat trickling down along the five fingers moistens even dry, hard rice, making it soft.

Atha tasmiṃ parimaddanamattenāpi sambhinnasobhe ālopaṃ katvā mukhe ṭhapite heṭṭhimadantā udukkhalakiccaṃ sādhenti, uparimā musalakiccaṃ, jivhā hatthakiccaṃ. Taṃ tattha suvānadoṇiyaṃ suvānapiṇḍamiva dantamusalehi koṭṭetvā jivhāya samparivattiyamānaṃ jivhāgge tanupasannakheḷo makkheti, vemajjhato paṭṭhāya bahalakheḷo makkheti, dantakaṭṭhena asampattaṭṭhāne dantagūthako makkheti. So evaṃ vicuṇṇitamakkhito taṅkhaṇaññeva antarahitavaṇṇagandhasaṅkhāraviseso suvānadoṇiyaṃ ṭhitasuvānavamathu viya paramajegucchabhāvaṃ upagacchati. Evarūpopi samāno cakkhussa āpāthaṃ atītattā ajjhoharitabbo hotīti evaṃ paribhogato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

Then, its beauty destroyed by the mere act of kneading, a morsel is made and placed in the mouth. The lower teeth accomplish the task of a mortar, the upper teeth the task of a pestle, and the tongue the task of a hand. There, like a dog’s lump of food in a dog’s trough, it is pounded by the tooth-pestles and turned over by the tongue. Thin, clear saliva at the tip of the tongue smears it; from the middle onwards, thick saliva smears it; and in places not reached by a tooth-stick, tooth-filth smears it. Thus pulverized and smeared, that food, its specific qualities of color, smell, and preparation immediately disappearing, attains a state of utmost loathsomeness, like a dog's vomit in a dog's trough. Even being of such a nature, because it has passed beyond the range of the eye, it must be swallowed. In this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of consumption.

298. Kathaṃ āsayato? Evaṃ paribhogaṃ upagato ca panesa anto pavisamāno yasmā buddhapaccekabuddhānampi raññopi cakkavattissa pittasemhapubbalohitāsayesu catūsu aññataro āsayo hotiyeva. Mandapuññānaṃ pana cattāro āsayā honti. Tasmā yassa pittāsayo adhiko hoti, tassa bahalamadhukatelamakkhito viya paramajeguccho hoti. Yassa semhāsayo adhiko hoti, tassa nāgabalapaṇṇarasamakkhito viya. Yassa pubbāsayo adhiko hoti, tassa pūtitakkamakkhito viya. Yassa lohitāsayo adhiko hoti, tassa rajanamakkhito viya paramajeguccho hotīti evaṃ āsayato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

298. How by way of the receptacle? Now, in this way, when this food has been consumed and is entering inside, for even Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and a wheel-turning monarch, among the four receptacles—bile, phlegm, pus, and blood—one or another receptacle indeed exists. For those of little merit, however, all four receptacles exist. Therefore, for one in whom the bile receptacle is predominant, it is extremely repulsive, like something smeared with thick madhuka oil. For one in whom the phlegm receptacle is predominant, it is like something smeared with the juice of nāgabalā leaves. For one in whom the pus receptacle is predominant, it is like something smeared with putrid buttermilk. For one in whom the blood receptacle is predominant, it is extremely repulsive, like something smeared with dye. Thus, in this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of the receptacle.

299. Kathaṃ nidhānato? So imesu catūsu āsayesu aññatarena āsayena makkhito antoudaraṃ pavisitvā neva suvaṇṇabhājane na maṇirajatādibhājanesu nidhānaṃ gacchati. Sace pana dasavassikena ajjhohariyati dasa vassāni adhotavaccakūpasadise okāse patiṭṭhahati. Sace vīsa, tiṃsa, cattālīsa, paññāsa, saṭṭhi, sattati, asīti, navutivassikena, sace vassasatikena ajjhohariyati. Vassasataṃ adhotavaccakūpasadise [M 1.0340] okāse patiṭṭhahatīti evaṃ nidhānato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

299. How by way of its place of deposit? That food, having been smeared by one or another of these four receptacles and having entered into the abdomen, is not deposited in a golden vessel, nor in vessels of gems, silver, and so on. But if it is consumed by a ten-year-old, it remains for ten years in a place like an unwashed cesspool. If it is consumed by one who is twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, or ninety years old, or if it is consumed by a hundred-year-old, it remains for a hundred years in a place like an unwashed cesspool. Thus, in this way, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of its place of deposit.

300. Kathaṃ aparipakkato? So panāyamāhāro evarūpe okāse nidhānamupagato yāva aparipakko hoti, tāva tasmiññeva yathāvuttappakāre paramandhakāratimise nānākuṇapagandhavāsitapavanavicarite [V 1.0336] atiduggandhajegucche padese yathā nāma nidāghe akālameghena abhivuṭṭhamhi caṇḍālagāmadvāraāvāṭe patitāni tiṇapaṇṇakilañjakhaṇḍaahikukkuramanussakuṇapādīni sūriyātapena santattāni pheṇapupphuḷakācitāni tiṭṭhanti, evameva taṃdivasampi hiyyopi tato purime divasepi ajjhohato sabbo ekato hutvā semhapaṭalapariyonaddho kāyaggisantāpakuthitakuthanasañjātapheṇapupphuḷakācito paramajegucchabhāvaṃ upagantvā tiṭṭhatīti evaṃ aparipakkato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

300. How by way of its undigested state? This food, having been deposited in such a place, for as long as it is undigested, remains in that very place—a region of utter darkness, extremely gloomy, pervaded by winds scented with various corpses, a place of extreme foulness and repulsiveness. Just as in the hot season, when an unseasonal cloud has rained down heavily, grass, leaves, pieces of old mats, and the corpses of snakes, dogs, and humans that have fallen into a cesspit at the gate of an outcaste village are intensely heated by the sun's heat and remain there covered with foam and bubbles; just so, all the food swallowed on that day, yesterday, and the day before, having become one mass, enveloped by a film of phlegm, and covered with foam and bubbles produced by being heated and boiled by the body-fire, reaches a state of extreme repulsiveness and remains there. Thus, repulsiveness should be reflected upon by way of its undigested state.

301. Kathaṃ paripakkato? So tattakāyagginā paripakko samāno na suvaṇṇarajatādidhātuyo viya suvaṇṇarajatādibhāvaṃ upagacchati. Pheṇapupphuḷake pana muñcanto saṇhakaraṇiyaṃ pisitvā nāḷike pakkhittapaṇḍumattikā viya karīsabhāvaṃ upagantvā pakkāsayaṃ, muttabhāvaṃ upagantvā muttavatthiñca pūretīti evaṃ paripakkato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

301. How by way of its digested state? When digested by the heated body-fire, it does not, like mineral ores of gold, silver, and so on, attain the state of gold, silver, and so on. But rather, releasing foam and bubbles, like pale fine earth ground on a grinding slab and put into a small tube, it reaches the state of feces and fills the repository for digested food; and it reaches the state of urine and fills the bladder. Thus, repulsiveness should be reflected upon by way of its digested state.

302. Kathaṃ phalato? Sammā paripaccamāno ca panāyaṃ kesalomanakhadantādīni nānākuṇapāni nipphādeti asammāparipaccamāno daddukaṇḍukacchukuṭṭhakilāsasosakāsātisārappabhutīni rogasatāni, idamassa phalanti evaṃ phalato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

302. How by way of its fruit? When properly digested, this food produces various foul things such as hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, and so on. When improperly digested, it gives rise to hundreds of diseases such as ringworm, itching, scabies, leprosy, a discoloring skin disease, consumption, cough, dysentery, and so on. This is its fruit. Thus, repulsiveness should be reflected upon by way of its fruit.

303. Kathaṃ nissandato? Ajjhohariyamāno cesa ekena dvārena pavisitvā nissandamāno akkhimhā akkhigūthako kaṇṇamhā kaṇṇagūthakotiādinā pakārena anekehi dvārehi nissandati. Ajjhoharaṇasamaye cesa mahāparivārenāpi ajjhohariyati. Nissandanasamaye pana uccārapassāvādibhāvaṃ upagato ekakeneva nīhariyati. Paṭhamadivase ca [M 1.0341] naṃ paribhuñjanto haṭṭhapahaṭṭhopi hoti udaggudaggo pītisomanassajāto. Dutiyadivase nissandento pihitanāsiko hoti vikuṇitamukho jegucchī maṅkubhūto. Paṭhamadivase ca naṃ ratto giddho gadhito mucchitopi ajjhoharitvā dutiyadivase ekarattivāsena viratto aṭṭīyamāno harāyamāno jigucchamāno nīharati. Tenāhu porāṇā –

303. How by way of its outflow? When being consumed, this food enters through one door, but when flowing out, it flows out from many doors: as eye-discharge from the eye, as earwax from the ear, and so on. Furthermore, at the time of consumption, it is consumed even with a great retinue. But at the time of outflow, having become feces, urine, and so on, it is expelled by oneself alone. Furthermore, on the first day, one who consumes it is also very delighted, uplifted, and filled with joy and gladness. On the second day, when it flows out, one has a contorted face, is disgusted, downcast, and pinches one's nose. Furthermore, on the first day, having swallowed it while being passionate, greedy, attached, and infatuated, on the second day, after it has stayed for just one night, one expels it while being dispassionate, weary, ashamed, and disgusted. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Annaṃ pānaṃ khādanīyaṃ, bhojanañca mahārahaṃ;

Ekadvārena pavisitvā, navadvārehi sandati.

“Food, drink, edibles, and meals worthy of the great— entering through one door, they flow out through nine.”

“Annaṃ [V 1.0337] pānaṃ khādanīyaṃ, bhojanañca mahārahaṃ;

Bhuñjati saparivāro, nikkhāmento nilīyati.

“Food, drink, edibles, and meals worthy of the great— one consumes them with a retinue, but when expelling, one hides.”

“Annaṃ pānaṃ khādanīyaṃ, bhojanañca mahārahaṃ;

Bhuñjati abhinandanto, nikkhāmento jigucchati.

“Food, drink, edibles, and meals worthy of the great— one eats them while greatly delighting, but when expelling, one is disgusted.”

“Annaṃ pānaṃ khādanīyaṃ, bhojanañca mahārahaṃ;

Ekarattiparivāsā, sabbaṃ bhavati pūtika”nti.

“Food, drink, edibles, and meals worthy of the great— after staying for a single night, all of it becomes putrid.”

Evaṃ nissandato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

Thus, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of its outflow.

304. Kathaṃ sammakkhanato? Paribhogakālepi cesa hatthaoṭṭhajivhātālūni sammakkheti. Tāni tena sammakkhitattā paṭikkūlāni honti, yāni dhotānipi gandhaharaṇatthaṃ punappunaṃ dhovitabbāni honti. Paribhutto samāno yathā nāma odane paccamāne thusakaṇakuṇḍakādīni uttaritvā ukkhalimukhavaṭṭipidhāniyo makkhanti, evameva sakalasarīrānugatena kāyagginā pheṇuddehakaṃ paccitvā uttaramāno dante dantamalabhāvena sammakkheti. Jivhātāluppabhutīni kheḷasemhādibhāvena, akkhikaṇṇanāsaadhomaggādike akkhigūthakakaṇṇagūthakasiṅghāṇikāmuttakarīsādibhāvena sammakkheti. Yena sammakkhitāni imāni dvārāni divase divase dhoviyamānānipi neva sucīni, na manoramāni honti. Yesu ekaccaṃ dhovitvā hattho puna udakena dhovitabbo hoti. Ekaccaṃ dhovitvā dvattikkhattuṃ gomayenapi mattikāyapi gandhacuṇṇenapi dhovato pāṭikulyatā vigacchatīti evaṃ sammakkhanato paṭikkūlatā paccavekkhitabbā.

304. How by way of its smearing? Even while being consumed, this food smears the hands, lips, tongue, and palate. Because they are smeared by it, they become repulsive—which, even when washed, must be washed again and again to remove the smell. When it has been consumed, just as husks, broken rice, and rice stalks rise to the surface when rice is cooking and smear the rim of the pot and the lid, so too, the body’s internal heat, which pervades the entire body, cooks it into a frothy discharge. This, rising up, smears the teeth as dental plaque. It smears the tongue, palate, and so on, as saliva, phlegm, and so on; and the eyes, ears, nose, and lower passages as eye-discharge, earwax, snot, urine, feces, and so on. Smeared in this way, these doors, even though washed day after day, are neither clean nor pleasant. Among them, after washing a certain one, the hand must be washed again with water. After washing a certain other, even when the hand is washed two or three times with cow-dung, clay, or scented powder, its repulsiveness does not depart. Thus, repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of its smearing.

305. Tassevaṃ [M 1.0342] dasahākārehi paṭikkūlataṃ paccavekkhato takkāhataṃ vitakkāhataṃ karontassa paṭikkūlākāravasena kabaḷīkārāhāro pākaṭo hoti. So taṃ nimittaṃ punappunaṃ āsevati bhāveti bahulīkaroti. Tassevaṃ karoto nīvaraṇāni vikkhambhanti. Kabaḷīkārāhārassa sabhāvadhammatāya gambhīrattā appanaṃ appattena upacārasamādhinā cittaṃ samādhiyati. Paṭikkūlākāraggahaṇavasena panettha saññā pākaṭā hoti. Tasmā imaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā icceva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

305. For one who reflects on repulsiveness in these ten ways, making it struck by thought and repeatedly struck by thought, morsel-food becomes manifest by way of its repulsive aspect.
