That one repeatedly resorts to, develops, and cultivates that sign. For one who does so, the hindrances are suppressed. Due to the profundity of morsel-food, it being an ultimate reality, the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration, without having reached absorption. Here, perception becomes manifest by means of grasping the repulsive aspect. Therefore, this meditation subject comes to be reckoned simply as 'the perception of repulsiveness in food'.

Imañca [V 1.0338] pana āhāre paṭikkūlasaññaṃ anuyuttassa bhikkhuno rasataṇhāya cittaṃ patilīyati patikuṭati pativaṭṭati. So kantāranittharaṇatthiko viya puttamaṃsaṃ vigatamado āhāraṃ āhāreti yāvadeva dukkhassa nittharaṇatthāya. Athassa appakasireneva kabaḷīkārāhārapariññāmukhena pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo pariññaṃ gacchati. So pañcakāmaguṇapariññāmukhena rūpakkhandhaṃ parijānāti. Aparipakkādipaṭikkūlabhāvavasena cassa kāyagatāsatibhāvanāpi pāripūriṃ gacchati, asubhasaññāya anulomapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti. Imaṃ pana paṭipattiṃ nissāya diṭṭheva dhamme amatapariyosānataṃ anabhisambhuṇanto sugatiparāyano hotīti.

Furthermore, for a monk who applies himself to this perception of repulsiveness in food, his mind shrinks, recoils, and turns away from craving for tastes. Like one with the purpose of crossing a wilderness who eats his son’s flesh, being free from intoxication, he partakes of food only for the purpose of crossing over suffering. Then, for him, with little difficulty, through the gateway of fully understanding morsel-food, lust connected with the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. Through the gateway of fully understanding the five strands of sensual pleasure, he fully understands the form aggregate. And for him, by way of the repulsive nature of undigested food and so on, the development of mindfulness directed to the body also reaches fulfillment, and he becomes one who has entered upon the practice that conforms with the perception of unattractiveness. Furthermore, relying on this practice, if he does not realize the state of having the deathless as its final end in this very life, he is bound for a happy destination.

Ayaṃ āhāre paṭikkūlasaññābhāvanāya vitthārakathā.

This is the detailed exposition on the development of the perception of repulsiveness in food.

Catudhātuvavatthānabhāvanā

The Development of the Analysis of the Four Elements

306. Idāni āhāre paṭikkūlasaññānantaraṃ ekaṃ vavatthānanti evaṃ uddiṭṭhassa catudhātuvavatthānassa bhāvanāniddeso anuppatto. Tattha vavatthānanti sabhāvūpalakkhaṇavasena sanniṭṭhānaṃ, catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vavatthānaṃ catudhātuvavatthānaṃ. Dhātumanasikāro, dhātukammaṭṭhānaṃ, catudhātuvavatthānanti atthato ekaṃ. Tayidaṃ dvidhā āgataṃ saṅkhepato ca vitthārato ca. Saṅkhepato mahāsatipaṭṭhāne āgataṃ. Vitthārato mahāhatthipadūpame rāhulovāde dhātuvibhaṅge ca. Tañhi –

306. Now, following the perception of repulsiveness in food, the instruction on the development of the analysis of the four elements, introduced as “one determination,” has been reached. Here, “determination” means ascertainment by way of its intrinsic nature and distinguishing marks. The determination of the four elements is the four-element determination. Attention to the elements, the element meditation subject, and the four-element determination are one in meaning. This has come in two ways: briefly and in detail. Briefly, it is found in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness. In detail, it is found in the Greater Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint, the Advice to Rāhula, and the Discourse on the Analysis of the Elements. For it is said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā catumahāpathe bilaso [M 1.0343] vibhajitvā nisinno assa, evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati, atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātū”ti –

“Just as, monks, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, would sit at a crossroads with it divided into portions, so too, monks, a monk reviews this very body, however it is situated or disposed, by way of the elements: ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’”

Evaṃ tikkhapaññassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa vasena mahāsatipaṭṭhāne (dī. ni. 2.378) saṅkhepato āgataṃ.

Thus, for one of sharp wisdom who practices the meditation subject of the elements, it is briefly presented in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 2.378).

Tassattho – yathā cheko goghātako vā tasseva vā bhattavetanabhato antevāsiko gāviṃ vadhitvā vinivijjhitvā catasso disā gatānaṃ mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte catumahāpathe koṭṭhāsaṃ [V 1.0339] katvā nisinno assa, evameva bhikkhu catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena ṭhitattā yathāṭhitaṃ. Yathāṭhitattāva yathāpaṇihitaṃ kāyaṃ atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu…pe… vāyodhātūti evaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati.

The meaning of that is: Just as a skilled cow-butcher or his apprentice, supported by food and wages, having killed a cow and dissected it, would be seated at the four great crossroads—described as the central place of the great highways going to the four directions—having made it into portions; just so, a bhikkhu reviews this body by way of the elements, just as it is established and disposed, on account of its being established in any one of the four postures, thus: 'In this body there is the earth element… the air element.'

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā goghātakassa gāviṃ posentassapi āghātanaṃ āharantassapi āharitvā tattha bandhitvā ṭhapentassapi vadhantassapi vadhitaṃ mataṃ passantassapi tāvadeva gāvītisaññā na antaradhāyati, yāva naṃ padāletvā bilaso na vibhajati. Vibhajitvā nisinnassa pana gāvīsaññā antaradhāyati, maṃsasaññā pavattati. Nāssa evaṃ hoti “ahaṃ gāviṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime gāviṃ harantī”ti. Atha khvassa “ahaṃ maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāmi, imepi maṃsaṃ haranti”cceva hoti, evameva imassāpi bhikkhuno pubbe bālaputhujjanakāle gihibhūtassapi pabbajitassapi tāvadeva sattoti vā posoti vā puggaloti vā saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā dhātuso na paccavekkhati. Dhātuso paccavekkhato pana sattasaññā antaradhāyati, dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati. Tenāha bhagavā “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā…pe… nisinno assa, evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu…pe… vāyodhātū”ti.

What is meant by this? Just as for a cow-butcher, whether while raising a cow, bringing it to the slaughter-place, having brought and tied it up there, killing it, or seeing it killed and dead, the perception 'cow' does not disappear for as long as he has not cut it up and divided it into portions. But for one who is seated after having divided it, the perception 'cow' disappears, and the perception 'meat' arises. The thought does not occur to him, 'I am selling a cow,' or 'These people are carrying a cow.' Rather, the thought occurs to him, 'I am selling meat,' and 'These people, too, are carrying meat.' Just so, for this bhikkhu too, formerly in the time of being a foolish worldling, whether as a householder or as one who has gone forth, the perception of 'a being,' 'a person,' or 'an individual' does not disappear for as long as he does not, after analytically breaking down the solidity of this very body as it is established and disposed, review it by way of the elements. But for one who reviews it by way of the elements, the perception of 'a being' disappears, and the mind becomes established by the power of the elements alone. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Just as, monks, a skilled cow-butcher… would be sitting; just so, monks, a bhikkhu… the air element.'

307. Mahāhatthipadūpame (ma. ni. 1.300 ādayo) pana – “katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ kharigataṃ upādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ[M 1.0344], kesā lomā…pe… udariyaṃ karīsaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ kharigataṃ upādinnaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati, āvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātū”ti ca,

307. Furthermore, in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta (The Great Elephant Footprint Simile Sutta), it is stated: "And what, friends, is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, that is hard, coarse, and clung to. That is to say: head hairs, body hairs... stomach contents, feces, or whatever else that is internal, belonging to oneself, that is hard, coarse, and clung to. This, friends, is called the internal earth element."

“Katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā āpodhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ āpo āpogataṃ upādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, pittaṃ…pe… muttaṃ, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ āpo āpogataṃ upādinnaṃ, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā āpodhātū”ti ca,

And, "And what, friends, is the internal water element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, that is water, of a watery nature, and clung to. That is to say: bile... urine, or whatever else that is internal, belonging to oneself, that is water, of a watery nature, and clung to. This, friends, is called the internal water element."

“Katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā tejodhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ tejo tejogataṃ upādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, yena ca santappati, yena ca jīrīyati, yena ca pariḍayhati, yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ [V 1.0340] sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ tejo tejogataṃ upādinnaṃ, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā tejodhātū”ti ca,

And, "And what, friends, is the internal fire element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, that is fire, of a fiery nature, and clung to. That is to say: that by which one is heated, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed with fever, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored undergoes proper digestion; or whatever else that is internal, belonging to oneself, that is fire, of a fiery nature, and clung to. This, friends, is called the internal fire element."

“Katamā cāvuso, ajjhattikā vāyodhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ vāyo vāyogataṃ upādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, uddhaṅgamā vātā, adhogamā vātā, kucchisayā vātā, koṭṭhāsayā vātā, aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā, assāso passāso iti vā, yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ vāyo vāyogataṃ upādinnaṃ, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, ajjhattikā vāyodhātū”ti ca –

And, "And what, friends, is the internal air element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, that is air, of an airy nature, and clung to. That is to say: upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, the in-breath and the out-breath; or whatever else that is internal, belonging to oneself, that is air, of an airy nature, and clung to. This, friends, is called the internal air element."

Evaṃ nātitikkhapaññassa dhātukammaṭṭhānikassa vasena vitthārato āgataṃ. Yathā cettha, evaṃ rāhulovādadhātuvibhaṅgesupi.

Thus it has been stated in detail with reference to a practitioner of the element meditation subject whose wisdom is not overly sharp. And as it is stated here, so too is it stated in the Rāhulovāda and Dhātuvibhaṅga Suttas.

Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā, ajjhattaṃ paccattanti idaṃ tāva ubhayampi niyakassa adhivacanaṃ. Niyakaṃ nāma attani jātaṃ sasantānapariyāpannanti attho. Tayidaṃ yathā loke itthīsu kathā adhitthīti vuccati, evaṃ attani pavattattā ajjhattaṃ, attānaṃ paṭicca paṭicca pavattattā paccattantipi vuccati. Kakkhaḷanti thaddhaṃ. Kharigatanti pharusaṃ. Tattha paṭhamaṃ lakkhaṇavacanaṃ, dutiyaṃ ākāravacanaṃ, kakkhaḷalakkhaṇā hi pathavīdhātu, sā pharusākārā hoti, tasmā kharigatanti [M 1.0345] vuttā. Upādinnanti daḷhaṃ ādinnaṃ, ahaṃ mamanti evaṃ daḷhaṃ ādinnaṃ, gahitaṃ parāmaṭṭhanti attho. Seyyathidanti nipāto. Tassa taṃ katamanti ceti attho. Tato taṃ dassento “kesā lomā”tiādimāha. Ettha ca matthaluṅgaṃ pakkhipitvā vīsatiyā ākārehi pathavīdhātu niddiṭṭhāti veditabbā. Yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñcīti avasesesu tīsu koṭṭhāsesu pathavīdhātu saṅgahitā.

Herein is the explanation of non-obvious terms. ‘Internal’ and ‘personal’—both these terms are, in the first place, designations for what is one's own. What is called ‘one's own’ means that which has arisen in oneself, included in one's own continuum; this is the meaning. Just as in the world, talk concerning women is called `adhitthī`, so too, because it occurs in oneself, it is called ‘internal’; and because it occurs in relation to oneself, it is also called ‘personal’. ‘Hard’ means stiff. ‘Coarse’ means harsh. Therein, the first is a term for the characteristic, the second a term for the manifestation. For the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, and it has a harsh manifestation; therefore, it is called ‘coarse’. ‘Grasped’ means firmly taken; it means firmly taken, held, and misapprehended thus: ‘I,’ ‘mine’. ‘Such as’ is a particle. Its meaning is: ‘Which is that?’ Then, showing that, he said: ‘head hairs, body hairs,’ and so on. And here it should be known that, by including the brain, the earth element is described in twenty aspects. By the phrase ‘Or whatever else there is,’ the earth element in the remaining three portions is also included.

Vissandanabhāvena taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ appotīti āpo. Kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena nānāvidhesu āpesu gatanti āpogataṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Āpodhātuyā ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ.

By its nature of flowing, it pervades this and that place; therefore, it is called `āpo` (water). By way of originating from kamma and so on, it is gone into various kinds of water; therefore, it is called `āpogataṃ` (gone to water). What is that? The characteristic of cohesion of the water element.

Tejanavasena tejo, vuttanayeneva tejesu gatanti tejogataṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Uṇhattalakkhaṇaṃ. Yena cāti yena tejodhātugatena kupitena ayaṃ kāyo santappati, ekāhikajarādibhāvena usumajāto hoti. Yena ca jīrīyatīti yena ayaṃ kāyo jīrati, indriyavekallataṃ balaparikkhayaṃ [V 1.0341] valipalitādibhāvañca pāpuṇāti. Yena ca pariḍayhatīti yena kupitena ayaṃ kāyo ḍayhati. So ca puggalo “ḍayhāmi ḍayhāmī”ti kandanto satadhotasappigosīsacandanādilepañceva tālavaṇṭavātañca paccāsīsati. Yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatīti yenetaṃ asitaṃ vā odanādi pītaṃ vā pānakādi khāyitaṃ vā piṭṭhakhajjakādi sāyitaṃ vā ambapakkamadhuphāṇitādi sammā paripākaṃ gacchati, rasādibhāvena vivekaṃ gacchatīti attho. Ettha ca purimā tayo tejodhātusamuṭṭhānā. Pacchimo kammasamuṭṭhānova.

It is tejo by way of sharpness. It is called 'included in fire' (tejagata) because it is included in the fire elements in the manner already stated. What is that? It is the fire element which has the characteristic of heat. And by what..., that is, by which agitated fire element this body is heated, becoming feverish by way of a one-day intermittent fever and so on. And by what it ages, that is, by which this body ages, reaching a state of impaired faculties, the exhaustion of strength, and the condition of wrinkled skin, grey hair, and so on. And by what it is consumed by fire, that is, by which agitated fire element this body is burned. And that person, crying out, “I am burning, I am burning!” longs for an ointment of butter washed a hundred times, gosīsa sandalwood, and the like, as well as the breeze of a palm-leaf fan. And by what what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted undergoes proper transformation, that is, by which this which is eaten, such as boiled rice; or drunk, such as beverages; or chewed, such as flour-cakes and savories; or tasted, such as ripe mangoes, honey, and molasses, is properly digested, reaching a state of separation by way of chyle, blood, flesh, fat, sinew, bone, marrow, and semen. Herein, the first three are of fourfold origin. The last is solely of kamma-origin.

Vāyanavasena vāyo, vuttanayeneva vāyesu gatanti vāyogataṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ. Uddhaṅgamā vātāti uggārahikkādipavattakā uddhaṃ ārohaṇavātā. Adhogamā vātāti uccārapassāvādinīharaṇakā adho orohaṇavātā. Kucchisayā vātāti antānaṃ bahivātā. Koṭṭhāsayā vātāti antānaṃ antovātā. Aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātāti dhamanijālānusārena sakalasarīre aṅgamaṅgāni anusaṭā samiñjanapasāraṇādinibbattakā vātā. Assāsoti antopavisananāsikavāto. Passāsoti bahinikkhamananāsikavāto. Ettha ca purimā pañca catusamuṭṭhānā. Assāsapassāsā [M 1.0346] cittasamuṭṭhānāva. Sabbattha yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñcīti iminā padena avasesakoṭṭhāsesu āpodhātuādayo saṅgahitā.

It is air by way of motion. It is called 'included in air' (vāyogata) because it is included in the air elements in the manner already stated. What is that? It has the characteristic of supporting. The upward-moving winds are winds that rise upwards, causing belching, hiccupping, and so forth. The downward-moving winds are winds that descend downwards, eliminating excrement, urine, and so forth. The winds that abide in the belly are winds external to the intestines. The winds that abide in the bowels are winds internal to the intestines. The winds that course through the major and minor limbs are winds that, following the network of vessels, pervade the entire body and its major and minor limbs, producing bending, stretching, and so on. In-breath is the wind entering through the nose. Out-breath is the wind exiting through the nose. Herein, the first five are of fourfold origin. In-breath and out-breath are solely of mind-origin. In all cases, by this phrase 'or whatever else there may be,' the water element and others are included in the remaining categories.

Iti vīsatiyā ākārehi pathavīdhātu, dvādasahi āpodhātu, catūhi tejodhātu, chahi vāyodhātūti dvācattālīsāya ākārehi catasso dhātuyo vitthāritā hontīti ayaṃ tāvettha pāḷivaṇṇanā.

Thus, in twenty aspects the earth element, in twelve the water element, in four the fire element, and in six the air element—thus, the four elements are expounded in forty-two aspects. This, for now, is the explanation of the Pāḷi here.

308. Bhāvanānaye panettha tikkhapaññassa bhikkhuno kesā pathavīdhātu, lomā pathavīdhātūti evaṃ vitthārato dhātupariggaho papañcato upaṭṭhāti. Yaṃ thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ, ayaṃ pathavīdhātu. Yaṃ ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ, ayaṃ āpodhātu. Yaṃ paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ, ayaṃ tejodhātu. Yaṃ vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ, ayaṃ vāyodhātūti evaṃ manasikaroto panassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Nātitikkhapaññassa pana evaṃ manasikaroto andhakāraṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti. Purimanayena vitthārato manasikarontassa pākaṭaṃ hoti.

308. Furthermore, in the method of development here, for a monk of sharp wisdom, the grasping of the elements in detail by way of 'Hairs of the head are the earth element, hairs of the body are the earth element,' and so on, appears to be a slow process. However, for one who attends thus: 'Whatever has the characteristic of hardness, this is the earth element. Whatever has the characteristic of cohesion, this is the water element. Whatever has the characteristic of maturation, this is the fire element. Whatever has the characteristic of support, this is the air element,' for him the meditation subject becomes manifest. But for one not of very sharp wisdom, when attending in this way, it becomes dark and unmanifest. For one who attends in detail according to the former method, it becomes manifest.

Kathaṃ[V 1.0342]? Yathā dvīsu bhikkhūsu bahupeyyālaṃ tantiṃ sajjhāyantesu tikkhapañño bhikkhu sakiṃ vā dvikkhattuṃ vā peyyālamukhaṃ vitthāretvā tato paraṃ ubhatokoṭivaseneva sajjhāyaṃ karonto gacchati. Tatra nātitikkhapañño evaṃ vattā hoti “kiṃ sajjhāyo nāmesa oṭṭhapariyāhatamattaṃ kātuṃ na deti, evaṃ sajjhāye kariyamāne kadā tanti paguṇā bhavissatī”ti. So āgatāgataṃ peyyālamukhaṃ vitthāretvāva sajjhāyaṃ karoti. Tamenaṃ itaro evamāha – “kiṃ sajjhāyo nāmesa pariyosānaṃ gantuṃ na deti, evaṃ sajjhāye kariyamāne kadā tanti pariyosānaṃ gamissatī”ti. Evameva tikkhapaññassa kesādivasena vitthārato dhātupariggaho papañcato upaṭṭhāti. Yaṃ thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ, ayaṃ pathavīdhātūtiādinā nayena saṅkhepato manasikaroto kammaṭṭhānaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Itarassa tathā manasikaroto andhakāraṃ avibhūtaṃ hoti. Kesādivasena vitthārato manasikarontassa pākaṭaṃ hoti.

How so? It is as when two monks are reciting a text with many abbreviations. The monk of sharp wisdom, after expanding the opening of the abbreviation once or twice, then proceeds with the recitation only by way of the two ends. Therein, the one not of very sharp wisdom would say: 'What kind of recitation is this? He does not even allow for the mere touching of the lips. When the recitation is done in this way, when will the text become familiar?' So he expands the opening of the abbreviation each time it appears and then recites. The other says to him: 'What kind of recitation is this? He does not allow one to get to the end. When the recitation is done in this way, when will the text reach its conclusion?' In this very same way, for the one of sharp wisdom, the grasping of the elements in detail by way of the hair of the head, etc., appears to be a slow process. For one who attends concisely by the method of 'Whatever has the characteristic of hardness, this is the earth element,' and so on, the meditation subject becomes manifest. For the other, attending in that way, it becomes dark and unmanifest. For one who attends in detail by way of the hair of the head, etc., it becomes manifest.

Tasmā imaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetukāmena tikkhapaññena tāva rahogatena paṭisallīnena sakalampi attano rūpakāyaṃ āvajjetvā yo imasmiṃ kāye thaddhabhāvo vā kharabhāvo vā, ayaṃ pathavīdhātu. Yo ābandhanabhāvo [M 1.0347] vā dravabhāvo vā, ayaṃ āpodhātu. Yo paripācanabhāvo vā uṇhabhāvo vā, ayaṃ tejodhātu. Yo vitthambhanabhāvo vā samudīraṇabhāvo vā, ayaṃ vāyodhātūti evaṃ saṃkhittena dhātuyo pariggahetvā punappunaṃ pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti dhātumattato nissattato nijjīvato āvajjitabbaṃ manasikātabbaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ vāyamamānassa nacireneva dhātuppabhedāvabhāsanapaññāpariggahito sabhāvadhammārammaṇattā appanaṃ appatto upacāramatto samādhi uppajjati.

Therefore, one who wishes to develop this meditation subject, being of keen wisdom, should first, having gone to a secluded place and being in solitude, advert to one's own entire physical body thus: 'Whatever in this body is the state of hardness or roughness, this is the earth element. Whatever is the state of binding or fluidity, this is the water element. Whatever is the state of maturing or heat, this is the fire element. Whatever is the state of supporting or impelling, this is the air element.' Having thus briefly grasped the elements, one should again and again advert to, attend to, and review them as 'earth element, water element,' and so on, as mere elements, as non-sentient, as non-living. For one who strives in this way, before long, a concentration arises that is merely access concentration, not having reached absorption; because it has natural phenomena as its object, it is comprehended by the wisdom that illuminates the distinction of the elements.

Atha vā pana ye ime catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ nissattabhāvadassanatthaṃ dhammasenāpatinā “aṭṭhiñca paṭicca nhāruñca paṭicca maṃsañca paṭicca cammañca paṭicca ākāso parivārito rūpantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchatī”ti (ma. ni. 1.306) cattāro koṭṭhāsā vuttā. Tesu taṃ taṃ antarānusārinā ñāṇahatthena vinibbhujitvā vinibbhujitvā yo etesu thaddhabhāvo vā kharabhāvo vā, ayaṃ pathavīdhātūti purimanayeneva dhātuyo pariggahetvā punappunaṃ pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti dhātumattato nissattato nijjīvato āvajjitabbaṃ manasikātabbaṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Tassevaṃ vāyamamānassa nacireneva dhātuppabhedāvabhāsanapaññāpariggahito sabhāvadhammārammaṇattā [V 1.0343] appanaṃ appatto upacāramatto samādhi uppajjati. Ayaṃ saṅkhepato āgate catudhātuvavatthāne bhāvanānayo.

Or alternatively, for the purpose of showing the non-sentient nature of the four great elements, the General of the Dhamma has stated: 'Depending on bone, and depending on sinew, and depending on flesh, and depending on skin, the enclosed space comes to be designated as "form"' (MN 1.240). These are the four parts that are spoken of. With regard to these, with the hand of wisdom that follows along the interval between each of them, having repeatedly disentangled them, one should grasp the elements by the very same method as before, thinking: 'Whatever in these parts is the state of hardness or roughness, this is the earth element.' Then, one should again and again advert to, attend to, and review them as 'earth element, water element,' and so on, as mere elements, as non-sentient, as non-living. For one who strives in this way, before long, a concentration arises that is merely access concentration, not having reached absorption, which is comprehended by the wisdom that illuminates the distinction of the elements and has natural phenomena as its object. This is the method of development in the determination of the four elements as taught in brief.

309. Vitthārato āgate pana evaṃ veditabbo. Idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetukāmena hi nātitikkhapaññena yoginā ācariyasantike dvācattālīsāya ākārehi vitthārato dhātuyo uggaṇhitvā vuttappakāre senāsane viharantena katasabbakiccena rahogatena paṭisallīnena sasambhārasaṅkhepato, sasambhāravibhattito, salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato, salakkhaṇavibhattitoti evaṃ catūhākārehi kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ.

309. However, regarding that which is taught in detail, it should be understood thus: A yogī who wishes to develop this meditation subject, one not of excessively sharp wisdom, should first learn the elements in detail in forty-two aspects in the presence of a teacher. Then, dwelling in a dwelling place of the type described, having completed all duties, gone to a secluded place, and withdrawn, the meditation subject should be developed in four ways: concisely with its components, by analysis with its components, concisely with its characteristics, and by analysis with its characteristics.

Tattha kathaṃ sasambhārasaṅkhepato bhāveti? Idha bhikkhu vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu thaddhākāraṃ pathavīdhātūti vavatthapeti. Dvādasasu koṭṭhāsesu yūsagataṃ udakasaṅkhātaṃ ābandhanākāraṃ āpodhātūti vavatthapeti. Catūsu koṭṭhāsesu paripācanakaṃ tejaṃ tejodhātūti vavatthapeti[M 1.0348]. Chasu koṭṭhāsesu vitthambhanākāraṃ vāyodhātūti vavatthapeti. Tassevaṃ vavatthāpayatoyeva dhātuyo pākaṭā honti. Tā punappunaṃ āvajjato manasikaroto vuttanayeneva upacārasamādhi uppajjati.

Therein, how does one develop it concisely with components? Here, a bhikkhu determines the aspect of hardness in the twenty bodily parts as 'the earth element.' In the twelve bodily parts, he determines the aspect of binding, which is included in liquids and designated as water, as 'the water element.' In the four bodily parts, he determines the digestive heat as 'the fire element.' In the six bodily parts, he determines the aspect of supporting as 'the air element.' For one determining thus, the elements become manifest. For one reflecting upon and attending to them again and again, access concentration arises in the very manner described.

310. Yassa pana evaṃ bhāvayato kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ijjhati, tena sasambhāravibhattito bhāvetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Tena hi bhikkhunā yaṃ taṃ kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhānaniddese sattadhā uggahakosallaṃ dasadhā manasikārakosallañca vuttaṃ. Dvattiṃsākāre tāva taṃ sabbaṃ aparihāpetvā tacapañcakādīnaṃ anulomapaṭilomato vacasā sajjhāyaṃ ādiṃkatvā sabbaṃ tattha vuttavidhānaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ayameva hi viseso, tattha vaṇṇasaṇṭhānadisokāsaparicchedavasena kesādayo manasikaritvāpi paṭikkūlavasena cittaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ, idha dhātuvasena. Tasmā vaṇṇādivasena pañcadhā pañcadhā kesādayo manasikaritvā avasāne evaṃ manasikāro pavattetabbo.

310. But for one for whom, while developing thus, the meditation subject does not succeed, it should be developed by analysis with its components. How so? That bhikkhu should, without diminishing any of that which was stated in the exposition of the mindfulness-of-the-body meditation subject—namely, the sevenfold skill in learning and the tenfold skill in attending to the thirty-two parts—do all that was instructed there, beginning with the verbal recitation of the skin-pentad and so on, forwards and backwards. This indeed is the difference: there, having attended to the hair, etc., by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, the mind is to be established by way of repulsiveness; here, it is by way of the elements. Therefore, having attended to the hair, etc., in five ways each by way of color and so on, at the end, attention should be directed thus:

311. Ime kesā nāma sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacamme jātā. Tattha yathāvammikamatthake jātesu kuṇṭhatiṇesu na vammikamatthako jānāti mayi kuṇṭhatiṇāni jātānīti, napi kuṇṭhatiṇāni jānanti mayaṃ vammikamatthake jātānīti, evameva na sīsakaṭāhapaliveṭhanacammaṃ jānāti mayi kesā jātāti, napi kesā jānanti mayaṃ sīsakaṭāhaveṭhanacamme jātāti, aññamaññaṃ [V 1.0344] ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti kesā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

311. These so-called hairs of the head are grown on the skin that wraps the skull-pan. In this regard, just as when blunt grasses have grown on the top of an anthill, the top of the anthill does not know, 'Blunt grasses have grown on me,' nor do the blunt grasses know, 'We have grown on the top of an anthill'; in the very same way, the skin that wraps the skull-pan does not know, 'Hairs of the head have grown on me,' nor do the hairs of the head know, 'We have grown on the skin that wraps the skull-pan.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, the so-called hairs of the head in this body are a separate part, insentient, indeterminate, void, devoid of a being, stiff—the earth element.

312. Lomā sarīraveṭhanacamme jātā. Tattha yathā suññagāmaṭṭhāne jātesu dabbatiṇakesu na suññagāmaṭṭhānaṃ jānāti mayi dabbatiṇakāni jātānīti, napi dabbatiṇakāni jānanti mayaṃ suññagāmaṭṭhāne jātānīti, evameva na sarīraveṭhanacammaṃ jānāti mayi lomā jātāti. Napi lomā jānanti mayaṃ sarīraveṭhanacamme jātāti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā [M 1.0349] ete dhammā. Iti lomā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

312. The hairs of the body are grown on the skin that wraps the body. In this regard, just as when dabba grass has grown in a deserted village site, the deserted village site does not know, 'Dabba grass has grown on me,' nor does the dabba grass know, 'We have grown in a deserted village site'; in the very same way, the skin that wraps the body does not know, 'Hairs of the body have grown on me,' nor do the hairs of the body know, 'We have grown on the skin that wraps the body.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, the so-called hairs of the body in this body are a separate part, insentient, indeterminate, void, devoid of a being, stiff—the earth element.

313. Nakhā aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu jātā. Tattha yathā kumārakesu daṇḍakehi madhukaṭṭhike vijjhitvā kīḷantesu na daṇḍakā jānanti amhesu madhukaṭṭhikā ṭhapitāti, napi madhukaṭṭhikā jānanti mayaṃ daṇḍakesu ṭhapitāti, evameva na aṅguliyo jānanti amhākaṃ aggesu nakhā jātāti. Napi nakhā jānanti mayaṃ aṅgulīnaṃ aggesu jātāti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti nakhā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

313. The nails are grown at the tips of the fingers and toes. In this regard, just as when boys play by piercing licorice seeds with darts, the darts do not know, 'Licorice seeds are placed on us,' nor do the licorice seeds know, 'We are placed on the darts'; in the very same way, the fingers and toes do not know, 'Nails have grown at our tips,' nor do the nails know, 'We have grown at the tips of the fingers and toes.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, the so-called nails in this body are a separate part, insentient, indeterminate, void, devoid of a being, stiff—the earth element.

314. Dantā hanukaṭṭhikesu jātā. Tattha yathā vaḍḍhakīhi pāsāṇaudukkhalakesu kenacideva silesajātena bandhitvā ṭhapitathambhesu na udukkhalā jānanti amhesu thambhā ṭhitāti. Napi thambhā jānanti mayaṃ udukkhalesu ṭhitāti, evameva na hanukaṭṭhīni jānanti amhesu dantā jātāti. Napi dantā jānanti mayaṃ hanukaṭṭhīsu jātāti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti dantā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

314. The teeth are grown in the jawbones. Herein, just as when carpenters set up posts in small stone mortars, having bound them with some kind of adhesive, the mortars do not know, “The posts are set in us,” nor do the posts know, “We are set in the mortars”; even so, the jawbones do not know, “The teeth are grown in us,” nor do the teeth know, “We are grown in the jawbones.” These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called ‘teeth’ in this body is a distinct component—insentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, and solid: the earth element.

315. Taco sakalasarīraṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhito. Tattha yathā allagocammapariyonaddhāya mahāvīṇāya na mahāvīṇā jānāti ahaṃ allagocammena pariyonaddhāti. Napi allagocammaṃ jānāti mayā mahāvīṇā pariyonaddhāti, evameva na sarīraṃ jānāti ahaṃ tacena pariyonaddhanti. Napi taco jānāti mayā sarīraṃ pariyonaddhanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā [V 1.0345] ete dhammā. Iti taco nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

315. The skin stands enveloping the entire body. Herein, just as in the case of a great lute enveloped by wet cowhide, the great lute does not know, “I am enveloped by wet cowhide,” nor does the wet cowhide know, “The great lute is enveloped by me”; even so, the body does not know, “I am enveloped by the skin,” nor does the skin know, “The body is enveloped by me.” These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called ‘skin’ in this body is a distinct component—insentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, and solid: the earth element.

316. Maṃsaṃ aṭṭhisaṅghāṭaṃ anulimpitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā mahāmattikalittāya bhittiyā na bhitti jānāti ahaṃ mahāmattikāya littāti. Napi [M 1.0350] mahāmattikā jānāti mayā bhitti littāti, evameva na aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo jānāti ahaṃ navapesisatappabhedena maṃsena littoti. Napi maṃsaṃ jānāti mayā aṭṭhisaṅghāṭo littoti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti maṃsaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

316. The flesh stands plastering the framework of bones. Herein, just as in the case of a wall plastered with thick clay, the wall does not know, “I am plastered with thick clay,” nor does the thick clay know, “The wall is plastered by me”; even so, the framework of bones does not know, “I am plastered with flesh of nine hundred different pieces,” nor does the flesh know, “The framework of bones is plastered by me.” These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called ‘flesh’ in this body is a distinct component—insentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, and solid: the earth element.

317. Nhāru sarīrabbhantare aṭṭhīni ābandhamānā ṭhitā. Tattha yathā vallīhi vinaddhesu kuṭṭadārūsu na kuṭṭadārūni jānanti mayaṃ vallīhi vinaddhānīti. Napi valliyo jānanti amhehi kuṭṭadārūni vinaddhānīti, evameva na aṭṭhīni jānanti mayaṃ nhārūhi ābaddhānīti. Napi nhārū jānanti amhehi aṭṭhīni ābaddhānīti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti nhāru nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

317. The sinews stand within the body, binding the bones. Herein, just as in the case of wall timbers bound by vines, the timbers do not know, “We are bound by vines,” nor do the vines know, “The wall timbers are bound by us”; even so, the bones do not know, “We are bound by sinews,” nor do the sinews know, “The bones are bound by us.” These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called ‘sinews’ in this body is a distinct component—insentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, and solid: the earth element.

318. Aṭṭhīsu paṇhikaṭṭhi gopphakaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Gopphakaṭṭhi jaṅghaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Jaṅghaṭṭhi ūruṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Ūruṭṭhi kaṭiṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Kaṭiṭṭhi piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ, piṭṭhikaṇṭako gīvaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhito. Gīvaṭṭhi sīsaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Sīsaṭṭhi gīvaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Gīvaṭṭhi piṭṭhikaṇṭake patiṭṭhitaṃ. Piṭṭhikaṇṭako kaṭiṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhito. Kaṭiṭṭhi ūruṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Ūruṭṭhi jaṅghaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Jaṅghaṭṭhi gopphakaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ. Gopphakaṭṭhi paṇhikaṭṭhike patiṭṭhitaṃ.

318. Among the bones, the heel bone stands supporting the ankle bone. The ankle bone stands supporting the shin bone. The shin bone stands supporting the thigh bone. The thigh bone stands supporting the hip bone. The hip bone stands supporting the backbone. The backbone stands supporting the neck bone. The neck bone stands supporting the skull. The skull is established on the neck bone. The neck bone is established on the backbone. The backbone is established on the hip bone. The hip bone is established on the thigh bone. The thigh bone is established on the shin bone. The shin bone is established on the ankle bone. The ankle bone is established on the heel bone.

Tattha yathā iṭṭhakadārugomayādisañcayesu na heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā jānanti mayaṃ uparime uparime ukkhipitvā ṭhitāti. Napi uparimā uparimā jānanti mayaṃ heṭṭhimesu heṭṭhimesu patiṭṭhitāti, evameva na paṇhikaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ gopphakaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti. Na gopphakaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ jaṅghaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti. Na jaṅghaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ ūruṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā [V 1.0346] ṭhitanti. Na ūruṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ kaṭiṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti. Na kaṭiṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti. Na piṭṭhikaṇṭako jānāti ahaṃ gīvaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti. Na gīvaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ sīsaṭṭhiṃ ukkhipitvā ṭhitanti. Na sīsaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ gīvaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitanti. Na gīvaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭake [M 1.0351] patiṭṭhitanti. Na piṭṭhikaṇṭako jānāti ahaṃ kaṭiṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitoti. Na kaṭiṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ ūruṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitanti. Na ūruṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ jaṅghaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitanti. Na jaṅghaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ gopphakaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitanti. Na gopphakaṭṭhi jānāti ahaṃ paṇhikaṭṭhimhi patiṭṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti aṭṭhi nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

Herein, just as in a pile of bricks, wood, cow dung, and so on, the lower ones do not know, “We stand supporting the upper ones,” nor do the upper ones know, “We are established on the lower ones”; even so, the heel bone does not know, “I stand supporting the ankle bone.” The ankle bone does not know, “I stand supporting the shin bone.” The shin bone does not know, “I stand supporting the thigh bone.” The thigh bone does not know, “I stand supporting the hip bone.” The hip bone does not know, “I stand supporting the backbone.” The backbone does not know, “I stand supporting the neck bone.” The neck bone does not know, “I stand supporting the skull.” The skull does not know, “I am established on the neck bone.” The neck bone does not know, “I am established on the backbone.” The backbone does not know, “I am established on the hip bone.” The hip bone does not know, “I am established on the thigh bone.” The thigh bone does not know, “I am established on the shin bone.” The shin bone does not know, “I am established on the ankle bone.” The ankle bone does not know, “I am established on the heel bone.” These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called ‘bone’ in this body is a distinct component—insentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, and solid: the earth element.

319. Aṭṭhimiñjaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ abbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā veḷupabbādīnaṃ anto pakkhittachinnavettaggādīsu na veḷupabbādīni jānanti amhesu vettaggādīni pakkhittānīti. Napi vettaggādīni jānanti mayaṃ veḷupabbādīsu ṭhitānīti, evameva na aṭṭhīni jānanti amhākaṃ anto miñjaṃ ṭhitanti. Nāpi miñjaṃ jānāti ahaṃ aṭṭhīnaṃ anto ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti aṭṭhimiñjaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

319. The bone marrow is situated within those various bones. Herein, just as in the case of bamboo joints and so on, into which cut rattan tips and so on have been inserted, the bamboo joints and so on do not know, “Rattan tips and so on are inserted in us,” nor do the rattan tips and so on know, “We are situated in the bamboo joints and so on”; even so, the bones do not know, “The marrow is situated within us,” nor does the marrow know, “I am situated within the bones.” These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called ‘bone marrow’ in this body is a distinct component—insentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, and solid: the earth element.

320. Vakkaṃ galavāṭakato nikkhantena ekamūlena thokaṃ gantvā dvidhā bhinnena thūlanhārunā vinibaddhaṃ hutvā hadayamaṃsaṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā vaṇṭupanibaddhe ambaphaladvaye na vaṇṭaṃ jānāti mayā ambaphaladvayaṃ upanibaddhanti. Napi ambaphaladvayaṃ jānāti ahaṃ vaṇṭena upanibaddhanti, evameva na thūlanhāru jānāti mayā vakkaṃ upanibaddhanti. Napi vakkaṃ jānāti ahaṃ thūlanhārunā upanibaddhanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti vakkaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

320. The kidneys are situated surrounding the heart-flesh, having been bound by a thick sinew that emerges from the throat with a single root, goes a little way, and then splits in two. Therein, just as in the case of two mango fruits bound by a stalk, the stalk does not know, 'The two mango fruits are bound by me,' nor do the two mango fruits know, 'We are bound by the stalk,' even so, the thick sinew does not know, 'The kidneys are bound by me,' nor do the kidneys know, 'We are bound by the thick sinew.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the kidneys in this body are a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

321. Hadayaṃ sarīrabbhantare uraṭṭhipañjaramajjhaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā jiṇṇasandamānikapañjaraṃ nissāya ṭhapitāya maṃsapesiyā na sandamānikapañjarabbhantaraṃ jānāti maṃ nissāya maṃsapesi ṭhitāti. Napi maṃsapesi jānāti ahaṃ jiṇṇasandamānikapañjaraṃ nissāya [V 1.0347] ṭhitāti, evameva na uraṭṭhipañjarabbhantaraṃ jānāti maṃ nissāya hadayaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi hadayaṃ jānāti ahaṃ uraṭṭhipañjaraṃ nissāya ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete [M 1.0352] dhammā. Iti hadayaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

321. The heart is situated within the body, relying on the middle of the rib cage. Therein, just as with a piece of meat placed relying on a worn-out iron-strip cage, the inside of the iron-strip cage does not know, 'The piece of meat is situated relying on me,' nor does the piece of meat know, 'I am situated relying on the worn-out iron-strip cage'; even so, the inside of the rib cage does not know, 'The heart is situated relying on me,' nor does the heart know, 'I am situated relying on the rib cage.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the heart in this body is a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

322. Yakanaṃ antosarīre dvinnaṃ thanānamabbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā ukkhalikapālapassamhi lagge yamakamaṃsapiṇḍe na ukkhalikapālapassaṃ jānāti mayi yamakamaṃsapiṇḍo laggoti. Napi yamakamaṃsapiṇḍo jānāti ahaṃ ukkhalikapālapasse laggoti, evameva na thanānamabbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ jānāti maṃ nissāya yakanaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi yakanaṃ jānāti ahaṃ thanānamabbhantare dakkhiṇapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti yakanaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

322. The liver is situated inside the body, relying on the right side in the space between the two breasts. Therein, just as with a pair of meat lumps stuck to the side of a pot sherd, the side of the pot sherd does not know, 'The pair of meat lumps is stuck on me,' nor does the pair of meat lumps know, 'We are stuck on the side of the pot sherd'; even so, the right side in the space between the breasts does not know, 'The liver is situated relying on me,' nor does the liver know, 'I am situated relying on the right side in the space between the breasts.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the liver in this body is a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

323. Kilomakesu paṭicchannakilomakaṃ hadayañca vakkañca parivāretvā ṭhitaṃ. Appaṭicchannakilomakaṃ sakalasarīre cammassa heṭṭhato maṃsaṃ pariyonandhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā pilotikapaliveṭhite maṃse na maṃsaṃ jānāti ahaṃ pilotikāya paliveṭhitanti. Napi pilotikā jānāti mayā maṃsaṃ paliveṭhitanti, evameva na vakkahadayāni sakalasarīre ca maṃsaṃ jānāti ahaṃ kilomakena paṭicchannanti. Napi kilomakaṃ jānāti mayā vakkahadayāni sakalasarīre ca maṃsaṃ paṭicchannanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti kilomakaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

323. Of the membranes, the covering membrane is situated enveloping the heart and the kidneys. The uncovered membrane is situated enmeshing the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body. Therein, just as when flesh is wrapped in a cloth, the flesh does not know, 'I am wrapped by the cloth,' nor does the cloth know, 'The flesh is wrapped by me'; even so, the kidneys and heart, and the flesh throughout the entire body, do not know, 'I am covered by the membrane,' nor does the membrane know, 'The kidneys, heart, and the flesh of the whole body are covered by me.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the membrane in this body is a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

324. Pihakaṃ hadayassa vāmapasse udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā koṭṭhamatthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitāya gomayapiṇḍiyā na koṭṭhamatthakapassaṃ jānāti gomayapiṇḍi maṃ nissāya ṭhitāti. Napi gomayapiṇḍi jānāti ahaṃ koṭṭhamatthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitāti, evameva na udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ jānāti pihakaṃ maṃ nissāya ṭhitanti. Napi pihakaṃ jānāti ahaṃ udarapaṭalassa matthakapassaṃ nissāya ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā [V 1.0348] ete dhammā. Iti pihakaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

324. The spleen is situated on the left side of the heart, resting on the upper side of the abdominal membrane. Therein, just as when a lump of cow-dung is situated resting on the upper side of a granary, the upper side of the granary does not know, 'The lump of cow-dung is resting on me,' nor does the lump of cow-dung know, 'I am resting on the upper side of the granary'; even so, the upper side of the abdominal membrane does not know, 'The spleen is resting on me,' nor does the spleen know, 'I am resting on the upper side of the abdominal membrane.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the spleen in this body is a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

325. Papphāsaṃ [M 1.0353] sarīrabbhantare dvinnaṃ thanānamantare hadayañca yakanañca upari chādetvā olambantaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā jiṇṇakoṭṭhabbhantare lambamāne sakuṇakulāvake na jiṇṇakoṭṭhabbhantaraṃ jānāti mayi sakuṇakulāvako lambamāno ṭhitoti. Napi sakuṇakulāvako jānāti ahaṃ jiṇṇakoṭṭhabbhantare lambamāno ṭhitoti, evameva na taṃ sarīrabbhantaraṃ jānāti mayi papphāsaṃ lambamānaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi papphāsaṃ jānāti ahaṃ evarūpe sarīrabbhantare lambamānaṃ ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti papphāsaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

325. The lungs hang suspended within the body's interior, between the two breasts, covering the heart and liver from above. Therein, just as the interior of an old granary does not know, 'A bird's nest is hanging within me,' nor does the bird's nest know, 'I am hanging inside the old granary,' even so, the body's interior does not know, 'The lungs are hanging within me,' nor do the lungs know, 'I am hanging within such a body.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the lungs in this body are a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

326. Antaṃ galavāṭakakarīsamaggapariyante sarīrabbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā lohitadoṇikāya obhujitvā ṭhapite chinnasīsadhammanikaḷevare na lohitadoṇi jānāti mayi dhammanikaḷevaraṃ ṭhitanti. Napi dhammanikaḷevaraṃ jānāti ahaṃ lohitadoṇiyā ṭhitanti, evameva na sarīrabbhantaraṃ jānāti mayi antaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi antaṃ jānāti ahaṃ sarīrabbhantare ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti antaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

326. The intestines are situated within the body's interior, extending from the throat passage to the rectum. Therein, just as, when the corpse of a beheaded snake is coiled and placed in a blood trough, the blood trough does not know, 'The snake's corpse is situated in me,' nor does the snake's corpse know, 'I am situated in the blood trough,' so too the body's interior does not know, 'The intestines are situated in me,' nor do the intestines know, 'I am situated in the body's interior.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, the intestines in this body are a distinct component—inanimate, undeclared, empty, without a living being, stiff—the earth element.

327. Antaguṇaṃ antantare ekavīsatiantabhoge bandhitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakaṃ sibbetvā ṭhitesu rajjukesu na pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakaṃ jānāti rajjukā maṃ sibbitvā ṭhitāti. Napi rajjukā jānanti mayaṃ pādapuñchanarajjumaṇḍalakaṃ sibbitvā ṭhitāti, evameva na antaṃ jānāti antaguṇaṃ maṃ ābandhitvā ṭhitanti. Napi antaguṇaṃ jānāti ahaṃ antaṃ ābandhitvā ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti antaguṇaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

327. The small intestine is situated amidst the large intestine, binding its twenty-one coils. Just as, when a coiled rope foot-mat is stitched together with cords, the coiled rope foot-mat does not know, 'The cords have stitched me,' nor do the cords know, 'We have stitched the coiled rope foot-mat,' so too the large intestine does not know, 'The small intestine has bound me,' nor does the small intestine know, 'I have bound the large intestine.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called the small intestine is a distinct part in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, rigid, the earth element.

328. Udariyaṃ udare ṭhitaṃ asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ. Tattha yathā suvānadoṇiyaṃ ṭhite suvānavamathumhi na suvānadoṇi jānāti mayi suvānavamathu ṭhitoti. Napi suvānavamathu jānāti [V 1.0349] ahaṃ suvānadoṇiyaṃ ṭhitoti, evameva na udaraṃ jānāti mayi udariyaṃ ṭhitanti[M 1.0354]. Napi udariyaṃ jānāti ahaṃ udare ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti udariyaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

328. The undigested food—that is, what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—is situated in the stomach. Just as, when dog vomit is in a dog's trough, the dog's trough does not know, 'Dog vomit is within me,' nor does the dog vomit know, 'I am in the dog's trough,' so too the stomach does not know, 'Undigested food is within me,' nor does the undigested food know, 'I am in the stomach.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called undigested food is a distinct part of this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, rigid, the earth element.

329. Karīsaṃ pakkāsayasaṅkhāte aṭṭhaṅgulaveḷupabbasadise antapariyosāne ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā veḷupabbe omadditvā pakkhittāya saṇhapaṇḍumattikāya na veḷupabbaṃ jānāti mayi paṇḍumattikā ṭhitāti. Napi paṇḍumattikā jānāti ahaṃ veḷupabbe ṭhitāti, evameva na pakkāsayo jānāti mayi karīsaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi karīsaṃ jānāti ahaṃ pakkāsaye ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti karīsaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

329. Feces is situated at the end of the large intestine, in what is known as the receptacle for digested food, which resembles a bamboo section of eight finger-breadths. Just as when fine, pale clay is kneaded and put into a bamboo section, the bamboo section does not know, 'Pale clay is situated in me,' nor does the pale clay know, 'I am situated in the bamboo section,' so too the receptacle for digested food does not know, 'Feces is situated in me,' nor does the feces know, 'I am situated in the receptacle for digested food.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called feces is a distinct part in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, rigid, the earth element.

330. Matthaluṅgaṃ sīsakaṭāhabbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā purāṇalābukaṭāhe pakkhittāya piṭṭhapiṇḍiyā na lābukaṭāhaṃ jānāti mayi piṭṭhapiṇḍi ṭhitāti. Napi piṭṭhapiṇḍi jānāti ahaṃ lābukaṭāhe ṭhitāti, evameva na sīsakaṭāhabbhantaraṃ jānāti mayi matthaluṅgaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi matthaluṅgaṃ jānāti ahaṃ sīsakaṭāhabbhantare ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti matthaluṅgaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto thaddho pathavīdhātūti.

330. The brain is situated inside the skull. Just as when a ball of dough is placed in an old gourd bowl, the gourd bowl does not know, 'A ball of dough is within me,' nor does the ball of dough know, 'I am inside the gourd bowl,' so too the inside of the skull does not know, 'The brain is within me,' nor does the brain know, 'I am inside the skull.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called the brain is a distinct part in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, rigid, the earth element.

331. Pittesu abaddhapittaṃ jīvitindriyapaṭibaddhaṃ sakalasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ. Baddhapittaṃ pittakosake ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā pūvaṃ byāpetvā ṭhite tele na pūvaṃ jānāti telaṃ maṃ byāpetvā ṭhitanti. Napi telaṃ jānāti ahaṃ pūvaṃ byāpetvā ṭhitanti, evameva na sarīraṃ jānāti abaddhapittaṃ maṃ byāpetvā ṭhitanti. Napi abaddhapittaṃ jānāti ahaṃ sarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitanti. Yathā vassodakena puṇṇe kosātakikosake na kosātakikosako jānāti mayi vassodakaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi vassodakaṃ jānāti ahaṃ kosātakikosake ṭhitanti, evameva na pittakosako jānāti mayi baddhapittaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi baddhapittaṃ jānāti ahaṃ pittakosake ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā[M 1.0355]. Iti pittaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko [V 1.0350] koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

331. Among the biles, unbound bile, connected to the life faculty, remains pervading the entire body. Bound bile remains in the bile sac. Therein, just as when oil remains pervading a cake, the cake does not know, 'Oil remains pervading me,' nor does the oil know, 'I remain pervading the cake,' so too, the body does not know, 'Unbound bile remains pervading me,' nor does unbound bile know, 'I remain pervading the body.' And just as when a sponge gourd pod is filled with rainwater, the sponge gourd pod does not know, 'Rainwater remains in me,' nor does the rainwater know, 'I remain in the sponge gourd pod,' so too, the bile sac does not know, 'Bound bile remains in me,' nor does bound bile know, 'I remain in the bile sac.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called bile is a distinct part in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, of the nature of broth, having the characteristic of binding, the water element.

332. Semhaṃ ekapatthapūrappamāṇaṃ udarapaṭale ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā upari sañjātapheṇapaṭalāya candanikāya na candanikā jānāti mayi pheṇapaṭalaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi pheṇapaṭalaṃ jānāti ahaṃ candanikāya ṭhitanti, evameva na udarapaṭalaṃ jānāti mayi semhaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi semhaṃ jānāti ahaṃ udarapaṭale ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti semhaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

332. Phlegm, about the measure of one pattha, is situated on the stomach lining. Just as when a layer of foam forms on the surface of a pond, the pond does not know, 'A layer of foam is upon me,' nor does the layer of foam know, 'I am on the pond,' so too the stomach lining does not know, 'Phlegm is upon me,' nor does the phlegm know, 'I am on the stomach lining.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called phlegm is a distinct part in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, of the nature of broth, having the characteristic of binding, the water element.

333. Pubbo anibaddhokāso yattha yattheva khāṇukaṇṭakappaharaṇaaggijālādīhi abhihate sarīrappadese lohitaṃ saṇṭhahitvā paccati, gaṇḍapīḷakādayo vā uppajjanti, tattha tattha tiṭṭhati. Tattha yathā pharasuppahārādivasena paggharitaniyyāse rukkhe na rukkhassa pahārādippadesā jānanti amhesu niyyāso ṭhitoti, napi niyyāso jānāti ahaṃ rukkhassa pahārādippadesesu ṭhitoti, evameva na sarīrassa khāṇukaṇṭakādīhi abhihatappadesā jānanti amhesu pubbo ṭhitoti. Napi pubbo jānāti ahaṃ tesu padesesu ṭhitoti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti pubbo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

333. Pus has no fixed location; it is found wherever in a region of the body that has been struck by stakes, thorns, weapons, flames, and so on, where blood has collected and festered, or where boils, abscesses, and the like arise; it is situated in those very places. Just as when sap flows from a tree due to being struck by an axe and so on, the places on the tree that were struck do not know, 'Sap is in us,' nor does the sap know, 'I am in the places on the tree that were struck,' so too, the regions of the body struck by stakes, thorns, and so on do not know, 'Pus is in us,' nor does the pus know, 'I am in those regions.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual consideration and reflection. Thus, what is called pus is a distinct part in this body—insentient, indeterminate, empty, without a living being, of the nature of broth, having the characteristic of binding, the water element.

334. Lohitesu saṃsaraṇalohitaṃ pittaṃ viya sakalasarīraṃ byāpetvā ṭhitaṃ. Sannicitalohitaṃ yakanaṭṭhānassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā ekapatthapūramattaṃ vakkahadayayakanapapphāsāni tementaṃ ṭhitaṃ. Tattha saṃsaraṇalohite abaddhapittasadisova vinicchayo. Itaraṃ pana yathā jajjarakapāle ovaṭṭhe udake heṭṭhā leḍḍukhaṇḍādīni temayamāne na leḍḍukhaṇḍādīni jānanti mayaṃ udakena temiyamānāti. Napi udakaṃ jānāti ahaṃ [M 1.0356] leḍḍukhaṇḍādīni tememīti, evameva na yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgaṭṭhānaṃ vakkādīni vā jānanti mayi lohitaṃ ṭhitaṃ amhe vā temayamānaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi lohitaṃ jānāti ahaṃ yakanassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ pūretvā vakkādīni temayamānaṃ ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti lohitaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre [V 1.0351] pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

334. Among the bloods, circulating blood, like bile, stands pervading the entire body. Collected blood, filling the lower part of the liver's location to the measure of one `pattha`, stands moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. Therein, regarding circulating blood, the determination is just like that for unbound bile. But as for the other, it is as when, in a crumbling pot that has been rained upon, the water moistens lumps of clay and so on at the bottom: neither do the lumps of clay and so on know, 'We are being moistened by water,' nor does the water know, 'I am moistening the lumps of clay and so on.' In the very same way, neither the lower part of the liver's location nor the kidneys and so on know, 'Blood is in me' or 'it stands moistening us.' Nor does the blood know, 'I stand filling the lower part of the liver's location and moistening the kidneys and so on.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called blood is a particular part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, like broth, has the characteristic of binding, and is the water element.

335. Sedo aggisantāpādikālesu kesalomakūpavivarāni pūretvā tiṭṭhati ceva paggharati ca. Tattha yathā udakā abbūḷhamattesu bhisamuḷālakumudanāḷakalāpesu na bhisādikalāpavivarāni jānanti amhehi udakaṃ paggharatīti. Napi bhisādikalāpavivarehi paggharantaṃ udakaṃ jānāti ahaṃ bhisādikalāpavivarehi paggharāmīti, evameva na kesalomakūpavivarāni jānanti amhehi sedo paggharatīti. Napi sedo jānāti ahaṃ kesalomakūpavivarehi paggharāmīti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti sedo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

335. Sweat, at times of heat from fire and so on, fills the pores of the head-hair and body-hair, and it both stands there and flows out. Therein, it is as with bundles of lotus stalks, lotus roots, water lilies, and lotus stems that have just been drawn out of the water: neither do the openings in the bundles of lotus stalks and so on know, 'Water is flowing from us,' nor does the water flowing from the openings in the bundles of lotus stalks and so on know, 'I am flowing from the openings in the bundles of lotus stalks and so on.' In the very same way, the pores of the head-hair and body-hair do not know, 'Sweat is flowing from us,' nor does the sweat know, 'I am flowing from the pores of the head-hair and body-hair.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called sweat is a particular part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, like broth, has the characteristic of binding, and is the water element.

336. Medo thūlassa sakalasarīraṃ pharitvā kisassa jaṅghamaṃsādīni nissāya ṭhito patthinnasineho. Tattha yathā haliddipilotikapaṭicchanne maṃsapuñje na maṃsapuñjo jānāti maṃ nissāya haliddipilotikā ṭhitāti. Napi haliddipilotikā jānāti ahaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ nissāya ṭhitāti, evameva na sakalasarīre jaṅghādīsu vā maṃsaṃ jānāti maṃ nissāya medo ṭhitoti. Napi medo jānāti ahaṃ sakalasarīre jaṅghādīsu vā maṃsaṃ nissāya ṭhitoti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti medo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto patthinnayūso ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

336. Fat is the thick grease that stands pervading the entire body of an obese person, and stands depending on the flesh of the calves and so on of a lean person. In this regard, just as in the case of a heap of meat covered with a turmeric-dyed worn-out cloth, the heap of meat does not know, 'The turmeric-dyed worn-out cloth is dependent on me,' nor does the turmeric-dyed worn-out cloth know, 'I am dependent on the heap of meat,' so too, neither does the flesh in the entire body or in the calves and so on know, 'Fat is dependent on me,' nor does the fat know, 'I am dependent on the flesh in the entire body or in the calves and so on.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called fat is a distinct part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, a thick, congealed fluid, having the characteristic of binding, and is the water element.

337. Assu [M 1.0357] yadā sañjāyati tadā akkhikūpake pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Tattha yathā udakapuṇṇesu taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakesu na taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakā jānanti amhesu udakaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakesu udakaṃ jānāti ahaṃ taruṇatālaṭṭhikūpakesu ṭhitanti, evameva na akkhikūpakā jānanti amhesu assu ṭhitanti. Napi assu jānāti ahaṃ akkhikūpakesu ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti assu nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

337. Tears, when they arise, fill the eye sockets and either stand or flow out. In this regard, just as the hollows of young palm seeds filled with water do not know, 'Water is in us,' nor does the water in the hollows of young palm seeds know, 'I am in the hollows of young palm seeds,' so too, the eye sockets do not know, 'Tears are in us,' nor do the tears know, 'I am in the eye sockets.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called tears is a distinct part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, like broth, has the characteristic of binding, and is the water element.

338. Vasā [V 1.0352] aggisantāpādikāle hatthatalahatthapiṭṭhipādatalapādapiṭṭhi nāsāpuṭanalāṭaaṃsakūṭesu ṭhitavilīnasneho. Tattha yathā pakkhittatele ācāme na ācāmo jānāti maṃ telaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitanti. Napi telaṃ jānāti ahaṃ ācāmaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitanti, evameva na hatthatalādippadeso jānāti maṃ vasā ajjhottharitvā ṭhitāti. Napi vasā jānāti ahaṃ hatthatalādippadesaṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitāti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti vasā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

338. Grease is the dissolved oil that stands, at times of heat from fire and so on, on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles, the backs of the feet, the bridge of the nose, the forehead, and the shoulder-blades. Therein, just as when oil is put into rice scum, the rice scum does not know, 'The oil stands, overspreading me,' nor does the oil know, 'I stand, overspreading the rice scum,' so too, the areas like the palms and so on do not know, 'Grease stands, overspreading me,' nor does the grease know, 'I stand, overspreading the areas like the palms and so on.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called grease is a distinct part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, like broth, has the characteristic of binding, and is the water element.

339. Kheḷo tathārūpe kheḷuppattipaccaye sati ubhohi kapolapassehi orohitvā jivhātale tiṭṭhati. Tattha yathā abbocchinnaudakanissande nadītīrakūpake na kūpatalaṃ jānāti mayi udakaṃ santiṭṭhatīti. Napi udakaṃ jānāti ahaṃ kūpatale santiṭṭhāmīti, evameva na jivhātalaṃ jānāti mayi ubhohi kapolapassehi orohitvā kheḷo ṭhitoti. Napi kheḷo jānāti ahaṃ ubhohi kapolapassehi orohitvā jivhātale ṭhitoti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti kheḷo nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

339. Saliva, when there is a suitable condition for its production, descends from both sides of the cheeks and stands on the surface of the tongue. Therein, just as in a small well on a riverbank with an uninterrupted flow of water, the bottom of the well does not know, 'Water stands in me,' nor does the water know, 'I stand on the bottom of the well,' so too, the surface of the tongue does not know, 'Saliva, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, stands on me,' nor does the saliva know, 'I, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, stand on the surface of the tongue.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called saliva is a distinct part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, lifeless, like broth, has the characteristic of binding, and is the water element.

340. Siṅghāṇikā [M 1.0358] yadā sañjāyati, tadā nāsāpuṭe pūretvā tiṭṭhati vā paggharati vā. Tattha yathā pūtidadhibharitāya sippikāya na sippikā jānāti mayi pūtidadhi ṭhitanti. Napi pūtidadhi jānāti ahaṃ sippikāya ṭhitanti, evameva na nāsāpuṭā jānanti amhesu siṅghāṇikā ṭhitāti. Napi siṅghāṇikā jānāti ahaṃ nāsāpuṭesu ṭhitāti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti siṅghāṇikā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

340. When mucus arises, it fills the nostrils and either remains or flows out. Therein, just as a shell filled with putrid curds does not know, 'Putrid curds are in me,' nor do the putrid curds know, 'I am in the shell,' so too, the nostrils do not know, 'Mucus is in us,' nor does the mucus know, 'I am in the nostrils.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called mucus is a distinct component in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, like broth, having the characteristic of cohesion, the water element.

341. Lasikā aṭṭhikasandhīnaṃ abbhañjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā asītisatasandhīsu ṭhitā. Tattha yathā telabbhañjite akkhe na akkho jānāti maṃ telaṃ abbhañjitvā ṭhitanti. Napi telaṃ jānāti ahaṃ akkhaṃ abbhañjitvā ṭhitanti, evameva na asītisatasandhayo jānanti lasikā amhe abbhañjitvā ṭhitāti. Napi lasikā jānāti ahaṃ asītisatasandhayo abbhañjitvā ṭhitāti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti lasikā nāma [V 1.0353] imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

341. Synovial fluid, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints, is present in the one hundred and eighty joints. Therein, just as an axle lubricated with oil does not know, 'Oil has lubricated me and is present,' nor does the oil know, 'I have lubricated the axle and am present,' so too, the one hundred and eighty joints do not know, 'Synovial fluid has lubricated us and is present,' nor does the synovial fluid know, 'I have lubricated the one hundred and eighty joints and am present.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called synovial fluid is a distinct component in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, like broth, having the characteristic of cohesion, the water element.

342. Muttaṃ vatthissa abbhantare ṭhitaṃ. Tattha yathā candanikāya pakkhitte amukhe ravaṇaghaṭe na ravaṇaghaṭo jānāti mayi candanikāraso ṭhitoti. Napi candanikāraso jānāti ahaṃ ravaṇaghaṭe ṭhitoti, evameva na vatthi jānāti mayi muttaṃ ṭhitanti. Napi muttaṃ jānāti ahaṃ vatthimhi ṭhitanti. Aññamaññaṃ ābhogapaccavekkhaṇarahitā ete dhammā. Iti muttaṃ nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto yūsabhūto ābandhanākāro āpodhātūti.

342. Urine is present inside the bladder. Therein, just as an uncracked pot without an opening placed in a cesspool does not know, 'Cesspool fluid is in me,' nor does the cesspool fluid know, 'I am in the uncracked pot,' so too, the bladder does not know, 'Urine is in me,' nor does the urine know, 'I am in the bladder.' These phenomena are devoid of mutual attention and reflection. Thus, what is called urine is a distinct component in this body—non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, like broth, having the characteristic of cohesion, the water element.

343. Evaṃ kesādīsu manasikāraṃ pavattetvā yena santappati, ayaṃ imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto paripācanākāro tejodhātūti, yena jīrīyati, yena [M 1.0359] pariḍayhati, yena asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto paripācanākāro tejodhātūti evaṃ tejokoṭṭhāsesu manasikāro pavattetabbo.

343. Having thus applied attention to the hair and other parts, [one should attend thus]: 'That by which [the body] is heated, this in this body is a distinct component, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, having the characteristic of maturing—the fire element.' 'That by which it ages...' 'That by which it is consumed by heat...' 'That by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted goes to proper digestion, this in this body is a distinct component, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, having the characteristic of maturing—the fire element.' In this way, attention should be applied to the components of the fire element.

344. Tato uddhaṅgame vāte uddhaṅgamavasena pariggahetvā adhogame adhogamavasena, kucchisaye kucchisayavasena, koṭṭhāsaye koṭṭhāsayavasena, aṅgamaṅgānusārimhi aṅgamaṅgānusārivasena, assāsapassāse assāsapassāsavasena pariggahetvā uddhaṅgamā vātā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto vitthambhanākāro vāyodhātūti, adhogamā vātā nāma, kucchisayā vātā nāma, koṭṭhāsayā vātā nāma, aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā nāma, assāsapassāsā vātā nāma imasmiṃ sarīre pāṭiyekko koṭṭhāso acetano abyākato suñño nissatto vitthambhanākāro vāyodhātūti evaṃ vāyokoṭṭhāsesu manasikāro pavattetabbo. Tassevaṃ pavattamanasikārassa dhātuyo pākaṭā honti. Tā punappunaṃ āvajjato manasikaroto vuttanayeneva upacārasamādhi uppajjati.

344. Then, having comprehended the upward-moving winds as upward-moving, the downward-moving winds as downward-moving, the winds in the belly as winds in the belly, the winds in the bowels as winds in the bowels, the winds that move through the limbs as winds that move through the limbs, and the in-breaths and out-breaths as in-breaths and out-breaths, [one should attend thus]: 'What are called the upward-moving winds in this body are a distinct component, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, having the characteristic of supporting—the wind element.' 'What are called the downward-moving winds...' 'What are called the winds in the belly...' 'What are called the winds in the bowels...' 'What are called the winds that move through the limbs...' 'What are called the in-breaths and out-breaths in this body are a distinct component, non-sentient, indeterminate, empty, non-living, having the characteristic of supporting—the wind element.' In this way, attention should be applied to the components of the wind element. For one who has thus applied attention, the elements become manifest. For one who repeatedly reflects upon and attends to them, access concentration arises in the very manner described.

345. Yassa pana evaṃ bhāvayato kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ijjhati, tena salakkhaṇasaṅkhepato bhāvetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Vīsatiyā koṭṭhāsesu thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīdhātūti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tattheva ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ [V 1.0354] āpodhātūti. Paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ tejodhātūti. Vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātūti.

345. But if for someone, while developing in this way, the meditation subject does not succeed, it should be developed by them by way of a summary of the characteristics. How? In the twenty components, the characteristic of hardness should be determined as the earth element. Therein, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element, the characteristic of maturing as the fire element, and the characteristic of supporting as the wind element.

Dvādasasu koṭṭhāsesu ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ āpodhātūti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tattheva paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ tejodhātūti. Vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātūti. Thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīdhātūti.

In the twelve components, the characteristic of cohesion should be determined as the water element. Therein, the characteristic of maturing as the fire element, the characteristic of supporting as the wind element, and the characteristic of hardness as the earth element.

Catūsu koṭṭhāsesu paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ tejodhātūti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tena avinibhuttaṃ vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātūti. Thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīdhātūti. Ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ āpodhātūti.

In the four components, the characteristic of maturing should be determined as the fire element. Inseparable from that, the characteristic of supporting as the wind element, the characteristic of hardness as the earth element, and the characteristic of cohesion as the water element.

Chasu [M 1.0360] koṭṭhāsesu vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātūti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tattheva thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīdhātūti. Ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ āpodhātūti. Paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ tejodhātūti. Tassevaṃ vavatthāpayato dhātuyo pākaṭā honti. Tā punappunaṃ āvajjato manasikaroto vuttanayeneva upacārasamādhi uppajjati.

In the six components, the characteristic of supporting should be determined as the wind element. Therein, the characteristic of hardness as the earth element, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element, and the characteristic of maturing as the fire element. For one who determines them in this way, the elements become manifest. For one who repeatedly reflects upon and attends to them, access concentration arises in the very manner described.

346. Yassa pana evampi bhāvayato kammaṭṭhānaṃ na ijjhati, tena salakkhaṇavibhattito bhāvetabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Pubbe vuttanayeneva kesādayo pariggahetvā kesamhi thaddhalakkhaṇaṃ pathavīdhātūti vavatthapetabbaṃ. Tattheva ābandhanalakkhaṇaṃ āpodhātūti. Paripācanalakkhaṇaṃ tejodhātūti. Vitthambhanalakkhaṇaṃ vāyodhātūti. Evaṃ sabbakoṭṭhāsesu ekekasmiṃ koṭṭhāse catasso catasso dhātuyo vavatthapetabbā. Tassevaṃ vavatthāpayato dhātuyo pākaṭā honti. Tā punappunaṃ āvajjato manasikaroto vuttanayeneva upacārasamādhi uppajjati.

346. But if for someone the meditation subject does not succeed even when developing it in this way, it should be developed by them by way of distinguishing the characteristics. How? In the very way previously stated, having comprehended the hair and so on, the characteristic of hardness in the hair should be determined as the earth element. Therein, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element, the characteristic of maturing as the fire element, and the characteristic of supporting as the wind element. Thus, in all the components, in each single component, the four elements are to be determined. For one who determines them in this way, the elements become manifest. For one who repeatedly reflects upon and attends to them, access concentration arises in the very manner described.

Apica kho pana vacanatthato, kalāpato, cuṇṇato, lakkhaṇādito, samuṭṭhānato, nānattekattato, vinibbhogāvinibbhogato, sabhāgavisabhāgato, ajjhattikabāhiravisesato, saṅgahato, paccayato, asamannāhārato, paccayavibhāgatoti imehipi ākārehi dhātuyo manasikātabbā.

Furthermore, the elements should be attended to by these modes: by way of etymology, by way of groups, by way of minute particles, by way of characteristics and so on, by way of origin, by way of diversity and unity, by way of divisibility and indivisibility, by way of similar and dissimilar nature, by way of the distinction between internal and external, by way of inclusion, by way of conditionality, by way of non-attention, and by way of the analysis of conditions.

347. Tattha vacanatthato manasikarontena patthaṭattā pathavī. Appoti āpiyati appāyatīti vā āpo. Tejatīti tejo. Vāyatīti vāyo. Avisesena pana salakkhaṇadhāraṇato [V 1.0355] dukkhādānato dukkhādhānato ca dhātūti. Evaṃ visesasāmaññavasena vacanatthato manasikātabbā.

347. Herein, one attending by way of etymology understands: it is ‘earth’ (pathavī) because it is spread out (patthaṭa). It is ‘water’ (āpo) because it pervades (appoti), or because it is imbibed (āpīyati), or because it causes increase (appāyati). It is ‘fire’ (tejo) because it torments (tejati). It is ‘wind’ (vāyo) because it moves (vāyati). In a general sense, however, they are called ‘elements’ (dhātu) because they bear their own characteristics, because they produce suffering, and because they are a basis for suffering. Thus, they should be attended to by way of etymology, in terms of the specific and the general.

348. Kalāpatoti yā ayaṃ kesā lomātiādinā nayena vīsatiyā ākārehi pathavīdhātu, pittaṃ semhanti ca ādinā nayena dvādasahākārehi āpodhātu niddiṭṭhā, tattha yasmā –
