348. By way of groups: The earth element is specified in twenty aspects by the method beginning with ‘hair of the head, hair of the body,’ and the water element is specified in twelve aspects by the method beginning with ‘bile, phlegm.’ Therein, because—

Vaṇṇo [M 1.0361] gandho raso ojā, catasso cāpi dhātuyo;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, hoti kesāti sammuti;

Tesaṃyeva vinibbhogā, natthi kesāti sammuti.

Color, odor, taste, nutritive essence, and also the four elements; from the combination of these eight dhammas, there is the convention ‘hair.’ From the separation of these very things, the convention ‘hair’ does not exist.

Tasmā kesāpi aṭṭhadhammakalāpamattameva. Tathā lomādayoti. Yo panettha kammasamuṭṭhāno koṭṭhāso, so jīvitindriyena ca bhāvena ca saddhiṃ dasadhammakalāpopi hoti. Ussadavasena pana pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti saṅkhaṃ gato. Evaṃ kalāpato manasikātabbā.

Therefore, hair is merely a group of eight dhammas. So too are body hairs and the rest. The portion here that is kamma-originated, together with the life faculty and the sex-determining phenomenon, also becomes a group of ten dhammas. But due to prominence, it is counted as the earth element or the water element. Thus, they should be attended to by way of groups.

349. Cuṇṇatoti imasmiṃ hi sarīre majjhimena pamāṇena pariggayhamānā paramāṇubhedasañcuṇṇā sukhumarajabhūtā pathavīdhātu doṇamattā siyā. Sā tato upaḍḍhappamāṇāya āpodhātuyā saṅgahitā, tejodhātuyā anupālitā vāyodhātuyā vitthambhitā na vikiriyati na viddhaṃsiyati, avikiriyamānā aviddhaṃsiyamānā anekavidhaṃ itthipurisaliṅgādibhāvavikappaṃ upagacchati, aṇuthūladīgharassathirakathinādibhāvañca pakāseti.

349. By way of minute particles: Indeed, in this body, if it were to be comprehended with a medium measure, the earth element—ground into a fine powder of atomic particles and become subtle dust—would amount to one doṇa. It is held together by half that measure of the water element, maintained by the fire element, and supported by the wind element, so it does not scatter or get destroyed. Not scattering and not being destroyed, it undergoes various transformations into the state of female and male characteristics, etc., and manifests the state of being small, large, long, short, firm, hard, and so on.

Yūsagatā ābandhanākārabhūtā panettha āpodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā tejānupālitā vāyovitthambhitā na paggharati na parissavati, apaggharamānā aparissavamānā pīṇitapīṇitabhāvaṃ dasseti.

The water element herein, having reached a state of liquid consistency and become a binding agent, is established on the earth element, maintained by the fire element, and supported by the wind element, so it does not flow down or seep out. Not flowing down and not seeping out, it shows a state of plumpness.

Asitapītādipācakā cettha usumākārabhūtā uṇhattalakkhaṇā tejodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā āposaṅgahitā vāyovitthambhitā imaṃ kāyaṃ paripāceti, vaṇṇasampattiñcassa āvahati. Tāya ca pana paripācito ayaṃ kāyo na pūtibhāvaṃ dasseti.

Furthermore, the fire element herein—which digests what is eaten, drunk, etc., which has the nature of heat, and which has the characteristic of warmth—being established on the earth element, held together by the water element, and supported by the wind element, ripens this body and brings about its accomplishment of complexion. And, being ripened by it, this body does not show a state of putrefaction.

Aṅgamaṅgānusaṭā [V 1.0356] cettha samudīraṇavitthambhanalakkhaṇā vāyodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā āposaṅgahitā tejānupālitā imaṃ kāyaṃ vitthambheti. Tāya ca pana vitthambhito ayaṃ kāyo na paripatati, ujukaṃ saṇṭhāti. Aparāya vāyodhātuyā samabbhāhato gamanaṭṭhānanisajjāsayanairiyāpathesu viññattiṃ dasseti, samiñjeti, sampasāreti, hatthapādaṃ lāḷeti. Evametaṃ itthipurisādibhāvena bālajanavañcanaṃ māyārūpasadisaṃ dhātuyantaṃ pavattatīti evaṃ cuṇṇato manasikātabbā.

Furthermore, the wind element herein—which pervades the major and minor limbs and has the characteristic of impelling and supporting—being established on the earth element, held together by the water element, and maintained by the fire element, supports this body. And, being supported by it, this body does not fall down but stands upright. Being impelled by another wind element, it shows intimation in the postures of going, standing, sitting, and lying down; it bends, it stretches, it moves the hands and feet. In this way, this mechanism of elements, which is like a conjured form that deceives foolish people through its appearance as a woman, man, etc., proceeds. Thus, the elements should be attended to by way of minute particles.

350. Lakkhaṇāditoti [M 1.0362] pathavīdhātu kiṃ lakkhaṇā, kiṃ rasā, kiṃ paccupaṭṭhānāti evaṃ catassopi dhātuyo āvajjetvā pathavīdhātu kakkhaḷattalakkhaṇā, patiṭṭhānarasā, sampaṭicchanapaccupaṭṭhānā. Āpodhātu paggharaṇalakkhaṇā, brūhanarasā, saṅgahapaccupaṭṭhānā. Tejodhātu uṇhattalakkhaṇā, paripācanarasā, maddavānuppadānapaccupaṭṭhānā. Vāyodhātu vitthambhanalakkhaṇā, samudīraṇarasā. Abhinīhārapaccupaṭṭhānāti evaṃ lakkhaṇādito manasikātabbā.

350. By way of characteristics, etc.: Having reflected on all four elements thus—‘What is the characteristic of the earth element? What is its function? What is its manifestation?’—one understands: the earth element has the characteristic of hardness, the function of being a foundation, and the manifestation of receiving. The water element has the characteristic of flowing, the function of augmenting, and the manifestation of holding together. The fire element has the characteristic of heat, the function of ripening, and the manifestation of providing softness. The wind element has the characteristic of supporting, the function of impelling, and the manifestation of conveying forward. Thus, they should be attended to by way of their characteristics, etc.

351. Samuṭṭhānatoti ye ime pathavīdhātuādīnaṃ vitthārato dassanavasena kesādayo dvācattālīsa koṭṭhāsā dassitā. Tesu udariyaṃ karīsaṃ pubbo muttanti ime cattāro koṭṭhāsā utusamuṭṭhānāva. Assu sedo kheḷo siṅghāṇikāti ime cattāro utucittasamuṭṭhānā. Asitādiparipācako tejo kammasamuṭṭhānova. Assāsapassāsā cittasamuṭṭhānāva. Avasesā sabbepi catusamuṭṭhānāti evaṃ samuṭṭhānato manasikātabbā.

351. By way of origin: These forty-two parts, beginning with hair, have been shown by way of a detailed exposition of the earth element and so on. Among them, these four parts—food in the stomach, feces, pus, and urine—arise solely from temperature. These four—tears, sweat, spittle, and nasal mucus—arise from temperature and consciousness. The fire that digests what is eaten, etc., arises solely from kamma. The in-breaths and out-breaths arise solely from consciousness. All the remaining parts arise from the four origins. Thus, they should be attended to by way of origin.

352. Nānattekattatoti sabbāsampi dhātūnaṃ salakkhaṇādito nānattaṃ. Aññāneva hi pathavīdhātuyā lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānāni. Aññāni āpodhātuādīnaṃ. Evaṃ lakkhaṇādivasena pana kammasamuṭṭhānādivasena ca nānattabhūtānampi etāsaṃ rūpamahābhūtadhātudhammaaniccādivasena ekattaṃ hoti. Sabbāpi hi dhātuyo ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ anatītattā rūpāni. Mahantapātubhāvādīhi kāraṇehi mahābhūtāni.

352. By way of diversity and unity: All the elements are diverse in terms of their own individual characteristics and so on. For the characteristics, functions, and manifestations of the earth element are indeed different; those of the water element and so on are different. Thus, though these elements are diverse by way of characteristics, etc., and by way of origin from kamma, etc., they have a unity by way of being material form, great elements, elements, phenomena, impermanent, and so on. To clarify, all the elements are material forms (rūpa) because they do not transcend the characteristic of being afflicted (ruppana). They are great elements (mahābhūta) for reasons such as their great manifestation.

Mahantapātubhāvādīhīti etā hi dhātuyo mahantapātubhāvato, mahābhūtasāmaññato, mahāparihārato, mahāvikārato, mahattā bhūtattā cāti imehi kāraṇehi mahābhūtānīti vuccanti.

Regarding ‘because of their great manifestation, etc.’: To elaborate, these elements are called ‘great elements’ for these reasons: because of their great manifestation; because of their similarity to great beings (like magicians); because of being maintained by many factors; because of their great alteration; and because of their greatness and their actual existence.

Tattha [V 1.0357] mahantapātubhāvatoti etāni hi anupādinnasantānepi upādinnasantānepi mahantāni pātubhūtāni. Tesaṃ anupādinnasantāne –

Among these, regarding ‘because of their great manifestation’: Indeed, these elements have manifested as great in both unappropriated and appropriated continuities. Regarding them in an unappropriated continuity:

Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharāti. –

“Two hundred thousand and four myriads; by such a measure in thickness is this earth reckoned.”

Ādinā nayena mahantapātubhāvatā buddhānussatiniddese vuttāva.

By this method and so on, their great manifestation was already stated in the Exposition of the Recollection of the Buddha.

Upādinnasantānepi [M 1.0363] macchakacchapadevadānavādisarīravasena mahantāneva pātubhūtāni. Vuttañhetaṃ “santi, bhikkhave, mahāsamudde yojanasatikāpi attabhāvā”tiādi.

In appropriated continuities too, they have manifested as great indeed by way of the bodies of fish, turtles, devas, asuras, and so on. For this has been said: “Monks, in the great ocean there are beings with an individual existence of even a hundred yojanas,” and so on.

Mahābhūtasāmaññatoti etāni hi yathā māyākāro amaṇiṃyeva udakaṃ maṇiṃ katvā dasseti, asuvaṇṇaṃyeva leḍḍuṃ suvaṇṇaṃ katvā dasseti.

As to 'because of their similarity to great beings (like magicians)': For just as a magician shows water, which is not a gem, having made it into a gem, and shows a clod, which is not gold, having made it into gold;

Yathā ca sayaṃ neva yakkho na yakkhī samāno yakkhabhāvampi yakkhibhāvampi dasseti, evameva sayaṃ anīlāneva hutvā nīlaṃ upādārūpaṃ dassenti, apītāni alohitāni anodātāneva hutvā odātaṃ upādārūpaṃ dassentīti māyākāramahābhūtasāmaññato mahābhūtāni.

and just as he, though being himself neither a yakkha nor a bird, shows the state of a yakkha and the state of a bird; even so, these elements, being themselves not blue, show the blue derived materiality; being themselves not yellow, not red, and not white, they show derived materiality that is yellow, red, and white. Thus, because of their similarity to a great being that is a magician, they are called great elements.

Yathā ca yakkhādīni mahābhūtāni yaṃ gaṇhanti, neva nesaṃ tassa anto na bahi ṭhānaṃ upalabbhati, na ca taṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhanti, evameva tānipi neva aññamaññassa anto na bahi ṭhitāni hutvā upalabbhanti, na ca aññamaññaṃ nissāya na tiṭṭhantīti acinteyyaṭṭhānatāya yakkhādimahābhūtasāmaññatopi mahābhūtāni. Yathā ca yakkhinīsaṅkhātāni mahābhūtāni manāpehi vaṇṇasaṇṭhānavikkhepehi attano bhayānakabhāvaṃ paṭicchādetvā satte vañcenti, evameva etānipi itthipurisasarīrādīsu manāpena chavivaṇṇena manāpena attano aṅgapaccaṅgasaṇṭhānena manāpena ca hatthapādaṅgulibhamukavikkhepena attano kakkhaḷattādibhedaṃ sarasalakkhaṇaṃ paṭicchādetvā bālajanaṃ vañcenti, attano sabhāvaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na dentīti vañcakattena yakkhinīmahābhūtasāmaññatopi mahābhūtāni.

Alternatively, just as when great beings such as yakkhas seize a certain being, their location is found neither inside nor outside that being, and yet it is not that they do not exist depending on that being; in the same way, these elements are found existing neither inside nor outside one another, and yet it is not that they do not exist depending on one another. Thus, because of having an inconceivable location, and also because of their similarity to great beings such as yakkhas, they are called great elements. Alternatively, just as great beings known as yakkhinīs deceive beings by concealing their own fearsome nature with pleasing colors, forms, and gestures, in the same way, these elements, in the bodies of women, men, and so on, deceive foolish people by concealing their own inherent characteristic, which is differentiated as hardness and so forth, with a pleasing skin color, a pleasing form of their own major and minor limbs, and with pleasing movements of the fingers, toes, and eyebrows, not allowing their own nature to be seen. Thus, because of their deceptiveness, and also because of their similarity to the great beings known as yakkhinīs, they are called great elements.

Mahāparihāratoti [V 1.0358] mahantehi paccayehi pariharitabbato. Etāni hi divase divase upanetabbattā mahantehi ghāsacchādanādīhi bhūtāni pavattānīti mahābhūtāni. Mahāparihārāni vā bhūtānītipi mahābhūtāni.

Because of great maintenance: because they must be maintained by great requisites. To elaborate, because these elements must be supplied day by day with great things such as food and clothing, they are beings that are maintained; thus, they are called great elements. Or, they are beings requiring great maintenance; thus also, they are called great elements.

Mahāvikāratoti etāni hi anupādinnānipi upādinnānipi mahāvikārāni honti. Tattha anupādinnānaṃ kappavuṭṭhāne vikāramahattaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Upādinnānaṃ dhātukkhobhakāle. Tathā hi –

Because of great alteration: To elaborate, these elements, whether unappropriated or appropriated, have great alteration. Among these, the greatness of the alteration of the unappropriated elements becomes manifest at the dissolution of the aeon. For the appropriated elements, it becomes manifest at the time of the disturbance of the elements. For so it is:

Bhūmito [M 1.0364] vuṭṭhitā yāva, brahmalokā vidhāvati;

Acci accimato loke, ḍayhamānamhi tejasā.

When the world is being burned by fire, the flame of the fiery one, having arisen from the earth, runs up as far as the Brahma world.

Koṭisatasahassekaṃ, cakkavāḷaṃ vilīyati;

Kupitena yadā loko, salilena vinassati.

When the world is destroyed by agitated water, then a single world-system of one hundred thousand koṭis dissolves.

Koṭisatasahassekaṃ, cakkavāḷaṃ vikīrati;

Vāyodhātuppakopena, yadā loko vinassati.

When the world is destroyed by the agitation of the wind element, then a single world-system of one hundred thousand koṭis is scattered.

Patthaddho bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho kaṭṭhamukhena vā;

Pathavīdhātuppakopena, hoti kaṭṭhamukheva so.

A body bitten by a kaṭṭhamukha snake becomes rigid, as it were; due to the agitation of the earth element, that body becomes rigid as if in the mouth of a kaṭṭhamukha snake.

Pūtiyo bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho pūtimukhena vā;

Āpodhātuppakopena, hoti pūtimukheva so.

A body bitten by a pūtimukha snake becomes putrid, as it were; due to the disturbance of the water element, that body becomes putrid as if in the mouth of a pūtimukha snake.

Santatto bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho aggimukhena vā;

Tejodhātuppakopena, hoti aggimukheva so.

A body bitten by an aggimukha snake becomes thoroughly heated, as it were; due to the disturbance of the fire element, that body becomes thoroughly heated as if in the mouth of an aggimukha snake.

Sañchinno bhavati kāyo, daṭṭho satthamukhena vā;

Vāyodhātuppakopena, hoti satthamukheva so.

A body bitten by a satthamukha snake is cut to pieces, as it were; due to the disturbance of the wind element, that body is cut to pieces as if in the mouth of a satthamukha snake.

Iti [V 1.0359] mahāvikārāni bhūtānīti mahābhūtāni.

Thus, because they are existent things that have great alterations, they are called the great elements.

Mahattā bhūtattā cāti etāni hi mahantāni mahatā vāyāmena pariggahetabbattā bhūtāni vijjamānattāti mahattā bhūtattā ca mahābhūtāni.

Regarding the phrase 'because of greatness and because of being existent': They are 'great' because they must be comprehended with great effort, and they are 'existent things' because they are manifest. Thus, because of greatness and because of being existent, they are called the great elements.

Evaṃ sabbāpetā dhātuyo mahantapātubhāvādīhi kāraṇehi mahābhūtāni.

In this way, all these elements are called great elements for reasons such as their great manifestation and so on.

Salakkhaṇadhāraṇato pana dukkhādānato ca dukkhādhānato ca sabbāpi dhātulakkhaṇaṃ anatītattā dhātuyo. Salakkhaṇadhāraṇena ca attano khaṇānurūpadhāraṇena ca dhammā. Khayaṭṭhena aniccā. Bhayaṭṭhena dukkhā. Asārakaṭṭhena anattā.

Furthermore, because they bear their own individual characteristics, because they produce suffering, and because they are a basis for suffering, all are called 'elements' (dhātu) as they do not go beyond the characteristic of an element. Because they bear their own individual characteristics and because they are established in accordance with their own momentary nature, they are called 'dhammas'. Because of their nature of perishing, they are 'impermanent' (aniccā). Because of their nature of being a danger, they are 'suffering' (dukkhā). Because of their nature of being without a core, they are 'not-self' (anattā).

Iti sabbāsampi rūpamahābhūtadhātudhammaaniccādivasena ekattanti evaṃ nānattekattato manasikātabbā.

Thus, there is a oneness of all of them by way of being form, a great element, an element, a dhamma, impermanent, and so on. In this way, they should be attended to in terms of their diversity and oneness.

353. Vinibbhogāvinibbhogatoti [M 1.0365] sahuppannāva etā ekekasmiṃ sabbapariyantime suddhaṭṭhakādikalāpepi padesena avinibbhuttā. Lakkhaṇena pana vinibbhuttāti evaṃ vinibbhogāvinibbhogato manasikātabbā.

353. Regarding separability and inseparability: These elements, arising together, are inseparable by location even in each single, most minute kalāpa, such as the pure octad. By characteristic, however, they are separable. In this way, they should be attended to in terms of separability and inseparability.

354. Sabhāgavisabhāgatoti evaṃ avinibbhuttāsu cāpi etāsu purimā dve garukattā sabhāgā. Tathā pacchimā lahukattā. Purimā pana pacchimāhi pacchimā ca purimāhi visabhāgāti evaṃ sabhāgavisabhāgato manasikātabbā.

354. Regarding similarity and dissimilarity: Although these elements are inseparable, among them the first two are similar because of heaviness, and likewise the latter two are similar because of lightness. However, the first two are dissimilar to the latter two, and the latter two are dissimilar to the first two. In this way, they should be attended to in terms of similarity and dissimilarity.

355. Ajjhattikabāhiravisesatoti ajjhattikā dhātuyo viññāṇavatthuviññattiindriyānaṃ nissayā honti, sairiyāpathā, catusamuṭṭhānā. Bāhirā vuttaviparītappakārāti evaṃ ajjhattikabāhiravisesato manasikātabbā.

355. Regarding the distinction between internal and external: The internal elements are the support for the consciousness-bases, the intimations, and the faculties; they are connected with the postures and arise from four causes. The external elements are of a kind opposite to what has been said. In this way, they should be attended to in terms of the distinction between internal and external.

356. Saṅgahatoti kammasamuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātu kammasamuṭṭhānāhi itarāhi ekasaṅgahā hoti samuṭṭhānanānattābhāvato[V 1.0360]. Tathā cittādisamuṭṭhānā cittādisamuṭṭhānāhīti evaṃ saṅgahato manasikātabbā.

356. As for grouping: the earth element that has kamma as its origin is grouped as one with the other elements that have kamma as their origin, because of the absence of difference in their origin. Similarly, that which has mind, etc., as its origin is grouped with those that have mind, etc., as their origin. Thus, the elements should be attended to by way of grouping.

357. Paccayatoti pathavīdhātu āposaṅgahitā tejoanupālitā vāyovitthambhitā tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ patiṭṭhā hutvā paccayo hoti. Āpodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā tejoanupālitā vāyovitthambhitā tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ ābandhanaṃ hutvā paccayo hoti. Tejodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā āposaṅgahitā vāyovitthambhitā tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ paripācanaṃ hutvā paccayo hoti. Vāyodhātu pathavīpatiṭṭhitā āposaṅgahitā tejoparipācitā tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ vitthambhanaṃ hutvā paccayo hotīti evaṃ paccayato manasikātabbā.

357. As for being a condition: The earth element, being held together by water, maintained by fire, and supported by air, becomes a foundation for the three great elements and is a condition. The water element, being established on earth, maintained by fire, and supported by air, becomes a binder for the three great elements and is a condition. The fire element, being established on earth, held together by water, and supported by air, becomes a maturer for the three great elements and is a condition. The air element, being established on earth, held together by water, and matured by fire, becomes a supporter for the three great elements and is a condition. Thus, the elements should be attended to by way of being a condition.

358. Asamannāhāratoti pathavīdhātu cettha “ahaṃ pathavīdhātū”ti vā, “tiṇṇaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ patiṭṭhā hutvā paccayo homī”ti vā na jānāti. Itarānipi tīṇi “amhākaṃ pathavīdhātu patiṭṭhā hutvā paccayo hotī”ti na jānanti. Esa nayo sabbatthāti evaṃ asamannāhārato manasikātabbā.

358. As for being without awareness: Herein, the earth element does not know, 'I am the earth element,' or, 'Being a foundation for the three great elements, I am a condition.' The other three also do not know, 'For us, the earth element, being a foundation, is a condition.' This is the method in all cases. Thus, the elements should be attended to by way of being without awareness.

359. Paccayavibhāgatoti [M 1.0366] dhātūnaṃ hi kammaṃ, cittaṃ, āhāro, utūti cattāro paccayā. Tattha kammasamuṭṭhānānaṃ kammameva paccayo hoti, na cittādayo. Cittādisamuṭṭhānānampi cittādayova paccayā honti, na itare. Kammasamuṭṭhānānañca kammaṃ janakapaccayo hoti, sesānaṃ pariyāyato upanissayapaccayo hoti. Cittasamuṭṭhānānaṃ cittaṃ janakapaccayo hoti, sesānaṃ pacchājātapaccayo atthipaccayo avigatapaccayo ca. Āhārasamuṭṭhānānaṃ āhāro janakapaccayo hoti, sesānaṃ āhārapaccayo atthipaccayo avigatapaccayo ca. Utusamuṭṭhānānaṃ utu janakapaccayo hoti, sesānaṃ atthipaccayo avigatapaccayo ca. Kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ mahābhūtaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānānampi mahābhūtānaṃ paccayo hoti cittādisamuṭṭhānānampi. Tathā cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Utusamuṭṭhānaṃ mahābhūtaṃ utusamuṭṭhānānampi mahābhūtānaṃ paccayo hoti kammādisamuṭṭhānānampi.

359. As to the analysis of conditions: indeed, for the elements, there are four conditions: kamma, mind, nutriment, and temperature. Among these, for those which are kamma-originated, only kamma is the condition, not mind and the others. For those which are mind-originated and the like, only mind and the like are the conditions, not the others. And for those which are kamma-originated, kamma is the generative condition; for the others, it is indirectly the decisive support condition. For those which are mind-originated, mind is the generative condition; for the others, it is the post-nascence condition, presence condition, and non-disappearance condition. For those which are nutriment-originated, nutriment is the generative condition; for the others, it is the nutriment condition, presence condition, and non-disappearance condition. For those which are temperature-originated, temperature is the generative condition; for the others, it is the presence condition and the non-disappearance condition. A great element that is kamma-originated is a condition for great elements that are also kamma-originated, and also for those that are mind-originated and the like. Likewise for a great element that is mind-originated and one that is nutriment-originated. A great element that is temperature-originated is a condition for great elements that are also temperature-originated, and also for those that are kamma-originated and the like.

Tattha kammasamuṭṭhānā pathavīdhātu kammasamuṭṭhānānaṃ itarāsaṃ sahajātaaññamaññanissayaatthiavigatavasena ceva patiṭṭhāvasena ca paccayo hoti, na janakavasena. Itaresaṃ tisantatimahābhūtānaṃ [V 1.0361] nissayaatthiavigatavasena paccayo hoti, na patiṭṭhāvasena na janakavasena. Āpodhātu cettha itarāsaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sahajātādivasena ceva ābandhanavasena ca paccayo hoti, na janakavasena. Itaresaṃ tisantatikānaṃ nissayaatthiavigatapaccayavaseneva, na ābandhanavasena na janakavasena. Tejodhātupettha itarāsaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sahajātādivasena ceva paripācanavasena ca paccayo hoti, na janakavasena. Itaresaṃ tisantatikānaṃ nissayaatthiavigatapaccayavaseneva, na paripācanavasena, na janakavasena. Vāyodhātupettha itarāsaṃ tiṇṇaṃ sahajātādivasena ceva vitthambhanavasena ca paccayo hoti, na janakavasena. Itaresaṃ tisantatikānaṃ nissayaatthiavigatapaccayavaseneva, na vitthambhanavasena, na janakavasena. Cittaāhārautusamuṭṭhānapathavīdhātuādīsupi eseva nayo.

Therein, the kamma-originated earth element is a condition for the other kamma-originated elements by way of co-nascence, mutuality, support, presence, and non-disappearance, and also by way of foundation, but not by way of generating. For the great elements of the three other continuities, it is a condition by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance, but not by way of foundation nor by way of generating. Herein, the water element is a condition for the other three kamma-originated elements by way of co-nascence and so on, and also by way of cohesion, but not by way of generating. For those of the three other continuities, it is a condition only by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance condition, not by way of cohesion nor by way of generating. Herein, the fire element is also a condition for the other three kamma-originated elements by way of co-nascence and so on, and also by way of maturing, but not by way of generating. For those of the three other continuities, it is a condition only by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance condition, not by way of maturing nor by way of generating. Herein, the air element is also a condition for the other three kamma-originated elements by way of co-nascence and so on, and also by way of supporting, but not by way of generating. For those of the three other continuities, it is a condition only by way of support, presence, and non-disappearance condition, not by way of supporting nor by way of generating. This same method should be understood also for the earth element and so on, originated from mind, nutriment, and temperature.

Evaṃ sahajātādipaccayavasappavattāsu ca panetāsu dhātūsu –

Thus, among these elements that proceed by way of conditions such as co-nascence and so on—

Ekaṃ paṭicca tisso, catudhā tisso paṭicca eko ca;

Dve dhātuyo paṭicca, dve chaddhā sampavattanti.

Depending on one, three proceed in four ways; and depending on three, one also proceeds in four ways. Depending on two elements, two proceed in six ways.

Pathavīādīsu [M 1.0367] hi ekekaṃ paṭicca itarā tisso tissoti evaṃ ekaṃ paṭicca tisso catudhā sampavattanti. Tathā pathavīdhātuādīsu ekekā itarā tisso tisso paṭiccāti evaṃ tisso paṭicca ekā catudhā sampavattati. Purimā pana dve paṭicca pacchimā, pacchimā ca dve paṭicca purimā, paṭhamatatiyā paṭicca dutiyacatutthā, dutiyacatutthā paṭicca paṭhamatatiyā, paṭhamacatutthā paṭicca dutiyatatiyā, dutiyatatiyā paṭicca paṭhamacatutthāti evaṃ dve dhātuyo paṭicca dve chadhā sampavattanti.

Indeed, among the earth element and others, depending on each one, the other three elements proceed. Thus, depending on one, three proceed in four ways. Similarly, among the earth element and others, each one proceeds depending on the other three. Thus, depending on three, one proceeds in four ways. Furthermore, depending on the first two, the latter two proceed; and depending on the latter two, the first two proceed. Depending on the first and third, the second and fourth proceed; depending on the second and fourth, the first and third proceed. Depending on the first and fourth, the second and third proceed; depending on the second and third, the first and fourth proceed. Thus, depending on two elements, two elements proceed in six ways.

Tāsu pathavīdhātu abhikkamapaṭikkamādikāle uppīḷanassa paccayo hoti. Sāva āpodhātuyā anugatā patiṭṭhāpanassa. Pathavīdhātuyā pana anugatā āpodhātu avakkhepanassa. Vāyodhātuyā anugatā tejodhātu uddharaṇassa. Tejodhātuyā anugatā vāyodhātu atiharaṇavītiharaṇānaṃ paccayo hotīti evaṃ paccayavibhāgato manasikātabbā.

Among them, the earth element, at the time of stepping forward, stepping back, and so on, is a condition for pressing down. That same earth element, when accompanied by the water element, is a condition for establishing. Furthermore, the water element, when accompanied by the earth element, is a condition for placing down. The fire element, when accompanied by the air element, is a condition for lifting up. The air element, when accompanied by the fire element, is a condition for carrying forward and carrying aside. Thus, the elements should be attended to by way of this analysis of conditions.

Evaṃ vacanatthādivasena manasi karontassāpi hi ekekena mukhena dhātuyo pākaṭā honti. Tā [V 1.0362] punappunaṃ āvajjato manasikaroto vuttanayeneva upacārasamādhi uppajjati. Svāyaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ vavatthāpakassa ñāṇassānubhāvena uppajjanato catudhātuvavatthānantveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

Indeed, even for one who attends in mind in this way, by way of the meaning of the words and so on, the elements become manifest through each single approach. For one who again and again adverts to and attends in mind to them, access concentration arises in the very way that was stated. Since this concentration arises through the power of the knowledge that determines the four elements, it is called the 'determination of the four elements'.

360. Idañca pana catudhātuvavatthānaṃ anuyutto bhikkhu suññataṃ avagāhati, sattasaññaṃ samugghāteti. So sattasaññāya samūhatattā vāḷamigayakkharakkhasādivikappaṃ anāvajjamāno bhayabheravasaho hoti, aratiratisaho, na iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu ugghātanigghātaṃ pāpuṇāti. Mahāpañño ca pana hoti amatapariyosāno vā sugatiparāyano vāti.

360. Furthermore, a monk devoted to this analysis of the four elements plunges into emptiness and eradicates the perception of a being. Because the perception of a being is eradicated, not adverting to conceptions of beasts of prey, yakkhas, rakkhasas, and so on, he becomes a withstander of fear and terror. He is a withstander of discontent and delight, and does not experience elation and dejection in regard to the desirable and undesirable. And furthermore, he becomes one of great wisdom, or has the deathless as his culmination, or has a happy destination as his resort.

Evaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ, yogivarasahassa kīḷitaṃ etaṃ;

Catudhātuvavatthānaṃ, niccaṃ sevetha medhāvīti.

Thus, this analysis of the four elements is of great power and is the sphere of play for a thousand excellent yogis; a wise one should always resort to it.

Ayaṃ catudhātuvavatthānassa bhāvanāniddeso.

This is the exposition of the development of the analysis of the four elements.

361. Ettāvatā ca yaṃ samādhissa vitthāraṃ bhāvanānayañca dassetuṃ “ko samādhi, kenaṭṭhena samādhī”tiādinā nayena pañhākammaṃ kataṃ, tattha “kathaṃ [M 1.0368] bhāvetabbo”ti imassa padassa sabbappakārato atthavaṇṇanā samattā hoti.

361. And thus far, regarding the task of questioning undertaken by the method beginning with 'What is concentration? In what sense is it concentration?' in order to explain the scope of concentration and the method of its development, therein the explanation of the meaning of this phrase, 'How is it to be developed?', is complete in every way.

Duvidhoyeva hayaṃ idha adhippeto upacārasamādhi ceva appanāsamādhi ca. Tattha dasasu kammaṭṭhānesu, appanāpubbabhāgacittesu ca ekaggatā upacārasamādhi. Avasesakammaṭṭhānesu cittekaggatā appanāsamādhi. So duvidhopi tesaṃ kammaṭṭhānānaṃ bhāvitattā bhāvito hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “kathaṃ bhāvetabboti imassa padassa sabbappakārato atthavaṇṇanā samattā”ti.

Here, this concentration is intended as only of two kinds: access concentration and absorption concentration. Therein, in the ten meditation subjects and in the preliminary-part consciousnesses of absorption, one-pointedness is access concentration. In the remaining meditation subjects, one-pointedness of mind is absorption concentration. Both these kinds are developed because those meditation subjects have been developed. Therefore it was said: 'the explanation of the meaning of this phrase, "How is it to be developed?", is complete in every way.'

Samādhiānisaṃsakathā

Discourse on the Benefits of Concentration

362. Yaṃ pana vuttaṃ “samādhibhāvanāya ko ānisaṃso”ti, tattha diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārādipañcavidho samādhibhāvanāya ānisaṃso. Tathā hi ye arahanto khīṇāsavā samāpajjitvā ekaggacittā sukhaṃ divasaṃ viharissāmāti samādhiṃ bhāventi, tesaṃ appanāsamādhibhāvanā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānisaṃsā hoti. Tenāha bhagavā “na kho panete, cunda, ariyassa [V 1.0363] vinaye sallekhā vuccanti. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā ete ariyassa vinaye vuccantī”ti (ma. ni. 1.82).

362. Now, regarding what was said, 'What is the benefit of the development of concentration?', therein the benefit of the development of concentration is five-fold, beginning with pleasant abiding in the present life. For so it is: when those Arahants whose taints are destroyed develop concentration, thinking, 'Having entered attainment, with one-pointed minds, we will dwell happily for the day,' their development of absorption concentration has the benefit of pleasant abiding in the present life. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'But these, Cunda, are not called practices of effacement in the Noble One’s Discipline. They are called pleasant abidings in the present life in the Noble One’s Discipline' (MN 8).

Sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhāya samāhitena cittena vipassissāmāti bhāvayataṃ vipassanāya padaṭṭhānattā appanāsamādhibhāvanāpi sambādhe okāsādhigamanayena upacārasamādhibhāvanāpi vipassanānisaṃsā hoti. Tenāha bhagavā “samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha. Samāhito, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5).

For learners and worldlings who develop concentration, thinking, 'Having arisen from attainment, we will practice insight with a concentrated mind,' both the development of absorption concentration—because it is the proximate cause for insight—and the development of access concentration—by the method of gaining an opportunity in confinement—have the benefit of insight. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'Monks, develop concentration. A monk who is concentrated, monks, understands things as they really are' (SN 22.5).

Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā abhiññāpādakaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya ekopi hutvā bahudhā hotīti vuttanayā abhiññāyo patthento nibbattenti, tesaṃ sati sati āyatane abhiññāpadaṭṭhānattā appanāsamādhibhāvanā abhiññānisaṃsā hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “so yassa yassa abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassa dhammassa [M 1.0369] cittaṃ abhininnāmeti abhiññāsacchikiriyāya, tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati sati āyatane”ti (ma. ni. 3.158; a. ni. 3.102).

For those who, having produced the eight attainments, enter the jhāna that is the basis for the super-knowledges, and emerging from that attainment, desire and produce the super-knowledges in the manner taught as, 'Having been one, he becomes many,' for them, when the supporting condition exists, because it is the proximate cause for the super-knowledges, the development of absorption concentration has the super-knowledges as its benefit. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'He directs his mind towards whatever phenomenon is to be directly realized by super-knowledge, for the sake of direct realization by super-knowledge; when the supporting condition exists, he attains the state of being capable of directly witnessing it in that very phenomenon.'

Ye aparihīnajjhānā brahmaloke nibbattissāmāti brahmalokūpapattiṃ patthentā apatthayamānā vāpi puthujjanā samādhito na parihāyanti, tesaṃ bhavavisesāvahattā appanāsamādhibhāvanā bhavavisesānisaṃsā hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ parittaṃ bhāvetvā kattha upapajjanti. Brahmapārisajjānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjantī”tiādi (vibha. 1024).

For those worldlings who have not declined from jhāna and who, whether aspiring to rebirth in the Brahma world or not, do not fall away from concentration, their development of absorption concentration has the benefit of a special existence because it leads to a special existence. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Having developed the first jhāna to a limited extent, where are they reborn? They are reborn into the companionship of the Brahmapārisajja devas,' and so on.

Upacārasamādhibhāvanāpi pana kāmāvacarasugatibhavavisesaṃ āvahatiyeva.

Furthermore, the development of access concentration indeed leads to a special fortunate existence in the sense-sphere.

Ye pana ariyā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā satta divasāni acittā hutvā diṭṭheva dhamme nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ patvā sukhaṃ viharissāmāti samādhiṃ bhāventi, tesaṃ appanāsamādhibhāvanā nirodhānisaṃsā hoti. Tenāha – “soḷasahi ñāṇacariyāhi navahi samādhicariyāhi vasībhāvatā paññā nirodhasamāpattiyā ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.34).

Furthermore, for those noble ones who, having produced the eight attainments, enter the attainment of cessation and, having been without mind for seven days, having reached cessation—Nibbāna—in this very life, develop concentration thinking, 'We will dwell happily,' for them, the development of absorption concentration has the attainment of cessation as its benefit. Therefore, it is said: 'Wisdom which is mastery through the sixteen courses of knowledge and the nine courses of concentration is the knowledge regarding the attainment of cessation.'

Evamayaṃ [V 1.0364] diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārādi pañcavidho samādhibhāvanāya ānisaṃso –

Thus, this is the fivefold benefit of the development of concentration, beginning with pleasant abiding in the present life:

“Tasmā nekānisaṃsamhi, kilesamalasodhane;

Samādhibhāvanāyoge, nappamajjeyya paṇḍito”ti.

Therefore, in the practice of developing concentration, which has many benefits and cleanses the stains of defilements, a wise person should not be negligent.

363. Ettāvatā ca “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti imissā gāthāya sīlasamādhipaññāmukhena desite visuddhimagge samādhipi paridīpito hoti.

363. And thus far, in the Path of Purification—taught by means of virtue, concentration, and wisdom in this verse, 'A wise man, established in virtue...'—concentration also has been fully elucidated.

Iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhimagge

Thus in the Path of Purification, composed for the delight of good people,

Samādhiniddeso nāma

The Exposition of Concentration

Ekādasamo paricchedo.

The Eleventh Chapter.

364. Paṭhamo [M 1.0370] sīlaniddeso. Dutiyo dhutaṅganiddeso;. Tatiyo kammaṭṭhānaggahaṇaniddeso. Catuttho pathavīkasiṇaniddeso. Pañcamo sesakasiṇaniddeso. Chaṭṭho asubhaniddeso. Sattamo chaanussatiniddeso. Aṭṭhamo sesānussatiniddeso. Navamo brahmavihāraniddeso. Dasamo āruppaniddeso. Paṭikkūlasaññādhātuvavatthānadvayaniddeso ekādasamoti.

364. The first is the Exposition of Virtue. The second is the Exposition of the Ascetic Practices. The third is the Exposition of Taking Up a Meditation Subject. The fourth is the Exposition of the Earth Kasiṇa. The fifth is the Exposition of the Remaining Kasiṇas. The sixth is the Exposition of Foulness. The seventh is the Exposition of the Six Recollections. The eighth is the Exposition of the Remaining Recollections. The ninth is the Exposition of the Divine Abidings. The tenth is the Exposition of the Formless Attainments. The Exposition of the Pair—the Perception of Repulsiveness and the Analysis of the Elements—is the eleventh.

Visuddhimaggassa paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part of the Visuddhimagga is finished.
